His Fulgens and Lucrece, played at Morton's household at Lambeth about 1497, is the earliest surviving secular English play, printed by John Rastell about 1512–16. He died about 1502.
authors.profile: Author of the first secular English drama. Fulgens and Lucrece dramatizes a humanist debate — whether nobility lies in birth or in virtue — as a Roman comedy of courtship, complete with a subplot in which two servants, A and B, compete for the audience's employment; his Nature is a full-scale morality play of man's fall and amendment. Both were played in Morton's great hall, the seedbed of the Tudor interlude.
authors.style: Debate framed as drama; the interweaving of serious argument and servant comedy; the morality convention put to secular and humanist use.
authors.concerns: True nobility and the claims of virtue over birth; the reform of manners; the education of the great household through play.
authors.significance: Bridging medieval morality and humanist comedy, Fulgens and Lucrece begins the secular English stage tradition that runs to the Elizabethan theatre.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate.
themes: Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer

authors.name: Henry More
authors.identity: The leading Cambridge Platonist; a poet-philosopher who defended a rational, spiritual Christianity against materialism and atheism, and who corresponded with Descartes and Anne Conway while writing philosophical and mystical treatises in verse and prose.
authors.biography: Born 12 October 1614 at Grantham, educated at Christ's College, Cambridge, where he became a Fellow (1639) and remained for life, declining preferment. He corresponded with Descartes (1648–49) and was the philosophical mentor of Anne Conway. His works include the Philosophical Poems (1647, including the 'Psychozoia' and 'Antipsychopannychia'), An Antidote Against Atheism (1653), Enthusiasmus Triumphatus (1656), and the Enchiridion Metaphysicum (1671), which argued against Cartesian mechanism and for the reality of spirit, extension, and the 'boniform faculty'. He defended belief in spirits and apparitions and died on 1 September 1687.
authors.profile: The Platonic philosopher-theologian who sought to reconcile reason, religion, and the new philosophy, opposing Hobbesian and Cartesian materialism with a spiritual, emanative metaphysics expressed in both verse and prose.
authors.style: Philosophical verse (Spenserian stanzas) and prose; Platonic and mystical argument; a serene, speculative, sometimes visionary style; and polemic against atheism and 'enthusiasm'.
authors.concerns: The existence and nature of spirit and God; reason and religion; the critique of materialism and of religious 'enthusiasm'; the immortality of the soul; and the relation of Descartes to Platonism.
authors.significance: More was the central figure of Cambridge Platonism, influencing Conway, Glanvill, and later Latitudinarian and Romantic thought; his correspondence with Descartes is a key document of seventeenth-century philosophy.
authors.uncertainty: More's life is documented through his works, correspondence, and a contemporary biography; his philosophical positions evolved and some attributions of influence are interpretive.

works.title: Enthusiasmus Triumphatus; or, A Brief Account of the Nature, Causes, Kinds, and Cure of Enthusiasm

authors.name: Henry of Huntingdon
authors.identity: historian; churchman; poet
authors.biography: Son of a Norman clerk and an English mother, and archdeacon of Huntingdon from c. 1110, he was commissioned by Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, to write a history of England; he travelled with the court, visited Rome (1139), and continued revising his Historia Anglorum until his death c. 1157.
authors.profile: Author of the Historia Anglorum (first version 1129, continued to 1154), the most widely read English chronicle of the twelfth century, and of verse epigrams including the satirical De contemptu mundi.
authors.style: Clear, vivid narrative with a moralist's relish for battles, plagues, and the falls of great men; the ubi sunt meditation and the contemptus mundi theme; patriotic celebration of the English past.
authors.concerns: The providential shape of English history; the transience of earthly power; the continuity of the English people through conquest.
authors.significance: The Historia Anglorum is a principal source for the Norman and Angevin periods and the classic expression of twelfth-century historical moralism.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; details of his career rest on his own book.
themes: Civil War, regicide, and the trial of the king
sources: The Poems of Thomas Gray, William Collins and Oliver Goldsmith

authors.name: Henry Vaughan
authors.identity: Anglo-Welsh physician, royalist, and metaphysical devotional poet; author of Silex Scintillans, whose mystical nature-poetry and longing for eternity distinguish him among Herbert's followers.
authors.biography: Born 1621 (baptised 16 April) at Newton St Bridget, twin brother of the alchemist Thomas Vaughan; educated privately and at Jesus College, Oxford, then trained in medicine. A royalist during the Civil Wars, he retired to his native Breconshire, practised medicine, and published Olor Iscanus (1651) and Silex Scintillans (1650, expanded 1655), influenced by Herbert. He also wrote prose devotional and hermetic works (The Mount of Olives, 1652) and translations of Nolle and Boece. He lived quietly through the Restoration at Newton and Alway, dying 23 April 1695.
authors.profile: The 'Silurist' whose verse seeks God through the natural world and childhood memory, marked by a mystic's sense of eternity glimpsed behind the material world ('intimations' later echoed by Wordsworth).
authors.style: Luminous nature imagery; a mystical, visionary quality; Herbert's influence tempered by a wilder, more personal imagination; emblematic structure; and Welsh landscape as the locus of spiritual experience.
authors.concerns: Eternity and the soul's pre-existence; nature as the book of God; childhood innocence; royalism and religious loyalty; hermetic and alchemical philosophy; death and resurrection.
authors.significance: Long neglected, Vaughan was recovered in the nineteenth century and prized by the Romantics and T. S. Eliot as a visionary metaphysical poet; 'The Retreat' and 'The World' are among the great English mystical lyrics.
authors.uncertainty: Much of Vaughan's life is obscure; his exact birth date and many details of his royalist activities and medical practice rest on inference and local records.

authors.name: Hester Chapone
authors.identity: Moralist and essayist, a Bluestocking associated writer best known for her conduct work Letters on the Improvement of the Mind.
authors.biography: Born Hester Mulso on 27 October 1727 at Twywell in Northamptonshire, the daughter of a clergyman, she was educated largely at home and became known in learned society, corresponding with Elizabeth Carter and moving in Bluestocking circles before marrying the lawyer John Chapone. Her Letters on the Improvement of the Mind (1773), addressed to young women, went through many editions, and she published further conduct and moral works, including Miscellanies in Verse and Prose (1775). She continued to write for the education of women into later life. She died at Hampton in 1801.
authors.profile: A writer of conduct and educational literature whose Letters shaped thinking about women's rational and moral improvement, making her one of the most widely read female didactic authors of her period.
authors.style: Clear, warm, rational didactic prose in the letter form; an accessible, moralizing tone; and an easy blend of religious seriousness with practical advice.
authors.concerns: The rational and moral education of women; conduct, religion, and duty; taste and the improvement of the mind; and friendship among the learned.
authors.significance: An important conduct writer and Bluestocking figure whose Letters on the Improvement of the Mind circulated widely and influenced ideas about female education in the late eighteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: Her broad life is documented; details of some minor writings and the precise chronology of her correspondence remain matters of editorial reconstruction.

works.title: Letters on the Improvement of the Mind

authors.name: Horace Walpole
authors.identity: English man of letters, antiquary, and politician, creator of the first Gothic novel and one of the most celebrated letter-writers of the century.
authors.biography: Born on 24 September 1717 in London, the son of Sir Robert Walpole, the first Prime Minister, he was educated at Eton and Cambridge and entered Parliament as a Whig. A lifelong man of letters, he built the Gothic villa at Strawberry Hill and wrote on art and antiquities. He published the novel The Castle of Otranto (1764), at first presented as a translation, and later the tragedy The Mysterious Mother (1768). His extensive letters, on society, politics, and literature, are a major historical source. He died on 2 March 1797.
authors.profile: The author of the founding Gothic romance and a prolific writer of tales, plays, antiquarian histories, and correspondence, whose work fused taste, antiquarianism, and a cultivated horror of the medieval past.
authors.style: Elegant, urbane, witty prose; deliberate archaism and romance convention in Otranto; a gossipy, polished epistolary style; and an antiquarian's eye for the picturesque and the marvelous.
authors.concerns: The revival of interest in the Middle Ages and Gothic taste; ancestry, prophecy, and the supernatural; the interplay of romance and reason; sociability and political gossip; and the aesthetics of terror and the picturesque.
authors.significance: The originator of the Gothic novel with The Castle of Otranto and a defining figure of eighteenth-century taste, antiquarianism, and letter-writing, whose influence shaped Gothic fiction and the Gothic Revival.
authors.uncertainty: His life is well documented; the chief uncertainty concerns the framing and initial pseudonymous or 'translated' presentation of The Castle of Otranto rather than his biography.

works.title: A Description of the Villa of Mr. Horace Walpole
Historic Doubts on the Life and Reign of King Richard the Third

authors.name: Hugh Blair
authors.identity: Scottish Presbyterian minister, rhetorician, and literary critic of the Scottish Enlightenment, the first professor of Rhetoric and Belles Lettres at Edinburgh.
authors.biography: Blair was born in Edinburgh, studied divinity there, and was ordained to a ministry in the Church of Scotland, rising to the leading Edinburgh congregations and becoming a prominent figure of the Moderate interest. He lectured on rhetoric and belles lettres and was appointed to the newly created chair of Rhetoric and Belles Lettres at the University of Edinburgh in 1762. His best-known work, Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres, was published in 1783, drawing on decades of teaching and becoming a standard text on taste, style, and criticism. He wrote influential sermons and critical essays, and his endorsements figured in the literary debates over Ossian and the ballad. He died in 1800.
authors.profile: A critic, rhetorician, and preacher who codified Enlightenment ideas of taste, style, and eloquence, defending polite letters, sensible religion, and the analysis of beautiful writing.
authors.style: A clear, measured, authoritative critical prose of definition, example, and classification of styles; a temperate homiletic voice in the sermons; and an emphasis on perspicuity, harmony, and decorum.
authors.concerns: The nature of taste, genius, and the sublime; rhetoric and the principles of eloquence; the history and criticism of style and genres; and the alliance of politeness with reasonable religion and morality.
authors.significance: A defining voice of the Moderate wing of the Scottish Enlightenment; his Lectures standardised rhetorical and literary-critical teaching for a century, and his judgments shaped taste in the Ossian and ballad debates.

works.title: Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres

authors.name: Hugh Kelly
authors.identity: Dramatist and poet, an Irish-born writer of sentimental comedy who became a prominent figure and government supporter on the London stage.
authors.biography: Born around 1739 in Ireland (his birthplace is given variously as Dublin or Killarney), the son of a publican, he worked as a staymaker and studied law before turning to the stage and journalism in London. Employed as a writer for government, he produced the successful sentimental comedy The False Delicacy (1768), followed by A Word to the Wise (1770), and wrote verse including the poem Thespis (1766). His rivalry with Oliver Goldsmith generated well-known theatrical and literary quarrels. He died in London on 3 February 1777.
authors.profile: A writer of sentimental and moral comedy and occasional verse, whose plays appealed to mid-century tastes for delicacy and virtue and who was a rival to Goldsmith in the competition for the comic stage.
authors.style: Sentimental comedy of delicate feeling and moral testing; neat comic plotting; conventional Augustan diction in his verse; and a polished, sometimes didactic tone.
authors.concerns: Virtue, delicacy, and moral feeling; the testing of character and reputation; the politics of the stage; and literary rivalry and patronage.
authors.significance: A leading comic dramatist of the 1760s and 1770s and a memorable rival of Goldsmith, whose career illustrates the intertwining of the stage, government propaganda, and literary politics in the period.
authors.uncertainty: His exact year and place of birth are uncertain, with Dublin and Killarney both claimed, and the full scope of his government-sponsored journalism is imperfectly recorded.

authors.name: Hugh Latimer
authors.identity: preacher; bishop of Worcester; martyr
authors.biography: Born of a yeoman family at Thurcaston about 1485; educated at Cambridge, where he was converted from conservative orthodoxy to the reformed faith in the 1520s. A preacher of extraordinary popular power, he became bishop of Worcester in 1535, resigned in 1539 over the Six Articles, and preached through the Edwardian years, notably the Sermon of the Plough (1548) and the Lent sermons before Edward VI (1549). Under Mary he was imprisoned with Ridley and Cranmer and burned at Oxford on 16 October 1555, urging Ridley: 'we shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out.'
authors.profile: The greatest English preacher of the Reformation. His printed sermons — above all the Sermon of the Plough and the Sermons before King Edward VI — are the classics of Tudor homiletics: plain, concrete, homely in metaphor, and fearless in their attack on landlords, enclosers, and corrupt clergy.
authors.style: The plain style made dramatic: rural simile, proverb, anecdote, and direct address; a yeoman's concreteness yoked to scriptural authority.
authors.concerns: Preaching as the cure of the commonwealth; social justice against enclosure and greed; the duty of bishops and landlords; the Word before ceremony.
authors.significance: The model of English preaching for a century and a principal voice of the Reformation's social conscience; his sermons document the moral crisis of mid-Tudor England.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

works.title: The Sermons before King Edward VI

sources: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, 7 volumes (Bury edition)

authors.name: Hwætberht
authors.identity: Latin riddler; abbot and scholar
authors.biography: A monk of Wearmouth-Jarrow from boyhood who studied in Ireland in his youth and took the religious name Eusebius. He succeeded Ceolfrith as abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow c. 716 and remained abbot until his death c. 747. He was a friend and correspondent of Boniface and a close associate of Bede, who dedicated works to him.
authors.profile: Author of the Aenigmata Eusebii, forty Latin riddles on encyclopedic subjects ranging from the alphabet and the liberal arts to the natural world, composed in the tradition of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
authors.style: Hexameter riddles marked by learned wordplay and allusive density, modelled closely on Aldhelm; the subjects move from grammatical abstraction to cosmology and natural history.
authors.concerns: The encyclopedic ordering of knowledge; the riddling description of creation; the transmission of Aldhelmian learning in Northumbria.
authors.significance: His riddles, together with Tatwine's, carried the Aldhelmian riddle tradition into the Northumbrian Renaissance and stand behind the vernacular riddle collection of the Exeter Book.
authors.uncertainty: Death date approximate (c. 747); the riddles are securely attributed by manuscript tradition.
sources: The Oxford Handbook of Tudor Literature, 1485–1603

authors.name: Isaac Watts
authors.identity: Independent minister, logician and the father of English hymnody, who taught Dissent to sing its own composed songs and wrote a textbook of reasoning used on both sides of the Atlantic.
authors.biography: Born at Southampton in 1674, the eldest of the children of a Southampton Nonconformist family whose father suffered imprisonment for religious meetings, he showed a remarkable gift for Latin as a child and was educated for the ministry under Dissenting tutors. He preached early and reluctantly, held a small charge in the country, and settled in London, where from the early 1690s he led the Independent assembly in Mark Lane and built one of the largest and most cultivated congregations in Dissent. His hymns and songs of worship began with the Horae Lyricae and the Hymns and Spiritual Songs of 1707, followed by Divine and Moral Songs for Children and by his bold paraphrases of the psalms, which provoked long disputes about whether congregations might sing anything not taken from the biblical psalter. His Logic, or the Art of Reasoning, his Improvement of the Mind and his theological and homiletic works made him a standard author for schools and preachers. Suspected by some of abandoning the Trinity, he was honoured with a doctorate and spent his last decades an invalid, still writing and visiting, until his death in November 1748; he was buried at Bunhill Fields.
authors.profile: The scholar-preacher of hymns and rules of thinking, who joined catechetical plainness to a lyricist's sense of meter and of congregational feeling.
authors.style: Clear, taught, unhurried prose in his logic and divinity; hymn verse in simple common measures with strong doctrinal structure and affective immediacy; a psalm paraphrase of dignified warmth.
authors.concerns: The signs, ideas and method of right reasoning; human composition in worship and the education of a singing people; the doctrine of the atonement and the disputed Trinity; childhood, catechism and the piety of the common Christian.
authors.significance: He invented the English congregation hymn and made it the vehicle of doctrine, and his Logic was a chief instrument of education for a century, used by Dissenters, Anglicans and the American colleges alike.
authors.uncertainty: The precise sequence of his early pastoral settlements is uncertain, and the authorship of a few works printed under his name has been debated.

works.title: Divine and Moral Songs for the Use of Children
The Psalms of David Imitated in the Christian Stile

authors.name: Izaak Walton
authors.identity: Anglican biographer and author of The Compleat Angler (1653), the beloved pastoral dialogue of fishing whose serene celebration of the contemplative country life made it one of the most reprinted books in English.
authors.biography: Born 9 August 1593 at Stafford; apprenticed to a linen-draper, he prospered as a haberdasher in London (Fleet Street and later Chancery Lane) and moved in literary circles. A devout royalist Anglican, he served the cause during the Civil Wars and at the Restoration. He wrote gentle biographies of John Donne (1640), Sir Henry Wotton, Richard Hooker, George Herbert (1670), and Robert Sanderson, collected as Walton's Lives. His masterpiece The Compleat Angler (1653), enlarged over five editions to 1676 (with Charles Cotton's second part on fly-fishing), became a classic. He retired to the country and died on 15 December 1683 at Winchester, aged 90.
authors.profile: The biographer of the devout and the angler of the contemplative life, whose unhurried, genial prose celebrates friendship, piety, and the pleasures of riverside retirement.
authors.style: Gentle, pastoral, conversational prose; dialogue form (Piscator, Venator, Auceps); a serene, pious tone; digressive quotation of verse and lore; and unpretentious charm.
authors.concerns: The contemplative and retired life; friendship and piety; the natural world of rivers and fish; Anglican devotion and modest virtue; and the celebration of simple pleasures.
authors.significance: The Compleat Angler has been continuously in print and is one of the most beloved of English books; Walton's Lives established a tradition of affectionate biographical portraiture and shaped the ideal of the Anglican 'holy life'.
authors.uncertainty: Walton's life is documented; his Lives blend fact with hagiographic affection and are not always reliable as biography, and his dates for some subjects are traditional.

works.title: The Compleat Angler; or, The Contemplative Man's Recreation

authors.name: James Beattie
authors.identity: Aberdeen professor and poet, the most widely read assailant of Humean scepticism, whose Essay on Truth (1770) and The Minstrel (1771) made him a European name.
authors.biography: Born at Laurencekirk in 1735, the son of a shopkeeper and small farmer, he was educated at Marischal College, Aberdeen, took his MA in 1753 and served briefly as a schoolmaster. He was appointed in 1760 to the Marischal chair of moral philosophy and logic, which he held for four decades, and married Mary Dun in 1767. The Essay on Truth (1770), a robust defence of common sense against the ideal system, made his reputation and earned him a pension from George III; the didactic poem The Minstrel, with its sketch of a young genius, followed in 1771 and was enlarged in 1773. His essays on poetry and music were gathered with the rest of his later writing in the Dissertations Moral and Critical of 1796, after the period covered here. He corresponded with Johnson and Witherspoon and was widely praised, and for a generation his name stood in the American colleges for the Christian answer to scepticism. He died in Aberdeen on 16 February 1803.
authors.profile: A professor of common sense and of taste, who argued that scepticism refutes itself in the ordinary belief of mankind and versified the same appeal to feeling.
authors.style: Confident, declamatory argument and good-humoured invective; descriptive and personifying verse in a meditative, Thomson-like manner; a didactic plainness of diction.
authors.concerns: The instincts and the first principles of knowledge; the reality of the external world and of other minds; genius, taste and the psychology of poetry; the moral sentiments and their cultural conditions.
authors.significance: For a generation he was the standard answer to Hume in Britain and above all in the American colleges, and his career shows both the strength and the superficiality of the common-sense assault on scepticism.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of his abolitionist writing and the extent of his debt to Reid's unpublished teaching are still debated.

works.title: The Minstrel; or, the Progress of Genius

authors.name: James Boswell
authors.identity: Scottish lawyer and autobiographer, immortal as the biographer and companion of Samuel Johnson and as a diarist of his own life and times.
authors.biography: Boswell was born in Edinburgh, the son of a judge, Lord Auchinleck, and was called to the Scottish bar. A restless, self-analysing young man, he travelled widely and met David Hume and Jean-Jacques Rousseau before becoming, in 1763, Johnson's devoted friend and would-be biographer. He wrote essays for his own periodical The Hypochondriack and travelled to London and to Corsica, recording a Journal of a Tour to Corsica (1768) with admiration for its patriots, and later a Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides (1785) with Johnson. His masterpiece, The Life of Samuel Johnson, appeared in 1791. In later years he lived at the family estate of Auchinleck and died in London in 1795; his frank private journal was printed only in the twentieth century.
authors.profile: A biographer, diarist, and essayist whose genius was for recording speech, personality, and the texture of daily life; his journals and Life of Johnson founded modern biographical and autobiographical realism.
authors.style: Vivid, intimate, anecdotal prose; faithful reproduction of talk and character; a self-exposing, confessional diary manner; and a mixture of Scotticism with cultivated Augustan ease.
authors.concerns: The study of character and genius; friendship, emulation, and self-knowledge; nationality, law, and politics; and the value of the everyday and the documentary record.
authors.significance: His Life of Johnson and his rediscovered journals make him a founder of modern biography and autobiography and one of the most valuable witnesses to eighteenth-century literary and social life.

works.title: Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides

authors.name: James Harrington
authors.identity: Political philosopher; author of The Commonwealth of Oceana (1656), an influential republican utopia that argued government follows the distribution of property and prescribed a balanced constitution, shaping Whig and American republican thought.
authors.biography: Born 3 January 1611 at Upton, Northamptonshire, educated at Trinity College, Oxford and the Middle Temple, travelling widely in Europe. He served as a groom of the bedchamber to Charles I (1647), remaining loyal in person while arguing republican principles, and was much affected by the king's execution. Imprisoned briefly, he published Oceana (1656), dedicated — provocatively — to Cromwell, arguing that political power rests on the 'balance' of landed property and proposing an ideal mixed republic with rotation of office and a secret ballot. He wrote further republican tracts (The Prerogative of Popular Government, 1658) and, after the Restoration, was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy and died, broken in health, on 11 September 1677.
authors.profile: The republican theorist whose materialist analysis of power and property and whose constitutional utopia Oceana provided a durable vocabulary of republicanism for the English and American revolutions.
authors.style: Argumentative political prose and utopian fiction; historical and classical analogy; constitutional scheming; and a dense, sometimes obscure, learned style.
authors.concerns: Republicanism and the balance of property; constitutional design, rotation, and the ballot; the rise and fall of states; civic virtue; and the critique of monarchy and of Hobbes.
authors.significance: Oceana profoundly influenced later republican and Whig thought, the 'country' ideology of the eighteenth century, and the American founders (Jefferson and Adams drew on Harrington's ideas of property, rotation, and the balanced constitution).
authors.uncertainty: Harrington's life is documented but his later imprisonment and decline are partly anecdotal; the reception of Oceana was shaped by its dedication to Cromwell and its suppression.

authors.name: James Hervey
authors.identity: Country clergyman and devotional writer, the most ornate of the meditative prose writers between Browne and the lake poets, author of Meditations among the Tombs (1746) and Theron and Aspasio (1755).
authors.biography: Born at Hardingstone in Northamptonshire in 1714 into a family of small means and many children, he was educated for the church at Oxford, where he sat at Lincoln College, and took holy orders. Delicate and retired by temperament, he served country parishes, chiefly in Suffolk, under the patronage of great neighbours, and passed his short life among books, correspondence and the composition of devotional essays. His Meditations among the Tombs (1746) made at once a new fashion for the graveyard reverie and a reputation for splendid, melancholy prose; other volumes of meditations, letters and dialogues followed, together with a psalmody and hymns. Theron and Aspasio (1755), a long set of dialogues on natural and revealed religion, was read by its author as a defence of scriptural Christianity against deism and by John Wesley as a masked enthusiasm, and the attack pursued him for the rest of his days. He died suddenly at the end of 1758, still in his forties, and his works were repeatedly reprinted and translated.
authors.profile: A rhetorician of devotion, who turned the cemetery, the grove and the fireside into stages for the meditation on death, providence and the soul.
authors.style: Richly ornamented, Latinate periodic prose; personification and apostrophe pressed to the edge of excess; dialogue and epistolary forms; a colour sense of leaves, twilight and marble that the next century would inherit.
authors.concerns: Death, immortality and the resurrection of the body; the evidences and the inward experience of revealed religion; the piety of natural scenery; taste, ornament and the uses of melancholy.
authors.significance: He fixed the graveyard meditation as a literary mode and supplied the ornate devotional prose that Johnson, the romantic naturists and the nineteenth-century tractarians all read; his controversy with Wesley sharpened the century's quarrel about enthusiasm and conversion.
authors.uncertainty: The details of his preferments and patronage are slight, and the chronology of his several volumes is confused by reissues and collected editions.

works.title: Theron and Aspasio; or, A Scriptural and Critical Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians

authors.name: James I of Scotland
authors.identity: poet; king
authors.biography: Captured at sea by the English in 1406 at the age of eleven, he spent eighteen years as a prisoner at the English court, where he received a full education in the company of Henry V's courtiers and poets. Released in 1424, he returned to rule Scotland with reforming vigour until his murder by conspirators at Perth on 21 February 1437.
authors.profile: Traditionally credited with The Kingis Quair (c. 1424), the dream vision in which the captive narrator sees his beloved and is consoled by the goddesses of love and fortune; the attribution rests on the poem's own claims and manuscript tradition.
authors.style: Graceful Chaucerian rhyme royal with an autobiographical frame; the fusion of Boethian consolation with courtly love vision; precociously Renaissance delight in nature and architecture.
authors.concerns: Love, fortune, and providence; the education and duties of a prince; captivity and deliverance.
authors.significance: The Kingis Quair is the fountainhead of the Scottish Chaucerian tradition and one of the great prison poems of European literature.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of the Quair to James I is traditional and widely accepted but not absolutely certain.
themes: Time, death, and immortality through verse
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Restoration Drama

authors.name: James Macpherson
authors.identity: Scottish scholar and literary forger, the Ossian, whose claimed ancient Gaelic epics won European fame and a long authenticity controversy.
authors.biography: Macpherson was born in Inverness-shire, educated briefly at Aberdeen and Edinburgh, and worked as a schoolmaster while collecting Highland ballads and Gaelic fragments. With the encouragement of Hugh Blair and other patrons he published Fragments of Ancient Poetry (1760), followed by Fingal (1761) and the epic Temora (1763), presented as translations of the ancient bard Ossian. The works were translated across Europe and admired by many, while critics, notably Samuel Johnson, charged him with forgery. He used the fame and a government pension to secure posts in colonial administration and later sat in the British Parliament. He died in 1796.
authors.profile: A maker of pseudo-primitive epic; his translations of Ossian offer a vast, dim, elegiac world of heroes, ghosts, and landscapes in a singularly hypnotic, rhythmic prose-poetry.
authors.style: High, cadenced, repetitive prose-verse; invocations, apostrophe, and broken parallelism; an intentionally archaic, primitive sublimity and melancholy.
authors.concerns: National and Celtic origins of poetry; primitive genius and the sublime of the elder world; memory, loss, and the passing of heroes; and the authenticity of literary tradition.
authors.significance: The Ossianic vogue was a European literary event that fed Romantic primitivism, melancholy, and nationalist epic; the ensuing forgery debate sharpened ideas of authenticity and folk-poetry collection.
authors.uncertainty: His exact date and place of birth are given as 1736 in Inverness-shire but only approximately; the degree to which he worked from genuine Gaelic tradition versus pure invention remains contested.

works.title: Fragments of Ancient Poetry, Collected from the Bards

authors.name: James Ramsay
authors.identity: Naval surgeon and West India clergyman whose Essay on the Treatment and Conversion of African Slaves (1784) supplied the abolitionist movement with its documentation and its moral case.
authors.biography: Born at Fraserburgh in Aberdeenshire in 1733 and educated for medicine, he served as a surgeon in the navy, was present in the West Indies, and after leaving the service settled as a planter's physician and then as a clergyman on the sugar islands, where he saw the working of the slave system at its worst and quarrelled with the island planters over it. Ordained and returned to England, he was given the living of Teston in Kent, where the Bouverie family became his friends and encouragement, and there he wrote his Essay on the Treatment and Conversion of African Slaves in the British Sugar Colonies (1784). Its companion volume, an Inquiry into the effects of stopping the African trade and opening a commerce with Africa, argued that emancipation and lawful trade would enrich the nation. The sugar interest answered him in a swarm of hostile pamphlets, attacked his conduct as a planter and as a clergyman, and pursued him over his account of the killing of mutinous ratings on a king's ship; he replied at length and lost certain friends by his stubbornness. He advised the committee formed in 1787 and instructed its members in the evidence of the colonies. He died in 1789, the year of Equiano's narrative, leaving the Teston circle to carry his arguments into Parliament.
authors.profile: The witness-clergyman, who made an accumulated case of particulars, dates and amounts out of twenty years of service in the slave-holding islands.
authors.style: Plain, accumulative, heavily evidenced prose; narrative of cases joined to statistical and scriptural argument; a surgeon's specification of wounds and punishments; occasional bitterness of reply.
authors.concerns: The treatment, conversion and education of enslaved people; the criminality of the trade and the duty of the nation; the economics of emancipation and of African commerce; the moral responsibility of the planter and the clergy.
authors.significance: His two books of 1784 converted a clerical protest into the printed evidence on which the organised abolition campaign of the following decade was built, and the circle he gathered at Teston became a nursery of the Clapham reformers.
authors.uncertainty: The dates of his island ministry and of his ordination are reported inconsistently, and the details of the controversy over the mutiny narrative are partisan on both sides.

works.title: An Inquiry into the Effects of Putting a Stop to the African Slave Trade, and of Granting Liberty to the Slaves in the British Sugar Colonies

authors.name: James Shirley
authors.identity: The leading Caroline dramatist; a prolific author of comedies of fashionable London manners and of tragedies and tragicomedies, whose work T. S. Eliot called the 'last of the Elizabethan playwrights' and whose verse lyric 'Death the Leveller' remains famous.
authors.biography: Born September 1596 in London, educated at Merchant Taylors' School, St John's College, Oxford, and St Catharine's, Cambridge. Converted to Catholicism, he taught school then turned to the stage, writing some thirty plays for the King's Men and Queen Henrietta's Men (1625–42), including The Wedding, Hyde Park, The Cardinal, and The Lady of Pleasure. During the Civil Wars he served as secretary to the royalist Earl of Newcastle; at the Restoration his old plays were revived with success. He died on 29 October 1666 in London, reportedly perishing with his wife in the Great Fire's aftermath.
authors.profile: The chronicler of Caroline fashionable society, whose comedies of intrigue, gallantry, and manners look forward to Restoration comedy, and whose tragedies show the late Jacobean taste for moral complexity and rhetorical set pieces.
authors.style: Polished verse and prose; witty, fashionable dialogue; intricate plots of courtship and intrigue; sententious moralising; and a lyric grace ('Only the actions of the just / Smell sweet and blossom in the dust').
authors.concerns: Manners, fashion, and the morals of the town; love, honour, and gallantry; political corruption and tyranny; death and the levelling of rank; and the fate of virtue.
authors.significance: Shirley was the principal dramatist of the Caroline theatre and the direct model for Restoration comedy; his plays kept the professional drama alive in style until the theatres closed in 1642.
authors.uncertainty: Shirley's life is documented in outline; the exact dates and authorship of some plays, and of his posthumous Six New Plays (1653), remain matters of scholarship.

authors.name: James Thomson
authors.identity: Scottish-born poet, best known for the blank-verse landscape cycle The Seasons, who helped introduce descriptive and sensuous nature poetry to English verse.
authors.biography: Thomson was born in the Scottish borders, the son of a minister, and studied divinity at the University of Edinburgh before abandoning the church for letters in London. He supported himself by tutoring and writing, and published Winter in 1726, soon expanding his descriptive pieces into The Seasons in its four-part edition of 1730. He wrote political and patriotic dramas, including Sophonisba (1730), and the Liberty poems (1734-1736). He enjoyed patronage associated with the Prince of Wales's circle at Leicester. He died suddenly in London in 1748.
authors.profile: A poet of nature, sensation, and civic patriotism; his central work observes the changing seasons in rich descriptive blank verse and infuses landscape with emotional and moral reflection.
authors.style: Sensuous, pictorial blank verse in long descriptive passages; accumulation of visual and atmospheric detail; a meditative, sometimes rapturous tone; and Miltonic diction and inversion.
authors.concerns: Nature as spectacle and moral teacher; the senses and the passions; British liberty, trade, and empire; the pleasure of the sublime and the picturesque; and the relation of landscape to feeling.
authors.significance: The Seasons transformed English nature poetry and anticipated the Romantic sensibility and the picturesque; it was one of the most influential and often-set poetic works of the eighteenth century.

authors.name: Jeremy Bentham
authors.identity: Law reformer and moral philosopher, founder of classical utilitarianism, who measured institutions by pleasure and pain and subjected the common law, the church and the prison to the test of utility.
authors.biography: Born in London in 1748 into a wealthy family of attorneys, a child prodigy in Latin and French law books, he was educated at Queen's College, Oxford, and was called to the bar in 1769, though he never practised and soon abandoned the profession to write on legislation. He inherited property and leisure, attached himself to no party, and passed his life in lodgings and in correspondence, drafting codes, inspecting prisons, and corresponding with rulers and reformers across Europe and America. Two long stays at the estates of his brother Samuel, the engineer in Russia, sharpened his ideas about inspection and the organisation of labour. He wrote against Blackstone in the 1760s, published the Fragment on Government anonymously in 1776, the Defence of Usury in 1787 and the Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation in 1789. His Panopticon scheme and his writings on colonies and on judicial procedure belong to the 1790s; the coded works edited for him by Dumont appeared in the 1800s, and his attack on Blackstone's Commentaries remained in manuscript until the twentieth century. He died in London in 1832, having asked that his body be dissected and preserved as his auto-icon.
authors.profile: A jurist of facts and consequences, whose vocabulary of utility, felicity and the greatest number recast moral and legal argument as an arithmetic of interests.
authors.style: Technical, taxonomic, tireless prose; long definitions, enumerated situations and coined terms; polemic conducted through analysis rather than rhetoric; a satirist's dryness about lawyers and priests.
authors.concerns: The greatest happiness principle; the anatomy of law, sovereignty and obligation; punishment, deterrence and the inspection of the idle; the interests of women, of colonial subjects and of animals; the corruption of church, university and common law.
authors.significance: He founded utilitarian ethics and systematic law reform, shaped Victorian policing, education and welfare legislation, and made the critical test of institutions their consequences for the greatest number.
authors.uncertainty: The order of his vast unpublished manuscripts, much of it first printed by editors after his death, makes the dating of his ideas a continual problem.

works.title: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation

authors.name: Jeremy Taylor
authors.identity: Anglican divine and devotional writer, called 'the Shakespeare of the divines'; his Holy Living (1650) and Holy Dying (1651) are the supreme prose achievements of Caroline Anglican piety, rich in imagery, learning, and moral casuistry.
authors.biography: Born August 1613 at Cambridge, son of a barber; educated at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge (BA 1630, MA 1634) and All Souls, Oxford. Patronised by William Laud and Charles I, he became a royalist chaplain, was twice imprisoned during the Civil Wars, and was deprived of his living. In seclusion in Wales he wrote his great devotional manuals Holy Living (1650) and Holy Dying (1651), and the casuistical Ductor Dubitantium (1660). At the Restoration he was consecrated Bishop of Down and Connor (1661) and Vice-Chancellor of Trinity College, Dublin; he died on 13 August 1667 at Lisburn.
authors.profile: The eloquent Caroline divine whose devotional prose combines baroque imagery, immense learning, and tender moral guidance, treating the whole of life as a preparation for a holy death.
authors.style: Lush, metaphorical, Latinate prose; abundant simile and classical and scriptural allusion; casuistical moral reasoning; and a rich, musical rhythm.
authors.concerns: Holy living and dying; Christian virtue, patience, and repentance; liberty of conscience and toleration (The Liberty of Prophesying, 1647); moral casuistry; and Anglican devotion.
authors.significance: Holy Living and Holy Dying shaped English devotional prose and the Anglican ideal of the good life and good death for centuries; Taylor's eloquence and advocacy of toleration mark him as one of the greatest prose writers and most liberal-minded of the Caroline divines.
authors.uncertainty: Taylor's life is documented; his imprisoned royalist years and some details of his preferment rest on tradition and ecclesiastical records.

works.title: The Rule and Exercises of Holy Dying
The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living

authors.name: John Arbuthnot
authors.identity: Aberdeenshire-born physician of Queen Anne, mathematician and wit, the inventor of John Bull and the author of the design argument that later natural theology reused.
authors.biography: Born at Marnoch in Aberdeenshire in 1667, the son of a Calvinist minister, he studied medicine at Aberdeen, took his degree in Scotland and removed to London, where he built a large and prosperous practice and was named one of the physicians to Queen Anne. He became the friend and adviser of Pope, Swift and Gay, and is held to have given the first impulse to the wits who met as the Scriblerus Club, while his own learned jokes about the arts and sciences supplied much of their matter. His essay on the usefulness of mathematical learning, published at the beginning of the century, put the argument from design in a form that was quoted for generations and that William Paley enlarged in his Natural Theology of 1802, long after the period covered here. In 1712 he wrote the History of John Bull, an allegory of the nation, its law and its trades, which gave English politics a permanent personification, and in the same year an essay on the art of political lying, an anatomy of party rhetoric. Pope addressed to him one of his most searching verses, and he died in London in February 1735.
authors.profile: A physician-mathematician who turned professional learning into political satire and moral argument, and whose allegory taught a nation to see itself as a character.
authors.style: Dry, learned, deadpan irony; the allegorical case history and the law suit as national portrait; precise definitions and enumerations; a populariser's clarity about mathematics and medicine.
authors.concerns: The evidence of design in nature and the uses of mathematical reasoning; the mechanics of party, credit and national interest; the character of the English constitution and its trades; the corruption of political language; the mixture of learning and quackery in the arts.
authors.significance: He gave Augustan politics its national allegory and its analysis of spin, carried the design argument into ordinary English prose, and stood at the centre of the circle that produced the greatest satires of the age.
authors.uncertainty: The ascription of individual pieces of Scriblerus work is unsettled, and the date of his London settlement and of his Scottish degree is variously reported.

works.title: An Essay Concerning the Art of Political Lying
The Works of Mr. Martinus Scriblerus

authors.name: John Aubrey
authors.identity: Antiquary, biographer, and gossip-collector; his Brief Lives — vivid, candid, anecdotal sketches of his famous contemporaries (Shakespeare, Hobbes, Donne, Bacon) — invented an intimate, factual mode of biography and preserved priceless literary history.
authors.biography: Born 12 March 1626 at Easton Piers, Wiltshire; educated at Trinity College, Oxford (no degree) and the Middle Temple. A gentleman antiquary and Fellow of the Royal Society (1663), he roamed the country recording monuments, folklore (Remains of Gentilisme and Judaisme), and the lives and sayings of learned men. A close friend of Hobbes (whose Life he wrote), he compiled his 'Minutes of Lives' — the Brief Lives — mostly in the 1660s–90s, not intended for publication. Ruined by lawsuits, he lived on others' charity and died in Oxford on 7 June 1697. His manuscripts, held by the Bodleian, were published in full only in the twentieth century.
authors.profile: The pioneer of intimate, empirical biography, whose frank, discursive, note-strewn 'Lives' capture the personalities, quirks, and scandals of the great with an unprecedented immediacy.
authors.style: Anecdotal, colloquial, note-form prose; candid reportage and quotation of others' testimony; digressive and unfinished quality; and an antiquarian accumulation of fact and folklore.
authors.concerns: Biography and personal character; antiquities, monuments, and folklore; the lives of the learned and of Hobbes; astrology and the supernatural; and the preservation of literary history.
authors.significance: Brief Lives is a unique and indispensable source for seventeenth-century literary and intellectual history and a founding work of modern, personal biography; Aubrey's methods anticipated the empirical, factual approach of later biographers.
authors.uncertainty: Aubrey's own life is documented through his manuscripts and correspondents; his Brief Lives are notes and gossip of varying reliability, requiring editorial caution.

authors.name: John Bale
authors.identity: playwright; polemicist; antiquary; bishop of Ossory
authors.biography: Born at Cove, Suffolk, on 21 November 1495; entered the Carmelite order at Norwich, then converted to the Reformation in the 1530s. He wrote King Johan (c. 1538), the first English history play and a weapon of Henrician propaganda; The Image of Both Churches (c. 1545), a running commentary on Revelation; and the Illustrium Maioris Britanniae Scriptorum Summarium (1548), the first bio-bibliography of British writers. Bishop of Ossory in Ireland in 1553, he fled abroad under Mary and returned under Elizabeth, dying at Canterbury in November 1563.
authors.profile: The founder of English literary history and of the Protestant history play. King Johan turned the chronicle matter of England into stage polemic, and the Summarium — enlarged at Basel in 1557–59 as the Scriptorum Illustrium Maioris Brytanniae Catalogus — preserved the names and titles on which later literary history rests.
authors.style: Furious polemical energy; the apocalyptic scheme of the two churches applied to history; catalogue and inventory as instruments of scholarship and propaganda alike.
authors.concerns: The identification of the pope with Antichrist; the English church and nation as God's elect; the record of British writers as proof of national dignity.
authors.significance: Inventor of the English history play and of English literary bibliography; his catalogues transmitted knowledge of the medieval English canon to the Renaissance.
authors.uncertainty: None significant.
themes: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations

works.title: The Chief Promises of God unto Man

sources: The Poems of Ossian and Related Works

authors.name: John Barbour
authors.identity: poet; chronicler; churchman
authors.biography: Archdeacon of Aberdeen and a clerk in the service of Robert II; he travelled repeatedly to England and France for study (Oxford and Paris) and royal business. His Brus, completed c. 1375, earned him a royal pension, and he died on 13 March 1395.
authors.profile: Author of The Brus (c. 1375), a verse chronicle of the wars of independence celebrating Robert Bruce and James Douglas; other works attributed to him (including a Troy book) are lost.
authors.style: Energetic octosyllabic couplets; vivid battle narrative and stirring speeches; the celebration of freedom ('A! Fredome is a noble thing!') within a providential frame.
authors.concerns: Scottish independence and national identity; the virtue of freedom against tyranny; chivalric loyalty.
authors.significance: The father of Scottish poetry and of Scottish national historical literature; the Brus is the first great work in Older Scots.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his other works are lost, so the canon rests on the Brus alone.
movements: Primitivism, the Bardic Revival and Ossian
sources: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler

authors.name: John Bunyan
authors.identity: Puritan preacher, nonconformist, and author of The Pilgrim's Progress (1678, 1684), the greatest allegory in English and one of the most widely read books ever written, born of his years of imprisonment for preaching without a licence.
authors.biography: Born November 1628 (baptised 30 November) at Elstow, Bedfordshire, son of a tinker; little educated, he served briefly in the Parliamentary army and followed his father's trade. After a profound spiritual crisis recounted in Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners (1666), he became a Baptist preacher at Bedford. Refusing to conform after the Restoration, he was imprisoned for twelve years (1660–72) and briefly again in 1675–76, during which he wrote and, likely, began The Pilgrim's Progress. Published in two parts (1678, 1684), it was an immediate and enduring popular success. He also wrote The Holy War (1682), The Life and Death of Mr Badman (1680), and much doctrinal and controversial prose. He died on 31 August 1688 in London after a stormy journey.
authors.profile: The tinker-preacher whose plain, biblical, vividly imaginative prose gave the Puritan pilgrimage of the soul an unforgettable narrative form, drawing its power from scripture, the vernacular, and his own tormented and triumphant experience.
authors.style: Allegory with concrete, homely, scriptural imagery; a plain, vigorous, rhythmic prose saturated with the Bible; vivid personification (Christian, Faithful, Apollyon, Mr Worldly Wiseman); and dream-frame narrative.
authors.concerns: Salvation, grace, and the pilgrim's journey; sin, despair, and assurance; the Christian life as warfare and pilgrimage; persecution and nonconformity; and the vanity of the world.
authors.significance: The Pilgrim's Progress is the supreme English allegory and a foundational text of Protestant spirituality, translated into hundreds of languages and influencing the novel, hymnody, and countless writers from Dickens to the present; Grace Abounding is a landmark of spiritual autobiography.
authors.uncertainty: Bunyan's life is documented through his own writings and Bedford church records; the exact circumstances and dates of his composition of The Pilgrim's Progress during imprisonment are traditional rather than certain.

works.title: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
The Holy War Made by Shaddai upon Diabolus, for the Regaining of the Metropolis of the World
The Life and Death of Mr. Badman
The Pilgrim's Progress from This World to That Which Is to Come (Part I)
The Pilgrim's Progress from This World to That Which Is to Come (Part II)

authors.name: John Capgrave
authors.identity: hagiographer; chronicler; Augustinian friar
authors.biography: Born at Lynn on 21 April 1393, he studied at Cambridge, joined the Augustinian friars, and became prior of their house at Lynn; he travelled to Rome in 1450 and died on 12 August 1464. The most learned English writer of his generation, he composed in both Latin and English.
authors.profile: Author of the Life of St Katharine (c. 1445), the Life of St Norbert, the Abbreuiacion of Cronicles, the chronicle of England to 1417, the pilgrimage guide Ye Solace of Pilgrimes, and numerous Latin commentaries and lives.
authors.style: Learned, well-ordered prose and Lydgatean verse; the devout scholar's care for accuracy and orthodoxy; the blending of chronicle and hagiography.
authors.concerns: The cult of St Katharine and the defence of learning; English history in the Lancastrian interest; orthodox devotion against Lollardy.
authors.significance: The leading East Anglian man of letters of the mid-fifteenth century; his Katharine is a classic of the learned saint's life.
authors.uncertainty: Little uncertain: his own works and the Lynn records document his career closely.
sources: The Spectator, 4 volumes

authors.name: John Clanvowe
authors.identity: poet; courtier; Lollard sympathizer
authors.biography: A knight of Richard II's household and lifelong companion of Sir William Neville, with whom he is buried at Constantinople, where both died in October 1391; their joint tomb, with its crossed swords, survives in Istanbul. A member of the 'Lollard knights' circle, he wrote both courtly and reforming works.
authors.profile: Author of The Two Ways (c. 1391), a Lollard-leaning devotional prose tract, and of The Boke of Cupide (The Cuckoo and the Nightingale, c. 1386), a Chaucerian dream poem long attributed to Chaucer.
authors.style: Graceful Chaucerian verse in the dream poem; plain, scriptural prose in the devotional tract.
authors.concerns: The two ways of life and death; the reform of the church; courtly love within a Christian frame.
authors.significance: The Two Ways is a principal document of the Lollard sensibility among the courtly elite, and the Boke of Cupide testifies to the immediate diffusion of Chaucerian poetry.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the extent of his personal Lollardy is debated.
sources: The Pilgrim's Progress

authors.name: John Colet
authors.identity: humanist; dean of St Paul's; founder of St Paul's School
authors.biography: Born in London in 1467, son of a Lord Mayor; studied at Oxford and in Italy. His Oxford lectures on the epistles of St Paul (c. 1497–1505) broke with scholastic method and made him the father of English humanism; he became dean of St Paul's in 1505 and founded St Paul's School in 1509, appointing William Lily its first master. He died on 16 September 1519. His grammatical treatise, the Aeditio, was printed in 1527.
authors.profile: The founder of the Oxford reform that produced English humanism. His Paul's lectures, teaching scripture from the plain text rather than the glosses, converted a generation — including Erasmus, who called him the ideal of the Christian humanist — and his Aeditio contributed the English accidence to the standard school grammar.
authors.style: Expository clarity aimed at the unlearned; plain-text biblical exposition; the reformer's impatience with ceremonial and gloss.
authors.concerns: The primitive church as model; education as the reform of Christendom; the layman's access to scripture.
authors.significance: The inspirer of Erasmus and More and the founder of the English humanist movement; his school and his lectures set the intellectual course of the Tudor century.
authors.uncertainty: None significant; the Aeditio's precise date of composition is approximate.

authors.name: John Dennis
authors.identity: English critic, playwright, and controversialist, a passionate early theorist of the sublime and one of the most quarrelsome and perceptive literary minds of his age.
authors.biography: Dennis was educated at a grammar school in Hertford and, by some accounts, at Cambridge, before briefly joining the army and then devoting himself to letters and the stage. He wrote tragedies, including Appius and Virginia (1709), and many critical works, among them The Advancement and Reformation of Poetry and Music (1701), The Grounds of Criticism in Poetry (1704), and treatises on the sublime, the operas, and the stage. He anticipated the Romantic enthusiasm he preached, and his quarrels, notably with Addison over Cato and with Pope and Steele, made him a notorious figure. A Whig and a devoted student of French classical criticism and of Longinus, he championed enthusiastick poetry. He died in 1734, in poverty and mental distress.
authors.profile: An aggressive, original critic and theorist of poetry and religion who, drawing on Longinus and Boileau, argued for enthusiastic imagination and the sublime against cold neoclassical regularity.
authors.style: Vehement, hyperbolic, often ranting critical prose; a rhetoric of enthusiasm and transports; sharp personal invective; and an earnest, sometimes incoherent eagerness in praise of the sublime.
authors.concerns: The sublime and enthusiastic imagination against rule; the relation of poetry to religion and passion; the defence of modern learning and national drama; and the corruption of critical taste.
authors.significance: A major forerunner of eighteenth-century and Romantic theories of the sublime and enthusiastic imagination; his critical writings, despite his notoriety, influenced Addison and later aesthetic thought.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is given as about 1657 from baptismal evidence, his exact birthplace is uncertain, and his claim to a university education rests on later testimony rather than firm records.

works.title: The Advancement and Reformation of Modern Poetry
The Grounds of Criticism in Poetry

authors.name: John Donne
authors.identity: Poet, preacher, and Dean of St Paul's; the greatest of the metaphysical poets, author of the Songs and Sonnets, the Holy Sonnets, the Anniversaries, the Devotions, and the sermons.
authors.biography: Born in London in 1572 into a recusant Catholic family (his mother was a daughter of John Heywood, and his uncle Jasper Heywood led the Jesuits); educated at Hart Hall, Oxford, and possibly Cambridge, and at Lincoln's Inn. He sailed on the Cadiz (1596) and Islands (1597) expeditions and was secretary to Sir Thomas Egerton before his secret marriage to Egerton's niece Anne More in 1601 wrecked his secular career ('John Donne, Anne Donne, Un-done'). After years of poverty and patronage-seeking, he took orders in 1615 at the king's urging, became Reader at Lincoln's Inn, Dean of St Paul's (1621), and the most famous preacher of the age. His poems circulated in manuscript in his lifetime (the Songs and Sonnets, Elegies, Satires, Holy Sonnets, the Anniversaries of 1611–12 on Elizabeth Drury); the Devotions upon Emergent Occasions appeared in 1624; the poems were first collected in 1633. He died on 31 March 1631 after preaching his own funeral sermon, 'Death's Duel'.
authors.profile: The poet of wit and the preacher of love: the Songs and Sonnets and Elegies are the great secular lyrics of the period, the Holy Sonnets and 'Good Friday, 1613. Riding Westward' its great devotional poems, and the sermons the summit of English pulpit prose.
authors.style: The dramatic opening, the extended conceit, the colloquial vehemence of an argumentative line, paradox and hyperbole, and the union of the erotic and the divine; in the sermons, a baroque prose of enormous periodic energy.
authors.concerns: The inseparability of body and soul; constancy and inconstancy in love; death, judgement, and resurrection; the discovery of the new philosophy and the decay of the old cosmos; the self as microcosm.
authors.significance: The greatest English metaphysical poet and one of the supreme preachers: his poetry was rediscovered by Grierson (1912) and Eliot as the alternative tradition to Spenserian sweetness, and shaped twentieth-century poetry; his Devotions ('No man is an island') and sermons remain classics of prose.
authors.uncertainty: Nearly all the poems are undated and circulated in widely varying manuscripts; the canon and ordering of the Songs and Sonnets depend on the 1633 and 1635 editions; several elegies' attributions remain contested.

authors.name: John Dryden
authors.identity: Poet laureate, dramatist, critic, and translator; the dominant literary figure of the Restoration, who perfected the heroic couplet, founded modern English criticism and verse satire, and moved between Puritan, royalist, and Catholic allegiances with the times.
authors.biography: Born 9 August 1631 at Aldwincle; educated at Westminster School and Trinity College, Cambridge (BA 1654). He supported Cromwell at his death (Heroic Stanzas, 1658) then hailed the Restoration (Astraea Redux, 1660). In London he married Lady Elizabeth Howard (1663), wrote heroic plays and comedies for the King's Company, became laureate and historiographer royal (1668), and defended the moderns and the English stage in An Essay of Dramatic Poesy (1668). His political satires Absalom and Achitophel (1681) and Mac Flecknoe (1682) and the religious poems Religio Laici (1682) and The Hind and the Panther (1687, after his conversion to Catholicism) mark his maturity. Deprived of his offices by the Protestant William III (1688), he turned to translation, producing the great Virgil (1697) and Fables Ancient and Modern (1700). He died 1 May 1700 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The versatile master of Restoration letters — playwright, laureate, critic, satirist, and translator — who established the heroic couplet as the standard medium of serious English poetry and created a durable critical vocabulary.
authors.style: The balanced, pointed heroic couplet; conversational yet elevated diction; satiric wit and character portraiture; a critical prose of clarity and good sense; and a translational idiom that naturalized the classics into contemporary English.
authors.concerns: The nature and decorum of drama and poetry; the quarrel of the ancients and moderns; political legitimacy, party, and succession; religious faith and conversion; the craft of translation and the history of the language.
authors.significance: Dryden created the Augustan style that Pope and Johnson inherited, founded English literary criticism, and produced the greatest political verse satire of the century; his translations made the classics central to English literary culture.
authors.uncertainty: Dryden's life is well recorded; his religious and political shifts are documented in his own poems and prefaces, though their sincerity has been debated.

Alexander's Feast; or, The Power of Music
All for Love; or, The World Well Lost
King Arthur; or, The British Worthy
The Satires of Decimus Junius Juvenalis and Aulus Persius Flaccus
The Tempest; or, The Enchanted Island
The Works of Virgil Translated into English Verse
To the Memory of Mr. Oldham

authors.name: John Duns Scotus
authors.identity: philosopher; theologian; Franciscan friar
authors.biography: The subtlest of the scholastic philosophers: he entered the Franciscans c. 1280, studied and taught at Oxford and Paris, and lectured on the Sentences at Oxford c. 1300–02 and Paris 1302–05; transferred to Cologne in 1307, he died there on 8 November 1308. His thought defined one of the two great schools of late medieval theology.
authors.profile: Author of the Ordinatio (his revision of the Oxford Sentences lectures, c. 1300–08), the Quaestiones Quodlibetales, and treatises on metaphysics, logic, and natural theology, including his famous proof of God's existence.
authors.style: Rigorous, compressed, terminologically innovative argument; the 'formal distinction' and the univocity of being; a dialectical subtlety that earned him the title Doctor Subtilis.
authors.concerns: The univocity of being and the nature of metaphysics; the freedom of God and of the will; the Immaculate Conception; individuation (haecceitas).
authors.significance: Founder of Scotism, which rivalled Thomism for centuries and shaped theology into the Reformation; among the most influential British philosophers of all time.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and early life approximate; the authenticity of parts of the corpus remains disputed.
themes: Female authorship and the woman writer
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Gothic Fiction

authors.name: John Dyer
authors.identity: Welsh-born poet and painter, associated with Thomson and the descriptive school, author of Grongar Hill and the georgic The Fleece.
authors.biography: Dyer was a Welshman, born about 1700, who first trained for a profession connected with architecture and surveying before turning to painting and poetry in the artistic circle around James Thomson and the Burlington set. His topographical poem Grongar Hill (1726) celebrates a Welsh landscape in light-reflective blank verse. He travelled in Italy and, back in Wales, farmed and wrote, producing the georgic The Fleece (1757), a poem on the Welsh wool trade. Weak memory and modest means marked his later years. He died in 1758.
authors.profile: A poet of landscape and the visual, whose descriptive and georgic verse reflects a painter's eye for colour, distance, and light and a patriot's attachment to Welsh scenery and industry.
authors.style: Clear, pictorial blank verse of space and colour; a sense of the distance and depth of a prospect; ease in the topographical and georgic mode; and a calm, contemplative, sensuous eye.
authors.concerns: The perception of landscape, distance, and light; patriotic and economic interest in the Welsh wool trade; retirement and rural labour; and the interplay of painting and poetry.
authors.significance: Grongar Hill is an early, much-admired poem of the picturesque prospect and a precursor of Romantic nature perception; Dyer helped link Thomson's descriptive verse to a Welsh topographical tradition.
authors.uncertainty: His year and place of birth are uncertain, given only as about 1700; the details of his early training and his later farming and mental decline rest on fragmentary accounts.

authors.name: John Evelyn
authors.identity: Diarist, author, horticulturist, and founding Fellow of the Royal Society; his long Diary (1641–1706) records the intellectual and public life of the age, and his Sylva (1664) — a plea for reforestation — was a pioneering work of natural history and one of the Society's first publications.
authors.biography: Born 31 October 1620 at Wotton, Surrey, educated at Balliol College, Oxford and the Middle Temple. He travelled Europe (1643–52), keeping a journal, and after the Restoration settled at Sayes Court, Deptford. A founder-member of the Royal Society (1662), he published Sylva; or, A Discourse of Forest-Trees (1664), Fumifugium (1661, on air pollution), and works on engraving, numismatics, and horticulture, and translated Lucretius and others. His Diary, kept over six decades, is the great public counterpart to Pepys's private one. A devout Anglican and royalist, he died on 27 February 1706.
authors.profile: The cultivated gentleman-scholar and improver whose wide-ranging diary, essays, and horticultural writings document the new science, the arts, and public affairs with learned, pious, and practical curiosity.
authors.style: Learned, observant, sometimes formal prose; the discursive diary and treatise; antiquarian and scientific detail; and a pious, improving tone.
authors.concerns: Horticulture, forestry, and the improvement of the land; the new science and the Royal Society; art, architecture, and engraving; air pollution and the environment; religion and public affairs.
authors.significance: Sylva is a landmark of natural history and environmental writing and helped reforest England for the navy; Evelyn's Diary is an invaluable record of the intellectual and cultural life of the seventeenth century, complementing Pepys.
authors.uncertainty: Evelyn's life and writings are thoroughly documented through his diary, letters, and family papers; his works are numerous and some are translations.

works.title: Sylva; or, A Discourse of Forest-Trees and the Propagation of Timber

authors.name: John Fisher
authors.identity: bishop of Rochester; theologian; cardinal; martyr and saint
authors.biography: Born at Beverley in 1469; educated at Cambridge, where he became Master of Michaelhouse and chancellor of the university, and the patron of Erasmus and of Greek studies. Bishop of Rochester from 1504, he was the confessor of Lady Margaret Beaufort and the most respected preacher of his age. Refusing the oath of supremacy, he was made a cardinal by Paul III and executed on 22 June 1535; canonized in 1935.
authors.profile: The great conservative preacher of the early Reformation. His sermons — against Luther (1521) and on the penitential psalms — are the classic statements of the old orthodoxy in the new age of print, and his commentary on the seven penitential psalms (1505, enlarged 1508) was the devotional bestseller of the early Tudor period.
authors.style: Scholastic learning in a plain, forceful pulpit style; the expository sermon built on the literal text; pastoral warmth under doctrinal rigour.
authors.concerns: The defence of the old faith; penance and the sacrament; the reform of the clergy from within; the university as the church's school.
authors.significance: The intellectual leader of English Catholicism in the crisis of the 1520s and 1530s; his life and death defined the conservative alternative to the Henrician settlement.
authors.uncertainty: None significant.
themes: The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales

authors.name: John Fletcher
authors.identity: dramatist
authors.biography: Baptized 20 December 1579 at Rye; son of Richard Fletcher, later Bishop of London. He was educated at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, and probably began writing for the stage about 1606. After his partnership with Beaumont he collaborated with Shakespeare (Henry VIII, The Two Noble Kinsmen) and with Massinger, and in 1616 succeeded Shakespeare as principal dramatist of the King's Men. He died of the plague in August 1625 and is buried in Southwark Cathedral.
authors.profile: Sole and collaborative canon of some fifty plays, including The Faithful Shepherdess (c. 1608), The Woman's Prize (c. 1611), The Island Princess (c. 1621), Rule a Wife and Have a Wife (1624), and, with Beaumont, Philaster, The Maid's Tragedy, and A King and No King.
authors.style: Supple, flowing blank verse with feminine endings; rapid plotting; a taste for surprise, disguise, and the reversals of tragicomedy.
authors.concerns: Honour, love, and friendship under pressure; the follies of tyranny; the pleasures of wit and gallantry.
authors.significance: His fluent verse and tragicomic plots set the pattern for Restoration drama; for the next half-century 'Beaumont and Fletcher' outran even Shakespeare at the box office.
authors.uncertainty: Shares in the fifty-play canon are often uncertain; the Beaumont–Fletcher division of labour remains debated.

authors.name: John Florio
authors.identity: translator; lexicographer; language teacher
authors.biography: Born in London in 1553, son of Michelangelo Florio, an Italian Protestant exile. He taught Italian to the court and nobility, served in the household of the Earl of Southampton, became reader in Italian to Queen Anne (1604), and groom of the privy chamber (1619). A friend of Jonson and Samuel Daniel, he died of the plague at Fulham in October 1625.
authors.profile: His Italian–English dictionaries A World of Words (1598) and Queen Anna's New World of Words (1611), the dialogue manuals First Fruits (1578) and Second Fruits (1591), and above all the translation of Montaigne's Essays (1603), one of the great translations in the language.
authors.style: A florid, expansive English that enlarges Montaigne's French into the idiom Shakespeare knew; a tireless coiner and collector of words.
authors.concerns: The transmission of Continental learning; language as national wealth; scepticism and the essay form.
authors.significance: His Montaigne gave English thought and letters — including Shakespeare's Tempest — direct access to the Essays, and his dictionaries record the Italian loan-words entering Elizabethan English.
authors.uncertainty: His role as possible editor for Southampton's circle remains a matter of speculation.

authors.name: John Ford
authors.identity: Caroline tragedian; the most intense and morbidly introspective of the later Jacobean-Caroline dramatists, author of 'Tis Pity She's a Whore, The Broken Heart, and Love's Sacrifice, whose plays explore transgressive passion, melancholy, and divided conscience.
authors.biography: Born c. 1586 at Ilsington, Devon (baptised 17 April), educated at Exeter College, Oxford and the Middle Temple (called to the bar 1620). He collaborated with Dekker, Rowley, and Webster on comedies and tragicomedies in the 1620s before writing his surviving solo tragedies in the early 1630s: Love's Sacrifice (1633), 'Tis Pity She's a Whore (1633), The Broken Heart (1633), and Perkin Warbeck (1634), with later comedies The Fancies Chaste and Noble (1638) and The Lady's Trial (1639). Little of his later life is recorded; he died c. 1639–40.
authors.profile: The tragedian of forbidden and self-destructive passion, whose plays probe incest, jealousy, and Stoic endurance with a melancholic, casuistical intensity and a detached moral ambiguity.
authors.style: Grave, formal blank verse; rhetorical lamentation and masque-like set pieces; a preoccupation with melancholy and Stoic self-mastery; and a disturbing moral neutrality toward transgression.
authors.concerns: Incestuous and forbidden desire; honour, jealousy, and reputation; melancholy and the divided self; Stoic endurance of suffering; and the ethics of passion versus social law.
authors.significance: Ford is the last great tragedian before the closing of the theatres; 'Tis Pity She's a Whore and The Broken Heart are central to the Caroline tragic canon and to modern interest in the psychology and transgression of Renaissance drama.
authors.uncertainty: Very little of Ford's biography is known; his birth and death dates are approximate, many of his works are lost, and his collaborations complicate attribution.

authors.name: John Foxe
authors.identity: martyrologist; church historian
authors.biography: Born at Boston, Lincolnshire, in 1516 or 1517. Educated at Brasenose and Magdalen College, Oxford, he resigned his fellowship over religious scruples, tutored in the households of the Protestant gentry, and fled to the Continent under Mary I, working at Basel as a proofreader for the printer Oporinus. He returned under Elizabeth and spent his later years as a preacher and writer in London, where he died on 8 April 1587.
authors.profile: Actes and Monuments of These Latter and Perilous Days — the 'Book of Martyrs' — first published in English in 1563 and greatly expanded in 1570, a vast church history built around the sufferings of Protestant martyrs from Wyclif to his own day.
authors.style: Massive documentary accumulation, vivid narrative set-pieces, and the rhetorical urgency of a man writing the history of his own cause.
authors.concerns: Providence in history; the true church against Antichrist; the testimony of the martyrs.
authors.significance: His book, ordered to be placed in every cathedral church, shaped English national and religious identity for three centuries and is a primary source for the Marian persecutions.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date uncertain (1516 or 1517).

authors.name: John Gay
authors.identity: English poet and dramatist, friend of Pope and Swift, best known for the ballad opera The Beggar's Opera and his Fables.
authors.biography: Born in Devon and apprenticed to a silkseller in London, Gay attached himself to the Augustan literary circle, befriending Pope, Swift, and John Arbuthnot, and joining the Scriblerus Club. Early poems such as Rural Sports, also called Trivia (1716), won notice. He wrote for the theatre in various modes, including pastoral and burlesque tragedy. His The Beggar's Opera (1728), a ballad opera satirising politics and the stage, was a great success and provoked political controversy that helped block his sequel Polly. His Fables, first and second collections appearing in 1727 and posthumously in 1738, remain famous. He died in London in 1732.
authors.profile: A versatile versifier and dramatist working in georgic, pastoral, fable, and burlesque, whose enduring achievements are the satiric ballad opera and the morally pointed fable.
authors.style: Lucid, unambitious Augustan diction; ease in popular and borrowed airs; epigrammatic moralising in the fables; and a genial, often sly satire rather than Swiftian ferocity.
authors.concerns: The corruption beneath social polish; the economics of crime and respectability; the rivalry between Italian opera and native drama; and the conduct of ordinary life as illustrated by beast-fable.
