authors.significance: The Pleasures of Imagination is a key early work of eighteenth-century aesthetic theory in verse, transmitting Shaftesbury, Addison, and associationism to a poetic audience and influencing later aesthetic thought.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is usually given as 1721 but sometimes 1722; the details of his medical practice and his London hospital connections are only partly documented.

authors.name: Mary Astell
authors.identity: Philosopher, polemicist, and early feminist; her A Serious Proposal to the Ladies (1694, 1697) argued for a women's educational institution and her Some Reflections upon Marriage (1700) exposed the double standard, making her a founder of English feminist argument.
authors.biography: Born 12 November 1666 at Newcastle upon Tyne, daughter of a coal merchant; deprived of formal education and a dowry by her father's early death, she moved to London (c. 1688) and, supported by a circle of aristocratic women patrons, became a prolific writer. A High Church Tory and intellectual correspondent of John Norris and George Hickes, she published A Serious Proposal to the Ladies (Part I 1694, Part II 1697), advocating a Protestant 'monastery' or academy for women's education, and Some Reflections upon Marriage (1700). She also wrote philosophical and theological works (The Christian Religion, 1705) and controversial pamphlets, and ran a charity school for girls in Chelsea in retirement. She died on 9 May 1731.
authors.profile: The rigorous female philosopher and polemicist who used Cartesian method and High Church theology to argue that women are rational souls entitled to education and to critique the inequalities of marriage and custom.
authors.style: Argumentative, ironic, and polemical prose; rhetorical questions and wit; philosophical reasoning applied to women's condition; and an earnest, hortatory tone.
authors.concerns: Women's education and rational capacity; marriage and the double standard; female friendship and community; religion and reason; and political and theological controversy.
authors.significance: Astell is a pioneering English feminist philosopher whose proposals for women's education and her critique of marriage anticipate later feminist thought; her recovery has made her central to the history of women's writing and of the Enlightenment debate on women.
authors.uncertainty: Astell's life is documented through her works, correspondence, and patrons; details of her early life and her Chelsea charity school rest on records and tradition.

works.title: A Serious Proposal to the Ladies, for the Advancement of Their True and Greatest Interest
Some Reflections upon Marriage, Occasion'd by the Duke and Duchess of Mazarine's Case
The Christian Religion, as Professed by a Daughter of the Church of God

authors.name: Mary Chudleigh
authors.identity: Poet and essayist, a learned gentlewoman known for her defense of women's education and capacity.
authors.biography: Born Mary Lee in August 1656 at Wonford near Exeter in Devon, the daughter of a Devon gentleman, she was largely self-educated through wide reading and correspondence. She married Sir John Chudleigh, a baronet. Her prose defense of women, An Essay to Defend the Womens Cause, circulated in manuscript and was printed in 1701, and her Poems on Several Occasions appeared in 1703, including verse on the soul, learning, and friendship. She moved in dissenting and learned circles. She was buried on 15 December 1710.
authors.profile: A poet and essayist of the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries whose work argues for women's rational and spiritual equality and explores themes of learning, friendship, virtue, and the soul.
authors.style: Measured heroic-couplet verse and plain, argumentative prose; an educated, conversational, often Platonic-tinged tone; and a didactic, moralizing seriousness of diction.
authors.concerns: The education and capacity of women; reason, virtue, and the immortality of the soul; friendship and learning; and the critique of Custom and prejudice.
authors.significance: An important figure in early feminist writing and in women's learned culture, whose essay and poems are central texts in the history of the seventeenth- and eighteenth-century debate about women.
authors.uncertainty: Her life is documented only in outline, and the dating of the composition and circulation of some works, including the essay first printed without her sanction in 1701, remains approximate.

works.title: An Essay to Defend the Women's Cause

authors.name: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
authors.identity: Translator, poet, and literary patron; the sister of Sir Philip Sidney and the most important female literary figure of the Elizabethan period after the queen.
authors.biography: Born 27 October 1561, daughter of Sir Henry Sidney; educated at home in French, Italian, and music. In 1577 she married Henry Herbert, second Earl of Pembroke, and made Wilton House a centre of letters; after her brother's death in 1586 she became his literary executrix, completing his verse translation of the Psalms (the Sidney Psalter) and supervising the publication of the Arcadia (1593). She translated Robert Garnier's Marc Antoine (1592) and Philippe de Mornay's Discours de la vie et de la mort (1592), wrote the pastoral dialogue for the queen's visit to Wilton (c. 1599), and patronized Spenser, Daniel, and Donne. She died of smallpox on 25 September 1621.
authors.profile: The presiding female patron of the Sidney circle, whose own translations — above all the 107 psalms of the Sidney Psalter — constitute one of the major poetic achievements of the period, uniting Reformed piety with the most sophisticated metrical experimentation in English.
authors.style: Metrical virtuosity (the Psalter uses over 120 different verse forms), learned paraphrase, and a devotional voice of disciplined intensity.
authors.concerns: The Protestant poetics of the psalm tradition; the consolation of mortality; the continuation of her brother's literary and religious legacy; female authorship within the bounds of aristocratic propriety.
authors.significance: The first English woman to sustain a major literary career as patron, editor, translator, and poet; the Sidney Psalter influenced Donne and Herbert and stands as the great English monument of the Genevan psalm tradition.
authors.uncertainty: The extent of her contribution to the Psalter (as against her brother's) is secure for Psalms 44–150; the degree of her editorial intervention in the 1593 Arcadia is debated.
influencedBy: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke

authors.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
authors.identity: Writer and philosopher and the most influential advocate of women's rational education of her generation.
authors.biography: Born on 27 April 1759 at Spitalfields in London into a family of limited means, she escaped an unhappy home, worked as a teacher and companion, and turned to letters in London, becoming associated with the publisher Joseph Johnson and radical intellectual circles. She published Thoughts on the Education of Daughters (1787) and the novel Mary (1788), alongside other works in the 1780s and early 1790s. Her famous Vindication of the Rights of Men appeared in 1790 and A Vindication of the Rights of Woman in 1792. After years abroad and a relationship with Gilbert Imlay and later marriage to William Godwin, she died on 10 September 1797 shortly after the birth of her daughter, the future Mary Shelley.
authors.profile: A polemicist, novelist, and essayist whose arguments for women's reason and education and whose accounts of feeling and society mark her as a founder of modern feminist thought and a distinctive Romantic-era writer.
authors.style: Passionate, argumentative prose combining Enlightenment rationalism with the language of sentiment; direct, urgent polemic; and a morally intense, self-conscious narrative voice in her fiction.
authors.concerns: The rational education and moral standing of women; virtue, independence, and citizenship; the critique of Custom and prejudice; feeling and reason; and the rights and duties of the individual in society.
authors.significance: One of the most important and enduring writers in the history of feminist argument, whose works in the 1790s shaped debates about rights, gender, and education and whose reputation has grown steadily since her own time.
authors.uncertainty: Her life is well documented, largely through Godwin's Memoirs, whose candid detail was itself contested; the precise dating and reception of some minor writings remain matters of editorial reconstruction.

works.title: On the Importance of Religious Opinions
Thoughts on the Education of Daughters

authors.name: Matthew Paris
authors.identity: chronicler; cartographer; artist; Benedictine monk
authors.biography: A monk of St Albans from 1217, he succeeded Roger Wendover as the abbey's chronicler in 1236 and made St Albans the foremost centre of English historical writing; friend and correspondent of Henry III, he travelled to Norway (1248) and died in 1259. He wrote, copied, and illuminated his own manuscripts with maps and drawings of exceptional skill.
authors.profile: Author of the Chronica Majora (begun c. 1240, continued to 1259), the greatest English chronicle of the thirteenth century; also the Historia Anglorum (abbreviation), the lives of the two Offas and of St Alban, and the Gesta Abbatum.
authors.style: Vivid, opinionated, encyclopedic narrative; fierce criticism of the king, the papacy, and the friars; the integration of maps, itineraries, and marginal drawings into the historical record.
authors.concerns: The liberties of the English church and kingdom against papal and royal encroachment; the moral judgement of rulers; the recording of contemporary events from documents and eyewitnesses.
authors.significance: The Chronica Majora is the indispensable narrative source for the reign of Henry III and a landmark of medieval book art as well as of historiography.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and parentage unknown; his surname may reflect continental training.
themes: Restoration politics: party, succession, and Exclusion
sources: The Cambridge Companion to the Eighteenth-Century Novel

authors.name: Matthew Prior
authors.identity: Poet and diplomat; a master of light verse, the burlesque, and the occasional poem, whose career under the patronage of Dorset and his diplomatic service produced the witty, polished poetry of the transition from Dryden to Pope.
authors.biography: Born 21 July 1664 in London, educated at Westminster School (where, per legend, the Earl of Dorset discovered him reciting Horace) and St John's College, Cambridge. Patronised by Dorset, he entered diplomacy and government service under the Earls of Portland and the Tories, serving at the negotiations of the treaties of Ryswick (1697) and Utrecht (1713) and as a Commissioner of Customs. He wrote the burlesque 'The City Mouse and Country Mouse' (with Montagu, 1687), Solomon on the Vanity of the World (1718), Alma, and many songs, tales, and epistles. He died on 18 September 1721.
authors.profile: The poet of urbane lightness, whose easy, witty verse and translations made him one of the most popular poets between Dryden and Pope and a model for the familiar style.
authors.style: Graceful octosyllabics and couplets; wit, irony, and colloquial ease; burlesque and mock-heroic; fable and tale; and a polished, Horatian lightness.
authors.concerns: Love and gallantry; the vanity of worldly ambition; politics and diplomacy; friendship and patronage; and moral philosophy in a light, Horatian key.
authors.significance: Prior's Poems on Several Occasions (1709) and later works were immensely popular; his light verse and translations helped form the Augustan taste and influenced Pope, who both admired and satirised him.
authors.uncertainty: Prior's life is well documented, though the anecdotes of his discovery by Dorset are partly legendary; his diplomatic career is recorded in state papers.

works.title: Solomon on the Vanity of the World
The City Mouse and Country Mouse

authors.name: Matthew Tindal
authors.identity: Civil lawyer and deist, author of Rights of the Christian Church (1706) and of Christianity as Old as the Creation (1730), the creed-book of eighteenth-century deism.
authors.biography: Born at Bere Ferrers in Devon, probably in 1657, the son of a clergyman, he went up to Oxford, where he sat at Lincoln and Exeter and became a fellow of All Souls. He conformed to Rome during the reign of James II and returned to the Church of England after the Revolution, an episode that sharpened his lifelong interest in church authority. The Rights of the Christian Church (1706) argued for a national establishment controlled by the state and answered his High Church critics; Vindiciae Judaeorum (1707) defended the Jewish nation against slanders. Christianity as Old as the Creation (1730), published anonymously as the work of a person of the Church of England, reduced the gospel to a republication of the religion of nature and provoked dozens of answers within a year. He died on 16 August 1733.
authors.profile: The systematiser of deism, who read Christianity as a moral institution whose truth must be measurable by a reason common to all nations.
authors.style: Arid, lawyerly, definitional prose; axioms and corollaries and exhaustive division of terms; a polemical coolness that invites reply rather than assent.
authors.concerns: The reasonableness and universality of natural religion; the civil rights of churches and the reach of state supremacy; priestcraft, mystery and the commerce of God with man; the interests of Israel and of toleration.
authors.significance: Christianity as Old as the Creation gave deism its mature form and forced the apologetic literature of the 1730s into a defensive debate about reason, revelation and the political power of clergy.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is only approximately fixed, and his principal works were issued anonymously, complicating attribution.

works.title: A Discourse of the Grounds and Reasons of the Christian Religion
Christianity as Old as the Creation
The Rights of the Christian Church Asserted

authors.name: Michael Drayton
authors.identity: Poet; the author of Idea, Poly-Olbion, and 'Since there's no help', the most prolific and professionally dedicated of the Elizabethan poets.
authors.biography: Born 1563 at Hartshill, Warwickshire, where he served as a page in the household of Sir Henry Goodere; possibly at Oxford for a time. He settled in London in the 1590s as a professional writer, publishing the sonnet sequence Idea (1594, revised to 1619), the historical legends (Mortimeriados 1596, revised as The Barons' Wars 1603; England's Heroical Epistles 1597), the pastoral Endimion and Phoebe (1595), and the vast topographical poem Poly-Olbion (1612, 1622), before the late odes and elegies of his Poems (1619) and The Muses Elizium (1630). He died in London on 23 December 1631 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The period's most devoted professional poet, who ranged across every genre — sonnets, epistles, odes, pastorals, topography, satire, and the 'nymphidia' fairy verse — and revised his canon continuously across five decades.
authors.style: Varied and capable rather than intense; the elegant sonnet, the sinewy epistle, the ambitious chorographical couplet of Poly-Olbion, and a late lyric grace ('Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part').
authors.concerns: English topography and the nation's antiquities; the historical memory of the Wars of the Roses; the poet's fame and the patronage system; love's vicissitudes.
authors.significance: The most complete professional man of letters of the age; Poly-Olbion is the great topographical poem of England, and his sonnets and odes remained in the anthologies that formed later English taste.
authors.uncertainty: Details of his early life and of his alleged service to the Goodere family rest on late testimony; much of his early work survives only in his own revisions.

authors.name: Miles Coverdale
authors.identity: Bible translator; bishop of Exeter
authors.biography: Born about 1488 in the North Riding of Yorkshire; educated at Cambridge and an Augustinian friar before converting to the Reformation. Working in Antwerp, he produced the first complete printed English Bible in 1535, and he edited the Great Bible of 1539, which was ordered to be read in every parish church. Bishop of Exeter in 1551, he went into exile under Mary and returned under Elizabeth, dying on 20 January 1569.
authors.profile: The translator of the first complete printed English Bible. The Coverdale Bible (1535), translating chiefly from German and Latin versions, gave the English church its Psalter — still sung as Coverdale's version in the Book of Common Prayer — and the Great Bible (1539) put an English Bible in every parish church, its wording (largely Tyndale's) forming the base of the Authorized Version.
authors.style: A flowing, musical prose less angular than Tyndale's; mastery of the cadence of the Psalms; the dignity of liturgical English.
authors.concerns: The complete vernacular Bible; the Psalter in English worship; the reform of the church through the Word.
authors.significance: Completed the English Bible and fixed the English Psalter; the Coverdale Psalms remain in liturgical use into the twenty-first century.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate; the exact place of printing of the 1535 Bible (Antwerp or Cologne) is debated.
themes: Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind

authors.name: Nathaniel Lee
authors.identity: Restoration tragedian; the leading exponent of heroic drama after Dryden, whose bombastic but powerful The Rival Queens (1677) held the stage for two centuries, and who collaborated with Dryden on Oedipus and The Duke of Guise.
authors.biography: Born c. 1653 at Waltham Abbey, Essex, son of a clergyman; educated at Westminster and Trinity College, Cambridge. He turned from brief attempts at law and teaching to the stage, writing heroic plays and tragedies including The Tragedy of Nero (1674), Sophonisba (1675), Gloriana (1676), and his great success The Rival Queens; or, The Death of Alexander the Great (1677). He collaborated with Dryden on Oedipus (1679) and The Duke of Guise (1682). Suffering from mental illness and alcoholism, he was confined in Bedlam (1684–88); released after the Revolution, he wrote The Princess of Cleve (1689) and died in poverty on 6 May 1692.
authors.profile: The passionate, sometimes ranting tragedian of the Restoration, whose heroic and blank-verse tragedies of overwhelming emotion and elevated rhetoric were enormously popular and long-lived on the stage.
authors.style: Elevated, bombastic rhetoric; heroic couplets and blank verse; scenes of violent passion and grandiose declamation; and, at best, real pathos and poetic power.
authors.concerns: Heroic passion, love, and glory; political conspiracy and tyranny; madness and the extremes of emotion; and the fate of great figures.
authors.significance: The Rival Queens was one of the most frequently performed plays from the Restoration into the nineteenth century; Lee's heroic tragedy carried the mode to its popular peak and influenced the acting style of the age.
authors.uncertainty: Lee's birth year is approximate and his biography, including his madness and Bedlam confinement, is documented but partly anecdotal.

works.title: Lucius Junius Brutus, Father of His Country
The Rival Queens; or, The Death of Alexander the Great

authors.name: Nennius
authors.identity: historian; compiler
authors.biography: Welsh scholar of the early ninth century, traditionally identified as the compiler of the Historia Brittonum; otherwise unknown.
authors.profile: The Historia Brittonum (c. 829/30) assembles genealogies, origin legends (including the Trojan foundation story of the Britons), the lives of St Patrick and St Germanus, and the earliest datable Arthur material — the list of Arthur's twelve battles culminating at Mount Badon.
authors.style: Composite, compilatory Latin prose of varied quality, drawing on earlier written and oral sources.
authors.concerns: The antiquity and identity of the Britons; the deeds of their heroes against the Saxons.
authors.significance: The earliest extended Arthurian text in insular literature and a major witness to British historical tradition.
authors.uncertainty: The prologue's attribution to Nennius is not found in all manuscripts; the work is composite and its authorship disputed.
sources: Middle English Dictionary

authors.name: Nicholas Love
authors.identity: translator; devotional writer; Carthusian prior
authors.biography: Prior of the Carthusian house of Mount Grace in Yorkshire (1410–21), where he oversaw the translation of the Meditationes Vitae Christi into English as the Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ (c. 1410), the most widely circulated devotional work in fifteenth-century England and one explicitly approved by Archbishop Arundel against Lollard translation.
authors.profile: Translator and adapter of the pseudo-Bonaventuran Meditationes Vitae Christi as the Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ, with extensive original additions.
authors.style: Affective, meditative prose designed to make the life of Christ present to the reader; conservative theology and smooth, accessible English.
authors.concerns: The orthodox channeling of lay devotion to the humanity of Christ; the containment of vernacular heresy.
authors.significance: The Mirror was the great bestseller of fifteenth-century English devotional prose, surviving in more manuscripts than any other Middle English text of its kind and shaping lay piety to the Reformation.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and early career unknown; death date approximate.

works.title: The Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ

sources: The Cambridge Companion to Christopher Marlowe

authors.name: Nicholas Rowe
authors.identity: English dramatist, poet, and editor, appointed Poet Laureate in 1715, celebrated for sentimental tragedy and an early scholarly edition of Shakespeare.
authors.biography: Rowe was educated at the Middle Temple and turned early to the stage. His first play, The Ambitious Statesman (1697), was followed by Jane Shore (1700) and The Fair Penitent (1703), the latter containing the villain Lothaire and often considered his finest. He wrote several further tragedies, including a Lucius Junius Brutus and a Lady Jane Grey. In 1709 he published an edition of Shakespeare, an early largely scholarly attempt to edit the plays and to give accounts of the actors, drawing on earlier sources and issued through the publisher Jacob Tonson. A Whig, he succeeded Thomas Tate as Poet Laureate in 1715 and died unexpectedly in London at the end of 1718.
authors.profile: A playwright of domestic and sentimental tragedy and a literary editor; his dramas turn on female virtue, seduction, and penitence, and his Shakespeare edition began the formal text-critical study of the plays.
authors.style: Smooth, decorous blank verse; moralising pathos; well-made tragic situations; and an editorial method marked by conjectural emendation and a taste for regularity and probability.
authors.concerns: Virtue under assault and the ethics of penitence; domestic and feminine suffering; national literary heritage and the canonisation of Shakespeare; and Whig political virtue.
authors.significance: His 1709 Shakespeare is a founding document of English literary scholarship and editing, and as laureate and dramatist he shaped early eighteenth-century taste in tragedy and commemorative verse.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace is not securely recorded; Rowe is associated with places in Buckinghamshire and the south, and the precise location of his birth remains uncertain.

authors.name: Nicholas Udall
authors.identity: playwright; schoolmaster; translator
authors.biography: Born at Southampton in 1504; educated at Winchester and Corpus Christi College, Oxford. Headmaster of Eton from 1534 (dismissed in 1541) and later of Westminster, he was a reformer who prospered under Edward VI and Mary alike. His Ralph Roister Doister, written about 1552, was printed about 1566. He died on 23 December 1556.
authors.profile: Author of the first English comedy. Ralph Roister Doister — five acts of Roman comedy built on Plautus's Miles Gloriosus, with the braggart soldier, the parasitic Merrygreek, and the London widow Dame Christian Custance — transplanted classical comic structure into English life and English verse, establishing the pattern the Elizabethan comedians followed.
authors.style: Doggerel couplets of deliberate comic roughness; the miles gloriosus and the cunning servant in English dress; songs and jigs built into the action.
authors.concerns: The imitation of Roman comedy; school drama as moral and rhetorical training; the comic punishment of vanity and presumption.
authors.significance: Wrote the first English comedy on the classical model, the direct ancestor of the Elizabethan stage comedy; his school drama linked the interlude tradition to the professional theatre.
authors.uncertainty: The precise date and first printing of Roister Doister are uncertain (c. 1552–53, printed c. 1566).
themes: Rural labour, depopulation, and the deserted village

authors.name: Olaudah Equiano
authors.birthplace: Essaka, in the interior of what is now Nigeria (contested; a birth in South Carolina has also been argued)
authors.nationality: British abolitionist writing of the African diaspora
authors.identity: Formerly enslaved mariner and author of The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African (1789), the founding text of the English-speaking slave narrative and of abolitionist argument.
authors.biography: Born about 1745, he recorded his childhood in the village of Essaka, in the interior of what is now southern Nigeria; the archival work of Vincent Carretta has raised the alternative that he was born in South Carolina, and the question is still debated. Brought into the trade as a child and carried to the West Indies, he was purchased by a naval officer, taken to England, christened and given the name by which he published, and afterwards served at sea in North America and the West Indies. In 1766 he bought his own freedom, worked as a mariner and merchant, went north with an Arctic voyage in 1773, settling in London, where he joined Methodist and abolitionist circles and made a living by his pen and his lectures. His Interesting Narrative appeared in 1789 by subscription, ran into several editions in his lifetime and was translated into several languages, and it became the standard account of the horrors of the middle passage. In 1791, after the period covered here, he was appointed to office in the Sierra Leone enterprise; he married an Englishwoman in 1792 and had children. He died in London in March 1797.
authors.profile: An autobiographer who combined the captive's narrative, the Methodist conversion account and the commercial self-assessment to make a claim on the reader's reason and pity.
authors.style: Clear, orderly, controlled first-person narrative; catalogues of ship, cargo, price and place used as evidence; horror reported without rant; a scriptural and civic vocabulary of liberty, brotherhood and redress.
authors.concerns: The evil and the economics of the slave trade; the capacity and the humanity of Africans; the religion of the converted captive; the rights of British subjects regardless of colour; the moral danger of colonial luxury to the metropole.
authors.significance: His Narrative was a decisive instrument of the abolitionist campaign and the earliest and most influential of the Atlantic slave narratives, still read as a foundation text of African-diaspora writing.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace, date of birth and the details of his early captivity remain contested, since the archival record does not confirm the account he printed of himself.

works.title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African. Written by Himself

authors.name: Oliver Goldsmith
authors.identity: Irish-born poet, essayist, novelist, and dramatist, a central figure of the London literary world, author of The Deserted Village, The Vicar of Wakefield, and She Stoops to Conquer.
authors.biography: Goldsmith was born in rural Ireland, the son of a clergyman, and studied medicine, spending time at Edinburgh and at a continental university before taking his degree; much of his student career is legendary. He went to London to live by his pen, working as an apothecary's assistant, a hack-writer, and a tutor, and became part of the group that founded The Club with Samuel Johnson and others. He wrote and edited widely, including the cosmopolitan essays The Citizen of the World (1760-1761). His poem The Traveller (1764), his novel The Vicar of Wakefield (1766), and the longer The Deserted Village (1770) established his fame, and his comedy She Stoops to Conquer (1773) revived laughter on the stage. He also wrote histories and natural histories. He died in London in 1774.
authors.profile: A writer of pastoral poetry, sentimental fiction, and laughing comedy who idealises rural abundance, childhood, and Christian innocence, and who attacks luxury, depopulation, and fashionable sentimental comedy on the stage.
authors.style: Clear, mellifluous heroic couplets in the pastoral poems; a warm, simple, often self-mocking prose; and easy, generous, laughing dramatic dialogue.
authors.concerns: Rural depopulation, luxury, and empire; the virtues of childhood and Christian simplicity; the rivalry between laughing and sentimental comedy; and the cosmopolitan comparison of nations and manners.
authors.significance: One of the most widely read writers of the later eighteenth century, in poetry, novel, and comedy alike; The Deserted Village became a touchstone of anti-commercial nostalgia, and his comedy redirected the English stage.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is disputed, given as 1728 or 1730, and his exact Irish birthplace and his scattered university career are partly mythologised by later accounts, especially by his friend and biographer Johnson.

works.title: An Enquiry into the Present State of Polite Learning in Europe
She Stoops to Conquer; or, The Mistakes of a Night
The Traveller; or, A Prospect of Society

authors.name: Orm
authors.identity: homilist; poet; Augustinian canon
authors.biography: An Augustinian canon, probably of Elsham Priory in north Lincolnshire, who composed the Ormulum, a vast collection of verse homilies on the gospels, c. 1180; his brother Walter is named in the dedication. Nothing else is recorded of his life.
authors.profile: Author of the Ormulum (c. 1180), some 20,000 short lines of gospel paraphrase and exegesis in the East Midland dialect; only about an eighth survives (Bodleian Library, MS Junius 1).
authors.style: A strictly regular unrhymed septenarius metre; a unique, systematic orthography (double consonants marking vowel length) of great value to historical linguists; plain homiletic exposition.
authors.concerns: The teaching of the gospels to the English laity in the vernacular; the reform of preaching after the Lateran emphasis on pastoral care.
authors.significance: The Ormulum is the most ambitious early Middle English religious work and a landmark in the history of English orthography and phonology.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from the dedication; dates approximate (c. 1150–1200).
themes: The Virgin Mary and Marian devotion
sources: The Book of Common Prayer: The Texts of 1549, 1559, and 1662

authors.name: Osbern Bokenham
authors.identity: poet; hagiographer; Augustinian friar
authors.biography: An Augustinian friar of Stoke by Clare, Suffolk, and doctor of divinity (Cambridge), who composed his Legends of Holy Women between 1443 and 1447 at the request of East Anglian patrons, several of them women. He died c. 1464.
authors.profile: Author of the Legends of Holy Women (1443–47), a collection of thirteen verse saints' lives — including those of Margaret, Anne, Katherine, Cecilia, and Mary Magdalene — with a substantial autobiographical prologue; also a prose treatise on the Mappula Angliae (a translation of Higden).
authors.style: Lydgatean verse with aureate diction; the female saint's life treated with tenderness and dramatic force; an unusually self-revealing authorial voice.
authors.concerns: The cult of female sanctity and its patronage by devout women; the legitimacy of vernacular hagiography.
authors.significance: The Legends are the principal fifteenth-century English monument of the female saints' lives and a major document of literary patronage by women.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; his career before the 1440s is unknown.
sources: Jonathan Swift: Critical, Scholastic, and Variorum Edition

authors.name: Ottobah Cugoano
authors.birthplace: the Gold Coast (the Fante coastal region of present-day Ghana; the town is given variously)
authors.nationality: British abolitionist writing of the African diaspora
authors.identity: Formerly enslaved writer and campaigner in London, author of Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species (1787), the century's most radical English abolitionist argument.
authors.biography: Born on the Gold Coast in the 1750s, he was kidnapped as a child, sold among the coastal forts and carried to Grenada, from which he was brought to England in the early 1770s. Named John Stuart in service, he remained in England a free man and joined the small circle of free Black Londoners clustered about Granville Sharp, for whom he acted as an intermediary and whose legal cases he helped to press. His Thoughts and Sentiments, published in 1787 and reprinted in the following years, argued from natural rights, scripture and the law of nations that the trade and slaveholding were crimes requiring restitution, and it demanded an end to the commerce rather than amelioration of it. He addressed the British public, the legislature and the slaveholders directly, and urged the commercial and religious advantages of an intercourse with Africa. He witnessed and advised in the campaigns of the later 1780s, and a shortened version of his book appeared in 1791. Nothing certain is known of him afterwards; he is usually supposed to have died about 1791.
authors.profile: A philosopher of natural rights from inside the experience of enslavement, who reasoned from first principles to restitution and to the equality of all mankind.
authors.style: Earnest, tightly argued prose of principle; scriptural and legal citation pressed into a single moral case; direct address to monarchs, merchants and slaves; a dignity that refuses apology.
authors.concerns: Natural liberty and the sin of man-stealing; the rights of Africans and the duties of Britain; restitution and compensation; the abolition of the trade rather than the reform of slavery; the religious and commercial future of Africa.
authors.significance: He supplied the abolitionist movement with its most uncompromising theoretical case and the first English book by a formerly enslaved writer to argue for total abolition, and his work stands beside Equiano's as a founding document of African-diaspora writing.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is approximate, the town of his birth is variously reported, and the date of his death is unknown; no record of him is certainly identified after 1791.

works.title: Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species, Humbly Submitted to the Justice of Great Britain by the Africans

authors.name: Philip Doddridge
authors.identity: Congregational minister and the principal teacher of his generation of Dissenting pastors, whose Family Expositor and Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul joined practical divinity to a wide philosophical charity.
authors.biography: Born in London in 1702, the youngest of twenty children, of whom only he and one sister reached adulthood, he was briefly apprenticed, then educated largely by his own reading with the help of neighbouring ministers, and began to preach as a teenager. He held a country charge at Kibworth Harborough and settled at Northampton, where he led a large congregation and kept the academy that educated many Dissenting ministers of the following generation. His writings were at once devotional, instructional and practical: the Family Expositor, a commentary for household reading issued in parts from 1739, the Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul (1745), sermons, letters and a psalmody, with posthumous collections of his lectures and hymns. His courtesy, his stress on the inward work of grace and his readiness to commend experimental religion across party lines made him the best-loved of the Dissenting divines; his works were read by Edwards and by the American revivalists, and his academy trained preachers for England and the colonies. A failing chest sent him south for the winter of 1750, and he died at Lisbon in October 1751.
authors.profile: A pastoral writer of method and tenderness who brought the academy, the family desk and the congregation into one plan of religious education.
authors.style: Warm, lucid, closely organised prose; commentary arranged for reading aloud in the family; case-divinity addressed to the conscience; a temperate ecumenical charity of phrase.
authors.concerns: The conduct and progress of religion in the soul; scripture read with the help of the learned and the critical; Dissenting education and the qualifications of the ministry; the duties of family worship; the friendship of Christians across parties.
authors.significance: He gave English Nonconformity its most influential programme of piety and ministerial training, and his books on the inner history of conversion shaped evangelical spirituality in Britain and America.
authors.uncertainty: Several of his works were assembled and edited after his death from sermons and lectures, so their dates and completeness are uncertain.

works.title: The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul

authors.name: Philip Massinger
authors.identity: dramatist
authors.biography: Baptized 24 November 1583 at Salisbury; son of a gentleman servant to the Herbert family. He studied at St Alban Hall, Oxford (1602–06), then went to London and collaborated with Fletcher, Dekker, and Field. After Fletcher's death in 1625 he became chief dramatist of the King's Men. He died suddenly on 17 March 1640 at his house on the Bankside and was buried in Fletcher's grave in Southwark Cathedral.
authors.profile: Some thirty plays survive, including The Roman Actor (1626), The City Madam (c. 1632), A New Way to Pay Old Debts (c. 1625), and The Bondman (1623); he completed Fletcher's unfinished work and wrote many plays in partnership.
authors.style: Careful construction, political earnestness, and a moral seriousness that made his comedies satires on greed and his tragedies studies of tyranny.
authors.concerns: The abuse of power; the corruption of wealth; justice and mercy in the state.
authors.significance: The last major dramatist of the pre-Civil War stage; his Sir Giles Overreach in A New Way to Pay Old Debts became one of the great actor's roles of the English repertoire.
authors.uncertainty: A period of obscurity and possible religious conversion (he was reputed a Catholic) in the 1610s is poorly documented.

works.title: A New Way to Pay Old Debts

authors.name: Queen Elizabeth I
authors.identity: monarch; poet; translator; orator
authors.biography: Born 7 September 1533 at Greenwich, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. Educated by Roger Ascham and others in the new humanist curriculum, she became queen in 1558 and reigned until her death on 24 March 1603 at Richmond Palace. Her learning, her speeches, and her poems made her one of the most literate monarchs in English history.
authors.profile: Poems including 'The Doubt of Future Foes' (c. 1571), 'On Monsieur's Departure' (c. 1582), and 'When I Was Fair and Young'; translations from Boethius, Horace, and Plutarch made in her youth; prayers and meditations; and the great public orations — the speech at Tilbury (1588) and the 'Golden Speech' to Parliament (1601).
authors.style: A pointed, antithetical, proverbial style in verse and a commanding rhetorical art in her speeches, learned and plain by turns.
authors.concerns: Kingship and its burdens; marriage, succession, and the body politic; divine protection and personal constancy.
authors.significance: Her speeches and poems made the queen herself a literary presence; the cult of Elizabeth pervades Spenser, Shakespeare, and the entire literature of her reign.
authors.uncertainty: A few poems are assigned to her by tradition rather than manuscript authority.

authors.name: Ralph Cudworth
authors.identity: Cambridge Platonist philosopher and theologian; his vast True Intellectual System of the Universe (1678) argued against atheism and materialism for a rational, divinely ordered cosmos and an innate moral sense, a major work of seventeenth-century philosophy.
authors.biography: Born 1617 at Aller, Somerset, educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, where he became Master (1654) and a leading figure of the Platonic circle. He served as Regius Professor of Hebrew, held livings, and was a correspondent of Temple's and an influential university figure (he tutored William Temple). His magnum opus, The True Intellectual System of the Universe (1678), the first part of a projected larger work, refuted 'atheism' through erudite argument and posited 'plastic natures' and innate moral ideas. Posthumous treatises on morality (A Treatise Concerning Eternal and Immutable Morality, 1731) were published later. He died on 26 February 1688.
authors.profile: The learned metaphysician whose encyclopaedic, erudite arguments for a rational, moral, divinely ordered universe represent the philosophical summit of Cambridge Platonism.
authors.style: Dense, erudite, argumentative prose; massive learning and citation; philosophical and theological reasoning; and a systematic, cumulative method.
authors.concerns: The existence of God and the refutation of atheism; the true intellectual system of the universe; innate moral ideas and eternal morality; free will; and 'plastic natures' as a middle principle.
authors.significance: Cudworth's True Intellectual System was a major philosophical work that influenced later thinkers (including Shaftesbury and the moral-sense school) and stands as the most systematic statement of Cambridge Platonist metaphysics and ethics.
authors.uncertainty: Cudworth's birth year is approximate and his life documented mainly through university and church records; much of his planned oeuvre was left unfinished or published posthumously.

works.title: The True Intellectual System of the Universe

authors.name: Ranulf Higden
authors.identity: chronicler; encyclopedist; Benedictine monk
authors.biography: A Benedictine monk of St Werburgh's abbey, Chester, where he spent his whole career, dying on 12 March 1364; his Polychronicon, a universal history and geography compiled from earlier writers, became the standard history of England, translated into English by John Trevisa in 1387 and printed by Caxton in 1482.
authors.profile: Author of the Polychronicon (completed c. 1327, continued to 1352), with its celebrated first book describing the geography of the world and of Britain, and of the Ars Componendi Sermones and other didactic works.
authors.style: The industrious compiler's art: orderly encyclopedic arrangement, clear Latin, and a moralizing attention to the marvellous; the Polychronicon's world-description was a favourite of later chroniclers and cartographers.
authors.concerns: The unity of sacred and secular history; the description of the world and of Britain; the moral instruction of the clergy.
authors.significance: The Polychronicon dominated English historical writing for two centuries and, in Trevisa's translation, became one of the great monuments of fourteenth-century English prose.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his continuations of the Polychronicon are hard to separate from those of his successors.
themes: Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
sources: The Novel: An Anthology of Criticism and Practice, 1700-1800

authors.name: Reginald Pecock
authors.identity: theologian; apologist; bishop
authors.biography: Fellow of Oriel College, Oxford, and successively bishop of St Asaph (1444) and Chichester (1450). The outstanding orthodox theologian of fifteenth-century England, he wrote in English to answer Lollardy by reason rather than force; his rejection of the church's reliance on authority and his defence of preaching earned him trial for heresy in 1457, public abjuration, and imprisonment at Thorney Abbey, where he died c. 1461.
authors.profile: Author of the Repressor of Over Much Blaming of the Clergy (c. 1449–55), The Book of Faith (1456), the Donet, the Folewer to the Donet, and other works of vernacular theology, most of them condemned and burned with him.
authors.style: A remarkable plain English of argument, invented vocabulary (e.g., 'unbileve' for infidelity), and dialectical method applied to vernacular controversy.
authors.concerns: The rational defence of orthodoxy; the 'doom of reason' against mere authority; the instruction of the laity.
authors.significance: The most original English theologian between Wyclif and the Reformation and a pioneer of philosophical prose in English; his condemnation dramatizes the fifteenth-century church's fear of vernacular theology.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; much of his corpus survives only in fragments or in his own summaries.

works.title: The Repressor of Over Much Blaming of the Clergy

sources: The Cambridge Companion to John Donne

authors.name: Richard Blackmore
authors.identity: English physician and ambitious religious epic poet, remembered chiefly as a target of Pope's satire in the Dunciad.
authors.biography: Blackmore was born in the west of England about 1654 and studied medicine at Exeter College, Oxford, taking his medical degree there and becoming a fellow of the College of Physicians. He practised as a physician in the west country and then in London, and was physician to William III. He published a long sacred epic, Creation (1712), a paraphrase of Job, and a sequel Paradise Regain'd (1718), together with poems on the mind and nature and medical and philosophical writings. His grand but heavily moralising verse drew ridicule from his rivals, and Pope mocked him in the Dunciad. He died in 1729.
authors.profile: A writer of didactic and religious epic who sought to render Miltonic verse into sober Protestant instruction; his ambition was greater than his reception.
authors.style: Weighty, moralising blank verse; elaborate scientific and theological paraphrase; a plain earnestness and diffuseness that contemporaries found tedious; and an addiction to poetic machinery of the mind.
authors.concerns: Providence, creation, and sacred history; the relation of medicine, body, and soul; natural philosophy and vitalism; and the defence of a pious, learned verse against the wit of the age.
authors.significance: A representative of the earnest sacred-epic and physico-theological tradition that his Augustan rivals displaced; his treatment in the Dunciad helped fix his posterity as a cautionary figure of misapplied ambition.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is given only as about 1654, and his exact birthplace in the west of England is not firmly established; the chronology of his medical career and publications is partly reconstructed.

authors.name: Richard Brinsley Sheridan
authors.identity: Playwright, poet, and Whig politician, the leading comic dramatist of the late eighteenth century and long owner and manager of Drury Lane.
authors.biography: Born on 30 October 1751 in Dublin, raised partly in England, and educated there, he entered the stage and politics through literary talent and marriage connections. His first play, The Rivals (1775), was an immediate success, followed by the comic opera The Duenna (1775) and his masterpiece The School for Scandal (1777). He became manager and part-owner of the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, and sat as a Whig Member of Parliament, a friend of Charles James Fox. Later comedies included The Critic (1797). Financial and political difficulties attended his last years. He died in London on 7 July 1816.
authors.profile: The foremost writer of Restoration-style comedy of manners in his age, whose witty, well-made comedies satirize hypocrisy, slander, and the manners of fashionable society.
authors.style: Brilliant, epigrammatic dialogue; the comedy-of-manners plot of masks and revelations; witty character types such as the malcontent and the rake; and a skilled balancing of sentiment and satire.
authors.concerns: Reputation, slander, and hypocrisy; wit and the manners of the fashionable world; sincerity versus affectation; and the politics of patronage and public life.
authors.significance: The most successful comic dramatist between Congreve and Wilde, whose School for Scandal and Rivals remain central to the repertory and to the study of eighteenth-century comedy.
authors.uncertainty: His life is well recorded, though the details of his education and early years and the precise chronology of some later political and financial events are sometimes variously given.

authors.name: Richard Brome
authors.identity: Caroline comic dramatist and former servant and protégé of Ben Jonson; author of robust, satirical city comedies such as The Antipodes, A Jovial Crew, and The Sparagus Garden, prized for their low-life energy and social observation.
authors.biography: Born c. 1590 (records are sparse); he served Ben Jonson as a menial and became his literary protégé ('my man', Jonson called him). From 1629 he wrote some fifteen comedies for the Salisbury Court, Queen Henrietta's, and other companies, including The Northern Lass (1629), Bartholomew Fair-ish city comedies, The Antipodes (1638), and A Jovial Crew (1641), the last major play before the theatres closed. He signed a notorious contract with the Salisbury Court theatre (1635–40). He survived into the Interregnum, dependent and impoverished, dying in 1652.
authors.profile: The most Jonsonian of the Caroline comic writers, whose satirical, energetic comedies of London low life, country gentry, and humours anticipate the social breadth of Restoration comedy.
authors.style: Vigorous prose and verse comedy; satire of humours and social types; realistic London and rustic settings; bawdy energy; and intricate farcical plotting.
authors.concerns: Social satire and the manners of town and country; wit, folly, and pretension; the world of beggars, players, and gallants; and the comic correction of humours.
authors.significance: Brome is the most important comic dramatist of the 1630s after Jonson's decline; his plays offer an unparalleled social portrait of Caroline London and directly influenced Restoration comedy, and A Jovial Crew was long popular in adaptation.
authors.uncertainty: Brome's life is very poorly documented; his birth date is conjectural, and the dating and company attribution of several plays are uncertain.

authors.name: Richard Crashaw
authors.identity: Metaphysical religious poet and Catholic convert; author of Steps to the Temple and Carmen Deo Nostro, whose ecstatic, sensuous, and baroque devotional verse — especially to St Teresa and the Virgin — is unique in English.
authors.biography: Born c. 1613 in London, son of a Puritan preacher; educated at Charterhouse and Pembroke Hall, Cambridge (Fellow of Peterhouse). A Laudian Anglican, he was ejected during the Civil Wars, converted to Roman Catholicism, and went into exile, first to Paris and then to Italy. He became a client of Cardinal Palotta and, in 1649, a canon of the Holy House of Loreto, where he died in July 1649. His Steps to the Temple (1646) was published in England; the Catholic Carmen Deo Nostro appeared in Paris in 1652.
authors.profile: The English poet most at home in the continental baroque, whose fervent Catholic imagination rendered the mystical ecstasy of the saints in lush, sensuous, and sometimes startlingly physical conceits.
authors.style: Baroque extravagance; sensuous and paradoxical imagery; the epigram and the witticism turned to devotion; musical repetition; and a Catholic and Counter-Reformation intensity alien to the Protestant mainstream.
authors.concerns: Mystical union and ecstasy; the Virgin Mary, Mary Magdalene, and St Teresa; martyrdom and the wounds of Christ; the conversion of the soul; the sensuous apprehension of the divine.
authors.significance: Crashaw is the principal English representative of continental baroque religious poetry; his 'Hymn to St Teresa' and his epigrams were admired by Cowley and, later, by the decadents and modern critics as the most sensuously daring of the metaphysicals.
authors.uncertainty: Crashaw's birth year (1612 or 1613) and the details of his conversion and exile are uncertain; his biography rests on scattered records and the testimony of Abraham Cowley.

authors.name: Richard de Bury
authors.identity: bibliophile; churchman; royal administrator
authors.biography: Born on 24 January 1287, he became tutor to the future Edward III, and thereafter the king's trusted servant: keeper of the privy seal, chancellor (1334–35), and bishop of Durham from 1333. An insatiable collector, he assembled one of the greatest libraries in England, and his household probably produced the Philobiblon, completed shortly before his death on 14 April 1345.
authors.profile: Author (or patron-author) of the Philobiblon (1344), the celebrated Latin treatise on the love of books, their care, and their lending — the first bibliophilic classic in English literature.
authors.style: Elegant, allusive Latin prose; the book personified as the companion of wisdom; practical rules for the custody of manuscripts enlivened by satire on careless clerks and students.
authors.concerns: The preservation and circulation of learning; the duties of clergy and princes to books; the reform of the universities.
authors.significance: The Philobiblon is the foundational text of English bibliophilia and a precious record of fourteenth-century book culture; de Bury's library fed Durham's later collections.
authors.uncertainty: The precise authorship of the Philobiblon (de Bury or his chaplain Robert Holcot) is debated.
themes: The New Science and experimental philosophy
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Alexander Pope

authors.name: Richard Hakluyt
authors.identity: geographer; editor; translator; clergyman
authors.biography: Born about 1552, probably in London; educated at Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, where his vocation was fixed when he saw a world map in his cousin's chamber. He lectured on geography at Oxford, served as chaplain to the English embassy in Paris (1583–88), and became rector of Wetheringsett, archdeacon of Westminster (1603), and a promoter of the Virginia enterprise. He died on 23 November 1616 and is buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: Divers Voyages Touching the Discovery of America (1582) and the great The Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffics and Discoveries of the English Nation (1589; vastly expanded 1598–1600), the documentary epic of English overseas enterprise.
authors.style: Editor rather than stylist: an unrivalled assembler of first-hand narratives, translated and arranged with patriotic purpose and scholarly care.
authors.concerns: The expansion of England; trade, colonization, and Protestant rivalry with Spain; the practical sciences of navigation and geography.
authors.significance: 'The prose epic of the modern English nation' (Froude); his collections became the sourcebook of English imperialism and shaped the language's sense of the world.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace approximate.

works.title: The Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffics and Discoveries of the English Nation

authors.name: Richard Holland
authors.identity: poet; churchman
authors.biography: A priest and secretary or chaplain to Archibald Douglas, Earl of Moray, for whom he composed the Buke of the Howlat (c. 1448); he later joined the exiled Douglases in England, was forfeited with them, and died c. 1483, perhaps in Orkney.
authors.profile: Author of the Buke of the Howlat (c. 1448), an alliterative beast-allegory in which the owl, ashamed of his ugliness, appeals through the birds to the pope and emperor, a satire on pride, flattery, and the Douglas family's enemies.
authors.style: The northern alliterative long line in intricate thirteen-line stanzas; the beast parliament as political allegory; a blend of heraldic pageantry and moral satire.
authors.concerns: Pride and humility; the flattery of courts; the honour of the Douglas family.
authors.significance: The Howlat is the last major alliterative poem of the Scottish tradition and a key document of Douglas politics and northern heraldry.
authors.uncertainty: Little is known of him; dates approximate and career reconstructed from Douglas records.
themes: The public theatre and the players' world
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

authors.name: Richard Hooker
authors.identity: theologian; apologist of the Church of England
authors.biography: Born at Heavitree near Exeter in early April 1554. Educated at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, he became a fellow, then Master of the Temple in 1585, where his famous controversy with the Puritan Walter Travers sharpened his defence of the established church. He became rector of Bishopsbourne in Kent, where he completed his great work; he died on 3 November 1600, cared for by his friend Lancelot Andrewes.
authors.profile: Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity — Books I–IV published 1593, Book V in 1597, and Books VI–VIII posthumously — the classic reasoned defence of the Elizabethan settlement against Puritan attack.
authors.style: Majestic, periodic prose of extraordinary clarity and dignity, argued with a sweet reasonableness that Izaak Walton celebrated and that set the standard for English theological prose.
authors.concerns: The relation of law, reason, and scripture; the nature of the church and of civil society; the grounds of political obligation.
authors.significance: The intellectual foundation of the Anglican via media; his theory of law and government influenced Locke and the mainstream of English constitutional thought.
authors.uncertainty: The authorship of the later books of the Polity is complicated by posthumous editing; parts of the last three books survive imperfectly.

works.title: Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity

authors.name: Richard Lovelace
authors.identity: Cavalier poet, courtier, and soldier; the archetype of the gallant royalist gentleman whose lyrics of love, honour, and imprisonment — 'To Althea, from Prison' and 'To Lucasta, Going to the Wars' — became the defining verse of the Cavalier cause.
authors.biography: Born 1616 (baptised 10 December at St Bride's, London), educated at Charterhouse and Gloucester Hall, Oxford, and a favourite of the court of Charles I. He served in the Bishops' Wars and, in 1642, presented the Kentish petition for the restoration of episcopacy, for which he was imprisoned in the Gatehouse; a second imprisonment (1648–49) followed his loyalty after the Civil War, during which he prepared his collection Lucasta (1649). He spent his later years in poverty in London, publishing Lucasta: Posthume Poems (1659 was posthumous; actually published 1660). He died in 1657, reportedly in great poverty.
authors.profile: The Cavalier gentleman-poet whose code of honour made 'I could not love thee, dear, so much, / Loved I not honour more' the motto of royalist gallantry.
authors.style: Elegant, musical lyrics; the argumentative conceit of love and honour; a gallant, dignified tone; and occasional metaphysical wit in the service of courtly feeling.
authors.concerns: Love and honour; loyalty to the king and the Cavalier cause; freedom of the spirit in imprisonment; friendship; and the consolation of poetry in defeat.
authors.significance: Lovelace's Lucasta is the classic Cavalier collection; his lyrics epitomise the royalist gentleman's ethos and remain among the most quoted poems of the seventeenth century.
authors.uncertainty: Lovelace's later life and the date and circumstances of his death are poorly documented; his reputation for a ruined, impoverished end rests partly on later tradition.

authors.name: Richard Price
authors.identity: Unitarian minister at Newington Green and one of the century's most influential moral philosophers, whose sermons on liberty made him a European authority on the rights of man.
authors.biography: Born at Bristol in 1723 and apprenticed to a glover, he found his vocation in the Dissent, studied mathematics, philosophy and a range of languages, and in the late 1750s became the minister of a small congregation at Newington Green, where he lived for the rest of his life. His Review of the Principal Questions in Morals (1769), a rigorous attack on sentiment and self-love as the foundation of right, gave him a philosophical rank beside Butler and Reid. Mathematical and demographic papers on annuities, life assurance and the value of marriage and mortality tables made him a Fellow of the Royal Society and an adviser to government on the funding of life. His sermons and tracts on the American Revolution, on the love of one's country, on toleration and on the corruptions of civil and ecclesiastical liberty were read, reviewed and answered across Britain, France and America. He died at Newington Green in June 1791, having refused richer preferment and stayed with his small meeting.
authors.profile: A moralist of reason and rights, who held that right and wrong are as fixed as the relations of number and that government exists only by the trust of the governed.
authors.style: Austere, tightly argued plainness; definitions and divisions carried into pulpit oratory; arithmetic and actuarial precision applied to human affairs; a sermonist's solemnity of appeal.
authors.concerns: Objective moral obligation against sentiment and interest; the reasonableness and corruptions of Christianity; the rights of individuals and the accountability of rulers; the valuation of life, annuities and population; the sin of the slave trade.
authors.significance: He supplied the rationalist morality and the doctrine of popular consent that made dissenting England a school of radical politics, and his actuarial work founded the mathematics of life assurance.
authors.uncertainty: The dating of his early conversion to Unitarian beliefs is loose, and the full text of several sermons survives only in reports made from shorthand.

works.title: A Discourse on the Love of Our Country
Observations on the Importance of the American Revolution, and the Means of Making It a Blessing to the Nations of Britain
Observations on the Nature of Civil Liberty, the Principles of Government, and the Justice and Policy of the Mother Country, respecting the Colonies

authors.name: Richard Rolle
authors.identity: mystic; devotional writer; hermit
authors.biography: Studied briefly at Oxford, then withdrew c. 1321 to become a hermit, finally settling near the Cistercian nunnery of Hampole in south Yorkshire, where he died in the Black Death (1349). The most widely read English spiritual writer of the fourteenth century, he was venerated as a saint, though never canonized.
authors.profile: Author of Latin treatises (Incendium Amoris, Emendatio Vitae, Melos Amoris) and English epistles (Ego Dormio, The Commandment, The Form of Living, addressed to the anchoress Margaret Kirkby) and of English psalm commentaries; his writings survive in hundreds of manuscripts.
authors.style: A highly personal, affective style built on the experience of 'fire, sweetness, and song' (calor, dulcor, canor); rhythmic prose with alliterative cadence; scriptural commentary fused with autobiography.
authors.concerns: The love of God as experienced warmth and song; the solitary life; the guidance of contemplatives, especially women recluses.
authors.significance: The father of the English mystical tradition: his affective spirituality shaped Rolle-influenced devotional prose for two centuries, and his English epistles are the earliest surviving writings of their kind.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his writings is debated; the medieval cult attributed miracles to him.
sources: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition

authors.name: Richard Steele
authors.identity: Anglo-Irish-born essayist, dramatist, and Whig publicist who founded the Tatler and co-founded the Spectator with Joseph Addison.
authors.biography: Born in Dublin and raised partly in England, Steele was educated at the Charterhouse and entered the army, buying a commission. He turned to writing and in 1709 founded the Tatler, a daily periodical of essays and news, soon joined by Addison. In 1711 the two launched the Spectator, to which Steele also contributed essays of feeling and reform. He wrote sentimental comedy, most successfully The Conscious Lovers (1722), and several political journals. A Whig member of Parliament, he fell into debt and estrangement from Addison in later life. After illness he retired to Wales, where he died in 1729.
authors.profile: A writer of familiar prose and sentimental drama, more impulsive and emotionally warm than Addison, who used the periodical to promote benevolence, fashion reform, and domestic feeling.
authors.style: Open, affectionate, sometimes hurried prose; a strong appeal to the heart rather than to judgement; lively character sketches; and an earnest, confessing moral voice.
authors.concerns: Reform of manners and duelling; benevolence and filial duty; Whig politics and religious toleration; and the sentimental education of the middle-class reader.
authors.significance: Inventor of the periodical essay through the Tatler and joint founder of the Spectator; a pioneer of sentimental comedy whose The Conscious Lovers dominated early eighteenth-century stage reform.
authors.uncertainty: His year and circumstances of birth are uncertain and commonly given only as about 1672; the precise division of labour between him and Addison in the Tatler and Spectator is still disputed.

authors.name: Robert Blair
authors.identity: Scottish Church of Scotland minister and poet, author of the meditative grave-poem The Grave, a landmark of the graveyard school.
authors.biography: Blair was born about 1699 and was ordained a minister of the Church of Scotland, where he became associated with the more liberal, Moderate interest in the kirk. He is remembered above all for his blank-verse poem The Grave (1743), a somber meditation on death and the resurrection that went through many editions and influenced the grave poetry that followed. He published sermons and devotional writings, but The Grave was his only poem of lasting note. He died in 1746.
authors.profile: A minister-poet whose single enduring work, The Grave, gives the eighteenth-century meditation on mortality an elevated, didactic, and pictorial blank-verse form.
authors.style: Grave, sonorous blank verse; accumulated images of burial, decay, and resurrection; sermon-like urgency; and a sustained mood of solemn meditation rather than narrative or wit.
authors.concerns: Death, the grave, and the hope of resurrection; the vanity of worldly distinctions before death; the equality of all in the tomb; and Christian consolation and judgement.
authors.significance: The Grave is a defining text of the graveyard school, alongside Young's Night Thoughts, shaping the later-eighteenth-century poetics of melancholy and mortality; Blair also belongs to the Moderate current of the Scottish kirk.
authors.uncertainty: His year and place of birth are uncertain and variously recorded; details of his Scottish charges and of the early illustration history of The Grave are imperfectly established.

authors.name: Robert Boyle
authors.identity: Natural philosopher and chemist, a founder of the Royal Society; his The Sceptical Chymist (1661) championed the new experimental method and corpuscular philosophy, and his pious writings defended Christianity as compatible with science.
authors.biography: Born 25 January 1627 at Lismore Castle, County Waterford, the youngest son of Richard Boyle, first Earl of Cork (the richest man in Britain); educated at Eton and in Europe (Geneva, Florence, where he read Galileo). Settling in England, he joined the 'invisible college' that became the Royal Society (chartered 1662), conducted experiments with his assistant Robert Hooke (inventor of the air pump), and formulated Boyle's law of gases. A devout Anglican, he wrote prolifically on both science and religion — The Sceptical Chymist (1661), Some Physico-Theological Considerations (1665), and works defending the faith — and endowed the Boyle Lectures. He died on 31 December 1691.
authors.profile: The experimental philosopher who separated chemistry from alchemy and medicine, argued for the corpuscular (mechanical) philosophy, and reconciled scientific enquiry with Christian piety in a clear, plain prose.
authors.style: Plain, experimental, methodical prose; detailed reports of apparatus and results; dialogic form (The Sceptical Chymist); and a pious, reasoned apologetic style.
authors.concerns: Experimental method and the corpuscular philosophy; chemistry, gases, and the air pump; the reconciliation of science and religion; the plain style of the new science; and natural theology.
authors.significance: Boyle is a founder of modern chemistry and of the experimental method, and his advocacy of the plain style and of physico-theology shaped both scientific writing and the religious defence of science; the Boyle Lectures continued his apologetic project for generations.
authors.uncertainty: Boyle's life and works are thoroughly documented; his scientific and religious writings are extensive and partly published posthumously.

works.title: New Experiments Physico-Mechanical, Touching the Spring of the Air

authors.name: Robert Burns
authors.identity: Scottish poet in English and in the Scots dialect, celebrated for songs, narrative, and lyric, and honoured as the national poet of Scotland.
authors.biography: Burns was born in Ayrshire to a poor tenant farmer and was largely educated at home and by informal tutoring, working the land from childhood. His Kilmarnock edition, Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect (1786), was an immediate success and took him to Edinburgh, where he moved among literary and aristocratic circles. Later he settled as an officer of excise and continued to collect and adapt Scottish songs, contributing to James Johnson's Musical Museum and to George Thomson's collections. His lyrics and songs, and his narrative and satiric poems, such as Tam o' Shanter (1790) and Holy Willie's Prayer, display a range of humour, sentiment, and radical sympathy. He died in Dumfries in 1796, aged thirty-seven.
authors.profile: A poet and songwriter of the common tongue, equally at home in tender lyric, bawdy, comic narrative, and democratic or religious satire, drawing on the native Scottish song and vernacular tradition.
authors.style: Vivid Scots vernacular diction and idiom; song-measures of great melodic fluency; direct, passionate, and often humorous address; and a blend of rustic naturalness with refined lyric sensibility.
authors.concerns: Common humanity and democratic fellow-feeling; the critique of religious hypocrisy and cant; the value of nature and vernacular song; nationality, friendship, and the dignity of the ordinary.
authors.significance: The national poet of Scotland and a seminal figure of the Romantic age and of vernacular and song literature; he elevated Scottish dialect poetry and became a global emblem of popular, egalitarian feeling.
authors.uncertainty: The authorship and dating of individual songs are often complicated by his free borrowing, adaptation, and reconstruction of traditional texts; some details of his political sympathies are disputed.

works.title: A Man's a Man for A' That
Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect

authors.name: Robert Burton
authors.identity: scholar; clergyman; prose writer
authors.biography: Born 8 February 1577 at Lindley, Leicestershire. Educated at Brasenose and Christ Church, Oxford, where he spent his life as student, tutor, librarian of Christ Church, and vicar of St Thomas's. A recluse among books, he died on 25 January 1640, having predicted his own death by horoscope; he is buried in Christ Church Cathedral.
authors.profile: The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621; five expanded editions in his lifetime, with a sixth posthumous in 1651), the vast encyclopedic treatise-disguised-as-self-cure written under the name 'Democritus Junior'.
authors.style: A prose of endless quotation, digression, and cataloguing — learned, humane, and often hilarious — that turns a medical treatise into a labyrinthine anatomy of everything.
authors.concerns: Melancholy in all its causes and cures; the vanity of learning; love, religion, and the passions as diseases of the mind.
authors.significance: A summa of Renaissance psychology and a fountainhead for Sterne, Lamb, and the whole tradition of English digressive prose.
authors.uncertainty: Almost all knowledge of his character comes from the book itself and from Anthony Wood's memoir.

authors.name: Robert Fabyan
authors.identity: chronicler; draper; alderman
authors.biography: A London draper, alderman, and sheriff (1493–94), Fabyan retired from civic life about 1502 and compiled his chronicle of England and France, which he finished by 1504 (with continuations to 1509). He died in London in 1513, and the work was printed by Richard Pynson in 1516 as The New Chronicles of England and France.
authors.profile: Author of the standard London chronicle of the early Tudor period. Organized annalistically around the mayors and sheriffs of London, Fabyan's chronicle supplied Shakespeare and the Tudor historians with the matter of English history from Brutus to Henry VII, and its verse interjections ('L'envoy') give it a distinctly civic literary character.
authors.style: The annalist's plain record, organized by civic year; occasional moralizing verse; a Londoner's eye for pageant, execution, and civic ceremony.
authors.concerns: The history of England and France as moral example; the dignity and record of the city of London.
authors.significance: The principal vernacular chronicle between the Brut tradition and Hall; a chief source of Tudor historical consciousness and of Shakespeare's history plays at second hand.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date unknown.
themes: Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination

works.title: The New Chronicles of England and France

authors.name: Robert Greene
authors.identity: dramatist; prose romancer; pamphleteer
authors.biography: Baptized 11 July 1558 in Norwich; took his BA at St John's College, Cambridge (1580) and MA from Clare Hall (1583), and was incorporated at Oxford. He came to London to live by the pen, married, abandoned his wife, and died in poverty on 3 September 1592 after a banquet of Rhenish wine and pickled herring, leaving the deathbed pamphlet Greene's Groatsworth of Wit, which contains the notorious 'upstart Crow' attack on Shakespeare.
authors.profile: The most prolific of the University Wits: plays include Alphonsus, King of Aragon (c. 1588), Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay (c. 1589), James IV (c. 1590), and Orlando Furioso (1591); romances include Pandosto (1588), the source of The Winter's Tale, and Menaphon (1589); pamphlets include the cony-catching series (1591–92) exposing the tricks of London's underworld.
authors.style: Euphuistic prose, romantic plotting, pastoral charm, and a pamphlet style of vivid, confessional journalism.
authors.concerns: The moral and financial perils of authorship; repentance; the underworld of London; the rivalries of the professional stage.
authors.significance: A central University Wit whose romantic comedy and prose fiction fed Shakespeare directly; his cony-catching pamphlets are landmarks of English prose realism and rogue literature.
authors.uncertainty: His repentances were staged for the press; the Groatsworth attribution is generally accepted though its circumstances are murky.

authors.name: Robert Henryson
authors.identity: poet; schoolmaster; notary
authors.biography: A university graduate ('Master') who served as schoolmaster of the grammar school of Dunfermline and as a notary public; his name appears in the records of Dunfermline Abbey in 1478. He died c. 1500. The finest of the fifteenth-century makars, he is grouped by Dunbar among the dead poets of the Lament for the Makaris.
authors.profile: Author of the Morall Fabillis of Esope (c. 1480s), the Testament of Cresseid (c. 1475–90), Orpheus and Eurydice, Robene and Makyne, and a body of shorter moral poems.
authors.style: Chaucerian forms infused with northern speech; rueful, compassionate irony; the beast fable raised to satiric and philosophical art; mastery of the 'ballat royal' stanza.
authors.concerns: Justice, prudence, and the social order; the tragedy of Cresseid as a drama of sin, punishment, and late repentance; mortality and consolation.
authors.significance: Universally ranked with Dunbar as the greatest of the makars; his Testament of Cresseid is the most powerful continuation of Chaucer ever written, and his Fabillis the summit of the European fable tradition in the vernacular.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; almost nothing is known of his life beyond the Dunfermline records.
movements: Gothic and the Literature of Terror

works.title: The Morall Fabillis of Esope the Phrygian

sources: The Cambridge Companion to English Literature, 1650–1740

authors.name: Robert Herrick
authors.identity: Cavalier poet and country parson; author of Hesperides (1648), a vast collection that joins pagan festivity, erotic lyrics, and devotional verse to a staunch Anglican and royalist piety rooted in rural Devon.
authors.biography: Born August 1591 in London (baptised at St Vedast), educated at St John's College, Cambridge (BA 1617, then transferred). A 'Son of Ben' in the London wit circles, he took orders and was presented to the living of Dean Prior in Devon (1629), where he served — grumbling at the rustic parishioners — until ejected by Parliament in 1647 as a royalist. He returned to London, published Hesperides (1648) and the religious Noble Numbers, then was restored to Dean Prior in 1662 after the Restoration and lived there until his death in October 1674.
authors.profile: The poet of 'gather ye rosebuds while ye may', whose Hesperides celebrates the seasonal rites, courtships, and superstitions of the English countryside with a classical gaiety shadowed by mutability and Anglican faith.
authors.style: Short, musical, epigrammatic lyrics; classical and rustic imagery; a light, mellifluous metrical variety; and the pairing of pagan 'Hesperides' with the Christian 'Noble Numbers'.
authors.concerns: Carpe diem and mutability; rural festivity and custom; erotic love and marriage; Anglican ceremony and royalist loyalty; death and the consolations of faith.
