authors.significance: Herrick is the greatest of the Cavalier lyricists in range and charm; Hesperides preserved the folklore and ceremonial culture of the English countryside and his lyrics have remained continuously popular.
authors.uncertainty: Herrick's life is documented mainly through his own poems and parish records; his exact attitudes and the arrangement of Hesperides remain matters of interpretation.

authors.name: Robert Hooke
authors.identity: Natural philosopher, inventor, and microscopist; his Micrographia (1665), with its spectacular engravings of the flea, the louse, and plant cells (he coined the word 'cell'), was a landmark of scientific illustration and of the literature of discovery.
authors.biography: Born 18 July 1635 at Freshwater, Isle of Wight; educated at Christ Church, Oxford, where he became assistant to Boyle (building the air pump) and later Professor of Geometry. A founder-member and Curator of Experiments to the Royal Society, he published Micrographia (1665), a sensational success, and made contributions across physics (Hooke's law of elasticity), astronomy, geology, and architecture (as Surveyor to the City of London after the Great Fire, working with Wren). He disputed priority with Newton over optics and gravitation. He died on 3 March 1703; no certain portrait of him survives.
authors.profile: The brilliant experimentalist and observer whose Micrographia opened an invisible world to readers through its prose descriptions and magnificent engravings, inspiring wonder and the new empirical vision.
authors.style: Descriptive, observational scientific prose; detailed accounts of apparatus and experiments; spectacular engraving and visual rhetoric; and a plain, empirical style.
authors.concerns: Microscopy and the structure of matter; experimental method and instrumentation; elasticity, light, and mechanics; geology and fossils; and architecture and rebuilding.
authors.significance: Micrographia is a founding work of microscopy and scientific illustration and influenced the literature and imagination of the new science (Pepys called it 'the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life'); Hooke's wide contributions made him a central figure of the Royal Society.
authors.uncertainty: Hooke's life is documented through Royal Society records and his diary; the destruction of his papers and the absence of a portrait have left his appearance and some achievements obscure.

works.title: Micrographia: or, Some Physiological Descriptions of Minute Bodies Made by Magnifying Glasses

authors.name: Robert Mannyng
authors.identity: chronicler; devotional writer; Gilbertine canon
authors.biography: A Gilbertine canon of Sempringham Priory, Lincolnshire, who spent part of his career at Sixhills. He translated the Anglo-Norman Manuel des péchés of William of Wadington as Handlyng Synne (begun 1303), the classic English manual of penance, and later composed the Chronicle (completed 1338), a verse history of England from Noah to Edward I based on Wace and Peter Langtoft.
authors.profile: Handlyng Synne (1303) made the casuistry of confession vivid through exemplary tales; the Chronicle (1338) is a principal vernacular history of England in the earlier fourteenth century.
authors.style: Plain, fluent couplets; the telling anecdote and moralized exemplum; skilful adaptation of French sources for a provincial English audience.
authors.concerns: Pastoral instruction of the laity; the moral meaning of English history.
authors.significance: Handlyng Synne is a cornerstone of Middle English penitential literature and a major source for the exemplum tradition; the Chronicle bridges the Brut tradition and the verse histories of the fourteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; details of his life come from his own prefaces.
sources: Tudor Drama before Shakespeare, 1485–1590: New Directions for Research, Criticism, and Pedagogy

authors.name: Robert Whittington
authors.identity: grammarian
authors.biography: Born at Lichfield about 1480; studied at Oxford, where he was laureated for grammar. He taught in London and wrote a series of grammatical and rhetorical textbooks, of which the Vulgaria (1520) — model sentences in Latin and English for schoolboys — is the most famous. He died about 1553.
authors.profile: The most successful school grammarian of the generation before Lily's Grammar was standardized. The Vulgaria's paired Latin and English sentences, drawn from everyday school and city life, are at once a textbook and a vivid picture of early Tudor London, and its jibes at Lily made it a document of the grammar wars of the 1520s.
authors.style: The schoolmaster's sentence-builder; colloquial English paired with schoolboy Latin; combative prefaces addressed to rival grammarians.
authors.concerns: The teaching of Latin through the vernacular; the rivalries of the grammar schools; the manners and language of London boys.
authors.significance: A principal maker of the Tudor school curriculum; the Vulgaria is a unique record of the spoken English of the early sixteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate.

authors.name: Roger Ascham
authors.identity: humanist; tutor to Elizabeth I; Latin secretary
authors.biography: Born at Kirby Wiske about 1515; educated at St John's College, Cambridge, where he taught Greek and reformed the pronunciation of it. Tutor to Princess Elizabeth from 1548 to 1550, he served as Latin secretary under Mary and Elizabeth. His Toxophilus (1545), a dialogue in praise of archery, won him a royal pension, and The Schoolmaster, begun about 1563, was published posthumously in 1570 by his widow. He died on 30 December 1568.
authors.profile: The most readable of the English humanist educators. Toxophilus is the first English treatise on a sport and a model of the plain style; The Schoolmaster — built around the instruction of the young Elizabeth — attacks Italianate corruption, prescribes the double translation of Latin, and records the educational practice of the age in the finest English prose between More and Hooker.
authors.style: The plain style refined into art: concrete, anecdotal, sinewy English that he explicitly opposed to the inkhorn inflation of his contemporaries.
authors.concerns: The education of the English governing class; the discipline of imitation and translation; the morality of travel; archery and bodily training as parts of the curriculum.
authors.significance: Tutor and intellectual model of Elizabeth I; The Schoolmaster governed English pedagogical theory for two centuries and remains the classic defence of the vernacular for learning.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate (1514 or 1515).

authors.name: Roger Bacon
authors.identity: philosopher; scientist; Franciscan friar
authors.biography: Educated at Oxford and Paris, where he lectured on Aristotle, he joined the Franciscans c. 1257 and, frustrated by the neglect of experimental science, sought the patronage of Pope Clement IV, for whom he composed the Opus Maius, Opus Minus, and Opus Tertium in 1267–68. He was condemned by his order c. 1278 and imprisoned, and died c. 1292.
authors.profile: Author of the Opus Maius (1267), a programmatic encyclopedia of the sciences — mathematics, optics, experimental science, moral philosophy, and the reform of learning — together with works on grammar, astronomy, alchemy, and the calendar.
authors.style: Urgent, polemical, encyclopedic prose; the advocacy of mathematics and experiment ('scientia experimentalis') as the foundation of knowledge; prophetic visions of technology (ships, cars, flying machines).
authors.concerns: The reform of the universities and of the church through science; the study of languages and texts; the practical power of knowledge.
authors.significance: The greatest scientific mind of the medieval West before the fourteenth-century natural philosophers; his experimental program made him the patron figure of early modern science in England (and the hero of Victorian legend).
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and the chronology of his Oxford years approximate; the circumstances of his condemnation are unclear.
themes: Carpe diem and the pleasures of the present
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Samuel Johnson

authors.name: Samuel Butler
authors.identity: Satirist and poet; author of Hudibras, the brilliant mock-heroic burlesque of Puritan hypocrisy that became one of the most quoted poems of the Restoration and defined English comic satire for a century.
authors.biography: Born c. 1612–13 at Strensham, Worcestershire; educated at the free school of Worcester and possibly Cambridge. He served in Puritan and royalist households, acted as steward to the royalist Sir William Waller, and after the Restoration held posts including secretary to the Lord President of the Marches at Ludlow. He published Hudibras in three parts (1663, 1664, 1678), a huge success celebrated by the court but poorly rewarded; he left a mass of unpublished 'characters' and notes (printed posthumously as Miscellaneous Thoughts, 1759, and The Genuine Remains, 1694). He died in poverty on 25 September 1680.
authors.profile: The scourge of Puritan cant, whose Hudibras attacked the hypocrisy of the Presbyterian Independents in rollicking doggerel and proverbial wit, coining countless phrases still in use.
authors.style: Comic octosyllabic couplets with absurd rhymes; mock-heroic and burlesque; a dense store of proverbs, puns, and learned-satiric allusion; and terse, epigrammatic 'characters' in prose.
authors.concerns: Hypocrisy, fanaticism, and false learning; royalist and Anglican loyalty; human folly and self-interest; and the satire of sectarian politics.
authors.significance: Hudibras was the most popular satire of the Restoration, a favourite of Charles II, and its mock-heroic technique directly influenced Dryden, Swift, and Pope's Dunciad.
authors.uncertainty: Butler's birth year is approximate and his early life obscure; his later poverty and the posthumous publication of his remains are documented but partly traditional.

works.title: Miscellaneous Thoughts and Posthumous Works of Samuel Butler

authors.name: Samuel Daniel
authors.identity: Poet and historian; the author of Delia, one of the first of the 1590s sonnet sequences, and of the long poem The Civil Wars, tutor to Lady Anne Clifford.
authors.biography: Born c. 1562 near Taunton, the son of a music master; educated at Magdalen Hall, Oxford. He served as tutor to William Herbert, later Earl of Pembroke, and travelled in Italy; his sonnet sequence Delia appeared in 1591–92 (appended to Astrophel and Stella in its first edition), followed by The Complaint of Rosamond (1592) and the tragedies Cleopatra (1594) and Philotas (1605). He was tutor to Lady Anne Clifford and groom of the chamber to Queen Anne; his Civil Wars (1595, revised to 1609) chronicled the Wars of the Roses. He died in October 1619 at Beckington, Somerset.
authors.profile: A laureate of moderate, musical verse — 'well-languaged Daniel' — whose sonnets, epistles, and philosophical poems (Musophilus, 1599) exemplify the Elizabethan ideal of learned eloquence in the service of moral reflection.
authors.style: Smooth, balanced, sententious verse; the plain-style reaction against Petrarchan conceit; an Augustan moderation of diction and rhythm that anticipates the seventeenth century.
authors.concerns: The uses of history as moral example; the fortunes of kings and the instability of power; poetry as the civilizing art; constancy in love and in the self.
authors.significance: A principal shaper of the Elizabethan sonnet vogue and of the verse-epistle and historical poem; his influence ran to Milton and the Augustans, and his Delia's 'Care-charmer Sleep' remains a classic.
authors.uncertainty: The year of birth (1562 or 1563) is uncertain; the extent of his rewriting of The Civil Wars across editions makes the poem's textual history complex.

authors.name: Samuel Johnson
authors.identity: English poet, essayist, lexicographer, and critic, the dominant man of letters of later-eighteenth-century England.
authors.biography: Johnson was born at Lichfield, studied at Pembroke College, Oxford, and after a brief schoolmastership returned to the Midlands before going to London to live by his pen. He wrote for the Gentleman's Magazine, and as editor produced the dictionary that defined English for a century, A Dictionary of the English Language (1755). Between 1750 and 1752 he wrote the moral weekly The Rambler, and later contributed to other periodicals including The Idler; the philosophical tale The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia appeared in 1759. His poetry includes London (1738) and The Vanity of Human Wishes (1749). A devoted Tory and Anglican and a founding member of The Club, he edited Shakespeare (1765) and wrote the Journey to the Western Islands (1775) and the Lives of the English Poets (1779-1781). He died in London in 1784.
authors.profile: A moralist, critic, and lexicographer of immense range, who practised the periodical essay, didactic verse, dictionary-making, textual editing, and biography, always subordinating fancy to judgement and common sense.
authors.style: Latinate, balanced, periodic prose of antithesis and generalisation; the weighty heroic couplet of his moral verse; a sententious, authoritative, common-sense tone; and a preference for truth over ornament.
authors.concerns: The regulation of the passions and the vanity of worldly hopes; the stability and authority of language; the criticism of literature by general nature; religion, duty, and mortality; and the common life.
authors.significance: The most authoritative English literary voice of his age, whose dictionary standardised the language and whose criticism set the terms for assessing poetry and the canon well into the nineteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: A probable congenital condition and an uncertain recovery from scrofula are described in accounts that mix fact with family legend; the dating of his early marriage and his first London writings is imperfect.

works.title: A Dictionary of the English Language
A Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language
Letter to the Earl of Chesterfield
Taxation Tyrannical; or, The Colonies and Britain Compared
The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia

authors.name: Samuel Pepys
authors.identity: Naval administrator and diarist; his Diary (1660–69), kept in shorthand and published only in the nineteenth century, is the most famous diary in English — a candid, vivid record of the Restoration, the Great Plague, and the Great Fire, and of his own private life.
authors.biography: Born 23 February 1633 in Salisbury Court, London, educated at St Paul's School and Magdalene College, Cambridge (BA 1654). Through the patronage of his cousin Edward Montagu (later Earl of Sandwich) he entered the Navy Office as Clerk of the Acts (1660), becoming an able administrator and later Secretary to the Admiralty. From January 1660 to May 1669 he kept a meticulous private diary in shorthand covering public affairs (the coronation, the Dutch Wars, the Plague of 1665, the Fire of 1666) and his own finances, ambitions, affairs, and domestic life. Failing eyesight ended the diary in 1669; he served as MP and President of the Royal Society (1684–86) but lost office after the Revolution. He died on 26 May 1703.
authors.profile: The incomparable diarist whose immediacy, curiosity, and unembarrassed self-revelation — of work, pleasure, money, sex, music, and public catastrophe — create an unrivalled portrait of Restoration England and of a single vivid personality.
authors.style: Spontaneous, detailed, colloquial prose in shorthand; a diary's day-by-day immediacy; candid self-scrutiny; vivid reportage of events; and an eye for the telling particular.
authors.concerns: Public affairs and naval administration; ambition, money, and social climbing; pleasure, music, theatre, and women; the Plague and the Fire; and the private conscience.
authors.significance: The Diary is a primary historical source of the first importance for the 1660s and a literary classic; its frankness and observational brilliance established the diary as a major form and Pepys as one of the most beloved figures in English letters.
authors.uncertainty: Pepys's Diary and letters are richly documented; the diary was deciphered only in the nineteenth century, and some shorthand passages remain uncertain in reading.

authors.name: Samuel Purchas
authors.identity: clergyman; compiler of travel narratives
authors.biography: Born at Thaxted, Essex, about 1577. Educated at St John's College, Cambridge, he took orders and served as chaplain and rector, most notably of St Martin Ludgate, London. He inherited Richard Hakluyt's unpublished papers and made them the core of his great collection. He died in 1626, probably in London.
authors.profile: Purchas His Pilgrimage (1613) and Hakluytus Posthumus, or Purchas His Pilgrimes (1625), the four-volume folio that continued and crowned Hakluyt's work of collecting the world's voyages.
authors.style: Compilatory and devout: he arranges others' narratives within a providential frame, adding moral reflection and apology for his 'pilgrimage' through the world's records.
authors.concerns: The spread of the Gospel and of English trade; the world as theatre of providence; the preservation of voyages from oblivion.
authors.significance: His Pilgrimes preserved many accounts that survive nowhere else and helped form the English colonial imagination in the seventeenth century.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

works.title: Hakluytus Posthumus, or Purchas His Pilgrimes

authors.name: Samuel Richardson
authors.identity: English printer and novelist, the master of the epistolary novel and one of the founders of the English novel tradition.
authors.biography: Born in 1689 (the year is accepted but not precisely documented, and details of his birthplace are uncertain), the son of a joiner, he was apprenticed to a printer and rose to become one of London's leading master printers and printer to the House of Commons. Late in life he turned to authorship, publishing the epistolary novel Pamela (1740), followed by the much longer Clarissa (1748) and Sir Charles Grandison (1753). His fiction drew on his experience of letter-writing and conduct material. He died on 1 July 1761.
authors.profile: The great eighteenth-century writer of the novel in letters, whose extended fictions dramatize the inner moral lives of their characters, especially women, and probe seduction, conscience, and social constraint through the unfolding present tense of correspondence.
authors.style: Epistolary form; intense psychological realism; an immediate, deliberating narrative voice; elaborate moral and sentimental rhetoric; and structural suspense built from letters that advance scene by scene.
authors.concerns: Virtue under pressure; female autonomy and vulnerability; conscience, duty, and temptation; the perils of the libertine; religion and morality; and the ethics of reading and sympathy.
authors.significance: One of the pivotal figures in the rise of the English novel, whose Pamela and Clarissa set new standards for psychological depth and whose epistolary method influenced writers across Europe for generations.
authors.uncertainty: His exact birth year and birthplace are not fully documented, and parts of his early life rest on inference from later records.

works.title: Clarissa; or, The History of a Young Lady
The History of Sir Charles Grandison

authors.name: Sarah Fielding
authors.identity: English novelist and children's writer, best known for David Simple and the pioneering children's novel The Governess.
authors.biography: Born on 8 November 1710 at East Stour in Dorset, the sister of Henry Fielding, she was educated in the family circle and remained close to her brother. She published The Adventures of David Simple (1744), later issuing sequels and contributing to the periodical contest and miscellany writing of the day. In 1749 she published The Governess; or, The Little Female Academy, often described as the first novel in English written expressly for children. She also translated and edited. She died on 9 April 1768 at Bath.
authors.profile: A novelist and moralist of a quieter, more reflective cast than her brother, whose fiction emphasizes sensibility, friendship, and female education, and who helped to create a native tradition of the story written for young readers.
authors.style: Sentimental and didactic prose; a simpler, more domestic realism than the picaresque; dialogic and moralizing structure; and a plainly addressed, instructive narrative voice suited to didactic and children's writing.
authors.concerns: Friendship, benevolence, and the education of the character; the situation and instruction of women and girls; sincerity versus worldly artifice; and the moral development of the young.
authors.significance: An important early woman novelist and a landmark figure in the history of children's literature in English, whose David Simple circulated widely and rivaled some of her brother's fiction in its day.
authors.uncertainty: Her exact birth and death dates are usually given but her life is unevenly documented, and parts of her early education and unpublished work remain imperfectly recorded.

works.title: The Governess; or, Little Female Academy
The History of the Adventures of David Simple

authors.name: Sir David Lindsay
altNames: Sir David Lindsay of the Mount
authors.identity: poet; playwright; herald; Lyon King of Arms
authors.biography: Born about 1486 at the Mount in Fife; attached to the court of James IV and the companion and usher of the young James V, whom he exhorted in The Dreme (1528). Lyon King of Arms from 1542 and a lord of session, he was the leading advocate of the reformed cause in Scottish letters. His Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis was played at Linlithgow in 1540 and enlarged at Cupar in 1552. He died about April 1555.
authors.profile: The major Scottish poet of the Reformation. The Dreme (1528) instructs the young king in a dream vision; The Testament of the Papyngo (1530) is a dying parrot's satire of court and clergy; and Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis — the great morality of the Scottish Reformation — stages the trial of the estates before King Humanitie, with John the Common-Weill the plaintiff and the vices of the church in the dock.
authors.style: Direct satirical address in fluent Scots; the dream vision and the testament turned to political use; the morality play expanded to a national parliament.
authors.concerns: The reformation of the Scottish church; the education of the king; the common weal against the estates; justice for the poor.
authors.significance: The poet of the Scottish Reformation and the author of its greatest dramatic work; the Satyre is the summit of Scots drama and was played and reprinted for generations.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the exact date of his death (1555) is uncertain within the year.

works.title: Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis

authors.name: Sir John Davies
authors.identity: Lawyer, statesman, and poet; author of Orchestra and Nosce Teipsum, the most accomplished philosophical poems of the Elizabethan period, and later attorney-general for Ireland.
authors.biography: Born in 1569 in Wiltshire; educated at Winchester and the Queen's College, Oxford, and the Middle Temple (called to the bar 1595). His Orchestra, or A Poem of Dancing was published in 1596, and Nosce Teipsum in 1599, both dedicated to Queen Elizabeth; he was disbarred in 1598 for striking Richard Martin in the Middle Temple hall, restored in 1601, and sat in the parliaments of James I. As solicitor-general (1603) and attorney-general (1606) for Ireland he administered the Ulster plantation and became speaker of the Irish parliament (1613); he returned to England as a judge in 1619, was lord chief justice briefly in 1626, and died on 8 December 1626.
authors.profile: A philosophical poet of unusual lucidity who turned the hardest questions of the soul into polished quatrains; Nosce Teipsum ('Know thyself') was celebrated by contemporaries as the proof that English verse could reason.
authors.style: The decasyllabic quatrain used with argumentative precision; elegant metaphysical wit without obscurity; the marriage of law, philosophy, and verse.
authors.concerns: The immortality of the soul and the nature of knowledge; the cosmic order expressed in the dance (Orchestra); the union of poetry and philosophy; the reform of Ireland and the duties of the magistrate.
authors.significance: The finest English philosophical poet before the metaphysicals, whose Nosce Teipsum was admired by Coleridge and remains the classic Elizabethan poem of self-knowledge.
authors.uncertainty: The poems' dates are approximate; the attribution of several epigrams between Sir John Davies and John Davies of Hereford has been a source of confusion since the seventeenth century.

authors.name: Sir John Denham
authors.identity: Poet and royalist administrator; author of Cooper's Hill (1642), the first great English topographical and reflective poem, whose balanced couplets established the model for Augustan nature-and-meditation verse.
authors.biography: Born 1615 (baptised at St Andrew Holborn), educated at Trinity College, Oxford, and Lincoln's Inn. His tragedy The Sophy (1642) and Cooper's Hill (1642) won him immediate fame. A moderate royalist, he served Charles I and Charles II on diplomatic missions and as Surveyor of the King's Works (1660, after Inigo Jones), was knighted in 1660, and suffered a much-publicised bout of madness in 1666. He died in March 1669 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The poet of the meditative landscape, whose view of the Thames from Cooper's Hill yoked topography, history, and moral reflection in the balanced couplet that Pope praised as 'strong sense ... most correctly writ'.
authors.style: The smooth, balanced closed couplet; topographical description as moral and political meditation; classical allusion; and a grave, sententious tone.
authors.concerns: Nature and order; the Thames, trade, and the English constitution; moderation and the 'golden mean'; royalist politics; and the relation of landscape to history and morality.
authors.significance: Cooper's Hill founded the English topographical and estate-mediation tradition that runs through Marvell, Pope ('Windsor-Forest'), and Thomson's Seasons, and its couplets shaped Augustan versification.
authors.uncertainty: Denham's life is well documented, including his madness and the scandal of his wife's death; the dating of Cooper's Hill's revisions (1642, 1650, 1655, 1668) is established.

authors.name: Sir John Suckling
authors.identity: Cavalier wit, courtier, and poet-playwright; famous for his rakish elegance, his sprightly songs, and his role as a dashing but ultimately tragic royalist, whose suicide in exile at thirty-three made him a legend of the Cavalier generation.
authors.biography: Born February 1609 at Whitton, educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn. He inherited a large fortune, travelled Europe, served in the Bishops' Wars (raising a troop at his own expense), and became a celebrated figure of the court wits around the Earl of Holland and Thomas Hobbes. He wrote plays (Aglaura, 1638; The Goblins, 1638) and lyrics, and was knighted in 1630. He took part in the First Army Plot (1641) to rescue the Earl of Strafford, fled to Paris, and died there in June 1642, reportedly by his own hand after a servant's insult. His Fragmenta Aurea was published in 1646.
authors.profile: The most fashionable Cavalier wit, whose careless grace and easy songs ('Why so pale and wan, fond lover?') embodied the rakish elegance of Charles I's court.
authors.style: Light, witty, conversational songs; a deliberately 'careless' aristocratic ease; satiric and bawdy verse; and dramatic prose and blank verse in his plays.
authors.concerns: Love and gallantry; wit and courtly fashion; royalist loyalty; sceptical libertinism; and the vanity of romantic pretence.
authors.significance: Suckling's lyrics and his legend as a doomed Cavalier made him an emblem of the Caroline court; his plays influenced Restoration comedy, and 'A Ballad upon a Wedding' is a lively social satire.
authors.uncertainty: The exact circumstances of Suckling's death (suicide or accident) are uncertain and were debated even by contemporaries.

authors.name: Sir Philip Sidney
authors.identity: Courtier, soldier, diplomat, and poet; the model of the Renaissance man whose posthumously published works founded the English sonnet sequence and the critical defence of poetry.
authors.biography: Born 30 November 1554 at Penshurst, eldest son of Sir Henry Sidney; educated at Shrewsbury School and Christ Church, Oxford, then travelled the continent (1572–75), witnessing the St Bartholomew's Day massacre and meeting continental humanists. At court he was a favourite of Elizabeth's diplomacy and a patron of letters (dedicatee of Spenser's Calender); his quarrel with the Earl of Oxford (1579) and his 'Letter to Queen Elizabeth' against the Anjou match (1579–80) marked his temporary rustication to Wilton, where he wrote the Arcadia. He served in Parliament, was knighted in 1583, and in 1585 was appointed governor of Flushing; he died on 17 October 1586 of a thigh wound received at Zutphen (famously giving his water to a dying soldier), and was mourned as the flower of English chivalry.
authors.profile: The courtier-poet who practised poetry as an aristocratic accomplishment rather than a profession — 'look in thy heart, and write'; his Defence of Poesy remains the period's central statement of the moral and cultural claims of literature, and Astrophel and Stella set the sonnet vogue of the 1590s in motion.
authors.style: Elegant courtly wit, the first sustained English sonnet sequence with a narrative of courtship, the mingling of prose romance and eclogue in the Arcadia, and a critical prose of luminous argument.
authors.concerns: The defence of poetry against Puritan attack; the education of the aristocrat in virtue and action; the psychology of desire and self-knowledge; Protestant politics and the duties of the public man.
authors.significance: The posthumous publication of his works (Arcadia 1590, Astrophel and Stella 1591, The Defence of Poesy 1595) made him the tutelary genius of the 1590s literary generation and the English type of the poet-hero.
authors.uncertainty: The dating of his major works rests on inference (the Arcadia is usually assigned to c. 1577–80, the Defence to c. 1579–81); none of his major works was printed in his lifetime by his own act.

authors.name: Sir Thomas Browne
authors.identity: Physician, antiquary, and prose stylist; author of Religio Medici (1643), Hydriotaphia (Urn Burial, 1658), and The Garden of Cyrus (1658), whose majestic, digressive, Latinate prose is among the richest in English and fuses faith, scepticism, and learned curiosity.
authors.biography: Born 19 October 1605 in London, educated at Winchester and Pembroke College, Oxford (BA 1626, MA 1629), then studying medicine at Montpellier, Padua, and Leiden (MD 1633). He settled as a physician in Norwich (1637), where he lived for the rest of his life, marrying Dorothy Mileham (1641) and fathering twelve children. Religio Medici, circulated in manuscript and printed without his consent (1643), made his name; he answered critics and published Pseudodoxia Epidemica (1646–72), a vast enquiry into 'vulgar errors', and the twin treatises Hydriotaphia and The Garden of Cyrus (1658). Knighted by Charles II in 1671, he corresponded with the Royal Society and died on 19 October 1682.
authors.profile: The physician-essayist who meditated on belief, death, and the wonders of the natural world in a grand, allusive prose, holding faith and sceptical enquiry in a richly personal balance.
authors.style: Sonorous, Latinate, digressive prose; paradox and learned allusion; a baroque richness of phrase; antiquarian and scientific curiosity; and a meditative, tolerant tone.
authors.concerns: Faith and reason; death, burial, and the resurrection; the errors of popular belief; nature, plants, and antiquities; the mystery of the self; and Christian tolerance.
authors.significance: Browne is one of the supreme English prose stylists, influencing Johnson, De Quincey, Lamb, and Woolf; Religio Medici created a new genre of personal, tolerant religious autobiography, and Urn Burial remains a masterpiece of meditative antiquarianism.
authors.uncertainty: Browne's life is well documented through his letters and Norwich records; the publication history of Religio Medici (pirated editions before his authorised text) is complex.

works.title: Pseudodoxia Epidemica; or, Enquiries into Very Many Received Tenets

authors.name: Sir Thomas Elyot
authors.identity: humanist; diplomat; lexicographer; political theorist
authors.biography: Born about 1490 into a family of west-country lawyers; he served Wolsey as clerk and became a diplomat and clerk of the king's council. Falling from favour in the 1530s, he devoted himself to letters: The Boke Named the Governour (1531), dedicated to Henry VIII, The Castle of Health (1534), and the first Latin–English dictionary (1538). He died on 26 March 1546.
authors.profile: The principal English theorist of humanist education and the gentleman magistrate. The Governour — drawing on Castiglione, Erasmus, and the Italian humanists — defined the curriculum, the virtues, and the physical training of the ruling class, and it introduced scores of classical commonplaces into English prose. His Dictionary (1538) founded English lexicography.
authors.style: Earnest, copious Ciceronian prose; the deliberate enrichment of English vocabulary from Latin; a moralist's directness beneath the classical apparatus.
authors.concerns: The education of princes and magistrates; the union of learning and virtue in the ruling class; the health of body and commonwealth; the capacities of the English language.
authors.significance: Author of the classic statement of the Tudor educational ideal, read by every Elizabethan schoolmaster, and of the dictionary that began the English lexicographical tradition.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.
themes: The sublime, terror, and the ruin
sources: Essays in the History of Ideas

authors.name: Sir Thomas More
authors.identity: humanist; lawyer; statesman; Lord Chancellor; martyr and saint
authors.biography: Born in Milk Street, London, on 7 February 1478, the son of a judge; page to Cardinal Morton; studied at Oxford and the Inns of Court. A friend of Erasmus from 1499, he translated Lucian with him, wrote the Latin epigrams, and published Utopia at Louvain in 1516. Entered royal service in 1517; undersheriff of London, speaker of the Commons (1523), chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and Lord Chancellor (1529–32). Refusing the oath of supremacy, he was imprisoned in the Tower in April 1534 and beheaded on 6 July 1535; canonized in 1935.
authors.profile: The presiding genius of English humanism. Utopia (1516) invented the fictional commonwealth; The History of King Richard III (c. 1513–18), written in both Latin and English, is the first great work of English historical prose and the source of Shakespeare's Richard III; the controversial dialogues of 1529–33 (A Dialogue Concerning Heresies, The Supplication of Souls, The Confutation of Tyndale's Answer) are the summit of Reformation polemic; and A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation (1534), written in the Tower, is a masterpiece of devotional prose.
authors.style: Irony, wit, and the dramatic management of dialogue; the plain English style of the later controversial works; Latinity of European standard in the epigrams and Utopia.
authors.concerns: The reform of Christendom and the commonwealth; the claims of conscience against the state; property, enclosure, and social justice; the defence of the old church against the new theology.
authors.significance: Author of the founding text of utopian fiction, the first classic of English historiography, and one of the great prose styles of the language; his life and death made him the exemplary conscience of the English Reformation.
authors.uncertainty: None significant; the dating of Richard III's composition remains approximate.
themes: Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding

works.title: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation
The History of King Richard III

sources: The Theory of Moral Sentiments (Cambridge Texts in the History of Philosophy)

authors.name: Sir Thomas North
authors.identity: translator; soldier; justice of the peace
authors.biography: Born 28 May 1535 in London, younger son of Edward North, 1st Baron North. Educated at Peterhouse, Cambridge, and Lincoln's Inn, he saw military service in Ireland and the Low Countries and later sat as a justice in Cambridgeshire. He died about 1603.
authors.profile: The Dial of Princes (1557, from Guevara via French) and the Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (1579) — his translation of Plutarch from Jacques Amyot's French, which became the single most important non-dramatic source for Shakespeare's Roman and Greek plays.
authors.style: A full, energetic, idiomatic English prose of remarkable dramatic vividness; Shakespeare followed it so closely that whole passages of the plays are North's sentences re-lined as verse.
authors.concerns: The exemplary lives of great men; counsel and conduct; the translation of classical wisdom for English readers.
authors.significance: North's Plutarch is the most consequential translation of the English Renaissance, the quarry of Julius Caesar, Coriolanus, Antony and Cleopatra, and Timon of Athens.
authors.uncertainty: Death date approximate; the records of his last years are scanty.

works.title: Plutarch's Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans

authors.name: Sir Thomas Wyatt
authors.identity: courtier; diplomat; poet
authors.biography: Born at Allington Castle, Kent, in 1503; educated at St John's College, Cambridge. A courtier and diplomat for Henry VIII — he was esquire of the body, ambassador in France, Italy, and Spain, and knighted in 1535 — he was twice imprisoned in the Tower: in 1536, during the fall of Anne Boleyn, and in 1541 on charges of treasonable correspondence. Released through the influence of Catherine Howard, he died of fever at Sherborne, Dorset, on 11 October 1542. His poems circulated in manuscript during his life; 96 were printed posthumously in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).
authors.profile: The founder of the English lyric tradition. He introduced the Petrarchan sonnet into English (translating and imitating the Rime sparse with rugged, deliberate roughness), wrote the great courtly lyrics ('They flee from me', 'Whoso list to hunt', 'My galley charged with forgetfulness'), the three verse epistles known as the Satires (c. 1536), and a paraphrase of the seven penitential psalms composed after his 1536 imprisonment.
authors.style: A difficult, compressed, colloquial style — enjambment against the rhyme, metrical irregularity used for dramatic emphasis, and the plain speech of the courtier set against Petrarchan convention.
authors.concerns: The dangers of court life under an absolute prince; the claims of truth against flattery; love, honour, and the unstable self; the psalmist's repentance as a model for the Tudor subject.
authors.significance: With Surrey, he established the sonnet, the courtly lyric, and the verse satire in English, providing the formal foundations of the Elizabethan poetic achievement; Tottel's printing of his verse made him the first modern English poet of the anthologies.
authors.uncertainty: The canon rests on manuscript attributions (principally the Egerton MS); the extent of his relationship with Anne Boleyn is conjectural.
themes: Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
sources: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano

authors.name: Sir Walter Ralegh
authors.identity: courtier; explorer; poet; historian
authors.biography: Born about 1554 at Hayes Barton, Devon. He fought in France and Ireland, rose at court through the favour of Elizabeth I, and was knighted in 1585. He organized the attempted Roanoke colony and expeditions to Guiana. After Elizabeth's death he was convicted of treason on flimsy evidence and imprisoned in the Tower (1603–16), where he wrote his History of the World. Released for the disastrous Guiana voyage of 1617, he was executed on 29 October 1618 on the old sentence.
authors.profile: The Discoverie of the Large, Rich and Beautiful Empire of Guiana (1596), the History of the World (1614), the Cynthia poems ('The Ocean to Cynthia' fragments), and lyrics such as 'The Lie', 'The Passionate Man's Pilgrimage', and the poem written the night before his death.
authors.style: A grave, plain, sententious style in prose; in verse, an introspective melancholy unusual in the Elizabethan court lyric.
authors.concerns: Fortune and the fall of greatness; colonial wealth and its moral cost; providence and the vanity of human glory.
authors.significance: The embodiment of the Elizabethan adventurer-intellectual; his History of the World was read for its stoic grandeur, and his myth has haunted English literature ever since.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the canon of his shorter poems rests on early anthologies and is partly uncertain.

works.title: The Discoverie of the Large, Rich and Beautiful Empire of Guiana

authors.name: Sir William Davenant
authors.identity: Poet, playwright, and impresario; the crucial bridge between the Caroline and Restoration stages, who kept drama alive during the Interregnum with 'entertainments' and the proto-opera The Siege of Rhodes, held one of the two Restoration theatre patents, and introduced women players and scenery to the English stage.
authors.biography: Born February 1606 in Oxford, son of a vintner (legend, fostered by Davenant, claimed Shakespeare as his father and godfather). He wrote masques and plays for the Caroline court, succeeded Jonson as poet laureate (1638), and was knighted (1651) for royalist service. During the Commonwealth he produced The Siege of Rhodes (1656) at Rutland House — often called the first English opera — evading the ban on plays as 'moral representations'. Imprisoned and pardoned for his part in royalist plots, he survived to hold, with Thomas Killigrew, the royal patent of 1660 that reopened the theatres; his Duke's Company introduced moveable scenery and, in 1660, the first professional actresses. He adapted Shakespeare (with Dryden, The Tempest, 1667) and died on 7 April 1668, buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The impresario-poet who modernised the English stage, blending masque, opera, and neoclassical drama, and whose Gondibert (1651) experimented with a new quatrain epic form praised by Hobbes.
authors.style: Masque and spectacle; the experimental four-line stanza of Gondibert; neoclassical dramatic theory; heroic and operatic forms; and a verse of public, philosophical ambition.
authors.concerns: The reform and moral justification of drama; Platonic and heroic virtue (Gondibert); the integration of music, scenery, and spectacle; royalist loyalty; and the new stagecraft.
authors.significance: Davenant founded the institutional and technical shape of the Restoration theatre — its patents, scenery, women players, and operatic ambitions — and mentored the young Dryden; without him the continuity of English drama across the Interregnum would have been broken.
authors.uncertainty: The claim that Davenant was Shakespeare's biological son is legend, not fact; his biography is otherwise well documented through theatre records and state papers.

works.title: The Tempest; or, The Enchanted Island

authors.name: Sir William Temple
authors.identity: Diplomat, statesman, and essayist; author of Observations upon the United Provinces (1673) and the elegant miscellaneous essays Of Gardens (1685) and Of Poetry, whose polished, urbane prose and patronage of Swift made him a central figure of late-century letters.
authors.biography: Born 25 April 1628 in London, son of Sir John Temple; educated at Bishop's Stortford and Emmanuel College, Cambridge (under Ralph Cudworth), travelling widely in Europe. He served as ambassador and negotiator (the Triple Alliance, 1668; the treaties of Nijmegen), and as Secretary of State (1679), before retiring to Moor Park, Surrey. There he wrote his Observations upon the United Provinces (1673), his Miscellanea (1680, 1690), and essays including 'Upon the Gardens of Epicurus' (1685), and employed the young Jonathan Swift as his secretary (1689–99). His 'Essay upon the Ancient and Modern Learning' (1690) provoked the Battle of the Books. He died on 27 January 1699.
authors.profile: The cultivated statesman-essayist whose clear, graceful, conversational prose exemplifies the polite ideal of the late seventeenth century and who introduced the Chinese garden and a cosmopolitan urbane taste to English letters.
authors.style: Polished, lucid, urbane prose; the short, balanced sentence; conversational ease; digressive reflection; and a Horatian ideal of retirement.
authors.concerns: Politics, diplomacy, and the Dutch republic; gardens, retirement, and the Epicurean ideal; the quarrel of the ancients and moderns; poetry and wit; and the conduct of public and private life.
authors.significance: Temple's essays shaped Augustan prose style and the taste for retirement and gardening; his patronage launched Swift, and his 'Ancient and Modern Learning' essay ignited the Battle of the Books that Swift and Wotton fought out.
authors.uncertainty: Temple's diplomatic career is well documented in state papers; his private life and the details of his relationship with Swift and his household are known through correspondence and memoirs.

works.title: Observations upon the United Provinces of the Netherlands

authors.name: Stephen Hawes
authors.identity: poet; groom of the chamber
authors.biography: Born about 1474, probably in Suffolk; educated perhaps at Oxford, he became groom of the chamber to Henry VII. His Pastime of Pleasure was printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1509 and The Example of Virtue about 1504; he died about 1523, the last significant poet of the Chaucerian-Lydgatian school.
authors.profile: The last of the medieval allegorists and a favourite of the early Tudor court. The Pastime of Pleasure recounts the education, courtship, and knightly career of the hero Graunde Amoure in rhyme royal and couplets, an allegorical summa of chivalric and learned ideals; The Example of Virtue traces the soul's progress through Youth to Age and Eternity.
authors.style: Aureate diction in the Lydgatian manner; rhyme royal handled with fluency; allegorical machinery of pilgrimage, tower, and tournament.
authors.concerns: The seven liberal arts; chivalric education and courtly love; the soul's moral progress; the poet's role as teacher of princes.
authors.significance: The bridge between the medieval allegorical tradition and Tudor court poetry; Spenser read him, and The Pastime of Pleasure kept the dream-allegory alive into the Renaissance.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; little is known of his life beyond his court service.

authors.name: Stephen of Ripon
authors.identity: hagiographer; Latin prose writer
authors.biography: A priest of Ripon and member of Bishop Wilfrid's household, conventionally identified with the Æddi Stephanus whom Bede says Wilfrid brought back from Kent as a singing-master (fl. c. 670-720). He accompanied Wilfrid on his journeys and wrote the Vita Sancti Wilfridi (c. 712-714) at the request of Acca of Hexham and Tatberht of Ripon. Nothing else is known of his life, and even his identification with Bede's 'Æddi' rests on a plausible but unproven equation.
authors.profile: The earliest identifiable Anglo-Latin biographer after the anonymous Lindisfarne life of Cuthbert. His Vita Wilfridi is a partisan defence of his hero against the charges of Wilfrid's enemies, cast in the conventions of late-antique hagiography.
authors.style: Vigorous, episodic narrative with a strong authorial voice; vivid set-piece scenes (Wilfrid's shipwreck, his Roman appeals, his deathbed); simpler and more direct Latin than Aldhelm's, with a notable absence of the hermeneutic manner.
authors.concerns: Episcopal authority and the primacy of Rome; the sanctity of a controversial political bishop; the deeds of the apostolic missionary as evidence of holiness.
authors.significance: His Vita Wilfridi is the earliest surviving biography written in England about a contemporary English churchman, and a principal source for the history of the seventh-century Northumbrian church and Wilfrid's career.
authors.uncertainty: Identification with Bede's Æddi Stephanus is traditional, not proven. Birth and death dates unknown; floruit c. 670-720.
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume III: 1189–1327

authors.name: Susanna Centlivre
authors.identity: English playwright, poet, and actress, widely considered the most successful female dramatist of the early eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born Susanna Freeman, though her maiden name is disputed, in Lincolnshire and baptized there around 1669, she was said to have been largely self-educated and to have entered the theatre early. She acted briefly and then turned to playwriting, becoming a dominant presence on the London stage in the reign of Queen Anne. Her best-known comedies include The Busie Body (1709), The Wonder: A Woman Keeps a Secret (1714), and A Bold Stroke for a Wife (1718). She also wrote a prologue and other occasional verse and was associated with Whig political circles. She died in London on 1 December 1723.
authors.profile: A prolific writer of city and manners comedies who specialized in brisk plots of mistaken identity, female cunning, and marriage intrigue, and whose plays remained a staple of the repertory long after her death.
authors.style: Sprightly, witty comic dialogue; well-made intrigue plots; stock and humours characters; clever, spirited heroines; and prose comedy designed for effective stage performance.
authors.concerns: Marriage, money, and social mobility; wit and the cunning of clever women; busybody culture and the manners of the town; and party and public life in Augustan London.
authors.significance: The most frequently performed woman playwright of her era in Britain, whose comedies helped shape the early-eighteenth-century stage and were revived and adapted throughout the century.
authors.uncertainty: Her maiden name and parentage (Freeman versus Carroll) and her exact birth year and birthplace are debated; her death is now fixed at 1 December 1723, though older sources long gave 1726, and parts of her early life are recorded only in unreliable or legendary accounts.

works.title: A Bold Stroke for a Wife
The Wonder: A Woman Keeps a Secret

authors.name: Tatwine
authors.identity: Latin riddler and theologian; grammarian
authors.biography: A Mercian by birth who became a monk at Breedon-on-the-Hill in Leicestershire, a house with Northumbrian connections. He was consecrated archbishop of Canterbury in 731, succeeding Berhtwald, and died in office in 734. Bede records his consecration in the Historia ecclesiastica.
authors.profile: Author of the Aenigmata, forty Latin riddles with a preface, on theological, philosophical, and grammatical subjects, and of a Latin grammar (Ars Tatuini) based on Donatus. His riddles are the first Latin riddle collection composed in England to survive complete.
authors.style: Compact hexameter riddles in the manner of Symphosius and Aldhelm, but with doctrine rather than natural history as their usual subject; the verse is plain and schoolmasterly rather than hermeneutic.
authors.concerns: The union of grammatical learning with theology; the encyclopedic description of creation through the riddle form; Christian teaching for the schoolroom.
authors.significance: With Aldhelm and Hwætberht he established the Anglo-Latin riddle tradition that fed into the vernacular Exeter Book Riddles; his grammar helped transmit the Insular grammatical tradition.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and place uncertain (Mercia by tradition); the attribution of the riddles and grammar to him is secure.
sources: English Literature in the Sixteenth Century, Excluding Drama

authors.name: Theodore of Tarsus
authors.identity: exegete, canonist, and teacher; Latin prose writer
authors.biography: Born in Tarsus in 602 and educated in the Greek East (probably at Antioch and Constantinople), he was living as a monk in Rome when Pope Vitalian consecrated him archbishop of Canterbury in 668, with Hadrian the African as his companion and adviser. Together they toured England, reformed the English church, and founded the school of Canterbury, where Greek and Latin learning, canon law, and biblical exegesis were taught. He died on 19 September 690.
authors.profile: The Laterculus Malalianus, a Latin exegetical and chronographical treatise on the life of Christ, is attributed to him (written at Canterbury in the 670s); the biblical commentaries from the Canterbury school preserve his and Hadrian's teaching; the penitential that circulates under his name is traditionally attributed to him. His school produced Aldhelm and the earliest English manuscript culture.
authors.style: In the Laterculus Malalianus, dense and sometimes idiosyncratic Latin shaped by Syriac and Greek exegetical sources, with a chronological apparatus; the Canterbury commentaries preserve an unusual blend of Greek and Latin patristic learning.
authors.concerns: The chronology and exegesis of the life of Christ; the union of Greek and Latin Christian learning; church order and penance; the education of an English clergy.
authors.significance: As organizer of the Canterbury school he is the founder of Anglo-Saxon Latin learning; his church reforms and synods (Hertford 672, Hatfield 679) unified the English church, and his teaching reached Bede's Northumbria through his pupils.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of the Laterculus Malalianus and the Penitential to him is traditional and widely accepted, but not beyond dispute. Birth and death dates are recorded by Bede.
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume B: The Sixteenth Century and the Early Seventeenth Century

authors.name: Thomas Campion
authors.identity: Poet, composer, and physician; the supreme English writer of the lute song, author of the airs and of the treatise on English metre Observations in the Art of English Poesy.
authors.biography: Born 12 February 1567 in London; educated at Peterhouse, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn, and took his medical degree at the University of Caen (1605), practising medicine in London. He published the Latin Poemata (1595), Observations in the Art of English Poesy (1602), the masque for Lord Hayes (1607), and above all the songbooks A Book of Airs (1601, with Philip Rosseter) and the Two, Third, and Fourth Books of Airs (c. 1613–17), for which he wrote both words and music. He died in London on 1 March 1620.
authors.profile: The one English poet-composer of the first rank: his airs — 'When to her lute Corinna sings', 'Rose-cheeked Laura', 'Never weather-beaten sail' — wed the Elizabethan lyric to the continental lute song with a musical economy unmatched in the language.
authors.style: Quantitative experiments in Latin and English; short-lined, song-like verse of classical restraint; an anti-rhyming polemic in the Observations belied by his own masterly rhymes.
authors.concerns: The union of music and poetry; classical prosody and the reform of English metre; the pleasures and deceits of love; moral and religious consolation.
authors.significance: The summit of the English lute-song tradition and a major figure in the history of English prosody; his airs remained in performance and shaped the lyric taste of the seventeenth century.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of several poems between Campion and his collaborators (notably Rosseter) is partly editorial; the dates of the later songbooks are inferred.

authors.name: Thomas Carew
authors.identity: Cavalier lyric poet and courtier of Charles I's household; admired by his contemporaries as perhaps the finest of the Caroline wits, he combined Jonsonian polish with Donnean wit in short, intense love poems.
authors.biography: Born c. 1595 at West Wickham, Kent, educated at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and the Middle Temple. After a dissolute youth and service abroad (in the household of the ambassador at The Hague, from which he was dismissed for 'scurrility'), he became a server-in-ordinary to Charles I and moved in the court literary circle. His elegy 'An Elegy upon the Death of the Dean of Paul's, Dr John Donne' (1633) is a key document of the metaphysical transition. His Coelum Britannicum (masque, 1634) and his Poems were published in 1640, shortly before his death in 1639/40.
authors.profile: The consummate Caroline court lyricist, whose poems fuse sensual elegance with intellectual wit in a manner Clarendon called the 'muses' most delicate son'.
authors.style: Polished, musical short lyrics; Donnean argument and conceit softened by Cavalier grace; sensuous wit; and a masterly control of the octosyllabic couplet.
authors.concerns: Love and desire; the pleasures and pains of courtship; poetry and immortality; the critique of Petrarchan convention; and courtly virtue.
authors.significance: Carew was ranked by contemporaries above most Cavalier poets; his synthesis of Donne and Jonson and his elegy on Donne make him central to understanding the metaphysical-to-Cavalier transition.
authors.uncertainty: Carew's birth and death dates are approximate and his life poorly documented; most of his poems were printed posthumously in 1640.

authors.name: Thomas Chatterton
authors.identity: English poet and forger, the marvellous boy, whose fabricated medieval Rowley poems and tragic early death made him a Romantic legend.
authors.biography: Chatterton was born in Bristol into a poor musical family and, as a boy connected with the church of St Mary Redcliffe, he discovered old manuscript documents he claimed were the work of a fifteenth-century monk, Thomas Rowley. From these he forged an entire pseudo-antique body of verse in a convincing archaic diction. He moved to London in 1770 to seek patronage and made a precarious living as a reporter and hack, also writing learned essays and poetry. Neglected and despairing, he died in London in 1770 by arsenic poisoning, aged seventeen. His story and the Rowley poems were taken up by Horace Walpole and later by the Romantics.
authors.profile: A poet of astonishing early gift who invented a medieval voice and persona; the Rowley pieces mix archaic pastiche with genuine lyric feeling, and his own later verse anticipates the grave and melancholy modes.
authors.style: Ingenious Rowley archaism of invented Middle-English diction; ballad and hymn measures; and in his modern verse a meditative, often melancholy descriptive and personifying style.
authors.concerns: The authenticity and romance of the literary past; imitation and forgery; the neglected genius and the cruelty of patronage; mortality and despair; and national poetic origins.
authors.significance: The Rowley forgeries stimulated the antiquarian revival of old English poetry and helped shape the Romantic cult of the doomed child-genius; his legend, told by Wordsworth, Keats, and others, became a literary myth.
authors.uncertainty: The circumstances and even the date of his death by suicide are partly legendary; the exact nature of the parish documents behind the Rowley forgeries is known chiefly from Chatterton's own unreliable accounts.

authors.name: Thomas Chestre
authors.identity: romance poet; translator
authors.biography: A late fourteenth-century English poet known only from his works, which name him 'Thomas Chestre' in their final lines; he flourished c. 1380–1400. Nothing else is recorded of his life.
authors.profile: Author of Sir Launfal (an English adaptation of Marie de France's Lanval), the romance Libeaus Desconus (from Renaud de Beaujeu's Le Bel Inconnu), and the romance Octavian; some scholarship also attributes The Isle of Ladies to him.
authors.style: Energetic tail-rhyme stanzas; brisk narrative compression of French sources; a fondness for the supernatural generosity of fairy mistresses and the rewards of loyalty.
authors.concerns: The adaptation of French courtly romance for English popular audiences; the claims of loyalty, love, and largesse.
authors.significance: A representative figure of the late Middle English tail-rhyme romance; his Sir Launfal is the fullest English treatment of the Lanval story and a staple of the Breton lay tradition in England.
authors.uncertainty: Dates and circumstances wholly unknown; the attributions rest on the poems' self-naming.
themes: Petrarchan desire and the sonnet mistress
sources: The Works of Aphra Behn

authors.name: Thomas Cranmer
authors.identity: archbishop of Canterbury; liturgist; theologian; martyr
authors.biography: Born at Aslockton on 2 July 1489; fellow of Jesus College, Cambridge. His suggestion that the universities should judge the validity of Henry VIII's marriage brought him to the king's notice; he became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1533 and presided over the annulment, the royal supremacy, and the dissolution. Under Edward VI he produced the two Books of Common Prayer (1549, 1552), the Book of Homilies (1547), and the Forty-Two Articles (1553). Under Mary he was tried, degraded, and — after recanting and then withdrawing his recantations — burned at Oxford on 21 March 1556, thrusting the hand that had signed the recantations first into the fire.
authors.profile: The architect of the English liturgy. The Book of Common Prayer is his monument: collects, services, and the prose of worship that fixed the devotional language of English for four centuries ('ashes to ashes, dust to dust'). He was the principal author of the first Book of Homilies (1547) and of the doctrinal statement of the Edwardian church.
authors.style: Ritual prose of unmatched gravity and compression: parallel phrasing, scriptural cadence, and the direct address of congregation by priest; a style built for the voice.
authors.concerns: Worship in the vernacular; the simplification of the liturgy on scriptural principles; royal supremacy and the reform of doctrine; the unity of the English church.
authors.significance: Author of the defining text of Anglican worship, still in daily use; the Prayer Book's prose ranks with Tyndale's Bible as the foundation of modern English devotional language.
authors.uncertainty: None significant; the division of authorship within the 1547 Homilies is partly editorial.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Taste, decorum, and the rules of art

works.title: A Defence of the True and Catholic Doctrine of the Sacrament

sources: Reflections on the Revolution in France

authors.name: Thomas Dekker
authors.identity: dramatist; pamphleteer
authors.biography: Born in London about 1572, probably of Dutch descent. He began writing for Henslowe's companies in 1598 and was imprisoned for debt in the Poultry Counter (1598–99). He collaborated with nearly every dramatist of the age — Jonson, Marston, Webster, Middleton, Ford, Massinger — and wrote some of the period's most vivid plague pamphlets. He died on 25 August 1632, still in debt.
authors.profile: Plays include The Shoemaker's Holiday (1599), Old Fortunatus (1599), Satiromastix (1601, with Marston, in the war of the theatres against Jonson), The Honest Whore (1604–05, with Middleton), and The Witch of Edmonton (1621, with Ford and Rowley); prose includes The Wonderful Year (1603) and The Gull's Hornbook (1609).
authors.style: Warmth, sentiment, and a Londoner's ear for the trades and cries of the city; his best scenes have a lyrical realism unmatched by his contemporaries.
authors.concerns: The dignity of citizens and craftsmen; plague and providence; the cheerful endurance of poverty.
authors.significance: The great celebrant of London's citizens; The Shoemaker's Holiday remains the most performed city comedy of its generation, and his pamphlets are major documents of urban life.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; little is known of his family and education.

authors.name: Thomas Deloney
authors.identity: balladeer; prose fiction writer; silk weaver
authors.biography: A silk weaver by trade, probably born in Norwich about 1560. He became the most popular ballad-maker of his generation; several of his broadsides offended the authorities, and he was briefly in trouble over a ballad on the scarcity of grain in 1596. He died in 1600, apparently in poverty, leaving the fiction on which his later fame rests.
authors.profile: The prose narratives Jack of Newbury (1597), The Gentle Craft (c. 1597–98), and Thomas of Reading (c. 1600), which turned the lives of English craftsmen and merchants into popular fiction, together with hundreds of ballads of which a handful survive.
authors.style: Plain, vigorous, humorous prose full of proverbs, workman's lore, and the speech of shop and street; a bourgeois realism new to English fiction.
authors.concerns: The dignity and prosperity of trade; the pleasures of the middling sort; charity, industry, and honest dealing.
authors.significance: The first English novelist of the working people; his fictions reached a readership far below the court and founded the tradition of popular prose romance.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace approximate; his surviving ballad canon is a fraction of a much larger lost output.

authors.name: Thomas Fuller
authors.identity: Anglican clergyman, historian, and wit; author of The Holy State and the Profane State (1642), a compendium of characters and maxims, and The History of the Worthies of England (1662), a pioneering biographical-topographical survey written in an energetic, proverbial style.
authors.biography: Born 1608 at Aldwincle, Northamptonshire (the same parish as Dryden); a prodigy educated at Queens' College, Cambridge (BA 1624/25) and Sidney Sussex College. He held various livings, served as a royalist chaplain during the Civil Wars, and was known for his preaching, memory, and wit. His major works include The Holy State (1642), Good Thoughts in Bad Times (1645), The Church-History of Britain (1655), and the posthumous Worthies of England (1662). A moderate during the Interregnum, he was restored at the Restoration and died on 16 August 1661 in London.
authors.profile: The learned, witty compiler and historian whose pithy, proverbial, digressive style and love of anecdotes and characters made him one of the most readable prose writers of the century.
authors.style: Terse, epigrammatic, proverbial prose; the 'character' sketch; abundant anecdote, pun, and quotation; a genial, learned wit; and a digressive, associative method.
authors.concerns: Moral and religious instruction; English history, biography, and topography; the virtues of the 'holy state' and the vices of the 'profane'; wit and wisdom; and moderation in the church.
authors.significance: Fuller's Worthies is a foundational work of English local history and biography, and his Church-History a pioneering ecclesiastical history; his prose style, full of quotable maxims, was widely admired and influential.
authors.uncertainty: Fuller's life is documented; the accuracy of some of his historical and biographical anecdotes was questioned even in his day and he himself admitted a love of a good story.

works.title: The History of the Worthies of England
The Holy State and the Profane State

authors.name: Thomas Gray
authors.identity: English poet and scholar, Professor of Modern History at Cambridge, whose Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard is among the most quoted poems in the language.
authors.biography: Gray was born in London and educated at Eton and at Peterhouse, Cambridge, where he later returned as a scholar and, from 1768, held the Professorship of Modern History. A careful, slow writer of small output, he published little in his lifetime, including the Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College and the Hymn to Adversity. His finest Pindaric odes, The Progress of Poesy and The Bard, appeared in 1757. His Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard (1751) brought him fame. He declined the laureateship and lived a studious, largely private life, close to a circle that included Horace Walpole. He died at Cambridge in 1771.
authors.profile: A poet of the graveyard, the meditative ode, and antiquarian romance; he combined neoclassical polish with a new interest in melancholy, the common dead, and the music and history of earlier English and Welsh verse.
authors.style: Exquisite diction and sonorous, Latinate word order; a restrained, melancholy dignity; Pindaric and Norse-influenced ode experiments; and an antiquarian taste for the ballad and the picturesque.
authors.concerns: Unfulfilled potential and the fate of obscure lives; death, memory, and the moral lesson of the grave; the history and progress of poetry; and the aesthetics of melancholy and the sublime.
authors.significance: The Elegy became the landmark of the graveyard school and a touchstone of sensibility, while his odes and editorial interests in old poetry helped open the way to Romantic and antiquarian taste.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is usually given as 1716, but some records support 1717; the dating of the Elegy's composition, long associated with the churchyard at Stoke Poges, is debated.

works.title: Elegy Written in a Country Church-Yard
Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College

authors.name: Thomas Heywood
authors.identity: dramatist; poet; prose writer
authors.biography: Born in Lincolnshire about 1573; studied at Emmanuel College, Cambridge. He was acting and writing for Henslowe's companies by 1598 and claimed to have had 'an entire hand, or at least a main finger' in 220 plays. He wrote pageants, translations, and compendious works of history and mythology, and died in Clerkenwell on 16 August 1641, one of the last survivors of the great Jacobean generation.
authors.profile: A Woman Killed with Kindness (1603), the domestic tragedy The English Traveller (c. 1627), the four-part Ages cycle (1611–32), The Fair Maid of the West (c. 1600), and the prose An Apology for Actors (1612), the period's chief defence of the stage.
authors.style: Plain, humane, middle-style verse; domestic settings; moral plots of patience and repentance that avoid the lurid excesses of his rivals.
authors.concerns: The dignity of the ordinary household; marital betrayal and forgiveness; the moral legitimacy of the theatre.
authors.significance: His domestic tragedy founded a genre that runs through Lillo to Ibsen; An Apology for Actors is the classic defence of the English stage.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the vast collaborative canon makes his exact share in many plays uncertain.

authors.name: Thomas Hobbes
authors.identity: Philosopher and political theorist; author of Leviathan (1649), the founding text of modern political philosophy, whose materialist, mechanistic system and prose of austere clarity transformed English thought and letters.
authors.biography: Born 5 April 1588 at Westport, Wiltshire (the year of the Armada — 'fear and I were born twins', he joked); educated at Magdalen Hall, Oxford. He served for decades as tutor and secretary to the Cavendish family (Earls of Devonshire), travelling Europe and meeting Mersenne, Gassendi, Descartes, and Galileo. Alarmed by the political crisis, he went into exile in Paris (1640–51), publishing De Cive (1642) and, in 1651, Leviathan, whose defence of absolute sovereignty and its Erastianism offended both royalists and Parliamentarians. He returned to England, was distrusted by the restored court, and, after the Clarendon attack and the 1666 parliamentary scrutiny of 'atheism', published little more political philosophy. His later works include Behemoth (1668–70) and an autobiography in verse. He died on 4 December 1679 at Hardwick.
authors.profile: The philosopher who derived the state from a contract among self-interested individuals in a 'war of every man against every man', and who wrote with a logical, powerful, and lucid prose that made philosophy English literature.
authors.style: Rigorous, deductive argument; a clear, forceful, sometimes ironic prose; striking metaphors (the state as 'Leviathan', life as 'nasty, brutish, and short'); and a materialist, mechanistic vocabulary.
authors.concerns: Sovereignty, the social contract, and the state of nature; materialism and mechanism; human nature, appetite, and reason; religion and its political control; and the philosophy of language and knowledge.
authors.significance: Leviathan founded modern political philosophy and social contract theory, profoundly influencing Locke, Rousseau, and all subsequent thought; Hobbes's materialism and prose style also made him a central, if feared, figure in English intellectual and literary history.
authors.uncertainty: Hobbes's life is well documented (including his own prose and verse autobiographies and Aubrey's Life); the sincerity of his religious professions remains debated.

works.title: Leviathan; or, The Matter, Forme, and Power of a Common-Wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civill
The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic

authors.name: Thomas Hoccleve
authors.identity: poet; clerk
authors.biography: A clerk of the Privy Seal office in Westminster from c. 1387 for some thirty-five years, he knew Chaucer personally and called himself his disciple; his poems — above all the autobiographical passages of the Series — record his anxiety, his 'maladie' of 1416, and the precarious life of a married office-holder. He died in 1426.
authors.profile: Author of the Regiment of Princes (1411), the classic English mirror-for-princes addressed to the future Henry V; the Series (c. 1419–21), a linked set of tales and complaints containing the first English poetic autobiography; and shorter poems including the Male Regle.
authors.style: Correct Chaucerian verse with a plain, personal voice; rueful self-portraiture; the adaptation of courtly and didactic forms to the experience of bureaucracy and illness.
authors.concerns: Good governance and the duties of princes; poverty, patronage, and the ethics of office; his own mental suffering and its consolation.
authors.significance: The first English poet to write extensively about his own life and illness; the Regiment is a principal document of Lancastrian political literature and of the Chaucerian inheritance.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the cause of his 1416 'maladie' remains debated.
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling
themes: The English vernacular and national letters
sources: The Diary of Samuel Pepys

authors.name: Thomas Kyd
authors.identity: dramatist; scrivener's son
authors.biography: Son of Francis Kyd, a London scrivener; baptized 6 November 1558. Probably attended Merchant Taylors' School. Little is known of his life before The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587), which made his name. In May 1593 he was arrested after papers denying the deity of Christ were found in his lodgings; he claimed they belonged to Christopher Marlowe, his former room-mate, and was tortured in Bridewell. He died in August 1594, buried on 15 August, in debt and obscurity.
authors.profile: Author of the most influential revenge tragedy of the age, The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587), with its play-within-the-play, its ghost of Don Andrea, and its hero Hieronimo; also wrote the tragedy Soliman and Perseda (c. 1592) and Cornelia (1594), a translation of Robert Garnier's Senecan tragedy, and is the probable author of the lost ur-Hamlet.
authors.style: Senecan rhetoric, ghosts and revenge choruses, dramatic irony, the device of the play within the play, and a blank verse line of strong end-stops that Marlowe and Shakespeare both learned from.
authors.concerns: Justice and its frustration; the morality of private revenge; the theatre's power to reveal concealed crime.
authors.significance: The founding figure of English revenge tragedy; The Spanish Tragedy was the most popular play of its generation and shaped Hamlet and a hundred imitations.
authors.uncertainty: Almost nothing certain about his education; the ur-Hamlet attribution is probable but not proven; several minor plays have been conjecturally assigned to him.

authors.name: Thomas Linacre
authors.identity: physician; humanist; founder of the Royal College of Physicians
authors.biography: Born about 1460, probably at Canterbury; studied at Oxford and in Italy, where he learned Greek from Politian and took a medical degree at Padua. Physician to Henry VIII, tutor of the young Thomas More, and founder of the Royal College of Physicians (1518), he translated Galen into Latin with unprecedented accuracy and wrote De Emendata Structura Latini Sermonis (1524), the first scientific Latin grammar by an Englishman. He died on 20 October 1524.
authors.profile: The English pioneer of Greek medicine and philology. His Galen translations (1517–23) restored the texts of ancient medicine to the West, and his Latin grammar, applying the new philology to the classical language, is a landmark of English humanism.
authors.style: The philologist's precision; translation as recovery of the original; grammar as science rather than schoolroom drill.
authors.concerns: The restoration of Greek learning; the reform of medicine on Galenic foundations; the accurate use of Latin among physicians and scholars.
authors.significance: Founded the scientific study of medicine in England and the College of Physicians; his translations and grammar made him, with Colet and Grocyn, one of the three pillars of the Oxford reform.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace approximate.

authors.name: Thomas Lodge
authors.identity: prose romancer; poet; dramatist; physician
authors.biography: Born in London in 1558, son of a Lord Mayor of London. Educated at Merchant Taylors' School and Trinity College, Oxford, he turned to literature, travelled to the Canaries and South America, then converted to Catholicism and took up medicine, graduating MD at Avignon in 1600. He practised in London until his death of the plague in September 1625.
authors.profile: The romance Rosalynde (1590) — the direct source of Shakespeare's As You Like It — the euphuistic romance Euphues' Shadow (1592), the mythological poem Scilla's Metamorphosis (1589), the satires A Fig for Momus (1595), the play The Wounds of Civil War (c. 1588), and the translation of Josephus (1602).
authors.style: Euphuism softened into pastoral lyricism; a fluent, musical prose of courtship, disguise, and greenwood virtue.
authors.concerns: Pastoral retreat and its therapeutic power; love and loyalty; the quarrel between poetry and the professions.
authors.significance: Through Rosalynde he gave Shakespeare one of his richest sources and helped fix the English pastoral romance as a form.
authors.uncertainty: The dates and details of his travels are reconstructed from allusions in his own works.

authors.name: Thomas Malory
authors.identity: prose writer; knight
authors.biography: Commonly identified with Sir Thomas Malory of Newbold Revel, Warwickshire, a War of the Roses knight with a long record of violence and imprisonment, who describes himself in the colophon of his book as 'knight prisoner' and prays for his deliverance.
