He completed Le Morte Darthur in prison in the ninth year of Edward IV (1469–70) and died on 14 March 1471; Caxton printed the work in 1485.
authors.profile: Author of Le Morte Darthur, the great prose compilation of the Arthurian legend in English, from the sword in the stone through the Grail quest to the death of Arthur and the ruin of the Round Table.
authors.style: A spare, rhythmic prose of paratactic clauses and ritual dialogue; the reduction of the French prose cycles to a single tragic arc; scenes of chivalry, combat, and pathos of enduring power.
authors.concerns: The ideals and contradictions of chivalry — loyalty, love, and treason; the costs of the Grail quest; the fall of a fellowship through sin.
authors.significance: Le Morte Darthur is the definitive English Arthurian book and the first great prose romance in the language; through Caxton's edition it fixed the Arthurian story for all subsequent English literature.
authors.uncertainty: The identification of the author with the Warwickshire knight is probable but not certain; the circumstances of composition are known only from the colophon.
sources: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden

authors.name: Thomas Middleton
authors.identity: dramatist; city chronologer; poet
authors.biography: Baptized 18 April 1580 in London; son of a bricklayer who left a comfortable estate. He matriculated at Queen's College, Oxford, in 1598 but left without a degree to write for the theatre. From 1613 he wrote the annual Lord Mayor's pageants, and in 1620 was appointed City Chronologer. His political allegory A Game at Chess (1624) — a satire on the Spanish match — became the greatest box-office success of the age and provoked a diplomatic uproar. He died at Newington Butts and was buried 4 July 1627.
authors.profile: The most versatile of the Jacobean professionals: city comedies (A Mad World, My Masters, 1605; A Trick to Catch the Old One, c. 1605; A Chaste Maid in Cheapside, 1613), tragedies (Women Beware Women, c. 1621; The Changeling, 1622, with Rowley; and — by the current consensus of attribution — The Revenger's Tragedy, 1606), and the political satire A Game at Chess (1624).
authors.style: Swift, sardonic wit; a fascination with money, appetite, and the mechanics of deceit; ferocious tragic irony; and a moral disgust that never blunts his comic energy.
authors.concerns: The corruptions of City and court; marriage as property transaction; the ethics of revenge; political and religious controversy.
authors.significance: The second great dramatist of the Jacobean age after Shakespeare and Jonson; A Game at Chess is a landmark of political theatre.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of The Revenger's Tragedy has shifted from Tourneur to Middleton on stylistic evidence; much of his output was collaborative and shares are sometimes disputed.

authors.name: Thomas Nashe
authors.identity: pamphleteer; satirist; dramatist; poet
authors.biography: Baptized November 1567 at Lowestoft; son of a curate. BA from St John's College, Cambridge (1586). He came to London about 1588 and earned a living by the pen, often in hardship. He fought the pamphlet war with Gabriel Harvey in the 1590s, fled London after the scandal of The Isle of Dogs (1597), and died in or about 1601, aged thirty-three.
authors.profile: Pierce Penniless His Supplication to the Devil (1592), The Unfortunate Traveller (1594) — the first picaresque novel in English — the anti-Puritan satire Christ's Tears over Jerusalem (1593), the play Summer's Last Will and Testament (1592, printed 1600), the erotic poem The Choice of Valentines, and the lost Isle of Dogs (1597), co-written with Ben Jonson, which closed the London theatres by order of the Privy Council.
authors.style: Furious verbal energy: colloquialism mixed with learned allusion, compound coinages, mock-heroic rhetoric, and the fastest, funniest prose of the decade.
authors.concerns: The condition of authorship without patronage; the hypocrisy of Puritans and pedants; urban poverty and plague; the grotesque body.
authors.significance: The great prose satirist of the 1590s and a pioneer of English fiction; his prose style was absorbed by Jonson, Dekker, and the pamphleteers who followed.
authors.uncertainty: Death date approximate; the circumstances of his last years are obscure.

works.title: Pierce Penniless His Supplication to the Devil

authors.name: Thomas Otway
authors.identity: Restoration tragedian; the master of pathetic, sentimental tragedy in blank verse, whose The Orphan (1680) and above all Venice Preserv'd (1682) were the most performed serious plays of the eighteenth century until superseded by later taste.
authors.biography: Born 3 March 1652 at Trotton, Sussex, educated at Winchester and Christ Church, Oxford, then briefly a soldier in Flanders. Turning to the stage, he wrote comedies (Alcibiades, 1675; Friendship in Fashion, 1678), the tragicomedies Titus and Berenice and Cheats of Scapin (1676–77), and his great tragedies The Orphan (1680) and Venice Preserv'd (1682), the latter inspired by the Popish Plot and starring the actors Thomas Betterton and Elizabeth Barry, with whom he was infatuated. He also wrote the verse tragedy Caius Marius (1679). He died in poverty on 14 April 1685, supposedly choking on bread after a long fast.
authors.profile: The poet of 'pathetic' tragedy, whose heroines and heroes of overwhelming, tender passion moved audiences to tears and created the sentimental mode that dominated the serious stage for a century.
authors.style: Passionate, tender blank verse; the tragedy of suffering innocence; scenes of heightened pathetic emotion; and a rhetoric designed to elicit tears and pity.
authors.concerns: Love, friendship, and betrayal; suffering innocence and female distress; political conspiracy and loyalty; the passions and their tragic cost; and sentimental virtue.
authors.significance: Venice Preserv'd held the stage continuously until the 1830s and was admired by Dryden, Pope, and Johnson; Otway's pathetic tragedy shaped the sentimental drama of the eighteenth century and the acting careers of Betterton and Barry.
authors.uncertainty: Otway's life is documented but romanticised; the story of his death by choking is traditional, and details of his military and amorous life are partly anecdotal.

works.title: The Orphan; or, The Unhappy Marriage
Venice Preserv'd; or, A Plot Discover'd

authors.name: Thomas Paine
authors.identity: Artisan, excise officer and the most powerful political pamphleteer of the Atlantic revolutions, whose Common Sense (1776) turned revolt into ordinary language.
authors.biography: Born at Thetford in 1737, the son of a Quaker staymaker, he served his father's trade, ran briefly and failed at several ventures, and became an officer of excise, a posting he lost after he had petitioned Parliament on his colleagues' pay. Frustrated and in debt, he went to London, fell in with Benjamin Franklin and reached Philadelphia at the end of 1774 with letters of introduction. He began to write for the Pennsylvania Magazine, where in March 1775 appeared his first and sharpest attack on American slavery, and in January 1776 Common Sense, arguing for independence and a republic in prose the mechanic could read. The American Crisis papers, written through the war, were read to Washington's troops; he served the American cause as a writer and in public office, and after the war was rewarded by several states. He returned to England in 1787, and his Rights of Man (1791) and the first part of The Age of Reason (1794), both after the period covered here, made him a prosecuted and then an exiled figure; he died in New York in 1809.
authors.profile: The democrat of plain style, who treated government as a common trade, monarchy as an imposture, and the reader's good sense as the only authority worth obeying.
authors.style: Short declarative sentences, homely metaphor and moral indignation; argument as address, with the cadence of a sermon and the directness of a handbill; sarcasm directed at rank and priestcraft.
authors.concerns: Natural rights and the consent of the governed; the corruption of hereditary and ministerial power; the sin and economics of slavery; deistical religion against priestly and scriptural authority; the interests of labouring men.
authors.significance: He made the case for American independence to the people who had to fight for it, and his later radicalism set the template for popular republicanism, free-thought agitation and the nineteenth-century radical press.
authors.uncertainty: His early manhood is dimly documented, and some of the works attributed to him in the 1770s have been disputed.

authors.name: Thomas Parnell
authors.identity: Anglo-Irish poet and Anglican clergyman, a friend of Pope and a member of the Scriblerus Club, admired for his meditative and light verse.
authors.biography: Parnell was an Irish scholar, commonly held to have been born about 1679 and educated at Trinity College Dublin, where he took holy orders in the Church of Ireland. He rose to hold benefices near Dublin and was archdeacon of Glendalough. Close to Alexander Pope and Jonathan Swift, he joined the Scriblerus Club, and Pope borrowed the theme of his own early Pastoral from Parnell's The Hermit. His short poems circulated in manuscript and periodicals during his lifetime, and a collected Poetical Works appeared posthumously in 1721. He died in Dublin in 1718.
authors.profile: A poet of modest output but high reputation, best known for a single reflective piece, The Hermit, together with light, witty songs and hymns that display ease and quiet moral feeling.
authors.style: Smooth Augustan couplets and lyric measures; a calm, meditative tone; graceful wit; and a plainness and sweetness praised by Pope as a model of true ease.
authors.concerns: Quietist contentment and retirement; moral self-examination; religious resignation; and the pleasantries and vanities of social life.
authors.significance: A transitional poet whose The Hermit anticipated the grave-mediation and churchyard current of later eighteenth-century verse, and a valued link within the Pope and Swift circle.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is uncertain and given as about 1679; some details of his Irish benefices and his family background rest on later biographical tradition.

works.title: Essay on the Different Stiles of Poetry
Peri Bathous, the Art of Sinking in Poetry
The Works of Mr. Martinus Scriblerus

authors.name: Thomas Percy
authors.identity: English scholar, bishop, and antiquary whose Reliques of Ancient English Poetry revived the ballad and shaped the study of old English verse.
authors.biography: Percy, born in Shropshire to a modest family, was educated at school in Shrewsbury and at Christ Church, Oxford, where he became a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries. In 1765 he published the Reliques of Ancient English Poetry, drawing on an old manuscript folio of ballads, which set off a great vogue for the popular ballad and influenced poets from Cowper and Burns to the Romantics. He edited and translated northern and antique material, including Five Pieces of Runic Poetry (1763) and a translation of Paul-Henri Mallet's Northern Antiquities, and prefaced the Reliques with a learned essay on the ancient minstrels. Advanced in the Irish church, he became Bishop of Dromore, where he died in 1789.
authors.profile: An antiquary-bishop and editor whose taste for the ballad, romance, and the early popular poetry of Britain made him a pivotal figure in the recovery and celebration of native literary tradition.
authors.style: In the Reliques, a taste for the simple lyric and the harmony of old ballads; in his own verse, easy, sometimes humorous antique and pastoral imitation; and a scholarly, glossarial editorial method.
authors.concerns: The native and popular origins of English poetry; ballad and romance as genres; national and northern literary antiquities; and the history and manners of the minstrels and their patrons.
authors.significance: The Reliques is one of the most influential anthologies in English literary history, launching the ballad revival, aiding the Romantic revaluation of popular poetry, and stimulating Burns and the later folk movement.
authors.uncertainty: His exact birthplace in Shropshire is given variously; the extent to which he silently revised and modernised the old ballads in the Reliques, rather than reproducing them, has long been debated.

authors.name: Thomas Reid
authors.identity: Minister and professor of Glasgow, founder of the school of common-sense philosophy, who answered the ideal theory of Locke, Berkeley and Hume by appealing to the first principles of human understanding.
authors.biography: Born in the manse at Strachan in the Mearns in 1710, the son of a Church of Scotland minister, he studied at King's College, Aberdeen, was licensed as a preacher in his teens and served the parish of New Machar from 1737. He left the ministry for teaching in 1752, when he was appointed regent in moral philosophy at King's College, Old Aberdeen, where the lectures sharpened his case against the ideal theory. His Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense (1764) argued that perception, memory and belief are original faculties that need no deduction, and that the way of ideas ends in Humean doubt. His Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense (1764) argued that perception, memory and belief are original faculties that require no deduction, and that the way of ideas ends in Humean doubt. Called in 1764 to the Glasgow chair of moral philosophy after Smith's resignation, he held it until failing health forced his retirement in 1781, publishing the Essays on the Intellectual Powers (1785) and the Essays on the Active Powers (1788). He died in Glasgow on 7 October 1796.
authors.profile: A pastor-philosopher who treated scepticism as a disease of theory and met it with an inventory of the mind's innate testimonies.
authors.style: Patient, encyclopaedic and repetitive exposition; classification of faculties and first principles; concrete appeals to sight, testimony and the language of common life, in a minister's measured tones.
authors.concerns: Perception, suggestion and the belief in external existence; the principles that precede reasoning; testimony, language and the rights of common sense; moral obligation, conscience and liberty of agency.
authors.significance: He gave philosophy its common-sense tradition, shaped the Scottish and American schools of mind, and set the problem of how to answer idealist scepticism that later thinkers from the Scottish realists to the twentieth century inherited.
authors.uncertainty: His published output is slight compared with his lectures, and the ordering of his intellectual development before 1764 must be reconstructed from manuscripts.

works.title: An Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense
Essays on the Active Powers of Man
Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man

authors.name: Thomas Sackville
authors.identity: poet; dramatist; statesman
authors.biography: Born in 1536 at Buckhurst, Sussex; educated at Oxford (Inner Temple, and Cambridge). He entered Parliament in 1558 and rose through the law and the council to become Baron Buckhurst (1567), a commissioner at the trial of Mary Queen of Scots, and Earl of Dorset and Lord Treasurer (1599–1608). He died suddenly at the council table at Whitehall on 19 April 1608.
authors.profile: Co-author with Thomas Norton of Gorboduc (performed 1561–62), the first English tragedy in blank verse, and author of the great 'Induction' and the 'Complaint of Henry Duke of Buckingham' contributed to A Mirror for Magistrates (1563), which he planned and edited with others.
authors.style: Grave, stately, Senecan moral verse; the Induction's descent into the underworld is the finest English poetry between Chaucer's death and Spenser.
authors.concerns: The dangers of a divided succession; the falls of princes; counsel and the commonwealth.
authors.significance: Gorboduc founded English tragedy and political drama; the Mirror for Magistrates he fathered became the great poetic storehouse of Elizabethan tragedy.
authors.uncertainty: The exact division of the Gorboduc acts between Sackville and Norton is unknown.

authors.name: Thomas Shadwell
authors.identity: Dramatist, Whig, and poet laureate; a self-professed disciple of Jonson who wrote vigorous comedies of humours and low life (Epsom Wells, The Squire of Alsatia) and whose quarrel with Dryden made him the target of Mac Flecknoe and the 'Og' of Absalom and Achitophel.
authors.biography: Born c. 1642 at Stanthall, Norfolk, educated at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn. A committed Protestant and Whig, he wrote some eighteen plays, including the comedies The Sullen Lovers (1668), Epsom Wells (1672), and The Squire of Alsatia (1688), the tragedy Psyche (1674), and the anti-Catholic The Lancashire Witches (1681). He succeeded Dryden as poet laureate and historiographer royal after the Revolution of 1688 (Dryden, a Catholic, having been deprived). He died on 19 November 1692.
authors.profile: The Jonsonian satirist-comedian of the Restoration, whose plays championed 'humours' comedy, Protestant Whiggism, and a plain, moral, low-comic realism against what he saw as the immorality and wit of Dryden's party.
authors.style: Comedy of humours and dialect; realistic low-life and provincial settings; moral satire; verse prologues and epilogues of political bite; and, in his operas and masques, spectacle.
authors.concerns: Protestant and Whig politics; the satire of vice, foppery, and popery; the moral purpose of comedy; Jonsonian 'humours'; and the defence of plain English sense.
authors.significance: Shadwell's importance lies both in his substantial, socially observant comedies and in his role as Dryden's antagonist — his defeat in the Mac Flecknoe quarrel made him a permanent emblem of literary dullness, though modern critics have reassessed his real comic talent.
authors.uncertainty: Shadwell's birth year is approximate; the Dryden–Shadwell quarrel is well documented, though Shadwell's reputation suffered from its partisan literary afterlife.

authors.name: Thomas Southerne
authors.identity: Irish-born Restoration dramatist; author of the pathetic tragedy The Fatal Marriage (1694) and of the stage adaptation of Behn's Oroonoko (1695), which held the repertory for over a century and made the 'noble slave' a staple of the eighteenth-century theatre.
authors.biography: Born 1660 at Stranorlar, County Donegal, educated at Trinity College, Dublin and the Middle Temple. He came to London, was befriended by Dryden (for whom he wrote a prologue), and produced comedies (The Wives' Excuse, 1691; The Maid's Last Prayer, 1693) and tragedies. His Oroonoko (1695), adapting Behn's novella into a tragedy with a comic subplot, and The Fatal Marriage (1694), built for the actress Elizabeth Barry, were enormously successful. He made a fortune from an Irish sinecure and a government post, retired from the stage early, and lived to the great age of 86, dying on 28 May 1746.
authors.profile: The successful practitioner of pathetic tragedy and the adapter who transmitted Behn's Oroonoko to the eighteenth-century stage in a form that shaped the period's imagination of slavery and noble suffering.
authors.style: Pathetic, sentimental blank verse; tragic suffering heroines; a mixture of tragedy and comic intrigue (in Oroonoko); and a commercially astute dramaturgy.
authors.concerns: Suffering innocence and pathetic tragedy; slavery and the 'noble savage'; love, marriage, and misfortune; and the moral appeal to pity.
authors.significance: Southerne's Oroonoko was the standard stage version of the story for 150 years and the vehicle through which Behn's anti-slavery narrative reached mass audiences; his pathetic tragedies exemplify the sentimental turn of Restoration serious drama.
authors.uncertainty: Southerne's life is documented; the extent of Dryden's hand in his early work and the sources of some plays are matters of scholarship.

works.title: The Fatal Marriage; or, The Innocent Adultery

authors.name: Thomas Sprat
authors.identity: Clergyman, poet, and historian of science; his History of the Royal-Society of London (1667) was the first account of the Society and a manifesto for the plain, factual prose style that the new philosophy demanded.
authors.biography: Born 1635 (baptised) at Henstridge, Dorset, educated at Wadham College, Oxford (Fellow), where he joined Wilkins's circle. He wrote a Pindaric ode on Cromwell (1659) and served as a chaplain and preacher after the Restoration. At the request of the Royal Society he composed its History (1667), celebrating its method and advocating a 'close, naked, natural way of speaking'. He rose in the church to become Dean of Westminster (1683) and Bishop of Rochester (1684), and was involved in the politics of James II's reign and the Revolution. He died on 20 May 1713.
authors.profile: The apologist and historian of the Royal Society whose prose ideal — plain, precise, free of rhetorical 'swelling' — became the manifesto for the modern scientific and plain style.
authors.style: Clear, expository, persuasive prose; historical narrative of an institution; advocacy of the plain style; and occasional Pindaric verse.
authors.concerns: The new experimental philosophy and its institution; the reform of language toward the plain style; the reconciliation of science and religion; and public and ecclesiastical affairs.
authors.significance: Sprat's History of the Royal-Society is the foundational document of the Society's early ideals and the classic statement of the plain-style programme, widely quoted in the history of science and of English prose.
authors.uncertainty: Sprat's birth year is approximate; his ecclesiastical and political career is documented, and his History is partly propagandistic for the Society's ideals.

works.title: The History of the Royal-Society of London for Improving of Natural Knowledge

authors.name: Thomas Traherne
authors.identity: Anglican priest, mystical prose writer, and poet, discovered only in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries; author of Centuries of Thankfulness and the Roman Forgeries, whose ecstatic celebration of innocent vision and divine felicity is unlike anything else in English.
authors.biography: Born c. 1636–37 in Hereford, son of a shoemaker; educated at Brasenose College, Oxford (BA 1656–57), and ordained, holding the living of Credenhill near Hereford (1657–72) while serving as chaplain to Sir Orlando Bridgman at Teddington from 1669. He wrote prolifically in prose and verse but published little in his lifetime (only the anti-Catholic Roman Forgeries, 1673). He died of smallpox on 27 September 1674. His major works — Centuries of Thankfulness, The Kingdom of God, and the poems — circulated in manuscript and were misattributed to Vaughan until Bertram Dobell's editions of 1903–08 established his fame.
authors.profile: The mystic of felicity and wonder, who celebrated the infant soul's apprehension of the infinite in the world and argued that happiness consists in rightly valuing creation as God's gift.
authors.style: A rhapsodic, cumulative prose of wonder and thanksgiving; long flowing 'centuries' or meditative paragraphs; visionary imagery of light, infinity, and childhood; and a lyric poetry of ecstatic innocence.
authors.concerns: Felicity and the desire for God; innocence and the vision of childhood; the infinity of the soul; gratitude and thanksgiving; the goodness of creation; free will and love.
authors.significance: Once unknown, Traherne is now recognised as a major mystical writer whose Centuries and poems anticipate Romantic and modernist celebrations of childhood vision and influenced figures from Christopher Smart to the twentieth century.
authors.uncertainty: Traherne's birth year is uncertain (1636 or 1637); his manuscripts were long misattributed, and the dating and arrangement of his works remain subjects of scholarship.

authors.name: Thomas Usk
authors.identity: poet; political writer; clerk
authors.biography: A London scrivener and clerk who attached himself first to the party of John of Northampton and then betrayed it to Nicholas Brembre and the royalist faction, serving as under-sheriff of Middlesex. Imprisoned after the Merciless Parliament of 1388, he wrote the Testament of Love in the Tower and was executed at Tyburn on 4 March 1388.
authors.profile: Author of the Testament of Love (c. 1384–88), an allegorical prose apologia in the Boethian and Chaucerian manner — for centuries printed as Chaucer's — in which Love consoles the imprisoned author and vindicates his political life.
authors.style: Elaborate allegorical prose with Chaucerian echoes; the fusion of love allegory with political self-defence; Boethian consolation adapted to a treason trial.
authors.concerns: The justice of his political career; fortune, free will, and the consolations of love and philosophy.
authors.significance: The Testament is the first major prose work in the Chaucerian line and a unique document of Ricardian factional politics; its false attribution to Chaucer long shaped the poet's canon.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of his political career come from hostile records.
movements: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy
sources: Leviathan: The English and Latin Texts

authors.name: Thomas Warton
authors.identity: English literary historian, poet, and scholar, professor at Oxford and Poet Laureate, best known for the foundational History of English Poetry.
authors.biography: Thomas Warton the younger, son of the poet Thomas Warton the elder and brother of the critic Joseph Warton, was educated at Oxford, where he became a fellow of Oriel College and later Professor of Poetry. He published early verse, including The Pleasures of Melancholy (1747), contributed odes written jointly with his brother, and wrote an Essay on the Genius and Writings of Pope. His lifelong work, The History of English Poetry, whose first volumes appeared in 1774, 1778, and 1781, pioneered the historical study of medieval and Renaissance verse and its French and Italian sources. He became Poet Laureate in 1785. He died in 1790.
authors.profile: A poet and a literary historian of romantic and antiquarian sympathies who, reacting against strict neoclassicism, prized imagination, the medieval tale, and the historical development of national literature.
authors.style: In his verse, a melancholy, descriptive, and occasionally antiquarian manner; in his History, a learned, digressive, source-hunting scholarly prose that valued imaginative romance and native tradition.
authors.concerns: The origins and historical development of English poetry; the romance tradition and its sources; the imagination versus rules; national literary identity; and the pleasures of melancholy and retirement.
authors.significance: The History of English Poetry is a founding work of English literary history and scholarship, establishing the study of medieval and early modern literature and anticipating Romantic interest in romance and imagination.
authors.uncertainty: He must be carefully distinguished from his father and his brother Joseph, also literary figures, and his exact birthplace is given variously; the completion and dating of the later volumes of his History are uneven.

works.title: Observations on the Faerie Queene of Spenser

authors.name: Tobias Smollett
authors.identity: Scottish novelist, pamphleteer, and historian, a vigorous picaresque writer and editor who was among the major novelists of his generation.
authors.biography: Born in 1721 (baptized in that year) at Dalquhurn in Dunbartonshire into a Scottish family, he was apprenticed to a printer in Glasgow and began writing. He moved to London, where his first novel, The Adventures of Roderick Random (1748), established his reputation, followed by The Adventures of Peregrine Pickle (1751), The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom (1753), and The Adventures of Sir Launcelot Greaves (1766). He edited periodicals and histories and traveled, including a journey that produced The Expedition of Humphry Clinker (1771). He died at Livorno on 17 October 1771.
authors.profile: A novelist of satiric vigor and abrasive humor whose picaresque journeys expose corruption, misanthropy, and the rougher edges of society, and whose late epistolary novel is a landmark of sentimental and travel-inflected fiction.
authors.style: Coarse, energetic, satirical realism; episodic picaresque plotting; caricatured and misanthropic characters; invective and humor; and in Humphry Clinker a comic polyphony of contrasting epistolary voices.
authors.concerns: National identity and Anglo-Scottish tension; cruelty and benevolence in society; travel, observation, and the state of the nation; the politics of faction; and misanthropy versus social feeling.
authors.significance: A leading figure in the rise of the novel and of Scottish letters within British culture, whose picaresque satires shaped later fiction and whose Humphry Clinker remains a touchstone of the comic epistolary novel.
authors.uncertainty: The year of his birth rests on baptismal records, and some details of his early life, apprenticeship, and the full extent of his journalistic and editorial work remain imperfectly documented.

works.title: A Journey Through France and Italy
The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom
The Adventures of Gil Blas of Santillane
The Adventures of Sir Launcelot Greaves

authors.name: Walter Hilton
authors.identity: mystic; devotional writer; Augustinian canon
authors.biography: Probably educated at Cambridge and trained in canon law before becoming an Augustinian canon of Thurgarton Priory, Nottinghamshire; he died on 24 March 1396. His writings circulated widely and were printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1494.
authors.profile: Author of the Scale of Perfection (Book I c. 1380s, addressed to an anchoress; Book II c. 1390s), the most influential English treatise on contemplation; of the Epistle on the Mixed Life, addressed to a devout layman; and of other works including Of Angels' Song and the translation of the Stimulus Amoris attributed to him.
authors.style: Measured, theologically precise prose; the famous image of the spiritual life as a ladder or scale; cautious discrimination between true and false mystical experience; clarity and pastoral warmth.
authors.concerns: The reformation of the soul in the image of God; the relation of active and contemplative lives; the discernment of spirits.
authors.significance: The classic systematizer of English mysticism; the Scale of Perfection remained a standard of English devotional reading into the seventeenth century (used by Augustine Baker and his circle).
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and early career conjectural; some works attributed to him are disputed.
sources: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

authors.name: Walter Map
authors.identity: satirist; courtier; churchman
authors.biography: A Herefordshire-born clerk of Welsh descent who studied at Paris and served Henry II as a royal justice and travelling ambassador; he attended the Lateran Council of 1179 and became a canon of St Paul's and archdeacon of Oxford. The archsatirist of the Angevin court, he died c. 1210.
authors.profile: Author of De Nugis Curialium (Courtiers' Trifles, c. 1181–92), a miscellany of satire, gossip, marvels, and history that preserves some of the earliest Arthurian and fairy material in Latin; the Goliardic poems once attributed to him are not his.
authors.style: Biting, allusive, deliberately disordered satire of the court and the religious orders; the anecdote raised to moral fable; a proto-Renaissance pessimism about the world he served.
authors.concerns: The vices of courts and monasteries; the vanity of worldly service; the relations of the sexes; the marvels of Wales and the Celtic past.
authors.significance: De Nugis is the supreme literary monument of the twelfth-century courtier's disenchantment and a key source for the early Arthurian and Herla/fairy traditions.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the De Nugis survives in a single manuscript and its text is unstable.
themes: Country retirement and the estate poem
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume D: The Romantic Period

authors.name: Werferth
authors.identity: translator; bishop
authors.biography: Bishop of Worcester from c. 872 to his death (c. 915); one of the scholars of King Alfred's court circle named by Asser.
authors.profile: Translator of Gregory the Great's Dialogues into Old English (c. 890s), a work commissioned by Alfred and prefaced by him; the earliest extensive Old English translation of a major patristic text.
authors.style: Faithful, competent Mercian-flavoured prose, somewhat more literal than the other Alfredian translations.
authors.concerns: The transmission of Gregory's hagiographical and pastoral teaching to a vernacular audience.
authors.significance: A key figure of the Alfredian translation program; his Dialogues preserve a major stage in the development of Old English prose.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the attribution of the translation rests on Asser's Life of Alfred and Alfred's own Preface.
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume II: 1042–1189

authors.name: William Baldwin
authors.identity: satirist; editor; corrector of printing
authors.biography: Born about 1515; a scholar of Oxford who became corrector of the king's printing under Edward VI and a prolific editor and compiler. His Treatise of Moral Philosophy appeared in 1547; his prose satire Beware the Cat, written in 1552–53, was printed in 1561. He planned and partly compiled A Mirror for Magistrates, printed in 1559 after his death. He died about 1563.
authors.profile: The author of the first English work of sustained prose fiction and the begetter of A Mirror for Magistrates. Beware the Cat — a night-long exchange of stories about cats, set in a London printing house and framed as a fantastic listening experiment — is the first English novel in embryo, and its anti-Catholic satire made it dangerous enough to be suppressed. The Mirror, which he edited and contributed to, became one of the most influential books of the Elizabethan age.
authors.style: Framed narrative in the plain style; printer's-shop realism; satirical fable with a serious theological edge.
authors.concerns: Protestant polemic against the old religion; the uses of fiction for truth-telling; the moral instruction of magistrates through the falls of great men.
authors.significance: A founding figure of English prose fiction and of the complaint tradition; his Mirror for Magistrates supplied subjects and rhetoric to Spenser, Shakespeare, and the whole Elizabethan tragic imagination.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; the division of authorship within the Mirror is editorial.
themes: Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history

authors.name: William Beckford
authors.identity: English writer, collector, and politician, the fabulously wealthy author of the Gothic-Oriental tale Vathek.
authors.biography: Born on 29 September 1760 in London, the son of William Beckford, twice Lord Mayor of London and a West Indian planter and politician, he inherited great wealth and entered public life as a Member of Parliament and briefly a sheriff. As a young man he wrote the Oriental romance Vathek, originally composed in French and published in English in 1786. He built the eccentric country house at Fonthill Abbey and pursued collecting and writing. He died on 2 May 1844.
authors.profile: The author of Vathek, a tale of oriental magnificence and forbidden knowledge that fused Gothic luxury with the Arabian Nights tradition and helped define the decadent and exotic strain in Romantic-era fiction.
authors.style: Ornate, sensational, orientalizing prose; lavish descriptive excess; a framing of wonder and magic; and a deliberate artificiality and luxury of detail inherited from the Arabian Nights vogue.
authors.concerns: Curiosity, power, and transgression; the pursuit of forbidden knowledge; orientalism and exotic magnificence; pleasure and damnation; and aesthetic luxury.
authors.significance: A distinctive and influential author of Gothic-Oriental fiction, whose Vathek became a landmark of the supernatural tale and an important source for later decadent and fantasy writing.
authors.uncertainty: His birth date is well attested; some details of the composition and translation history of Vathek, and of the dating of his writings, remain subjects of scholarly note rather than of real dispute.

authors.name: William Blackstone
authors.identity: Oxford don, serjeant at law, judge and Tory MP, whose four-volume Commentaries on the Laws of England (1765-1769) made English law a readable rational system.
authors.biography: Born in Cheapside in London in 1723, the posthumous son of a City merchant, he was educated at a London grammar school and at Pembroke College, Oxford, with the help of relations, and was elected a fellow of All Souls. Called to the bench of the Middle Temple and practising on the Oxford and home circuits, he won fame by a book on gavelkind and by lecturing on English law, which led to his appointment as the first Vinerian professor in 1758. His Analysis of the Laws of England (1756) and his Discourse on the Study of the Law (1765) prepared the Commentaries, published in four parts between 1765 and 1769 and immediately made his name. He sat in the Commons, was appointed to the bench of the Common Pleas and knighted in 1770, and was transferred to the King's Bench in 1779, where his rigorous, sometimes unpopular judgments tested his own theory of law. He died in London on 14 February 1780.
authors.profile: The great systematiser and apologist of the common law, who presented its intricacies as an ordered, decent and largely admirable inheritance.
authors.style: Clear, stately, judicious prose that explains difficulty without hiding it; balanced periods and a scholar's courtesy; historical narrative used to legitimate existing doctrine.
authors.concerns: The reasonableness and continuity of the common law; the rights of persons and of things; the nature of law, sovereignty and the reach of parliamentary authority; the legal condition of servants, women, children and colonial subjects; the relation of law to religion and morality.
authors.significance: The Commentaries became the standard education of English-speaking lawyers for two centuries and, with their American reprints, one of the chief sources of early American legal and political vocabulary; Bentham's attack on them opened the age of law reform.
authors.uncertainty: The order and dating of his lectures and of the several editions of the Commentaries, which he revised to his death, are complex and disputed.

works.title: An Analysis of the Laws of England
Commentaries on the Laws of England

authors.name: William Camden
authors.identity: antiquarian; historian; herald; schoolmaster
authors.biography: Born 2 May 1551 in the Old Bailey, London. Educated at Christ's Hospital and St Paul's School, then at Magdalen and Christ Church, Oxford. He taught at Westminster School (1575–97), where his pupils included Ben Jonson, and ended his career as Clarenceux King of Arms (1597). He died on 9 November 1623 at Chislehurst, Kent.
authors.profile: Britannia (1586, in Latin; English translation by Philemon Holland, 1610), the chorographical description of Britain, and the Annales of the reign of Elizabeth I (1615–25).
authors.style: Exact, methodical, elegant Latin and an English style of grave plainness; the scholar's impartiality joined to patriotic purpose.
authors.concerns: The recovery of British antiquity; the writing of sober, documented history against legend; national identity through the past.
authors.significance: The father of English antiquarianism; his Britannia launched the great tradition of county and national history that runs through the seventeenth century and beyond.
authors.uncertainty: The accuracy of the Annales on some episodes is disputed by later historians.

authors.name: William Caxton
authors.identity: printer; translator; merchant
authors.biography: A Kentish mercer who spent three decades in the Low Countries, rising to governor of the English merchants at Bruges, where he learned printing at Cologne and produced the first book printed in English, his own Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (Bruges, c. 1473–74). In 1476 he set up the first English press at Westminster, printing some hundred books — Chaucer, Malory, Gower, Lydgate, the Golden Legend, and his own translations — before his death c. 1491.
authors.profile: Printer and translator: the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (c. 1473–74), The Game and Playe of the Chesse (1474), the History of Reynard the Fox (1481), the Golden Legend (1483), and numerous prologues and epilogues that constitute a body of critical prose.
authors.style: Lucid, idiomatic translation from French sources; a merchant's plain style enriched by courtly vocabulary; the prologues' genial self-presentation as servant of the 'comyn wele'.
authors.concerns: The provision of good books in English; the standardization of the language ('ouer rude termes' and the dialect of Kent); the moral and chivalric education of the nobility and gentry.
authors.significance: The introducer of printing to England: his press fixed the form of the English classics, began the standardization of written English, and made the fifteenth century's literature the sixteenth century's inheritance.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the exact site and date of his first printing remain debated.
themes: The education of princes and magistrates

works.title: Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye

sources: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne

authors.name: William Collins
authors.identity: English lyric poet of the Odes, associated with Gray and with the rise of imaginative, impassioned, and personified poetry.
authors.biography: Collins was born at Chichester, the son of an insurer, and studied at Winchester College and at Queen's College, Oxford. A volume of odes appeared in 1746 but sold poorly and was effectively withdrawn, and the pieces came to be prized chiefly after his death. Later poems such as Ode on the Poetical Character and his oriental and Persian imitations mark his range. Mental illness and early death cut short his career; he was tended in his last years by his lifelong friend the painter Joseph Hammell, and he died at Chichester in 1759. Gray, who admired him, did much to secure his posthumous reputation.
authors.profile: A short-lived lyric poet whose best work casts abstract qualities as personified figures in an atmosphere of imaginative reverie, enthusiasm, and melancholy; he stands between the Augustans and the pre-Romantics.
authors.style: Rich, sustained personification; lyric and ode measures of great musicality; elevated, sometimes archaic diction; and an intoxicating, enthusiastic imaginative tone distinct from Pope's point.
authors.concerns: The power of imagination and poetic enthusiasm; the personified emotions and qualities of the mind; the appeal of the exotic, the supernatural, and melancholy; and the poet's isolation.
authors.significance: One of the most important lyric poets between Pope and the Romantics; his odes were championed by Samuel Johnson and later admired for prefiguring Romantic imagination and sensibility.
authors.uncertainty: The number and publication history of his odes are complicated by the suppression of his 1746 volume and later editorial reconstruction; the nature and onset of his mental illness are imperfectly documented.

works.title: Odes on Several Descriptive and Allegorical Subjects
The Passions: An Ode for Music

authors.name: William Congreve
authors.identity: The greatest master of the comedy of manners; author of The Way of the World (1700), Love for Love (1695), and the tragedy The Mourning Bride (1697), whose flawless comic prose and brilliant repartee represent the summit of English wit comedy.
authors.biography: Born 24 January 1670 at Bardsey, Yorkshire, son of an army officer; raised in Ireland and educated at Kilkenny and Trinity College, Dublin. He came to London, studied law at the Middle Temple, and astonished the town with The Old Bachelor (1693), followed by The Double Dealer (1693), Love for Love (1695), and The Mourning Bride (1697, the most successful tragedy of the decade). His masterwork The Way of the World (1700) was coolly received, and, sensitive to criticism and enjoying a comfortable government sinecure and the friendship of the Whig Junto (and a long liaison with Henrietta Godolphin, Duchess of Marlborough), he wrote little after 1700. He died on 19 January 1729 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The consummate artist of comic prose, whose plays achieve a perfection of wit, structure, and tone — 'the prose Shakespeare' — treating the negotiation of love, marriage, and money in a society of manners with ironic elegance.
authors.style: Brilliantly epigrammatic prose; the 'proviso' scene of negotiated marriage; balanced, ironic repartee; elegant plotting; and, in The Mourning Bride, sonorous blank-verse declamation.
authors.concerns: Wit and true wit; love, marriage, and money; hypocrisy, affectation, and scandal; the social code of the town; and the relation of art and manners.
authors.significance: The Way of the World is universally regarded as the finest comedy of manners in English; Congreve defined the genre, influenced Sheridan and Wilde, and his tragic lines ('Musick has charms to soothe a savage breast') became proverbial.
authors.uncertainty: Congreve's life is well documented; his early retirement from writing is explained by his finances, health, and sensitivity to criticism, though the reasons remain partly conjectural.

authors.name: William Cowper
authors.identity: English poet and hymn-writer of the evangelical and sentimental age, whose Task and Olney Hymns opened a new nature poetry and whose life was marked by depression and religious terror.
authors.biography: Cowper was born in Hertfordshire, the son of a clergyman, was called to the bar, and after a breakdown and an attempt at self-destruction found a measure of religious assurance in evangelical Christianity. He lived much of his life in retirement under the shelter of the Hill family, at Olney and later in Norfolk. With John Newton he contributed to the Olney Hymns (1779), writing such hymns as God Moves in a Mysterious Way. His long conversational poem The Task (1785) established his fame, followed by translations of Homer and shorter poems including The Castaway and an account of his despair. Plagued all his life by melancholy and by a recurring conviction of reprobation, he died in 1800.
authors.profile: A poet of retirement, domestic life, nature, and religious feeling, who combined the descriptive, meditative, and comic-familiar modes and wrote with startling honesty of depression and faith.
authors.style: Smooth, conversational blank verse of the familiar line; descriptive tenderness and homely humour; a passionate, troubled religious lyricism; and a gift for hymn and melancholy song.
authors.concerns: Providence, evangelical assurance, and despair; the consolation of rural and domestic life; anti-slavery and humane feeling; nature, retirement, and melancholy; and the critique of luxury and city life.
authors.significance: A leading poet of sensibility and the evangelical revival and one of the most influential nature poets before the Romantics, admired by Wordsworth and Coleridge for the honesty and feeling of his verse.
authors.uncertainty: A lifelong fear of eternal reprobation makes his own accounts of his religious states hard to date precisely; the chronology of his breakdowns and his late poem on despair is partly conjectural.

authors.name: William Dunbar
authors.identity: poet; courtier; priest
authors.biography: A graduate of St Andrews (MA 1479) and a Franciscan novice in his youth, he served from c. 1500 as a clerk and poet at the court of James IV, for whom he wrote the celebratory poems of the marriage to Margaret Tudor (1503); he received a royal pension from 1500. He disappears from record after the battle of Flodden (1513), and died c. 1520.
authors.profile: Author of some eighty poems preserved chiefly in the Bannatyne and Maitland manuscripts: the Lament for the Makaris (c. 1505), The Goldyn Targe, The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo (c. 1500–07), the flying with Kennedy, the dream allegories, and the great occasional verse of the court.
authors.style: The most technically virtuosic of the makars: aureate magnificence (The Goldyn Targe) alternating with scabrous colloquial satire (the Tretis); the refrain, the flying, the alliterative line, and the French formes fixes all mastered; a voice by turns celebratory, venomous, elegiac, and devout.
authors.concerns: The vanity of life and the power of death (Timor mortis conturbat me); the hypocrisies of court and clergy; the duties and pleasures of the royal court.
authors.significance: With Henryson, the greatest poet of medieval Scotland; the Lament for the Makaris is one of the supreme elegies in the language and gave the Scottish tradition its name.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; his clerical status and career details are conjectural.
themes: Order and degree: the body politic

works.title: The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo

sources: The Cambridge Companion to Milton, 2nd edition

authors.name: William Langland
authors.birthplace: probably Cleobury Mortimer, Shropshire, or the Malvern Hills area
authors.identity: poet; satirist; allegorist
authors.biography: Almost everything known of him is inferred from Piers Plowman, whose dreamer 'Will' is a long-clothed clerk of the Malvern country, married, and living in London in poverty among the Cornhill folk; the poem's A-text (c. 1367–70), B-text (c. 1377–79), and C-text (c. 1386–88) show a career of continuous revision. He is commonly identified with the William Langland recorded at Oxford and in London in the 1390s, though the identification is uncertain.
authors.profile: Author of Piers Plowman, the greatest English allegorical poem: a sequence of dream visions in which Will searches for Truth, Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest amid the estates of fourteenth-century England.
authors.style: Unrhymed alliterative long lines of extraordinary range — satiric, homiletic, apocalyptic, tender; the allegorical dream vision fused with estates satire and biblical exegesis; the personification of abstract virtues with concrete social observation.
authors.concerns: The reform of society and church through penance and truth; the theology of grace and merit; poverty, labour, and the social order.
authors.significance: With Chaucer and Gower, the third summit of Ricardian poetry; Piers Plowman became the rallying text of reformist and radical traditions (it was read by the rebels of 1381 and printed by the Tudor reformers) and one of the most studied poems in English.
authors.uncertainty: Biography almost entirely conjectural; the attribution of the poem rests on manuscript rubrics and internal evidence.
sources: The Poems of Andrew Marvell

authors.name: William Law
authors.identity: Nonjuring clergyman and devotional writer, author of A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life (1728) and of the Christian perfection tracts that shaped Methodist and Anglo-Catholic piety.
authors.biography: Born at King's Cliffe in Northamptonshire in 1686, he was educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and held a fellowship there. He refused the oaths to the Hanoverian succession in 1715, lost his fellowship and spent the following decade as a schoolmaster in London. Retiring to his birthplace in 1727, he lived there, writing and governing his household, until his death in 1761. In 1726 he entered the stage controversy with an attack on theatrical entertainment as a snare of Satan; in 1728 A Serious Call applied the rules of devotion to the ordinary hours of a gentleman's or a lady's day. From the 1730s his letters on the spirit of prayer and on the spirit of faith set him against Bishop Warburton; with the help of the lawyer William Bryan he edited and translated Jacob Boehme and printed a selection of Boehme's works in 1745.
authors.profile: A practical diviner of the daily closet, whose prose makes the whole of life, and not its religious intervals, an offering.
authors.style: Plain, urgent, exact devotional prose; moral portraiture and example; a rule-of-life cadence of precept, reproof and prayer; later a mystical exuberance of type and figure.
authors.concerns: The universality of devotion; Christian perfection and the death of self-will; church, oath and civil obedience; the stage, dress and the amusements of the world; the hidden God of Boehmean mysticism.
authors.significance: The Serious Call made him the most read English devotional writer between Bunyan and the Tractarians; it formed the religious imagination of Samuel Johnson and of the Oxford movement, and his mystical writings fed Methodist and Anglo-Catholic holiness.
authors.uncertainty: His reasons for conforming outwardly after 1727 are debated, and the serial publication of his letters makes their chronology awkward.

works.title: A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life

authors.name: William Lily
authors.identity: grammarian; first High Master of St Paul's School
authors.biography: Born at Odiham about 1468; studied at Oxford and in Italy, where he learned Greek. Appointed by John Colet as the first High Master of St Paul's School in 1512, he wrote the Latin grammar that, revised by Colet and Erasmus, became the standard school grammar of England. He died in February 1522 (new style 1523).
authors.profile: Author of the grammar that schooled England for three centuries. The Short Introduction of Grammar ('Lily's Grammar'), with its English accidence and its Latin Brevissima Institutio, was prescribed by royal proclamation under Henry VIII and Edward VI and memorized by every grammar-school boy from Shakespeare to Johnson — who quotes it, and its misquotations, throughout the literature of the period.
authors.style: The schoolmaster's clarity: paradigms, rules in English for boys, Latin examples; a grammar written to be memorized.
authors.concerns: The reform of Latin teaching on humanist principles; the founding of a public grammar school; the union of Greek learning with Christian education.
authors.significance: The author of the most widely used textbook in English history; Lily's Grammar structured the linguistic formation of the entire literate class of early modern England.
authors.uncertainty: The exact division of the grammar's authorship among Lily, Colet, and Erasmus is editorial.
genres: Moral Philosophy and the Theory of Society

authors.name: William Mason
authors.identity: English poet, dramatist, and garden theorist, author of blank-verse tragedy and essays on poetry and gardening, associated with pre-Romantic sensibility.
authors.biography: Mason, sometimes called the younger to distinguish him from a kinsman of the same name, was educated at Westminster School and Queen's College, Oxford, and inherited an estate at Nuthall in Nottinghamshire. His Poems (1754) won immediate attention, and he followed with elegiac and didactic verse, including essays on eclogues and on garden design. He turned to blank-verse historical tragedy with Elfrida (1763) and Caractacus (1769), and he wrote a Life of his friend Thomas Gray. A keen gardener and man of letters, he corresponded widely within the literary circles of the age. He died at Nuthall in 1797.
authors.profile: A poet, dramatist, and man of letters whose work spans the sentimental elegy, the garden essay, and declamatory blank-verse tragedy, reflecting the movement from Augustan taste toward pre-Romantic feeling.
authors.style: Correct, elevated blank verse; didactic ease in the essay poem; mournful sensibility in the elegy; and a rhetorical, declamatory grandeur in the tragedies, with a cultivated taste for the picturesque garden.
authors.concerns: Taste and the design of gardens; moral and heroic virtue in historical drama; friendship, biography, and literary memory; melancholy, retirement, and religious consolation.
authors.significance: A transitional figure of later-eighteenth-century letters whose garden writings and blank-verse tragedy reflect the spread of picturesque taste and pre-Romantic sensibility; his Life of Gray is an important literary document.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace is given variously in biographical accounts; the precise chronology of his poems and essays, and his relation to the older William Mason of the same family, require careful distinction.

works.title: Edwin and Morcar, the Earls of Mercia and Northumberland

authors.name: William of Malmesbury
authors.identity: historian; Benedictine monk
authors.biography: A monk and librarian of Malmesbury Abbey, where he spent his whole career, becoming precentor and, late in life, refusing the abbacy; he died c. 1143. The greatest English historian since Bede, he gathered his materials from libraries across England and corresponded with the learned of his day.
authors.profile: Author of the Gesta Regum Anglorum (first version 1125, revised to c. 1135), the Gesta Pontificum Anglorum (1125), the Historia Novella (c. 1140–43), and saints' lives including those of Wulfstan, Dunstan, and Aldhelm.
authors.style: Polished, allusive Latin modelled on classical historians; critical assessment of sources; a gift for anecdote and character; patriotic pride in English history tempered by Norman loyalties.
authors.concerns: The continuity of the English kingdom from the Anglo-Saxons to his own day; the moral exemplarity of history; the recovery of the English past after the Conquest.
authors.significance: The founder of critical English historiography after Bede; his Gesta Regum is the principal narrative source for Anglo-Norman history and the model for the century's chroniclers.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; his Anglo-Saxon sources were largely lost in the Reformation.
sources: The Life of Samuel Johnson, 6 volumes (Birkbeck Hill edition)

authors.name: William of Ockham
authors.identity: philosopher; logician; political theorist; Franciscan friar
authors.biography: A Franciscan who studied and taught at Oxford, where his teaching was denounced to the papal court at Avignon (1324); while awaiting judgement he became embroiled in the Franciscan poverty controversy, fled Avignon with Michael of Cesena in 1328, and spent the rest of his life under the protection of the emperor Louis of Bavaria at Munich, writing political works against the papacy until his death in 1347.
authors.profile: Author of the Summa Logicae (c. 1323), the Ordinationes on the Sentences, the Quodlibeta, and a series of political treatises on poverty and papal power.
authors.style: The 'razor' of terminist logic: relentless elimination of superfluous entities and distinctions; a new theory of signs and mental language; clear, devastating polemic in the political works.
authors.concerns: The foundations of logic and knowledge; universals and nominalism; the limits of papal power; apostolic poverty.
authors.significance: The most consequential English philosopher of the Middle Ages: his nominalism reshaped European philosophy and theology (via Buridan, the via moderna, and Luther), and his political theory laid groundwork for conciliarism and modern notions of sovereignty.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his early works rests on internal evidence.
themes: Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
sources: The Rise of the Novel: Studies in Defoe, Richardson and Fielding

authors.name: William Paley
authors.identity: Archdeacon of Carlisle and the century's master of utilitarian divinity, whose Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy (1785) made happiness and obedience the whole of duty.
authors.biography: Born at Peterborough in July 1743, the son of a clergyman who later became headmaster of the free school at Giggleswick, he was educated at that school and at Christ's College, Cambridge, where an idle first year was retrieved by hard reading, a fellowship and a tutorship that made him the most successful coach of his university. He took orders in the Church of England, held a succession of northern livings at Musgrave, Dalston and Appleby, and was made archdeacon of Carlisle in 1782. His Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy (1785) soon became a standard university text and the target of reviewers who thought it reduced virtue to expedience. His argument for the undesigned coincidence of the apostolic letters appeared in the Horae Paulinae of 1790, and his Evidences of Christianity (1794) and Natural Theology (1802), both later than the period covered here, long stood as textbooks in the schools of theology. He was installed at Bishopwearmouth in his last years and died on 25 May 1805.
authors.profile: A clear-eyed churchman who wrote the morality of obedience and the evidences of belief for a reading public that wanted argument in plain terms.
authors.style: Conversational, concrete and unornamented; cases and common-life examples carried through a single rule; the plainness of a good tutor, with a polemicist's patience in reply.
authors.concerns: Utility as the measure of duty; the obligations imposed by civil government and by the established church; the evidences of revelation and the credibility of miracle; design in nature and the relation of pleasure to virtue.
authors.significance: He gave utilitarian ethics its first systematic ecclesiastical form and supplied the teleological argument in the version Mill and Darwin had to answer; his textbooks governed English theological education for a generation.
authors.uncertainty: The order in which his preferments and lecture texts were produced is complicated by posthumous edition and by his own revisions.

works.title: The Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy

authors.name: William Robertson
authors.identity: Minister of the Church of Scotland, principal of Edinburgh and royal historiographer, whose History of America (1777) made philosophical history a professional discipline in Britain.
authors.biography: Born at Borthwick near Langholm in 1721, the son of a country clergyman, he was educated at Edinburgh, entered the ministry and served a southern parish before he removed to Edinburgh and became one of the city's most fashionable preachers. The History of Scotland (1759) established him as the leading historian of his generation, and the great work on the reign of Charles V (1769) displayed his command of archives and of the European sixteenth century. Appointed principal of the University of Edinburgh in 1762 and royal historiographer, he at last produced the History of America (1777), three volumes of sources, geography, conquest and character which were translated across Europe, and the History of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth (1787). His disquisition on the ancients' knowledge of India came in 1791, after the period with which this record deals. He was a leader of the moderate interest in the church, a friend of Hume, Smith, Ferguson and Home, and died in 1793.
authors.profile: The historian of states and religions who wrote narrative as instructed enquiry, combining Scottish church politics with the sources of the Spanish and Italian archives.
authors.style: Dignified, lucid, well-paced narrative; disquisitions and notes carrying the argument; a preacher's moral seriousness and an editor's restraint; balance of character, cause and consequence.
authors.concerns: The origins of American civilisation and conquest; the political and religious history of Europe in the age of Charles V; feudal law, ranks and the rise of the commons; the character of Queen Elizabeth and of the Reformation.
authors.significance: He professionalised historical writing in Britain, gave the English-speaking world its standard account of America's discovery and conquest, and set the model of philosophic narrative that Gibbon and the nineteenth century inherited.
authors.uncertainty: His early parish years are documented thinly, and his use of other men's manuscripts and collections has been re-assessed by later scholarship.

works.title: The History of the Progress and Termination of the Roman Republic
The History of the Reign of the Emperor Charles V

authors.name: William Roper
authors.identity: biographer; lawyer; More's son-in-law
authors.biography: Born about 1496; a lawyer of Lincoln's Inn who married Margaret, Thomas More's eldest daughter, in 1521, and lived in More's household at Chelsea for sixteen years. He wrote The Life of Sir Thomas More between about 1553 and 1558 from intimate memory; it circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1626. He died on 4 January 1578.
authors.profile: Author of the first great English biography of a private man. The Life of Sir Thomas More — the portrait of the Chancellor at Chelsea: his prayers, his jests, his relations with his family, and his final refusal of the oath — is the classic of Tudor life-writing and the foundation of the More legend that Shakespeare's play and the later tradition inherited.
authors.style: Plain, affectionate, anecdotal prose; the vivid recalled dialogue of the Chelsea household; a son-in-law's reverence without hagiographical inflation.
authors.concerns: The memory and example of More; conscience against the state; the sanctity of the family and the household.
authors.significance: Established the English biographical tradition and supplied the human More to every later age; a primary source of the first importance for the English Reformation.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

works.title: The Life of Sir Thomas More

authors.name: William Shakespeare
authors.identity: Playwright, poet, and actor; the central figure of English literature, author of some 39 plays, 154 sonnets, and two narrative poems.
authors.biography: Baptized 26 April 1564 at Stratford-upon-Avon, son of the glover and alderman John Shakespeare; educated at the Stratford grammar school. He married Anne Hathaway in 1582 (children Susanna, and the twins Hamnet and Judith), and by 1592 was established in the London theatre (Greene's 'upstart crow' attack). He wrote for the Lord Chamberlain's Men (from 1594) and its successor the King's Men (from 1603), was a sharer in the Globe (1599) and Blackfriars, and prospered as actor, playwright, and investor, buying New Place in Stratford in 1597. The narrative poems Venus and Adonis (1593) and The Rape of Lucrece (1594) were his first printed works; the Sonnets appeared in 1609. He retired to Stratford around 1613 and died there on 23 April 1616; the First Folio of his plays was published by Heminges and Condell in 1623.
authors.profile: The supreme dramatist of the language and its greatest poet of the human interior: his histories, comedies, tragedies, and romances transformed every genre they touched, and his sonnets reinvented the Petrarchan sequence as a meditation on love, time, and art.
authors.style: Unmatched range of register — from the euphuistic wit and sonneteering of the early plays to the metaphysical density of the great tragedies and the late romances' verse of reconciliation; mastery of blank verse, prose, and song; the invention of character through soliloquy.
authors.concerns: Kingship, legitimacy, and the body politic; love, jealousy, and self-deception; time, mortality, and the immortality of art; the theatre itself as the mirror of nature; conscience and the divided self.
authors.significance: The measure of English literature: his works constitute the largest single achievement of the language's canon, translated into every tongue and performed continuously since the 1590s.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of the plays rests on printed dates, records of performance, and stylistic evidence; the authorship of several plays (Titus Andronicus, Pericles, Henry VIII, The Two Noble Kinsmen, Edward III, Sir Thomas More) is collaborative, and the biographical record between 1585 and 1592 is a blank.

authors.name: William Shenstone
authors.identity: English poet and gardener, of the Leasowes, a pastoral writer and letter-writer whose ornamental garden became an eighteenth-century landmark of taste.
authors.biography: Shenstone was born into the Worcestershire gentry, educated at Halesowen and at Pembroke College, Cambridge, and succeeded to the family estate, the Leasowes, which he laid out as a celebrated ornamental farm. He wrote the pastoral poem The Schoolmistress (1742) and other pastorals, songs, and epistles, publishing his Poetical Works in a collected form in 1763. His letters and his critical and horticultural writings circulated among friends and were partly printed after his death, notably his account of the Leasowes and his essays on taste and gardening. He died unmarried at the Leasowes in 1763.
authors.profile: A poet of retirement, rural sympathy, and sensibility, and a practised maker of landscapes; his verse and his garden together embody the cult of the picturesque and the ornamented farm.
authors.style: Gentle, conversational pastoral and occasional verse; Spenserian and Thomsonian descriptive influence; a warm, familiar, sometimes digressive epistolary prose; and an aesthetic of artless variety.
authors.concerns: Rural life and the education of rustic minds; taste, the picturesque, and the design of landscapes; retirement, friendship, and benevolence; and the integration of art and nature.
authors.significance: A central figure in the development of the English landscape garden and picturesque taste, and a respected pastoral and epistolary writer linking Thomson's nature poetry to later sensibility.
authors.uncertainty: His exact birthplace is given variously in accounts of the Worcestershire parish; the precise dating of his garden improvements and of the circulation of his letters and essays remains partly conjectural.

authors.name: William Tyndale
authors.identity: Bible translator; reformer; martyr
authors.biography: Born in Gloucestershire about 1494; educated at Oxford (BA 1512, MA 1515) and Cambridge. Denied episcopal patronage for an English Bible, he left England in 1524 and worked in Germany and the Low Countries: his New Testament was printed at Worms in 1526 and smuggled into England; the Pentateuch followed in 1530 and a revised New Testament in 1534. Betrayed at Antwerp in 1535, he was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde on 6 October 1536.
authors.profile: The father of the English Bible. His translations — made from the Greek of Erasmus and the Hebrew — gave English scripture its enduring shape: the Authorized Version of 1611 retains perhaps ninety per cent of his New Testament phrasing. As a polemicist he wrote the most effective Reformation tracts in English: The Obedience of a Christian Man (1528), The Parable of the Wicked Mammon (1528), The Practice of Prelates (1530), and An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue (1531).
authors.style: The plain style at its greatest: short sentences, monosyllabic Saxon diction, and rhythms tuned for reading aloud; learned argument made colloquial and urgent.
authors.concerns: The authority of scripture over church and prince; justification by faith; the translation of the Word into every ploughboy's language; the duty of obedience and its limits.
authors.significance: The principal architect of English biblical prose and of the language of English devotion; his translation work shaped the King James Bible and, through it, the speech of the English-speaking world.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of his early Gloucestershire life rest on Foxe's Acts and Monuments.
themes: The public sphere, print, and the periodical

works.title: An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue
The Obedience of a Christian Man
The Parable of the Wicked Mammon

sources: A Treatise of Human Nature (Clarendon Edition of the Works of David Hume)

authors.name: William Wycherley
authors.identity: Restoration dramatist; author of the two fiercest comedies of manners, The Country Wife (1675) and The Plain Dealer (1676), whose savage wit and moral seriousness about lust, hypocrisy, and jealousy set him apart from his more elegant contemporaries.
authors.biography: Born c. 1640–41 at Clive, Shropshire, educated at Queen's College, Oxford, the Middle Temple, and in France (where he briefly became a Catholic before reverting). He served at sea in the Second Dutch War and moved in court circles. His plays — Love in a Wood (1671), The Gentleman Dancing-Master (1672), The Country Wife (1675), and The Plain Dealer (1676) — won him fame but little money. A secret marriage to the Countess of Drogheda ruined him; he spent seven years in the Fleet for debt, was briefly reconciled to his father, and lived in obscurity and poverty until, in old age, he married a young heiress days before his death on 1 January 1716, leaving his manuscripts to the young Alexander Pope.
authors.profile: The most savage and morally earnest of the Restoration comic writers, whose comedies expose sexual appetite, jealousy, and hypocrisy with a harsh, near-Jacobean intensity beneath the manners-comedy surface.
authors.style: Biting, energetic dialogue; intrigue plotting drawn from Molière and the Spanish; sexual frankness and dark comedy; and a moral seriousness unusual in the comedy of manners.
authors.concerns: Lust, jealousy, and cuckoldry; social and sexual hypocrisy; the corruption of town and country; misanthropy and plain dealing; and the vanity of pretence.
authors.significance: The Country Wife and The Plain Dealer are among the greatest English comedies; Wycherley's moral ferocity influenced Congreve and later satirists, and his late-life friendship with Pope linked Restoration and Augustan letters.
authors.uncertainty: Wycherley's birth year is uncertain (c. 1640–41) and much of his biography, especially his marriages and debts, is recorded only in anecdotal sources.

works.title: Love in a Wood; or, St. James's Park

authors.name: Wulfstan
authors.identity: homilist; lawgiver; archbishop
authors.biography: Bishop of London 996–1002, bishop of Worcester 1002–1016, and archbishop of York 1002–1023; the principal counselor and draftsman of law under kings Æthelred II and Cnut.
authors.profile: Author of the Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (1014), the most famous Old English sermon, preached in the crisis of the Danish invasions; the Institutes of Polity (a treatise on the orders of Christian society); the Canons of Edgar; the law codes of Æthelred and Cnut; and a series of eschatological homilies (De Antichristo, De falsis deis) warning of the approaching end.
authors.style: A distinctive, urgent rhythm built on two-stress phrases, alliteration, intensifying repetition, and cumulative word-pairs; the most recognizable idiolect in Old English prose.
authors.concerns: National repentance; social order and the duties of each estate; the coming of Antichrist; the law of God as the foundation of earthly law.
authors.significance: With Ælfric, the last great writer of Old English prose; his homilies and law codes shaped the response of the English church and state to the conquest of 1016.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and early career unknown; the canon of his writings rests on stylistic analysis.

works.title: Wulfstan's Eschatological Homilies (De Antichristo, De falsis deis, and related sermons)

sources: Dictionary of Old English: A to I online

authors.name: Wulfstan the Cantor
authors.identity: poet; hagiographer
authors.biography: Monk and precentor of the Old Minster, Winchester, active in the 990s; a leading figure of the literary culture of the Benedictine Reform.
authors.profile: Author of the Narratio metrica de Sancto Swithuno (c. 996), a verse life of St Swithun with an important prose preface describing the rebuilding of the Old Minster; also credited with the Life of St Æthelwold.
authors.style: Accomplished Latin hexameters in the classical revival manner of the tenth-century reform; encomiastic tone.
authors.concerns: The cult of the saints as the glory of the reformed church; the commemoration of Winchester's patrons and builders.
authors.significance: The principal Latin poet of the late Old English period; his Narratio is a major source for the architecture and liturgy of the Old Minster.
authors.uncertainty: Little biographical detail known; attributions of the Æthelwold life debated.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500

authors.name: Ælfric Bata
authors.identity: Latin colloquy writer; schoolmaster
authors.biography: A pupil of Ælfric of Eynsham who identifies himself by the nickname 'Bata' and addresses his master with affectionate humour in the colloquies. He probably taught at a monastic school in the first quarter of the eleventh century (fl. c. 1005-1025). His life is otherwise unknown.
authors.profile: Author of the Colloquia and the Colloquia difficiliora, Latin conversation manuals modelled on Ælfric's Colloquy but far more expansive and boisterous: they dramatize daily life in the monastic school with dialogue about food, drink, beatings, and petty theft.
authors.style: Colloquial, hyperbolic Latin with a taste for comic exaggeration and insult; the texts deliberately enlarge the vocabulary of daily life beyond the classroom classics.
authors.concerns: The teaching of spoken Latin; the discipline and everyday realities of the monastic school; the relationship between master and pupil.
authors.significance: His colloquies preserve a uniquely vivid picture of eleventh-century English school life and document the vitality of the vernacular-Latin classroom tradition founded by Ælfric.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from his texts; floruit approximate (c. 1005-1025); birth and death dates unknown.
sources: The Cambridge History of Early Modern English Literature

authors.name: Ælfric of Eynsham
authors.identity: homilist; hagiographer; grammarian; translator
authors.biography: Educated at Winchester under Bishop Æthelwold, the leading figure of the Benedictine Reform; monk and mass-priest at Cerne Abbas (c. 987–1005); first abbot of Eynsham (1005–c. 1010). The greatest and most prolific writer of Old English prose.
authors.profile: Author of the two series of Catholic Homilies (c. 989–995), the Lives of Saints (c. 993–998), the Grammar and Glossary (the first Latin grammar in a European vernacular), the Colloquy, translations of Genesis and other Old Testament books (the Old English Hexateuch), De temporibus anni, pastoral letters, and numerous shorter homilies and treatises.
authors.style: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of extraordinary clarity and control — a deliberately plain style designed to be read aloud and understood; careful avoidance of apocryphal excess.
authors.concerns: Orthodox teaching for clergy and laity; the dignity and capacity of the English language; the education of the young; resistance to superstition and error.
authors.significance: The culmination of the Old English prose tradition; his works circulated more widely than any other vernacular prose of the period and influenced English religious writing for centuries.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; several works are attributed to him on stylistic grounds.
