sources: Beowulf: A Verse Translation

authors.name: Æthelweard
authors.identity: chronicler; ealdorman; patron
authors.biography: Ealdorman of the western provinces and descendant of King Æthelred I; patron of Ælfric of Eynsham; died c. 998.
authors.profile: Author of the Chronicon (c. 980), a Latin version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle down to 973, written for his kinswoman Matilda, abbess of Essen, with a famous prologue praising King Alfred.
authors.style: Dense, hermeneutic Latin of the sort parodied by his contemporary William of Malmesbury's sources; learned vocabulary and Grecisms.
authors.concerns: The antiquity and dignity of the West Saxon royal line; the cultivation of Latin learning among the secular aristocracy.
authors.significance: An important witness to the text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and to lay Latin literacy in late Anglo-Saxon England.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; identification with the ealdorman Æthelweard of the charters is standard but rests on prosopography.
sources: The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

authors.name: Æthelwold of Winchester
authors.identity: monastic reformer; Latin and Old English prose writer; translator
authors.biography: Born into a noble Winchester family c. 904-909, brought up at the court of King Æthelstan, and ordained with Dunstan. He became a monk at Glastonbury under Dunstan, was made abbot of the derelict monastery of Abingdon (c. 954), and in 963 was appointed bishop of Winchester, where he expelled the secular clerics of the Old and New Minsters and installed monks. He was the most radical and effective leader of the Benedictine Reform, a teacher of Ælfric, and a patron of manuscript production and the arts. He died on 1 August 984.
authors.profile: Author of the Regularis Concordia (c. 970), the customary that unified English monastic observance under royal patronage; traditionally credited with the Old English translation of the Rule of St Benedict (c. 960s) and associated with the Old English New Minster Charter (966) and possibly the Benedictine Office. His school at Winchester created the standardized literary language ('Winchester words') used by Ælfric.
authors.style: In the Regularis Concordia, clear expository Latin organized for practical liturgical use, with vivid prescriptions for ceremony (the Visitatio Sepulchri, the 'tropes'); in the vernacular Rule, plain idiomatic Old English translating Benedict's Latin closely.
authors.concerns: Uniformity of observance; the king as protector of reformed monasticism; the education of monks in Latin and the vernacular; the liturgy as the centre of the religious life.
authors.significance: The architect of the English Benedictine Reform and of the alliance between the crown and the reformed monasteries; his Winchester school and standardized Old English shaped the literary language of the late tenth century and of Ælfric's and Wulfstan's prose.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate (c. 904-909). The attribution of the Old English Benedictine Rule and Benedictine Office to him is traditional and widely but not universally accepted.
movements: English Petrarchism and the Sonnet Vogue
themes: Women's experience and the feminine voice

works.title: The Old English Rule of St Benedict

sources: TEAMS Middle English Texts Series

works.title: 'Tis Pity She's a Whore
works.description: John Ford's notorious tragedy of incestuous love between the siblings Giovanni and Annabella in Parma, and of Giovanni's murder of his sister and his entrance bearing her heart on his dagger.
works.plot: Governing himself by passion rather than religion, Giovanni declares his love to his sister Annabella; she yields, marries the noble Soranzo to conceal her pregnancy, is discovered, and is killed by Giovanni, who then dies fighting Soranzo's followers.
works.significance: The most powerful and most discussed Caroline tragedy; it pushed the theatre's moral limits further than any contemporary play and remains a central text in the study of early modern incest and tragic passion.
works.meter: Blank verse of sustained lyric intensity, with Ford's characteristic repetition and lament.
works.context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Phoenix in Drury Lane, probably c. 1629-33, and published in 1633 with a remarkable author's dedication defending the play's seriousness.
works.characters: Giovanni; Annabella; Soranzo; the Friar Bonaventura; Vasques; Grimaldi; Bergetto; Philotis; Richardetto; Hippolita
works.structure: Five acts of a single, tightly driven tragic action with subordinate comic plots, ending in the public catastrophe at the cardinal's feast.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ford on the 1633 title page; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Bold Stroke for a Wife
altTitles: A Bold Stroke for a Wife: A Comedy
works.form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: The author's best-known comedy, a comic campaign in which a clever lover wins an heiress by personating the several guardians who have been charged with keeping her from him. It is a sustained satire on religious and political cant, each guardian standing for a species of enthusiasm.
works.plot: A colonel loves a young woman whose fortune is controlled by four guardians, a Quaker, a nun, a Whig knight and a Tory general, each pledged to keep her from him. He and his friends disguise themselves as a Quaker preacher, a confessor and a petitioning politician, and by playing each guardian's own cant against him they obtain her consent. The exposure of the tricks reconciles the guardians and the lovers marry.
works.significance: It is the most durable English comedy about enthusiasm as a social language, and a central text for the study of the woman dramatist in the Augustan theatre; its personation structure was a model for later comedy of disguise.
works.meter: Predominantly prose dialogue with verse epilogue, the humour carried by the stylised cant of each guardian - Quaker plainness, Romish casistry, party phraseology.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in February 1718, in the season of the Whig split and the Jacobite scare, and held a repertory place through the century; its portraits of Quaker and papist enthusiasts draw on the controversy comedy of the previous age.
works.characters: Colonel Fainwell; Miss Lovely; Obadiah Prim the Quaker; the nun Perpetua; Sir Simon Affection; the Tory general
works.structure: Five-act comedy built on a single conceit of successive personation, with an epilogue and prologue addressing the party divisions of the house; the disguise scenes are arranged as set pieces of mimicry.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the play was published with the author's name, though the pirated acting editions of the century alter its lines.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Book of Airs
works.description: The songbook of 1601 by Thomas Campion (words and music) and Philip Rosseter (music): twenty-one lute songs and one masque song, including 'My sweetest Lesbia', 'Follow thy fair sun', 'When to her lute Corinna sings', and 'I care not for these ladies' — the volume that made Campion the supreme English lyricist of the lute-song golden age.
works.plot: No plot: the airs set the commonplaces of love — carpe diem, the lady's beauty, the lover's complaint, the joys of country over court — each song a perfected miniature in the courtly lyric tradition.
works.significance: The classic of the Elizabethan lute-song tradition — poetry and music fused as nowhere else in the language, and a touchstone for every later English lyricist.
works.meter: Short-line lyric stanzas of exquisite finish — trochees, iambs, and the quantitative experiments of Campion's 'observations' — composed for music and printed with tablature.
works.context: Published 1601 in the first great decade of the English ayre, alongside Dowland's and Jones's books; Campion's preface defends the new union of English verse and music against the metrical pedants.
works.characters: the singer-lover; Lesbia; Corinna; the beloved ladies
works.structure: A printed songbook of twenty-one airs plus the masque song, arranged for voice and lute (some also for viol consort), in the standard format of the English ayre books.
works.attributionNotes: Words by Campion throughout, with one masque song; music by Campion for half the airs and by Rosseter for the rest.

editions.title: The Works of Thomas Campion

works.title: A Chaste Maid in Cheapside
works.description: Middleton's comedy of London's sexual economy: the goldsmith Yellowhammer's daughter Moll, betrothed by her parents to the decadent knight Sir Walter Whorehound, loves the poor Touchwood Junior; the city's trades in food, sex, and legitimacy — the Allwits' household, the promoters, the puritans feasting at a christening — fill the play, until Sir Walter's ruin and Moll's mock-death restore the lovers.
works.plot: Sir Walter finances the Allwits and fathers their 'children' while courting Moll; Touchwood Senior's fertility and his brother's love-plot run through the middle acts; the christening feast and the arrest of the gallants expose the city's corruptions; and the final scene, with Moll's pretended death and revival, joins the lovers and topples the knight.
works.significance: The sharpest of the Jacobean city comedies — a play that makes money, sex, and religion a single system of exchange.
works.meter: Prose and verse of Middleton's quickest, cruellest wit, with the christening scene's hypocritical feasting as its summit.
works.context: Performed by the Lady Elizabeth's Men at the Swan in 1613 and printed in 1630; its satire of the Jacobean marriage market and puritan hypocrisy is the most scathing of the age.
works.characters: Moll Yellowhammer; Touchwood Junior; Touchwood Senior; Sir Walter Whorehound; Yellowhammer; Maudlin Yellowhammer; the Allwits; the Kixes; the promoters; the wench; the puritans
works.structure: A five-act cross-section of Cheapside — multiple households joined by Sir Walter's purse — in Middleton's most populous and corrosive comic design.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: A Chaste Maid in Cheapside (New Mermaids)

works.title: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists
works.description: John Wesley's canonical hymnal, gathered from the brothers' earlier collections into some five hundred and twenty-five hymns, his last great editorial act and the book Methodism long sang from. He meant it as a compact scripture of heart and doctrine, its order teaching the whole Methodist way of salvation in verse.
works.plot: The collection orders the Christian and Methodist life from general hymns of praise through the acts and sufferings of Christ, the operations of the Spirit, the states of the believer, the means of grace, the sacraments, and the seasons of the year, a walk through divinity in song. Its nucleus is Charles Wesley's lyric theology, with the best of Watts, Doddridge, and the older hymnists admitted beside John's own translations and paraphrases. The editor pruned, altered, and regularized the texts of forty revival years into a single honest compass of experimental religion. Its preface states the design plainly: that the people called Methodists should own the whole of their religion and hope in one small book they could sing.
works.significance: It is the parent of almost all later Methodist hymnals and one of the most influential hymn books in the language, fixing the canon of Charles Wesley's lyrics in the worship of the whole communion.
works.meter: The common, long, short, and varied eight-line hymn metres of Augustan psalmody, the texts regularized in diction and measure by the editor.
works.context: Published in 1780 as the societies entered the last decade under John Wesley's sole governance, it deliberately canonized the revival's song against the multiplicity of earlier collections and became the standard of Methodist worship.
works.structure: An ordered hymnal in heads following the course of divinity and the church year, with preface and indices by subject and first line.
works.attributionNotes: Edited throughout by John Wesley; the majority of hymns are Charles Wesley's, with others by Watts, Doddridge, and earlier hands.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Collection of Psalms and Hymns
works.description: The Wesleys' first London hymn collection, issued in 1738 for the society they met with and drawing on the psalter versions and hymns then in use among the Oxford and London methodists. It carries the earliest printed fruits of Charles Wesley's hymnwriting alongside metrical psalms and the brothers' translations.
works.plot: The collection sets David's psalms in metrical version beside hymns for the chief seasons and doctrines: Advent, Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, repentance, faith, and the last things. Its prefatory address pleads the conscience of the writers in choosing and mending the old versions, and its hymns already display Charles's gift for first-person assurance and tender doctrine. The volume thus forms a bridge from the Psalm-singing of the Church of England to the full Methodist hymnody of the Bristol collections.
works.significance: It marks the moment the Wesleyan movement began to sing in print, the first public shape of the revival's lyric theology and the ancestor of the great Methodist collections.
works.meter: Common, long, and short metre psalm stanzas and hymn measures of iambic lines; the language plain and singable, after the style of the earlier methodist psalmody.
works.context: Published in London in 1738 in the months of Aldersgate and the societies' forming, after the Oxford Psalm and Hymn pocket book of 1733 and before the Bristol Hymns and Sacred Poems of 1739.
works.characters: the London society
works.structure: A dual collection, psalms in metre followed by hymns arranged by seasons and subjects, with preface and occasional doxologies.
works.attributionNotes: Prepared by John and Charles Wesley; Charles is the author of the new hymns, the psalter versions being collaborative and largely rehandled from earlier hands.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Defence of the True and Catholic Doctrine of the Sacrament
altTitles: The Defence of the True and Catholike Doctrine of the Sacrament of the Body and Bloud of Our Saviour Christ
works.description: Cranmer's principal theological work, published in 1550, defining the eucharist against both transubstantiation and mere memorialism; the fullest statement of the Reformed doctrine of the sacrament in English.
works.plot: The book argues from scripture and the fathers that Christ is truly but spiritually present in the eucharist, received by faith; it refutes the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation (against Stephen Gardiner) and the Zwinglian reduction of the sacrament to a bare sign, distinguishing 'sacramentally' from 'corporally', and it defends the vernacular liturgy and communion in both kinds.
works.significance: The classic English statement of the Reformed eucharist and Cranmer's most sustained piece of theological prose; it fixed the middle course of Anglican sacramental doctrine for centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1550 during Cranmer's ascendancy under Edward VI, in the controversy with Bishop Stephen Gardiner (imprisoned for his opposition); the doctrine of the Defence shaped the communion rite of the 1552 Prayer Book, and Cranmer recanted it under Mary before renouncing his recantations at the stake in 1556.
works.structure: Five books of doctrinal argument with patristic citation, cast as a reply to Gardiner's defence of the corporal presence.

works.title: A Description of the Villa of Mr. Horace Walpole
altTitles: A Description of the Villa of Mr. Horace Walpole at Strawberry Hill
works.form: antiquarian description and catalogue of a collection
works.description: A room-by-room account of the author's Gothic villa at Strawberry Hill, its collections, its chapels and its libraries, written for the guidance of visitors and printed at his own instance. It is the founding document of the Gothic revival house as a literary and antiquarian artefact.
works.plot: The description leads the visitor through the exterior and the several apartments, reporting the arrangements of the Gothic chambers, the painted glass, the armour, the books and the relics with their provenances. It explains the taste and the scholarship that assembled them, and defends the villa's imitations of the old styles as faithful and instructive. The account of the collection ends with the library and the collections of prints and drawings, the whole forming a theory of antiquarian pleasure.
works.significance: It established the model of the described Gothic house and is the primary source for the taste, the antiquarian methods and the humour of the century's most famous literary residence.
works.meter: A plain descriptive prose of measurement, provenance and modest comment, with the epigraphic and heraldic phrases of the antiquarian tradition.
works.context: Printed in 1784 in the season of the vogue for Strawberry Hill and of the author's late quarrels over the authenticity of the relics he displayed; the villa itself, built and altered over some thirty years, is the work the book describes.
works.structure: A topographical and inventory description ordered by the plan of the house, with inserted catalogues and historical notes on individual pieces; there is no argument beyond the tour.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work was printed by the owner's direction, and the later editions were enlarged by other hands after his death.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Dialogue Concerning Heresies
altTitles: A Dialogue of Sir Thomas More, Knight
works.description: More's first and longest English polemical work against the Lutheran heresy, cast as a four-book dialogue between More and a young 'messenger' sent by a friend who is tempted by the reformers.
works.plot: In Book I More defends the veneration of images, pilgrimages, and miracles; Book II discusses the authority of the Church and the corruption of Tyndale's New Testament translation; Book III refutes Luther's and Tyndale's views on faith and works; Book IV defends the clergy and the burning of heretics, arguing that Luther's doctrine leads to sedition and the destruction of the sacraments.
works.significance: The major English Catholic response to the early Reformation, documenting the doctrinal battle over scripture and tradition, and one of the fullest exhibits of More's prose — combative, witty, and colloquial — outside the Latin works.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written 1528–29 after More had read Tyndale's New Testament and his Obedience of a Christian Man; part of the print war between More (with Bishop John Fisher) and the English reformers conducted under Bishop Tunstall's licence to read heretical books.
works.characters: Thomas More (as speaker); The Messenger
works.structure: Four books of continuous dialogue; the anonymous messenger relays objections while More answers at length with authorities, anecdotes, and comic deflation of the reformers.

works.title: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation
works.description: More's last and greatest English work, written in the Tower of London while awaiting execution, a dialogue in which an elderly Hungarian uncle instructs his nephew on bearing tribulation, especially the fear of death under persecution.
works.plot: Set in Hungary on the eve of a Turkish invasion, the dialogue moves from the general consolation of tribulation, through the temptations of fear, scruple, and despair, to the specific comfort of martyrdom, culminating in the uncle's meditation on the passion of Christ as the pattern of all suffering.
works.significance: The masterpiece of English devotional prose of its age, and one of the great prison writings in the language; its controlled serenity under sentence of death has made it the most widely read of More's English works.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the Tower between More's arrest (April 1534) and execution (6 July 1535), after his refusal of the Oath of Succession; the manuscript was smuggled abroad and first printed in London by Richard Tottel in 1553, under Mary I.
works.characters: Anthony (the uncle); Vincent (the nephew)
works.structure: Three books of dialogue between the aged Anthony and his nephew Vincent, with inset parables and a famous treatment of the temptation to suicide; the fictional frame thinly veils More's own imprisonment.

editions.title: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation (The Yale Edition of the Complete Works of St. Thomas More, vol. 12)
editions.editor: Louis L. Martz and Frank Manley

works.title: A Dictionary of the English Language
altTitles: A Dictionary of the English Language, in Which the Words are Derived from the Originals, and Illustrated in Their Different Significations by Examples from the Best Writers (first edition title)
works.form: two-volume folio dictionary with a prefixed grammar and prospectus; lexicographical and philological writing
works.description: The two folio volumes that settled the lexicography of English for half a century and remained the standard authority until the Oxford English Dictionary. Johnson gave some 42,773 words and illustrated their senses with a vast body of literary quotations, treating the language as a national literature rather than as a set of logical terms. The work was performed largely by Johnson's own labour, assisted by a small body of clerks, on the booksellers' contract signed in 1747.
works.plot: Each entry gives the orthography, the etymology where it can be traced, the parts of speech and the senses arranged from the primary to the derived, each authenticated by a quotation from an approved writer. Johnson's discussions of the difficulty of fixing a living language, of the limits of etymology and of the treatment of low or indecent words are recorded in the Grammar and the Plan prefixed to the volumes, and the illustrative citations - Shakespeare, Milton, Dryden, Pope and hundreds more - amount to an anthology of English writing.
works.significance: It established quotation-as-evidence, the historical treatment of senses and the idea that a dictionary is a record of a literature, all of which passed into later lexicons; it also created the modern image of the independent professional writer. Its definitions remain a literary document, and the work is a central text for eighteenth-century theories of language, usage and national letters.
works.meter: Prose of extreme compression in the definitions, with the illustrative quotations supplying the rhythm and the authority; the Grammar is written in the same periodic style as the Plan.
works.context: Produced in the decade after Chesterfield's indifference to projects for an English academy and in the same years as the Rambler papers; the booksellers' share system, the labour of the six copying clerks and Johnson's lodging in Gough Square provide the physical conditions of the work, and the Seven Years' War had already begun when it was published.
works.structure: A reference work: an alphabetical macrostructure, preceded by the Plan and a Grammar of the English tongue; no narrative order, but a strict microstructure of word, etymology, senses, examples.
works.attributionNotes: Johnson is the author of the whole design and of the definitions; the clerks and later bibliographers assisted the execution, and the etymologies relied on the philology then available, including Junius, Skinner and Tooke's predecessors.

editions.title: The Yale Edition of the Works of Samuel Johnson (21 volumes)
editions.editor: W. Jackson Bate and James L. Clifford (general editors)

works.title: A Discourse of the Grounds and Reasons of the Christian Religion
works.description: Collins's historical-critical pamphlet, treating Christianity as a this-worldly political phenomenon whose grounds lie in Jewish messianic expectation and whose reasons for assent are those of the Jewish religion it answered. Published amid the Woolston trials, it provoked a swarm of replies and a parliamentary outrage.
works.plot: Collins argues that the Jews expected a temporal Messiah, and that the first preachers addressed purely political hopes shaped by that expectation. On this account Christianity's rise is explained by causes within history: a deluded expectation later corrected by an allegorical reading after the failure of the temporal kingdom. The spiritualizing interpretation, he suggests, is a shift that saved the sect from extinction and made prophecy serve whatever happened. He closes with a proposal: the true Messiah remains to come, and the grounds of Christian assent, being historical and political, are weaker than those of the Jewish religion they displaced.
works.significance: It is the most political of the deist attacks, turning the evidences inside out by explaining religion from the interests it served, and a decisive provocation for the historical and moral apologetics of the following decades.
works.meter: Level, deadpan argumentative prose, with startling conclusions reached through a series of apparently neutral historical enquiries.
works.context: Published in 1724, the same year as Tindal's Christianity as Old as the Creation and in the shadow of Woolston's libel trial; the House of Commons resolved to prosecute the author, making it a cause celebre of the deist decade.
works.structure: A compact single discourse moving from the political state of the Jews, through the causes of Christianity's rise, to the allegorizing solution and a concluding query about the true Messiah.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Discourse on the Love of Our Country
altTitles: A Discourse on the Love of Our Country, on a Review of the Revolution of 1688
works.description: Price's sermon to the Revolution Society on the centenary of the Glorious Revolution, delivered two months after the fall of the Bastille and read as a blessing upon the French Revolution. It defined true love of country as attachment to liberty and to the rights of mankind, not to soil, state, or church establishment, and it provoked Burke's Reflections directly.
works.plot: Price argues that the love of our country, rightly understood, is a moral attachment to the commonwealth of free people, not a jealous patriotism set against the rest of the world. He reviews the English Revolution of 1688 as a real assertion of the rights of mankind, and insists that the same principles authorize the French people's resistance to tyranny; the glory of Britain lies in having taught the lesson, not in reserving it. He warns that churches and courts which turn religion into an engine of state betray both, and closes with a universalist prayer for the progress of liberty, knowledge, and virtue among all nations. The discourse was answered by loyal addresses, by clerical replies, and above all by Burke.
works.significance: It is the great text of cosmopolitan British radicalism and the book that called Burke into print, defining the argument about the rights of nations and the love of country that ran through the revolutionary decade.
works.meter: Sermonic prose of grave, sustained warmth, the periods built by parallel and antithesis, its rhetoric deliberately pacific and universal.
works.context: Delivered on 4 November 1789 to the Revolution Society at the Old Jewry in the first fever of the French Revolution, printed by the author's appointment and reprinted within the year; it was the immediate occasion of Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France.
works.structure: A single commemorative sermon, the centenary meditation opening into a universal theory of liberty and its love.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Fragment on Government
altTitles: A Fragment on Government; or, A Comment on the Commentaries
works.description: Bentham's anonymous first book, a savage critique of Blackstone's Commentaries that made the greatest legal oracle of the age the enemy of rational law. Its preface planted the principle of utility - the greatest happiness of the greatest number - at the foundation of legislation, and its commentary exposed fiction, prescription, and mystery as the armour of misrule.
works.plot: Against Blackstone's account of original contract and passive obedience, Bentham argues that government rests on the obedience actually rendered, and that the test of institutions is their utility, not their antiquity or the lawyer's applause. He dissects the Commentaries passage by passage: the state of nature fable, the fictional contract, the praise of English law's mystery and its trifling with the people's interest under the name of ease. The celebrated passages expose Blackstone's apology for the equity of the judges, the vagueness of natural law, and the treason-law's tyranny, until the famous declaration that the standard of right and wrong is the greatest happiness of the greatest number. The fragment thus turns a commentary into a manifesto for radical reform.
works.significance: It founded utilitarian radicalism and the critique of the common-law mystique, gave the English reform movement its watchword and its method, and made its author, unknown for years, the legislator of the reforming century.
works.meter: Ferocious, vivid, quotational prose, the polemical repetition of an opponent's own phrases turned against him by emphasis and scorn.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1776, the year of the Wealth of Nations and Common Sense, after Bentham's youthful revolt in the Temple from Blackstone's lectures; its first public detection as Blackstone's critic scandalized the profession.
works.structure: A double work: a preface of principle and then a running paragraph-by-paragraph commentary on selected sections of Blackstone.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously, with only the advertisement's clues; authorship known within the circle of Bentham's friends and declared openly in later years.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A General History of the Pyrates
altTitles: A General History of the Pyrates, From Their First Rise and Settlement in the Island of Providence
works.form: collective biography and historical narrative in prose
works.description: The chief narrative source for the lives of the great pirates of the American station, compiled and dramatised as a history of the profligate colony of the Bahamas. Its first volume is a continuous series of captains' lives, and its style is a hybrid of the criminal biography, the sea narrative and the moralising tale.
works.plot: The work traces the rise of pyrating after the peace discharged the privateers, describes the settlement at New Providence under Hornigold and the seizures made by the new confederacy, and then gives the careers, customs, articles, trials and deaths of the principal captains. It dwells on Roberts's articles and discipline, on the terrors of Teach, and on the female pirates' disguise and capture. It moralises throughout on the inevitable end of the pyrating course, so that even the successful captains are reported into the gallows or the desert.
works.significance: It is the sourcebook of the modern image of piracy, the black flag, the articles and the ship's democracy, and one of the most influential of the Newgate-derived prose series; its uncertain authorship makes it a test case for the attribution of hack history.
works.meter: Plain narrative prose of the criminal life, with sea-cant, trial reportage and the abrupt sentences of the hanging report; the inserted documents preserve official and notarial styles.
works.context: Published in London between 1724 and 1728 in the wave of public interest following the vice-admiralty trials of the pirates, and drawing on the court records, the colonial news sheets and the captains' own depositions.
works.characters: Henry Every; Blackbeard; Bartholomew Roberts; Henry Jennings; Charles Vane; Anne Bonny; Mary Read
works.structure: A serial of biographical lives inside a short historical introduction, with inserted documents such as articles and trial reports; a second volume extends the series with a more evidently inventive manner.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution disputed: the first volume was entered in the name of Captain Charles Johnson, a pseudonym many scholars have identified with the novelist and pamphleteer of the same publishing circle, while others deny the identification and question the second volume; the record is held for that disputed ascription and the pseudonym alone is named in the text.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Journal of a Voyage to Lisbon
altTitles: The Journal of a Voyage to Lisbon
works.form: travel journal and personal narrative in prose
works.description: The account of a dying man's sea passage, written by an author who sailed for Lisbon in the hope of health and died on the way home. It mixes the journal of the voyage, the complaint of the ship's company and a serious meditation on the conduct of a physician and the resignation of a man who expects to die.
works.plot: The traveller, broken by illness and obliged to leave England, describes his departure, the passage and his sufferings on board, with the behaviour of his own family and of the other passengers under the same trial. He reports the quarrels, the sickness, the crew and the treatment of the sick by the ship's surgeon, arriving at Lisbon in a condition little amended. The journal closes with the return homeward and the traveller's death, which the publishers' advertisement disclosed.
works.significance: It is the most affecting of the century's dying autobiographies and a crucial companion to the fiction, its candid account of the body and of domestic weakness confirming the argument of the last novel.
works.meter: A plain diary prose of the daily entry, with the heightened periodic manner reserved for the closing meditations on death.
works.context: Written in the autumn of 1754 and published a few months after the author's death in Lisbon in October of that year, in the season of his retirement from the office and of the controversy over his conduct as a magistrate.
works.characters: the travelling author; his wife and attendants; the ship's company and the surgeon; the fellow passengers of the Lisbon packet
works.structure: A dated prose journal of a single crossing, continuous in its observation and rising to a set of reflective conclusions on sickness, death and the duties of those who attend them.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published posthumously from the writer's own journal, with a prefatorial advertisement of the circumstances of his death.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Journal of the Plague Year
altTitles: The Journal of the Plague Year
A Journal of the Plague Year: Being Observations or Memorials, of the Most Remarkable Occurrences
works.description: A week-by-week history of the London visitation of 1665, compiled as a journal by a surviving citizen and published in 1722. It is neither a memoir nor an invention but a deliberately documentary fiction, assembled from bills of mortality, medical broadsides and the city's own alarm.
works.plot: H.F., a stay-and-watch baker, follows the sickness from its first appearance in parishes north of the river through the closing of houses, the weekly bills, the heaps of dead, the flight of the court and the greed of doctors and officers. He reports the Aldgate burying-ground, the mad people, the poor, and the French church; he records his own narrow escapes, his visit to a doctor's house, and the disorder of the streets. The journal ends as the mortality falls with the cold weather and the city recovers.
works.significance: It is the model of empirical urban narrative in English fiction and a foundational text for the history of the epidemic as a literary form, its mixture of statistic and fear defining how the disaster city is later fictionalised.
works.meter: Austere prose of numeration and specification, with bills, tables and parish totals quoted as authority; the rhetorical heightening is confined to the passages of remonstrance with the city's wickedness.
works.context: Written nearly sixty years after the event during a period of continental plague scares, and built on the bills of mortality, visitation archives and printed accounts of 1665; its publication coincided with a wider antiquarian revival of interest in the city's catastrophe.
works.characters: H.F. the baker; his brother the physician; the watchmen, searchers and buryers of the parishes; the doctors and the mountebanks
works.structure: A dated and partly weekly serial journal, impersonal and statistical in the outer parts and anxiously first-person in the visits and wanderings; the observing 'I' stands inside an impersonal civic record.
works.attributionNotes: The text was inscribed with the initials 'H.F.' and long read as a genuine memoir; attribution to the author of the 1719-22 fiction is now generally accepted on stylistic and bibliographical grounds and is here recorded as single authorship.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Journey Through France and Italy
altTitles: A Journey Through France and Italy, in a Series of Letters
works.description: A book of travels in letters from an English invalid travelling with his family through France into the north of Italy, written during a residence abroad and published some years after the writer's death. It mixes the guidebook, the medical complaint and the moral essay, and is one of the most readable of the century's continental tours.
works.plot: The traveller conducts his family from Dover through France, complains of the posts, the inns, the cooks and the beggars, and praises the laws and the politeness that make travelling easy. He enters Italy by Genoa and passes to Pisa and Livorno, where the climate and the medical advice are weighed; the letters report the companies, the opera and the antiquities. The final part recommends the Italian residence to consumptive English patients and judges the nations by their accommodation of the sick.
works.significance: It stands with the great travel books of the century as a document of the continental tour and of the medical geography of exile, and it supplies the circumstances of the author's last years.
works.meter: A testy and idiomatic epistolary prose, with the enumerative energy of the complaint and the balanced manner of the political observation.
works.context: Composed during the author's residence at Nice in the years after the peace of 1763, and published posthumously in 1776 in the season of the vogue for the Italian tour and the health-travel of the English.
works.characters: the travelling invalid and his family; the physicians and the innkeepers; the companies of the waters and of the opera
works.structure: A continuous series of letters arranged by route, with digressions on commerce, government, medicine and taste; the itinerary supplies the order and the invalid's temper the unity.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after his death from his own letters and papers.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Jovial Crew
altTitles: A Jovial Crew; or, The Merry Beggars
works.description: Brome's most admired comedy, in which three gentlewomen run away to join a band of strolling beggars, and their idyll of freedom is tested by hunger, lust, and the law before they return home.
works.plot: Rachel, Amy, and the widow Springlove's daughters abandon their comfortable homes for the beggars' life; the beggar community is ruled by the mysterious Patrico, and the experiment ends with marriage and the reintegration of the runaways.
works.significance: Brome's masterpiece and the most substantial dramatic treatment of English beggar life in the period; it is a key text for Caroline social history and for the development of comic realism.
works.meter: Prose dominant, with songs and verses.
works.context: Performed at Drury Lane in 1641, just before the theatres closed; the play was popular again after the Restoration and inspired several adaptations, including the ballad opera The Jovial Crew (1731).
works.characters: Rachel; Amy; Meriel; Oldrents; Hilliard; Springlove; Patrico; Randall; Vincent; Martin
works.structure: Five acts, alternating between the gentleman's houses and the beggars' barn, with an unusually detailed portrait of vagrant society.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Brome; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Jubilate Agno
works.form: Devotional and encyclopaedic poem in responsive measure, related to the litany, to the psalms and to the hymn; surviving in author's manuscript and unprinted for two centuries.
works.description: Christopher Smart's immense poem of universal rejoicing, written during his years of confinement and retirement and not printed in his lifetime. It is structured as a responsive sequence of pairs, each joining some creature, object or abstraction to another in the duty of praising God, and it expands from the animal kingdom to the alphabet, to the languages of the world, to the poet's own person and history. Its mixture of theology, natural history, philology and autobiography is without analogue in English verse.
works.plot: There is no narrative, only an enormous act of doxology. The poem proceeds in responsive pairs, in which a member of creation is set to rejoice with another, and it passes through cats, dogs, birds, insects, the elements, the parts of the body, the letters, the tongues ancient and modern, and the institutions and professions of men. The governing argument is that all being is under an obligation to praise, and that the poet, whose own case and wrongs are repeatedly pleaded in the middle of the doxology, stands as an example of the created thing that refuses or is unable to complete its part. The effect is at once encyclopaedic and intensely personal, and the poem's logic is that of a litany rather than of a discourse.
works.significance: It is one of the few entirely original large forms created in English religious poetry, and its recovery established Smart as a central rather than eccentric figure of Augustan letters; its prosody, its catalogue method and its fusion of natural history with praise anticipate much later poetry. It is also the principal document of the age's quarrel between enthusiasm and reason.
works.meter: The pair-verse of the poem: a long line divided by a caesura into two responding parts, with the reiterated formulas 'for' and 'let ... rejoice with ...', producing a prosody of parallelism and accumulation closer to Hebrew and to chant than to any Augustan measure.
works.context: It was composed during the poet's confinement, the same period that produced the 'Song to David' and the other poems of the retirement, and it belongs to the culture of enthusiasm, religious melancholy and psalm-praise which the Augustan public found so difficult to classify. Its survival in manuscript made it a twentieth-century discovery, and its publication changed the terms of Smart's reputation.
works.characters: The Creator addressed and praised; the whole catalogue of creatures, letters and languages; the poet's own self, 'for I' clauses of defence and complaint
works.structure: A continuous responsive sequence in paired half-lines, with the response of the priest and the people marked, broken into sections by the change of subject and by the poet's intrusive personal passages; no closure was supplied by the author.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Smart is unquestioned; the difficulty is bibliographical, not authorial. The poem survived only in his manuscript and was not printed in the eighteenth century, so no publication year can be recorded and the field is left null; the composition years are given as the span of the confinement, which is the accepted but not precisely dated account.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Letter Concerning Toleration
works.description: Locke's argument for religious toleration, written in Latin in Holland in 1685 and published anonymously in 1689 in William Popple's English translation; it separates the ends of civil government from the care of souls.
works.plot: The magistrate's power extends only to civil interests — life, liberty, health, and property; the care of souls belongs to no one but God, and persecution cannot produce sincere belief; therefore the state must tolerate all religions that do not threaten civil peace.
works.significance: The classic statement of the case for religious toleration and a foundational text of liberal pluralism; three further letters followed in 1690, 1692, and 1704.
works.meter: Clear Latin prose, widely read in Popple's English translation.
works.context: Written in 1685 after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, in correspondence with Philip van Limborch; published in 1689 at Gouda in the same year as the Revolution settlement.
works.structure: A single continuous letter addressed to an unnamed friend.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as Epistola de Tolerantia; the English translation was by William Popple; Locke's authorship was suspected but not acknowledged.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Mad World, My Masters
works.description: Middleton's early city comedy of tricks: the rake Follywit, disguised as a lord and then as a player, gulls his rich grandfather Sir Bounteous Progress; the courtesan Frank Gullman is passed off as a virgin; and the bawdy plot of Penitent Brothel and the Harebrain household runs alongside — the whole a 'mad world' of disguises whose final scene dissolves into the play-within-the-play of The Slip.
works.plot: Follywit robs his grandfather three times over in three disguises; the gullings of the 'virgin' Gullman and the jealousy comedy of Harebrain interweave; the final robbery turns into the play performed before Sir Bounteous, who is robbed as he watches — the trick revealed only in the last lines, when Follywit marries Gullman with his grandfather's blessing.
works.significance: The wittiest of Middleton's early comedies — a laboratory of the trick-plot and the play-within-the-play he would perfect.
works.meter: Prose and verse in Middleton's swift, sardonic mix, with the mock-tragedy of the players as its final parody.
works.context: Performed by the Children of Paul's in 1605 and printed in 1608; its frank bawdry answered the fashion of the private-theatre comedies.
works.characters: Follywit; Sir Bounteous Progress; Frank Gullman; Penitent Brothel; Harebrain; Mistress Harebrain; the Succubus (appearing as Mistress Harebrain); the players
works.structure: A five-act intrigue of triple disguise built on the trick-play device, with the play-within-the-play as its climactic joke on the audience as well as the gull.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: A Man's a Man for A' That
altTitles: For A' That, and A' That
works.form: song lyric and political hymn in the Scottish vernacular, in the radical verse tradition of the 1790s
works.description: Burns's democratic anthem, which asserts that rank, ribbons and titles are nothing against the worth of the honest man, and that the true aristocracy is that of virtue and character. The song gathers the language of the 1790s radical argument about precedence and desert into a strophic hymn of equality, closing with the prophecy of a day when the brotherhood of man shall be more than a phrase. It is the most quoted of all verses on human equality in Scottish.
works.plot: The speaker catalogues the marks of worldly distinction - the coat of arms, the livery, the belt and the star, the flattery of menials - and insists that none of them makes the man better than his poor neighbour. The independent mind, poor and unpatented, is declared the true nobility, and the external rendings of rank are set against the worth of the upright heart. The final stanza looks forward to the coming time when man shall be a brother to man for a' that, turning the song's invective into a promise.
works.significance: It has become the standard lyrical statement of human equality in the language, quoted at inaugurations, funerals and political meetings, and a touchstone for the history of democratic sentiment. Its union of vernacular song with a political proposition makes it a central text of the literature of the nations in the 1790s.
works.meter: Four-beat Scots stanzas with the burden-like return of the phrase a man's a man for a' that, adapted to an air; the diction is colloquial, abrupt and full of monosyllables.
works.context: Written in the later Dumfries years, when the repressive measures following the French war and the agitation over parliamentary reform sharpened the language of rank and desert in Scotland; the song belongs to the same 1790s argument as the Address to the Deil and Tam o' Shanter in its contempt for precedence and for the trappings of nobility.
works.characters: The upright poor man; the hireling and slave of rank; the 'rulers' and 'wrigglers' of precedence
works.structure: A strophic argument in the manner of a song, each verse restating and intensifying the proposition of the refrain, ending with the prophetic closing stanza.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is variously assigned by the biographers within the last years of Burns's life, and the song was not printed in his lifetime, so the composition range entered here is deliberately broad and publication_date is left null.

works.title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
works.description: Shakespeare's fairy comedy of lovers, artisans, and the dream-wood: four Athenian lovers flee into the forest, the fairy king and queen quarrel over an Indian boy, Puck's love-juice scrambles every affection, and the 'rude mechanicals' rehearse the tragedy of Pyramus and Thisbe — the whole resolved at dawn into Theseus's wedding feast and the play-within-the-play.
works.plot: Hermia must marry Demetrius or die; she flees with Lysander, pursued by Demetrius and Helena; Oberon's magic makes both men love Helena; Titania, enchanted, dotes on Bottom the weaver in his ass's head; all is set right by dawn, and the mechanicals' catastrophic performance of 'Pyramus and Thisbe' crowns the triple wedding.
works.significance: The most perfect English comedy of the supernatural, and the play through which most of the world first meets Shakespeare.
works.meter: Lyric blank verse for the lovers and fairies, prose for the mechanicals, with the songs and charms of the fairy scenes.
works.context: Probably written for an aristocratic wedding about 1595–96; its 'rude mechanicals' satirize the artisan theatre culture of Elizabethan London.
works.characters: Theseus; Hippolyta; Lysander; Demetrius; Hermia; Helena; Oberon; Titania; Puck (Robin Goodfellow); Nick Bottom; Peter Quince; Francis Flute; Egeus
works.structure: Four interwoven plots — court, lovers, fairies, artisans — braided through the night and united in the final act's play-within-the-play.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: A Mirror for Magistrates
works.description: The great Elizabethan collection of 'complaints', planned by Thomas Sackville and others as a continuation of Lydgate's Fall of Princes: the ghosts of England's fallen rulers and nobles — from Albanact and Cordila to Richard III and the Duke of Buckingham — rise before the poets and tell their tragedies, warning magistrates against ambition, flattery, and misrule; Sackville's own 'Induction' and 'Complaint of Buckingham' crown the 1563 edition.
works.plot: In Sackville's Induction, the poet descends with Sorrow into the underworld and meets the train of the fallen; each ghost then speaks his or her complaint — the causes of the fall anatomized in de casibus form — in poems by Sackville, Baldwin, Ferrers, Churchyard, and others across the successive editions.
works.significance: The great poetic quarry of Elizabethan tragedy — the book Shakespeare, Marlowe, and the chroniclers all mined for their falls of princes.
works.meter: Rhyme royal and varied stanzas, with Sackville's Induction in his stateliest blank verse and rhyme.
works.context: The first edition (1559) was suppressed for its treatment of living magnates; the fuller editions of 1563 and later became the storehouse of plots and moral themes for the Elizabethan history play.
works.characters: Sorrow; the poet; the ghosts of Richard III, the Duke of Buckingham, Jane Shore, Cardinal Wolsey, Lord Hastings, the Black Prince, and many others
works.structure: A frame (the poets meeting to continue Lydgate) enclosing a series of dramatic monologues by the ghosts of the great, in the medieval de casibus tradition revived for Tudor statecraft.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative, planned by Sackville and written chiefly by William Baldwin and George Ferrers, with Sackville's Induction and Buckingham; individual attributions follow the early editions.

works.title: A Modest Defence of Publick Stews
altTitles: A Modest Defence of a Publick Stew
A Modest Defence of Publick Stews; or, An Essay Upon Whoring
works.description: Mandeville's notorious polemical pamphlet proposing licensed public brothels ('stews') as a remedy for the social miseries of clandestine prostitution, seduction, and venereal disease. Its calm institutional logic, applied to the most censurable subject, makes it both a piece of social planning and an experiment in the rhetoric of Mandevillian paradox.
works.plot: The essay first states the problem in terms of the failure of law and morality to suppress private prostitution, which spreads disease and ruins women and families unseen. It then proposes regulated stews, arguing by analogy with the management of the poor, the army, and the taxes that what cannot be prevented can be supervised, taxed, and made innocent of its worst harms. Objections from religion, modesty, and policy are enumerated and answered one by one with the pamphlet's signature deflating arithmetic of consequences. The conclusion holds that a legislature which consults 'the Nature of the Beast' rather than its ideals will secure public health and quiet where sermons have failed.
works.significance: It remains Mandeville's boldest test of whether public policy should reason from things as they are rather than as piety wishes them, and a key document of eighteenth-century debates about prostitution, regulation, and the language of projects.
works.meter: Plain, reasoningly colloquial prose,ironically modelled on the tones of a modest proposal, with lists of objections and answers driving its rhythm.
works.context: Published in London in 1724 with a letter to the Grand Jury of Middlesex, in the immediate aftermath of the Fable's prosecution and of the 'Mauduit' affair; it engages the same licensed-immorality debate that the Reformation of Manners societies and the Gin Age produced.
works.structure: A single sustained argumentative pamphlet: statement of the mischief, proposal, systematic confutation of objections, and practical peroration.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed without serious doubt to Mandeville, who signed related material and defended the pamphlet's premises within his own system; the imprint does not name him.

works.title: A Modest Proposal
altTitles: A Modest Proposal for Preventing the Children of Poor People from Being a Burthen to Their Parents or Country
works.description: Swift's ironical project for Ireland, in which a compassionate calculator proposes that the children of the poor be fattened and sold as food, and computes the profit to the landlord, the shopkeeper and the kingdom.
works.plot: The projector states the misery of the breeders in Dublin, dismisses the expedients of others, then lays down the arithmetic of the infants' carcases, their skins and their use for the tables of the rich, and closes by listing the objections he has already answered.
works.significance: It is the most quoted single satire in English and the permanent example of what the ironised first person can do to a society's moral arithmetic, especially its calculation of human bodies as commerce.
works.meter: The smooth arithmetical prose of political arithmetic, with the parenthesis of tender feeling and the exact figures of the computation.
works.context: Printed in the depth of the Irish distress after the failure of the linen trade and the abortive schemes for the kingdom, when the pamphlets of political economy were proposing population and export as the remedy for poverty.
works.characters: the projector; the knowing American of his acquaintance; the poor breeders and their children; the landlords and the shopkeepers
works.structure: A single short tract in the form of a disinterested proposal, moving from the statement of the pressure, through the computation, to the catalogue of the scheme's additional advantages.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the tract appeared anonymously with a fabricated Irish imprint in its first issue.

works.title: A New Way to Pay Old Debts
works.description: Massinger's comedy of the extortioner's fall: Sir Giles Overreach, who has swallowed the estates of his neighbours through mortgage and fraud, plots the marriage of his daughter Margaret to the young Lord Lovell; the conspiracy of the just — Welborne's recovery of his lands, Lady Allworth's pretended favour, and the servants' evidence — brings Overreach to the mad scene in which he is dragged off 'in a frenzy', his schemes destroyed and his daughter married to the man she loves.
works.plot: Welborne, ruined by Overreach, is raised by Lady Allworth's courtesy and wins his lands back through Overreach's own greed; Overreach forces Margaret toward Lovell, who instead promotes her marriage to Allworth; the double exposure — the deeds and the daughter's defiance — breaks the extortioner; and the final scene's madness ('The devil has left his shape') closes the comedy on the ruin of the usurer.
works.significance: The last great comedy of the pre-Civil War stage — and the vehicle of one of the English theatre's most durable villains.
works.meter: Blank verse and prose in Massinger's careful, moral style, with Overreach's mad scene as the great actor's moment it became.
works.context: Written about 1625 and printed in 1633; Overreach was modelled on the notorious extortioner Sir Giles Mompesson; the role became the property of the great actors from the Restoration to the twentieth century.
works.characters: Sir Giles Overreach; Frank Welborne; Margaret Overreach; Tom Allworth; Lady Allworth; Lord Lovell; Justice Greedy; Marrall; Will-do; the parson; the servants
works.structure: A five-act city comedy of the Jonsonian school, built on the double plot of Welborne's restoration and Margaret's marriage, with Overreach's fall as its moral engine.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: A New Way to Pay Old Debts (New Mermaids)

works.title: A Nocturnal Reverie
works.description: Anne Finch's celebrated night-piece, in which the poet describes the peace and beauty of the natural world by moonlight and the freedom of the imagination in solitude, until daylight and the world's cares return — a poem Wordsworth praised as the finest nature poem between Milton and himself.
works.plot: In a night of perfect calm the speaker contemplates the sleeping landscape, the freedom of the birds and her own fancy, and the liberty of the night, until 'a rude voice' and the approaching day break the spell and recall her to the world.
works.significance: A precursor of Romantic nature poetry, admired by Wordsworth, and one of the finest descriptive lyrics by a woman of the period.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of quiet, sensuous description with a contemplative, almost Romantic tone.
works.context: Composed in the 1680s–90s and circulated in manuscript among Finch's literary circle; published in her Poems on Several Occasions (1713).
works.characters: the poet; nature; Ardelia (her pastoral name)
works.structure: A single meditative blank-verse-couplet reflection on a night scene, framed by the return of day.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: A Paraphrase upon Part of the Book of Job
altTitles: A Paraphrase on Part of the Book of Job
A Paraphrase upon the Book of Job
works.description: Young's late blank-verse paraphrase of Job, which turns the patriarch's trial into a further Night Thought on affliction, the silence of providence and the immortality of the sufferer.
works.plot: The paraphrase follows the argument of Job and his friends, the adversary's license and the calamities of the righteous man, and reads the poem as a proof of patience and of a life to come, ending in the restoration and the moral application.
works.significance: It is the last great English verse paraphrase of Job before the century's end, and it completes the meditation on affliction and immortality which the Complaint had opened.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines in the Miltonic and Youngian manner, with the inflated period and the apostrophic interruption.
works.context: Published in the closing years of Young's life, in the season of the argument from the suffering of the righteous, of the Job revivals in devotional poetry and of his own quarrel with the critics of the Complaint.
works.characters: Job; the friends of Job; the adversary; the voice out of the whirlwind
works.structure: A continuous poetic paraphrase of the biblical book, with the speeches of Job, the friends and the divine answer rendered in the manner of the Complaint.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the pamphlet was issued anonymously and the author's name is supplied by the known signature of his other pieces.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Philosophical Inquiry Concerning Human Liberty
works.description: Anthony Collins's libertarian manifesto, the first sustained English argument that liberty is a power of acting according to the determination of the will, and that necessity so understood is compatible with, indeed the condition of, freedom. It attacks the doctrine of liberty of indifference as unintelligible and self-contradictory.
works.plot: Collins defines liberty as a power of acting according to the will's determination, and argues that every act of the will is determined by its object or by preceding causes. The liberty of indifference, a power to choose either way without preponderating motive, he shows to be unintelligible, since an undetermined choice would be mere chance and not agency. He then presses the moral and theological consequences: a determined will can still be free in the only sense that matters for praise, blame, and law. The closing chapters answer the objection that necessity destroys religion and morality, and defend the compatibility scheme against its clerical opponents.
works.significance: It fixed the vocabulary of the liberty-necessity debate in English for half a century, providing the hard libertarian position against which Hutcheson, Hume, and Reid defined their own schemes.
works.meter: Clear, terse argumentative prose with scholastic distinctions handled lightly; the chapters close on sharp either/or dilemmas.
works.context: Published in 1717 during the noise made by Collins's earlier Essay on the Use of Reason and his dispute with Clarke, and part of the freethinking campaign that Hume's later writings on liberty and necessity would answer.
works.structure: A short treatise in ten chapters: definitions, the history of the controversy, the confutation of indifference, the affirmative argument, and replies to moral and religious objections.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language
altTitles: Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language, Humbly Submitted to the Publick by Samuel Johnson
The Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language
works.form: printed prospectus and critical dissertation in formal balanced prose
works.description: The prospectus and manifesto issued to launch the Dictionary, addressed nominally to the Earl of Chesterfield and the nine other booksellers who subscribed for the work. It sets out the method, the historical scope and the philosophy of a dictionary of an untreated, unauthorised modern language, and distinguishes an orthoepist, a grammatist and a critic. It is at once a working proposal, a piece of self-justification, and one of the finest occasional prose performances of the century.
works.plot: Johnson argues that English has never been settled by a national academy, and that the attempt to fix a living language is in itself vain: words and meanings change with the commerce and literature of a nation. He proposes to register rather than to regulate, to collect the vocabulary from the best writers within a limited historical period, and to illustrate each word with quotations that both authenticate the sense and preserve the literary record. The Plan reviews previous English and Continental lexicons, defends the division of labour he has contracted for with the booksellers, and closes with a frank claim to have carried the work through without patronal assistance.
works.significance: The Plan is the foundational statement of English philological self-consciousness, replacing the dream of an academy with the authority of usage and the evidence of quotations, a practice that still governs historical lexicons. Its frank account of the economics of authorship makes it a key document for the professionalisation of letters, and its closing pages were long read as the manifesto of independent labour.
works.meter: Prose; periodic sentences of Latinate weight, tricolon and balanced clause, in the manner of the attached dedication; no verse.
works.context: Issued in 1747 after the booksellers of London had contracted with Johnson for a dictionary on the model of the French Academy's, in the same decade as the repeated but failed projects for an English academy and the debate over ascertaining the language that Swift had opened in 1712. The subscription and copyright economy of the trade, and the example of the French and Italian lexicons, set the terms of the proposal.
works.structure: A continuous epistolary essay: dedication to Chesterfield, historical account of previous dictionaries and of the absence of an English academy, statement of method and of the three provinces of the lexicographer, and a personal peroration on the conditions of authorship.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested, though the Plan was written under contract and in the shadow of a booksellers' subscription list; the coolness of Chesterfield, which Johnson recorded in the letter of 1755, belongs to the later correspondence rather than to this document.

works.title: A Play of Love
works.description: John Heywood's debate interlude on the pains and pleasures of love, printed by William Rastell in 1534; the first English play devoted wholly to the analysis of courtship.
works.plot: A man loved but not loving pleads his case against a man loving but not loved, each claiming the sharper pain; their debate is referred to a woman neither loving nor loved, who judges between them; the argument moves through the paradoxes of desire to a reconciliation in which the four parties pair off, demonstrating that love's pleasures and pains are inseparable.
works.significance: The first sustained dramatic treatment of love in English and the purest example of the debate-interlude form; it links medieval love-casuistry to the Renaissance comedy of courtship.
works.meter: Couplets with stanzaic lyric interludes
works.context: Printed in 1534, the year of the Act of Supremacy; the play belongs to the courtly debate tradition of the early Tudor household, drawing on the amatory casuistry of the medieval demande d'amour and anticipating the love-debates of Elizabethan drama.
works.characters: Lover Not Loved; Loved Not Loving; Neither Lover Nor Loved; Both Lover and Loved
works.structure: A formal disputation in two parts, with the Vice 'Neither-lover-nor-loved' as referee and a concluding judgement that resolves the debate into mutual pairing.

works.title: A Political Romance
works.form: allegorical prose satire and political squib
works.description: A short squib on the politics of the northern church, in which the possessions and dignities of a see are represented as a family estate disputed by greedy relations. It was printed privately and suppressed almost at once, and its suppression is the best-documented quarrel of the author's Yorkshire years.
works.plot: The affairs of an ancient manor and its offices are thrown into confusion by the designs of a steward and a faction of dependants, who would divide the profits and dispose of the lady of the house. The several parties plead their rights in a style of mock-legal and romantic gallantry, until the whole scheme is exposed as a traffic in dignities. The tale ends in the defeat of the project and in an ironical apology to the offended readers.
works.significance: It is the earliest publication of the author and the key to the personal and ecclesiastical material that later surfaces in the fiction, and its suppression is a case study in the practical limits of Augustan libel.
works.meter: A dense parodic prose of the romantic and the conveyancing styles, with the personated legal phrases of the real quarrel reproduced for effect.
works.context: Written in 1759 in the heat of the dispute over the York diocesan offices and the family interests of the author's own circle, and withdrawn by the printer after threats of an action for scandal; the affair is recorded in the letters of the year.
works.characters: the personated dignitaries of the northern church; the scheming steward and his faction; the lady of the manor and her dependants
works.structure: A brief continuous allegorical tale in the romantic and lawyerly manner, the persons standing transparently for the parties of the diocese; the design is a single sustained joke of personation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; printed without the author's name and identified in his correspondence and by the parties attacked.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Priest to the Temple
works.description: Herbert's prose manual of pastoral practice, written for the guidance of country clergy; in short chapters it describes the parson's character, duties, preaching, catechising, visiting, and conduct, presenting the ideal of the devoted, humble, and practical parish priest.
works.plot: Each chapter ('The Parson's Character', 'The Parson Preaching', 'The Parson in Circuits', etc.) offers practical and spiritual counsel, arguing that the parson must know and love his flock, teach plainly, and sanctify every part of life.
works.significance: A classic of Anglican pastoral literature, valued for its humane wisdom and its influence on Izaak Walton's Life of Herbert and on the ideal of the country parson in English letters.
works.meter: Plain, homely, wise prose with occasional proverbial turns and scriptural allusion.
works.context: Written c. 1632 at Bemerton and circulated in manuscript; published in 1652 as part of Herbert's Remains, it reflects the Laudian and practical devotional ideals of the Caroline church.
works.characters: the country parson; his parishioners
works.structure: A series of short prose chapters forming a complete guide to the pastoral office.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
