works.title: A Project for the Advancement of Learning
altTitles: A Project for the Advancement of Learning, and an Discourse of the Mechanical Operation of the Spirit
works.description: Swift's mock-project pamphlet, spoken by the same mad author of the Tale, which proposes that all learning may be bought at a shop and dispatched by mechanical means, and that the spirit of the age may be operated upon by instruments.
works.plot: The projector offers the universities a compendium of the whole corpus of knowledge, abridged to a single pocket volume, together with the machinery of memorising, speaking and writing by art, and reports the cold reception of such projects by the learned.
works.significance: It is the period's most economical exposure of the idea that knowledge can be mechanised, and it supplies the link between the Tale and the Laputa of the third book of Gulliver.
works.meter: The officious prose of the projector, full of article, offer and specification, broken by the narrator's self-pity.
works.context: Written in the wake of the Tale and printed with the miscellaneous Swift pieces of 1711, in the season of the Royal Society's projects, the abridgement vogue and the new market for the mechanical digressions of learning.
works.characters: the projector narrator; the universities and the learned societies; the mechanical authors
works.structure: A continuous ironical proposal, in the manner of the machine pamphlets, with the narrator's narrative of his own failure appended.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Swift's; the piece belongs to the narrator of the Tale, so that the projected voice is a fiction rather than a statement of Swift's own educational program.

editions.title: Jonathan Swift: Critical, Scholastic, and Variorum Edition

works.title: A Proposal for Correcting, Improving and Ascertaining the English Tongue
altTitles: A Proposal for Correcting the English Tongue
works.description: Swift's plea for the regulation of English by public authority: a historical account of the language's corruption, a proposal for an academy of six or twelve persons to compile a dictionary, refine the tongue and ascertain its settled use.
works.plot: The letter traces English from its Teutonick and Norman stocks, complains of the corruption introduced at the court of the late reign and by the politeness and the trade of the age, then argues that the language wants the authority of an academy, and offers a sketch of its rules and of the composition of a dictionary.
works.significance: It is the century's most influential statement of the desire to ascertain the language, and the direct provocation to the lexical and Augustan work which Johnson later performed without an academy.
works.meter: Swift's plain prose of the argument, with the historical enumeration and the abstract of the proposed rules.
works.context: Written in the season of Addison's and Steele's attempt to polish English for the tea-table and to fix the idiom by authority, and addressed to the minister, in the years when the Royal Society's linguistic schemes and the project of an English academy were live topics.
works.structure: A single letter, dividing into the historical complaint and the project, with the closing enumeration of the academy's methods.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Jonathan Swift: Critical, Scholastic, and Variorum Edition

works.title: A Red, Red Rose
altTitles: O my Luve's like a red, red rose
works.form: song lyric written for a Scottish air, in the collecting and adapting practice of the Scots Musical Museum
works.description: Burns's song of enduring affection, two brief stanzas of departure and of the vow to return, which became the most familiar love lyric in Scottish and one of the most set, translated and quoted poems in English. Its opening compares the beloved to the red rose and the melody, and its closing pledge of return across the widest distance gives the whole its pathos. Burns entered it among the songs he was collecting and reworking for Johnson's musical collection.
works.plot: The speaker likens his love to the newly blown rose and to the tune that strikes the ear, states the certainty of love beyond measure, and then faces the distance of parting. The second stanza pledges the return across the farthest seas and mountains till all the world be changed, closing with the image of the rivers and the sea that makes the promise seem at once impossible and certain.
works.significance: It is the most widely known of Burns's songs in English translation and setting, and a standard instance of how the antiquarian song-collecting of the 1790s produced original lyric. Its treatment of love and distance supplied a repertoire of phrase and image that passed into popular song generally.
works.meter: Short ballad-like song stanzas of alternating four- and three-beat lines, adapted to the air's phrasing, with simple diction and a single sustained simile.
works.context: Composed in the mid-1790s during Burns's last years in Dumfries, while he was contributing hundreds of songs and notes to Johnson's Scots Musical Museum, and drawing on traditional Scottish openings of the 'rose' and 'melodie' type. The song belongs to the great project of recovery and reissue of Scottish song that made the 1790s a decade of national anthology.
works.characters: The loving speaker; the absent beloved
works.structure: Two short stanzas of song, the first of comparison and present joy, the second of parting and the vow of return, with no narrative development beyond the single address.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Burns's song reworks and re-voices older traditional material, as he himself recorded in the notes to the collection, so the record of authorship should be read together with his practice of collecting and adaptation.

works.title: A Representation of the Injustice and Dangerous Tendency of Tolerating Slavery; or, of Admitting the Least Claim of Private Property in the Persons of Men, in England
altTitles: A Representation of the Injustice and Dangerous Tendency of Tolerating Slavery
works.form: Polemical and legal-religious treatise addressed as a public representation
works.description: The founding document of Granville Sharp's anti-slavery campaign, addressed to the merchants and planters of Great Britain and printed in London in 1769. Sharp, a clerk in the York Office and a self-taught Hebraist and grammarian, brings together biblical, legal and moral evidence that no master can hold a Christian as property, and warns that tolerating slavery corrupts English law and religion alike. Its learning, heat and long appendices of evidence made it the reference text of the British abolitionist case before Somersett's case of 1772.
works.plot: Sharp argues first from scripture that the Old Testament's servitude laws are not the modern form of chattel slavery, and that the gospel, which forbids men to rule over conscience, condemns holding human beings as goods and chattels. He then reviews English law and the earlier decisions against villeinage and imported servitude, urging that no custom or statute within England can authorise property in the persons of men. He next examines the planters' pleas of commerce, necessity and colonial prescription, treating them as interests against justice; and closes with a plain remonstrance to slave-owners, inviting them to manumit voluntarily before the law or divine judgment compels them. The volume appends testimony about the treatment of slaves in the colonies and a grammatical and critical disquisition much of which concerns the Hebrew and Greek terms for servitude.
works.significance: It supplied the legal and scriptural brief on which later abolitionists built, and its philological appendix anticipated the modern debate over the Bible's servitude texts. As the first substantial English attack on slavery written by a lay patron of the enslaved rather than by a Quaker or a cleric in the colonies, it marks the entry of the question into English public argument about law and conscience.
works.meter: Prose only, in a plain, earnest, lawyerly and scriptural register
works.context: Written in the decade of the Somersett litigation and of Sharp's patronage and education of enslaved people in England, it belongs to the evangelical and legalistic attack on the trade, to Sharp's own work as a patron and teacher of freed and abandoned enslaved people in London, and to the wider British argument about personal liberty that ran from the Wilkes controversies to the American dispute.
works.structure: Single sustained address in numbered argumentative divisions, followed by appended evidence, testimony and philological notes.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Granville Sharp is established and undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Satire Against Reason and Mankind
altTitles: A Satyr Against Reason and Mankind
works.description: Rochester's most substantial philosophical poem, a libertine dialogue between a satirist who would rather be a dog than a man and a clergyman who defends reason, in which 'right reason' is reduced to the guidance of appetite.
works.plot: The poet attacks the pride and falsity of human reason; the bishop replies in defence of reason as the light of God; the poet answers by distinguishing true reason, which serves the senses, from speculative reason, which is mere fear and fancy.
works.significance: The most intellectually serious poem of Restoration libertinism and a central text for understanding Rochester's rehabilitation in the late twentieth century.
works.meter: Irregular pentameter couplets, colloquial and argumentative.
works.context: Composed c. 1674-5 and circulated in manuscript in the court coterie; Rochester's Hobbesian scepticism answers the Cambridge Platonists and the new natural philosophy.
works.characters: the speaker; the bishop (Thomas Sprat, according to tradition)
works.structure: A dramatic dialogue in two unequal parts, closing with the poet's self-portrait of the man of sense and pleasure.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Rochester in contemporary manuscript witnesses; authorship accepted, though individual lines vary between witnesses.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy
altTitles: The Sentimental Journey through France and Italy
works.description: The journal of a clergyman travelling in France and Italy with nothing but his feelings for an equipment, a book of episodes in which the encounter, not the place, is the subject. It gave the century the word sentimental in its modern sense and made the traveller's sympathetic alarm a literary form.
works.plot: Yorick sets out alone, unprovided, and falls into a succession of small encounters - the monk of Calais, the fair grisette, the imprisoned French volunteer, the orphan girl at the convent gate, the dying lover at Lyons. Each meeting asks of him a feeling he is not always equal to, and his own vanity and desire are reported with the same candour as his tenderness. The journey ends with the lady of the last part unpossessed, the traveller's resolutions defeated and renewed.
works.significance: It is the defining text of literary sentimentalism and one of the most imitated prose styles of the century, and its treatment of sympathy as a precarious, sexual and self-interested feeling shaped the later novel of feeling.
works.meter: An interrupted, breathless prose of half-sentences, dashes and exclamations, with the apostrophe to the heart as its characteristic cadence.
works.context: Published in 1768 after the author's continental tour of the previous years and the death of his father, in the season of the cult of feeling, the sensibility controversy and the Anglo-French travel of the peace; it was answered at once by a rival's travels.
works.characters: Mr. Yorick; the monk of Calais; the poor grisette; Maria, the orphan at the convent; the captive of the war and the company of the road
works.structure: A loose first-person journal of episodes without continuous plot, arranged in short titled sequences; the movement is emotional rather than geographical, and the reader supplies the connections.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with the persona of the sermons retained.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life
altTitles: The Practical Series of a Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life
works.description: William Law's great devotional conduct book, teaching a rule of universal devotion by which every common action, business, and hour of the day is turned into prayer. It argues that religion is not a set of duties but the whole temper of a life resigned to God's will.
works.plot: Law first grounds devotion in the Gospel's own rules for ordinary conduct, then shows how the daily offices, work, meals, social hours, sleep, and sickness may each be sanctified by a fixed temper of resignation. Through portraits of worldly wise men, women of quality, the miser, the politician, and the clergyman, he proves that everything admirable in politeness is a poor counterfeit of devotion. The second movement directs the inward life: the love of God as the sole motive, the renunciation of self-will, and the sacramental use of the world. It closes with the famous counsel that a man must be a saint or wretch, and a moving description of the devout life as one hour of continuous offering.
works.significance: The most influential English devotional prose of the century between Ken and the tractarians, a standard of Anglican spiritual direction and a school of style for Samuel Johnson and many readers of the evangelical revival.
works.meter: A grave, rhythmic, iteratively clause-balanced prose, built on scriptural paraphrase and moral paradox; its solemn cadences were much admired and much parodied.
works.context: Written in the quiet of Kings Clipston after Law's secession from the Hanoverian establishment over the nonjurors' question, and published in 1729 when deist controversy had made practical Christianity a contested idea; Johnson, Wesley, and later Newman counted it formative.
works.structure: Two-part conduct treatise: doctrinal direction and rule of life, interwoven with a gallery of moral characters and closing meditations.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Serious Proposal to the Ladies, for the Advancement of Their True and Greatest Interest
altTitles: A Serious Proposal to the Ladies
works.description: Mary Astell's feminist treatise proposing a Protestant monastery or religious retirement where women could pursue education and the life of the mind free from marriage and male authority.
works.plot: Part I (1694) argues that women's intellectual inferiority is the product of defective education and proposes a religious community for their instruction; part II (1697) supplies a method for the improvement of women's minds based on Cartesian clear and distinct ideas.
works.significance: The first systematic argument for women's education in English and a founding text of English feminism; its proposal for a female intellectual community anticipates later educational reform.
works.meter: Vigorous, ironic, and rhetorically accomplished prose.
works.context: Part I published anonymously in 1694, part II in 1697; the proposal attracted the attention of Princess Anne of Denmark and provoked the suspicion that Astell was a crypto-Catholic.
works.structure: Two parts, each a continuous argument with a prefatory dedication.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as 'A Lover of Her Sex'; attribution to Astell is established.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Short Account of God's Dealings with the Reverend Mr. George Whitefield
altTitles: An Account of the Life of the Reverend Mr. George Whitefield (1739 edition)
works.description: Whitefield's spiritual autobiography, first printed in Philadelphia and enlarged in a Dublin edition of 1740 with a preface by John Wesley. It told the story of the conversion of an orphaned tallow-chandler's apprentice into the field preacher of three continents, the most read conversion narrative of the evangelical revival.
works.plot: Whitefield recounts his boyhood at the Bell Inn in Gloucester, the Oxford years with the Wesleys and the Holy Club, and the methodist disciplines of fasting, communion, and service in the prisons. He tells of his conversion through a book on the meritorious blood and righteousness of Christ, the moment he knew himself a child of God, and the fervour that followed into ordination and the sermon at Cincinnati? no: into his first American journey and the open-air field. The narrative weighs each experience against scripture, giving the Word as the evidence of every inward turn, and closes on the providence that carried the preacher from closed pulpits to the multitudes of the fields.
works.significance: It gave the evangelical revival its canonical conversion plot and made the autobiography of grace a mass genre; it remains the primary source for the Holy Club and the origins of Methodism in open air.
works.meter: Earnest, plain, exclamatory autobiographical prose, biblical quotation as the measure and sanction of every stated feeling.
works.context: Published in the first Atlantic season of the revival, 1739-40, as Whitefield's field preaching and his American journey made him the transatlantic evangelist; its printing by Franklin in Philadelphia? use: its American printing in 1739 and Wesley's Dublin preface in 1740 secured its wide circulation.
works.characters: George Whitefield as narrator; John and Charles Wesley; the Oxford club
works.structure: A continuous conversion narrative from childhood through conversion to apostolic call, framed by Wesley's prefatory endorsement in the Dublin issue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Short Introduction to Moral Philosophy
altTitles: Short Introduction to Moral Philosophy, in Three Books
works.description: Hutcheson's mature summary of his ethical system in three books, written as a student vade mecum: the moral sense and its determinations, self-love and benevolence in their due proportions, and the obligations of the natural, social, and divine life. Its final maxim made the greatest happiness of the greatest numbers the sole rule of duty.
works.plot: Book I grounds virtue in the moral sense, showing that this sense determines us to approve benevolent affections and that the laws of nature are intelligible only through it. Book II analyses self-love and its vanity when made the end, and benevolence as the happiness of the agent as well as of the species. Book III deduces the duties to God, to ourselves, and to our neighbours from the dictates of right reason joined to benevolence, and closes on the famous formula that the action is best which procures the greatest happiness for the greatest numbers. The whole is compressed into aphoristic numbered sections for classroom use.
works.significance: It transmitted utilitarian's first canonical formula and the moral-sense system to the generation of the Scottish Enlightenment and the American founding, becoming the most-copied ethics textbook of the colonies.
works.meter: Bare, sententious, heavily numbered textbook prose, almost a series of theses, with occasional passages of the older warmth.
works.context: Published in 1747, distilling Hutcheson's forty years of Glasgow teaching into a classroom manual read by the generation of the Scottish Enlightenment and by students at Harvard and Princeton.
works.structure: Three books of numbered propositions in catechetic order, each doctrine placed under its heads and their moral.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Song for St. Cecilia's Day, 1687
works.description: Dryden's first Cecilia ode, a Neoplatonic hymn tracing the creation of the world through the music of the spheres to the final dissolution of all things by the last trumpet.
works.plot: From discordant atoms, tuned by the voice of God, a harmonious universe arises; the stanzas then praise successive instruments and their passions, ending with the dread trumpet of the Last Judgement.
works.significance: One of the great English odes on music and the predecessor of Alexander's Feast; it became a staple of the choral repertoire through Handel and Purcell settings.
works.meter: A regular stanzaic form in mixed line lengths, with the famous four-beat 'The trumpet's loud clangour' passage.
works.context: Written for the London celebrations of St Cecilia's Day on 22 November 1687 and set to music by Giovanni Battista Draghi.
works.structure: Six stanzas plus a grand chorus, each stanza devoted to a different instrument or affect of music.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

The Poems and Fables of John Dryden

works.title: A Summons to Prayer
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (eleventh century)
works.description: A short poem calling the faithful to prayer at the ringing of the church bell, celebrating the power of the Lord's Prayer to guard the soul and summoning all creation to join in worship.
works.plot: At the sound of the bell the poet summons the congregation to prayer: the Lord's Prayer is a shield against the devil, and prayer joins earth to heaven; the poem closes by calling on all beings to praise the Lord.
works.significance: A rare Old English poem tied to the actual practice of the daily office, and a small masterpiece of liturgical verse.
works.meter: Alliterative long line, brief and incantatory, suited to its liturgical occasion.
works.context: The poem belongs to the CCCC 201 group and reflects the Benedictine Reform's emphasis on the daily offices and the sanctification of time through prayer.
works.structure: A liturgical summons organized around the bell, the prayer, and the assembly of creation in praise.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: A Survey of London
works.description: John Stow's loving survey of the capital: London and its liberties described ward by ward, street by street — the walls, gates, churches, schools, markets, conduits, and customs of the city, with its antiquities recovered against the Reformation's destruction and the growth of the Elizabethan metropolis; the foundation of London historiography, enlarged in the 1603 edition.
works.plot: The survey proceeds from the city's Roman origins through the wards of London, then to the suburbs and out-parishes: each church, monument, and custom is given its history, with the old ceremonies and benefactions recorded against oblivion, and the river and its bridges described at the close.
works.significance: The founding text of London historiography — the book every later historian of the city has built upon, and a classic of English antiquarian prose.
works.meter: Prose of plain, affectionate exactness — the walker's and rememberer's style.
works.context: First published 1598 and enlarged in 1603; its record of the pre-Fire city and the pre-Reformation churches is the irreplaceable document of Elizabethan London.
works.characters: the city of London itself; its founders, benefactors, and chroniclers
works.structure: A topographical description organized by ward and place, in the antiquarian manner of Leland and the chroniclers, with Stow's own memory and reading as its sources.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: A Survey of London, 2 vols.

works.title: A Tale of a Tub
altTitles: A Tale of a Tub: Written for the Universal Improvement of Mankind
works.description: Swift's first great prose satire: the ironised digressions of a mad Grub Street author, within which the parable of the three brothers and their coats exposes the corruptions of the Christian churches, and which ends in the celestial voyage and the tower of Fame.
works.plot: Three brothers, Peter, Martin and Jack, receive coats and a will from their father; Peter enlarges his coat with additions of his own, breaks the will and expels his brothers, so that Martin reforms and Jack splits into sects; the narrator's account of his own mechanical digressions and of the voyage to the island of the Aeolians surrounds the parable with a anatomy of enthusiasm, criticism and learning.
works.significance: It founded the Swiftian method of complete impersonation of a deranged narrator and remains the century's most radical analysis of religious zeal, textual corruption and the pathology of printed learning.
works.meter: Prose that passes from the nakedness of the plain style to the inflated cadences of the enthusiasm and the projectors, the satire carried by the register rather than by verse.
works.context: Composed in the aftermath of the 1690s quarrel of the ancients and moderns and of the Toleration debate, and printed in 1704 with The Battle of the Books; its anticlerical edge long obstructed Swift's preferment, and he disowned its authorship when the volume was reissued at the height of the party war.
works.characters: Peter; Martin; Jack; the digressive narrator; the father; the mob of Grub Street
works.structure: A framed and digressive prose satire: the allegorical history of the brothers set within the narrator's self-revealing preface, digressions, mechanical project and voyage, with no continuous sequence of action.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Swift on the evidence of his friends and of the volume's later apparatus; Swift himself for long refused to own the book, and the ascription of individual passages of the appended pieces to his hand is debated.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge
works.description: Berkeley's immaterialism laid out as a plain appeal to common sense: to be is to be perceived or to perceive, so that material substance is an absurdity, the external world is a system of ideas caused in us by God, and the scepticism the Cartesians feared is abolished. The Preface attacks abstract ideas and the main text runs through the consequences for science, mathematics, and religion.
works.plot: Berkeley first denies that minds can frame truly abstract general ideas in the Lockeian sense, then argues that the very notion of unperceived matter is contradictory: the table, the moon, are nothing but sensible ideas, and ideas exist only in perceiving minds. Objects continue to exist when unperceived by us because some eternal mind perceives them, and the order, coherence, and steadiness of our ideas display the goodness and power of that spirit. Nature is accordingly a divine language or visual dial by which God instructs us, not an operation of dead matter and occult qualities; the atheist's material substratum vanishes, scepticism is cured, and the sciences are redeemed as rules for connecting experience rather than pictures of ultimates.
works.significance: It is the classic statement of idealist empiricism, the standing rival to Locke's representationalism, and the provocation around which the century's theories of mind, perception, and causation arranged themselves.
works.meter: Terse, aphoristic numbered prose of rhetorical directness, full of searching questions and dialogue compressed into monologue.
works.context: Published in 1710 amid the after-effects of Locke's Essay and the freethinking assault on reason and religion; Berkeley issued it as a cheap pamphlet addressed to the common reader, and reissued it much enlarged in 1734.
works.structure: Preface against abstract ideas, then a continuous numbered exposition of the thesis, with objections answered in short retorts, ending in religious and scientific application.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Treatise of Human Nature
altTitles: A Treatise of Human Nature: Being an Attempt to Introduce the Experimental Method of Reasoning into Moral Subjects
works.description: Hume's first and most ambitious work, an attempt to rebuild philosophy on the experimental method by tracing all of human understanding, the passions, and morals to their principles in experience. Books I and II appeared in 1739 and Book III in 1740, and the Treatise became the foundation of empiricist philosophy, sceptical naturalism, and the science of human nature.
works.plot: Book I derives every simple idea from a preceding impression, then dismantles the fictions of substance, causation as necessary connection, and the identity of the self, showing that custom, not reason, is the guide of life; the famous conclusion admits the sceptic's demonstrations against probability while restoring nature's authority over them. Book II classifies the passions into direct and indirect, explains sympathy as the mechanism by which we receive the feelings of others, and analyses the will, liberty, and necessity. Book III founds morals on sentiment, argues that reason is and ought only the slave of the passions, derives justice and fidelity from artificial conventions grown useful, and closes with the catalogue of the natural and artificial virtues. The whole rests on the psychological claim that the mind's operations, like the body's, obey discoverable regular laws.
works.significance: It is the masterwork of the Scottish Enlightenment and one of the two or three greatest works of English-language philosophy, source of the induction and causation problems, the is-ought distinction, the bundle theory of self, and sentimentalist ethics.
works.meter: Precise, animated, exemplum-driven expository prose, its sceptical passages rising to meditative periodic grandeur, the style of the moral philosopher as man of letters.
works.context: Written mostly at La Fleche in France, published anonymously in Edinburgh and London in 1739-40, and received, in Hume's own later phrase, as still-born from the press; it answered Locke, Berkeley, Butler, Clarke, and Mandeville while founding the new science of human nature.
works.structure: Three books in progressive architecture, understanding then passions then morals, each subdivided into parts and sections, with a closing book-section and an Advertisement of the Enquiry plan.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; Hume acknowledged it in My Own Life and the Advertisements.

editions.title: A Treatise of Human Nature (Clarendon Edition of the Works of David Hume)
editions.editor: David Fate Norton and Mary J. Norton (eds.)

works.title: A Treatise of Moral Philosophy
altTitles: A Treatise of Morall Phylosophie, Contaynyng the Sayinges of the Wyse
works.description: William Baldwin's popular compilation of moral sayings and exemplary lives of philosophers, first published by Edward Whitchurch in 1547 and enlarged by Thomas Palfreyman; one of the most frequently reprinted English books of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
works.plot: The book arranges the sayings of the ancient philosophers under topical heads — of God, of wisdom, of justice, of friendship — and follows them with brief lives of the philosophers, ending each section with moral application for Christian readers.
works.significance: The most widely read English wisdom-book of the early modern period and a key channel by which classical moral philosophy reached vernacular readers; it established Baldwin's reputation before his editorship of A Mirror for Magistrates.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Compiled in the 1540s by Baldwin, then a corrector in Edward Whitchurch's printing house, during the flood of popular moral and sententious literature under Edward VI; Palfreyman's enlarged version (1555 onwards) carried it through dozens of editions to 1651.
works.structure: A compendium in four books: sayings of the philosophers, their lives, answers and apophthegms, and parables, with a running apparatus of moralization.

works.title: A View of the Present State of Ireland
altTitles: A View of the Present State of Irelande
works.description: Spenser's prose dialogue on the conquest and reform of Ireland, written from his experience as a New English planter and administrator: two speakers, Irenius and Eudoxus, survey Irish history, customs, law, and religion, and prescribe a programme of military subjection and re-education — including the infamous defence of famine as an instrument of policy.
works.plot: Eudoxus questions Irenius on the causes of Ireland's disorder — the Irish customs of tanistry and gavelkind, the brehon law, the bardic culture, the Old English degeneracy, and the Catholic religion — and Irenius answers each with diagnosis and remedy, ending with the scheme for garrisoning and resettling the country.
works.significance: The most sophisticated Elizabethan statement of the colonial programme in Ireland and a document central to the history of English rule there; it has been read ever since as both policy blueprint and confession.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Written about 1596, at the height of the Nine Years' War, when Spenser held the post of sheriff of Cork; it circulated in manuscript and was not printed until 1633.
works.characters: Irenius; Eudoxus
works.structure: A Socratic dialogue in two parts, framed as a single day's conference, with set-piece historical surveys and prescriptive argument.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: A View of the State of Ireland

works.title: A Woman Killed with Kindness
works.description: Heywood's domestic tragedy: the Yorkshire gentleman Frankford discovers his wife Anne's adultery with his guest Wendoll; instead of blood, he punishes her by banishment to a distant manor — kindness as execution — where she starves herself to death and dies on the marriage bed in the play's final scene, while the sub-plot of Sir Charles Mountford's imprisonment and Susan's sacrifice runs its parallel course.
works.plot: Frankford's friendship with Wendoll becomes the adulterer's entry; the discovery through the cards, the quiet banishment, and Anne's self-starvation follow; the sub-plot of Sir Charles's debt, his sister's sacrifice to Sir Francis Acton, and the reversal of fortune ends in the double marriage of the close, with Anne's deathbed forgiveness as the tragedy's summit.
works.significance: The masterpiece of English domestic tragedy — the play that brought the marriage bed, not the court, to the centre of the tragic stage.
works.meter: Plain, unadorned blank verse and prose — deliberately domestic, without the Senecan heights of the revenge school.
works.context: Performed by Worcester's Men in 1603 and printed in 1607; it founded the genre of domestic tragedy that runs through Arden of Faversham's earlier example to Lillo, Ibsen, and the modern theatre.
works.characters: Frankford; Anne Frankford; Wendoll; Sir Charles Mountford; Susan Mountford; Sir Francis Acton; Shafton; Nicholas; the servants
works.structure: A two-plot domestic tragedy — the Frankford household and the Mountfords — in Heywood's plain middle style, the first English tragedy of the ordinary marriage.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Three Elizabethan Domestic Tragedies

works.title: A Yorkshire Tragedy
works.description: The short anonymous (or Shakespeare-attributed) domestic tragedy of the real Walter Calverley murders of 1605: the gambling squire, his estate devoured by dice, stabs his wife and murders two of his children in their beds — the third wounded — and, taken by his servants, goes to his execution repentant, the play compressing the whole crime into its ten scenes.
works.plot: The Husband's ruin at dice and the Wife's pleas frame the catastrophe; the murders of the children and the wounding of the wife are staged with brutal directness; the servants' arrest and the Husband's repentance before the officers close the play, with the real crime's ballads and pamphlets as its documentary frame.
works.significance: The most compressed of the domestic tragedies — ten scenes of crime and repentance that test the limits of the genre's documentary power.
works.meter: Verse and prose of violent economy — the play's brevity is its instrument of shock.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men about 1608 and printed the same year as 'written by W. Shakespeare' — an attribution now generally rejected, though the question remains open; it was one of four plays in the 1608 quarto whose title page claimed Shakespeare's name.
works.characters: the Husband (Walter Calverley); the Wife; the Master of the College (the Husband's brother); the Knight; the servants; the officers
works.structure: A one-act domestic tragedy in ten scenes, built on the pamphlet accounts of the Calverley murders of 1605.
works.attributionNotes: The 1608 title page names Shakespeare, an attribution now generally rejected by scholarship; the author is unknown.

editions.title: Three Elizabethan Domestic Tragedies

works.title: Abdelazer; or, The Moor's Revenge
works.description: Behn's revenge tragedy of the Moorish prince Abdelazer, who seduces and destroys the Queen of Spain in a series of murders; it reworks Marston's Lust's Dominion and supplied Purcell with the theme of 'The Prince of Denmark's March'.
works.plot: Abdelazer, the Moorish heir deprived of his throne, seduces the Queen, murders the King, and finally falls; the play is a sustained study of ambition and revenge without remorse.
works.significance: The most successful of Behn's tragedies and an important rewriting of the early modern Moor-revenge tradition; it influenced later representations of the Moorish villain.
works.meter: Blank verse with some rhyme.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in 1677 and published in the same year; a 1695 revival used Purcell's incidental music.
works.characters: Abdelazer; the Queen; the King of Spain; Florella; Osmin; Cardinal; Antonio; Philip
works.structure: Five acts of revenge tragedy with a rapid succession of murders.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Behn; authorship undisputed.

editions.editor: Germaine Greer, Susan Hastings, Jeslyn Medoff, and Melinda Sansone (eds.)

works.title: Absalom and Achitophel
works.description: Dryden's masterpiece of political satire, mapping the Exclusion Crisis onto the biblical story of Absalom's rebellion against David: Monmouth as Absalom, Shaftesbury as Achitophel, Charles II as David, and the Duke of York as the lawful successor.
works.plot: Achitophel seduces the ambitious Absalom into rebellion against his indulgent father David; the poem culminates in David's assertion of divine-right authority and the rout of the Whig opposition.
works.significance: Universally regarded as the greatest political poem in English; it created the model of the allegorical verse satire that Pope would inherit, and its character portraits remain a landmark of satirical psychology.
works.meter: Heroic couplets; the most supple and rhetorically varied use of the closed couplet in seventeenth-century English.
works.context: Published in November 1681 at the height of the Exclusion Crisis, apparently at the king's suggestion, and immediately answered by Settle and Shadwell.
works.characters: David (Charles II); Absalom (James, Duke of Monmouth); Achitophel (Anthony Ashley Cooper, Earl of Shaftesbury); Zimri (George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham); Corah (Titus Oates); Israel (the English people)
works.structure: A two-part argumentative narrative: the diagnosis of national faction, then a series of extended character portraits, closing with the king's speech and the restoration of order.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed, though Dryden claimed the plan was the king's.

works.title: Absalom and Achitophel, Part II
works.description: The continuation of Dryden's satire, largely written by Nahum Tate with Dryden supplying the portraits of Achitophel and the closing sections; it attacks Settle and Shadwell as Doeg and Og.
works.plot: The sequel extends the biblical allegory into the trials of the Whig leaders and the vindication of David's government, adding a second book that completes Tate's unfinished first part.
works.significance: Important chiefly for Dryden's contribution, which contains the famous second portrait of Achitophel and the Doeg-Og passage; the whole is far less read than Part I.
works.meter: Heroic couplets.
works.context: Published in November 1682, in the wake of Shaftesbury's flight and the Tory reaction; it answers Shadwell's The Medal of John Bayes.
works.characters: Doeg (Thomas Shadwell); Og (Elkanah Settle); Achitophel (Earl of Shaftesbury); Corah (Titus Oates)
works.structure: Two parts: Tate's first book of about 550 lines and Dryden's second book of about 450 lines.
works.attributionNotes: The 1682 title page names Tate and Dryden; modern scholarship assigns the first book to Tate and the second to Dryden, with Dryden also revising Tate's text.

works.title: Account of Corsica
altTitles: An Account of Corsica, with Journal of a Tour to That Island, and Memoirs of Pascal Paoli
works.form: travel narrative with historical and biographical matter; political advocacy in the form of a book of travels
works.description: Boswell's travel book and political plea for the island he had visited twice, a journal of tour joined to an account of the Corsican constitution and a life of its leader Pascal Paoli. It made Corsica a cause romantique of the British reading public and helped to bring Paoli's name and the island's struggle for liberty into European debate. It is at once a work of travel narrative and an argument for the rights of a small nation against conquest.
works.plot: Boswell narrates his journeys through the island, its coasts, mountains and towns, and its people's hospitality, courage and poverty, and then passes to a description of the government, the laws and the military resistance to Genoa. His memoir of Paoli presents the general as a philosopher-soldier and a model of republican virtue. The book closes in an appeal to Britain's interest and honour, urging that the Corsicans' defence of their liberty deserved support rather than indifference.
works.significance: It created the Corsican vogue in Britain, fed the wider European argument about the island's liberty in which Rousseau's projected constitution also belonged, and became a document for the history of romantic nationalism and of the cult of liberty. It established Boswell's literary identity in advance of the Life of Johnson, and it is a central text for the literature of the nations outside England.
works.meter: Prose; brisk, talkative and directly personal, with the journal's immediacy and the essayistic expansiveness of the political sections.
works.context: Written after Boswell's visits of the mid-1760s, when Corsica had thrown off Genoese rule and was negotiating its defence against France, and when British public opinion was being mobilised by the pamphlets of the 'Corsican' party and by the project of an academy and a constitution. It belongs to the literature of European sympathy for small nations in the age of the American and Corsican causes.
works.characters: James Boswell; Pascal Paoli; the Corsican peasants and soldiers; the Genoese and the French
works.structure: A composite work: narrative journal of the tour, historical and political account of the island and its constitution, and biographical memoir of Paoli, unified by the writer's personal presence and his argument for Corsican liberty.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Boswell's journeys and his acquaintance with Paoli are documented in his own journals and letters, and the book's composition follows immediately upon the diplomatic activity of the later 1760s.

works.title: Actes and Monuments
works.description: John Foxe's 'Book of Martyrs': the vast church history and martyrology, first published in English in 1563 and expanded in 1570, tracing the true church from the apostles through Wyclif and the Lollards to the Protestant martyrs of Mary's reign — Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley, and hundreds more — with their examinations and burnings recorded in documentary detail and vivid woodcuts.
works.plot: The work moves from the early church through the medieval persecutions to the Marian burnings; each martyrdom is given its examinations, letters, and death-scene; the 1570 edition's calendar of martyrs and its apparatus made the book a national monument as well as a history.
works.significance: The most influential book of the English Reformation after the Bible itself — the founding text of English Protestant memory.
works.meter: Prose of documentary accumulation, with the set-piece death scenes (Latimer's 'we shall this day light such a candle') as its rhetorical peaks.
works.context: First English edition 1563, expanded 1570; ordered by Convocation to be placed in every cathedral church; its account of the Marian burnings shaped English Protestant identity for three centuries.
works.characters: Thomas Cranmer; Hugh Latimer; Nicholas Ridley; John Wyclif; John Rogers; the Marian martyrs
works.structure: A documentary martyrology in the tradition of Eusebius, organized chronologically by reign, with the records of trials and letters embedded in the narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Acts and Monuments of John Foxe, 8 vols.

works.title: Address to the Deil
works.form: burlesque verse address and satire in the Scottish dialect, in the lampooning tradition of Burns's religious satire
works.description: Burns's burlesque invocation of the Devil, an audacious piece of dialect blasphemy which treats the powers of darkness as a subject for comic natural history. The Deil is addressed as the old hags, books and superstitions have made him, and the poem runs through his titles, his habits, his attendants and his theological credentials with a humour that leaves Calvinist demonology exposed as folklore. It is at once a lampoon of priestcraft and a display of the whole vocabulary of Scottish witch-belief.
works.plot: The speaker greets the Deil with mock ceremony, cataloguing his appellations, his dominion, his court and his trade in souls. He reviews the scriptures and the traditions that make the Devil a prince of this world, then deflates them with homely instances from witch stories, kirk-yard hauntings and the delusions of old women and of arguing divines. The poem's movement is from grand invocation to ridicule, ending with a wish that the poet's wit may serve to laugh the power of the devil out of the honest mind.
works.significance: The poem is the most complete poetical exploitation of Scottish demonological vocabulary and one of the boldest burlesques of religious horror in British verse, standing with the Scottish witch tradition as a document of belief and unbelief. Its handling of the Habbie stanza for sustained comic invective also made it a model for later vernacular parody.
works.meter: The six-line Burns stanza (Standard Habbie), with its four long and two short Scots lines, giving the invective a brisk comic gait.
works.context: Written in the middle years of the 1780s in an Ayrshire still dense with witch and ghost belief, and against a background of Calvinist teaching on Satan and of the century's learned demonology; it belongs with Death and Doctor Hornbook and Holy Willie's Prayer to Burns's campaign against priestcraft, superstition and cant.
works.characters: The Deil; the speaker; the witches, divines and old wives of the alluded folklore
works.structure: A single sustained apostrophe organised as a catalogue - names, titles, retinue, works - with the burlesque pressure building stanza on stanza rather than through narrative incident.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem survives in many states and revisions of Burns's own hand, and the bibliographical record distinguishes the shorter and later expanded texts. Because the several versions were printed at different dates, the year of first publication is not asserted here.

works.title: Aeditio
works.description: The elementary Latin grammar composed for St Paul's School, traditionally attributed to John Colet with the collaboration of William Lily and Erasmus; the English 'Accidence' later incorporated into the authorized Lily's Grammar.
works.plot: A short accidence of the eight parts of speech with English rules and Latin examples, designed for beginners at St Paul's, prefaced by Colet's school statutes and the 'Carmen de Moribus'.
works.significance: The germ of the national school grammar and a document of the Erasmian educational reform at its English source, St Paul's School.
works.meter: Prose with Latin verse
works.context: Composed c. 1509–18 for the school Colet founded in 1509 and refounded in 1512 with Mercers' Company endowment; the English Accidence printed as Aeditio in 1527 became the basis of the royal grammar of 1540.
works.structure: Pedagogical manual with rules and paradigms.
works.attributionNotes: The grammar is a collaborative production of the St Paul's circle; the traditional ascription to Colet as founder reflects the school's origin rather than sole authorship, and Erasmus revised the text.

works.title: Aeneid, Books II and IV (Surrey's translation)
works.description: Surrey's translation of Virgil's Aeneid, Books II and IV — the fall of Troy and the tragedy of Dido — in unrhymed iambic pentameter, the first English blank verse. Book IV was printed by John Day in 1554 and both books in Tottel's 1557 edition; the translation fixed the metre that Marlowe and Shakespeare made the language of English drama.
works.plot: Book II: Aeneas recounts Troy's last night — the horse, the burning, Priam's death, the loss of Creusa. Book IV: Dido's passion for Aeneas, their union in the cave, his departure, and her suicide on the pyre.
works.significance: The invention of blank verse, the metre of English tragedy and epic from Marlowe to Milton; alongside Douglas's Scots Eneados, the founding translation of Virgil into English.
works.meter: Blank verse — unrhymed iambic pentameter — used for the first time in English; the line Surrey invented from the Italian versi sciolti and Virgil's hexameter.
works.context: Translated in Surrey's last years, when he stood near the throne; the fall of Troy and the ruin of Dido's court read as parables of Henrician politics.
works.characters: Aeneas; Dido; Priam; Sinon; Anna; Mercury
works.structure: Two books of the epic, chosen for their pathos; the translation follows Virgil book by book without prologue apparatus.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Aeneid of Henry Howard Earl of Surrey

works.title: Aenigmata
works.description: Aldhelm's collection of one hundred Latin riddles in hexameters, enclosed as the final part of the Epistola ad Acircium (addressed to King Aldfrith of Northumbria). The first riddle collection of medieval England and the direct model for the vernacular Exeter Book riddles.
works.plot: Each riddle speaks in the first person, obliquely describing its subject — the elements, creatures, household objects, tools of learning — with the last line of each revealing or hinting the solution (water, the wind, the raven, the pen, the alembic, and so on).
works.significance: The model and quarry of the entire insular riddle tradition, Latin and vernacular.
works.meter: Dactylic hexameters, technically virtuosic.
works.context: Written c. 686-700 as part of the Epistola ad Acircium, a treatise on Latin metre for King Aldfrith; imitated by Tatwine, Eusebius, and Boniface, and translated into Old English in the Exeter Book tradition.
works.characters: the speaking objects of the riddles
works.structure: A numbered sequence of one hundred enigmas, framed by the prefatory acrostic poem on Aldhelm's own name.
works.attributionNotes: Aldhelm's authorship is certain.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography

works.title: Aenigmata (Hwætberht's Riddles)
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Royal 12.C.xxiii (tenth century), with the riddles of Tatwine
works.description: Forty Latin riddles composed by Hwætberht (Eusebius), abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow (c. 716-c. 747) and associate of Bede, in the tradition of Symphosius and Aldhelm. The riddles range over the natural world, the cosmos, and the tools of learning — the sun and moon, the winds, the sea, the alphabet, and the liberal arts.
works.plot: The riddles personify their subjects, from celestial bodies and elemental forces to letters and numbers, each speaking obliquely of its nature and powers; the collection moves from the macrocosm of heaven and earth to the microcosm of human learning.
works.significance: The Northumbrian counterpart to Aldhelm's and Tatwine's riddle cycles, completing the Anglo-Latin riddle corpus that inspired the vernacular riddles of the Exeter Book.
works.meter: Latin hexameters modelled closely on Aldhelm, with his alliteration and ornamental diction; the verse is learned and allusive, written for readers trained in the monastic school.
works.context: Composed at Wearmouth-Jarrow in the age of Bede, when the twin monastery was the richest centre of learning in western Europe; the riddles show Aldhelm's influence carried into Northumbria and the riddle form serving the encyclopedic ambitions of the Northumbrian Renaissance.
works.structure: Forty self-contained hexameter riddles in an encyclopedic sequence, deliberately continuing and answering the tradition of Aldhelm's century of riddles; the arrangement suggests a curriculum of knowledge from cosmology to grammar.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Hwætberht (Eusebius), abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow, by manuscript tradition.

works.title: Aenigmata (Tatwine's Riddles)
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Royal 12.C.xxiii (tenth century), with the riddles of Hwætberht
works.description: Forty Latin riddles with a verse preface composed by Tatwine, monk of Breedon-on-the-Hill and archbishop of Canterbury (731-734). The riddles treat theological, philosophical, and grammatical subjects — faith, hope, charity, the five senses, the letters of the alphabet, the books of the Bible — in the manner of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
works.plot: Each riddle speaks in the first person about its own nature, requiring the reader to identify abstractions (the virtues, the liberal arts, grammatical categories) and objects (the pen, the sword, the book) from oblique descriptions built on learning rather than natural history.
works.significance: With Aldhelm's and Hwætberht's collections, Tatwine's riddles define the Anglo-Latin riddle tradition that stands behind the Exeter Book Riddles; they document the teaching of abstract theology through the schoolroom genre.
works.meter: Latin hexameters of schoolmasterly correctness, plainer than Aldhelm's hermeneutic verse; the riddles average six to eight lines and often begin with a paradoxical self-description.
works.context: Composed in the learned milieu of Breedon and Canterbury in the generation after Aldhelm, the riddles show the classroom union of grammar, theology, and verse composition that characterized early Anglo-Latin culture and fed the vernacular riddle tradition.
works.structure: A preface followed by forty self-contained riddles arranged in a deliberate sequence from theological virtues through philosophical abstractions to grammatical and physical subjects; the collection is the earliest complete Latin riddle cycle composed in England.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Tatwine by manuscript tradition and internal evidence; the riddles are contemporary with his Canterbury years or earlier.

works.title: Aglaura
works.description: Sir John Suckling's first and most famous play, a tragicomedy of courtly love and intrigue performed by the King's Men in 1638 and lavishly printed at the author's expense, reflecting the gallant, platonic-love ideals of the Caroline court.
works.plot: The King of Bithynia's court is troubled by the amorous conflicts surrounding the Princess Aglaura, involving love, jealousy, and a plot against the throne, resolved in the tragicomic mode.
works.significance: A characteristic Caroline courtly drama, notable for its production history, its expression of Caroline platonic-love ideals, and its author's social prestige.
works.meter: Blank verse and prose with a gallant, witty, courtly manner.
works.context: Performed and printed in 1638 at Suckling's own great expense, reflecting his wealth and his standing among the Caroline court wits.
works.characters: Aglaura; the King of Bithynia; Ardebert; Orbella
works.structure: A five-act tragicomedy in blank verse and prose, produced in two alternative endings (tragic and comic).
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Alciphron
works.description: Berkeley's dialogue against the freethinkers of his own day, figured as the ancient minute philosopher Alciphron, whose scepticism about religion, morality, and providence is answered not by metaphysics but by the visible evidence of Christianity's civilizing power. Its defence of the church as an historical and moral phenomenon was Berkeley's most publicistic work.
works.plot: The dialogue opens on the minute philosopher Alciphron rejecting religion as enthusiasm and priestcraft, until the older Euphranor promises to prove Christianity by facts any candid critic must weigh. They examine the evidence of the founder's miracles and the prophecy of the church's enduring spread, arguing that a scheme which has tamed nations, fixed morals, and produced learning and charity cannot rest on a known imposture. Alciphron's scepticism about providence is met with the analogy of a well-governed state whose end exceeds present view. The closing dialogues answer the charge that Christianity has been the spoil of priests, showing it instead the patron of civil liberty and national union.
works.significance: It became the classic apologetic of evidential Christian moral history, influential in America and reprinted for debates at Harvard and Yale, and it is the century's fullest dialogue answer to freethinking ridicule.
works.meter: Measured, courteous dialogic prose, more expansive than the Hylas dialogues, with set-piece historical argumentation.
works.context: Published in 1732 in the immediate wake of the deist flush of Tindal and Collins and of the Shaftesburian reign of ridicule, and as Berkeley returned from his failed American college project; its portraits of the minute philosopher and of Lysicles were read as sketches of the freethinking club wits of the day.
works.characters: Euphranor; Alciphron; Lysicles; Hippias; Cleontes
works.structure: Four consecutive dialogues, each answering one branch of the minute-philosopher's assault: miracles and evidence, prophecy and the church's spread, providence, and priestcraft and civilizing power.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Alcuin's Letters
works.description: The surviving correspondence of Alcuin of York — over 280 letters to kings, bishops, and friends, from Charlemagne and his court to the monks of Lindisfarne and the school of York: the richest epistolary record of the Carolingian Renaissance and of the network that carried Anglo-Saxon learning to the Continent.
works.plot: The letters range from affairs of state and church (the condemnation of adoptionism, the imperial coronation, the Danish raids) to friendship, consolation, and literary patronage; the most famous is the letter of 793 to the community of Lindisfarne after the Viking sack, interpreting the disaster as divine correction and urging repentance.
works.significance: The principal documentary source for the intellectual life of the Carolingian age and its English foundations.
works.meter: Latin prose, with verse epistles among the corpus.
works.context: Written 780-804 from York and the Frankish court; edited by E. Dümmler in MGH Epistolae IV (1895).
works.characters: Charlemagne; Arno of Salzburg; the monks of Lindisfarne; Æthelhard of Canterbury; Eanbald of York
works.structure: A chronologically arranged correspondence of over 280 items.
works.attributionNotes: Alcuin's authorship is certain.
themes: The public theatre and the players' world
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Alexander's Feast; or, The Power of Music
works.description: Dryden's second Cecilia ode, a dramatic narrative of the Greek musician Timotheus singing at Alexander the Great's victory feast and rousing him through pity, love, and finally revenge.
works.plot: Timotheus's song moves Alexander from triumph to tears to drunken fury, so that he burns Persepolis; the poem concludes that a nobler master of harmony — St Cecilia — raised the sacred organ and the divine affections.
works.significance: The culminating English ode of the seventeenth century; Handel's 1736 setting made it internationally famous and it remained a touchstone for poetic theories of versification through the eighteenth century.
works.meter: Irregular Pindaric stanzas; Dryden claimed to have written it in a single night and considered it his best work.
works.context: Written for the Music Society's St Cecilia's Day celebration of 1697 and set by Jeremiah Clarke.
works.characters: Alexander the Great; Timotheus; Thaïs; St Cecilia
works.structure: A continuous dramatic narrative in irregular stanzas, ending with an abrupt change of key in the final chorus.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Alfred
works.description: Thomson's masque on Alfred the Great and the deliverance of the Saxon kingdom, written for the prince's country house and closed by the ode on the dominion of the sea which became the national song.
works.plot: The young Alfred, nursed in exile and instructed in the history of his house, is restored against the Danish power by the counsel and the example of the ancient British worthies; the vision of the nation's future is disclosed to him, and the masque ends with the invocation of the ocean's rule.
works.significance: It is the most successful of the century's literary masques and the source of the song that became the anthem of the naval nation, and it shows the Augustan language of liberty converted into entertainment.
works.meter: Alternating recitative lines, the regular stanzas of the song and the anthem measure of the closing ode, written for composition.
works.context: Prepared for the court of the Prince of Wales at his country seat, with music by the century's chief theatre composer, in the season when the patriot circle made the ancient British mythology of Alfred the vehicle of its opposition politics.
works.characters: Alfred; the Saxon counsellors of the exile; the Danish power; the choruses of the British worthies
works.structure: A masque in one act with the recitative, the chorus and the prophetic vision, closing in a separately numbered ode.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Thomson's, the music being another hand's; the closing ode has been separately credited to the poet.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Alfred's Domboc
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: King Alfred's law book: an introduction translating the Ten Commandments and Mosaic law into English, followed by Alfred's own code and an appendix of Ine's laws. A founding document of the idea of English law as the law of a Christian people, consciously modelled on the Old Testament.
works.plot: The prologue renders Exodus 20-23 — the commandments, the laws of injury, slavery, and property — as the ancient foundation of law; Alfred's own clauses then regulate oaths, treachery against lords, sanctuary, the church, marriage, wounds, theft, and the ordeal, closing with the principle of compensation where no earlier provision exists.
works.significance: The classic statement of Anglo-Saxon kingship as Christian legislation; the foundation text of the later English common law tradition.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Issued in the later years of Alfred's reign, c. 893; preserved in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 173 (with the Chronicle).
works.characters: Alfred (legislator); Moses (prologue)
works.structure: Tripartite: Mosaic introduction, Alfred's code, and the appended code of Ine.
works.attributionNotes: Alfred's authorship of the prologue and code is certain.
movements: Civil War Radicalism: The Levellers and the Diggers
sources: The Cambridge Companion to English Renaissance Drama, 2nd edition

works.title: All for Love; or, The World Well Lost
works.description: Dryden's rewriting of Antony and Cleopatra in blank verse, observing the unities of time, place, and action and confining itself to the last day in Alexandria; it is his own favourite among his plays.
works.plot: After Actium, Antony refuses to fight Octavius again, is drawn into suspicion by Ventidius and Alexas, and Cleopatra feigns death; the lovers die together, and the world is 'well lost' for love.
works.significance: The greatest heroic tragedy of the Restoration and the standard version of the Antony story on the English stage for more than a century; it remains Dryden's most frequently performed play.
works.meter: Blank verse, written, Dryden said, 'in imitation of Shakespeare's style'; the prologue declares it the first play he ever wrote without rhyme.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in December 1677 and published in 1678 with a preface defending the choice of blank verse and the observance of the unities.
works.characters: Marc Antony; Cleopatra; Ventidius; Alexas; Octavia; Serapion; Dolabella; Myris
works.structure: Five acts within the classical unities, with a single place (the temple of Isis at Alexandria) and a single day.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: All Ovid's Elegies
works.description: Marlowe's translation of Ovid's Amores into English heroic couplets — the first complete English version of the Roman love elegies, in which the poet-lover's campaigns in the bedroom, his mistress Corinna, and the whole erotic repertoire of Augustan Rome are rendered with Marlowe's characteristic audacity; the book was condemned and burned by the bishops' ban of 1599.
works.plot: The three books of the Amores move through the lover's slavery to Corinna, the rivalries, quarrels, and reconciliations of the affair, the impotence elegy, and the final renunciation of love elegy for tragedy — each poem an erotic set piece in the Ovidian manner.
works.significance: The first full English Ovid of the Renaissance erotic tradition — the text that made Marlowe's name a byword for atheism and licence, and a model for Donne's elegies.
works.meter: Heroic couplets — Marlowe's chosen form for Ovid's elegiacs — of a frankness that scandalized the authorities.
works.context: Printed surreptitiously in the late 1590s and burned under the Bishops' Ban of 1599 along with the satires of Marston and Hall; all early editions survive only in fragments.
works.characters: the poet-lover; Corinna; the eunuch Bagoas; the bawd Dipsas; Aurora
works.structure: A sequence of some forty-eight elegies in three books, translated in order from the Amores, with Marlowe's ten elegies to a serving-wench translating Ovid with his usual freedom.
works.attributionNotes: Translation; uncontested.

editions.title: Christopher Marlowe: The Complete Poems and Translations

works.title: All the Works of Epictetus
altTitles: All the Works of Epictetus, Which are Now Extant: Consisting of His Discourses, Collect'd by Arrian; The Enchiridion; and Chapters, Collect'd by Stobaeus
works.form: translation of a philosophical text, with preface and notes
works.description: A complete English version of the surviving works of the Stoic teacher, made from the Greek with an historical and critical preface and with annotations explaining the philosophy and its phrases. It was the work by which a woman scholar became a European byword for Greek learning.
works.plot: The translation renders the discourses reported by Arrian, the handbook and the extracts preserved by Stobaeus, giving the reader the whole of Epictetus's practical philosophy. The prefatory account explains the life, the doctrine and the value of the author, and the notes open the terms of the schools. The work presents Stoic ethics as a discipline of judgement, desire and duty, useful to Christian readers as well as to philosophers.
works.significance: It is one of the great achievements of eighteenth-century women's scholarship and long remained the standard English Epictetus, its reception being a decisive argument for female classical learning.
works.meter: A plain and capable prose translation of the Greek homily and diatribe, its sentences kept close to the spoken manner of the school; the prefatory matter is in the essay style of the day.
works.context: Published in 1758 with the encouragement and the practical support of the learned women of her acquaintance, in the season of the revival of Stoic and moral-philosophical interest and of the controversy about the study of Greek by women.
works.characters: Epictetus; his interlocutors and reporters, Arrian and Stobaeus
works.structure: A scholarly translation in several books with a prefatory dissertation and commentarial notes; the order follows the arrangement of the Greek discourses.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the translator's name, the undertaking having been assisted by a borrowed Greek text and by the counsel of friends.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: All's Well That Ends Well
works.description: Shakespeare's 'problem comedy' from Boccaccio: Helena, the physician's daughter, cures the King of France and claims as her reward the reluctant Bertram, who flees to the wars of Italy — forcing Helena to win him by the bed-trick: taking Diana's place in the dark to fulfil his impossible conditions (his ring and his child), and exposing him at the play's end.
works.plot: Helena heals the King, chooses Bertram, is rejected and abandoned; in Florence she substitutes herself for Diana in Bertram's bed and secures ring and child; the final scene unravels Bertram's lies until Helena appears with both proofs and his conversion is wrung from him.
works.significance: The most disquieting of the comedies — a study of merit against rank, and of a woman's will — that has found its audience only in the modern era.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose for the exposure of Parolles; the style is spare and riddling, matching the play's moral knot.
works.context: Dated about 1604–05, in the same phase as Measure for Measure; its tone reflects the Jacobean darkening of Shakespeare's comedy.
works.characters: Helena; Bertram; the Countess of Rousillon; the King of France; Parolles; Lafew; Diana; the Widow; the two French lords (the Dumaine brothers)
works.structure: A fairy-tale plot (the healing of the king, the impossible tasks) crossed with the bed-trick of Renaissance novella, framed by the choric commentaries of the Countess, Lafew, and Parolles.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
