The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Antonius
authors: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
works.description: Mary Sidney Herbert's translation of Robert Garnier's Senecan tragedy Marc-Antoine (1578), the first English version of a French classical tragedy: a closet drama in which Mark Antony, after Actium, debates his ruin with his friends and Cleopatra, and falls on his sword.
works.plot: Antony, defeated and despairing, rejects the counsel of his followers, is reproached and forgiven by Cleopatra, and kills himself; the play closes with the chorus's meditation on Fortune and with Cleopatra's grief and resolve.
works.significance: The bridge by which French neoclassical tragedy entered English, and the first English tragedy of Cleopatra.
works.meter: Blank verse with rhyming choruses, matching Garnier's French alexandrines with English iambic pentameter.
works.context: Published in 1592, amid the English vogue for Senecan tragedy and the Pembroke circle's literary patronage; it anticipated the Antony plays of Shakespeare and Daniel.
works.characters: Mark Antony; Cleopatra; Charmian; Philostratus; Lucilius; the Chorus of Egyptians
works.structure: Five acts of Senecan structure with choruses, designed for reading rather than performance.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by Mary Sidney Herbert from Robert Garnier's Marc-Antoine (1578); uncontested.

editions.title: The Collected Works of Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
editions.editor: Margaret P. Hannay, Michael G. Brennan, and Mary Ellen Lamb (eds.)

works.title: Antony and Cleopatra
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of empire and desire: the ageing Antony, caught between Rome and Egypt, duty and Cleopatra, loses the world at Actium and, hearing the false report of her death, falls on his sword; Cleopatra, refusing Octavius's triumph, dies by the asp, and the play ends with the lovers' deaths transfigured into myth.
works.plot: Antony's dalliance in Alexandria draws him back to Rome and the marriage to Octavia; the breach with Caesar sends him back to Cleopatra; the sea-fight at Actium is lost when she flies and he follows; his rage, her feigned death, his botched suicide, and her staged one complete the tragedy — 'I am fire and air' — with Caesar left to bury them side by side.
works.significance: The greatest English poem of erotic grandeur — the tragedy in which the lovers outgrow tragedy itself.
works.meter: A hyperbolic, sensuous verse of superlatives — Enobarbus's barge speech its summit — with the prose of Egypt's court as the foil to Roman plainness.
works.context: Written about 1606–07 from North's Plutarch, whose phrasing Shakespeare follows at the barge and the death scenes; the play's imperial themes shadow the Jacobean debate over empire and union.
works.characters: Mark Antony; Cleopatra; Octavius Caesar; Enobarbus; Octavia; Charmian; Iras; Lepidus; Pompey; Alexas; Eros; Dolabella; the Clown
works.structure: A tragedy of scenes, not acts — forty-two rapid movements between Rome and Alexandria — in which the lovers' deaths are deliberately drawn out across the final acts as ceremony and apotheosis.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Apollonius of Tyre
works.form: prose romance in Old English prose
works.description: The Old English prose translation of the Historia Apollonii regis Tyri — the story of the shipwrecked prince Apollonius, his lost wife and daughter, and their final reunion: the first prose romance in English and the ancestor of Shakespeare's Pericles and of the Apollonius tradition that runs through Gower and the Middle Ages.
works.plot: Apollonius of Tyre, having solved the riddle of the incestuous king Antiochus, flees by sea; shipwrecked at Pentapolis, he wins the king's daughter in marriage; at sea their daughter is born and the queen, apparently dead, is cast overboard in a sealed coffin; the daughter, raised at Mytilene, is sold to a brothel-keeper but preserves her honour by her wisdom; the story ends in the great recognition scene, when the family is reunited at Ephesus and Mytilene.
works.significance: The first English prose romance; the bridge between the classical romance tradition and the Middle English romances and Shakespeare's Pericles.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated c. 1000-1050 from the Latin Historia Apollonii (a late antique romance); the unique manuscript is Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201, which also contains Wulfstan's homilies.
works.characters: Apollonius; Antiochus; Arcestrates of Pentapolis; the queen; the daughter (Thasia); Athenagoras of Mytilene
works.structure: A continuous romance narrative of adventure, loss, and recognition, in the incest-riddle frame of the Latin source.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translator.

works.title: Apology for the Life of Colley Cibber
works.form: Autobiographical memoir and theatrical history in prose.
works.description: An autobiographical memoir published in 1740 after the writer's retirement from the stage, at once a defence of a career and the richest contemporary account of the London patent theatre in its first brilliant half-century. Written in a garrulous, self-admiring prose that rarely distinguishes vanity from evidence, it reviews the author's own plays and acting, the quarrels and collapses of the companies he helped to manage, and the attacks of his enemies, the most formidable of which had long since enthroned him as the emperor of dullness.
works.plot: The narrative runs from a boyhood in the theatre world and a first sight of a play to management at Drury Lane, feuds with rival companies and with the poets who succeeded, and final retirement; it is interrupted by set defences of the author's treatment of the Shakespearean text, of his own dramatic writings, and of the actors and actresses he employed. Passages of portraiture of players, managers and their noble patrons are worked up from memory and were repeatedly borrowed by later historians of the stage. The memoir prints or paraphrases the prologues, epilogues and occasional verses by which its author had advertised himself, and quotes the insults levelled at him at length so as to return them with good humour.
works.significance: It is the principal source-book for the company history, repertory and acting style of the London stage between the 1680s and the 1730s, and the standard illustration of how a manager turned autobiography into reply. Historians use its testimony with caution because self-love governs its dates and its judgments, and its apology for adapting the national dramatist to modern taste is the fullest contemporary defence of that practice.
works.context: The memoir was put together in the years of the author's retirement, when the theatre he described had been reconstituted by new managers and licences, and when the satire that had made his name a byword for dullness was still in circulation. It belongs to the flourishing of theatrical memoir and anecdote that also produced the biographical prefaces of the play collections of the 1730s and 1740s, and it is a specimen of the Augustan practice of answering lampoon with autobiography.
works.characters: the author himself as boy, actor, manager and old man; the players and actresses of the two patent houses; the booksellers and rivals with whom he quarrelled; the noble patrons and box-keepers of the theatre
works.structure: Continuous first-person prose narrative running in one line from youth to old age, with documentary matter - verses, letters, the published records of quarrels - embedded in it and with digressive chapters on the drama and on editorial dealings with the national dramatist.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Appius and Virginia
works.form: tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: Dennis's blank-verse Roman tragedy, drawn from the decemviral history of Livy, in which the lust of the mighty magistrate for a plebeian maid and the father's pious murder of her become a study of corrupt power, chastity and republican fury. Severe in its moral register and unstinted in its invective against the decemvirs, it is the dramatic illustration of the theories of enthusiasm and of the terrors of virtue set out in the treatises of 1701 and 1704. Its failure at the playhouse and the quarrel over its re-use by other authors made it also the most famous case in the century of the professional writer's grievance.
works.plot: Appius, one of the decemvirs, designs to get Virginia, the betrothed of Icilius, by a judicial fiction of sale, and uses his authority to defeat her advocates in the forum; Virginius, her father, rather than yield her to the tyrant's power, kills her in the street with a sentence that at once frees and destroys her; the outraged commons secede, the decemviral yoke is attacked, and Appius, stripped of office and abandoned by his patrons, dies in captivity. The play thus moves from the corruption of law into tyranny, to private catastrophe, and then to the restoration of public liberty.
works.significance: Its severity and its political indignation made it a permanent exemplum of the neglected Augustan tragedian, and the anecdote attached to it entered the common lore of authorial property in dramatic texts; it also survives as the practical test case of a critical theory that demanded terror, enthusiasm and moral gravity in the same play.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter, declamatory and heavily sententious, with long impassioned periods and a deliberate accumulation of terror-words proper to Dennis's account of poetical enthusiasm.
works.context: First acted in London in 1709, in a season when the theatre was contested ground for Whig and Tory interpretations of Roman liberty; it held the stage for only a very short run, and the later revival of its scenes in another company's play provoked Dennis's well-known public protest against the appropriation of his work.
works.characters: Appius Claudius; Virginia; Virginius; Icilius; the seceding commons of Rome
works.structure: Regular five-act tragedy in the neoclassical manner, with a public forum action, a central recognition and killing, and an offstage political resolution; the catastrophe is reported rather than represented, and the political action closes the design.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Dennis's ownership of the text is documented by his own publication and by the anecdote of the reclaimed scenes.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Arcadia
works.description: Sidney's prose romance written for his sister Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke: the 'Old Arcadia' (c. 1577–80, complete in five books or acts) is a tragicomic tale of two princes in disguise among the shepherds of Arcadia; the unfinished 'New Arcadia' (c. 1584–86) reworks the first books into a heroic romance of chivalric adventure; the composite edition of 1593 joined the revised books to the old ending.
works.plot: Princes Musidorus and Pyrocles, in love with the princesses Pamela and Philoclea, disguise themselves as a shepherd and an Amazon to gain access to the secluded royal household; their courtships, the rebellion of the commons, the trial of the princes for the supposed death of King Basilius, and the oracles that haunt the plot drive the action of the Old Arcadia, while the New Arcadia expands it with the wars of the rebel Amphialus and the captivity episodes.
works.significance: The most influential prose fiction of the English Renaissance — the model for a century of romances and the direct ancestor of Wroth's Urania and of Shakespeare's borrowed plots.
works.meter: Prose of elaborate periodic balance, with verse eclogues in many stanza forms at the act divisions.
works.context: Written in retirement at Wilton after Sidney's withdrawal from court (1579) and revised in the mid-1580s; printed after his death in 1590 and, with his sister's composite arrangement, in 1593.
works.characters: Pyrocles; Musidorus; Philoclea; Pamela; Basilius, King of Arcadia; Gynecia; Euarchus; Amphialus; the shepherds Dorus and Strephon
works.structure: An interlaced romance in prose with verse eclogues between the books, deliberately organized by Sidney into 'five acts' on the model of drama.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the 1593 composite text was assembled by Mary Sidney Herbert.

editions.title: The New Arcadia

works.title: Arden of Faversham
altTitles: The Lamentable and True Tragedy of Master Arden of Faversham
works.description: The anonymous domestic tragedy of the real murder of Thomas Arden of Faversham in 1551: his wife Alice and her lover Mosby hire a succession of bungling assassins — Black Will and Shakebag among them — whose attempts fail comically until the murder is done in Arden's own house; the killers are caught, and the play ends with the executions and Alice's burning, 'the sin of murder' its homiletic close.
works.plot: Alice's adultery and Arden's blindness to it set the plot; the hired murders fail through fog, chance, and cowardice; the final ambush in the parlour succeeds; the discovery of the body, the flight of the murderers, and the punishment of all — including Alice, who dies 'bewailed' only by her guilt — complete the tragedy's documentary arc.
works.significance: The founding text of English domestic tragedy — the first play to make an English household and an English murder the matter of tragedy.
works.meter: A plain, powerful verse (and prose) of the provincial scene — the play's very anonymity has invited attribution to Shakespeare, Kyd, and others.
works.context: Printed in 1592 and performed by the Admiral's Men; based on the notorious Faversham murder of 1551 as told in Holinshed; it is the first English play of a real, recent, and domestic crime.
works.characters: Thomas Arden; Alice Arden; Mosby; Black Will; Shakebag; Greene; Michael; Franklin; the Mayor of Faversham; Susan; Clarke the painter
works.structure: A five-act tragedy built directly on Holinshed's account of the real 1551 murder, with the comic failures of the assassins as its counterpoint to the horror.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attributions to Kyd, Shakespeare, and others have been proposed but none is proven.

editions.title: Arden of Faversham (Revels Plays)

works.title: Areopagitica
altTitles: Areopagitica: A Speech of Mr. John Milton for the Liberty of Unlicenc'd Printing
works.description: Milton's prose speech to Parliament (24 November 1644) against the Licensing Order of 1643, arguing that prior censorship of books destroys learning, virtue, and truth, and that a free people must be trusted to choose good over evil — the classic English defence of freedom of the press.
works.plot: Milton traces the history of licensing from the Inquisition, argues that books contain the 'life-blood of a master spirit', distinguishes the testing of virtue from its seclusion, and contends that truth will prevail in a free and open encounter.
works.significance: One of the foundational texts of the argument for free speech and a free press, still quoted in constitutional and press-freedom debates, and a masterpiece of English prose.
works.meter: Eloquent, Latinate prose with a powerful oratorical rhythm and dense classical allusion.
works.context: Published during the Civil War against Parliament's 1643 licensing order; it drew on Milton's own experience of unlicensed publication and the collapse of censorship.
works.structure: A classical oration in prose, modeled on Isocrates's Areopagiticus, moving through historical example, argument, and eloquent peroration.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under Milton's name.

works.title: As You Like It
works.description: Shakespeare's pastoral comedy, adapted from Thomas Lodge's Rosalynde: Duke Senior, exiled to the Forest of Arden, is joined by his daughter Rosalind (disguised as the boy Ganymede), her cousin Celia, the clown Touchstone, and eventually the melancholy Jaques and the reformed usurper — while Orlando's love-verses to Rosalind hang on every tree.
works.plot: Orlando, robbed of his birthright, flees to Arden; Rosalind, banished, tutors him in love while disguised as Ganymede; the usurping Duke is converted on the forest's edge; and the play ends with four weddings and the god Hymen's masque, followed by Rosalind's epilogue.
works.significance: The definitive English pastoral comedy and the vehicle of Shakespeare's greatest comic heroine.
works.meter: Alternating prose and blank verse — Rosalind's prose wit against Orlando's verses — with the songs 'Under the greenwood tree' and 'It was a lover and his lass'.
works.context: Written 1599, the year of the Globe's opening, from Lodge's Rosalynde (1590); the forest reimagines the Ardennes through Warwickshire memory.
works.characters: Rosalind; Orlando; Celia; Touchstone; Jaques; Duke Senior; Duke Frederick; Oliver; Adam; Silvius; Phebe; Audrey; William; Corin; Charles the wrestler
works.structure: A movement from court to forest and back, built on the contrast of the two worlds and on the play's chain of love-dialogues, with the 'Seven Ages of Man' speech and the songs of Amiens as set pieces.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Astraea Redux
altTitles: Astraea Redux: A Poem on the Happy Restoration & Return of His Sacred Majesty Charles the Second
works.description: Dryden's first public poem, celebrating the Restoration of Charles II in May 1660 and announcing the young poet's allegiance to the returning monarchy; it recasts the civil wars as a national illness now cured by the king's return.
works.plot: The poem traces the disorder of the Interregnum, praises General Monck's role, and celebrates Charles II as the providential healer of the nation, drawing on biblical and classical typology.
works.significance: Established Dryden's public reputation and set the tone for the political panegyric of the Restoration; a benchmark for his later development.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in closed iambic pentameter, with occasional alexandrines; one of the earliest displays of Dryden's mature couplet.
works.context: Written within weeks of Charles II's landing at Dover on 25 May 1660 and published in the same year.
works.structure: A panegyric in three movements: the diagnosis of national disorder, the mechanism of restoration, and the prophetic blessing on the new reign.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden on the title page of the 1660 quarto; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Astrophel and Stella
works.description: The first great English sonnet sequence: 108 sonnets and eleven songs tracing the love of Astrophel (the star-lover) for Stella (the star) — widely read as Sidney's love for Penelope Devereux, Lady Rich — from first sight through desire, frustration, and the lady's marriage to another, to the renunciation of the last sonnets.
works.plot: Astrophel falls in love with Stella at first sight; he pleads, she rebuffs; she marries Lord Rich; the poems anatomize every phase of the love — reason versus desire, sleep and dreams, the stolen kiss, jealousy, absence — until the final sonnets turn from the vain suit.
works.significance: The fountainhead of the Elizabethan sonnet vogue: Spenser, Daniel, Drayton, and Shakespeare all wrote in its wake.
works.meter: The English (Shakespearean-type) sonnet form of Sidney's own stamp — abab abab cdcd ee — with hexameter final lines in several sonnets.
works.context: Composed about 1581–82 in the circle of the Earl of Oxford's and Sidney's London; printed posthumously in 1591 by Thomas Newman in an unauthorized edition, which launched the vogue of the sonnet sequence.
works.characters: Astrophel; Stella; Lord Rich (alluded to); Cupid; Reason; Virtue
works.structure: A sequence with a genuine plot — courtship, crisis, renunciation — varied by the eleven songs inserted at points of dramatic action.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the biographical reading as Sidney and Penelope Devereux is a later interpretation, not a fact in the text.

editions.title: The Poems of Sir Philip Sidney

works.title: Athelston
works.description: A dark romance of kingship and treason, unique in the canon: the king Athelston, swayed by the traitor Wymond, puts his sworn brother and his family to the ordeal of fire, and is saved from tyranny only by the intervention of the archbishop and the test of the fire itself. Its grim political realism makes it unlike any other English romance.
works.plot: Four messengers become sworn brothers; Athelston becomes king, and the envious Wymond persuades him that Earl Egeland plots treason; Athelston's violence against the earl's pregnant wife and children is halted when the archbishop curses him and the ordeal of fire acquits the innocent, exposing Wymond and restoring the fellowship.
works.significance: The most politically serious of the English romances — a study of tyranny, sanctuary, and the ordeal — and a favourite text for the romance's engagement with law and kingship.
works.meter: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas, often grimly emphatic.
works.context: Composed c. 1355–80 in the East Midlands, drawing on the legend of St Edmund and on baronial and ecclesiastical politics; preserved uniquely in Cambridge, Gonville and Caius College, MS 175.
works.characters: Athelston; Wymond; Egeland; Edyff; the archbishop
works.structure: A compact tragedy of misrule in three movements (oath, slander, ordeal), with the archbishop's excommunication as its pivot.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Auld Lang Syne
works.form: song lyric in the Scottish vernacular, collected and reworked from traditional material for a musical anthology
works.description: The song of old acquaintance and of remembrance, in which the pairs of friends who have run the world together ask whether the times of 'auld lang syne' shall be forgotten. Burns presented it to Johnson as a recovered old song rather than as an invention, and his own stanzas gave the traditional phrase its enduring form. It has since become the most performed commemorative song in the English-speaking world.
works.plot: The speaker proposes that the partners in former merriness should drink a cup of kindness yet for the sake of the old days, recalling the runs over the braes and the talks before they were parted by years and distance. The refrain insists on the phrase itself, converting a drinking song's occasion into a general meditation on memory, friendship and the passage of time, and closing with the pledge of remembrance.
works.significance: It is the most widely performed and most universally recognised song in the language, and the exemplar of the way Burns's collecting practice could make an old phrase into a new poem. It also stands as a document of the 1790s effort to define a national song repertory against imported opera and English popular air.
works.meter: Ballad stanzas of alternating four- and three-beat lines with a refrain, set to the air Burns associated with the words; the diction is plain and the syntax colloquial.
works.context: Sent by Burns to Johnson in 1793 with a letter describing it as taken down from an old man's recitation and as belonging to the store of ancient Scottish song; the phrase and title had already been used by Allan Ramsay, and Burns's work is an act of recovery and revision within the collecting culture of the Scottish Musical Museum.
works.characters: The speaker and the old friend or friends toasted
works.structure: A strophic song with a fixed refrain, each verse adding a remembered scene to the toast, the argument carried by the return of the phrase auld lang syne.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Burns is uncontested for the familiar text, but the song is expressly a recovery and reworking of earlier traditional verse, and the standard editions record the anterior phrase and Ramsay's use of the title; the composition date follows Burns's letter to Johnson.

works.title: Aureng-zebe; or, The Great Mogul
works.description: Dryden's heroic play on the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb's succession struggle, notable for its more restrained hero and for Dryden's prefatory doubt about the value of rhyme.
works.plot: The aged emperor Shah Abbas is suspected of loving his son Aureng-zebe's mistress Indamora; the prince's constancy and filial duty survive a rebellion by his brother Morat, and order is restored.
works.significance: The last of Dryden's heroic plays and the point at which he turned away from rhyme toward blank verse in All for Love; it marks the end of the heroic drama's ascendancy.
works.meter: Rhymed heroic couplets, with a looser and more conversational movement than in The Conquest of Granada.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1675 and published in 1676, dedicated to the Earl of Mulgrave; the prologue's complaint about 'the dull duties of a poet's trade' reflects Dryden's growing disenchantment with rhyme.
works.characters: Aureng-zebe; Indamora; Shah Abbas; Morat; Nourmahal; Arban; Benducar
works.structure: Five acts in the heroic manner with a single main action and a rival brother subplot.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Autumn
works.description: The fourth of Thomson's seasonal poems, on the harvest, the gleaning, the vine and the melancholy of the closing year, with the celebrated account of the poet's own love and the meditation on the season of the mind.
works.plot: The poem follows the year to its ripening and its ingathering, the harvest field, the orchard and the vineyard, the mists and the melancholy of the evening, and ends with the tale of Cynia and the poet's retreat to contemplation and to the hymn of the season.
works.significance: It gave English verse its enduring imagery of autumn, harvest and melancholy evening, and its meditation on the seasons of the mind is the direct ancestor of the mid-century night and graveyard poem.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines of the most sustained richness in the sequence, with the long evening period and the inserted lyric ode.
works.context: Issued at the close of the first publication of the four seasons, when the poem of the harvest and of melancholy was the most fashionable species of descriptive writing.
works.characters: the reapers and the gleaners of the harvest field; the maid of the inset tale; the contemplative poet
works.structure: A descriptive progression through the operations of the harvest, with the inset love tale and the closing meditative retreat.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Azarias
altTitles: The Canticle of the Three Youths
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious narrative poem with embedded canticle
works.description: A poem on the ordeal of the three youths — Azarias, Ananias, and Misael — in Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace, based on Daniel 3 and on the canticle of praise they sing from the flames. The poem shares a substantial passage with the Junius manuscript poem Daniel.
works.plot: The three youths refuse to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image and are cast into the furnace; protected by the angel of God, they walk unharmed amid the flames and sing a canticle of praise in which all creation is summoned to bless the Lord, from the heavens and waters to the beasts and the sons of men.
works.significance: Together with Daniel it shows how Old English poets rendered the canticles of the liturgy in the native heroic idiom, turning scriptural praise into alliterative poetry.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the canticle's catalogues of creation are carried by parallel alliterative phrases in the liturgical style.
works.context: The story of the three youths was read typologically in Anglo-Saxon England: the furnace prefigured both the Incarnation (the fire that does not burn) and the Church's endurance under persecution. The poem is closely related to Daniel in the Junius manuscript.
works.characters: Azarias, Ananias, Misael, Nebuchadnezzar
works.structure: A bipartite structure: a brief narrative of the ordeal followed by the long canticle of praise, a liturgical catalogue of creation in the manner of the Benedicite.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The relationship with Daniel (shared lines) is a standing crux of Old English scholarship; the two poems may derive from a common source or one from the other.
themes: Rural labour, depopulation, and the deserted village

works.title: Bald's Leechbook
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Royal 12.D.xvii (mid-tenth century, Winchester)
works.description: The most ambitious medical work in any early medieval vernacular: a systematic Old English leechbook in three books, compiled at Winchester in the mid-tenth century and named for Bald and Cild, the physicians named in its metrical colophon. It organizes hundreds of remedies for ailments from head to foot, drawing on Latin medical learning translated into English.
works.plot: Book I treats external ailments (head to toe), Book II internal diseases, and Book III a miscellany of surgical procedures, with remedies drawn from Greek, Latin, and native traditions; the work instructs the physician in diagnosis, pharmacy, bloodletting, and surgery, and includes charms as well as herbal and mineral preparations.
works.significance: The earliest substantial medical treatise in any western European vernacular, invaluable for the history of medicine and of Old English scientific prose, and a demonstration of the vernacular's capacity for technical writing.
works.context: Compiled in the Winchester milieu on the eve of the Benedictine Reform, the Leechbook shows the court's patronage of practical learning and the translation of Mediterranean medicine into English; it is the ancestor of the Middle English medical manuscript tradition.
works.structure: A systematic reference work organized by ailment and body-part (a capite ad calcem), with numbered remedies under each heading; the third book is looser, mixing surgery, obstetrics, and charms.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous compilation; the colophon names Bald as owner and Cild as writer, not as authors of the medical content.

editions.title: Leechdoms, Wortcunning, and Starcraft of Early England

works.title: Bartholomew Fair
works.description: Jonson's comedy of the fair: on St Bartholomew's Day, the whole of London pours into Smithfield — the justice Adam Overdo in disguise, the hot Puritan Zeal-of-the-Land Busy, the gallants Winwife and Quarlous, the pig-woman Ursula and her booth, the puppet-show of Hero and Leander — in a play whose carnival world exposes every pretension, and whose induction mocks its own audience's 'warrant' for the satire.
works.plot: Overdo patrols the fair to 'enormities' in disguise; Busy denounces the fleshpots and falls to the pig; the gallants win the rich widow and the ward through the fair's games; the cutpurse Edgeworth and the bawd Whit ply their trades; and the last act's puppet trial before Overdo ends with the puppets' own argument and the universal pardon of the fair.
works.significance: The greatest carnival play in English — a comedy that swallows its own satire and leaves the audience judged along with the fair.
works.meter: Almost wholly prose — the most populous and idiomatic prose of Jonson's career — with the puppets' verse as the final parody.
works.context: First performed at the Hope theatre on 31 October 1614, before James I; printed 1631; its 'enormities' satire answers the puritan attacks on the stage Jonson had answered in his own person.
works.characters: Adam Overdo; Dame Overdo; Zeal-of-the-Land Busy; Winwife; Quarlous; Bartholomew Cokes; Grace Wellborn; Wasp; Ursula the pig-woman; Leatherhead (Lantern); Joan Trash; Edgeworth; Whit; Justice Trouble-All; the Puppets
works.structure: A deliberately sprawling carnival structure — no single plot, but a cross-section of the fair in five acts, with Overdo's exposures as the running joke and the puppet trial as the finale.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, 7 vols.
editions.editor: David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (gen. eds.)

works.title: Bede's Death Song
works.manuscriptDate: St Gallen, Stiftsbibliothek 254 (ninth century or earlier); Northumbrian version in Cambridge, University Library Kk.5.16 (the Moore Bede, c. 737)
works.description: A five-line alliterative poem, the last words of the dying Bede, recorded in the Epistola Cuthberti de obitu Bedae. The poet meditates on the soul's necessary journey out of the body and the judgment each man must face for his deeds. It is the earliest datable Old English poem.
works.plot: Bede, near death, reflects that no man's wisdom can outrun his need to consider, before departing, what judgment his soul will receive for the good and evil he has done.
works.significance: The earliest datable poem in English, and a uniquely documented case of vernacular verse preserved with its author, date, and occasion of composition.
works.meter: Five lines of classic alliterative verse in the Northumbrian dialect, preserved with Latin paraphrase; the earliest securely datable example of English poetry.
works.context: Recorded by Bede's pupil Cuthbert in the letter describing the master's death on 26 May 735; the poem circulated in two dialect versions and in many manuscripts of the Historia ecclesiastica, often with a Latin translation.
works.characters: Bede (speaker)
works.structure: Five alliterative long lines in two movements: the inevitability of the soul's departure, and the reckoning of deeds before the judge.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Bede in the Epistola Cuthberti, composed, according to the letter, on his deathbed; the attribution is accepted by modern scholarship, though the poem circulated anonymously in some manuscripts.

works.title: Behemoth; or, The Long Parliament
works.description: Hobbes's history of the English civil wars in the form of a dialogue, written in old age as a companion to Leviathan and suppressed by Charles II, but printed without authority in 1679 and after Hobbes's death in 1682.
works.plot: In four dialogues between A and B, Hobbes explains the causes of the civil wars as the spread of seditious doctrines from the Presbyterians, the Independents, and the universities, and the ambition of the parliamentary leaders.
works.significance: Hobbes's own interpretation of the events that produced Leviathan and a key text for understanding his theory of sedition and the role of universities and clergy in politics.
works.meter: Conversational prose dialogue.
works.context: Written c. 1668-70; Charles II refused permission to publish it, and it appeared in an unauthorised edition in 1679 and an authorised edition in 1682.
works.characters: A (the narrator); B (the questioner); Charles I; Cromwell; the Long Parliament
works.structure: Four dialogues covering 1640 to 1660.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Hobbes; the 1679 edition was unauthorised and Hobbes complained of its errors.

editions.title: Leviathan: The English and Latin Texts
editions.publisher: Clarendon Press (Clarendon Edition of the Works of Thomas Hobbes)

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Believe as You List
works.description: Massinger's political tragedy on the false Sebastian of Portugal, suppressed by the Master of the Revels for its treatment of a recent alliance and then rewritten; it survives in the author's manuscript with Sir Henry Herbert's annotations.
works.plot: A young man claiming to be the lost King Sebastian of Portugal is recognised by many, pursued by Spain, and finally exposed as an impostor; the play explores the politics of belief and dynastic legitimacy.
works.significance: The most important surviving manuscript of a Caroline play, documenting the workings of censorship; it is also Massinger's most serious political tragedy.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: First drafted in 1631 and banned by Herbert as seditious because of its allusion to the Anglo-Spanish alliance; Massinger recast the story in a Roman setting and the revised version was licensed on 6 May 1631.
works.characters: Antiochus (the false Sebastian); Titus Flaminius; the Roman Senate; Marcella; Sulpitius
works.structure: Five acts following the pretender's rise, recognition, and exposure.
works.attributionNotes: The authorial manuscript is signed 'P.M.' and is universally accepted as Massinger's holograph.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Beowulf
works.description: The greatest surviving poem in Old English: a heroic epic of 3,182 alliterative lines recounting the deeds of the Geatish hero Beowulf against the monster Grendel, Grendel's mother, and, fifty years later, a dragon. It combines the legendary history of Scandinavia with a profound Christian meditation on heroism, mortality, and the limits of earthly glory.
works.plot: The young hero Beowulf sails from Geatland to Denmark to rid King Hrothgar's hall Heorot of the man-eating monster Grendel, whom he defeats in a night combat; he then tracks Grendel's mother to her underwater lair and slays her. Rewarded and honoured, he returns home and eventually rules the Geats for fifty years, until a dragon, enraged by the theft of a cup from its hoard, ravages his kingdom; the aged king kills the dragon but dies of his wounds, and the poem ends with his funeral pyre and the foreboding of his people's doom.
works.significance: The foundational epic of English literature; the first extended poetic masterpiece in any Germanic vernacular; a touchstone for subsequent English poetry (Tolkien, Auden, Heaney) and for the study of Germanic legend.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre: four stresses per line divided by a caesura; formulaic diction, kennings, and variation throughout.
works.context: Composed somewhere between the age of Bede and the eve of the Conquest, and copied c. 1000 in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv); its heroes belong to sixth-century Scandinavia (Hygelac's raid on Frisia, c. 521, is historical), while its audience was Christian Anglo-Saxon England.
works.characters: Beowulf, Hrothgar, Grendel, Grendel's mother, the dragon, Wiglaf, Hygelac, Unferth, Wealhtheow, Scyld Scefing
works.structure: A bipartite structure (youthful Danish adventures; old age and the dragon) framed by the funerals of Scyld Scefing and Beowulf; interlaced with digressions — the Finnsburh episode, the Sigmund lay, the Swedish-Geatish wars, and the 'Lay of the Last Survivor' — that mirror and darken the main action.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; authorship_status reflects scholarly consensus. Ascribed to no known poet.

editions.title: Beowulf: A Verse Translation
Klaeber's Beowulf and The Fight at Finnsburg
editions.editor: R. D. Fulk, Robert E. Bjork, and John D. Niles (eds.)

sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume A: The Middle Ages

works.title: Bevis of Hampton
works.description: One of the most popular of all Middle English romances: the adventures of Bevis of Southampton, sold into heathen lands by his mother's treachery, who wins the Saracen princess Josian, fights dragons and giants, and at last reclaims his English inheritance. Its vigorous, episodic narrative survived in verse, prose, and print into the seventeenth century.
works.plot: Bevis's mother plots his father's murder and marries the murderer; the boy is sold overseas, but wins fame and the love of Josian; after adventures in Armenia, Cologne, and England — including his defeat of the dragon of Cologne and his final siege of Southampton — he regains his lands and ends his days as a monk with Josian.
works.significance: The archetypal popular romance: its immense circulation (Chaucer's Sir Thopas parodies its tail-rhyme form) makes it central to the history of English popular reading.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets, later rewritten in tail-rhyme in some manuscripts.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 from an Anglo-Norman original (Boeve de Haumtoun); preserved in six manuscripts, the Auchinleck (c. 1330) foremost, and repeatedly printed from c. 1500 to the seventeenth century.
works.characters: Bevis; Josian; Ascopard the giant; Saber; the dragon of Cologne; King Ermin
works.structure: A sprawling episodic quest in the Auchinleck manner, with exile, conversion, combat, and restoration as its repeating units.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Beware the Cat
altTitles: Beware the Cat: The First English Novel
works.description: William Baldwin's anti-Catholic prose satire of 1552–53, in which a company of men swap stories proving that cats can speak and understand; printed posthumously in 1561 and often claimed as the first English novel.
works.plot: The narrator, Master Streamer, overhears a conversation among the household of John Young while lodged at the printing house; the talk turns to cats, and Gregory Streamer relates how, having eaten a cat, he gained the power to understand animal speech, recounting the trial of Mouse-slayer before the cat parliament and the bawdy doings of cats and priests — a satire on Catholic superstition, oral tradition, and the credulity of tale-collectors.
works.significance: Claimed as the first English novel for its sustained prose fiction and self-conscious narrative framing; it is also a sophisticated satire on storytelling, tradition, and the authority of print, anticipating the narrative experiments of the Elizabethan period.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in 1552–53 at the press of John Day, where Baldwin worked; its satire of Catholic ritual (the cat's mass) fitted the Edwardian Reformation moment, and by its printing in 1561 (with a prefatory epistle to John Young) the political climate had changed again.
works.characters: Master Streamer (narrator); Gregory Streamer; Mouse-slayer; Grimalkin; John Young (the printer)
works.structure: A framed narrative in three orations, with inset stories (the cat's life of Grimalkin, the trial of Mouse-slayer) and a self-conscious apparatus of marginal glosses and running commentary on the reliability of oral report.
works.attributionNotes: Printed anonymously in 1561 with initials 'G. B.'; the attribution to William Baldwin rests on the prefatory matter and the internal evidence of the printing-house setting, and is accepted by modern scholarship.

editions.title: Beware the Cat: The First English Novel
editions.editor: William A. Ringler, Jr., and Michael Flachmann

works.title: Bishop Burnet's History of His Own Time
works.description: Burnet's posthumous history of England from the Restoration to the Treaty of Utrecht, written from his own experience as a bishop and courtier and published in two volumes in 1724 and 1734.
works.plot: The history narrates the reigns of Charles II, James II, William III, and Anne, with candid portraits of the leading statesmen and a Whig interpretation of the Revolution.
works.significance: One of the most important primary sources for the history of Restoration and Revolution politics; its portraits and anecdotes were widely quoted by Macaulay and later historians.
works.meter: Lively, anecdotal, sometimes careless prose of a participant historian.
works.context: Written from 1683 until Burnet's death in 1715; published by his son Thomas in 1724 and 1734.
works.characters: Charles II; James II; William III; Anne; Shaftesbury; Clarendon; Halifax; Rochester
works.structure: Two volumes covering 1660 to 1713, with digressions on the reigns before.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Burnet; published posthumously by his son.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Blickling Homilies
works.description: A collection of eighteen anonymous Old English homilies for the church year, preserved in the Princeton Blickling manuscript: the earliest substantial vernacular sermon collection, contemporary with the first series of Ælfric's Catholic Homilies but plainer and more popular in style. Contains the famous vision of hell and of the places of the souls ('the three utterances of the soul').
works.plot: The homilies treat the major feasts — Annunciation, Palm Sunday, Easter (with the harrowing of hell), Rogationtide, Ascension, Pentecost, the Assumption, and the feasts of the apostles — expounding the gospel readings with vivid narrative expansions: the descent into hell, the soul's journey after death, and the architecture of the otherworld.
works.significance: The principal witness to the pre-Ælfrician homiletic tradition and to vernacular eschatological imagery.
works.meter: Old English prose; occasional rhythmical passages.
works.context: Copied c. 971, probably in Mercia or East Anglia; the manuscript (Princeton, Scheide Library, MS 71) is closely contemporary with the Beowulf manuscript's milieu.
works.characters: the evangelists' figures (Christ, the apostles, Mary, the blessed and the damned)
works.structure: Eighteen independent homilies in calendar order, each built on a gospel pericope with exegetical and exemplary digressions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to John Donne

works.title: Boece
works.description: Chaucer's prose translation of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, the work that above all others shaped his thought: the dialogue between the imprisoned Boethius and Lady Philosophy on fortune, free will, providence, and the sovereign good. Made c. 1380–86 with the aid of the commentary tradition, it is the foundation of the Boethian strain that runs through all his poetry.
works.plot: Boethius, imprisoned and awaiting death, laments his fall until Lady Philosophy appears and, through a graduated argument in prose and verse (the metres), cures him: showing that fortune is mutable by nature, that true happiness lies in God, that evil men are punished by their own wickedness, and that providence and free will are compatible.
works.significance: The most consequential translation Chaucer made: through it, the Consolation became English literature's native philosophical idiom, from Chaucer to Elizabeth I's translation and beyond.
works.meter: Prose translation of the whole, metres included, dense with the philosophical vocabulary Chaucer coined or naturalized.
works.context: Composed c. 1380–86, drawing on the Latin text and the commentary of Nicholas Trevet; its influence pervades Chaucer's mature poems (Troilus, the Knight's Tale, the ballades) and the whole English Boethian tradition.
works.characters: Boethius; Lady Philosophy
works.structure: Five books of alternating prose and metrical sections, in the Menippean form of the original; Chaucer renders the metres in prose, with explanatory glosses from the commentaries.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure (named in the Retraction).

editions.title: The Riverside Chaucer

works.title: Bohoursky
works.form: war elegy and occasional meditative poem, in the Ossianising manner of the late century
works.description: Cowper's late war elegy on a Russian general killed in the storming of Ochakov, a short poem that turns a printed notice of a stranger's death into a meditation on honour, pity and the cost of arms. It mourns the fallen commander as a brave and humane soldier and sets the horrors of a stormed town against the praise of the man who died in the breach. It is characteristic of Cowper's last decade in its mixture of northern romantic colour and Christian regret.
works.plot: The poem recalls the general's conduct and courage, the storm of the place and his death in the attack, and then asks what glory can mean for a Christian who must count the slain. It dwells on the spectacle of the field and the breach, on the pity that survives the battlefield, and on the uncertainty of fame, closing with the sense that the warrior's reward is a mourned name rather than a triumph.
works.significance: It is the best of Cowper's short war poems and a useful instance of how the 1790s made a remote general's death an occasion of Christian pity, an argument later central to the literature of war. Its handling of printed report into reflection shows the late topographical voice turned to contemporary history.
works.meter: Stanzaic iambic verse of Cowper's late manner, with a solemn slow movement and much monosyllabic weight.
works.context: Written in 1789 on the printed accounts of the Russo-Turkish war and the storming of Ochakov, at the close of a decade in which Cowper was deeply interested in the news of Europe and in the morality of war; his late poems on the Russian campaigns and on the French Revolution belong to the same journalistic and providential imagination.
works.characters: The Russian general Bohoursky; the assailants and defenders of the town; the mediating poet
works.structure: A brief epitaphic meditation in continuous stanzas, moving from the notice of the death to the description of the assault and to the reflection on honour and pity.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem's occasion is the printed account of the Russian general's death in the Russo-Turkish war, and its date rests on the printing of 1789.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Boniface's Letters
works.description: The correspondence of the missionary Boniface and his circle — some 150 letters exchanged with popes, kings, and above all the English friends and pupils who sustained his mission (Eadburga, Bugga, Leoba, Lull, Egbert of York): the most vivid documentary record of the Anglo-Saxon missions to the Continent.
works.plot: The letters carry the whole business of the German mission: requests for books and prayers, reports of synods and conversions, the felling of the sacred oak at Geismar, appeals for English nuns and scholars, consolations, and the last letters before the martyrdom at Dokkum (754); several are verse epistles with riddles for the nuns of Wessex.
works.significance: The richest source for the Anglo-Saxon missionary movement and for the literary culture of its female religious correspondents.
works.meter: Latin prose with verse epistles.
works.context: Written 716-754 from the mission field in Frisia and Germany; edited by M. Tangl, MGH Epistolae Selectae I (1916).
works.characters: Boniface; Lull; Leoba; Eadburga of Minster-in-Thanet; Bugga; Egbert of York; Daniel of Winchester; Pope Gregory II and III
works.structure: A correspondence of c. 150 letters, including letters addressed to Boniface.
works.attributionNotes: The core letters are Boniface's own; the collection includes his correspondents.
themes: Colonial enterprise and the New World
sources: The Poems of Alexander Pope, Twickenham Edition (11 volumes)

works.title: Brief Lives
works.description: John Aubrey's vast collection of biographical memoranda on the notable men of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries — Bacon, Hobbes, Shakespeare, Donne, Milton, Harvey, and hundreds more — compiled as notes for Anthony Wood's Athenae Oxonienses and never published in his lifetime.
works.plot: The entries are informal, gossipy, and anecdotal, recording physical appearance, habits, sayings, and eccentricities alongside dates and facts, in Aubrey's own hurried hand with gaps and marginal queries.
works.significance: The most vivid and most human biographical source for seventeenth-century England; Aubrey's method of personal recollection and physical detail anticipates modern biography, and the Lives have been continuously read since their publication.
works.meter: Informal, hurried, anecdotal prose, often in note form.
works.context: Compiled chiefly between 1669 and 1696, partly for Anthony Wood; the manuscripts passed to the Bodleian and were first printed in part in 1813.
works.characters: Thomas Hobbes; William Shakespeare; John Milton; Francis Bacon; John Donne; William Harvey; Sir Walter Raleigh
works.structure: An alphabetical collection of biographical memoranda, many incomplete, with Aubrey's characteristic asterisks and queries.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Aubrey; the manuscripts are in his own hand.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Britannia
works.description: William Camden's chorographical description of Britain, published in Latin in 1586 and enlarged through six editions (the English translation by Philemon Holland appearing in 1610): the island's name, peoples, counties, towns, and antiquities — Roman, Saxon, and medieval — surveyed county by county in the work that founded English antiquarianism and taught the nation its own past.
works.plot: The book proceeds from the general description of Britain and its inhabitants through the counties of England, Wales, Scotland, and Ireland: each county's etymology, history, noble families, and antiquities set down with the new documentary scholarship of the age.
works.significance: The founding work of British antiquarianism — the book that made the island's past a subject of systematic knowledge.
works.meter: Latin prose of classical elegance (translated by Holland into the full Elizabethan English of 1610).
works.context: First edition 1586, dedicated to Burghley; Camden's Britannia launched the great tradition of county histories and the Society of Antiquaries' programme, and its 1610 English version made the past accessible to the nation.
works.characters: Britain itself; the Britons, Romans, Saxons, and Normans; the noble families and antiquaries
works.structure: A chorography in the classical tradition (Ptolemy, Pausanias), organized geographically by county, with the apparatus of sources and the author's correspondence as its scholarly frame.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the English translation of 1610 is Philemon Holland's.

editions.title: Britannia, 2nd edn, 4 vols.

works.title: Britannia (Thomson)
works.description: Thomson's patriotic poem, calling on the national spirit and the naval force of the island and urging that Britain's safety lies in the command of the sea and in the virtue of a free people.
works.plot: The poem summons the genius of the country, remembers its ancient and modern deliverances, and argues that the naval and commercial power of Britain is the instrument of her liberty against the ambition of the continent.
works.significance: It is one of the founding texts of the British naval-patriotic lyric, the immediate context of the odes on the rule of the ocean which the following years made national.
works.meter: The martial and anthem-like measures of the national ode, with the short stirring line and the recurring summons; the precise stanzaic scheme of the first issue is not asserted here.
works.context: Written in the years of the disputes over the navy and the commercial system that preceded the war of the Spanish succession, when the government's pacific economy was being attacked by the patriot writers in the language of the island's sea power.
works.characters: the genius of Britannia; the navy and the merchant; the threatened nation
works.structure: A continuous patriotic argument in the ode-like measures of the anthem, with the historical recollection and the direct address to the nation.
works.attributionNotes: Disambiguated in the title from Camden's LATIN Britannia already in this database; the poem here is Thomson's.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Bussy D'Ambois
works.description: Chapman's tragedy of heroic virtue at court: the poor gentleman Bussy d'Ambois, raised by the Duke of Anjou to the French court, defies the great, wins the love of the married Tamyra, and is destroyed by her husband Montsurry's trap — dying on his feet, propped against the wall, 'like a Roman' whose spirit cannot be killed.
works.plot: Bussy arrives at court in poverty and virtue, quarrels and triumphs with the courtiers, and is loved by Tamyra; the friar's conjuring reveals the affair to Montsurry; the revenge plot — the summoned spirits, the forced confession, the ambush — kills the friar and corners Bussy; his death speech turns defeat into apotheosis, and Tamyra's final letters close the tragedy.
works.significance: The great English tragedy of heroic self-assertion — the play in which the Renaissance individual asserts himself against the court and the stars.
works.meter: Chapman's dense, oracular blank verse — packed with stoic sententiae — reaching its height in Bussy's death speech.
works.context: Based on the historical Bussy (d. 1579) as reported in French chronicles; performed about 1604 and printed in 1607, with a revised text in 1641.
works.characters: Bussy d'Ambois; Tamyra; Montsurry; the Duke of Anjou (Monsieur); the King of France; the Guise; the Friar; Pero; Behemoth and the spirits
works.structure: A five-act Senecan tragedy of the heroic mode, with the friar's necromancy and the spirits (Behemoth and the rest) as its supernatural machinery.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Bussy D'Ambois (Revels Plays)

works.title: Caelica
works.description: Fulke Greville's sequence of 109 short poems, written over some three decades: it begins as a Petrarchan sequence to 'Caelica' and 'Myra', then turns through political and philosophical verse to the great religious poems of renunciation ('Down in the depth of mine iniquity', 'Sion lies waste') with which it ends.
works.plot: The lover's courtship of Caelica gives way to meditations on the fall of princes, the vanity of earthly love, and the corruption of the will, until the final poems renounce the world for God.
works.significance: The bridge between the Elizabethan sonnet vogue and the metaphysical and devotional poetry of the next generation; its late religious poems rank with the greatest of the century.
works.meter: Varied short forms — songs, sonnets, and stanzaic meditations — in Greville's characteristically compressed, gnomic style.
works.context: Composed from the 1580s onward by the friend and biographer of Sidney, who served Elizabeth and James in high office; printed posthumously in the 1633 volume Certain Learned and Elegant Works.
works.characters: the poet-lover; Caelica; Myra; Cynthia
works.structure: A sequence in three movements — love, politics, religion — recording a lifelong spiritual itinerary.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Poems and Dramas of Fulke Greville, 2 vols.

works.title: Caius Marius
works.description: Otway's Roman tragedy, which grafts a Romeo-and-Juliet love story onto the civil wars of Marius and Sulla and was read as a political allegory of the Exclusion Crisis.
works.plot: Young Marius loves Lavinia, the daughter of the Sullan Crassus; the factions' hatred destroys them, and the play ends with Marius's death and Lavinia's.
works.significance: An important document of Whig political drama and of the Restoration use of Roman history as a mirror for contemporary politics.
works.meter: Blank verse with a large borrowing from Romeo and Juliet in the balcony scene.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in 1679 during the Exclusion Crisis; the political application was so pointed that the play was suppressed in 1680.
works.characters: Caius Marius; Young Marius; Lavinia; Sulla; Crassus; Juno; Metellus
works.structure: Five acts combining Roman history with a Shakespearean love tragedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Otway; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Calisto and Melebea
altTitles: A New Comedy in English in Manner of an Interlude
works.description: An anonymous English adaptation of the first four acts of Fernando de Rojas's Celestina, printed by John Rastell c. 1525–30; the first English version of the Spanish classic.
works.plot: Calisto, rejected by Melibea, seeks the help of the old bawd Celestina, who wins the lady for him by her arts; the fragment (the play survives incomplete) follows the first movement of Rojas's tragicomedy through the lovers' meeting, ending before the deaths that close the original.
works.significance: The first English adaptation of the Celestina and an early witness to Anglo-Spanish literary exchange; it extends the range of the interlude to tragicomic romance and anticipates the Elizabethan stage's use of continental fiction.
works.meter: Couplets with stanzaic songs
works.context: Printed c. 1525–30, probably by John Rastell, whose press had connections to the Spanish trade through the More circle (More's daughter married into the Rastell family, and Vives was in England); the Celestina, the great Spanish masterpiece of 1499, was thus introduced to English readers a generation before Mabbe's full translation.
works.characters: Calisto; Melibea; Celestina; Sempronio; Parmeno
works.structure: A scene-by-scene dramatization of the opening of the Celestina, compressed into interlude form, with the bawd's character preserved in translation.
works.attributionNotes: No author is named; the play has been attributed to John Rastell on the evidence of the press and the More circle's Spanish connections, but the attribution is conjectural.

works.title: Campaspe
works.description: Lyly's court comedy of the painter's triumph: Alexander the Great, in love with his captive Campaspe, commissions her portrait from the painter Apelles — who falls in love with her himself; the emperor, discovering the mutual love, renounces her and gives the couple his blessing, proving himself 'Alexander' in magnanimity as in conquest.
works.plot: Alexander's philosophers (Diogenes in his tub, Plato, Aristotle) and generals debate around the love affair; Apelles paints and conceals his love; the courtiers' plots to part the lovers fail; and the play ends with Alexander's renunciation and the painter's marriage, the emperor's 'discipline' the play's moral.
works.significance: The first English high comedy of the court — the play that founded the elegant, debating tradition Jonson and the Restoration inherited.
works.meter: Prose throughout — the Euphuistic manner transferred to the stage — with the songs of the finale.
works.context: Performed before Elizabeth I by the Children of Paul's and the Chapel children on the same day (1 January 1584) in the 'battle of the theatres' between the two boy companies; printed the same year.
works.characters: Alexander; Campaspe; Apelles; Diogenes; Plato; Aristotle; Hephestion; Parmenio; Manes; Psyllus; the pages
works.structure: A five-act classical comedy on the Italian model, built of debate scenes — the philosophers' wit, the generals' counsel — with the painter's studio as its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Complete Works of John Lyly, 3 vols.

works.title: Caractacus: A Dramatic Poem
works.form: Dramatic poem / closet tragedy with a strong lyrical and descriptive element; regular acts; printed with prefatory and dedicatory matter and with the author's account of the subject's sources.
works.description: Mason's most admired tragedy, and a work he labelled a 'dramatic poem' rather than a play, partly because it was written for a circle of subscribers and for the reader's theatre as much as for the pit. Its subject is the British chief Caractacus, defeated by Rome, carried in chains to Italy and displayed in triumph before the emperor, and there outdoing his captors in the dignity with which he speaks of liberty and of his country. The machinery of Druids and of British superstition gives the poem its religious and sublimer colour.
works.plot: The action is built on the collision between Roman imperial splendour and captive British virtue. Caractacus, having lost his kingdom in the field, keeps his sovereignty in the language he uses at Rome, refusing the concessions that would make his captivity comfortable. Around him the poem arranges the expected attachments of love and friendship, and the Druidic element supplies prophecy, sacred grove and solemn rite, all of which Mason treats as a national priesthood of great moral elevation. The dramatic interest is thereby concentrated not in the plot but in the set-piece of the conquered man before the conqueror, where the language of liberty is spoken with a force the contemporary reader recognised as the sublimity of unrhymed verse achieved.
works.significance: For decades it was the standard example of modern English blank verse and of the patriotic 'British' subject treated in elevated measure, and it was praised for exactly that by later critics of the poetical revival. It also became a schoolroom and elocutionary text, and its Druidical machinery is a notable stage in the eighteenth-century imaginative recovery of the Celtic past.
works.meter: Blank verse of a carefully modulated kind, with short sententious lines for declamation and longer, more rhythmic periods for the Druidical and descriptive passages; Mason's practice here was commonly cited by later editors of the blank-verse controversy as evidence that unrhymed measure could be made 'musical'.
works.context: Published in the year after the fall of Quebec, when British patriotic feeling and the cult of ancient 'British' liberty were unusually available to a poet, and in the middle of the critical debate about dramatic measure. Mason composed it largely in private and issued it by subscription, a publishing route that let a clergyman-poet keep the dignity of the work independent of theatrical managers.
works.characters: Caractacus; the Druids of the British grove; the court of the emperor Claudius at Rome
works.structure: A five-act dramatic poem whose movement is episodic rather than tightly plotted, rising to the Roman triumph and the audience with the emperor as its rhetorical centre.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem carries Mason's name in the first edition and its making is documented in his correspondence and in his later collected edition. Its first stage representation, whenever it came, is not asserted here.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Carew's Poems
works.description: The posthumous collection of Thomas Carew's lyrics (1640), including 'A Song: Ask Me No More', 'The Spring', 'The Primrose', and the celebrated elegy 'Upon the Death of the Dean of Paul's, Dr John Donne', which praised Donne for purging poetry of 'th'hyperboles' and is a key document of the metaphysical transition.
works.plot: The poems explore love, desire, beauty, and time with Donnean wit and Cavalier grace; the elegy on Donne assesses his achievement and marks the passing of the metaphysical master.
works.significance: Carew's Poems fuse Donne and Jonson and include the period's most important critical elegy on Donne; they are central to the metaphysical-Cavalier transition.
works.meter: Polished octosyllabics and songs with metaphysical argument and sensual elegance.
works.context: Published in 1640, shortly after Carew's death, by his friend Thomas Walkley; it established his reputation as the finest of the Caroline wits.
works.characters: the poet; mistresses; John Donne (in the elegy)
works.structure: A collection of short lyrics, songs, elegies, and the masque, unified by Carew's courtly and metaphysical sensibility.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Carmen Deo Nostro
altTitles: Carmen Deo Nostro, Te Decet Hymnus, Sacred Poems
works.description: Crashaw's posthumous Catholic collection, published in Paris in 1652 with an emblematic frontispiece of the crucifix, containing his mature hymns — including the great 'Hymn in Adoration of the Blessed Sacrament' and the hymns to St Teresa — in an ecstatic, baroque devotion.
works.plot: The hymns celebrate Catholic doctrine (the Eucharist, the Name of Jesus, the saints, St Teresa's mystical ecstasy) in fervent, sensuous verse marked by paradox, repetition, and intense religious feeling.
works.significance: The principal English work of Catholic baroque devotion, its hymn to St Teresa and 'Adoration of the Blessed Sacrament' are among the most ecstatic religious poems in English.
works.meter: Musical, incantatory verse with baroque repetition and paradox; emblematic and visionary imagery.
works.context: Written after Crashaw's conversion and exile; published at Loreto/Paris in 1652, three years after his death, by his friend Thomas Carre, with the poet's own drawings.
works.characters: Christ; the Virgin; St Teresa; the saints
works.structure: A collection of hymns, epigrams, and religious verse with emblematic apparatus, unified by Catholic devotional subjects.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published posthumously.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Catholic Homilies
altTitles: Ælfric's Catholic Homilies, First and Second Series
works.description: Ælfric's two series of forty sermons for the church year (c. 989-995), the masterpiece of Old English prose: orthodox, elegantly plain expositions of the gospel readings, written in the rhythmical alliterative style and prefaced by a Latin preface deploring the doctrinal errors of the anonymous homiletic tradition. The most widely copied vernacular preaching text of the Anglo-Saxon period.
works.plot: Each homily expounds the pericope of the day with patristic learning made lucid for the laity — the feasts of Christ and the saints, the parables, the miracles — carefully distinguishing orthodox doctrine from apocryphal excess; the two series together provide a complete homiletic cycle for the year in the order of the liturgical calendar.
works.significance: The summit of the Old English homiletic tradition and the foundation of standard literary Old English.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of Ælfric's mature 'plain style'.
works.context: Composed at Cerne Abbas c. 989-995 at the request of the ealdorman Æthelweard and his son Æthelmær; over thirty manuscripts and fragments survive.
works.characters: Christ; the saints of the calendar
works.structure: Two series of forty homilies each, organized by the church year; each homily opens with the gospel text in English and proceeds by exegesis, exemplum, and exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Ælfric's authorship is certain.
themes: Reformation faith and the authority of scripture

editions.title: Ælfric's Catholic Homilies: The First Series (EETS SS 17)

sources: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton

works.title: Cato
works.form: tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: Addison's serious tragedy of the last days of Cato of Utica, written as a demonstration that regular neoclassical drama in blank verse could teach Stoic virtue and resignation to providence. It was the most acted, read and imitated English tragedy of the first half of the eighteenth century.
works.plot: After Thapsus the defeated Cato refuses Caesar's clemency and holds Utica; his friend Lucilius dies by poison in a scene of Stoic obedience, the treachery of Sempronius is exposed, and Juba's suit for Marcia fails; Cato secures the safety of those about him, reconciles public liberty with resignation to providence, and kills himself, the catastrophe being reported rather than shown.
works.significance: It fixed for a generation the model of the rational moral tragedy and made Roman liberty and Christian resignation a national schoolroom exemplum, admired across party lines, imitated on the stage and in the closet, and answered by the later tragedy of feeling.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat blank verse of the moderated post-Dryden line, with balanced antithetical periods and sententious closures; the speeches are built as declamatory rhetorical units.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in the spring of 1713, during the party struggle over the peace settlement, when the theatre was an arena of political interpretation; the play was praised in The Tatler in the season of its first performance, and the rival Whig and Tory press each claimed it.
works.characters: Cato; Caesar; Lucilius; Sempronius; Marcia; Juba
works.structure: Five-act regular tragedy closely observing the unities of time, place and action, moving from the council at Utica through the discovery of the conspiracy to the protagonist's suicide and its reportage.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Addison's authorship is documented by his own publication and by contemporary correspondence.

editions.title: The Spectator, 4 volumes

works.title: Cecilia; or, Memoirs of an Heiress
works.form: novel of manners and of the marriage market
works.description: The history of an heiress whose fortune makes her the property of everyone who desires it, and who is worn between the claims of several marriages and the demands of a society that cannot conceive of a woman with money acting for herself. It is the broadest and most public of the author's novels, ending in a catastrophe the century's readers thought severe.
works.plot: Cecilia Beverley, left an estate on condition that her husband take the name, is courted by a lawyer of merit and by a young fellow of fashion, while her guardians consult their own interest in the choice. She is carried to Bristol and into the companies of the town, is drawn into a friend's distress and loses money at the card table through the artifice of a designing relation. She at last accepts the suit of the man she had undervalued, and his death from a wound received in defence of her reputation exposes the world that destroyed him. The novel closes on her renunciation of society and her retirement, the heiress having purchased her independence at the price of every attachment.
works.significance: It is the most complete analysis of the position of the propertied woman in the fiction of the century before the age of its author's rivals, and its argument about independence shaped the later novel of women's circumstance.
works.meter: An ample, reflective third-person prose with the free indirect report of the heroine's opinion, and the epistolary and conversational set pieces of the earlier novel retained in modified form.
works.context: Published by subscription in 1782, in the season of the debates on women's property, the law of marriage and the influence of the fashionable circle; its author was by then a recognised novelist and a member of the Bluestocking society.
works.characters: Cecilia Beverley; Mr. Belfield; the young man of fashion; her guardians and their families; Madame de Burgh; the friends of the town and of Bristol
works.structure: Third-person narration in five or six volumes, with the heroine's consciousness reported rather than voiced, and a public plot of debts, assemblies and the law; the conclusion is a retirement rather than a marriage.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after the anonymous first novel, the issue by subscription being recorded in its own lists.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Cely Letters
works.description: The business correspondence of the Cely family, London wool merchants of the Staple of Calais, 1472–88: some 250 letters and papers recording the wool trade, shipping, politics, and daily life of a merchant family in the age of Edward IV and Richard III. The most vivid surviving record of English commercial life in the fifteenth century.
works.plot: The letters pass between the brothers Robert, Richard, and George Cely in London and Calais and their factors, recording the buying and shipping of wool, prices and freights, news of the wars in France and at home (including the fall of Richard III), and the family's hunting, hawking, and domestic affairs.
works.significance: The classic document of fifteenth-century English commerce and the merchant's English, complementing the Paston archive's gentry perspective.
works.meter: Prose: brisk, practical mercantile English, of great linguistic value.
works.context: Written 1472–88, when the Celys' Calais staple stood at the centre of England's wool economy; discovered in 1860 among the family's papers and edited by H. E. Malden (1900).
works.characters: George Cely; Richard Cely the elder and younger; William Maryon; the Calais factors
works.structure: A documentary archive of business correspondence, chronological in arrangement, spanning sixteen years.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative (family and factors); authorship_status reflects the archive's collective character.

editions.title: The Cely Letters 1472–1488

works.title: Centuries of Thankfulness
works.description: Thomas Traherne's great mystical prose meditations — four 'centuries' of numbered paragraphs celebrating God's goodness, the soul's felicity, and the wonder of creation as apprehended by an innocent eye — unpublished in his lifetime and discovered and printed only in the early twentieth century.
works.plot: The Centuries argue that true happiness consists in rightly valuing and enjoying God's creation, recover the infant soul's vision of infinity, and exhort gratitude and thanksgiving as the path to felicity.
works.significance: The Centuries are a unique achievement in English mystical prose, anticipating Romantic celebrations of childhood vision and influencing later spiritual and literary writers.
works.meter: Rhapsodic, cumulative, rhythmic prose of wonder, with visionary imagery of light, infinity, and childhood.
works.context: Written in the early 1670s and left in manuscript; misattributed to Henry Vaughan until Bertram Dobell acquired and published them in 1908, revealing a major unknown mystic.
works.characters: the soul; God; the self in childhood
works.structure: Four 'centuries' of 100 numbered meditative paragraphs each (partly incomplete), forming a cumulative rhapsody of wonder and thanksgiving.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested once Dobell established Traherne's authorship; the manuscripts were long misattributed to Vaughan.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Characteristics of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times
