works.title: Elene
altTitles: The Finding of the True Cross
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: Cynewulf's longest signed poem (1,321 lines), on the legend of the Finding of the True Cross: the empress Helena, mother of Constantine, journeys to Jerusalem, compels the Jews to reveal the site of the Crucifixion, and recovers the cross. The poem is a masterpiece of typological narrative, casting Helena as a heroic queen and the cross as the sign of victory.
works.plot: Constantine, granted a vision of the cross before battle, sends his mother Helena to Jerusalem; her search, the interrogation of the Jew Judas (who resists, is imprisoned, converted by a sign, and baptized as Cyriacus), the miraculous finding of the three crosses, the proof by resurrection of a dead youth, the conversion of the Jews, and Helena's building of churches; the epilogue carries Cynewulf's runic signature and his meditation on judgment and poetry.
works.significance: The richest treatment in early English poetry of the cross as sign of victory; the locus classicus of Cynewulf's typological art.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the signature passage is among the most ornate in the corpus.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 121v-133v); based on the Latin Acta Cyriaci tradition of the Inventio crucis legend.
works.characters: Elene (Helena); Constantine; Judas/Cyriacus; Satan (in the debate with Judas)
works.structure: A conversion narrative in the heroic manner, organized around three debates (Constantine's vision, Helena's interrogations, Judas's conversion) and closing on the runic signature.
works.attributionNotes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes.
themes: Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
sources: The Novel: An Anthology of Criticism and Practice, 1700-1800

works.title: Eleonora: A Panegyrical Dedication
works.description: Dryden's commissioned character-poem on an unnamed lady, written for the Earl of Abingdon in memory of his wife, whom the poem calls only Eleonora.
works.plot: The poem sets out to describe Eleonora's virtues in an ordered portrait of her soul, mind, and conduct, and concedes the impossibility of doing her justice in verse.
works.significance: An important experiment in the 'character' as a poetic form and a revealing document of Dryden's professional circumstances in the 1690s.
works.meter: Heroic couplets.
works.context: Composed in 1691-2 for a fee of £100 from the Earl of Abingdon; Dryden complained that he could not write a character-poem on commission.
works.characters: Eleonora (the Countess of Abingdon)
works.structure: A panegyrical character study in a continuous argument, deliberately refusing narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Eloisa to Abelard
works.description: Pope's verse epistle from Heloise to Abelard, written in the Ovidian manner as a confession of a love that the convent cannot extinguish; the poem analyses the passion of religious and erotic love confused in one mind.
works.plot: Eloisa, abbess in the cloister, writes to the man who has abandoned her to her vows: she recounts her education and their love, argues with her own guilt, and resolves finally to preserve his fame by her silence and her unhappiness.
works.significance: It gave English poetry its most quoted study of a woman's divided consciousness, and it became the standard model for the poetic epistle of feeling for half a century.
works.meter: Heroic couplets made nervous by exclamation, apostrophe and broken syntax, the periodic closure repeatedly delayed by the passion it describes.
works.context: Written after the letters of Abelard and Heloise had been made English and adapted by the early-eighteenth-century theatre, and in the same season as the controversy over female desire and the convent in the Gothic and sentimental tale.
works.characters: Eloisa; Abelard
works.structure: A single letter in verse, progressing from address to narrative memory, to self-examination and passion's quarrel with duty, to a closing resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Poems of Alexander Pope, Twickenham Edition (11 volumes)

works.title: Emaré
works.description: A Breton lay on the Constance legend: the princess Emaré, cast out by her incestuous father, drifts across the sea in a boat with her child, and through the marvellous cloth she weaves and the recognitions it brings, is restored to her husband and kingdom. The legend Chaucer used for the Man of Law's Tale, told as a fairy-tale of patient suffering.
works.plot: Emaré, given a magic cloth by the emperor, refuses her father's marriage proposal and is set adrift; she marries the king of Galys, is slandered by her wicked mother-in-law and cast out again with her son Segramour; after years in Rome, her husband finds her and all are reconciled.
works.significance: The most artful English version of the Constance story and a central text for the romance's treatment of incest, exile, and female patience.
works.meter: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas.
works.context: Composed c. 1400, probably in the north-east Midlands, from the Constance legend (ultimately Trivet's chronicle, as in Chaucer); preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ii.
works.characters: Emaré; her father the emperor; the king of Galys; the wicked mother-in-law; Segramour
works.structure: A double exile-and-return plot organized by the magic cloth and the repeated sea voyages, in the Constance tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Emblems
works.description: Francis Quarles's emblem book (1635), the most popular work of verse in seventeenth-century England, in which each of five books pairs an engraved emblem with a biblical motto, epigram, and moral verse, making religious meditation vivid and accessible to a mass readership.
works.plot: Each emblem presents a picture and motto drawn from scripture (largely the Song of Songs, Job, and Hosea) followed by meditative verse that moralises the image for the reader's devotion.
works.significance: Emblems shaped the popular religious imagination of the period and influenced Bunyan's allegory; it is the classic English emblem book and a key text of devotional culture.
works.meter: Varied verse forms (quatrains, couplets) accompanying engraved emblems, in a plain, proverbial, sometimes homely style.
works.context: Published in 1635 and reprinted constantly through the century and beyond; it was read by the devout and by Bunyan, and was both hugely popular and later critically scorned.
works.characters: the soul; Christ; biblical figures
works.structure: Five books of emblem-and-verse units, adapted from the Jesuit emblem books of Hugo Pia and others.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Enchiridion
works.form: didactic and scientific prose (computus) in Latin and Old English
works.description: Byrhtferth of Ramsey's bilingual manual of computus and the related sciences (c. 1011), written in alternating Latin and English: the fullest surviving treatise on the Anglo-Saxon science of time — the calendar, the lunar cycles, number symbolism, and the harmony of the cosmos — composed for the instruction of the young monks of Ramsey.
works.plot: The manual explains the computation of Easter, the course of the sun and moon through the zodiac, the elements, the ages of the world and of man, the symbolic meanings of numbers, and the figures of grammar and rhetoric, all ordered to the liturgical year and the contemplation of the world's design.
works.significance: The richest surviving witness to the scientific culture of the Benedictine Reform.
works.meter: Bilingual prose with verse passages.
works.context: Composed 1011 at Ramsey Abbey by Byrhtferth, pupil of Abbo of Fleury; unique manuscript: Oxford, Bodleian Library, Ashmole 328.
works.characters: the young monks of Ramsey (addressees)
works.structure: Four books of didactic exposition, alternating between Latin and English, with diagrams and tables.
works.attributionNotes: Byrhtferth's authorship is certain (he names himself).
themes: Petrarchan desire and the sonnet mistress
movements: Garrick and the Regenerated London Theatre
sources: The Works of Aphra Behn

works.title: Endymion
altTitles: Endymion, the Man in the Moon
works.description: Lyly's allegorical court comedy: Endymion's hopeless love for the moon-goddess Cynthia casts him into a forty-year sleep from which only her kiss can wake him; the intrigues of the sorceress Dipsas and the braggart Sir Tophas complicate the court, and the play ends with Endymion's awakening and the famous reading of Cynthia as the Queen whose 'virtue' the play mirrors.
works.plot: Endymion renounces Tellus for Cynthia; Tellus's jealousy and Dipsas's enchantment cast him asleep; his friend Eumenides quests for the cure, and the riddle of the fountain directs him to the kiss; the sub-plot of Sir Tophas's mock-chivalry and the pages' comedy runs alongside; Cynthia's kiss wakes the sleeper, and the play closes on the praises of her constancy.
works.significance: The most influential of the Elizabethan court allegories — the model of the dream-play of royal favour and disfavour.
works.meter: Prose for the court scenes, verse for the enchantments and the finale, with the songs of the fairies.
works.context: Performed at court in 1588 and printed in 1591; the play's veiled allusions to Leicester's fall and the Queen's favour have kept its allegory a critical puzzle for four centuries.
works.characters: Endymion; Cynthia; Tellus; Eumenides; Semele; Dipsas; Sir Tophas; Geron; Corsites; the Fairies; the pages (Epiton, Samias, Dares)
works.structure: A five-act court allegory with a fairy-tale centre (the sleep, the quest, the cure) and a burlesque chivalric sub-plot.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Complete Works of John Lyly, 3 vols.

works.title: Eneados
works.description: Douglas's complete translation of Virgil's Aeneid into Scots couplets, completed on 22 July 1513 — the first full translation of the poem in any British language — with a thirteenth book from Mapheus Vegius, and a prologue to each book in which the translator speaks of the Scottish seasons, his art, and his critics. Printed at London in 1553.
works.plot: Virgil's epic entire: Aeneas's flight from Troy, the wanderings, the tragedy of Dido, the descent to the underworld, and the wars in Italy — with Vegius's supplement completing the hero's apotheosis.
works.significance: The first complete British Aeneid and the summit of Scots humanist translation; its prologues are the finest nature poetry in Scots, and the translation passed Virgil to the northern Renaissance.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in vigorous Scots; the prologues alternate aureate and plain registers with seasonal description.
works.context: Completed in the year of Flodden (1513), when the Scottish court and much of its nobility were destroyed; Douglas's translation of the epic of exile and foundation speaks to a nation in crisis.
works.characters: Aeneas; Dido; Turnus; Anchises; Venus; Juno
works.structure: Twelve books of the Aeneid plus the thirteenth book of Vegius; each book preceded by a prologue, of which the seasonal prologues (VII, XII, XIII) are the most celebrated.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Virgil's Aeneid Translated into Scottish Verse by Gavin Douglas

works.title: England's Birth-Right Justified
altTitles: England's Birth-Right Justified Against All Arbitrary Usurpation
works.description: John Lilburne's principal Leveller pamphlet, in which he claims that the free-born people of England possess an inalienable birth-right of liberty that no parliament or king may take away.
works.plot: Lilburne argues that arbitrary imprisonment, taxation without consent, the monopoly of the law, and the power of the great are all violations of the birth-right of every free-born Englishman, and that the people's representatives must be accountable.
works.significance: A foundational text of English radicalism and of the doctrine of popular sovereignty; its language of birth-right influenced the Leveller Agreements and, through them, later democratic theory.
works.meter: Fierce, urgent, colloquial prose of the pamphlet wars.
works.context: Published in October 1645 during the civil wars, while Lilburne was serving in the parliamentary army; it laid the intellectual foundations of the Leveller movement.
works.structure: A single polemical tract with a dedicatory epistle.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Lilburne; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Enthusiasmus Triumphatus; or, A Brief Account of the Nature, Causes, Kinds, and Cure of Enthusiasm
works.description: Henry More's influential analysis of religious enthusiasm as a disease of the imagination, published in his Collection of Several Philosophical Writings and directed against the sectarian excesses of the Commonwealth.
works.plot: More identifies enthusiasm with the disturbance of the animal spirits, with melancholy, with ignorance, and with the pride of private revelation, and proposes reason, self-examination, and the discipline of the church as its cure.
works.significance: The standard seventeenth-century treatment of enthusiasm and a key text in the history of the psychology of religion; it influenced Shaftesbury, Swift's Tale of a Tub, and the eighteenth-century debate on fanaticism.
works.meter: Learned, argumentative prose.
works.context: Published in 1656 during the Commonwealth, when the sects proliferated; More was a Cambridge Platonist concerned to defend a rational Christianity against both enthusiasm and materialism.
works.structure: A single treatise in sections.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Henry More; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Epicene
works.description: Jonson's comedy of noise and silence: Morose, who cannot bear sound, marries the 'silent woman' Epicene to disinherit his nephew Dauphine — only to find his bride a torrent of talk, his house invaded by the collegiate ladies and the barber Cutbeard, and the play's last trick the revelation that Epicene is a boy, Dauphine's instrument, and the marriage void.
works.plot: Dauphine plots to break his uncle's will: the silent bride, the mock divorce consultation, and the siege of Morose's house by the Otiers' collegiates drive the old man to any terms; the contract signed, Dauphine strips the boy of his disguise and the play ends on the audience's own exposure to satire.
works.significance: The most audacious of Jonson's comedies of sex and gender — the play Restoration comedy learned its tricks from.
works.meter: Predominantly prose — Jonson's most assured comic prose — with the wit-duels of Truewit as its set pieces.
works.context: First performed by the Children of the Queen's Revels at Whitefriars, 1609; its boy-bride was played by a boy, doubling the play's game with gender; printed in the 1616 Folio.
works.characters: Morose; Dauphine; Epicene; Truewit; Clerimont; Sir John Daw; Sir Amorous La Foole; Captain Otter; Mistress Otter; Cutbeard; Mavis; the collegiates
works.structure: A five-act farce of escalating noise and counter-plot, with the collegiate ladies' scenes as a satire of female learning and the divorce farce as its centrepiece.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, 7 vols.
editions.editor: David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (gen. eds.)

works.title: Epigrammata
altTitles: Epigrammata clarissimi disertissimique viri Thomae Mori
works.description: More's collected Latin epigrams, printed together with his Utopia in 1518, including translations from the Greek Anthology, satirical and courtly verse, and the poems on his own fortune and on kingship.
works.plot: The collection has no single argument; it ranges from verse translations of Greek epigrams made with William Lily, through witty satires on astrologers and courtiers, to the programmatic 'Progymnasmata' and poems celebrating the accession of Henry VIII.
works.significance: The finest Latin verse written by an Englishman of the early Renaissance and a showcase of the Erasmian revival of classical epigram; the coronation poems mark the beginnings of English Renaissance panegyric.
works.meter: Elegiac couplets, hendecasyllables, and other classical metres
works.context: Composed across More's humanist career from the late 1490s; the Progymnasmata with Lily (an exercise translating Greek epigrams) dates from c. 1503–04; the collection was printed by Froben at Basel in 1518 together with the third edition of Utopia.
works.structure: A printed miscellany grouped by type: translations from the Greek Anthology, original epigrams, and the coronation poems of 1509.

works.title: Epigrams
works.description: Jonson's collection of 133 epigrams, printed in the 1616 Folio of his Works: poems of praise to the great and good of his acquaintance (Lucy, Countess of Bedford; the Sidneys; Donne; Shakespeare), and poems of satiric castigation to the vicious — 'On Court-Worm', 'On Gut', 'On My First Son', and the epitaphs on his children among them — the classical epigram remade as a moral instrument.
works.plot: No plot: the collection alternates poems of praise and blame, with the commendatory poems to patrons and fellow poets balancing the satires of fools and knaves, and the personal elegies (on his son, on his first daughter) at the collection's heart.
works.significance: The foundation of the English epigram tradition and the seedbed of the Augustan moral couplet.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of lapidary finish — the model for the Augustan couplet of the next century.
works.context: Written across Jonson's career and collected for the 1616 Works, the first folio of an English playwright's own canon; 'To the Memory of My Beloved, the Author, Mr. William Shakespeare' appeared separately in the 1623 Folio.
works.characters: the poet; the named patrons and poets (Lucy, Countess of Bedford; Donne; Shakespeare; the Sidneys); the satirized types (Court-Worm, Gut, Poet-Ape)
works.structure: A book of 133 short poems in the Martial tradition, arranged as a gallery of virtues and vices, prefaced by Jonson's defence of the genre.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, 7 vols.
editions.editor: David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (gen. eds.)

works.title: Epistle on the Mixed Life
works.description: Walter Hilton's epistle addressed to a wealthy layman, probably a lord, teaching the 'mixed life' — the life that joins the active works of mercy and the duties of estate with the inner practice of contemplation. It is the classic English statement that contemplation is not the preserve of monks: lay people in the world may and should live the contemplative life in their degree.
works.plot: Hilton distinguishes three lives — active, contemplative, and mixed — and argues that the mixed life, combining works of charity and governance with prayer and meditation, is the life of prelates and devout lay lords; he then teaches his addressee the practice of this life in his daily affairs.
works.significance: The founding text of the 'mixed life' tradition that legitimized lay contemplation and shaped the spirituality of the fifteenth-century gentry.
works.meter: Plain, authoritative prose of the Hilton school.
works.context: Composed c. 1385, when the growth of lay piety and the demand for vernacular guidance was transforming English religious life; preserved in numerous manuscripts, often with the Scale of Perfection.
works.characters: Hilton (writer); the devout layman (addressee)
works.structure: A single epistle in two movements: the doctrine of the three lives, and its application to the recipient's estate.
works.attributionNotes: Hilton's authorship secure.

works.title: Epsom Wells
works.description: Thomas Shadwell's most popular comedy, set at the Epsom mineral wells, in which the fashionable world of gallants, cits, and country justices is exposed in a series of comic intrigues.
works.plot: The rake Bellamour pursues Lucia while the city couple Woodly and Mrs Woodly play at adultery; the country justice Clodpate and his wife are gulled, and all is resolved in marriage.
works.significance: Shadwell's finest comedy and a principal example of his Jonsonian 'humours' method; it held the stage into the eighteenth century through adaptation.
works.meter: Prose dominant.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in Dorset Garden in 1672 and published in 1673, dedicated to the Duke of Newcastle; Shadwell claimed to have drawn the characters from life at the wells.
works.characters: Bellamour; Woodly; Lucia; Carolina; Mrs Woodly; Justice Clodpate; Mrs Clodpate; Bumpkin; Lucy
works.structure: Five acts of humours comedy with a strong Jonsonian comic portrait in Clodpate.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shadwell; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Essay on the Different Stiles of Poetry
altTitles: An Essay on the Different Stiles of Poetry
works.description: Parnell's short verse essay on the styles proper to the several kinds of poetry, arguing that the numbers of verse must be chosen for the subject and that the harmony of the line is a matter of judgment rather than of rule.
works.plot: The essay distinguishes the lofty, the smooth and the loose measures, censures the affectation of harmony for its own sake, and commends the poet who suits his stiles to his design.
works.significance: It is one of the earliest and most readable English poems on style and numbers, and it stands beside the Essay on Criticism for its account of imitation in verse.
works.meter: Heroic couplet, with the illustrative lines deliberately imitating the measures under discussion.
works.context: Published in the years of the quarrel over rhyme, blank verse and the harmony of the couplet, when the periodical essay, Dennis's criticism and Pope's Essay on Criticism were making versification a public argument.
works.structure: A continuous argument in verse, opening with the occasion and closing in a character of the finished poet.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the printing history of the piece is obscure and it survives chiefly in the collected editions of Parnell's poems.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Essays in Verse and Prose
works.description: Cowley's posthumous essays (1668) — 'Of Myself', 'Of Solitude', 'Of Gardens', 'Of Liberty', 'Of the Late Civil War', and 'Of Plants' — which champion retirement, the country life, and the new experimental philosophy, and helped establish the familiar, conversational English essay.
works.plot: The essays reflect on retirement and the value of solitude, the love of gardening and the countryside, liberty, the recent Civil Wars, and the Royal Society's programme, in a personal, digressive, hortatory manner.
works.significance: Cowley's essays shaped the Restoration familiar essay and the ideal of cultivated retirement, influencing Steele, Addison, and Johnson, and linked literature to the Royal Society's ideals.
works.meter: Graceful, conversational prose with occasional verse; a cultivated, reflective tone.
works.context: Written after Cowley's retirement to Chertsey following the Restoration and published posthumously in 1668; 'Of Plants' is an Englishing of his Latin De Plantis and engages the new science.
works.structure: A collection of familiar essays, some with verse interspersed, on moral and philosophical subjects.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published posthumously.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Essays Moral and Political
altTitles: Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary (1741-42 volumes)
Essays Moral and Political, Vol. I
works.description: Hume's first popular publications, two volumes of essays (1741-42) on taste, passion, the stoics, the jealousy of trade, party, and the balance of power, which established his literary reputation where the Treatise had failed. They introduced the essay as an instrument of the new psychology of refinement and modern politics.
works.plot: The moral essays argue that refinement of the age softens the man rather than enervates him, that a true delicacy of taste depends on a sound sense joined to passion, and that the ancient stoic ideal of extirpating the passions is an enthusiastic self-deception; the modern essayist counsels the regulation rather than the destruction of feeling. The political essays analyse the vices of party, the jealousy of trade as a groundless zero-sum fear, the blessings of industry, civility, and refinements, and the delicate balance of authority and liberty in a modern commonwealth. Essays on the first principles of government ground political obligation in convention and utility rather than an original contract. Together they sketch the 'taste and temperament' of commercial modernity the later writings would theorize.
works.significance: They made Hume a man of letters before he was a philosopher, fixed the classic essays on taste and the jealousy of trade, and supplied the humane public philosophy that the Enquiries and History later carried.
works.meter: The clear, balanced middle style of the polite essay, periodic where meditative, pointed where polemical, with its signature generalizations in short declaratives.
works.context: Volume I appeared in Edinburgh in 1741 and Volume II in 1742, during Hume's failed embassy and clergymen's uproar over the Treatise, and after the pattern of the Spectator papers was already worn; Hume's essays reinvented the form as moral philosophy in undress.
works.structure: A miscellany of independent essays in two volumes, ordered moral then political and historical, with no sustained argument across papers.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: A Treatise of Human Nature (Clarendon Edition of the Works of David Hume)
editions.editor: David Fate Norton and Mary J. Norton (eds.)

works.title: Essays on the Active Powers of Man
works.form: Analytical treatise in moral philosophy, essay by essay
works.description: The second half of Thomas Reid's planned division of the human mind, published in Edinburgh in 1788 after the Essays on the Intellectual Powers of 1785. Its seven essays analyse what a person does rather than what a person knows: agency, will, motive and freedom, conscience, the moral power, and the authority of the understanding over conduct. It is the mature statement of the common-sense school's philosophy of action and of its defence of liberty against Hume and Hartley.
works.plot: Reid begins by distinguishing active power from mere event, arguing that the very notion of cause is drawn from our consciousness of our own agency. He then examines the will, motive and the relation of volition to desire, and maintains that a free agent is an efficient cause whose choices are determined by neither necessity nor the strongest motive. The following essays treat moral agency, the conscience as a judge pronouncing upon character and not only upon actions, and the principles of action in brute animals and in human art and science. Finally Reid argues that sound judgment, or common sense, governs practice as much as belief, so that the same original principles which direct the understanding direct conduct.
works.significance: It is the principal eighteenth-century defence of human liberty and of the moral sense against sceptical analysis, and the source of Reid's influential account of conscience as a judicial faculty. Its philosophy of action, largely neglected in its own century, has been recovered by recent work on agency and free will, and it completes the Common-Sense programme that shaped Reid's American disciples.
works.meter: Prose only, in a plain, patient, lecture-derived analytical style
works.context: Written in the last Aberdeen and Edinburgh decades of Reid's life, after the Intellectual Powers and amid the controversy over Humean necessity and Priestley's materialism, it belongs to the Scottish Enlightenment's systematic reconstruction of the faculties and to the Common-Sense school's debate with the physiology of Hartley.
works.structure: Seven sequential essays of analytical moral psychology, advancing from the analysis of agency to the will, moral obligation, conscience and the governance of common sense in action.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Thomas Reid is established and undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man
works.form: philosophical essays on the mental powers
works.description: Reid's mature encyclopaedia of the mind, the Glasgow lectures of the 1770s? keep general: the mature summing-up of common-sense philosophy, eight essays on the powers of perception, memory, consciousness, conception, judgment, reasoning, and taste. It is the fullest statement of the anatomy of the human understanding after Locke and the companion to its successor volume on the active powers.
works.plot: The first essays analyse the power of perception in its original and acquired forms, the perceptions that make a landscape readable to the eye, and the roles of memory and consciousness as the direct testimony of the mind. Conception, the conceptions of primary and secondary qualities, and the general conceptions by which language works, are then distinguished from the principles of judgment, the self-evident first principles of common sense which the sceptic must borrow before he can argue. The closing essays examine the power of reasoning and the province of taste and criticism. Throughout, Reid answers the sceptical account of belief and the geometry of probabilities, reasserting that the natural faculties are, and must be, the measure of their own trustworthiness.
works.significance: It consolidated the school of common-sense philosophy into the century's great alternative account of the mind and remains the standard text of the non-sceptical Scottish epistemology that shaped the American common-sense tradition through Reid's Scottish pupils and their descendants.
works.meter: The plain, cumulative, exemplum-rich prose of the lecture-room, with long definitions and numbered first principles delivered in a tone of candid remonstrance.
works.context: Published in 1785 after years of Glasgow lectures and amid the running Scottish response to Hume and to Beattie's Essay on Truth, it preceded the companion volume on the active powers and was widely reviewed and soon translated on the continent.
works.structure: Eight essays in the manner of the Glasgow lectures, each on one intellectual power, arranged from perception through judgment to reasoning and criticism.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Essays on Various Subjects, in Prose and Verse
altTitles: Essays on Various Subjects, in Prose and Verse. By the Author of Sensibility
works.description: A collection of occasional essays, tales and verses gathered from the author's papers of the previous five years and published in the same season as her first tragedy. It shows the range of her early moral and sociable writing, from the character and the familiar letter to the short tale of feeling.
works.plot: The volume passes from the essay on manners and on the duties of the heart to the narrative illustrations of the same themes, the tales exhibiting the errors of a good-nature ungoverned by principle. Its verses address friends and occasions, and its closing pieces turn from the world of the tea-table to the claims of religion and of seriousness. The design throughout is to recommend an active and disciplined virtue over the passive refinement of the age.
works.significance: It fixed her early reputation as a moral essayist and is the base from which her later conduct writing and her religious work were developed; several of the pieces were reprinted separately through the decade.
works.meter: Argumentative prose of the mid-century essay for the discursive pieces, and heroic couplets and lyrical stanzas for the verse, the two being kept in the polite middle register.
works.context: Published in 1777 in the season of the author's establishment in the London and Bath circles and of her first successes on the stage, in the same years as the quarrel between the sensibility writers and their moral critics.
works.structure: A miscellany of prose essays, inset tales and occasional verse, arranged with the longer argumentative pieces first and the shorter pieces following; no continuous plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with the advertisement of the previous poem.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Euphues and His England
works.description: Lyly's sequel: Euphues and his friend Philautus sail for England, where the courtship of the ladies — Camilla, Surius's sister, and the rest — and the praises of Elizabeth I, the English court, and English women fill the book, in the second and final installment of the Euphuistic diptych.
works.plot: The voyage, the arrival in Dover, and the tour of England's marvels frame the main action: Philautus courts the ladies, Euphues plays the counsellor, and the long debate on love, beauty, and constancy ends with the famous 'glass for Europe' — the encomium of Queen Elizabeth that closes the book.
works.significance: The completion of the Euphuistic diptych and a founding text of English literary nationalism.
works.meter: The Euphuistic prose at its ripest, with the encomium of Elizabeth as its set piece.
works.context: Published in 1580, the year of Drake's circumnavigation and the Jesuit mission's arrival; its celebration of England answered the national mood and fixed Euphues as the English style's patron.
works.characters: Euphues; Philautus; Camilla; Lady Flavia; Surius; Fidus; Psellus; Queen Elizabeth (praised in the encomium)
works.structure: A travel frame enclosing the courtship debates, letters, and the concluding praise of England, mirroring the first book's structure.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Complete Works of John Lyly, 3 vols.

works.title: Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit
works.description: Lyly's first Euphues book and the fountain of Euphuism: the young Athenian Euphues comes to Naples, where the friendship with Philautus, the love of Lucilla, and her inconstancy teach him the anatomy of wit — the whole told in the balanced, antithetical, simile-laden prose that took England by storm and gave the decade its style.
works.plot: Euphues wins Philautus's friendship and then Lucilla's love, betraying his friend; Lucilla's fickleness (she turns to Curio) punishes the traitor; the debate on love, the letters of counsel, and Euphues's departure close the book with the moral anatomy — 'wit' dissected into its deceits and remedies.
works.significance: The most influential prose style of the English Renaissance — the book that taught a generation to write, and to think in balances.
works.meter: Prose of elaborate Euphuistic balance — antithesis, isocolon, and the zoological similes of Pliny's natural history.
works.context: Published in 1578 and reprinted a dozen times by 1600; the style it founded was imitated by Greene, Lodge, and the court, and parodied by Shakespeare and Nashe within the decade.
works.characters: Euphues; Philautus; Lucilla; Curio; the old gentleman of Naples; the ladies of Naples
works.structure: A moral romance in the manner of the Italian questioni d'amore: narrative framed by debate, letters, and the concluding 'Cooling Card' against love.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Complete Works of John Lyly, 3 vols.

works.title: Evelina; or, A Young Lady's Introduction to the World
altTitles: Evelina, A Young Lady's Introduction to the World
works.description: The history of a young woman of unknown birth introduced by her guardian's family into London and Bristol society, told in her letters home to the grandfather she has never known. Its publication was anonymous and its immediate success surprised its author, who had thrown it out as a juvenile exercise.
works.plot: Evelina Anville, the daughter of a private and disobliged marriage, is taken by her grandfather Lady Howard's connection into the company of the Mirvan family. She is annoyed by Madame Duval, her mother's relation, insulted and compromised in the gardens and at the assemblies, and carried through the theatre, the balls and the rackets of the town. At Bristol she is robbed and rescued, and in London her conduct under continual provocation is vindicated; the discovery of her birth and her grandfather's consent prepare the marriage with the man she has deserved.
works.significance: It created the comedy-of-manners novel written by a woman and is the standard account of the initiation of a girl into the sexual and social grammar of polite London; its influence on the later novel of observation is very large.
works.meter: A carefully graded epistolary prose, the heroine's letters polite, naive and increasingly articulate, the comic letters of Captain Mirvan and of Madame Duval carrying the broad humour; the style of the reporting letters is the book's chief instrument.
works.context: Published in London in 1778 by a young woman writing from the household of the musical family of the Drury Lane manager, in the season of the new attention to the manners of the town, the assemblies and the public gardens, and of the quarrel over women's novels.
works.characters: Evelina Anville; Mr. Villars; Lady Howard; Mrs. and Miss Mirvan; Captain Mirvan; Madame Duval; Lord Ormont; the servants and the assistants of the town
works.structure: A novel in a series of letters, principally from Evelina to Mr. Villars, with the letters of others supplying the report of her conduct; the sequence of public amusements forms the social anatomy of the book.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; issued anonymously as by a lady in the first edition, its authorship being declared by the writer in the second and later editions and established by her papers.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Every Man in His Humour
works.description: Jonson's first great comedy of humours, performed by the Lord Chamberlain's Men with Shakespeare in the cast: the jealous merchant Kitely, the braggart Captain Bobadill, the town gull Matthew, and the poetaster's crew are all 'humorous' — each ruled by an obsession — until the exposure of the final act lets the sane (Clement, Wellbred) judge the fools, in a London whose names Jonson later anglicized from the Italian setting.
works.plot: Old Knowell worries over his son's London dissipations; Kitely suspects his wife; Bobadill boasts and fights by words only; the gulls and their plots collide at Cob's house, and Justice Clement's court of the final scene administers the comic verdicts — including the purging of the humours by the 'vent' of exposure.
works.significance: The foundation of Jonson's comic method and of the English comedy of character — the template for Restoration and eighteenth-century comedy alike.
works.meter: Mostly prose in the 1616 Folio revision, with the verse of the earlier Italian version smoothed away — the first great prose comedy of the English stage.
works.context: Performed 1598 at the Curtain by the Chamberlain's Men (Shakespeare played Old Knowell); Jonson revised the play, resetting it in London, for the 1616 Folio of his Works.
works.characters: Kitely; Dame Kitely; Captain Bobadill; Edward Knowell; Brainworm; Wellbred; Stephen; Matthew; Justice Clement; Downright; Bridget; Cob; Tib
works.structure: A unified-plot comedy on the classical model — one city, one day, one action — built on the humours theory announced in the Induction and resolved in the judgment scene.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, 7 vols.
editions.editor: David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (gen. eds.)

works.title: Everyman
works.description: The most famous of the English moralities, translated from the Dutch Elckerlijc (c. 1495) around 1500: Everyman, summoned by Death to render his account, finds that Fellowship, Kindred, Goods, and even his own Strength and Beauty desert him, and that only Good Deeds — and Knowledge, Confession, and the priesthood — go with him into the grave. Its stark allegory of death has kept it on the stage for five centuries.
works.plot: God, seeing mankind sunk in worldly love, sends Death to Everyman with the summons to his reckoning; one by one his companions refuse the journey — Fellowship, Kindred, Cousin, Goods — until Good Deeds, weakened by his neglect, sends him to Knowledge, who leads him through Confession and penance to the sacraments; at the grave, Strength, Discretion, Beauty, and the Five Wits desert him in turn, and only Good Deeds descends with him, as the angels receive his soul.
works.significance: The classic English play of death and the reckoning: its allegory has made it the most performed medieval English drama in the modern world.
works.meter: Couplets and stanza forms, plain and weighty, with the Dutch original's structure faithfully kept.
works.context: Translated from the Dutch Elckerlijc (c. 1495) c. 1500 and printed by Richard Pynson and John Skot c. 1510–1535; continuously performed since, including modern productions (Hofmannsthal's Jedermann at Salzburg descends from it).
works.characters: Everyman; Death; God; Fellowship; Kindred; Cousin; Goods; Good Deeds; Knowledge; Confession; Strength; Discretion; Beauty; the Five Wits; the Angel; the Doctor
works.structure: A single-movement morality of the final journey, with the successive desertions of the companions as its pitiless rhythm and the doctrine of the reckoning as its frame.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; translated from the Dutch, whose authorship is likewise disputed.

editions.title: Everyman and Mankind

works.title: Exodus
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 590 lines on the Israelites' crossing of the Red Sea, from the Junius manuscript: a bravura reworking of Exodus 13-14 in which Moses becomes a heroic leader and the crossing a nautical epic, prefiguring the Christian's passage through the waters of baptism and the harrowing of hell.
works.plot: After a prologue on Moses and the law, the poem narrates the pursuit of the Israelites by Pharaoh's host, the pillar of cloud and fire, the parting of the waters, the drowning of the Egyptians, and the Israelites' division of spoils on the far shore; it closes with an allegorical exegesis of the crossing (the 'keys of the deep', the 'spiritual meanings') and allusions to Noah, Abraham, Solomon's temple, and the end of the world.
works.significance: The most stylistically daring of the Old Testament poems; its sea imagery is a high point of Old English diction.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of unusual density; famous kennings for the sea ('the whale's road', 'the swan's riding-place').
works.context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11, pp. 143-171); the poem is often linked with the Cædmonian school of biblical paraphrase mentioned by Bede.
works.characters: Moses; Pharaoh; the Israelites; Abraham; Noah
works.structure: Narrative epic with an extended typological epilogue; the abrupt shifts of scene (Noah, Abraham, the temple) have prompted theories of textual disruption.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the Cædmonian attribution is traditional only.
themes: Country retirement and the estate poem
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume D: The Romantic Period

works.title: Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air
altTitles: Experiments upon Different Kinds of Air
works.description: Priestley's founding reports of pneumatic chemistry, the first volume published in 1774 and the series extended through the 1780s, in which he isolated and named the airs, fixed air, dephlogisticated air and the rest, and made the study of gases a science. The work established his European fame and transformed the chemistry of the atmosphere.
works.plot: Priestley describes his method of collecting airs over water and quicksilver, and reports the generation of fixed air from fermentation, chalk, and living mice, showing its abundance in ordinary processes. He proves that common air is indefinitely alterable, that mice and flame consume and corrupt it, and that dephlogisticated air, obtained by heat from mercurial calcine and niter, is air purified beyond compare, in which a candle burns with unparalleled lustre and animal life is prolonged. He then trials nitrous, phlogisticated, and alkaline airs, the composition and the respirability of each, the later volumes extending these discoveries through the 1780s. The narrative insists that the airs are chemical individuals, not modifications of a single element.
works.significance: It created the chemistry of gases and is one of the foundational experimental records of modern chemistry; its discovery of oxygen, however interpreted within the phlogiston scheme, stands among the turning points of the science.
works.meter: Homely, exact laboratory prose: operation, observation, inference, with occasional rhapsody at the wonders disclosed.
works.context: Begun at Leeds and Birmingham after the Electricity history, amid the phlogiston controversies and Priestley's nonconformist ministry; the first volume appeared in 1774, and the series was soon rebuilt by Lavoisier into the oxygen chemistry and answered by the British phlogistonists.
works.structure: Serial volumes of reported experiments, each a chain of trials with the apparatus described, the observation, and the inference, the later volumes answering critics.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Explanatory Notes Upon the New Testament
altTitles: Wesley's Explanatory Notes on the New Testament
works.description: John Wesley's one-volume commentary on the New Testament, verse by verse, the most widely circulating English exegesis of Methodism and a deliberate distillation of Bengelius, Grotius, Lightfoot, and the practical writers. It gave the preachers and a lay readership a complete working interpretation of the text in English.
works.plot: Wesley prints the received English text in sense paragraphs and follows each verse with notes that paraphrase, clear the idiom, weigh the sense against other translators, and press the practical and experimental meaning. The notes are strongest on justification by faith, assurance, inward sanctification, and Christian perfection, doctrines he reads through the whole of the epistles and Gospels; he handles prophecy, the church, and the sacraments with a return to primitive antiquity. Difficulties of gospel chronology and the Pauline argument receive plain, workmanlike solutions. The whole is a manual of the New Testament made for preachers on horseback and pious families.
works.significance: It became the working New Testament of early Methodism on both sides of the Atlantic and remains the fullest witness to Wesley's exegetical mind and his doctrine of experimental religion.
works.meter: Condensed, abbreviated note prose of marginal shorthand made discursive, its sentences pared to the practical point.
works.context: Produced in the thick of Wesley's preaching ministry and the society's growth, published in 1754 for the use of the Methodists, it gathered earlier continental and English annotation into a standard of Methodist scriptural reason joined to heart-religion.
works.structure: A continuous verse commentary on the books of the New Testament in canonical order, paragraph by paragraph.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Expugnatio Hibernica
works.description: Gerald of Wales's history of the Anglo-Norman invasion and conquest of Ireland (1169–85), framed as a panegyric of Henry II and of Gerald's own relatives among the conquerors, the Geraldines; composed from 1188 and read publicly at Oxford in 1188 or 1189.
works.summary: Gerald recounts the coming of the Normans under Strongbow and the campaigns that established English lordship in Ireland, devoting special attention to the deeds of the FitzGeralds, to the character of the Irish, and to the prophecies and prodigies attending the conquest.
works.significance: The foundational narrative of the English presence in Ireland, shaped by family partisanship but indispensable as the earliest extended account of the conquest; a model of twelfth-century historical rhetoric.

works.title: Fables (First Collection)
altTitles: Fables by John Gay, Part the First
works.description: Gay's first collection of the beast fables, cast in the manner of the Eastern and classical apologue and applied, in the dedication and the moral, to the court, the city, the stage and the marriage market of his own country.
works.plot: A succession of short tales of beasts, birds and insects, each closing with an application: on credulity and the guide who leads the rash, on the great and their favourites, on the tyrant and his courtiers, on the traveller and the city, and on the marriage market.
works.significance: It restored the fable to the English canon as a form of social and political realism, and it long stood in the schoolroom beside Aesop and later with the century's own collection of the short moral tale.
works.meter: Heroic couplet in the plainest narrative use, with the short sententious close that carries the moral.
works.context: Published by subscription in the year of the Beggar's Opera's first run, when the vogue for eastern tales and for La Fontaine's imitators had made the apologue a vehicle of national comment; the dedication commends the instruction of a princess of the House of Hanover.
works.characters: the beasts and birds of the apologues; the court, the city and the theatre they figure
works.structure: A collection in numbered books of independent fables, each with its own narrative and appended application, unified only by the dedicator's frame.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the collection reworks earlier apologue material, and Gay acknowledges his Eastern and classical obligations.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Fables (Second Collection)
altTitles: Fables by John Gay, Part the Second
works.description: Gay's second and last collection of fables, prepared for publication shortly before his death and more openly personal and political than the first, with the poet's own retirement and independence as its recurring subject.
works.plot: Independent apologues of beasts, plants and the domesticks of the world, each with its application, several of them taking the fortunes of court friendship, the poet's patron and the dangers of the great.
works.significance: It completes the most considerable English fable sequence of the century and preserves the image of the poet's protected retirement which the age attached to Gay's memory.
works.meter: Heroic couplet, more reflective and sometimes more broken than in the first collection, with the lyric insertion in the closing fable.
works.context: Composed across the 1730s, after the suppression of Polly and the withdrawal of the theatre patronage, and published in the year of Gay's death in the subscription manner he had used for the first collection.
works.characters: the beasts and trees of the apologues; the court friend and the poet
works.structure: A collection in books of separate fables with their morals, framed by the poet's retirement among his books and closing with the fable of the old apple-tree.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Fables Ancient and Modern
works.description: Dryden's last volume, a collection of verse translations and adaptations from Homer, Ovid, Boccaccio, and Chaucer, dedicated to the Duke of Ormond and prefaced by his famous account of translation.
works.plot: The volume contains, among others, Palamon and Arcite (from Boccaccio's Teseida), The Cock and the Fox (from Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale), The Wife of Bath Her Tale, Theodore and Honoria, Cymon and Iphigenia, and the twelfth book of Ovid's Metamorphoses.
works.significance: The greatest achievement of Dryden's late career and a founding document of English translation theory; Palamon and Arcite and the preface are canonical texts in the history of Chaucer reception.
works.meter: Heroic couplets throughout, including the celebrated octosyllabic-free Chaucerian adaptations rendered in five-beat lines.
works.context: Published in March 1700, two months before Dryden's death, by subscription after he had been stripped of the laureateship in 1689.
works.characters: Palamon; Arcite; Emily; Chaunticlere; Pertelote; Reynard; Theodore; Honoria; Cymon; Iphigenia; the Wife of Bath
works.structure: A miscellany of narrative poems unified by the preface's theory of translation as the art of conveying a dead author's spirit in the living language.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Fall of Princes
works.description: John Lydgate's monumental translation (over 36,000 lines) of Boccaccio's De Casibus Virorum Illustrium, commissioned by Humphrey Duke of Gloucester and completed in 1438: a procession of the falls of princes from Adam to King John of France, moralized by the ghostly narrator Boccaccio himself. The encyclopedic English 'tragedy' of fortune, and the ancestor of the Mirror for Magistrates.
works.plot: The poet, in a Boethian frame, receives the sorrowing Boccaccio, who recounts example after example of greatness overthrown — Nimrod, Saul, Priam, Alexander, Caesar, Nero, Arthur, and the modern princes — each tale closing with the moral of fortune's wheel; the work ends with the falls of the French and English kings and a defense of poetry itself.
works.significance: The great English poem of the falls of princes and the conduit by which Boccaccio's tragic vision became the Tudor theory of tragedy; its influence on the Elizabethan stage is direct.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas with prose links, aureate and copious.
works.context: Commissioned by Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, in 1431 and completed in 1438, during the wars in France and the king's minority; printed by Pynson (1494) and continuously read; the Mirror for Magistrates (1559) descends directly from it.
works.characters: Lydgate (dreamer); Boccaccio (narrator); the fallen princes of history
works.structure: Nine books of exemplary falls within the dream-vision frame, with the envoy to Duke Humphrey as its patronage climax.
works.attributionNotes: Lydgate's authorship secure.

editions.title: Lydgate's Fall of Princes

works.title: False Delicacy
works.form: sentimental comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: A sentimental comedy of a young woman who loses the man she loves by an over-scrupulous reserve, written to prove that virtue itself may err by excess of refinement. It was the successful rival of a kindred play of the same season and took the argument for sentimental reformation of the stage.
works.plot: A lady of exalted principles conceals her affection from the lover she has promised, from a false notion of modesty, and by her silence gives his family the opening for another match. A second pair, less refined and more frank, carry the underplot of honest inclination, and the friends and guardians divide the counsel of the world. The exposure of the mistake restores the first lovers, the comedy closing on the argument that a delicacy which costs a woman her happiness is false.
works.significance: It is the standard example of the sentimental comedy in its hour of triumph, and the season's pamphlets on the two species of comedy make it a fixed point in the history of the century's genre quarrel.
works.meter: A smooth prose dialogue of delicate refinement and sententious argument, the emotional moments raised into short declamations of principle.
works.context: First performed at Covent Garden in January 1766 in the same season and on the same bill as the rival comedy of the same quarrel, the contest being made the occasion of a public debate on the laughing and the sentimental comedy by the authors of both sides.
works.characters: the lady of the false delicacy of the title; the lover lost by her reserve; the guardian and the friends who misadvise; the frank pair of the underplot
works.structure: Five-act comedy of concealed feeling and mistaken counsel, with the underplot of the frank pair set against the main plot of scruple; the moral case is argued directly in the dialogue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with the prefatory argument on the design.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Fantomina; or, Love in a Maze
altTitles: Fantomina; or, Love in a Maze. By a Fine Lady
works.description: A short amatory tale in which a young woman, pursued no longer than she chooses to be, pursues a young officer by successive disguises, inventing for him one fictional person after another. It is the most praised of its author's fictions, a compact study of the masquerade of identity and of the economics of the sexual chase.
works.plot: Seeing a young officer at a public exhibition, a lady of quality resolves to be enjoyed by him on her own terms; she lodges near him as a poor woman, is bought and resold by him, and then personates a wanton, a neighbour and finally a man to keep his desire alive. Each invention is exhausted and replaced by another until the last disguise, that of a rival male, forces him to flee the town; she then appears in her own person and renews the pursuit from the beginning.
works.significance: It has been recovered as a masterpiece of early feminist narrative, its serial personation being read as an analysis of gender as performance and of the novel's own dependence on disguise.
works.meter: Lucid, ironic prose with the free-indirect reporting of the heroine's calculations, and a rhetorical heightening borrowed from romantic diction but turned to comedy.
works.context: Published in 1725 in a collected volume of the author's short fictions, in the season of the revival of the masquerade operas and of the controversy over the novel of intrigue; its own tale of disguise is a commentary on the theatre of the town.
works.structure: A single continuous third-person tale with a close ring composition: the last scene restores the first, so that the maze of the title is formally completed; the disguise episodes are arranged in escalating irony.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published as by 'a fine lady' and gathered under the author's name in her collected fiction.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Festial
works.description: John Mirk's cycle of English sermons for the feasts of the church year, composed c. 1380s at Lilleshall Abbey: lively, exemplum-rich homilies designed for parish priests to read to their congregations, from Advent through the temporale and sanctorale to the dedication of the church. The most popular sermon collection of late medieval England.
works.plot: Each sermon expounds the day's feast — its history, its scripture, and its moral — with the miracle stories and exempla that made the Festial famous: the monk and the birds, the usurer's bees, the proud lady's punishment — and closes with practical instruction for the parish.
works.significance: The classic of the English late medieval sermon and the principal record of orthodox parish preaching in the age of Lollardy; its exempla are a treasury of popular piety.
works.meter: Plain, animated prose with verse tags and exemplary narrative.
works.context: Composed by the Augustinian canon John Mirk, prior of Lilleshall, in the 1380s, for the 'ignorant' parish clergy; it spread across England in some forty manuscripts and was printed by Caxton (1483) and repeatedly thereafter.
works.characters: the exemplary figures of the tales
works.structure: A cycle of seventy-four (or more) sermons following the church year, in the homiletic-exemplary manner.
works.attributionNotes: Mirk's authorship secure (he names himself in the preface).

editions.title: John Mirk's Festial

works.title: Fingal
works.form: Ancient epic in the restored or reconstructed manner, in books, with argument or analysis prefixed to each book and with introductory and explanatory dissertation; accompanied by a group of shorter songs and laments.
works.description: Macpherson's first long Ossianic poem, offered as an ancient epic in six books on the deeds of Fingal, the Caledonian hero, together with several shorter translated poems. It greatly enlarges the manner of the 'Fragments' into a narrative machine of invasions, single combats, ghosts and bardic recitation. Its publication, with a prefacial dissertation, provoked both enthusiasm in Europe and attack at home.
works.plot: The epic frame is a war in which the forces of the north and of Ireland contend, and Fingal, aged, venerable and supreme in judgement as well as in arms, leads his Caledonians to the relief of the distressed. The action is interrupted and deepened by the recursive method of the poems: bards sing the past, heroes recount their own sorrows, and the ghosts of the departed appear to hasten or to lament a death. Love, friendship and the observance of hospitality are the governing virtues, and the great motive power is grief, expressed in lamentation over the slain and over fallen greatness. The shorter poems appended are mostly laments and narratives of private calamity, and they supply the tenderness the epic's battles refuse.
works.significance: It is the founding text of the Ossianic vogue in its full epic form, and one of the most widely translated and imitated poems of the later eighteenth century in Europe; its machinery of grief, mist, ghosts and heroic moderation supplied preromantic poetry with a whole repertoire. Its claim to have supplied Britain with an ancient epic of its own remains the centre of the authentication controversy.
works.meter: Unrhymed cadenced verse of great uniformity and weight, with inversion, accumulation of epithets, and long rolling periods; the measure is deliberately unlike heroick couplet or blank verse of the Augustan school, and was admired as a recovery of ancient harmonious barbaric numbers.
works.context: Published in 1762, in the war years, when Scottish and English readers were being offered national epics on every side, and when the dissertation on ancient poetry prefixed to the work was itself a contribution to the criticism of taste and sublimity. The volume's success established Macpherson's position and his claim to have recovered a Homeric-age literature from the Gaelic.
works.characters: Fingal; his sons and warriors; the heroes and heroines of the appended poems; the spirits of the dead and the reciting bards
works.structure: An epic in six books with a strongly episodic and recursive organisation: the present action is repeatedly suspended by songs, recitations and visions of the past, so that the temporal structure is that of an ancient tradition recollected by bards rather than of a continuous plot.
works.attributionNotes: Recorded as disputed because Macpherson published the work as a translation of an ancient epic and contemporaries, and many since, have held that the ancient original is largely or wholly his own composition, made from such Gaelic tradition as he genuinely gathered. The ascription to 'Ossian' and to the ancient bards is not verifiable; Macpherson's own responsibility for the printed text is undisputed.

editions.title: The Poems of Ossian and Related Works

works.title: Five Varieties of Blank Verse
altTitles: Five Varieties of Blank Verse, which are found to have been practised by some of our best English Poets
works.form: Critical treatise in versification, printed as a separate tract and reissued among the apparatus of the collected editions of old English poetry; its method is definitional and illustrative, with quoted specimens.
works.description: A short metrical treatise by Percy, issued as a companion to the historical criticism of the 'Reliques', which distinguishes five varieties of unrhymed English verse and traces them from the age of Gower to that of Milton. It is one of the earliest attempts in English to describe the history of blank verse as a system of measurable forms rather than as a single practice, and it belongs to the editorial apparatus of the antiquarian revival of native poetry.
works.plot: The treatise argues that English unrhymed verse is not one measure but several, and it sets out the varieties with specimens of each, arranged in chronological order so that the reader may see the progress of the metre towards the established iambic pentameter of the later poets. The point is both technical and national: the Old English and early writers had a metrical art of their own, and the modern habit of reading them as irregular or barbarous arises from ignorance of the distinction. Percy's evidence is scanned quotation, and his method is that of the antiquary-critic who lets specimens carry the argument. The essay thus supports the larger case of the 'Reliques', that native antiquity deserves critical as well as historical attention.
works.significance: It is a foundation-stone of the history of English metrics, the first systematic attempt to classify the varieties of unrhymed native verse, and it prepared the way for the later scholarship of the early English measures and for the antiquarian defence of blank verse as a national form.
works.meter: Prose argument on verse: the subject-matter is the analysis of English accentual and syllabic measures, including the long unrhymed line, the twelve-syllable line of the Romance school, and the several varieties of the decasyllable, with scanning of each.
works.context: It appears with the first vogue of the 'Reliques' and in the middle of the 1760s debate about old English verse, blank verse and the rules, in which the antiquaries were revising the neoclassical account of the metrical history of the language. It is a scholarly by-product of the ballad collection's enterprise.
works.structure: A continuous argument in a single short tract: proposition, definition and naming of each variety, illustrative specimens in sequence, and concluding remarks on the ascent of the measure to Milton.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Percy is regular and undisputed. Its precise first-print circumstances and its relation to the several editions of the 'Reliques' are complicated, and the composition dates are not fixed; the year recorded is that of its publication as a separate metrical tract of the same moment as the collection.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Floris and Blancheflour
works.description: An idyllic romance of young love, adapted from the Old French Floire et Blancheflor: the Saracen prince Floris and the Christian captive Blancheflour, brought up together, are parted by his parents, and Floris pursues her to the emir's tower in Babylon, where love and loyalty overcome jealousy and force. The gentlest of the early English romances.
works.plot: Floris's parents sell Blancheflour to merchants to end the match; she is taken to the emir of Babylon's harem tower; Floris follows, bribes his way in, is discovered in the maidens' tower, and is saved from death when the lovers' mutual devotion moves the emir to mercy and their marriage.
works.significance: The classic English romance of young love and constancy, and a key witness to the transmission of the sentimental romance from France to England.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets, gently lyrical in tone.
works.context: Composed c. 1250 in the south-east from the French Floire et Blancheflor (c. 1150), one of the most widely translated romances of the Middle Ages; preserved in four English manuscripts from c. 1300 onward.
works.characters: Floris; Blancheflour; the emir of Babylon; Clarice; Darys the porter
works.structure: A quest-romance in two movements (parting; pursuit and rescue), with the tower and the garden as symbolic settings.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Fowre Hymnes
works.description: Four philosophical hymns on love and beauty — 'An Hymne in Honour of Love', 'An Hymne in Honour of Beautie', 'An Hymne of Heavenly Love', and 'An Hymne of Heavenly Beautie' — in which the Platonism of earthly desire is answered and completed by the Christian ascent to divine love.
works.plot: The first two hymns celebrate Cupid's power and the beauties of the beloved as earthly ladder; the second pair, written (the dedication says) to 'reform' the first, ascend through the creation to the love of Christ and the beauty of the divine wisdom enthroned in heaven.
works.significance: The classic English statement of the Neoplatonic ladder of love, and a key text for the devotional Platonism of the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Rhyme royal, with an elevated, liturgical diction.
works.context: Published in 1596 with a dedicatory epistle to the Countess of Cumberland and the Countess of Warwick explaining that the first two hymns were written in youth, the second two in maturity.
works.characters: the poet as lover and worshipper
works.structure: Two matched pairs of hymns, the earthly pair answered point by point by the heavenly pair in a deliberate palinode.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Yale Edition of the Shorter Poems of Edmund Spenser
editions.editor: William A. Oram, Einar Bjorvand, Ronald Bond, Thomas Cain, Alexander Dunlop, and Richard Schell (eds.)

works.title: Fragmenta Aurea
altTitles: Fragmenta Aurea: A Collection of All the Incomparable Pieces
works.description: The posthumous collection of Suckling's poems and plays (1646), including his best-loved lyrics — 'Why so pale and wan, fond lover?', 'A Ballad upon a Wedding', and 'The Session of the Poets' — which capture the rakish wit and careless grace of the Cavalier generation.
works.plot: The lyrics treat love, gallantry, friendship, and wit with an easy, sceptical charm, deflating romantic pretension while celebrating the pleasures of court life.
works.significance: Fragmenta Aurea is the classic record of Cavalier wit and song; 'Why so pale' and 'A Ballad upon a Wedding' remain among the most lively lyrics of the century.
works.meter: Light, witty, conversational songs with a deliberately 'careless' aristocratic ease.
works.context: Published in 1646, four years after Suckling's death in exile, by his friends, with an engraved frontispiece; it preserved the voice of the doomed Cavalier court.
works.characters: the poet; mistresses; fellow wits
works.structure: A collection of songs, poems, letters, and four plays, gathered by friends after Suckling's death.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published posthumously.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
