works.title: Fragments of Ancient Poetry, Collected from the Bards
works.form: Anthology of translated fragments in prose-verse arrangement, with prefatory and paratextual matter asserting their antiquity and their source language; the unit is the short lyric or the broken narrative.
works.description: James Macpherson's first Ossianic publication: a thin collection of short pieces offered as translations from the Gaelic or Erse of 'ancient bards', with the names of the heroic cycle attached to them. It appeared anonymously, with a list of subscribers prefixed, and its success sent its author into the Highlands to collect more. It is the opening document of one of the great literary controversies of the century.
works.plot: There is no sustained argument, only a series of brief lyrical and narrative fragments: invocations of heroes, laments for the dead, addresses to the night, to mountains and to departed glory. The pieces are unified by a tone of mournful sublimity and by a supposed antiquity, since the speaker throughout is a bard of an unrecorded heroic age reporting what older bards sang. The effect the collection aims at is the impression of a native epic tradition surviving in ruins, and its politics of the fragment is deliberate: what is missing is made to appear lost rather than never written. The book's dedication and advertisements frame the fragments as a national restoration of ancient Scottish poetry, and they promised further and larger recoveries.
works.significance: It started the Ossian phenomenon and with it the European fashion for the primitive sublime, the forged or reconstructed national epic, and the cult of the bard. Its manner is traceable through the following decade's poetry, and its controversy set the terms in which authentication, national literary property and editorial honesty were debated.
works.meter: A stern, inverted, cadenced English prose-verse of long periods and heavy latinate diction, modelled on no existing English measure; the irregular 'ancient' rhythm was one of the features that readers seized on as evidence of sublimity and sceptics seized on as evidence of imposition.
works.context: It was published in Edinburgh in 1760, in the moment after the 'Forty-five' when Scottish Highland antiquity was being simultaneously romanticised and policed, and within the wider European argument about primitive genius, Homer and the origins of national poetry that had been sharpened by Hurd, Blair and the Warton circle. Hugh Blair's encouragement and the subscription model made the first collection possible.
works.characters: The supposed ancient bards; the heroes and heroines of the Gaelic cycle invoked in the fragments
works.structure: A collection of independent short pieces, sequenced for variety of tone rather than chronology, prefaced by subscriber list and advertisements and annotated with the names of the heroes and the occasions of the songs.
works.attributionNotes: Macpherson is the author in the sense that he produced and published the texts; whether he translated genuine Gaelic and Irish sources or largely composed his 'ancients' himself has been disputed from 1760 to the present, and the 'ancient bard' authorship the title asserts is certainly not verifiable. The present record assigns the book to Macpherson and marks the ancient attribution as disputed.

editions.title: The Poems of Ossian and Related Works

works.title: Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay
works.description: Greene's romantic comedy of Oxford magic and Suffolk love: Friar Bacon, England's great magician, works his brazen head and his glass of distant seeing while the Prince of Wales, the earls, and the keeper's daughter Margaret of Fressingfield play out their love-plot — the play moving between the scholars' cell and the country fair to its double ending of broken magic and honest marriage.
works.plot: Prince Edward and Lacy both love Margaret; Lacy woos her in the prince's name and wins her for himself; the prince's rage, the rivals' duel, and the disguises of the middle acts complicate the match; Bacon's glass shows the fathers' deaths and is shattered; the brazen head speaks 'Time is, Time was, Time is past' and falls; and the play ends with the marriages and the friar's renunciation of magic.
works.significance: The masterpiece of the University Wits' romantic comedy — the play in which magic, love, and England's own legends met on the popular stage.
works.meter: Blank verse for the court and scholars, prose for the rustics — the mixed style that became the Elizabethan comic norm.
works.context: Performed about 1589 and printed in 1594; its Oxford setting and national hero-magician answered the vogue for conjuring plays after Faustus.
works.characters: Friar Bacon; Friar Bungay; Prince Edward; Lacy, Earl of Lincoln; Margaret of Fressingfield; the Keeper; Miles; the two scholars (the sons of Lambert and Serlsby); the Devil (in the conjuring); the brazen head
works.structure: A two-world comedy — the university cell and the Fressingfield household — braided by the magic glass, in Greene's most accomplished construction.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: James IV (Revels Plays)

works.title: Friendship in Death
altTitles: Friendship in Death: In Twenty-Six Letters, Between Two Persons of Distinction, Of the Other World
works.description: A series of letters between two departed friends who write to each other from their tombs in Westminster Abbey, reviewing the lives they have left and the affections they have not lost. It is one of the most original of the pious fictions of the early century, and a landmark both of the women's friendship tradition and of the literature of the other world.
works.plot: Two women long deceased carry on a correspondence from their respective sepulchres, each reporting the state of the other's family and the changes of the world below. They review their own past conduct, the trials of marriage, the uses of study and the comfort of religion, and they intercede and sympathise with one another across the boundary of death. The letters pass to the deaths of those still living and to the reunions of the friends, the whole closing on the hope of a friendship perfected in another state.
works.significance: It stands between the conduct fiction and the novel of female friendship, and its device of the correspondence of the dead anticipates both the Gothic letter and the sentimental fiction of bereavement; it was long read and reprinted through the century.
works.meter: A warm and elevated epistolary prose of the female devotional style, with the apostrophes to the dead and to the Abbey as its characteristic movement; some of the pieces are versified.
works.context: Published in 1728 by a poet already known as the author of pious verse and of the poems of the earlier years, in the season of the vogue for the letters of the dead and for the conversation of the other world, an amusement that had been licensed by the essays of the previous generation.
works.characters: the two departed friends who write from their tombs; the surviving families and friends reported to them; the several characters of the inset histories
works.structure: A serial epistolary fiction of short letters, the sequence of correspondents and of posthumous reports supplying the order; the inset histories of the living make it a collection of tales within a correspondence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and reprinted in the posthumous collections of her works.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Fulgens and Lucrece
works.description: Henry Medwall's interlude of the wooing of Lucrece, performed at the household of Cardinal Morton; the earliest surviving secular English play, printed by John Rastell c. 1512–16.
works.plot: The Roman senator Fulgens promises his daughter Lucrece to the suitor of greater nobility, Publius Cornelius or Gaius Flaminius; the debate on true nobility (virtue versus birth) is interwoven with a subplot in which two serving-men, A and B, woo Lucrece's maid and re-enact the contest in comic parallel. The play breaks off in the unique surviving copy before the conclusion.
works.significance: The first surviving secular English play and a landmark in the transition from medieval moral drama to Renaissance comedy; its debate on true nobility and its pairing of serious and comic plots anticipate the structure of Elizabethan drama.
works.meter: Rhyme royal and couplets, with prose dialogue in the comic scenes
works.context: Written for performance at a feast given by Cardinal John Morton (probably Christmas 1497), in whose household Medwall was chaplain; the play adapts Buonaccorso da Montemagno's De vera nobilitate (translated by John Tiptoft c. 1460), and Rastell's printing (c. 1512–16) preserved it for the sixteenth-century stage tradition.
works.characters: Fulgens; Lucrece; Publius Cornelius; Gaius Flaminius; A (servant); B (servant); Joan (Lucrece's maid)
works.structure: Two-part interlude alternating the serious debate of the senators with the comic subplot of the servants, with direct addresses to the banqueting audience.

editions.title: The Plays of Henry Medwall

works.title: Gallathea
works.description: Lyly's pastoral comedy of disguise and desire: to appease Neptune's demand for the fairest virgin of the land, the fathers of Gallathea and Phillida disguise both girls as boys; the two 'youths' fall in love with each other, and the play ends with Venus's promise that 'one of them' shall be transformed into a man — a resolution whose gender the text leaves teasingly open.
works.plot: Neptune's sacrifice is evaded by the two disguises; the shepherds' loves and the fair's episodes (Rafe, Robin, and the alchemist) fill the middle; the 'boys'' mutual love complicates everything; and the final scene, with Diana and Venus contending, produces the metamorphosis promise and the virgin's reprieve.
works.significance: The most daring of Lyly's gender comedies — the play in which the Elizabethan stage's play with sexual identity becomes the plot itself.
works.meter: Prose with verse for the divine scenes — the gods speak verse, the mortals prose, in Lyly's careful decorum.
works.context: Probably performed at court on 1 January 1588, the Armada year; printed 1592; its same-sex desire, licensed by the boy actors' convention, has made it a touchstone of queer reading of the Renaissance stage.
works.characters: Gallathea; Phillida; Neptune; Venus; Diana; Cupid; the fathers (Tityrus and Melibeus); Hebe; the fair folk (Rafe, Robin, the Alchemist, the Mariner)
works.structure: A five-act pastoral built on the cross-dressing device, with the fair scenes and Neptune's wrath as frame and counterpoint.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Complete Works of John Lyly, 3 vols.

works.title: Gammer Gurton's Needle
altTitles: A Ryght Pithy, Pleasaunt and Merie Comedie: Intytuled Gammer Gurtons Nedle
works.description: The classic English village farce of the lost needle, composed c. 1552–53, probably at Christ's College, Cambridge, and printed in 1575; the second of the two earliest English comedies (with Ralph Roister Doister).
works.plot: Gammer Gurton's precious needle is lost while mending the breeches of her servant Hodge; the whole household turns out to search, suspicion falls on the neighbour Dame Chat, and the village curate Doctor Rat is beaten in a confusion of break-ins and brawls; the needle is at last discovered — in the seat of Hodge's breeches — with a resounding yell, and the company shares the ale in reconciliation.
works.significance: One of the two founding comedies of the English stage: its picture of village life, its rich dialect comedy, and its plot of the lost needle set the pattern for English farce from Shakespeare's Merry Wives to the twentieth century.
works.meter: Rhyming couplets ('rhyming fourteeners'), with the famous drinking song 'Back and side go bare'
works.context: Composed c. 1552–53, with the title-page attribution of the 1575 edition to 'Mr. S. Master of Art' generally identified as William Stevenson of Christ's College, Cambridge, where the play was probably acted; it belongs to the university revival of classical comedy in the 1550s.
works.characters: Gammer Gurton; Hodge; Diccon the Bedlam; Dame Chat; Doctor Rat; Master Bayly; Tib; Cock
works.structure: Five acts in a single village setting, modelled on Roman comedy but filled with native farce: the plot turns on the lost object, the false accusation, and the comic discovery.
works.attributionNotes: The 1575 title page ascribes the play to 'Mr. S. Master of Art', identified by modern scholarship (most fully by Charles W. Whitworth) as William Stevenson of Christ's College, Cambridge; the attribution is probable rather than certain.

editions.title: Three Sixteenth-Century Comedies

works.title: Genesis A
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 2,935 lines paraphrasing Genesis 1-22, from the creation and the fall of the angels to the sacrifice of Isaac. The longest of the Junius manuscript poems, it is the foundational Old Testament epic of the period, composed in the plain style of the 'Cædmonian' school.
works.plot: The poem recounts the fall of the rebel angels, the six days of creation, the fall of Adam and Eve and their expulsion, Cain and Abel, the generations to Noah, the Flood and the covenant, the tower of Babel, and the story of Abraham to the near-sacrifice of Isaac, concluding with the promise of the seed.
works.significance: The earliest sustained biblical epic in English; a primary witness to the vernacular reception of scripture.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre in a relatively plain, narrative style.
works.context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11); its opening lines were long known as 'Cædmon's Genesis' from the early editor Junius's attribution.
works.characters: God; Adam; Eve; Satan; Cain; Abel; Noah; Abraham; Sarah; Isaac; Lot
works.structure: Continuous biblical paraphrase in epic form, with an interpolated passage (Genesis B, lines 235-851) translated from Old Saxon treating the fall in greater detail.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attribution to Cædmon is traditional and no longer accepted.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Eighteenth-Century Poetry

works.title: Genesis B
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 617 lines, interpolated into Genesis A (lines 235-851), translated from an Old Saxon original and containing the most celebrated scenes of the fall in Old English: Satan's proud rebellion ('better for me to be a king in hell'), the temptation of Adam by the disguised tempter, and the grief of Eve.
works.plot: The poem opens with Satan's boast against God and his binding in hell; an envoy demon journeys to Eden and, taking the form of a serpent, tempts first Adam (unsuccessfully) and then Eve, deceiving her with the promise of a vision of heaven; Eve eats and persuades Adam; the poem closes on their shame and the beginning of repentance, with the original ending lost in the transition back to Genesis A.
works.significance: Contains the finest dramatic treatment of the fall in early English poetry; its Satan anticipates Milton's in power and pathos, a connection first argued by Sievers in 1875.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, with occasional hypermetric lines betraying the Old Saxon original.
works.context: Translated into Old English from an Old Saxon poem (possibly connected with the ninth-century Heliand milieu) and interpolated into Genesis A in the Junius manuscript; the Old Saxon original survives only in a few Vatican fragments.
works.characters: Satan; the Tempter (demon); Adam; Eve
works.structure: A dramatic expansion of the fall narrative built on lengthy speeches — Satan's monologue, the tempter's persuasions, Eve's lament — unique in the corpus for its psychological interest.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the interpolation was first detected by Eduard Sievers (1875).
themes: Restoration politics: party, succession, and Exclusion
sources: The Cambridge Companion to the Eighteenth-Century Novel

works.title: Gentleness and Nobility
works.description: A debate interlude on the nature of true nobility, printed by John Rastell c. 1529 and attributed to Rastell (or, by some, to John Heywood); an early dramatic statement of the humanist case that virtue, not birth, makes the gentleman.
works.plot: A Knight, a Merchant, and a Ploughman dispute whether gentleness resides in ancestry or in virtue; the Ploughman, arguing that nobility of birth without worth is empty, is supported against the Knight's hereditary claims, and the debate — refereed by the Philosopher — concludes with the definition of true gentleness as virtuous living, with a sharp satire of idle gentlemen who live off others' labour.
works.significance: The first English play devoted wholly to the question of true nobility, and a rare dramatic voice for the commonwealth critique of hereditary privilege; it anticipates the social debates of Elizabethan drama.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Printed c. 1529, in the year of the Reformation Parliament; the play's defence of labour and its satire of idle gentry voice the social criticism of the humanist commonwealth tradition (More's Utopia, Starkey's Dialogue), and its attribution to Rastell connects it to the More circle.
works.characters: The Knight; The Merchant; The Ploughman; The Philosopher
works.structure: A formal disputation in two parts, with the Philosopher as moderator and the three estates as speakers; the debate is enlivened by comic abuse between the Knight and the Ploughman.
works.attributionNotes: Printed without author's name; the play is traditionally attributed to John Rastell (whose press produced it), with John Heywood also proposed; modern scholarship accepts Rastell as the likeliest author without certainty.

works.title: Gesta Regum Anglorum
altTitles: Deeds of the Kings of the English
works.description: William of Malmesbury's history of the English kings from the arrival of the Anglo-Saxons (449) to the twenty-eighth year of Henry I (1127–28), the most learned English history of the twelfth century, deliberately modelled on Bede and written with a polished Latinity that set a new standard for English historiography.
works.summary: Five books carry the narrative from the adventus Saxonum through the kings of Wessex and the Norman Conquest to Henry I; the work combines narrative history with biography, anecdote, and documentary research, drawing on a library of sources now partly lost and on William's own travels and enquiries.
works.significance: The outstanding English historical work between Bede and the later twelfth century; a model of critical method and style, cited and pillaged by later chroniclers, and a primary witness to Anglo-Saxon history after the Conquest.

editions.title: Gesta Regum Anglorum
editions.editor: R. A. B. Mynors, R. M. Thomson, and M. Winterbottom (eds.)

works.title: Gloria I and II
altTitles: The Greater and Lesser Doxology Poems
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious lyric (liturgical paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: Two short Old English versifications of the liturgical Gloria: Gloria I (57 lines) paraphrases the Greater Doxology sung at Mass, praising the Trinity and Christ the Lamb of God; Gloria II (20 lines) is a brief rendering of the doxology of praise to Father, Son, and Spirit.
works.plot: Gloria I moves from the angels' song of praise through the attributes of the persons of the Trinity to Christ the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, ending with a prayer for mercy. Gloria II offers a compact doxology in verse.
works.significance: Evidence of the Old English church's project of rendering the central texts of the liturgy into the vernacular poetic idiom.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the balanced parallelism appropriate to liturgical praise; the shorter poem is notably compact.
works.context: The Benedictine Reform's devotion to the liturgy gave new prominence to the sung ordinary of the Mass; vernacular paraphrases like these made its texts accessible to those whose Latin was limited.
works.structure: Both poems are direct liturgical paraphrases; Gloria I is organized by the successive clauses of the Gloria in excelsis, closing with the Agnus Dei petitions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The two poems are separate compositions.
themes: Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind

works.title: Godfrey of Bulloigne
works.description: Edward Fairfax's translation of Tasso's Gerusalemme Liberata (1581), under the title Godfrey of Bulloigne, or the Recovery of Jerusalem (1600): the crusaders' siege and taking of Jerusalem — Godfrey's command, Rinaldo's enchantment in Armida's garden, Tancred and Clorinda's tragedy — in English ottava rima of grave and musical fidelity, the translation Dryden ranked with the originals.
works.plot: The Christian army besieges Jerusalem; the pagan enchantments of Armida and Ismeno delay the victory; Rinaldo is rescued from the garden of Armida; the duel of Tancred and Clorinda, the battles, and the final assault take the city; and the poem ends with Godfrey's worship at the Sepulchre.
works.significance: The great English Tasso — the version through which the Italian romantic epic entered English poetry, and a landmark of translation as an art.
works.meter: Ottava rima (abababcc) of sustained dignity and sweetness — the metre Fairfax naturalized for English heroic verse.
works.context: Published 1600, in the decade of the English epic translations (Harington's Ariosto, Sylvester's Du Bartas); Fairfax's Tasso was read by the Spenserians and praised by Dryden as the model of translation.
works.characters: Godfrey of Bouillon; Rinaldo; Armida; Tancred; Clorinda; Erminia; Peter the Hermit; Ismeno; Solyman; Argantes
works.structure: Twenty cantos of ottava rima following Tasso's order, with Fairfax's 'Allegory of the Poem' appended as the moral key.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by Fairfax; uncontested.

editions.title: Godfrey of Bulloigne: A Critical Edition of Edward Fairfax's Translation of Tasso's Gerusalemme Liberata
editions.editor: Kathleen M. Lea and T. M. Gang (eds.)

works.title: Godly Queen Hester
altTitles: A New Interlude Drawn out of the Holy Scripture of Godly Queen Hester
works.description: An anonymous interlude on the biblical story of Esther, printed in 1561 but composed c. 1525–29; a political allegory in which the virtuous queen and her wise counsellor save the realm from the wicked minister.
works.plot: King Ahasuerus, misled by the proud Aman, signs a decree against the Jews; Queen Hester, advised by the wise Mardocheus, intercedes with the king at the risk of her life, exposes Aman's malice, and obtains his overthrow and the deliverance of her people — with the collop-eating scene of Aman's gluttony played as comic Vice-business.
works.significance: The first surviving English dramatization of the Esther story and a striking example of the interlude as political counsel; it shows biblical drama absorbing the new humanist debate on counsel and tyranny.
works.meter: Couplets with stanzaic passages
works.context: Composed c. 1525–29, almost certainly for a noble household: the story of Esther had long served as an allegory of good counsel and royal deliverance, and the play has been read (by Greg Walker and others) as a veiled commentary on the fall of Wolsey, in which the virtuous queen intercedes against an overmighty minister.
works.characters: King Ahasuerus; Queen Hester; Mardocheus; Aman; Ardion (Aman's servant); Hardydardy; Pride; Adulation; Ambition
works.structure: A continuous interlude alternating the counsel scenes of Hester and Mardocheus with the comic scenes of Aman and his servants, ending in judgement and the elevation of Mardocheus.

works.title: Goostly Psalmes and Spirituall Songes
works.description: Miles Coverdale's collection of metrical psalms, hymns, and carols translated from the German (chiefly Luther), printed c. 1535; the first English hymn book, intended for congregational singing.
works.plot: Forty-one pieces — metrical versions of the psalms, Luther's hymns (including 'Ein feste Burg' as 'Our God is a defence and tower'), the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and canticles — each with its tune indicated, prefaced by an epistle on the right use of psalmody in church and home.
works.significance: The first English hymn book and the beginning of English congregational song; its psalms anticipate the metrical psalters of Sternhold and Hopkins, and its translation of 'Ein feste Burg' entered the English hymnic tradition.
works.meter: Metrical stanzas in ballad and hymn metres, set to German tunes
works.context: Printed c. 1535 during Coverdale's continental exile, drawing on the Wittenberg hymn books; Henry VIII's 1546 proclamation against 'ballads, rhymes, and lewd songs' included it among the books to be burned, and only one complete copy survives (Queen's College, Oxford).
works.structure: A hymn book arranged by liturgical use, with a preface on singing and notes of the tunes to which the pieces are set.

works.title: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
works.description: Bunyan's spiritual autobiography, written in Bedford Gaol during his twelve-year imprisonment for preaching without a licence, which records his agonising struggle with doubt, temptation, and the assurance of salvation.
works.plot: Bunyan traces his life from a childhood of swearing and bell-ringing through his conversion under John Gifford, his long torments of doubt and despair, his reading of Luther's Commentary on Galatians, and his final assurance of grace; the narrative is organised around biblical typology rather than chronology.
works.significance: The greatest spiritual autobiography in English and a foundational text of the Protestant confessional tradition; it supplied the raw material of inner experience that Bunyan transformed into the allegory of The Pilgrim's Progress.
works.meter: Vigorous, colloquial prose saturated with biblical language, especially the Psalms, Paul, and Hebrews.
works.context: Written in 1666 during Bunyan's first long imprisonment (1660-72) and published in the same year with a preface addressed to his Bedford congregation; a seventh edition appeared before his death.
works.characters: John Bunyan (the narrator); John Gifford; his first wife; his second wife Elizabeth; the Bedford congregation
works.structure: A first-person retrospective narrative in numbered paragraphs, with scriptural glosses on the margins, following the pattern of the Pauline conversion.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Bunyan; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Pilgrim's Progress
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Grammar and Glossary
works.form: grammar and didactic prose in Old English
works.description: Ælfric's Latin grammar written in English — the first grammar of Latin composed in any European vernacular — with its companion glossary of Latin words arranged by subject. A landmark in the history of education and of the vernacular as an instrument of learning.
works.plot: The Grammar adapts the Excerptiones de Prisciano to teach the parts of speech, declensions, and conjugations entirely through the medium of English, explaining Latin forms with English equivalents; the Glossary lists vocabulary by topics (the body, kinship, the church, tools, birds, beasts) in Latin with English glosses.
works.significance: The first vernacular Latin grammar in Europe; a milestone in the history of English education.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Composed c. 998, when Ælfric was at Cerne Abbas or Eynsham; at least fifteen manuscripts survive, evidence of its use in schools into the twelfth century.
works.characters: the schoolboys of Eynsham (addressees)
works.structure: A systematic school grammar in sections on the eight parts of speech, followed by the thematic glossary.
works.attributionNotes: Ælfric's authorship is certain.
themes: Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: The Graveyard School and Preromantic Meditation
sources: The English Poems of George Herbert

works.title: Gulliver's Travels
altTitles: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World
works.description: Swift's four-part voyage satire, narrated by the surgeon and captain Lemuel Gulliver, which reduces the scale of mankind to Lilliput, enlarges it in Brobdingnag, sends him to the flying island and the projectors of the Academy, and ends among the Houyhnhnms and the Yahoos.
works.plot: Gulliver is cast away and reaches a nation of six-inch men whose politics, war and parties are a miniature of Europe; then a land of giants where his own species is judged; then the projects of the mechanicks and the shades of the dead; and finally a country of rational horses whose human brutes, the Yahoos, force him to see his own kind as vermin, till his return and his disgust.
works.significance: It is the century's largest satiric fiction, converting the travellers' tale into an anatomy of human pride, and it founded the tradition of the constructed utopian and satirical voyage that runs to the nineteenth century.
works.meter: The deliberately unadorned prose of the navigator's log, with the exact measurement, the enumeration of customs and the flat statement of the most outrageous conclusion.
works.context: Written in the years between the fall of the Harley ministry and Swift's retirement to Dublin, and published anonymously in 1726 at a moment when the travel narrative and the new fiction of Defoe were making the invented first person respectable; the contemporary key identified nearly every personage of the first part.
works.characters: Lemuel Gulliver; the court and army of Lilliput; the farmer and the queen of Brobdingnag; the sages of the flying island; the Houyhnhnms; the Yahoos
works.structure: Four independent voyages in the first person, in the plain manner of the travel relation, each with its own ascent from curiosity to judgment; the sequence tightens from the political satire of the first two to the philosophical conclusion of the fourth.
works.attributionNotes: Published as the work of Lemuel Gulliver, initially a surgeon and lately a captain, with the printer's pretence of an unauthorised copy; Swift's authorship was understood at once and is uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Guthlac A
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 818 lines on the Mercian hermit Guthlac of Crowland: his arrival in the fenland retreat, his battles with the demons who tempt and torment him, and his vindication by the apostle Bartholomew. Based on Felix's Latin Vita, the poem turns the saint's spiritual warfare into heroic combat in the native manner.
works.plot: The young Mercian warrior Guthlac, renouncing war, takes up the solitary life in the fens of Crowland; demons assault his cell, carry him to the gates of hell, and accuse him of pride; the apostle Bartholomew commands his release and the devils obey; Guthlac returns victorious, and the poem closes with his death and the angels' reception of his soul.
works.significance: The classic vernacular treatment of the hermit-warrior and of the fenland as spiritual battlefield.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, with the diction of heroic combat applied to spiritual warfare.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 32b-44b); source: Felix of Crowland's Vita Sancti Guthlaci (c. 730-740).
works.characters: Guthlac; the demons; Bartholomew; the angels
works.structure: A hagiographical epic in the heroic mode: renunciation, the demonic wars (a psychomachia in narrative form), heavenly vindication, and death; speeches dominate the central combat scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
sources: The Works of Mary Wollstonecraft, 7 volumes

works.title: Guthlac B
works.description: A poem of 561 lines on the death of St Guthlac of Crowland, from the Exeter Book: the saint's illness, his last conversation with his servant Beccel, and the ascent of his soul, which flies like a bird to heaven. Distinct from Guthlac A in style and emphasis, it is one of the most tender poems in the corpus.
works.plot: Stricken with his final illness, Guthlac instructs his disciple Beccel, foretelling his own death on the seventh day; his soul departs like a bird to the heavenly home, and a light shines over the fen; Beccel, instructed to tell his sister Pega, buries him and the poem closes with a prayer. The poet's meditation on death — 'death is no man's friend' — frames the narrative.
works.significance: The finest Old English poem on the death of a saint; its bird-image for the soul's flight is among the period's most memorable figures.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; gentler and more meditative than Guthlac A.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 44b-52b); source: Felix's Vita Sancti Guthlaci.
works.characters: Guthlac; Beccel; Pega; the angels
works.structure: A single, intimate deathbed narrative: prophecy, farewell dialogue, and the ascent of the soul, framed by prologue and prayer.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; distinct authorship from Guthlac A is generally accepted.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
sources: Reflections on the Revolution in France

works.title: Guy of Warwick
altTitles: The Romance of Guy of Warwick
works.form: romance in couplets and tail-rhyme stanzas
works.description: The longest and one of the most widely read of the English romances, in couplets and tail-rhyme stanzas: the career of Guy, earl of Warwick, who wins the lady Felice by feats of arms, then renounces the world to fight as God's champion and die as a hermit. Its hero was England's favourite romance champion for three centuries.
works.plot: Guy, a steward's son, wins Felice through tournaments and foreign wars; struck by remorse, he leaves her to do penance as a pilgrim, returning in disguise to defend England against the giant Colbrond at Winchester; recognized only at his death, he is buried by Felice, who follows him in holiness.
works.significance: The romance of Guy fixed the image of the penitent knight in English culture and remained a bestseller until the Civil War; it is central to the study of romance readership.
works.meter: Couplets in the Auchinleck version; tail-rhyme stanzas in later copies.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 from Anglo-Norman sources, drawing on Warwick legend and the cult of Guy; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript and many later copies and prints, into the seventeenth century.
works.characters: Guy; Felice; Colbrond the giant; Reinbrun (their son); Herhaud
works.structure: A two-part structure — chivalric career, then penitential career — with the Colbrond episode and the deathbed recognition as climaxes.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Hakluytus Posthumus, or Purchas His Pilgrimes
works.description: Samuel Purchas's four-volume continuation of Hakluyt's collections: the voyage narratives and geographical documents left unpublished at Hakluyt's death — the travels of the East and West Indies, the relations of China and Japan, the Arctic voyages, and the Virginia enterprises — gathered and framed in Purchas's 'pilgrimage' of the world's records, the great Jacobean storehouse of travel literature.
works.plot: No single plot: the Pilgrimes arranges its hundreds of narratives by region and voyage — Purchas's own summaries and moral reflections interlacing the documents — from the voyages of the ancients to the discoveries of his own day.
works.significance: The great Jacobean continuation of Hakluyt — the book that carried the age of discovery's records into the age of colonization.
works.meter: Prose of many hands within Purchas's devout editorial frame.
works.context: Published 1625, the year of Purchas's death and of the Virginia Company's dissolution; the collection preserved many accounts that survive nowhere else and fed the English imagination of empire for two centuries.
works.characters: the voyagers and travellers (Hudson, Baffin, Cavendish, and hundreds of others)
works.structure: Four folio volumes of documentary compilation, with Purchas's prefaces, indices, and the running apparatus of his editorial 'pilgrimage'.
works.attributionNotes: Compiled and edited by Purchas from Hakluyt's papers and other sources; uncontested.

editions.title: Hakluytus Posthumus or Purchas His Pilgrimes, 20 vols.

works.title: Hali Meiðhad
works.description: An alliterative prose epistle in praise of virginity, addressed to young women contemplating the religious life, in the AB language of the Katherine Group. It contrasts the blessedness of the virgin bride of Christ with the miseries of married life, in a rhetorical tradition going back to patristic treatises on virginity.
works.plot: The author extols virginity as the highest estate, describes the joys of the heavenly bridegroom, and — in famously vivid passages — details the pains and humiliations of marriage and childbearing to urge his readers to choose the better part.
works.significance: The classic Middle English statement of the virginity ideal, and a prime exhibit of the period's energetic anti-matrimonial rhetoric (the counterpart of the Wife of Bath's prologue).
works.meter: Rhythmical, heavily alliterative prose of the AB language group.
works.context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands, in the circle of Ancrene Wisse; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34 and BL Cotton MS Titus D.xviii.
works.characters: the virgin reader (addressee); Christ as bridegroom
works.structure: A single sustained exhortation moving from praise of virginity through satiric anatomy of marriage to the rewards of the heavenly marriage.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Hamlet
altTitles: The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of revenge and consciousness: the ghost of Hamlet's father charges him to avenge his murder by Claudius, who now wears the crown and the queen; Hamlet's feigned madness, the play-within-the-play ('The Mousetrap'), the deaths of Polonius and Ophelia, and the final duel — poisoned rapier and cup — in which the stage is cleared of the whole royal house.
works.plot: Hamlet tests the ghost's word by staging a murder-play before the king; Claudius's guilt is exposed; Hamlet spares the praying king, kills Polonius, is sent to England with a death warrant he reverses; Ophelia drowns; Laertes returns for revenge; and the poisoned duel at Elsinore kills Gertrude, Laertes, Claudius, and Hamlet himself, with Fortinbras inheriting Denmark.
works.significance: The most famous play ever written — the tragedy of modern consciousness itself, and the summit of the English language's claim on world literature.
works.meter: The widest range in Shakespeare — soliloquy, prose, song, the Player's speech, the graveyard quibbles — with 'To be or not to be' at its centre.
works.context: Written about 1600–01 in the wake of the lost ur-Hamlet and of the death of Shakespeare's son Hamnet; the three texts (Q1 1603, Q2 1604–05, F 1623) present the classic problem of Shakespearean textual scholarship.
works.characters: Hamlet; Claudius; Gertrude; the Ghost; Polonius; Ophelia; Laertes; Horatio; Rosencrantz; Guildenstern; Fortinbras; Osric; the First Gravedigger
works.structure: A five-act revenge tragedy infinitely deferred and interiorized — soliloquies, plays, and feigned madness displacing action — until the catastrophe of Act 5.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the relationship of the three early texts remains the central problem of its bibliography.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition
Hamlet (Arden Shakespeare, 3rd series)

works.title: Handlyng Synne
works.description: Robert Mannyng of Brunne's English verse adaptation (begun 1303) of the Anglo-Norman Manuel des péchés of William of Wadington: a manual of penance in some 12,000 lines expounding the commandments, the deadly sins, the sacraments, and the art of confession, illustrated with scores of exemplary tales. It is the classic Middle English penitential handbook.
works.plot: The poem moves systematically through the commandments and sins, each doctrine illustrated by cautionary exempla — the dancing carolers cursed by a priest, the usurer, the witch of Ely — and concludes with instruction on confession, contrition, and satisfaction.
works.significance: The principal English treatment of penance between the thirteenth-century homilies and Chaucer's Parson's Tale (which draws on related material), and a treasury of the exemplum tradition.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of plain, efficient didactic verse in the Lincolnshire dialect.
works.context: Begun in 1303 by the Gilbertine canon Robert Mannyng at Sempringham Priory, Lincolnshire, translating Wadington's manual for an English lay audience; preserved in the Vernon and Bodleian Digby manuscripts among others.
works.characters: the exemplary sinners and saints of the tales
works.structure: A didactic sequence organized by commandment, sin, and sacrament, with narrative exempla inset throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed by the author's own preface to 'Robert of Brunne'.

works.title: Havelok the Dane
altTitles: The Lay of Havelok the Dane
works.description: A Lincolnshire romance of some 3,000 lines on the dispossessed prince Havelok, brought up as a kitchen-boy at Grimsby, whose royal birthmark, strength, and marriage to the princess Goldeboru lead to the recovery of the thrones of Denmark and England. Its sympathetic depiction of labouring life and its Lincolnshire topography make it unique among the romances.
works.plot: The orphaned Havelok is saved from the usurper Godard by the fisherman Grim, who flees with him to England; in disguise he serves as a kitchen hand at Lincoln, where the usurper Godrich marries the princess Goldeboru to him in mockery; Havelok's revealed royalty, his defeat of the usurpers, and his double coronation conclude the poem.
works.significance: One of the finest English romances: its realism about work and poverty, and its fusion of folk-tale, dynastic, and hagiographical elements, make it a classic of the genre.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with marked northern (East Midland/Lincolnshire) dialect features.
works.context: Composed c. 1280–90 in Lincolnshire, drawing on local legend (Grimsby's foundation) and Anglo-Norman sources (Lai d'Haveloc, Gaimar); preserved uniquely in Bodleian Library, Laud Misc. 108.
works.characters: Havelok; Goldeboru; Grim the fisherman; Godard; Godrich; Ubbe
works.structure: A double exile-and-restoration plot (Havelok and Goldeboru in parallel), with an interpolated miracle episode and a long climactic battle.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

editions.title: Havelok

works.title: Henrietta
works.form: novel; domestic and moral prose fiction
works.description: A novel of a portionless young woman, a poor relation in a great house, whose virtue is tried by presumption, by a fraudulent seduction and by the world's readiness to believe the worst of a woman alone. It is darker and more analytical than the author's earlier fiction and much concerned with the opinion of the world as a tribunal.
works.plot: Henrietta, dependent on relations of consequence, is pursued by a man of fortune who offers protection rather than marriage, and later by one whose design is outright seduction. She defends herself with spirit, is compromised in appearance, and must bear the verdict of society while the men who injured her are spared. Her constancy and the exposure of her persecutors prepare a marriage on equal terms, the narrative arguing that a woman's reputation is a social construction.
works.significance: It is one of the most acute mid-century analyses of the sexual double standard in fiction and a key text in the development of the novel of the unprotected woman.
works.meter: An argentine prose of reflection and reported conversation, with the narrator's essays on female dependency interrupting the narrative.
works.context: Published in 1758, in the decade of the mid-century novel's turn to the analysis of reputation and dependency, and after the author's critical work on the drama had fixed her place in letters.
works.characters: Henrietta; her protectress and the great family; the two pursuers, one coarse and one designing; the suitor who finally offers equality
works.structure: Third-person narration in two volumes with a strong current of moral essay; the plot turns on the difference between Henrietta's conduct and the world's report of it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Henry IV, Part 1
altTitles: The First Part of Henry the Fourth
works.description: The first play of the Henriad proper: Prince Hal's education between the tavern of Falstaff and the field of Shrewsbury, where he kills the rebel Hotspur and redeems his reputation — the comedy of Eastcheap and the tragedy of the Percys joined in the greatest of the English history plays.
works.plot: Hotspur and the Percys rebel against the king they helped make; Hal plays truant with Falstaff until the crisis calls him to arms; at Shrewsbury he saves his father, kills Hotspur, and leaves Falstaff to counterfeit death and claim the honour — a claim the prince allows, 'for my part, if a lie may do thee grace, I'll gild it with the happiest terms I have'.
works.significance: Contains Shakespeare's greatest comic creation in Falstaff, and his profoundest study of a prince's education in power.
works.meter: The fullest range of Shakespeare's early style: Hotspur's verse, Falstaff's prose, Hal's movement between them, and Glendower's Welsh lyricism.
works.context: Written about 1596–97 from Holinshed and the anonymous Famous Victories of Henry V; Oldcastle's name was changed to Falstaff after protest from the Cobham family.
works.characters: Prince Hal (Henry, Prince of Wales); Sir John Falstaff; King Henry IV; Hotspur (Henry Percy); the Earl of Worcester; the Earl of Northumberland; Owen Glendower; the Earl of Douglas; Poins; Bardolph; Mistress Quickly; Lady Percy
works.structure: A double plot of court/camp and tavern braided by Hal's movement between the two worlds, with the Gadshill robbery as hinge and the battle as convergence.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Henry IV, Part 2
altTitles: The Second Part of Henry the Fourth
works.description: The darker sequel: rebellion flickers out at Gaultree Forest, the king sickens under the weight of his usurped crown, Falstaff conscripts the rag-tag army of Gloucestershire and runs up his tavern score, and the play ends with the new king's public rejection of his old companion — 'I know thee not, old man' — and Falstaff's ruin.
works.plot: Northumberland's rebellion collapses; Prince John tricks the rebels into disbanding; the dying king and Hal are reconciled; Henry V's coronation is followed by the rejection of Falstaff and the justice's promise of the new reign.
works.significance: The most sombre of the histories — a study of the costs of power whose rejection scene is among the most painful in the canon.
works.meter: Prose dominates the Falstaff scenes and verse the court; the play's elegiac music belongs to its age and sickness.
works.context: Written about 1597–98; its Epilogue promises the further adventures of Falstaff, fulfilled instead in The Merry Wives of Windsor.
works.characters: Prince Hal; Sir John Falstaff; King Henry IV; the Lord Chief Justice; Prince John of Lancaster; the Earl of Northumberland; the Archbishop of York; Justice Shallow; Justice Silence; Pistol; Doll Tearsheet; Mistress Quickly; Bardolph; Poins; Lady Percy
works.structure: A chronicle of endings — of rebellion, of reign, of friendship — built on scenes of age, disease, and memory, with the Gloucestershire justices and the tavern as the comic underworld.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Henry V
altTitles: The Life of Henry the Fifth
works.description: The climax of the second tetralogy: the Chorus's apology for the 'wooden O' frames the epic of Agincourt — Henry's claim to France, the traitors at Southampton, Harfleur's breach, the night before battle, and the victory of the 'band of brothers' — followed by the comic peace of the wooing of Katherine.
works.plot: Henry, urged by the church and provoked by the Dauphin's tennis balls, invades France; the campaign moves through Harfleur to Agincourt, where the outnumbered English win; the play closes with the treaty of Troyes and the king's rough wooing of the French princess.
works.significance: The national epic of the English stage — and, in its ambivalences, the most debated of the histories in every age of war.
works.meter: The great set speeches — 'Once more unto the breach', the Crispin's Day oration — in verse, against the prose of the soldiers and the dialect comedy of the captains.
works.context: Written 1599, the year of the Globe and of Essex's Irish expedition (to which the Chorus looks forward); the play made Agincourt the founding myth of English arms.
works.characters: King Henry V; the Chorus; the Duke of Exeter; Fluellen; Pistol; Bardolph; Nym; Mistress Quickly; the Dauphin; the Constable of France; Katherine; Princess of France; Alice; Montjoy; Williams; the King of France
works.structure: A choric five-act epic, each act introduced by the Chorus, alternating the high rhetoric of war with the low comedy of the tavern remnants (Bardolph, Pistol, Fluellen) and ending in the romance of the wooing scene.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Henry VI, Part 1
altTitles: The First Part of Henry the Sixth
works.description: The first play of Shakespeare's earliest tetralogy, probably written in collaboration: the loss of France, the rise and burning of Joan la Pucelle (Joan of Arc), the quarrels of Gloucester and Winchester, and the white rose and the red plucked in the Temple Garden that plant the Wars of the Roses.
works.plot: Henry V's funeral opens the play; the French recover their towns through Joan's victories; Talbot, the English Achilles, dies at Bordeaux; the factions of York and Lancaster form in England; and the play ends with Suffolk's capture of Margaret of Anjou as Henry's bride — and his own instrument.
works.significance: The foundation of the English history-play cycle, and the apprenticeship of its greatest master.
works.meter: Early blank verse, often stiff and end-stopped, with the play's documentary sweep compensating for its poetic unevenness.
works.context: The Talbot scenes were celebrated by Nashe in 1592; the play is the first in the sequence that runs through Richard III.
works.characters: King Henry VI; Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester; the Bishop of Winchester; Richard, Duke of York; the Earl of Warwick; Talbot; Joan la Pucelle; Charles the Dauphin; the Duke of Suffolk; Margaret of Anjou; Edmund Mortimer
works.structure: An episodic chronicle alternating English and French scenes, unified by Talbot's tragedy and the growth of the court factions.
works.attributionNotes: Generally regarded as collaborative (the shares of Nashe and others are debated); assigned to Shakespeare by the Folio.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Henry VI, Part 2
altTitles: The First Part of the Contention
The Contention of the Two Famous Houses of York and Lancaster
works.description: The second play of the tetralogy: the fall of Duke Humphrey of Gloucester, the rebellion of Jack Cade, and the rise of Richard, Duke of York, through the disintegration of Henry VI's England toward the first battle of St Albans.
works.plot: The court faction destroys Gloucester; York exploits the Cade rebellion to test his claim; the play's great set pieces — Gloucester's murder, the miracle at St Albans, Cade's insurrection — carry England from anarchy to open war, with Margaret and Suffolk's fall along the way.
works.significance: The first English play to put the whole commonwealth — commons, court, and crown — on stage together.
works.meter: Blank verse growing more assured, with the prose of the Cade scenes as the first great crowd-comedy in English drama.
works.context: The Cade rebellion scenes dramatize the 1450 rising through Elizabethan anxieties about the commons; printed in 1594 as The First Part of the Contention.
works.characters: King Henry VI; Queen Margaret; Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester; Eleanor Cobham; the Duke of Suffolk; the Duke of York; Jack Cade; the Earl of Warwick; the Cardinal (Beaufort); Lord Say; Dick the butcher
works.structure: A chronicle of successive falls (Gloucester, Suffolk, Cade) leading to York's armed claim, in the de casibus pattern of the Mirror for Magistrates.
works.attributionNotes: Possibly collaborative with Marlowe or Nashe in debated shares; the Folio canon is followed here.

editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Henry VI, Part 3
altTitles: The True Tragedy of Richard Duke of York
works.description: The third play of the tetralogy: the Wars of the Roses in full blood — York's death on the molehill at Wakefield, Margaret's taunting of him with the paper crown, the slaughter of young Rutland, and the rise of Richard of Gloucester through the battles of Towton, Barnet, and Tewkesbury to his soliloquized ambitions at the play's end.
works.plot: York breaks his oath and claims the crown; the wars swing between Lancaster and York; Edward IV wins the throne and marries Elizabeth Woodville; Warwick changes sides and dies at Barnet; and Richard murders Henry VI in the Tower, then turns to the audience to announce his design on the crown.
works.significance: The bridge from the Henry VI plays to Richard III — and the first sketch of Shakespeare's greatest villain.
works.meter: Blank verse of mounting power, culminating in Richard's first great soliloquy.
works.context: Written about 1590–91, the play's cycles of revenge answered the Senecan fashion while its national matter spoke to the post-Armada moment.
works.characters: King Henry VI; Queen Margaret; Richard, Duke of York; Edward IV; George, Duke of Clarence; Richard, Duke of Gloucester; the Earl of Warwick; Lady Grey (Elizabeth Woodville); the Duke of Exeter; Rutland; Clifford
works.structure: A rapid battle-chronicle built on reversals of fortune, with Richard's emergence as the play's climactic revelation.
works.attributionNotes: Possibly collaborative in debated shares; the Folio canon is followed here.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Henry VIII
altTitles: The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eighth
works.description: The last of the history plays, written with John Fletcher: the pageant-like fall of Buckingham, the trial and divorce of Katherine of Aragon, the rise of Anne Bullen and of Cranmer, and the christening of the infant Elizabeth — ending in Cranmer's prophecy of the golden age to come under the 'maiden phoenix'.
works.plot: Buckingham falls to Wolsey's faction; the king's conscience turns against his marriage; Katherine defends herself at the legatine trial; Wolsey's fall follows; Anne is crowned and Elizabeth christened, with Cranmer's prophetic blessing on the new reign.
works.significance: The Stuart court's official version of the Reformation, and the last flowering of the history play Shakespeare had invented.
works.meter: Verse of late-Shakespearean looseness with Fletcherian run-on lines; the trial scene of Katherine is its moral and poetic summit.
works.context: First performed 29 June 1613 at the Globe, when the firing of the chambers set the theatre alight and burned it down — the play's alternate title, All Is True, is the one recorded at that performance.
works.characters: King Henry VIII; Cardinal Wolsey; Queen Katherine of Aragon; Anne Bullen; the Duke of Buckingham; Thomas Cranmer; the Duke of Norfolk; the Duke of Suffolk; Gardiner; Cromwell; the Old Lady
works.structure: A series of state show-scenes — trials, coronations, christenings — in the masque-like mode of late Jacobean spectacle, structured as successive falls and risings.
works.attributionNotes: Collaboration with John Fletcher established by stylistic and metrical evidence; the Folio assigns the play to Shakespeare alone.
