works.title: Lacnunga
works.form: medical manual and charm collection (Old English prose and verse)
works.description: A less orderly but more eclectic collection of remedies, charms, and prayers than Bald's Leechbook, compiled in the early eleventh century. It is best known for preserving the pagan-tinged metrical charms — above all the Nine Herbs Charm — alongside Christian prayers and learned Latin-derived recipes.
works.plot: The collection gathers remedies for wounds, fevers, eye and ear complaints, and childbirth, mixing herbal preparations with spoken charms and ritual instructions; its metrical charms invoke Woden and the herbs' powers while concluding with Christian formulas, in a characteristic fusion of traditions.
works.significance: The richest source of Old English charms, including the great Nine Herbs Charm, and a unique window onto the interface of learned medicine, popular healing, and pagan survival in late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.meter: The embedded charms are in alliterative verse (the Nine Herbs Charm, the Journey Charm); the surrounding recipes are plain instructional prose.
works.context: The manuscript belongs to the late Old English period's flourishing of vernacular medicine, when remedies circulated in monastic and lay households; the charms preserve elements of Germanic pre-Christian ritual under a Christian surface, a central document of the 'Christian-pagan synthesis'.
works.structure: A compilation in no strict order, grouping remedies by source rather than ailment; the metrical charms stand out from the surrounding prose as the collection's literary high points.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous compilation; the name 'Lacnunga' ('Remedies') is editorial, from the first remedy's heading.

editions.title: Anglo-Saxon Remedies, Charms, and Prayers from British Library MS Harley 585: The Lacnunga

works.title: Lament for the Makaris
works.description: William Dunbar's elegy on the poets ('makaris') of Scotland and the world (c. 1505, 100 lines): a procession of the dead — Chaucer, Lydgate, Gower, Henryson, and the court poets of the Stewart kings — each stanza closed by the refrain 'Timor mortis conturbat me' (the fear of death troubles me). The greatest short elegy of the Scottish tradition, and the poem that gave the makars their name.
works.plot: The poet, reflecting that all things must die, calls the roll of the dead poets: first the great English trio of Chaucer, Gower, and Lydgate, then the Scottish makers — Barbour, Hary, Holland, and above all 'the noble rhetor' Henryson — and finally the court poets of his own youth, closing with the fear of death and the petition that God provide for the poet before he joins them.
works.significance: One of the great elegies in the language: its roll-call fixed the canon of the makars and its refrain became the proverbial voice of late medieval mortality.
works.meter: Four-line stanzas with the Latin refrain, austere and musical.
works.context: Composed c. 1505 at the court of James IV, when Dunbar's generation was passing and the print era beginning; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508); it names the Scottish tradition 'makaris' for all later criticism.
works.characters: Dunbar (speaker); the dead poets (Chaucer, Gower, Lydgate, Barbour, Hary, Henryson, and others)
works.structure: Twenty-five stanzas of single-movement elegy, the refrain tolling each catalogue entry, in the ubi sunt tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Dunbar's authorship secure.

editions.title: The Poems of William Dunbar

works.title: Lancelot of the Laik
works.description: A Scottish romance of some 3,500 lines adapting the French prose Lancelot: Arthur's war with Galiot, Lancelot's secret love for Guinevere, and the dream-vision in which the lover's conscience anatomizes his state. The only Scottish Arthurian romance, composed in the age of the makars for a court that read both Chaucer and the French cycles.
works.plot: Arthur, weakened by tyranny and war with the rebel Galiot, is saved by Lancelot, who fights incognito and compels Galiot's submission; the second half turns inward, as a dream allegory of love's joys and pains lays bare Lancelot's adulterous devotion to the queen.
works.significance: The sole Scottish Arthurian romance and a significant witness to the reception of French Arthurian prose in the Stewart court.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in Older Scots, with aureate ornament.
works.context: Composed c. 1460–79 in Scotland, adapting the French prose Lancelot and the amatory allegory tradition; preserved uniquely in Cambridge University Library MS Kk.1.5 (c. 1500).
works.characters: Lancelot; Arthur; Guinevere; Galiot
works.structure: A two-part structure — chivalric war, then amatory dream vision — that joins the French romance of arms to the Chaucerian allegory of love.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Laterculus Malalianus
altTitles: The Laterculus Malalianus of Theodore of Tarsus
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 139 (twelfth century)
works.description: A Latin exegetical and chronographical treatise on the life of Christ, attributed to Theodore of Tarsus, archbishop of Canterbury, and written at Canterbury in the 670s. Based on the Greek chronography of John Malalas, it expounds the gospel account of Christ's life in the light of eastern exegesis and computes the ages of the world; it is the principal surviving witness to the school of Theodore.
works.plot: The treatise moves through the life of Christ from the Incarnation to the Passion, glossing each episode with eastern exegetical traditions (on the Virgin, the baptism, the temptations, the crucifixion) and interweaving chronographical calculations of the world's ages drawn from Malalas's chronicle, concluding with eschatological reflection on the last things.
works.significance: The earliest theological work composed in England, and the founding document of the Canterbury school that made England a centre of Greek-influenced Latin learning; a unique witness to the eastern roots of Anglo-Saxon exegesis.
works.context: Written when Theodore and Hadrian were building the school of Canterbury, the treatise shows the direct importation of Greek and Syriac learning into England; the same exegetical traditions appear in the Canterbury biblical commentaries preserved in Milan, and Theodore's pupils carried them into the Northumbrian Renaissance of Bede.
works.structure: A continuous exegetical treatise organized by the gospel narrative, with digressions into chronology and typology; the style is dense and allusive, marked by the Greek learning of its source.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Theodore of Tarsus on the basis of its Greek sources, its Canterbury origin, and its consistent transmission with Theodore's school texts; the attribution is widely accepted but rests on inference rather than explicit ascription.

works.title: Layamon's Brut
works.description: Layamon's verse chronicle of Britain, some 16,000 lines adapting Wace's Roman de Brut with additions from Welsh and English tradition, from the Trojan Brutus to the Saxon conquest, including the fullest early English account of King Arthur. It is the first major treatment of the Arthurian legend in English.
works.plot: Following the Trojan Brutus's settlement of Britain, the poem recounts the line of British kings — Lear, Cymbeline, and above all Arthur, whose conquests, Round Table, and death it narrates at length — down to the Saxon victory and Arthur's prophesied return.
works.significance: The first Arthurian epic in English and the bridge from the alliterative tradition to Middle English romance; its Arthur material influenced the entire subsequent Arthurian tradition in England.
works.meter: A hybrid line blending the native alliterative half-line with loose rhyme and French-derived couplets; formulaic and archaic diction.
works.context: Composed by the priest Layamon of Areley Kings, Worcestershire, c. 1190–1215, in the generation after the loss of Normandy, when English was re-emerging as a literary language; preserved in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ix (earlier, longer) and Cotton MS Otho C.xiii (later, shortened, fire-damaged).
works.characters: Brutus; King Lear; Arthur; Guinevere; Merlin; Vortigern; Hengest; Cadwalader
works.structure: A continuous regnal chronicle organized by successive kings, with Arthur as its structural and emotional centre.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship secured by the prologue's self-naming of Layamon, priest of Ernleye (Areley Kings).

editions.title: Layamon's Brut, or Hystoria Brutonum
editions.editor: W. R. J. Barron and S. C. Weinberg (eds.)

works.title: Le Morte Darthur
altTitles: The Whole Book of King Arthur and of His Noble Knights of the Round Table
works.description: Sir Thomas Malory's great prose compilation of the Arthurian legend, completed in prison in 1469–70 and printed by Caxton in 1485: from the sword in the stone and the winning of Guinevere, through the adventures of Lancelot, Tristram, and the Grail quest, to the breaking of the Round Table, the last battle, and Arthur's passing to Avalon. The definitive English Arthurian book.
works.plot: Malory weaves the French prose cycles and English alliterative poems into a single tragic narrative: Arthur's accession and marriage, the founding of the Round Table, the quests and loves of its knights, the Grail quest that divides the fellowship, the adultery of Lancelot and Guinevere, and the final war against Mordred in which Arthur falls — his body borne to Avalon, his epitaph 'Rex quondam Rexque futurus'.
works.significance: The summit of English Arthurian literature and the conduit of the Arthurian story to Spenser, Tennyson, and the modern novel; its vision of chivalry — at once idealized and doomed — is the period's most enduring legacy.
works.meter: Prose: paratactic, ritual, and rhythmic, with the famous Malorian cadence of balanced clauses and repeated key words.
works.context: Completed by the 'knight prisoner' Thomas Malory in the ninth year of Edward IV (1469–70), during the Wars of the Roses; Caxton's 1485 print fixed the text for three centuries until the discovery of the Winchester manuscript (1934) revealed the pre-print version.
works.characters: Arthur; Lancelot; Guinevere; Gawain; Tristram; Isolde; Galahad; Merlin; Morgan le Fay; Mordred
works.structure: Eight books (Caxton's twenty-one divisions) of interlaced adventure compressed into linear narrative, with the Grail and the Lancelot-Guinevere tragedy as the arcs that break the fellowship.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Sir Thomas Malory of Newbold Revel (d. 1471) on the evidence of the colophons; the identification is widely though not universally accepted.

editions.title: The Works of Sir Thomas Malory
editions.editor: Eugène Vinaver (ed.); rev. P. J. C. Field

works.title: Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres
works.form: critical treatise and professorial textbook, with anthologised extracts and commentaries
works.description: The published substance of Blair's professorial course at Edinburgh, the first institutional chair of rhetoric and belles lettres in Britain, and the most influential textbook of taste and composition of its generation. It joins a theory of taste, a history of the styles of writing and an analysis of the genres - epic, tragedy, ode, satire, the periodical essay - with precepts on pronunciation and elocution. For half a century it was the standard manual of literary judgment in Britain and America.
works.plot: The lectures begin with the principles of taste and with the sublime and the beautiful, proceed through the historical stages of literature and the study of the ancient and modern writers, and then examine the species of composition in prose and verse, the passions, the figures, the kinds of style and the rules of delivery. Blair argues that taste is founded on common sense and on the sympathy of mankind, that genius must be disciplined by rule and by the ancients, and that the criticism of a work must consult the sentiments and the manners of its own age.
works.significance: It codified the century's criticism of taste, sublimity and genre into a teachable system and became the grammar of literary judgment for the nineteenth century, for readers and for institutions on both sides of the Atlantic. Its treatment of primitive and national poetry, of the sublime and of elocution also makes it an index to the movements of taste that produced the graveyard and the ballad revivals.
works.meter: Prose; clear, temperate and exemplary, written to be a model of the styles it prescribes, with the illustrative extracts supplying the metrical variety.
works.context: Delivered after Blair's appointment to the new Edinburgh chair and published in 1783, in the full tide of the Scottish Enlightenment's analysis of taste, sympathy and the progress of the arts, and in the same years as the vogue of the fine arts and of the history of literature. Its use in universities and academies made it a vehicle of the period's educational programme.
works.structure: A course of lectures in three broad parts - the principles of taste and the history of literature, the species of composition with illustrative extracts and remarks, and elocution and delivery - each number a self-contained lesson with examples.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the lectures are those of Blair's course at Edinburgh, and the printed edition was prepared by him from the matter used in teaching, with several later editions revised.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Legends of Holy Women
works.description: Osbern Bokenham's collection of thirteen verse lives of female saints, written 1443–47 at the request of a circle of East Anglian patrons, several of them women: Margaret, Anne, Christine, the Eleven Thousand Virgins, Faith, Agnes, Dorothy, Mary Magdalene, Katherine, Cecilia, Agatha, Lucy, and Elizabeth of Hungary. The major fifteenth-century English legendary of women's sanctity.
works.plot: Each life narrates the saint's birth, conversion, and martyrdom (or holy death), with the debates, torments, and miracles of the genre; the framing prologues record the patrons who commissioned each legend, making the work a document of literary patronage as much as of hagiography.
works.significance: The principal fifteenth-century English collection of female saints' lives and a uniquely documented instance of women's literary patronage in the period.
works.meter: Couplets and rhyme royal in the Lydgatean style, aureate but warm.
works.context: Composed 1443–47 by the Augustinian friar Osbern Bokenham of Stoke by Clare, Suffolk, for Lady Katherine Denston, Isabel Hunt, and other East Anglian gentry women; preserved in BL Arundel MS 327 (the author's own manuscript).
works.characters: St Margaret; St Anne; St Katherine; St Mary Magdalene; St Cecilia; and the other saints; Bokenham (narrator)
works.structure: A sequence of independent verse legends, each with its own prologue naming the patron, in the Chaucerian-Lydgatean manner.
works.attributionNotes: Bokenham's authorship secure; he names himself and his patrons throughout.

works.title: Lessons for Children
works.form: children's educational prose and verse, in the graduated reading-lesson tradition
works.description: Barbauld's elementary books for the very young, begun in 1778 and issued in graduated classes, the first widely successful example in English of a reading course calculated for the mind of a child. The lessons move from single words and short dialogues about the household, the animals and the weather to longer narrative and moral pieces as the child's capacity grows. Their method of steady progression, of the familiar object and of the question-and-answer dialogue made them the model of children's teaching books for a century.
works.plot: The earliest classes consist of short exchanges about things within a child's reach, naming, seeing and doing, and pass by easy steps to little stories and to the plainest duties of kindness, truthfulness and attention. Later classes introduce narrative, fable and reflection, still pitched to the child's experience and governed by the principle that instruction should follow the interests of the learner. The whole proceeds on the conviction that the mind of a child is to be led, not driven, and that pleasure is the proper engine of learning.
works.significance: It is the founding text of English literature written for the nursery and the direct ancestor of the progressive reading series, and it changed expectations of what a child could be given to read. Its doctrine of instruction through pleasure and familiar objects became orthodoxy in elementary education and in children's writing.
works.meter: Plain short sentences and dialogue in the earliest classes, with simple rhymed and rhythmic pieces introduced as the series proceeds.
works.context: Written in the train of Locke's thinking on education and of the new interest in the education of infancy, and in the practical context of Barbauld's own teaching circle and of the nonconformist academies; the books belong to the 1770s revolution in the literature made for children, which treated the child as a reader with rights of its own.
works.characters: The child addressed; the instructing voice of the book; the household and animal figures of the dialogues
works.structure: A graded series of short lessons in several classes or parts, each rising in difficulty, arranged for sequential use rather than as a continuous story.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the classes appeared successively from 1778 and the dates of the several parts differ, so the composition start is left null with the series described in the note.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Letter to the Earl of Chesterfield
altTitles: Letter to the Right Honourable Philip Stanhope, Earl of Chesterfield, 7 February 1755
works.form: familiar letter in the state paper manner; epistolary prose of the Augustan school
works.description: The brief reply that closed Johnson's nine years of expectation of patronage, sent days before the publication of the Dictionary after Chesterfield had revived his acquaintance at its approach. Its courteous refusal - that favour is unwelcome when it comes 'delayed till I am indifferent, and cannot enjoy it; till I am obstinate, and cannot repay it' - is the most celebrated letter in English literary history and the classic statement of the independent professional writer. It was copied, circulated and printed soon after and became part of the lore of letters.
works.plot: Johnson recounts how he first approached Chesterfield nine years earlier, was repulsed, and nonetheless worked on without help; he observes that the Earl has now thought it convenient to remember him, and declines the favour on the ground that it comes too late to be welcome. He insists that he has needed no patron and will owe no obligations he cannot repay, and closes with a wish for the Earl's happiness that is decorously but unmistakably cold. The argument is not a personal quarrel but a claim about the dignity and self-sufficiency of learned labour.
works.significance: The letter fixed the image of authorship against patronage for the next century and supplied the standard anecdote of Johnson's independence. It is a touchstone for the history of the literary marketplace, and its rhetoric has been read as the perfect example of the period's controlled, judicial prose.
works.meter: Prose, balanced and judicial in cadence, moving from ironic gratitude to the famous refusal that favour arrives 'delayed till I am indifferent, and cannot enjoy it; till I am obstinate, and cannot repay it', and ending with a decorately cold wish for the Earl's happiness.
works.context: Written in the week before the Dictionary was issued, when the subscription and copyright economy of bookselling had already made the old aristocratic patronage relation embarrassing to both parties; Chesterfield's own letters to his son had publicly recommended a very different model of literary dependence.
works.characters: Samuel Johnson; Philip Stanhope, Earl of Chesterfield
works.structure: A single brief formal letter of a few short paragraphs, ordered chronologically through the history of the acquaintance and rhetorically from courtesy to refusal to the closing wish.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the letter is documented by Johnson's holograph copies and by early print, though no holograph of the final version survives.

works.title: Letters from Dorothy Osborne to Sir William Temple
works.description: The seventy-seven surviving letters written by Dorothy Osborne to William Temple during their long courtship in 1652-4, in which she discusses her family's opposition to the match, the books she is reading, and the state of the country under the Commonwealth.
works.plot: The letters trace the progress of the courtship against Osborne's brother's opposition and her own reluctance; they range freely over literature, gossip, politics, and the difficulty of a woman's position.
works.significance: The finest English letters of the seventeenth century and a crucial document of women's writing; their spontaneous style was admired by Virginia Woolf and they are the standard by which later familiar letters are judged.
works.meter: An easy, natural, unselfconscious prose that is the earliest great example of familiar English letter-writing.
works.context: Written 1652-4, during the Commonwealth, when Osborne was confined at Chicksands and Temple was travelling; they married in 1654.
works.characters: Dorothy Osborne; Sir William Temple; Sir Peter Osborne; Osborne's brother Henry
works.structure: A sequence of letters over about two years, with gaps.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Osborne; the manuscripts were printed in 1847 from the family papers (first partly published in 1713).

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Letters on the Improvement of the Mind
altTitles: Letters on the Improvement of the Mind, Particularly with Regard to the Conduct of the Life
Letters on the Improvement of the Mind
works.form: conduct and educational letters; familiar essay in epistolary form
works.description: A series of letters of instruction to a young woman, on the government of the temper, the use of learning, the choice of company, religion and the conduct of the common day. It became one of the most widely read of the century's female conduct books and passed through many editions.
works.plot: The correspondent is guided through the duties of the mind, the culture of the understanding, the discipline of the passions and the ordering of time and fortune. Learning is recommended for judgement rather than for show, and the dangers of sensibility, of company and of expense are weighed with practical counsel. The later letters turn to religion, to the conduct of the understanding in divine matters and to the duties of the active life.
works.significance: It is a central text of the practical education of women in the later eighteenth century and a document of the Bluestocking argument that improvement of the mind and conduct of the life are one subject.
works.meter: A clear, warm and unrhetorical epistolary prose of the middle style, with the balanced sentence of moral advice and the occasional quotation of the poets.
works.context: Published in 1773 from the circle of the Bluestocking correspondents, whose letters on female education and taste had prepared the public for such a work, and in the season of the new attention to the academies and to women's rational improvement.
works.structure: A serial of familiar letters on connected heads, the sequence moving from the culture of the mind to the conduct of the life and to religion; each letter closes with a practical direction.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after the circulation of the letters among friends.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Letters to Serena
altTitles: Letters to Serena, Occasioned in a Stay in France
works.description: Toland's Spinozist-tinged philosophical letters, written during and after a stay in France, which develop a necessitarian, materialist account of mind, matter, and the eternity of the species. The letters to his correspondent Serena are prefixed by a discourse on the eastern philosophy arguing that European learning derived from the East.
works.plot: The prefatory discourse maintains that philosophy migrated east-to-west and that the Greeks learned from barbarian sages, demoting the miracle of Greek originality. The letters then argue that motion is essential to matter, so that an immaterial, unmoved mover is unintelligible; thought likewise arises in organized matter, and the mind is not a separable substance. From this Toland draws the eternity of the universe and of the species of creatures, against creation out of nothing and against the doctrine of a naturally mortal soul, reading Genesis as a natural history of this world only. Personal immortality is dissolved into the perpetuity of nature, and religion is reinterpreted as the homage of a mind that contemplates the whole.
works.significance: It introduced a Spinozist necessitarianism into English philosophical letters and became a standard citation in the pantheist scares of the century; its eastern-philosophy thesis early globalized the history of ideas.
works.meter: Supple epistolary prose, argumentative but conversational, with long distinctions worked out through examples and retorts.
works.context: Written after Toland's 1707-08 continental visit, where he studied the reception of Spinoza on the continent, and published amid the post-Clarke debates on the soul and on the sufficiency of reason.
works.characters: Serena (the addressee); the writer
works.structure: A sequence of familiar letters on connected philosophical topics, framed by a prefatory historical discourse.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Leviathan; or, The Matter, Forme, and Power of a Common-Wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civill
works.description: Hobbes's masterwork of political philosophy, in which the commonwealth is conceived as an artificial man whose soul is sovereignty, founded on a covenant by which individuals transfer their right of self-government to an absolute sovereign.
works.plot: Part I ('Of Man') sets out Hobbes's materialist psychology and his state of nature, in which life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'; part II ('Of Common-Wealth') derives the sovereign's absolute authority from the social contract; part III ('Of a Christian Common-Wealth') subordinates the church to the state; part IV ('Of the Kingdom of Darkness') attacks scholastic and papal claims.
works.significance: The foundational text of modern political philosophy and of social contract theory; it transformed the vocabulary of politics, founded the modern theory of sovereignty, and provoked responses from Locke, Rousseau, and every subsequent theorist of the state.
works.meter: A powerful, lucid English prose deliberately free of rhetorical ornament; Hobbes's style became a model of the plain philosophical sentence.
works.context: Composed in Paris during Hobbes's exile and published in London in 1651, two years after the execution of Charles I; it was condemned by royalists and by Presbyterians alike and was later attacked in Parliament as an encouragement to atheism.
works.structure: Four parts in 47 numbered chapters, with the famous engraved frontispiece of the giant sovereign composed of his subjects.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Hobbes; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Liberty
altTitles: Liberty, a Poem, in Three Parts
works.description: Thomson's didactic poem on civil and moral liberty, in three parts: the ancient and modern history of free states, the constitution of Britain, and the relation of liberty to the arts, commerce and the sentiments of the individual.
works.plot: The poet invokes Liberty and traces her causes and effects in commonwealths and in the British constitution, argues that trade and independence are the guardians of the state, and passes in the last part to the culture of the mind, the fine arts and the virtue which alone can preserve a free people.
works.significance: It is the century's most ambitious attempt to make the history of free government the subject of a serious didactic poem, and it supplied the vocabulary of liberty later used by the American and the British radical traditions.
works.meter: Blank verse of the seasonal manner, more declamatory and more sententious than the descriptive poems, with the apostrophic invocation.
works.context: Published in the years of the patriot-Whig opposition to the Walpole administration, when the country language of liberty, independent property and the standing army was being renewed in poetry and in the journals.
works.characters: the goddess Liberty invoked; the patriot and the statesman; the free commonwealths of the example
works.structure: Three separately issued parts, each an argument of history, reflection and apostrophe, with the inserted episodes of the Swiss and Dutch deliverers and of the patriot.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Life of King Alfred
works.description: Asser's biography of King Alfred, written in 893 by the Welsh bishop of Sherborne: the principal contemporary portrait of the king — his childhood, illnesses, wars against the Vikings, piety, and program of learning — and the main source for the Alfredian Renaissance.
works.plot: The life follows Alfred from birth (849) through his education and accession (871), the Viking wars culminating in Edington (878) and the treaty with Guthrum, the rebuilding of London and the kingdom's defences, and the gathering of scholars — Werferth, Plegmund, Æthelstan, Grimbald, John the Old Saxon — for the translation program; an annalistic section covers the years to 887, and the work ends with Alfred's daily round of prayer, judgment, and study.
works.significance: The primary source for Alfred's reign and the only near-contemporary biography of an Anglo-Saxon king.
works.meter: Latin prose of the ninth-century insular school.
works.context: Composed 893 at the West Saxon court; the unique manuscript (British Library, Cotton MS Otho A.xii) was largely destroyed in 1731, and the text rests on the 1574 edition and sixteenth-century transcripts.
works.characters: Alfred; Asser (narrator); Guthrum; Werferth; Plegmund; Ealhswith
works.structure: Biography modelled on Einhard's Charlemagne, with an embedded chronicle of the years 849-887 and anecdotal set-pieces (the story of the cakes is a later interpolation).
works.attributionNotes: Asser's authorship is stated in the text and generally accepted after long debate.
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume B: The Sixteenth Century and the Early Seventeenth Century

works.title: Lily's Grammar
works.description: The authorized Latin grammar of the English schools, compiled from the grammars of William Lily and John Colet, edited and revised by Erasmus, and imposed by royal proclamation of Henry VIII in 1540 as the single grammar to be used in all schools.
works.plot: A textbook in two parts: the English 'Introduction of the Eight Parts of Speech' (the Accidence) and the Latin 'Brevissima Institutio' (syntax and prosody), with the famous prefatory poem 'Carmen de Moribus' on schoolboy manners.
works.significance: The most influential textbook in the history of English education: in use (as the 'Eton Grammar') for three centuries, it shaped the Latinity of every educated English writer from Shakespeare to Johnson, and its jingling rules became proverbial.
works.meter: Prose with Latin verse paradigms
works.context: The grammar grew out of Colet's statutes for St Paul's School (c. 1509), Lily's part in its composition, and Erasmus's revisions; after Lily's death (1522) it was printed in various forms until the royal proclamation of 1540 and the authorized edition of 1549 standardized it, making it the one book every grammar-school boy knew.
works.structure: Two-part pedagogical manual, with rules, paradigms, and examples arranged for memorization.
works.attributionNotes: A collaborative compilation traditionally credited to William Lily as first high master of St Paul's; Colet and Erasmus contributed substantially, and the standard attribution to Lily is conventional rather than strictly authorial.

works.title: Linacre's Galen translations
altTitles: The Galen Translations of Thomas Linacre
works.description: Thomas Linacre's Latin translations of six treatises of Galen, printed by Richard Pynson between 1521 and 1523, which restored the Greek Galen to European medicine and established Linacre as the founder of the English school of medical humanism.
works.plot: The translations cover Galen's De sanitate tuenda, Methodus medendi, De temperamentis, De naturalibus facultatibus, De pulsuum usu, and De symptomatum differentiis, rendered into a purified humanist Latin from the Greek texts Linacre collated.
works.significance: The founding texts of English medical humanism: by purging the medieval Latin Galen of Arabist corruption, Linacre transformed European medical education and helped found the Royal College of Physicians (1518), of which he was first president.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Translated c. 1517–23 after Linacre's Greek studies under Chalcondyles and Politian in Italy; Pynson printed the treatises in 1521–23, and they were reprinted on the continent, remaining the standard Latin Galen for over a century.
works.structure: Six separate treatises translated and printed with prefaces to Henry VIII and to Linacre's medical colleagues.

works.title: Lives (Walton)
altTitles: The Lives of Doctor John Donne, Sir Henry Wotton, Mr Richard Hooker, Doctor George Herbert, and Doctor Robert Sanderson
works.description: Walton's five biographies of Donne (1640), Wotton (1651), Hooker (1665), Herbert (1670), and Sanderson (1678), collected in 1670 and revised until his death in 1683; they created the modern English literary biography and the hagiographic ideal of the Anglican divine.
works.plot: Each life presents its subject as a model of Christian virtue: Donne the penitent preacher, Wotton the courtier-diplomat, Hooker the learned divine, Herbert the country parson, Sanderson the casuist.
works.significance: The Lives established Walton as the founder of English biographical prose and shaped the Anglican devotional ideal of the holy life; modern scholarship has shown their factual liberties, but their literary influence is immense.
works.meter: A deceptively simple, warm prose of anecdote and character.
works.context: Written across the civil wars, Commonwealth, and Restoration; the Life of Donne was based on Walton's personal knowledge and on Donne's own papers.
works.characters: John Donne; Sir Henry Wotton; Richard Hooker; George Herbert; Robert Sanderson
works.structure: Five separate lives, each with a portrait, letters, and verses.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Walton; the Life of Donne has been shown to borrow heavily from Donne's own writings and from earlier sources.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Lives of Saints
works.form: hagiography (saints' lives) in Old English prose
works.description: Ælfric's collection of saints' lives, passions, and legends (c. 993-998), composed for his patron Æthelweard: the largest vernacular hagiographical collection of the Anglo-Saxon period — virgins, martyrs, kings, and hermits of the universal church, told in Ælfric's rhythmical prose with his characteristic doctrinal care.
works.plot: The lives recount the passions of the early martyrs (Agnes, Alban, Lucy, the Forty Soldiers), the deeds of the virgin saints (Æthelthryth, Agatha, Cecilia), the kings and missionaries of England (Edmund, Oswald, Swithun, Cuthbert), and the great ascetics (Antony, Basil, Martin, Benedict) — each life framed by Ælfric's homiletic introductions and conclusions drawing out the moral for his audience.
works.significance: The fullest vernacular hagiography of the period; the principal vehicle of the saints' cults in late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose.
works.context: Composed at Cerne Abbas c. 993-998; the principal manuscript is British Library, Cotton MS Julius E.vii.
works.characters: the saints of the collection; Æthelweard and Æthelmær (patrons)
works.structure: A collection of over thirty independent lives, each a self-contained narrative homily.
works.attributionNotes: Ælfric's authorship is certain.
sources: The Poems of Andrew Marvell

works.title: London
altTitles: London: A Poem in Imitation of the Second Satire of Juvenal
works.form: verse satire in the Juvenalian manner, an Augustan 'imitation' rather than a literal translation
works.description: Johnson's first published poem, a vigorous translation-of-argument of Juvenal's third satire that replaces the ancient Rome with the London of George II. The speaker Thales retires to a remote country village rather than endure the corruption, insecurity and snobbery of the capital, while Johnson's own indignation at the treatment of the poor, the Scotch immigrant and the dependent writer breaks through the Roman mask. It is the founding document of Johnson's literary career and of his lifelong quarrel with metropolitan patronage and moneyed pride.
works.plot: Thales, disgusted with London, resolves to leave it and persuade his friend to join him in a rational rural retirement. The poem then catalogues the evils of the city: the insecurity of property, the tyranny of the rich over the poor, the degeneracy of the great house and its flattered heir, the corruption of the law, the theatre and the court, and the insolence of wealth in high life. Scottish poverty and the waves of immigration south are given a famous passage of indignation, and the embers of Roman jealousy of foreign arts are turned on the fashionable importation of Italian opera and Continental taste. The conclusion returns to the defence of honest poverty, the pleasures of study and the hope that verse may preserve virtue from contagion.
works.significance: The poem announced Johnson as the leading satiric voice of the generation after Pope and established the moral vocabulary - independence, dependence, the dignity of poverty, suspicion of commercial splendour - that informs Rasselas and the periodical essays. Its handling of the Scottish immigrant makes it a central text for eighteenth-century writing about the nations, and its couplet practice widened the Augustan line for later moral poets.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, with a heavy, polysyllabic and Latinate diction, occasional triple and dactylic rhymes, and long periodic sentences running across several couplets.
works.context: Written after Johnson's failed schoolmastership at Market Bosworth and his London literary apprenticeship, and published in the politically charged years of Walpole's ministry, when the excise scheme of 1737 and the growing quarrel with Spain had made the rhetoric of national corruption and ministerial influence a everyday subject of debate. Its attack on corrupt wealth and on the treatment of dependents addressed the anxieties of the newly professional Grub Street letters that Pope and Swift had already mapped.
works.characters: Thales; Astrella; Licentia; Corydon; the unnamed friend and addressee
works.structure: A single sustained argument in two loosely joined movements, the invective against London and the praise of retirement, framed as a dialogue between Thales and an unnamed friend and closed by an address to the muse; the Juvenalian progression is interrupted by strongly personal passages.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Johnson's authorship is documented by his own publication and by later bibliographical and copyright evidence.

works.title: Love and a Bottle
works.description: Farquhar's first comedy, a lively if derivative play of intrigue in which the Irish adventurer Roebuck arrives in London with nothing but love and a bottle and sets about marrying an heiress.
works.plot: Roebuck, newly arrived from Ireland, pursues the heiress Lucinda while his servant and the town's rogues complicate the plot; the intrigue is resolved in marriage.
works.significance: The debut of the last important Restoration dramatist and the beginning of the transition from the comedy of manners to the sentimental comedy of the eighteenth century.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Performed at Drury Lane in 1698 and published in 1699; Farquhar was a young Irish actor turned playwright after a stage accident.
works.characters: Roebuck; Lucinda; Leanwell; Clear; Sabina; Mrs Gainall; Lyrick
works.structure: Five acts of intrigue comedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Farquhar; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love and Honour
works.description: Davenant's tragi-comedy of love tested by honour, in which a noble lady disguises herself as a poor servant to try the constancy of her lover before the war separates them.
works.plot: Evadne, beloved of the noble Prothall, disguises herself to test his faith; a series of misunderstandings, a supposed death, and a battlefield reunion resolve the conflict between love and honour.
works.significance: Davenant's first major success and a key example of Caroline tragicomedy; it also shows the beginnings of his interest in music and spectacle that would produce The Siege of Rhodes.
works.meter: Blank verse with songs.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men at the Blackfriars in 1634 and published in Davenant's collected Plays of 1639.
works.characters: Evadne; Prothall; Alphonso; Melora; the Duke; Aurelio
works.structure: Five acts with a disguise-testing plot and a final recognition.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Davenant; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Love Divine, All Loves Excelling
altTitles: A Hymn for the Inner Room
works.description: Charles Wesley's great hymn of sanctifying love, a short lyric in which the soul prays to be bound to its Lord and made all the love it beholds. It stands among the most admired hymns in English and among the highest achievements of Charles Wesley's later Bristol period.
works.plot: The hymn opens on the captive soul's address to divine love, fixed and bound by the bands of its own choosing, and moves through petition for the lamp of pure flame and anticipation of the marriage supper of the Lamb. Its central desire is entire consecration, that the heart be fixed, abiding, and cleaving to its God, and the closing stanzas ask the loss of self in God, the soul dyed with the love of Christ, and a close in praise. The argument is Methodist perfectionism turned into lyric yearning, doctrine as amorous address. Each stanza advances the surrender one degree farther toward the wish to be all love.
works.significance: A summit of English hymnody and of the lyric of religious desire, anthologized universally and the model of the Methodist sanctification hymn; its imagery shaped later devotional verse and hymn-tune pairing.
works.meter: Stanzas of the eight-syllable trochaic seven-line measure known in hymnals as 7.7.7.7.7.7.7, with paired internal rhymes that give the verse its urgency; the received text runs to six stanzas and is now sung to tunes such as HYFRYDOL and NICAEA.
works.context: Composed at Bristol in 1762, in Charles Wesley's mature season of hymns for the societies' social worship and the inner room, the year of his wife's death and of some of his deepest lyrics, though the hymn's own first appearance is disputed among the small collections of these years.
works.structure: A single continuous lyric in six stanzas, from captivity and petition to union and doxology.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love for Love
works.description: Congreve's most popular comedy, in which the improvident Valentine, disinherited by his father and pressed by his creditors, feigns madness to escape a forced marriage and finally wins Angelica.
works.plot: Valentine signs away his inheritance to Trapland and Forester; his father Sir Sampson Legend tries to marry him to Miss Prue; the scheming Angelica and the mad prophet Tattle are entangled until the plot resolves in Valentine's recovery and marriage.
works.significance: The most frequently revived of Congreve's comedies in his own lifetime and a principal model for eighteenth-century comedy; its treatment of debt and disinheritance is unusually sharp social commentary.
works.meter: Prose of great variety, from high wit to coarse farce.
works.context: First performed at the new Lincoln's Inn Fields Theatre on 30 April 1695, the opening of the breakaway actors' company under Betterton, and published the same year.
works.characters: Valentine; Angelica; Sir Sampson Legend; Ben Legend; Tattle; Mrs Frail; Miss Prue; Foresight; Jeremy; Trapland; Buckram; Scandal
works.structure: Five acts with a rich comic subplot of the nurse, the astrologer Foresight, and the country Miss Prue.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Congreve; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love in a Wood; or, St. James's Park
works.description: Wycherley's first comedy, a sprawling intrigue play set in St James's Park, in which masked gallants and ladies pursue one another through a series of night adventures.
works.plot: Several couples are entangled in the fashionable world of the Park and the Exchange; disguises, duels, and betrayals are resolved in a set of marriages, with the virtuous Dapperwit exposed as a wit.
works.significance: An early and uneven but energetic comedy that anticipates Wycherley's later severity; its portrait of the Park is a valuable document of Restoration London.
works.meter: Prose dominant with some verse.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1671 and published in 1672, dedicated to the Duchess of Cleveland.
works.characters: Ranger; Vincent; Lydia; Martha; Dapperwit; Mrs Crossbite; Alderman Gripe; Simon
works.structure: Five acts with multiple plots and a low comic subplot of the city.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Wycherley; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love in Excess; or, The Fatal Enquiry
altTitles: Love in Excess: Or, The Fatal Enquiry
works.form: prose romance; amatory novel in several parts
works.description: The first and most ambitious of the amatory novels of its period, issued in parts over several years and built as a chain of interlaced histories of passion, seduction and betrayal. It sets the pattern of the long romance of the erring lover that its author afterwards dominated, and its tales of ruined women are narrated with a rhetoric of pity.
works.plot: A young gentleman of fortune pursues an heiress and meets refusals, while in the tales within the narrative other lovers are tried by seduction, discovery and revenge. Brothers and rivals abduct, disguise and betray; women of condition are ruined by inquiry into their past, and the several histories converge through letters and unexpected recognitions. The closing parts resolve the errors by revelation of birth and the forgiveness of the offended.
works.significance: It is the founding text of the amatory novel as a long form and the work that made its author the central female prose fiction-writer of the 1720s; its treatment of female complicity and male constancy shaped the genre down to the novelists of the 1740s.
works.meter: High romantic prose of apostrophe, exclamation and elaborated syntax, with letters and reported speeches; the style is consciously ornamented and emotionally intensified.
works.context: Published in parts between 1719 and 1722 in the efflorescence of the three-volume romance, succeeding the translation-based fashion and competing directly with the scandalous fiction of the same booksellers.
works.structure: A serial multi-volume romance with embedded tales and a frame of continuous narration; the interlacing of stories is deliberate and the sequence of parts extends the suspense over years of publication.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the parts were published with the author's name after the success of the early issues, and she reissued the whole in revised form in the following decade.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love's Labour's Lost
works.description: Shakespeare's most verbally extravagant comedy: the King of Navarre and his three lords swear a three-year vow of study, fasting, and no women — a vow broken at once by the arrival of the Princess of France and her ladies, whose wit outmatches the men's until the play's astonishing turn: news of the Princess's father's death converts the comedy into a year of penance and a set of unfinished songs.
works.plot: The lords woo the ladies in disguise and are exposed; the pedants Holofernes and Nathaniel stage the pageant of the Nine Worthies and are mocked; and just as the marriages are to be concluded, Marcade enters with the news of the French king's death, and the ladies impose their year-long conditions on the suitors.
works.significance: The summit of Elizabethan verbal comedy and the play in which Shakespeare's lyric genius first runs free.
works.meter: The highest proportion of rhyme in Shakespeare, with sonnets, songs, and the prose of the pedants' Latinity.
works.context: Written about 1594–95 amid the French succession crisis and the Euphuistic wordplay fashion it both satirizes and surpasses; first printed in quarto, 1598.
works.characters: Ferdinand, King of Navarre; Berowne; Longaville; Dumaine; the Princess of France; Rosaline; Maria; Katherine; Boyet; Don Armado; Holofernes; Nathaniel; Costard; Jaquenetta; Moth
works.structure: A plotless, tournament-like comedy of wit built on symmetrical scenes of courtship, masque, and pageant, ending in the deliberately anti-comic 'dialogue' of Spring and Winter songs.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

works.title: Love's Last Shift; or, The Fool in Fashion
works.description: Colley Cibber's first comedy, in which the rake Loveless is reformed by his long-suffering wife Amanda; the play's famous double structure — libertine comedy in the first half, moral reform in the second — provoked Vanbrugh's answer in The Relapse.
works.plot: Loveless, believing Amanda a stranger, seduces her in disguise; she reveals herself and he is reformed; the comic subplot of Sir Novelty Fashion satirises the fashionable fop.
works.significance: Usually cited as the first sentimental comedy in English and the pivot between Restoration libertinism and eighteenth-century moral reform; Cibber's career as actor-manager of Drury Lane shaped the Georgian stage.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Performed at Drury Lane in January 1696 with Cibber himself as Sir Novelty Fashion; the role made him famous and the play was a great success.
works.characters: Loveless; Amanda; Sir Novelty Fashion; Young Worthy; Snap; Narcissa; Flareit
works.structure: Five acts with a sharp generic shift at the centre that critics have called the origin of sentimental comedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Cibber; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love's Sacrifice
works.description: Ford's tragedy of unwarranted jealousy, in which the Duke of Pavy, persuaded by his secretary Nibrassa, believes his duchess Bianca unfaithful to him with his friend Fernando, and kills her before learning the truth.
works.plot: The Duke marries Bianca but loves his friend Fernando more; Fernando and Bianca love each other chastely; the malicious secretary sows suspicion; the Duke murders Bianca and Fernando, then kills himself in remorse.
works.significance: A notable Caroline reworking of the Othello situation, and an important example of Ford's preoccupation with honour and the destruction of innocence.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Published 1633, performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Phoenix.
works.characters: the Duke of Pavy; Bianca; Fernando; Nibrassa; Fiormonda; Colona; Petruchio
works.structure: Five acts following the Othello pattern of jealousy induced by a villain and resolved in catastrophe.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ford on the 1633 title page; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister
works.description: Behn's epistolary novel in three parts, based on the real scandal of Lord Grey of Warke's elopement with his wife's sister, in which Philander seduces Silvia and she descends through a series of lovers into prostitution and political intrigue.
works.plot: Philander writes to Silvia, his sister-in-law; they elope; he tires of her and takes another mistress; Silvia responds by seducing and abandoning a series of men, becoming a courtesan and finally a political agent of Monmouth's rebellion.
works.significance: The first major English epistolary novel and a decisive step toward the eighteenth-century novel of Richardson and Laclos; its portrayal of a woman's sexual and political agency was unprecedented.
works.meter: Prose with interpolated verse.
works.context: Published in three parts between 1684 and 1687, at the time of the Monmouth Rebellion; it is a roman à clef on the Grey-Sisters scandal.
works.characters: Philander; Silvia; Calista; Octavio; Don Alonzo; Cesario; the Countess
works.structure: Three parts (1684, 1685, 1687) of letters with narrative interludes, the first substantial English epistolary fiction.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in parts; attribution to Behn is long-established and undisputed.

editions.editor: Germaine Greer, Susan Hastings, Jeslyn Medoff, and Melinda Sansone (eds.)

works.title: Lucan's Pharsalia Translated
altTitles: Lucan's Pharsalia Translated into English Verse
works.description: Rowe's verse translation of Lucan's civil-war epic, the work by which the English reader of the early century knew the wars of Caesar and Pompey and the Stoic Cato.
works.plot: The translation follows Lucan's argument of the breach between Caesar and Pompey, the flight from Rome, Pharsalia and the suicide of Cato, with the poet's own reflections on the loss of Roman liberty running through the narrative.
works.significance: It was the standard English Lucan of the first half of the century, and its translator was later made the point of a satiric joke about the rendering that outdoes its original.
works.meter: Heroic couplet of the regular Augustan kind, straining to carry Lucan's declamation and his apostrophes.
works.context: Published in the years when the republicanism and the liberty of the Roman commonwealth were being read into the quarrels of the British constitution, and when the translation of the classics had become a profession's work.
works.characters: Caesar; Pompey; Cato; Lucan as the translated author
works.structure: A book-by-book verse translation of the ten books of the Pharsalia, with the preface, the arguments and the explanatory notes.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the volume's later issues were revised and part of the prefatory matter has been assigned to another hand.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Lucasta
works.description: Richard Lovelace's collection of Cavalier verse (1649), named for his mistress Lucy Sacheverell ('Lucasta'), containing his most famous lyrics — 'To Althea, from Prison', 'To Lucasta, Going to the Wars', and 'The Grasshopper' — which made the code of love and honour the motto of the royalist gentleman.
works.plot: The poems celebrate love, friendship, loyalty, and liberty of spirit even in prison and defeat, arguing that honour and constancy survive political ruin ('Stone walls do not a prison make, / Nor iron bars a cage').
works.significance: Lucasta is the classic Cavalier collection; 'To Althea' and 'To Lucasta' are among the most quoted poems of the seventeenth century and define royalist gallantry.
works.meter: Musical, dignified lyrics in varied meters with argumentative conceits of love and honour.
works.context: Lovelace prepared the collection during his imprisonment in the Gatehouse (1648–49) for his royalist loyalty; it was published in 1649, the year of the regicide.
works.characters: the poet; Lucasta; Althea; fellow Cavaliers
works.structure: A collection of songs, odes, elegies, and occasional verse unified by the Cavalier ethos and the figure of Lucasta.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; a posthumous second part appeared in 1659/60.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Lucius Junius Brutus, Father of His Country
works.description: Lee's republican tragedy on the expulsion of the Tarquins and the founding of the Roman republic, banned by the Lord Chamberlain in 1680 for its allegedly republican politics.
works.plot: Brutus feigns idiocy under the tyrant Tarquin; after the rape of Lucretia he leads the revolt, and sacrifices his own sons for treason rather than betray the new republic.
works.significance: An important document of Whig political sentiment in the drama and a forerunner of the eighteenth-century republican tragedies of Addison and Thomson; its suppression is a classic case of Restoration censorship.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Prohibited from performance in 1680 by the Lord Chamberlain on the ground that it contained 'very scandalous expressions and reflections upon monarchical government'; printed in 1681 during the Exclusion Crisis.
works.characters: Lucius Junius Brutus; Tarquin; Lucretia; Teraminta; Titus; Tiberius; Collatinus; Herminius
works.structure: Five acts of political tragedy culminating in the hero's filial sacrifice.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Lee; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Lusty Juventus
works.description: A Protestant morality interlude of the youth Juventus, tempted by Hypocrisy and the devil but restored by Good Counsel and God's Merciful Promises; printed c. 1550 with the author's name given as R. Wever.
works.plot: Juventus (Youth), fresh from his conversion, is tempted by the devil's instruments — Hypocrisy, Fellowship, and Abominable Living — who draw him into sin and despair; Good Counsel and Knowledge recall him, God's Merciful Promises assures him of forgiveness through Christ, and the play ends with Juventus's restoration and a call to the audience to follow his example.
works.significance: The most explicitly doctrinal of the Edwardian moralities and a prime example of the interlude as Reformation propaganda; its title character became the proverbial type of the reformed youth.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages
works.context: Composed in the early years of the Edwardian Reformation (c. 1547–53) and printed c. 1550; its polemic against hypocrisy and works-righteousness and its emphasis on justification by faith make it a direct dramatic expression of Protestant doctrine for a young audience.
works.characters: Juventus; Good Counsel; Knowledge; God's Merciful Promises; The Devil; Hypocrisy; Fellowship; Abominable Living
works.structure: A continuous morality play of temptation, fall, and restoration, with the devil and Hypocrisy as the comic Vices and a concluding address to the young.
works.attributionNotes: The title page names 'R. Wever' as author; nothing further is known of him, and the ascription cannot be independently confirmed.

works.title: Lycidas
works.description: Milton's pastoral elegy for Edward King, a Cambridge contemporary drowned off the Irish coast in 1637, written for the memorial volume Justa Edouardo King; it mourns the young poet's death, indicts the corrupt clergy, and consoles with the promise of resurrection and fame in heaven.
works.plot: The shepherd-poet mourns Lycidas, questions divine justice, invokes the Muse and St Peter (who denounces the 'blind mouths' of the corrupt church), hears the tale of Lycidas's drowning and apotheosis, and finds consolation in the belief that he is 'sunk low, but mounted high' as the genius of the shore.
works.significance: Widely regarded as the greatest pastoral elegy in English, Lycidas combines personal grief, political and religious satire, and visionary consolation in a uniquely wrought form.
works.meter: A varied and intricately rhymed pastoral stanza of irregular line lengths, with carefully placed short lines and refrains.
works.context: Written in 1637 for the collection Justa Edouardo King Naufrago (1638); it draws on the pastoral elegiac tradition from Theocritus and Virgil to Spenser, transfigured by Milton's Puritan faith and anticlerical anger.
works.characters: the uncouth swain (Milton); Lycidas (Edward King); St Peter; the Muse; Jove
works.structure: A pastoral elegy in irregular verse, moving from grief and doubt through the prophetic denunciation by St Peter to Christian consolation and the poet's turn to 'pastures new'.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; signed 'J.M.' in the 1638 volume and included in the 1645 Poems.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton
editions.editor: William Kerrigan, John Rumrich, and Stephen M. Fallon (eds.)

works.title: Mac Flecknoe
altTitles: Mac Flecknoe: A Satire upon the True-blew-Protestant Poet, T. S.
works.description: Dryden's short mock-heroic satire on Thomas Shadwell, imagining the dull poet Richard Flecknoe abdicating his empire of nonsense and choosing Shadwell as his heir.
works.plot: Flecknoe, monarch of the realm of dullness, delivers a coronation speech naming Shadwell as his successor; Shadwell is crowned amid burlesque pomp and vanishes through a trapdoor.
works.significance: The first sustained mock-heroic in English and the direct model for Pope's The Dunciad; it established the 'empire of dullness' conceit that dominated Augustan satire.
works.meter: Heroic couplets used to comic effect by sustaining an epic register throughout.
works.context: Written between about 1678 and 1682, circulated in manuscript, and printed without Dryden's name in 1682; it arises from the quarrel over dramatic criticism that began with The Essay of Dramatic Poesy.
works.characters: Richard Flecknoe; Thomas Shadwell (Sh—-); Henry VIII's ghost; Arion
works.structure: A single continuous mock-coronation scene in elevated epic diction, ending with the sudden comic collapse of the hero.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in 1682 and ascribed to Dryden by contemporaries; attribution undisputed.

works.title: Macbeth
works.description: Shakespeare's shortest tragedy, of ambition and the supernatural: the Scottish general Macbeth, told by the Weird Sisters that he shall be king, murders Duncan in his sleep and enters a reign of blood — Banquo's murder, the apparitions' riddling prophecies, the slaughter of Macduff's family — until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane and the tyrant falls to the man 'not of woman born'.
works.plot: The prophecies kindle Macbeth's ambition and Lady Macbeth steels him to the murder; the crown brings only sleeplessness and escalating violence; Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking confession and death precede the final battle, where the equivocations of the witches are fulfilled and Macduff beheads the tyrant.
works.significance: The supreme English tragedy of evil's self-entrapment — the shortest road to the heart of darkness the stage has ever built.
works.meter: The densest verse in Shakespeare — image packed and accelerated — with the witches' tetrameter charms and the Porter's prose as deliberate descents.
works.context: Written 1606 for the new king, James I, the patron of the company and the author of Daemonologie; the play's Scottish matter, witchcraft, and Banquo's royal line all court the Stuart interest.
works.characters: Macbeth; Lady Macbeth; Banquo; the Weird Sisters; Duncan; Macduff; Lady Macduff; Malcolm; Donalbain; Ross; Lennox; the Porter; Fleance
works.structure: A single-line tragedy of mounting speed, structured by the three prophecies and their ironic fulfilments, with the banquet scene as its turning point and the sleepwalking scene as its moral climax.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the Hecate scenes may be later interpolations (possibly by Middleton).
