works.title: Prothalamion
works.description: A wedding song ('spousal verse') written for the double marriage of the daughters of the Earl of Worcester, Elizabeth and Katherine Somerset, celebrated at Essex House on the Thames in 1596; the poem follows the bridal procession along the river and closes with the refrain 'Sweet Thames, run softly, till I end my song'.
works.plot: The poet, walking the Thames bank in dejection, sees two swans (the brides) float down the river attended by nymphs; the vision becomes the wedding procession itself, and the poem blesses the marriages and the house of Essex.
works.significance: One of the two great English wedding odes, and the source of a refrain that became a byword of English poetry.
works.meter: The Spenserian stanza with a refrain line, lending the poem its processional music.
works.context: Written in 1596 in the orbit of the Earl of Essex, to whom the poem glances in its praise of Essex House; published the same year.
works.characters: the poet; Elizabeth and Katherine Somerset (the brides); the nymphs of Thames and Lee
works.structure: Ten stanzas with a refrain, moving from the poet's melancholy through the visionary river scene to the ceremonial blessing of the brides.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Yale Edition of the Shorter Poems of Edmund Spenser
editions.editor: William A. Oram, Einar Bjorvand, Ronald Bond, Thomas Cain, Alexander Dunlop, and Richard Schell (eds.)

works.title: Pseudodoxia Epidemica; or, Enquiries into Very Many Received Tenets
works.description: Browne's encyclopaedic survey of popular errors, in seven books examining and correcting the received beliefs of his time about natural history, medicine, geography, history, and Scripture.
works.plot: Book I analyses the causes of error; books II-IV treat errors concerning animals, plants, minerals, and man; books V-VII treat errors of history, chronology, and Scripture.
works.significance: The greatest English work of popular scepticism and one of the most important documents of seventeenth-century intellectual life; it influenced Baconian empiricism and the Royal Society's programme.
works.meter: Learned, allusive prose of great compression; the work went through five editions in Browne's lifetime.
works.context: Published in 1646, in the midst of the civil wars; it belongs to the new empirical spirit that would found the Royal Society, though Browne's method is as much scholarly as experimental.
works.structure: Seven books of learned enquiry organised by subject, each entry stating the received opinion and Browne's correction.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Browne; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Ralph Roister Doister
works.description: Nicholas Udall's five-act comedy of the braggart Ralph Roister Doister, written c. 1552–54 and printed c. 1566–67; generally regarded as the first English comedy.
works.plot: Ralph Roister Doister, a vainglorious suitor encouraged by the parasite Merrygreek, woos Dame Christian Custance, who is betrothed to the merchant Gawin Goodluck; his letters and verses are read to her as insults, and his siege of her house ends in a comic battle with her maids, the braggart routed by a broom; the play closes with the lovers reunited and Roister Doister invited to dinner — folly corrected without malice.
works.significance: The first English comedy: it transplants the Roman braggart soldier and parasite into a London setting, joins classical form to native farce, and inaugurates the line that runs through Gammer Gurton's Needle to Shakespeare and Jonson.
works.meter: Irregular rhyming couplets ('rhyming fourteeners'), with songs
works.context: Written c. 1552–54, probably for performance by the boys of Westminster School (Udall was headmaster there from 1555, earlier at Eton); drawing on Plautus's Miles Gloriosus and Terence's Eunuchus, it belongs to the academic revival of Roman comedy that would produce Gammer Gurton's Needle and the school drama of the 1560s.
works.characters: Ralph Roister Doister; Matthew Merrygreek; Dame Christian Custance; Gawin Goodluck; Tristram Trusty; Madge Mumblecrust; Tibet Talkapace; Annot Alyface
works.structure: Five acts modelled on the Roman comedy of Plautus and Terence, with a braggart soldier, a parasite, and a reunion plot; the action is domestic and the verse a rollicking doggerel.

editions.title: Three Sixteenth-Century Comedies

works.title: Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye
altTitles: The Recuyell of the Histories of Troy
works.description: William Caxton's translation of Raoul Lefèvre's French Recueil des histoires de Troyes, begun in Bruges in 1468 and completed in Cologne in 1471, and printed by Caxton at Bruges in 1473–74 as the first book printed in English. A courtly Troy compilation made for the Burgundian duchess Margaret of York, it inaugurated both Caxton's career and the English printed book.
works.plot: The compilation recounts the deeds of Hercules and the first destruction of Troy, then the rebuilding of the city under Priam and the second war — the rape of Helen, the battles before Troy, the deaths of Hector and Achilles, and the fall of the city through the wooden horse.
works.significance: The first book printed in English and the founding text of the English print tradition; its Troy matter carried the medieval romance of antiquity into the print era.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's early style, French-inflected and courtly, before his London plainness matured.
works.context: Begun in Bruges in 1468 for Margaret of York, sister of Edward IV, and printed at Bruges c. 1473–74 — the first English printed book; Caxton's famous prologue records his despair over the labour of translation and the duchess's command to finish.
works.characters: Hercules; Jason; Priam; Hector; Achilles; Paris; Helen; Ulysses
works.structure: Three books in Lefèvre's arrangement, translated in full, with Caxton's prologue and epilogue recording the circumstances of its making.
works.attributionNotes: Caxton's authorship of the translation and printing is documented in his own prologue and epilogue.

editions.title: The Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye

works.title: Redemption
works.description: Blackmore's last large religious poem, a sacred epic of the redemption of mankind which carries the Miltonic measure of Creation into the history of the fall and the work of the Saviour.
works.plot: The poem reviews the fall of man and the promise of redemption, the training of the Old Testament and the coming, teaching and passion of Christ, and closes on the application of the saving work to the conscience of the reader.
works.significance: It completes the series by which the physico-theological and the sacred epic were attempted in Miltonic blank verse, and it documents the isolation of a once fashionable poet from the taste that had superseded him.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines in the Miltonic manner, sustained through the longest of Blackmore's religious poems.
works.context: Published in the closing years of the century's first great quarrel over the poem of religion, when Blackmore's verse had long been the target of the Scribleran burlesque of the art of sinking.
works.characters: the poet; the redeeming Saviour; Satan; the figures of the Old and New Testament narrative
works.structure: A continuous sacred narrative in numbered books, with the theological reflection interposed in the poet's own voice.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Regularis Concordia
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius A.iii (mid-eleventh century) and Cotton Faustina B.iii
works.description: The customary drawn up at the Council of Winchester (c. 970) under Æthelwold of Winchester to unify the observance of all English monasteries: a national supplement to the Rule of St Benedict, adapting continental customaries from Fleury and Ghent to English conditions and binding the reformed houses together under royal protection.
works.plot: The Concordia sets out the daily, weekly, and yearly round of the monastic life — the hours of prayer, the psalms and canticles, the ceremonies of the great feasts, the commemoration of the king and queen, and the dramatic rites of Holy Week, including the earliest recorded Visitatio Sepulchri (the 'Quem quaeritis' dialogue) in England.
works.significance: The founding document of the unified English monasticism of the late tenth century, and the source of the earliest English dramatic text (the Visitatio Sepulchri), making it a landmark in the history of English theatre as well as of monasticism.
works.context: Produced at the high point of the Benedictine Reform under King Edgar (959-975), the Concordia institutionalized the alliance of crown and monastery: the king and queen are commemorated in the daily office, and the text was issued with royal authority for all houses.
works.structure: A prologue addressed to King Edgar, followed by a systematic customary organized by the liturgical day and year; the prescriptions culminate in the elaborated rites of the Triduum, with the dialogue of the three Marys and the angel at the Easter sepulchre.
works.attributionNotes: Written by Æthelwold of Winchester, who names himself as the compiler; the text is securely attributed.

editions.title: Regularis Concordia Anglicae Nationis

works.title: Religio Laici
altTitles: Religio Laici: or, A Layman's Faith
works.description: Dryden's philosophical poem defending the Anglican via media against both Catholic tradition and Protestant private judgement, written while he was still a conforming member of the Church of England.
works.plot: The poem argues that Scripture is the sole rule of faith but is obscure in places, that private interpretation leads to chaos, and that the established church's tradition supplies the necessary authority.
works.significance: A key text in the history of English apologetics and the immediate predecessor of Pope's Essay on Man; it also marks the religious position Dryden abandoned when he converted to Catholicism in 1685-6.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, deliberately roughened, with frequent alexandrines and triplets.
works.context: Published in November 1682, after Dryden's translation of Simon's Criticial History; it responds to the Deist and Socinian challenge to revelation.
works.structure: A continuous argumentative poem with a prose preface defending its 'fugitive' method and rough verse.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

The Poems and Fables of John Dryden

works.title: Religio Medici
altTitles: Religio Medici: Its Author's Name is Thomas Browne
works.description: Sir Thomas Browne's meditative confession of faith, written privately in the 1630s and pirated in 1642 before Browne issued his own authorised text in 1643; it is the founding work of English introspective prose.
works.plot: In two parts Browne sets out his religious faith and his moral philosophy: the first defends his adherence to the Church of England against the charges of atheism and scepticism, the second explores charity and the duty to one's neighbour.
works.significance: The most influential work of English prose of the seventeenth century after the Authorised Bible; it created the genre of the personal religious meditation in prose and influenced Montaigne's English readers, Coleridge, Lamb, and Virginia Woolf.
works.meter: A richly Latinate, periodic prose with a strong personal cadence; Browne's style became the model of English 'character' writing.
works.context: Written while Browne was practising medicine, probably in the late 1630s; circulated in manuscript and printed without his consent in 1642, then authorised in 1643 with his own preface.
works.structure: Two parts of continuous meditative prose without formal division into chapters in the first edition.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Browne; he authorised the 1643 edition after the pirated 1642 printing.

editions.title: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Reliques of Ancient English Poetry
works.form: Anthology of editorial collection: ballads, songs, romances and fragments, printed with preface, essays, arguments, annotations and glossary; the founding model of the scholarly-popular national anthology.
works.description: Thomas Percy's three-volume collection of early English ballads, songs and other poetical remains, with prefatory essays, historical and critical notes and a life of several of the old poets: the book that made the native ballad tradition available to the polite reader and turned it into a subject of criticism. It drew on a recovered manuscript folio of ballads and on printed copies, and it presented the material in a carefully arranged historical order. Its editorial practice, modernising and repairing the old texts, was at once its popular strength and the ground of the quarrel about it.
works.plot: As a collection its argument is a history of English poetry told in specimens: that the native tradition, from the minstrelsy of the north through the ballad and the romance, possessed a genuine pathos, harmony and strength of description which the later 'polite' age undervalued. The volumes interleave heroic songs, ballads of love and chivalry, fragments of old romance, and pieces of lyric and devotional poetry, with critical remarks on each and with the famous defence of the 'antient' poets in the prefacial essay on minstrelsy. Percy also let the reader see the editorial hand: texts were amended, completed from other copies, and in places composed or interpolated where the original was judged defective, in the belief that he was restoring an ancient author's meaning. The collection thus argues two things at once, that English poetry has an ancient native inheritance, and that a modern editor of taste is its rightful guardian.
works.significance: It is the single most influential book of old English poetry of the century: it formed the taste of the Romantic poets for the ballad, revived the native tradition as a source of poetical pleasure, and established the anthology-with-notes as a critical genre. Both its method and its materials were answered and extended by later collectors, and its influence on the ballad revivals of the 1780s and 1790s is direct.
works.meter: The whole range of early English verse as Percy understood it: ballad stanzas of common and of long measure, the stanzaic forms of the native romance, and the several kinds of old English verse he set out to distinguish; the printed texts are smoothed toward modern regularity.
works.context: It appears at the centre of the 1760s revival of interest in national antiquity, alongside Chatterton's Rowley forgeries, Macpherson's Ossian and the debates over primitive genius, and it was edited by a clergyman-antiquary with patrons in the great houses, later himself a bishop in Ireland. Its appearance also coincides with the quarrel over editorial fidelity, in which Percy was attacked for modernising and for pretending to restore what he had in fact rewritten.
works.characters: The anonymous and named old poets and 'minstrels' whose songs are collected; the editors and printers whose copies are collated; Percy himself as the arranging and annotating voice
works.structure: A chronological and thematic anthology in three volumes, each book of specimens preceded or followed by historical and critical observation, with a preliminary essay and with notes, glossaries and life accounts attached to individual pieces.
works.attributionNotes: Percy is the editor and the responsibility for the arrangement, essays and the amended texts is his; the individual poems are of course anonymous and attributed within the volumes with varying degrees of confidence. Some pieces were printed from the folio manuscript he recovered, others from broadsides and earlier copies, and a number were repaired or completed by the editor, which is the notorious part of the book's attribution history.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Remarks on Several Parts of Paradise Lost
works.description: Addison's serial criticism of Milton's epic, first conducted as papers in The Spectator: it reads Paradise Lost as a work of sublime original genius disciplined by scriptural and classical learning, and defends its machinery, its diction and its allegory against the objections of the French neoclassical rules.
works.plot: Successive remarks take the fable, the characters, the machinery of angels, the episodes of limbo and of Pandemonium, the similes and the versification, arguing that Milton's faults are those of a genius and that his subject gives him a sublimity the classical epics could not reach.
works.significance: It established the Augustan rehabilitation of Milton and, through its account of the sublime and of allegorical machinery, supplied the vocabulary that later eighteenth-century criticism and the graveyard poets inherited.
works.meter: Prose of exemplary periodic balance, continuously reinforced by quoted hexameter and couplet passages from Milton and the ancients.
works.context: Delivered in the year of the quarrel over the unities and over the value of blank verse, when Tonson's cheap Milton and Dennis's and Bentley's rival criticisms made the national epic a contested property.
works.structure: A linked sequence of short critical dissertations, one per paper, each opening on a passage and closing with a general rule of taste.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested Addison; a single passage's share has occasionally been queried by bibliographers of the joint paper.

editions.title: The Spectator, 4 volumes

works.title: Resignation
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A first-person penitential prayer in which the speaker, an exile and outcast from his lord's favour, submits himself wholly to God's will and prays for guidance through the storms of life. The poem fuses the secular conventions of the exile's lament with Christian devotion.
works.plot: The speaker, alienated from his earthly lord and wandering in misery, turns to God as his true protector, acknowledging that he has suffered for his sins, and prays for wisdom, steadfastness, and a safe passage through life's sea of troubles to the heavenly home.
works.significance: A major example of the Old English religious lyric's absorption of elegiac conventions, and a witness to the penitential spirituality of late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.meter: Standard alliterative long line with the formulaic diction of the elegiac tradition; the poem is textually imperfect, with apparent lacunae.
works.context: The poem belongs to the late Old English religious lyric, where the conventions of heroic exile poetry were appropriated for penitential devotion; comparable to The Wife's Lament in its fusion of personal loss and landscape imagery.
works.structure: A sustained first-person prayer in which the imagery of exile, sea-voyage, and homelessness is progressively reinterpreted as the soul's spiritual condition; some editors detect a break in the middle of the text suggesting an incomplete or composite poem.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The title 'Resignation' is an editorial convenience, not in the manuscript.
themes: Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination

works.title: Respublica
works.description: An anonymous Protestant morality play of the commonwealth, written for performance at Christmas 1553 during the first months of Mary I's reign; a sophisticated political allegory of the misgovernment of the 1540s.
works.plot: Respublica, the widowed commonwealth, is robbed by Avarice and his crew — Oppression, Adulation, and Insolence (disguised as Policy, Honesty, and Authority) — who plunder her goods and divide them among themselves; the four sisters People, Verity, Peace, and Justice return, strip the thieves of their disguises, and restore the commonwealth, with Mercy pronouncing judgement and the audience promised amendment under the new queen.
works.significance: The most politically sophisticated of the sixteenth-century moralities: its allegory of the commonwealth, its disguised Vices, and its address to the monarch anticipate the political drama of the Elizabethan stage, and it documents the mid-Tudor crisis of counsel and plunder.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic speeches
works.context: Performed at Christmas 1553, evidently by a company of boys, in the first months of Mary's reign; the play's allegory of the plunder of the commonwealth under Edward VI's ministers (Somerset and Northumberland) and its restoration under the Catholic queen marks a rare moment when the morality tradition served immediate dynastic politics.
works.characters: Respublica; Avarice; Adulation; Oppression; Insolence; People; Verity; Peace; Justice; Mercy; Nemesis
works.structure: Five acts of morality allegory applied to contemporary politics, with the Vice Avarice doubling his disguises and a final scene of restoration and loyal address to Mary I.
works.attributionNotes: No author is named in the manuscript; Nicholas Udall has been proposed by some scholars, but the attribution remains unproven, and the work is treated as anonymous.

works.title: Revelations of Divine Love
works.description: Julian of Norwich's account of the sixteen revelations ('showings') she received during a grave illness on 8 May 1373, in two versions — the Short Text written soon after, and the Long Text, the fruit of some twenty years of meditation, completed c. 1393. Its theology of divine love — 'all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' — and of Jesus as mother makes it the greatest work of English mysticism and the first book in English known to be by a woman.
works.plot: At the point of death, the thirty-year-old Julian receives a series of visions of Christ's Passion, the Virgin, the world's littleness (the hazelnut), and the Lord's meaning: that love is his meaning; the Long Text unfolds these showings into a theology of sin, suffering, divine motherhood, and the 'great deed' by which all shall be made well.
works.significance: The summit of the English mystical tradition: the first major theological work by an English woman, and a text of the first importance for the history of women's writing and of Christian theology.
works.meter: Plain, meditative prose of extraordinary depth; homely images (the hazelnut) carrying speculative theology.
works.context: The showings occurred in Norwich on 8 May 1373; Julian became an anchoress at St Julian's church and wrote the Short Text shortly after and the Long Text c. 1393; Margery Kempe visited her c. 1413; the Long Text circulated in manuscript and in the printed editions of Serenus Cressy (1670).
works.characters: Julian (visionary); Christ; the Virgin Mary; the fiend
works.structure: Eighty-six (or more) chapters of vision, exposition, and prayer, organized by the order of the showings and the decades of their meditation.
works.attributionNotes: The author is known only as Julian of Norwich (from her church); her name in the world is unknown.

editions.title: The Writings of Julian of Norwich

works.title: Reynard the Fox
altTitles: The History of Reynard the Fox
The Historye of Reynart the Foxe
works.description: William Caxton's translation of the Dutch prose Reinaert de Vos, printed at Westminster in 1481: the beast epic of the fox Reynard, whose crimes are arraigned at the court of King Noble the lion, and whose cunning turns every accusation — and his own execution — into the ruin of his accusers. Caxton's print brought the European Reynard tradition to English readers and printers alike.
works.plot: Summoned to the lion's court to answer the complaints of the wolf Isengrim, the bear Bruin, and the other beasts, Reynard tricks each accuser in turn, confesses to save his neck, and is sent on pilgrimage only to murder his escort; his enemies' heads decorate his house, and the lion makes him his counsellor — the trickster triumphant.
works.significance: The classic English Reynard and the ancestor of the beast satire that runs through Spenser's Mother Hubberds Tale to the seventeenth-century Reynard reprints; a landmark of Caxton's publishing program.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's plain, lively narrative style at its best.
works.context: Translated by Caxton from the Dutch and printed in 1481, in the same year as his Godfrey of Boulogne; it fed a long English print tradition of Reynard editions and the beast satire of the sixteenth century.
works.characters: Reynard the Fox; King Noble the Lion; Isengrim the Wolf; Bruin the Bear; Tibert the Cat; Chanticleer the Cock
works.structure: A beast epic in episodic form: arraignment, defence, confession, and triumph, in the framework of the animals' court.
works.attributionNotes: Caxton's translation documented in his own colophon.

editions.title: The History of Reynard the Fox

works.title: Richard II
altTitles: The Tragedy of King Richard the Second
works.description: Shakespeare's lyrical tragedy of deposition, opening the second tetralogy: Richard's misgovernment, the quarrel of Bolingbroke and Mowbray, and the king's fall from the throne of England — the first English history play written entirely in verse, culminating in Richard's murder at Pomfret and the new king's guilt.
works.plot: Richard banishes Bolingbroke and seizes his inheritance on Gaunt's death; Bolingbroke returns to claim his own, and the king's support melts away; in the deposition scene Richard unkings himself before Parliament; the plot of Aumerle is discovered, and Exton, reading Henry's wish, kills Richard in prison.
works.significance: The great English meditation on kingship, legitimacy, and the theatre of power — the seed of the Henriad that follows.
works.meter: Entirely in verse, much of it rhymed — Richard's elegiac lyricism is the play's signature music.
works.context: Written 1595 and printed 1597; the deposition scene was omitted from the early quartos for political reasons, and the play was notoriously performed on the eve of Essex's rising in 1601.
works.characters: King Richard II; Henry Bolingbroke; John of Gaunt; the Duke of York; the Duke of Aumerle; Thomas Mowbray; the Queen; Northumberland; the Bishop of Carlisle; Exton; the Gardener
works.structure: A five-act fall of princes, symmetrical in its structure of deposition, prophecy, and fulfilment, with the garden scene as the play's emblem of the commonwealth.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Richard III
altTitles: The Tragedy of King Richard the Third
works.description: Shakespeare's first great tragedy, completing the first tetralogy: Richard, Duke of Gloucester, murders his way to the crown through his brothers, his nephews (the Princes in the Tower), and his allies, seducing and discarding Lady Anne along the way, until the ghosts of his victims curse him at Bosworth and Richmond's victory ends the Wars of the Roses and plants the Tudor line.
works.plot: Richard announces his villainy in the opening soliloquy, eliminates Clarence, Hastings, Buckingham, Rivers, and the young princes, weds Anne and then plans her death; at Bosworth the procession of ghosts damns him and blesses Richmond, who slays him and marries Elizabeth of York.
works.significance: The first fully achieved Shakespearean tragedy of character, and the role that has defined the tragic actor from Burbage to Olivier.
works.meter: A verse of rhetorical virtuosity — Richard's soliloquies are among the most quoted in the canon — with the stichomythia of the wooing scene.
works.context: Written about 1592–93 from More's History of King Richard III via the chronicles of Hall and Holinshed; the Tudor myth of Richard's monstrosity serves the founding ideology of the Elizabethan state.
works.characters: Richard, Duke of Gloucester (Richard III); the Duke of Buckingham; Lady Anne; Queen Elizabeth; Queen Margaret; the Duke of Clarence; Lord Hastings; King Edward IV; the Duchess of York; Henry, Earl of Richmond; the two young Princes
works.structure: A Senecan revenge-cum-chronicle play driven by Richard's direct address — the audience as confidant — and crowned by the symmetrical dream of ghosts.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Robert Mannyng's Chronicle
works.description: Robert Mannyng of Brunne's verse history of England from Noah and the Trojan Brutus to the death of Edward I (1307), completed in 1338: the first part translates Wace's Roman de Brut, the second Peter Langtoft's French chronicle. It is the principal vernacular chronicle in English verse between Layamon and the fifteenth century.
works.plot: The poem narrates British and English history in sequence — Brutus, Arthur, the Saxon kings, the Norman Conquest, and the Plantagenet reigns — with particular fullness on the baronial wars of the thirteenth century.
works.significance: The chief English verse chronicle of the fourteenth century and a key witness to the national, vernacular historical consciousness of the period.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in the first part, six-line tail-rhyme stanzas in the second.
works.context: Completed in 1338 by Mannyng, Gilbertine canon of Sempringham, at Sixhills, for the instruction of lay readers in English history; preserved in two manuscripts, BL Harley MS 1317 and Lambeth Palace MS 131.
works.characters: Arthur; the English kings from William I to Edward I; Simon de Montfort
works.structure: A two-part regnal chronicle (Brut section; Langtoft section) with patriotic and didactic digressions.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Mannyng in the poem's own colophon.

works.title: Robinson Crusoe
altTitles: The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, of York, Mariner
works.form: novel; prose fiction in the form of a spiritual autobiography and travel relation
works.description: A first-person narrative of a mariner cast away for twenty-eight years on an uninhabited island near the mouth of the Orinoco, presented as a true history and a penitential life. It joins an extremely detailed account of material survival - building, planting, pottery, calendaring - to a providential reading of the narrator's own sins and mercies. Published in April 1719 and struck off in several issues that year, it made the individual survivor narrative the central plot of English prose fiction.
works.plot: Against his father's counsel of a middle station the York mariner sails, is taken by Sale pirates, escapes, plants a plantation in Brazil, and is wrecked in a course that leaves him sole survivor on a shore. He salvages the ship, builds a fence and a country house, learns by trial and error to make boards, earthenware, bread and goats' milk, keeps a journal, and reads scripture, gradually interpreting his preservation as conversion. He discovers a footprint, then cannibal feasts, saves a captive whom he names Friday, and with Friday and a Spaniard fights off further visitors. An English ship arriving after a mutiny carries him home by way of Brazil and land travel through hostile country, and the closing narrative reports his plantation wealth and a second, briefly summarised marriage.
works.significance: It established the material-realist individual narrative as the governing model of the rising English novel, and its treatment of labour, property, dominion and providence has made it the founding text for debates about middle-class identity, colonial possession and the philosophy of the isolated mind.
works.meter: Unornamented prose of the low or business style, with periodic sentences, accounting clauses, inventories and repeated temporal markers ('first', 'then', 'about'); the rhythm is documentary rather than rhetorical, and the couple of passages of elevated meditation are marked off by scriptural quotation.
works.context: Written in the spring and summer of 1719 out of real and romanced sources, including the marooned Alexander Selkirk, Spanish-American trade geography and the project-mongering literature of the 1690s, and printed in the same decade as the expansion of the plantation and slave trades. Its title-page assertion that the narrator is the author answered the contemporary vogue for detected 'memoirs'.
works.characters: Robinson Crusoe; Friday; Xury; the Portuguese captain of the Lisbon trade; the captain of the Brazil plantation; the mutineer mate; the Spaniard
works.structure: Continuous first-person retrospect, with embedded journal entries at the centre and a list-and-inventory mode of description; the frame of an edited 'original' account allows the narrator to comment on his own earlier blindness.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work was published without the writer's name, and the two continuations, advertised as by the same hand, establish continuity of authorship.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Roman Forgeries
altTitles: Roman Forgeries: Giving an Account of False Records
works.description: Traherne's only work published in his lifetime: an anti-Catholic polemic exposing spurious documents and legends in Roman tradition (the Donation of Constantine, fictitious councils and decrees), arguing for Protestantism on grounds of historical truth.
works.plot: Traherne catalogues and refutes alleged forgeries and false records in the Roman church's history, contending that the truth of a religion can be tested by the authenticity of its documents and tradition.
works.significance: Important as Traherne's only lifetime publication and as a document of seventeenth-century anti-Catholic polemic; it contrasts with his unpublished mystical writings.
works.meter: Argumentative, learned prose of controversial divinity.
works.context: Published in 1673 amid the anti-Catholic controversies that preceded the Popish Plot and the Exclusion Crisis, reflecting Traherne's Anglican commitment.
works.structure: A polemical treatise of historical argument and refutation.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Romeo and Juliet
altTitles: The Most Excellent and Lamentable Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet
works.description: Shakespeare's lyric tragedy of young love: the star-crossed children of Verona's feuding houses meet at the Capulet feast, marry in secret, and are destroyed by chance and haste — the deaths of Mercutio and Tybalt, the exile, the sleeping potion, and the double suicide in the tomb that reconciles the houses too late.
works.plot: Romeo and Juliet fall in love across the family feud; Friar Laurence marries them; the street brawl kills Mercutio and Tybalt and exiles Romeo; the Capulets press Paris's suit; Juliet takes the friar's potion; the undelivered letter dooms the lovers; and the play ends with the discovery in the tomb and the prince's judgment on 'a glooming peace'.
works.significance: The archetype of the love tragedy in world literature — the play that fixed 'star-crossed lovers' in the language and on every subsequent stage and screen.
works.meter: The lovers' first dialogue is a shared sonnet; the play's verse runs from Mercutio's prose fantasia on Queen Mab to Juliet's aubade, with the final couplets of the tomb scene.
works.context: Written about 1595–96 from Arthur Brooke's poem Romeus and Juliet (1562) via continental novella; printed in quarto in 1597 and in a fuller text in 1599.
works.characters: Romeo; Juliet; Friar Laurence; Mercutio; Tybalt; the Nurse; Benvolio; Lord and Lady Capulet; Lord and Lady Montague; Paris; Prince Escalus
works.structure: A five-act tragedy of accelerating momentum — comedy in the first two acts, catastrophe in the last — built on the sonnet-form exchanges of the lovers and the antitheses of love and hate.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Rosalynde
works.description: Lodge's pastoral romance, the direct source of Shakespeare's As You Like It: Rosader (Orlando), disinherited by his brother, flees to the forest of Arden, where the banished king, the disguised Rosalynde, and the shepherds' loves play out the courtships, disguises, and recognitions of the greenwood — the whole styled 'Euphues' golden legacy' and salted with eclogues.
works.plot: Saladyne's cruelty drives Rosader to the forest; Rosalynde, banished by the usurper Torismond, walks there disguised as Ganymede; the lovers' meetings in disguise, the lion's attack, the rescue of Saladyne, and the final scene's restorations — the true king, the brothers, and the three marriages — close the romance in Arden's court.
works.significance: The pastoral romance that became one of Shakespeare's greatest comedies — the greenwood's prose and the stage's poetry in one tradition.
works.meter: Euphuistic prose with pastoral verse, in Lodge's sweetest and most musical register.
works.context: Published 1590, at the height of the pastoral vogue; Shakespeare followed its plot closely in As You Like It (1599), keeping the forest, the disguises, and even the names of Phoebe and Adam.
works.characters: Rosader; Rosalynde (Ganymede); Saladyne; Alinda (Aliena); Torismond; Gerismond the exiled king; Phoebe; Montanus; Corydon; Adam Spencer
works.structure: A prose romance of exile and disguise in the pastoral mode, with verse eclogues and the euphuistic style of its subtitle.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Rosalynde: Euphues Golden Legacie

works.title: Roxana
altTitles: The Fortunate Mistress: Or, a History of the Life and Most Surprising Adventures of a Lady
works.form: novel; confessional and picaresque prose fiction
works.description: The last and most searching of the great fictional confessions of the 1720s, the career of a woman who converts her own person into an asset and rises from a silk-stockinger's daughter to the mistress of a duke and the envy of the town. It is the most coolly ironic of the series, withholding the penitence its heroine repeatedly promises and making the reader wait for an ending the narrative refuses to supply.
works.plot: Married against her inclination and then abandoned by a husband ruined in trade, she persuades herself that virtue is a word used by the poor to keep them poor, and becomes successively the wife, mistress and pensioner of a series of men in England and on the Continent, accumulating fortunes in Holland and Paris. She returns to London, is courted by a nobleman whom she refuses to marry, discovers that a former husband and her own daughter have tracked her down, and ends in want and remorse, the loss of her child and the collapse of her design being the catastrophe she cannot argument her way out of.
works.significance: It is the most radical study of the marriage market in early fiction and a key text for the debate about whether the eighteenth-century novel could represent female desire without punishing it; its unfinished ending has generated a large critical literature.
works.meter: An elaborate argumentative prose of casuistry, full of self-interrogation, exclamation and the repeated counting of stocks; the colloquy with Amy supplies a dialogue of conscience inside the monologue.
works.context: Published in 1724 in the wake of the South Sea bubble and its aftermath of fortune-hunters and bigamy scandals, and drawing on the continental travel and money-market knowledge of the author's earlier project writing.
works.characters: Roxana; her husband the silk merchant; the Scottish landowner; the Duke of M.; the Dutch merchant; Susan, the lost daughter; Amy, the confidante
works.structure: First-person confessional retrospect with a self-consciously unfinished close; the irony is generated by the gap between the narrator's casuistry and the events she reports, and the Dutch and French sections slow into a series of reckonings.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the name Roxana is the heroine's own assumption in the narrative and the convenient title established by later editors.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Salmacida Spolia
works.description: The last masque performed at the court of Charles I, presented at Whitehall on 21 January 1640 with designs by Inigo Jones and with the young Prince Charles and his brothers among the masquers.
works.plot: Discord, in the person of a malicious spirit, has troubled the land; Wisdom and the genius of Britain, embodied in the king, restore concord, and the masquers descend to dance with the ladies.
works.significance: The final Caroline masque and a poignant document of a court culture on the eve of destruction; it also marks Davenant's official succession to Jonson as laureate.
works.meter: Verse and song with prose description; Inigo Jones's scenery and machinery.
works.context: Presented at Whitehall in January 1640, months before the calling of the Short Parliament and the collapse of Charles's personal rule; Davenant had been made Poet Laureate in 1638 on Jonson's death.
works.characters: Discord; Wisdom; the Genius of Britain; the masquers
works.structure: The standard court masque form: antimasque of discord, main masque of harmony, and the revels.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Davenant as laureate; Jones's designs are documented.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum
works.description: Aemilia Lanyer's volume of sacred poetry, one of the first books of poems published by an Englishwoman: the long title poem on Christ's Passion — with its celebrated 'Eve's Apology' defending women against the blame of the Fall — framed by the eleven dedicatory poems to the great ladies of the court and followed by 'The Description of Cooke-ham', the first country-house poem in English.
works.plot: The Passion poem narrates Christ's betrayal, trial, and crucifixion through the eyes of the women who followed him, with Pilate's wife's dream and the 'Eve's Apology' arguing women's innocence and worth; the dedications praise the Queen, the Countess of Pembroke, and the other patronesses; and Cooke-ham celebrates the estate of Margaret Clifford, Countess of Cumberland, in the farewell of its trees and walks.
works.significance: A founding text of English women's poetry — the first sustained feminist argument in English verse, and the first country-house poem.
works.meter: Rhyme royal for the Passion poem, with the varied stanzas of the dedications and the elegiac couplets of Cooke-ham.
works.context: Published 1611, in the year of the King James Bible, by a woman of the court's margins; its argument for women's learning and worth answered the querelle des femmes with theology, and its Cooke-ham preceded Jonson's 'To Penshurst' in the country-house genre.
works.characters: Christ; Pilate's wife; Eve; the women of Jerusalem; Margaret Clifford, Countess of Cumberland; Anne Clifford; the dedicatees
works.structure: A tripartite volume — dedications, Passion poem, country-house poem — organized as a woman's address to women, the patrons and readers its intended audience.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Poems of Aemilia Lanyer

works.title: Samson Agonistes
works.description: A Greek tragedy in English on the blind Hebrew hero Samson, written to be read rather than performed: imprisoned and blinded by the Philistines, Samson moves from despair to renewed faith and, at the feast of Dagon, pulls down the temple, destroying himself and his enemies in an act of divine vengeance.
works.plot: Samson laments his blindness and capture; he is visited in turn by the Chorus of Danites, his father Manoah, his wife Dalila, and the giant Harapha; summoned to make sport before the Philistine lords at the temple of Dagon, he prays for strength, topples the pillars, and dies triumphantly with his enemies.
works.significance: The greatest English example of classical closet tragedy, it fuses Greek form with Hebrew subject and Milton's own condition, and has generated sustained debate about its violence, its politics, and its catharsis.
works.meter: Blank verse with choruses in varied lyric meters, using the Greek tragic forms of strophe and antistrophe.
works.context: Published with Paradise Regained in 1671; the blinded, politically defeated hero has long been read as a figure of Milton himself after the Restoration, and the play engages the problem of violent divine justice.
works.characters: Samson; the Chorus of Danites; Manoah; Dalila; Harapha; the Philistine Officer; the Messenger
works.structure: A classical drama observing the unities of time and place, with chorus, stichomythia, messenger, and catharsis, modeled on Sophocles and Aeschylus.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the title page notes it was 'never intended' for the stage.

The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton
editions.editor: William Kerrigan, John Rumrich, and Stephen M. Fallon (eds.)

works.title: Sapho and Phao
works.description: Lyly's mythological court comedy: the ferryman Phao, made beautiful by Venus, is loved by the queen Sapho; Venus, jealous of the queen she meant to humble, afflicts Phao with love of herself; and the play resolves through Cupid's arrows and Sybilla's lore into Sapho's triumph over Venus and the renunciation of Phao's love.
works.plot: Venus, angered by Sapho's chastity, arms Cupid against her; the arrows misfire, Phao is loved and Sapho infatuated; the court's debates (between the scholars and the women) anatomize love; Sybilla's counsel and Venus's flight end the play with Sapho restored to rule and Phao banished from desire.
works.significance: The classic of the Elizabethan mythological court play — a genre in which the Queen's own image was negotiated on stage.
works.meter: Prose of Euphuistic balance, with songs and the debate set pieces.
works.context: Performed at court in 1584 and printed the same year; its Sapho is read as a mirror of Elizabeth I, and its love-psychology answers the Alençon courtship debates of the early 1580s.
works.characters: Sapho; Phao; Venus; Cupid; Sybilla; the court ladies; the scholars; the pages
works.structure: A five-act mythological debate-comedy of the Ovidian type, with the low comedy of the pages and servants as counterpoint.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Complete Works of John Lyly, 3 vols.

works.title: Satires
works.description: Donne's five formal verse satires of the 1590s — on the foppish courtier, the corrupt lawyer, religion and the quest for true church, the court, and the suitors and officers of the law — the poems that established the English formal satire and prompted the 1599 ban on satires, with their Juvenalian 'railing' and their portrait of Elizabethan London's vices.
works.plot: Each satire is a walk through a vice — the courtier's affectations, the lawyer's bribes, the sects' errors, the court's vanity, the law's extortion — with the poet as reluctant companion and ironist, and the third satire's 'On a huge hill, / Cragged and steep, Truth stands' as the sequence's moral summit.
works.significance: The foundation of English formal satire — the model for Pope's couplet and for every later poet of the town's vices.
works.meter: Rough, deliberately harsh heroic couplets — 'strong lines' — whose jagged enjambment and parenthesis imitated the speech of the town and the Roman satirists' abruptness.
works.context: Written 1593–98, in the decade that also produced the satires of Hall and Marston; the bishops' ban of 1599, which ordered the burning of satires, answered this vogue directly.
works.characters: the satirist; the fop; the lawyer; the courtier; the officers and suitors
works.structure: Five numbered satires in the formal Roman manner, each a single scene or progress through the city, in the couplet form Donne hardened into an instrument of speech.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: John Donne: The Complete English Poems
The Complete Poems of John Donne

works.title: Sawles Warde
works.description: An allegorical homily in AB-language prose on the custody of the soul: the house of the body is governed by Wit and Will, guarded by the five senses, threatened by the devil, and comforted by the virtues and the joys of heaven. It adapts Hugh of St Victor's De Anima and is the earliest extended allegory of the inner life in English prose.
works.plot: Wit (reason), with his wife Will, rules the soul's house; the messenger Fear of Death warns of the devil's assaults; the virtues — Prudence, Strength, Moderation, Righteousness — and the vision of the heavenly bliss fortify the household against temptation.
works.significance: A foundation stone of English allegory: its personified psychology anticipates the moralities (The Castle of Perseverance) and the dream allegories of the fourteenth century.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative AB-language prose.
works.context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands, adapting Hugh of St Victor; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34, BL Cotton MS Titus D.xviii, and Royal MS 17 A.xxvii.
works.characters: Wit; Will; Fear of Death; the Virtues; the Devil
works.structure: A continuous allegorical narrative built on the house/castle metaphor, with set-piece descriptions of the pains of hell and the joys of heaven.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Scots Wha Hae
altTitles: Scots, wha hae wi' Wallace bled
works.form: persona song and war lyric set to a traditional march air, in the national-song mode of the 1790s
works.description: Burns's war-song written in the voice of Bruce addressing his men before Bannockburn, and the most powerful political lyric of the 1790s in Scotland. Under the cover of the fourteenth-century battle it speaks the language of liberty and of servile dependence in the present, and its challenge - who will be a slave, who a freeman - made publishers hesitate to print it anonymously as an old song. It is the classic instance of Burns turning national history into a democratic battle hymn.
works.plot: Bruce calls on the Scots who bled with Wallace to remember the days that made their names, and sets the tyrant's hirelings against the freemen who fight for their own land. The song demands the choice of slavery or liberty in the strictest terms, promises the reward of victory and the shame of the slave, and ends with the call to share the battle and its prize. The historical speaker makes the contemporary application unmistakable without naming it.
works.significance: It became one of the national songs of Scotland and a standard text of the literature of liberty, admired for its concentration and for its way of making medieval history speak to contemporary radicalism. Its use as a battle and commemorative hymn, and its place in the song repertory of the nations, make it a central document of the 1790s bardic revival.
works.meter: Four-beat Scots lines in short stanzas with a strong march rhythm, adapted to the air of Bruce's March; the diction is imperious and monosyllabic, with the refrain-like closing address.
works.context: Composed in the summer of 1793, in the excitement and repression that followed the French Revolution and the trials of the king, when Burns's radical sympathies were constrained by his office in the excise, to which he had been appointed in 1789; it was contributed to Johnson's musical collection as a song of the northern nation, and its publication raised the question of political offence.
works.characters: Robert the Bruce; the Scots host; Edward of England as the tyrant; Wallace as the remembered leader
works.structure: A short strophic song in the persona of Bruce, each stanza advancing the exhortation from memory of Wallace to the present choice, the threat of the tyrant, and the final rally.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is fixed by Burns's own letter to Johnson in the summer of 1793, and the printing of the song in the musical collection is documented, though the volumes' issue dates have been variously reckoned.

editions.title: The Poems of Robert Burns, 3 volumes

works.title: Seasons for Fasting
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Additional MS 43703 (a sixteenth-century transcript by Laurence Nowell of the lost Cotton Otho B.xi)
works.description: A poem of some 230 lines on the proper observance of the Ember fasts, defending the English custom of four seasonal fasts against the laxity of those who fast only once a year, and citing biblical and canonical authority for the practice. The text breaks off imperfectly.
works.plot: The poet rebukes priests who observe the Ember days wrongly, argues from scripture (Moses, Elijah, the Ninevites, Christ's forty days) that fasting is commanded, sets out the correct times of the four seasonal fasts, and attacks drunken priests; the poem ends incomplete amid a catalogue of fasts.
works.significance: A rare Old English poem on a live question of ecclesiastical discipline, valuable for its picture of eleventh-century religious controversy and its fusion of homiletic and satirical verse.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the homiletic urgency of Wulfstan's prose; the text is incomplete, and some lines are metrically irregular.
works.context: The poem belongs to the late Old English period's debates over ecclesiastical discipline, contemporary with Wulfstan's legislation on fasting and the reform of the clergy; its strictures on drunken priests echo the reformers' campaigns.
works.structure: An argumentative structure: rebuke, biblical proof-texts, prescription of the fasts, and invective against clerical abuses, in the manner of Wulfstanian homiletic verse.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The poem's Wulfstanian manner has suggested to some scholars an origin in his circle, but no attribution is established.

works.title: Sejanus His Fall
works.description: Jonson's Roman tragedy of the favourite's fall: the ambitious Sejanus, minister of Tiberius, destroys the house of Germanicus piece by piece and rises toward the throne itself — until Tiberius's letter from Capri, read in the Senate, turns the city against him, and the mob tears him to pieces in the streets, his children executed, his statues melted down.
works.plot: Sejanus corrupts and removes Drusus, Agrippina, and their sons; the senators' servility and the informers' trade fill the middle acts; the emperor's withdrawal and the counter-plot of Macro prepare the fall; the Senate scene reverses Sejanus's fortunes in a single letter, and the final act follows the executioners through the city's vengeance.
works.significance: The first great English political tragedy of the Jacobean age and the founding text of the Roman play's documentary tradition.
works.meter: A grave, scholarly blank verse with extensive marginal annotation in the printed text — the play as documented history.
works.context: Performed at the Globe in 1603 (with Shakespeare in the cast), then revised for print in 1605, with Jonson's marginal notes citing his classical authorities; it landed him before the Privy Council on charges of 'popery and treason'.
works.characters: Sejanus; Tiberius; Macro; Silius; Arruntius; Agrippina; Drusus; Livia; the Senate; Cordus; Natta; Eudemus
works.structure: A five-act tragedy of state built on Tacitus, with the Senate scenes as its rhetorical engine and the messenger's report of the mob's savagery as its climax.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the original Globe version contained a share by another hand, which Jonson replaced for the printed text.

editions.title: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, 7 vols.
editions.editor: David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (gen. eds.)

works.title: Sensibility
altTitles: Sensibility. A Poem. In Two Parts
works.description: A moral essay in couplets on the culture of feeling, distinguishing a true from a false sensibility and arguing that tenderness without principle is a form of self-love. It was the first considerable poem of its author and established her reputation in the fashionable literary world.
works.plot: The poet examines the temper of the age, in which the refinement of feeling has been mistaken for virtue, and shows the man of sensibility pursuing his own pleasure under the colour of sympathy. Examples of the false and the real are contrasted - the suffering of the poor, the distress of friendship, the duties that a feeling heart evades. The second part passes to the consolation of religion and to the assertion that sensibility must be governed by duty and by the hope of another world.
works.significance: It is one of the clearest early statements of the case against the ethics of feeling, and it announced a career that was to span the century's passage from fashionable sensibility to evangelical duty.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of the Augustan school, with the closed and balanced antithesis of the sententious line and the occasional pathetical pause.
works.context: Published in 1773, in the height of the cult of sensibility and of the first attacks upon it, and written by a young woman of the Bath and London literary circles who was shortly to become a dramatist and a conduct writer.
works.structure: A discursive poem in two parts, opening with a complaint of the manners of the age, passing through instances and characters, and closing in an elevation of principle.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and reprinted in her collected verse.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Sensus Communis: An Essay on Wit and Humour
altTitles: Sensus Communis, an Essay on Wit and Humour
authors: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
works.description: Shaftesbury's essay on wit, written as a friendly critique of Anthony Collins's Essay Concerning the Use of Reason and issued the same year as the Letter Concerning Enthusiasm. It proposes ridicule as the proper test of wit and of whatever claims assent, and distinguishes true raillery, which supports sociability and liberty of thought, from the spleen and ignorance of the mere witling.
works.plot: The essay opens on the character of a book and the conditions of free examination, then passes to an anatomy of wit and humour, classifying wits by their governing humour. Shaftesbury insists that ridicule, like reason, must be exercised freely and without fear, since a doctrine or religion that cannot endure to be ill-used deserves to be. He distinguishes genuine raillery, addressed to opinions and manners, from personal abuse, and traces modern wit to a mixture of the fine and the humorous. The argument closes with a defence of good manners in raillery and an appeal to common sense as the public standard of the ridiculous.
works.significance: It gave the century its most influential account of ridicule as a criterion of truth and civility, directly conditioning Addison's papers, Pope's doctrine of wit, and later theories of humour and the comic.
works.meter: Conversational, pointed prose in the manner of a letter to a friend, rich in distinctions, short definitions, and barbed asides; passages of rhythmic tripartite enumeration give it the feel of spoken raillery.
works.context: Printed in 1709 amid the freethinking debates opened by Collins and Toland, and written in dialogue with the author of A Discourse of the Liberty of the Press, whose press Shaftesbury praises while disagreeing with his conclusion. It forms part of what became the Characteristics.
works.structure: A single discursive essay in loose epistolary form, moving from the conditions of free enquiry through a classification of wits to the doctrine of ridicule as test.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Serious Reflections During the Life and Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
altTitles: Serious Reflections During the Life and Afflicting Circumstances of Robinson Crusoe
works.form: meditative and didactic prose essays in a fictional persona
works.description: The third Crusoe volume, a collection of meditations, dialogues and practical essays put into the mouth of the retired islander. It abandons narrative for moral reflection on providence, solitude, the fear of man, temperance and the duties of a master, and is organised as a set of numbered serious thoughts.
works.plot: The narrator, now settled and prospering, meditates on the religious meanings of his preservation, debates with imagined interlocutors the questions of conscience and enthusiasm, reflects on the condition of servants, wives and children, and argues that a Christian's true business is the government of his own passions. The volume adds visionary and allegorical papers on the invisible world, including a dialogue with the soul and a description of the world of spirits.
works.significance: It supplies the strongest internal evidence of the moral and religious frame that contemporaries read in the first volume, and its mixed reception marked the boundary between fiction and edification in the early-eighteenth-century book trade.
works.meter: Serious plain prose of the conduct-book manner, with balancing clauses, scriptural tags and the interrogative turn of meditation; the allegorical papers admit a more ornate visionary rhetoric.
works.context: Published in the same year as the second volume and in the wake of controversies over enthusiasm and natural religion, it draws on the Puritan tradition of the serious meditation and on the 1710s vogue for soliloquy on the passions.
works.characters: Robinson Crusoe; the imagined interlocutor; Friday as a figure of natural religion; the narrator's own soul
works.structure: A serial of short reflective papers rather than a continuous plot, with inset dialogues and a few narrative fragments; the Crusoe persona functions as a mask for a moralist.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested, though the volume has conventionally been treated as the weakest of the three; the title-page carries the same fictional persona as its warrant.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Sermo Lupi ad Anglos
altTitles: The Sermon of the Wolf to the English
works.description: Wulfstan's most famous sermon, preached in the crisis year 1014 as the Danish conquest of England was completed: an impassioned jeremiad interpreting the Viking devastation as God's punishment for the nation's sins, culminating in the vision of the enslaved nation — 'an Englishman is not worth more to a Dane than a dog'. The masterpiece of Old English pulpit rhetoric.
works.plot: The sermon catalogues the nation's sins — betrayal of lords, perjury, oppression of the poor, the violation of churches — and reads the tribulations of Æthelred's reign (the treachery of Eadric Streona, the burning, plundering, and enslavement of the people) as the biblical pattern of divine wrath; it calls the nation to repentance before the last things overtake it, in a crescendo of Wulfstan's two-stress rhythms.
works.significance: The greatest Old English sermon and the classic statement of the period's theology of national sin.
works.meter: Wulfstan's rhythmical prose: two-stress phrases, alliteration, anaphora, and word-pairs ('byman and bærnan' — burn and ravage).
works.context: Preached in 1014, after the expulsion of Æthelred and before Cnut's final conquest (1016); preserved in five manuscripts, including British Library, Cotton MS Nero A.i.
works.characters: Wulfstan (preacher, as 'Lupus'); the English nation
works.structure: A single continuous exhortation built on the antithesis of sin and punishment, with the historical crisis framed as the fulfilment of prophecy.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan's authorship is certain ('Lupus' is his Latin signature).

editions.title: The Homilies of Wulfstan

sources: The Pilgrim's Progress

works.title: Sermon of the Plough
works.description: Hugh Latimer's most famous sermon, preached at Paul's Cross on 18 January 1548 and printed the same year; the classic Protestant sermon of social criticism, built on the text of the sower.
works.plot: Taking the gospel of the sower, Latimer expounds the 'plough' of preaching, the 'seed' of God's word, and the spiritual husbandry required of clergy and laity alike; he attacks the idleness of prelates ('unpreaching prelates'), the rack-renting of landlords, and the neglect of the poor, calling the realm to the work of the spiritual plough — a sustained sermon of estates satire turned to gospel ends.
works.significance: The most celebrated English sermon of the Reformation: its homely agricultural allegory and its fearless attack on clerical and landlord abuses made it the model of the Protestant pulpit's social criticism from the sixteenth century to the nineteenth.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Preached at Paul's Cross on 18 January 1548, in the first months of Edward VI's reign, as part of the reform campaign against images and non-residence; printed by John Day in 1548 and reprinted through the century, the sermon made Latimer the voice of the Edwardian Reformation's social conscience.
works.structure: A single sermon structured by the parable's allegory — the plough, the seed, the soil — with digressions into the abuses of church and commonwealth.

editions.title: Sermons by Hugh Latimer

works.title: Sermons (Hugh Blair)
works.form: published pulpit oratory and practical divinity, in the polite sermon tradition of the eighteenth century
works.description: The collected sermons of Blair, minister of St Giles's in Edinburgh and the most widely read Scottish preacher of his generation, issued from the later 1770s and reprinted across the English-speaking world. They exhibit the temperament of moderated Augustan pulpit oratory: practical, moral, polished, addressed to the feelings and to the conduct of ordinary life rather than to doctrinal controversy. Their success made Blair the standard model of the polite sermon and a central presence in the rhetoric of the Scottish Enlightenment.
works.plot: The discourses take up the duties of the Christian life - the government of the passions, the duties of social and family conduct, the improvement of the mind, the conduct of affliction and the hope of a future state - and expound their texts with an orderly argument from observation of human feeling to practical application. Blair's handling of the parables and of the gospel history is narrative and affective, and his perorations press the auditor toward self-examination without invoking terrors.
works.significance: The Sermons were among the most reprinted religious books of the age, admired for their style by Blair's Scottish auditors and by the French and German translators who used them. They supply the practical counterpart to the Lectures on Rhetoric and remain the standard illustration of polite pulpit oratory in the culture of feeling.
works.meter: Prose; the balanced period, the graduated triple, the measured cadence and the clear syllabic emphasis for which Blair's theory of elocution was written into his own practice.
works.context: Preached and collected in the decades of Blair's incumbency at St Giles's and of his Edinburgh professorship of rhetoric and belles lettres, when the moderated Calvinism of the Scottish church and the culture of feeling met in the pulpit, and when the sermon was a literary genre with a substantial print market.
works.structure: A serial volume of separately preached discourses, each a single argument with an opening explication of the text, a progression of reflections and a closing application; the several series were gathered in successive volumes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the several series of Blair's Sermons appeared across the later eighteenth century and the volumes are documented by his own publication of them, so the date entered here is that of the first collected series, with the later volumes described in the note.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel
altTitles: Fifteen Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel
Sermons, Founded on Several Occasions, Preached at the Rolls Chapel, in Chancery Lane
works.description: Butler's early sermon sequence on human nature, conscience, and the authority of reflection, preached at the Rolls in the 1720s and published as a philosophical defence of the natural constitution of moral agents. Its central claim, that conscience is by nature authoritative in man, answers Mandeville, Hobbes, and Shaftesbury at once.
works.plot: Butler argues first that human nature is a system, not a heap of instincts, in which self-love and benevolence are naturally implanted and commonly coincide. Against psychological egoism he shows that particular passions have their own objects, and that pursuing them, not self, is the true path to happiness. Reflection or conscience surveys our actions and approves or disapproves with a natural authority that is one of degree as well as strength; to follow it is the case of the whole creature. The later sermons treat self-deception, the pursuit of pleasure, and the respect owing to conscience, grounding religion in the same constitution that grounds morality.
works.significance: The Preface and sermons anticipated the theories of benevolence, conscience, and authority debated by Hume, Reid, and the intuitionists, and remain the most-cited eighteenth-century text in moral philosophy besides the Treatise.
works.meter: The plain, exact, cumulative prose of the pulpit turned to analytic purpose: distinction after distinction, quietly weighted, with an unwonted precision of definition.
works.context: Preached between 1719 and 1725 before a Rolls audience drawn from the chancery bar, amid the Mandeville and Shaftesbury debates on self-love; the sermons were published in 1726 with a Preface that became a locus classicus of moral philosophy.
works.structure: A collected series of fifteen sermons with an analytical Preface, each sermon isolating one branch of the argument from human nature.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Sermons upon Several Occasions (Tillotson)
altTitles: The Works of the Most Reverend Dr John Tillotson
works.description: The collected sermons of John Tillotson, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1691, published posthumously by his chaplain Ralph Barker; they are the model of latitudinarian preaching and were among the most widely read religious works of the eighteenth century.
works.plot: The sermons expound a rational, moral, and tolerant Christianity: the reasonableness of revelation, the duties of charity and justice, the evil of strife and persecution, and the practical character of true religion.
works.significance: Tillotson's sermons defined latitudinarian prose style and were a principal influence on Addison, Swift's models of plain preaching, and the moral temper of eighteenth-century Anglicanism.
works.meter: Clear, balanced, plain prose that became the standard of English pulpit eloquence.
works.context: Tillotson preached at St Lawrence Jewry and at court through the Restoration and after the Revolution; he was made Archbishop of Canterbury in 1691 and died in 1694; the folio of his Works appeared in 1696.
works.structure: A collection of occasional sermons arranged by subject and occasion.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Tillotson; the posthumous collection was edited by Ralph Barker.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Shakespear Illustrated
altTitles: Shakespear Illustrated: Containing the Genuine Plot of His Best Plays, Proving That They Are Translations from the Italian, Spanish and French
Shakespear Illustrated, with Essays Proving His Plays Translations
works.form: critical treatise with comparative abstracts of sources
works.description: A critical collection proving from the antecedent tales that the plots of Shakespeare's best plays are borrowed from Italian, Spanish and French originals, each play being faced with an abstract of the source. Its prefatory discourse on the properties of drama is an early statement of neoclassical plot doctrine in English criticism.
works.plot: The work examines a sequence of the plays - among them Othello, Measure for Measure, All's Well That Ends Well, Romeo and Juliet and The Taming of the Shrew - and sets against each the story Shakespeare found. It shows the plot as given, the alterations as made, and argues that the poet's judgement rather than his invention is to be praised or blamed. The prefatory discourse draws the conclusion that fidelity to probability and to the unities is the measure of dramatic merit.
works.significance: It is an important document of source study before scholarship and of the eighteenth-century argument about Shakespeare's obligations to the romance tradition, anticipating later source criticism.
works.meter: Plain argumentative prose of the mid-century critical essay, with the quoted abstracts in a deliberately bald narrative style.
works.context: Published in 1753 in two volumes, in the season of the great editions of Shakespeare and of the quarrel over his regularity, and written by a novelist-critic with access to the Italian and Spanish sources through translation.
works.structure: A series of comparative essays, each pairing an abstract of the source with remarks on the play, framed by a general discourse on the drama; the argument is cumulative and evidential.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name, though early bibliographers occasionally misassigned it.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Shakespeare's Sonnets
works.description: The 154 sonnets printed in 1609, with the long poem 'A Lover's Complaint' appended: a sequence to a beautiful young man urging him to marry and immortalizing him in verse, shadowed by a rival poet and by the 'dark lady' of the later sonnets — the greatest sonnet collection in the language, and the most argued-over book of poems in English literary history.
works.plot: The first seventeen sonnets press the youth to marry; the middle poems anatomize love, jealousy, absence, and the rival poet; the dark lady sequence (127–152) turns on lust and self-betrayal; and the final poems rework Cupid and the cures of love, closing with 'A Lover's Complaint' spoken by a forsaken maid.
works.significance: The summit of the English sonnet tradition; its identities, erotic shapes, and textual mysteries have made it a permanent site of scholarship and dispute.
works.meter: The Shakespearean sonnet (abab cdcd efef gg) brought to its definitive form, with 'A Lover's Complaint' in rhyme royal.
works.context: Composed across the 1590s and early 1600s, partly circulating in manuscript; printed by Thomas Thorpe in 1609 with the dedication 'To the onlie begetter of these insuing sonnets, Mr. W.H.' — the most famous crux in English bibliography.
works.characters: the poet; the young man (Fair Youth); the dark lady; the rival poet; the maid (in the Complaint)
works.structure: A sequence of 154 sonnets with a detectable narrative arc — courtship, crisis, self-reproach — followed by the appended complaint.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Shakespeare's; the identities of the Fair Youth, the dark lady, and 'Mr. W.H.' remain unknown.

works.title: Shamela
works.form: short epistolary burlesque and prose satire
works.description: A short burlesque of the servant-girl novel, published anonymously in the same season as its original, which turns the heroine's letters into the devices of an artful seductress pursuing her aim. It is the earliest and sharpest of the answers to the conduct fiction, arguing from inside the form that its morality was interested.
works.plot: Shamela Andrews, a country servant with an eye on her mistress's estate, writes letters home rehearsing her own arts of attack and defence. She is courted, resisted and finally complied with on her own schedule, her scruples being the scruples of design, and she secures a proposal from the squire while keeping the old woman and the parson in play. The piece ends with her married and in possession, the pretence of virtue having served the whole design.
works.significance: It invented the technique of the ideologically inverted parody and remains the standard instance of the eighteenth-century argument that the novel of moral reward was a fiction of interest; it also led directly to the author's own theory of comic prose.
works.meter: A debased copy of the servant style, with the idiom and misspellings of the original mocked and the candid sentences of the design breaking through the piety.
works.context: Published in April 1741, three months after the conduct novel it answers, in a season crowded with its imitations and abridgements; the pamphlet war over the education of women and the price of virtue formed its immediate context.
works.characters: Shamela Andrews; Squire Booby; Parson Williams; Mrs. Slipslop; the old lady of the family
works.structure: An epistolary burlesque in a single short volume, the letters' dates and self-exposures replacing the original's suspense; the prefatorial apparatus directs the reading as party attack.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution long anonymous and established by internal evidence, the contemporary advertisement and later acknowledgment; recorded here as single.
