works.title: The Battle of the Books
altTitles: The Battle of the Books: A Paper, which was Read in a Great Club
works.description: Swift's short ironic allegory of the quarrel of the ancients and the moderns, in which the spider and the bee dispute over their claims to invention and to the honey of the hive, and the modern critick is defeated in the library of St James's.
works.plot: The narrator enters the court library at the moment when the ancient and modern books fall out; the spider, who spins all things from his own bowels, and the bee, who gathers from abroad and digests what it collects, plead their rival causes, and the battle of the ants, the wasp and the critick ends with the ancient party's discomfiture and a joke at the author's expense.
works.significance: It fixed the image of the two kinds of writer, the spider and the bee, and turned the rules-of-art quarrel into a durable piece of English literary mythology.
works.meter: Plain Swiftian prose of the fable and the character, with the balanced pleading of the two rivals and the abrupt deflating close.
works.context: Written in the season of Wotton's and Bentley's engagement over the quality of modern learning and of Temple's essay on ancient and modern discipline, and printed with the Tale of a Tub in 1704; it is the founding document of the Scribleran war against the modern critick.
works.characters: the spider; the bee; the wasp; the critick; the narrator who reports the scene
works.structure: A brief narrative frame containing an allegorical dispute and a battle piece, closed by an authorial rebuke to the reporter.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the piece was long circulated in manuscript before its 1704 printing.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Beaux' Stratagem
works.description: Farquhar's last and greatest comedy, written on his deathbed, in which the fortune-hunters Archer and Aimwell arrive at Lichfield to repair their ruined estates and encounter the unhappily married Mrs Sullen.
works.plot: Archer and Aimwell take turns posing as lord and servant at Lichfield; Aimwell courts Dorinda, Archer is drawn into the unhappy marriage of Mrs Sullen and Sullen; a highway robbery, a French invasion scare, and the discovery that Aimwell is not the real lord resolve the plot in marriage and reconciliation.
works.significance: The finest comedy of the early eighteenth century and the culmination of the Restoration tradition; its treatment of divorce and of provincial English society was ahead of its time, and it has been continuously revived since.
works.meter: Prose of remarkable richness and speed.
works.context: Performed at the Queen's Theatre in the Haymarket on 8 March 1707 and published the same year; Farquhar died in March or April 1707, weeks after the first performance.
works.characters: Archer; Aimwell; Mrs Sullen; Sullen; Dorinda; Lady Bountiful; Cherry; Boniface; Gibbet; Count Bellairde; Foigard
works.structure: Five acts with the celebrated bedroom scene (III.iii) in which Archer and Mrs Sullen debate marriage and divorce.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Farquhar; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Beggar's Opera
works.description: Gay's ballad opera, proposed by Pope as a burlesque of the Italian heroic opera, in which the highwayman, the thief-taker and the Newgate clerks are made to sing the airs of the town, and the criminal economy of the city is staged as the mirror of high life.
works.plot: Macheath, the gay highwayman, is betrayed by Peachum to Lockit and to the gallows, having married both Polly and Lucy; the rival fathers scheme, the gang quarrels, and the last-minute reprieve, protested by the Beggar who superintends the piece, exposes the convention by which the hero of quality escapes the rope.
works.significance: It created the ballad opera, made the criminal underworld the true subject of a musical entertainment, and remains the century's most sustained identification of the gallows and the drawing room as one economy.
works.meter: Ballad and song stanzas of the street and the theatre, set to borrowed airs, alternating with prose dialogue; the metres are those of the popular tune rather than of the dramatic blank verse.
works.context: First performed and printed in the season of the London opera companies' triumph with Handel's Italian dramas, and of the South Sea collapse, when the language of credit, the press gang and the property of the stage were all in dispute; the work was licensed without difficulty and became the most pirated text of the decade.
works.characters: Macheath; Peachum; Lockit; Polly Peachum; Lucy Lockit; the gang; the Beggar; the Player
works.structure: An opera in three acts with spoken dialogue between the airs, framed by the Beggar's argument with the poet and the composer about probability and about the fate of the hero.
works.attributionNotes: Gay's, on the plan suggested by Pope; the airs, the tunes and the many pirated keys and continuations are other men's work.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Belle's Stratagem
works.form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: The most successful comedy by a woman dramatist of the late eighteenth century, in which a young woman determined to be won rather than to win pursues the man she loves through a series of disguises. Its heroine's stratagems make it the most direct descendant on the stage of the amatory fiction of the earlier century.
works.plot: Letitia Hardy, promised to a young man of fortune who does not know her worth, resolves to make him pursue her by assuming a different woman each night, first as a neighbour's daughter and then in other persons of the town. Her friend and the gallants of her father's circle are drawn into the design, and the lovers' fathers make their own plans of marriage. The last stratagem brings the lover to a declaration, and the discoveries justify the heroine's conduct and complete the match.
works.significance: It holds the place of the century's most durable comedy by a woman playwright and is a key text for the history of the female plotter in drama and of the theatrical revival of romantic disguise.
works.meter: A bright prose dialogue of retort and affected persons, with the disguised speeches carrying the satire of fashionable address; the songs and letters serve as set pieces.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1780, in the season in which the woman dramatist became a regular attraction of the theatres and in which the old device of personation was revived for a polite audience.
works.characters: Letitia Hardy; Dorilton, the lover she must win; her friend of the stratagems; the fathers who arrange the matches; the gallants and the imposed-with company
works.structure: Five-act comedy of personation, the successive disguises supplying the movement and the final recognition the close; the heroine's management of the plot is the play's governing interest.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after her first successes, though some of her verse had circulated earlier under a poetic signature.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Bestiary
works.description: A Middle English bestiary of 802 lines, probably of East Anglian origin, describing the nature of the lion, eagle, serpent, stag, whale, and other creatures and drawing from each a moral and allegorical lesson, in the tradition of the Physiologus. It is the earliest English bestiary to survive in the vernacular.
works.plot: Each animal's natural history — the lion's sleep with open eyes, the whale luring sailors, the phoenix's rebirth — is expounded as a figure of Christ, the devil, or the Christian soul.
works.significance: The link between the Old English Physiologus poems and the later English bestiary tradition, and a vivid example of medieval allegorical natural history in the vernacular.
works.meter: Irregular rhyming couplets of varying length, with some alliterative ornament.
works.context: Composed c. 1250, translated from the Latin Physiologus of Theobaldus; preserved uniquely in BL Arundel MS 292, with Norwich connections.
works.characters: the animals (lion, eagle, serpent, stag, fox, spider, whale, siren, elephant, turtle-dove, panther, dove)
works.structure: A sequence of discrete animal exempla, each divided between natural description (natura) and moralization (significacio).
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Boke Named the Governour
works.description: Elyot's treatise on the education and conduct of the English ruling class, the first major work of English political and educational theory written in the vernacular rather than Latin.
works.plot: The first book prescribes the upbringing of a future governor from infancy — nurses, tutors, the curriculum of classical authors, music, painting, and physical exercise. The second book treats the virtues proper to a ruler: justice, fortitude, temperance, wisdom, and the golden mean. The third discusses the cardinal virtues and their application in counsel and judgement.
works.significance: A founding text of English humanism in the vernacular: it established the ideal of the educated magistrate, coined or first recorded many English words ('education', 'encyclopaedia'), and remained an authority on gentlemanly conduct for two centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written c. 1530–31 while Elyot, a diplomat and clerk, was out of royal favour after Wolsey's fall; dedicated to Henry VIII, it drew on Castiglione's Il Cortegiano and Patrizi's De regno, and shaped the humanist programme of gentlemanly education institutionalized in the grammar schools.
works.structure: Three books of systematic exposition, dense with citation of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and Plutarch, and illustrated with exemplary stories of classical princes.

editions.title: The Book Named the Governor

works.title: The Book of Common Prayer (1549)
altTitles: The First Prayer Book of Edward VI
The Booke of the Common Prayer and Administracion of the Sacramentes
works.description: The first Book of Common Prayer, compiled chiefly by Thomas Cranmer and imposed by the Act of Uniformity of 1549 as the single liturgy of the English church; the foundational text of Anglican worship.
works.plot: The book replaces the medieval service books (missal, breviary, manual, pontifical) with one English liturgy: Morning and Evening Prayer, the collects, the order for Holy Communion, baptism, confirmation, matrimony, visitation of the sick, burial, and the ordination rites, with the psalter and lectionary — retaining much medieval devotion while recasting the eucharist as a communion of all the people in both kinds.
works.significance: The greatest single achievement of English liturgical prose: Cranmer's collects ('whose service is perfect freedom', 'read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest') entered the language itself, and the book's cadences shaped English prose from Hooker to the Authorized Version and beyond.
works.meter: Prose with psalmody
works.context: Drafted in 1548–49 by Cranmer with a committee of bishops and divines, authorized by the first Act of Uniformity (January 1549), and introduced at Whitsun 1549, provoking the Prayer Book Rebellion in Devon and Cornwall; the book was revised in 1552 (the Second Prayer Book), restored by Elizabeth in 1559, and its language survives in the 1662 book used for four centuries.
works.structure: A complete liturgical manual arranged by rite, with rubrics, calendar, and lectionary; the prose is Cranmer's — sonorous, cadenced, and scriptural.
works.attributionNotes: The book is the work of Cranmer and his committee; the title page names no author, and the record attributes the compilation to Cranmer as chief author, following universal scholarly usage.

editions.title: The Book of Common Prayer: The Texts of 1549, 1559, and 1662

works.title: The Book of Faith
works.description: Reginald Pecock's vernacular treatise of 1456 on the nature of faith and its relation to reason, written in the last years before his condemnation: faith, he argues, is a species of knowledge grounded in evidence and reason, not mere belief on authority — the doctrine that brought him to trial and abjuration. It survives in the author's own manuscript.
works.plot: Pecock analyzes faith as intellectual assent produced by the 'doom of reason' on credible testimony, distinguishes it from opinion and knowledge, answers the objections of the 'unbilevers', and defends the lay person's right and duty to understand what he believes.
works.significance: The boldest medieval English statement of the rationality of faith, and the terminus of vernacular theology before the Reformation.
works.meter: Argumentative English prose, technical and precise.
works.context: Completed in 1456, a year before Pecock's trial; its rationalism was among the charges against him, and the work survives only in the Trinity College, Cambridge, autograph manuscript (MS B.14.45).
works.characters: none (theological treatise)
works.structure: Two books of philosophical-theological analysis, in the scholastic quaestio manner adapted to English.
works.attributionNotes: Pecock's authorship secure.

works.title: The Book of Homilies
altTitles: Certain Sermons or Homilies Appointed by the King's Majesty to Be Declared and Read
works.description: The first official book of sermons of the Church of England, issued in 1547 under the direction of Thomas Cranmer (who wrote several of the homilies himself) to be read in parish churches; a principal vehicle of Reformation doctrine for the laity.
works.plot: Twelve homilies expound the Protestant faith in plain English: on scripture, the misery of mankind, salvation by faith alone, good works, Christian love, against swearing and perjury, against strife, obedience to rulers, and against whoredom and adultery — each designed to be read from the pulpit by clergy who could not preach.
works.significance: The official voice of the English Reformation for ordinary congregations: the homilies translated Protestant doctrine into a national plain style and remained binding on the church for three centuries, feeding directly into the religious language of the Elizabethans.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Issued in 1547, the first year of Edward VI, as part of the royal Injunctions requiring the homilies' use; the homily 'Of Good Works' and others are Cranmer's own, and the second book (with the famous homily 'Against Disobedience and Wilful Rebellion') followed in 1571, making the two books the official theology of the Elizabethan church.
works.structure: Twelve self-contained sermons, each with a scriptural text, exposition, and application, written for oral delivery by non-preaching clergy.
works.attributionNotes: The book is a collaborative production of Cranmer, Thomas Becon, and other reformers; the record attributes it to Cranmer as the supervising compiler, following standard scholarship, while noting the collaboration.

works.title: The Book of Margery Kempe
works.description: The dictated spiritual autobiography of Margery Kempe of King's Lynn (c. 1436–38), commonly called the first autobiography in English: her conversion after childbirth, her marriage and vow of chastity, her uncontrollable weeping at the thought of the Passion, her pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome, and Santiago, and her examinations for heresy before the archbishops of Canterbury and York. A unique document of female lay piety and of fifteenth-century English life.
works.plot: Margery recounts her visionary conversations with Christ, her struggle with her husband for chastity, her travels through Europe and the Holy Land, her clashes with hostile clergy and her vindications, her visit to Julian of Norwich, and her old age caring for her ailing husband — the whole narrated in the third person through her scribes.
works.significance: The first autobiography in English and the earliest extended account of a laywoman's religious life; its frankness about body, marriage, and authority has made it a founding text of women's literary history.
works.meter: Direct, colloquial prose, vivid in dialogue and detail, mediated by her scribes.
works.context: Dictated c. 1436–38, with a second book of the 1430s–40s, in the East Anglian culture of orthodox lay devotion shadowed by the Lollard trials; the complete text was lost until the discovery of the manuscript in 1934 (BL Additional MS 61823), and first published in 1936.
works.characters: Margery Kempe; John Kempe (her husband); Julian of Norwich; Christ (in dialogue); the archbishops
works.structure: Two books of episodic autobiography, moving between mystical colloquy and the social world of East Anglian towns, courts, and pilgrim routes.
works.attributionNotes: Margery Kempe's authorship (by dictation to scribes) is recorded within the book itself.

editions.title: The Book of Margery Kempe
editions.editor: Sanford Brown Meech and Hope Emily Allen (eds.)

works.title: The Book of St Albans
altTitles: The Book of Hawking, Hunting, and Heraldry
works.form: courtesy book and household manual (verse and prose)
works.description: The gentleman's handbook printed at St Albans in 1486: treatises in verse and prose on hawking, hunting, and heraldry, together with the terms of venery and the 'companies of beasts', traditionally attributed to Dame Juliana Berners, prioress of Sopwell. It is the classic English manual of the gentleman's arts, reprinted and expanded into the seventeenth century.
works.plot: The book instructs the reader in the falconer's and hunter's crafts — the mews, the lure, the chase of the hart, the terms of the hunt — and in the blazoning of arms, closing with the famous catalogues of collective nouns ('a parliament of rooks', 'a murmuration of starlings') that fixed the English vocabulary of the field.
works.significance: The foundational English manual of the gentleman's arts: its venery terms entered the language and its heraldry shaped Tudor and Stuart practice.
works.meter: Mixed: the hawking and hunting treatises in rhyme royal and couplets, the heraldry in prose.
works.context: Printed at the schoolmaster press of St Albans in 1486 (a colophon names 'the schoolmaster of St Albans'), in the post-Caxton provincial print boom; the attribution to Juliana Berners appears in the 1496 de Worde reprint.
works.characters: none (manual)
works.structure: A compilation of distinct treatises (hawking; hunting; arms; blazoning) in the practical-manual tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dame Juliana Berners (prioress of Sopwell) in the 1496 reprint; the attribution is traditional and doubted. authorship_status reflects this traditional attribution.

works.title: The Book of the Duchess
altTitles: The Deth of Blaunche the Duchesse
works.description: Chaucer's earliest major poem (1,334 lines in octosyllabic couplets), a dream vision elegy for Blanche, Duchess of Lancaster, who died in 1368: the insomniac dreamer overhears a grieving knight in black, whose lament for his lost lady — 'White' — unfolds the ideal of courtly love into a meditation on death and consolation. The poem that founded the English dream-vision tradition.
works.plot: The dreamer, sleepless from an eight-year love-sickness, reads Ovid's tale of Ceyx and Alcyone and falls asleep; in his dream he meets the Man in Black, who tells of his long service to Fortune and of the peerless lady White whom he won and has now lost; only the dreamer's blunt question — 'she is dead?' — breaks the elegy's obliqueness, and the dream ends with the hunting of the hart and the poem's closure on the word 'king'.
works.significance: The first great English dream poem and the foundation of Chaucer's mature art; its fusion of consolation, allegory, and courtly elegy shaped the entire English dream-vision tradition.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of courtly grace, adapted from Machaut and the Roman de la Rose.
works.context: Composed c. 1368–72, commemorating Blanche of Lancaster (d. 12 September 1368), first wife of John of Gaunt, Chaucer's patron; the poem's courtly audience would have recognized the dead duchess in the knight's 'White'.
works.characters: the Dreamer; the Man in Black; Lady White; Fortune
works.structure: A double frame (reading; dream) enclosing the knight's elegiac autobiography, in the French dit manner; the wordplay on 'White', 'hart/heart', and 'king' ties consolation to allegory.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure; the occasional reference to Blanche is universally accepted.

editions.title: The Riverside Chaucer

works.title: The Bowge of Courte
works.description: Skelton's first major poem, a dream satire in rhyme royal: the dreamer Drede boards the ship Bowge of Courte, where the personified vices of the court — Flattery, Suspicion, Harvy Hafter, Disdain, Riot, Deceit — successively menace and betray him, until he leaps overboard. It is the founding text of the Tudor court-satire tradition.
works.plot: Drede, standing at the shore, is invited aboard the Bowge of Courte; each passenger woos him and then turns on him, and the poem breaks off as he prepares to leap from the ship to save his life.
works.significance: The first sustained court satire of the English Renaissance, combining the dream vision of Chaucer with the estates satire of the Middle Ages and setting the pattern for the complaint literature of the sixteenth century.
works.meter: Seven-line rhyme royal stanzas, handled with Chaucerian fluency but a distinctly satirical edge.
works.context: Written at the turn of the century, when Skelton was moving from court service to the country living at Diss; its portrait of court corruption anticipates his later anti-Wolsey satires.
works.characters: Drede (the dreamer); Flattery; Suspicion; Harvy Hafter; Disdain; Riot; Deceit
works.structure: Dream vision with prologue; an allegorical sea voyage in which successive encounters with the courtly vices build to a single climactic decision to abandon the court.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; printed by Wynkyn de Worde about 1499.

editions.title: John Skelton: The Complete English Poems

works.title: The British Recluse
altTitles: The British Recluse: A Pastoral Romance
works.form: pastoral romance in prose with interspersed verse
works.description: A short pastoral romance in which a retired lady and her companion recount the course of their loves in a cultivated English landscape. It is the author's deliberate domestication of the French heroic pastoral into English scenes, with songs and dialogues interspersed among the narrated histories.
works.plot: Two gentlewomen, withdrawn from the town and its disappointments, pass their retirement in a British grove, where they tell and answer one another's histories of service, constancy and betrayal. Their own loves are reported in the manner of pastoral gallantry, trials of fidelity intervene, and the tales close in reconciliation rather than in tragedy. The frame presents retirement itself as the moral condition of the narrative.
works.significance: It shows the persistence of the heroic pastoral mode inside the emerging novel and is a document of the woman writer's control of the romance tradition, later reworked by the same hand in the novel of conduct.
works.meter: Ornamented romantic prose relieved by short lyric songs and dialogues in the conventional pastoral measures of the day.
works.context: Published in 1728 in a volume issued with a comic opera adaptation, in the season of the pastoral revival and of the quarrel over the theatre's licentiousness; its retirement theme answers the town satire of the same years.
works.structure: A framed pastoral with embedded tales and interspersed songs; the dialogue of the two narrators gives the sequence and the recessional structure of the romance.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the tale was gathered under the author's name in her collected fiction and reissued in the 1730s.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Broken Heart
works.description: Ford's stately tragedy set in Sparta, in which the enforced marriage of Penthea to the aged Bassanes destroys her love for Orgilus, and the play ends in a chain of ritual deaths.
works.plot: Orgilus, cheated of his love Penthea by her brother Ithocles' ambition, returns in disguise; Ithocles loves the Spartan princess Calantha, whose father the king dies; Orgilus kills Ithocles, Penthea starves herself, and Calantha dies of a broken heart.
works.significance: Ford's most artistically controlled tragedy and the clearest Caroline example of a tragedy of honour, obligation, and emotional starvation.
works.meter: Blank verse with lyric interludes and songs, of unusually measured and elegiac cadence.
works.context: Published in 1633; probably written for a private playhouse or for court reading, given its restrained action and heavy lyricism.
works.characters: Orgilus; Penthea; Ithocles; Calantha; Bassanes; the King of Sparta; Tecnicus; Christalla
works.structure: Five acts of a slow, ceremonially patterned tragedy in which the final scene of deaths is framed by the wedding masque.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ford on the 1633 title page; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Brothers
works.description: Young's domestic tragedy of two brothers, one of whom is condemned for a capital offence against a family's honour, drawn from the recent criminal case reported in the ordinary accounts of the town.
works.plot: A seduced woman's accusation, a mistaken identity and the pursuit of the brothers through the stages of flight, trial and sentence bring one to the scaffold, while the father's anguish and the brother's devotion fill the play's intervals of pathos.
works.significance: It is the founding example of the English tragedy of the gallows and of the middle-rank family, the dramatic complement to Lillo's London merchant, and it fixed Young's reputation as the poet of mourning.
works.meter: Blank verse deliberately reduced to the nearest speech of grief, with the short exclamatory line and the address to the sufferer.
works.context: Written and acted in the year of the Beggar's Opera's triumph, when the criminal case on the stage and in the ordinary was a popular species and when the controversy over laughing and sentimental comedy was opening.
works.characters: the two brothers; the injured woman; the father; the judges and officers of the law
works.structure: Five acts of domestic calamity in the plainest tragic manner, with the trial and the execution as the two public crises framing the family's private distress.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Brus
works.description: John Barbour's verse chronicle of Robert Bruce and the Scottish wars of independence, completed c. 1375 in some 14,000 octosyllabic lines: the murder of the Red Comyn, the crowning at Scone, the years of guerrilla warfare, and the great victory at Bannockburn (1314), with James Douglas as the poem's second hero. The first great work of Scottish literature and the fountainhead of the nation's heroic self-image.
works.plot: The poem follows Bruce from the killing of Comyn and his coronation through defeat, exile, and the legendary perseverance of the spider episode to the recovery of the kingdom castle by castle, the battle of Bannockburn, the raids of Douglas into England, and the king's death — all framed by the poem's great theme, that 'fredome is a noble thing'.
works.significance: The first great poem in Scots and the founding text of Scottish national literature; Burns's 'Scots Wha Hae' and the whole Bruce tradition descend from it.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of energy and speed, in Older Scots.
works.context: Completed in 1375 by the archdeacon of Aberdeen, in the court of Robert II (Bruce's grandson), when the Stewart dynasty needed a heroic past; preserved in two manuscripts (1487, 1489) and printed in 1571.
works.characters: Robert Bruce; James Douglas; Edward II; Edward Bruce; the Scottish and English armies
works.structure: Twenty books of continuous narrative in the romance-chronicle manner, with set-piece battles and speeches, closed by the king's death and the poet's envoy.
works.attributionNotes: Barbour's authorship secure (named in the text and the royal records).

editions.title: Barbour's Bruce
editions.editor: Matthew P. McDiarmid and James A. C. Stevenson (eds.)

works.title: The Brut Chronicle
works.description: The Middle English prose Brut, the most popular secular text in late medieval England: a chronicle of Britain from the Trojan Brutus through the Arthurian kings to the fourteenth century, with continuations carrying the story through the Wars of the Roses. Over 180 manuscripts survive in English — more than any other secular work — and Caxton's print (1480) made it the standard popular history of England.
works.plot: The chronicle narrates the legendary British history of the Brut tradition — Brutus, Lear, Arthur — then the Saxon, Norman, and Plantagenet reigns, with the continuations adding the Lancastrian and Yorkist wars; its plain, annalistic prose made it the layman's history of England.
works.significance: The bestselling secular book of the English Middle Ages: its diffusion defines the popular historical culture out of which Tudor history writing grew.
works.meter: Plain, formulaic prose of the chronicle tradition.
works.context: The earliest version was made in the later fourteenth century, probably in London, from French and Latin sources; it was expanded continuously through the fifteenth century (the 'common version' to 1419, continuations to 1461 and later) and printed by Caxton in 1480.
works.characters: Brutus; Arthur; the kings of England to Edward IV
works.structure: A regnal chronicle in the Brut tradition, open-ended and continuously continued by successive compilers.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous and compilational.

works.title: The Buke of the Howlat
works.description: Richard Holland's Scottish alliterative beast-allegory of some 1,000 lines, composed c. 1448 for the Douglas family: the owl, ashamed of his ugliness, appeals through the assembly of birds to the pope and the emperor, each bird vying in flattery, until Dame Nature restores him to his proper worth. A satire of pride, courts, and flattery, and the last major alliterative poem of the tradition.
works.plot: The howlat, complaining of his feathers, is counselled by the peacock to seek redress; the birds assemble in parliament before the pope and emperor, but the debate degenerates into mutual slander and sycophancy, until Nature intervenes, clothes the owl in dignity, and the poem ends with the Douglas heraldry and the family's praise.
works.significance: The last major alliterative poem in the British tradition and a key document of Douglas politics, heraldry, and the Scottish reception of the Alliterative Revival.
works.meter: Thirteen-line alliterative stanzas with rhyme and wheel, in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1448 by Richard Holland, secretary to Archibald Douglas, Earl of Moray, for the Douglas family at a moment of their power; preserved in the Asloan and Bannatyne manuscripts (c. 1515, 1568).
works.characters: the Howlat; the Peacock; the Pope; the Emperor; Dame Nature; the birds of the parliament
works.structure: A beast-parliament in the Chaucerian manner, framed by the owl's complaint and closed by the heraldic celebration of the Douglases.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Richard Holland on the evidence of the poem's colophon and Douglas records.

works.title: The Busie Body
works.form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: A city comedy of gossip, project and guardianship, the play that established its author as the most successful woman dramatist of the early eighteenth century. Its busy-bodies, a pair of meddling widows who superintend everyone's affairs, frame a plot of a fortune-hunting colonel, a ward and her several suitors.
works.plot: An amorous colonel arrives in London resolved to make his court to a rich ward, and finds her guarded by two busy-body neighbours who report his designs and arrange her marriage to a fool. His servant and the ward's lovers counterplot, a ball and its gig of the age assemble the company, and the final division of the lady's property among three competitors exposes the arithmetic of the marriage market. The busy-bodies themselves are outwitted and reconciled to the younger pair.
works.significance: It is the central instance of the post-Restoration city comedy rewritten for a Whig commercial audience, and a landmark in the history of women's professional playwriting; its treatment of female guardianship and of the price of an heiress anticipates the comic novel.
works.meter: Brisk prose dialogue with the irregular mixture of verse passes usual in early-eighteenth-century comedy; the scenes run on quick repartee and the interruption of gossip.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1709 and frequently revived; the division-of-property scene was read aloud in the House of Commons in 1719 during the debate on the bill against patent projecting, a mark of how topical its satire on project and gossip had become.
works.characters: the two busy-body neighbours; the fortune-hunting colonel; his witty servant; the wealthy ward; her three competing suitors; the projectors of the age
works.structure: Five-act city comedy in prose and verse with a strictly interlocked main and underplot; the scenes of the busy-bodies' surveillance provide the comic engine and the division-of-property set piece the climax.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the play was published with the author's name and its success was registered in the pirated editions and revivals of the following decades.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Canterbury Tales
works.description: Chaucer's unfinished masterpiece and the supreme achievement of Middle English literature: a frame-tale collection in which some thirty pilgrims journeying from the Tabard Inn to Canterbury agree to a storytelling contest, the tales ranging from the Knight's romance and the Miller's fabliau to the Wife of Bath's prologue, the Pardoner's sermon, and the Parson's treatise. Begun c. 1387 and left unfinished at Chaucer's death in 1400.
works.plot: In the General Prologue the narrator joins a company of pilgrims — knight, miller, reeve, wife of Bath, pardoner, summoner, nun's priest, and the rest — each vividly portrayed; Harry Bailly, the Host, proposes the tale-telling game, and the tales that follow answer and quarrel with one another across the whole range of medieval genres, from courtly romance (Knight, Squire, Franklin) through fabliau (Miller, Reeve, Shipman, Merchant) and saint's life (Second Nun, Prioress) to sermon (Pardoner), beast fable (Nun's Priest), and the closing penitential treatise of the Parson.
works.significance: The most influential single work of English literature: its pilgrims, its tales, and its frame established the English tradition of comic realism, dramatic monologue, and narrative irony that runs through Shakespeare to the novel.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of unprecedented flexibility, with rhyme royal, tail-rhyme, and prose for special effects; the decasyllabic line perfected.
works.context: Composed c. 1387–1400 in London, drawing on Boccaccio, Ovid, Boethius, and the estates tradition; the pilgrimage to Becket's shrine at Canterbury supplied the frame; circulated in some eighty manuscripts and printed by Caxton (1476–78) and his successors, making it the foundation of the English printed canon.
works.characters: the Narrator; the Host (Harry Bailly); the Knight; the Miller; the Reeve; the Wife of Bath; the Pardoner; the Friar; the Summoner; the Nun's Priest; the Parson; and the other pilgrims
works.structure: A frame narrative (the pilgrimage, the Host's game) enclosing twenty-four tales grouped into ten fragments; the links between tales stage the pilgrims' quarrels and judgments, and the work's unfinished state is part of its design.
works.attributionNotes: Uniquely well attested: Chaucer's authorship of the Tales is not in doubt, though the ordering of the fragments and some links are editorial.

editions.title: The Riverside Chaucer

works.title: The Cardinal
works.description: Shirley's last tragedy, written in Ireland and performed at the Cockpit in 1641, in which a scheming cardinal forces a marriage that leads to poisoning, madness, and death.
works.plot: The Cardinal, thwarted in his own designs on the Duchess of Pavia, compels her to marry his protégé Columbo; when she loves the soldier Alvarez instead, Columbo kills him, and the Duchess poisons the Cardinal and herself.
works.significance: A late and vigorous Caroline revenge tragedy, notable for its portrait of ecclesiastical ambition and for closing Shirley's career.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Composed during Shirley's Irish period and revived at the Cockpit in 1641, on the eve of the civil wars; printed in Shirley's Six New Plays of 1653.
works.characters: the Cardinal; the Duchess of Pavia; Columbo; Alvarez; Celinde; Hernando
works.structure: Five acts of revenge tragedy with a catastrophic denouement.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shirley; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Careless Husband
works.form: Domestic comedy in five acts in prose dialogue, written for a particular acting company and printed from the theatre's text.
works.description: A comedy brought out by the Drury Lane company at the end of 1704 and printed in the following year, which keeps the machinery of Restoration sexual intrigue but redirects it towards the reformation of a rake and the reconciliation of a married couple. Its central conceit, a woman's virtue tested while she lies unsuspecting and asleep, supplied the eighteenth century's most celebrated showcase for an actress. The play is habitually cited as the hinge between the libertine comedy of the 1690s and the sentimental domestic drama of the following generations.
works.plot: Sir Charles Easy, a hot-tempered and inattentive husband, has come to believe that his wife Lady Easy has countenanced the addresses of Lord Careless, a gay seducer whose boast is that no woman has yet refused him. The jealousy of the husband and the vanity of the rake are answered by a stratagem of the wife's own: she writes the assignation, then contrives that she shall be found asleep in a posture that seems to invite surprise. Lord Careless, admitted to the chamber and discovering the unconscious lady, contends with himself, leaves the written appointment unfilled, and abandons the design. In the underplot the young fop Sir Easy Foppington, lately and unwillingly married, makes a fool of himself in courtship of the housemaid, and the valet Moody is detected in picking his master's pocket. Convinced by these proofs of his wife's constancy, Sir Charles asks her pardon; the reformed rake is reconciled to the family he had traduced, and the comedy closes with forgiveness and marriages.
works.significance: It is the standard example of the century's turn from libertine wit to sentimental proof of female constancy, and it gave the stage a situation, a woman's virtue tested in her own unconsciousness, that novelists of the next generation and later domestic drama exploited. Its mixed inheritance of intrigue and moral seriousness makes it a fixed reference point in accounts of how English comedy changed after 1700.
works.meter: Familiar prose speech with quick re-partee and deliberate pauses, the pauses carrying the moral weight of the sleeping scene; the customary prologue and epilogue spoken to the audience are in closed couplets.
works.context: The manager-actor who wrote it had helped to run the Drury Lane company since the patent lapsed in 1695, and the piece answers the stage-anti-stage campaign of the 1690s by offering a comedy in which seduction is refused and reform is won on the stage. The fop plot continues the city-marriage and chambermaid intrigue that the same management had made its stock in trade. The play held the repertory through the century and remained a trial of skill for leading performers.
works.characters: Sir Charles Easy; Lady Easy; Lord Careless; Sir Easy Foppington; Moody the valet; the chambermaid courted by the young fop
works.structure: Five-act stage comedy with a main plot and a fop underplot tightly linked by their shared subject of tried virtue; the movement runs from suspicion through a single staged trial of a woman's constancy to public vindication and marriage, with the sleeping scene at the centre as the turning-point.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Castaway
works.form: meditative lyric on an occurrent disaster, in the graveyard-school manner of gloom and self-analysis
works.description: Cowper's shortest and starkest poem, founded on the wreck of an East Indiaman in which one seaman, described as deranged, was said to have been lost, and turning the incident into a figure of the poet's own spiritual exposure. The speaker watches the thoughtless crew about their business while the abandoned man lies at the mast foot, and the wreck becomes an image of the soul for whom no pity and no hope remain. It is the most intense of the preromantic lyrics of desolation.
works.plot: The poem reports the wreck, the crew's exertions and the fate of the abandoned seaman who, past reason and past hope, was left to the sea. The speaker then draws the moral likeness: he too is exposed without pity, without prayer and without the sympathies that keep others from despair. The closing stanzas refuse consolation, identifying the castaway with a man abandoned both of God and man, and leave the figure of the storming sea as the poem's last image.
works.significance: It is the poem by which Cowper is most often read as a precursor of Romantic despair, and one of the strongest lyrics of abandonment in English. Its identification of a public news-item with private spiritual state makes it a document of the culture of feeling and of the graveyard meditation.
works.meter: Ballad-like stanzas of alternating four- and three-beat lines with a solemn rhyme, the measure giving the poem its hymn-like severity.
works.context: Written in January 1785 on the news of the loss of an East Indiaman eastward, in the same months in which Cowper's religious depression was returning; the wreck lies near the centre of the decade's interest in maritime disaster, providence and the limits of sympathy.
works.characters: The lost seaman; the surviving crew; the meditative speaker
works.structure: A brief narrative in short stanzas, passing from the reported wreck to the meditative identification of the speaker with the castaway and ending without consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is fixed by Cowper's own letter, and the year usually given for the first printing is 1786, a reckoning followed here with the qualification recorded in the bibliographical note.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Castle of Health
works.description: Elyot's vernacular treatise on diet and regimen, the first substantial English medical handbook written by a layman for lay readers.
works.plot: The book surveys the four humours and complexions, the properties of foods and drinks, sleep, exercise, and the regimen proper to each age and season, advising the reader how to preserve health through moderation and self-knowledge.
works.significance: A landmark in the vernacularization of medicine and natural knowledge in Tudor England, influential on later dietary literature and a document of humanist attitudes to the body.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the mid-1530s and printed by Thomas Berthelet in 1539 (with editions to 1610); Elyot's attempt to bring learned medicine into English paralleled his linguistic programme in The Governour.
works.structure: Four books of systematic exposition, compiled from Galen, Hippocrates, and the medieval regimen literature.

works.title: The Castle of Indolence
altTitles: The Castle of Indolence: An Allegorical Poem
works.description: Thomson's last and most finished allegorical poem, in the Spenserian measure: a knight is allured into the castle of Indolence, its slumber, its luxury and its self-consuming sweetness, and is delivered by the sight of the wizard's own punishment and of the castle's fall.
works.plot: Two companions, the lover of labour and the lover of ease, come to the enchanted castle; the slumbry of its inhabitants, the pleasures of its gardens and the tales of its enchanter's love hold the indolent guest fast, until the philosophy of the active life and the destruction of the place recover him to virtue.
works.significance: It restored the Spenserian stanza to English verse, and it remains the period's most complete poem on the temptation of ease, answering the season's own moral economy with an allegory of the unspent life.
works.meter: The nine-line Spenserian stanza, revived by Thomson for this poem and used with a sensuous richness of sound that made the measure a permanent option for English allegory.
works.context: Conceived in the early 1730s as a burlesque of the poet's own company and long retouched before its publication in the year of his death, when the Spenserian revival, the poetry of retirement and the moral argument about industry were all active.
works.characters: the two guests of the castle; the enchanter of the place and his fair one; the personified indolence and her crew
works.structure: Two cantos of continuous allegorical narrative, with the inserted tale of the enchanter and his fair one, the personified crew of the castle and the moral conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Castle of Otranto
altTitles: The Castle of Otranto. A Story. Translated by William Marshal, Gent. From the Original Italian of Onuphrio Murelli
works.form: Gothic romance and tale of terror
works.description: A Gothic tale of a tyrant prince of Apulia, his giant helmet, his murdered son and the prophecy that his castle and name would fall to the rightful possessor, published as a translation from an Italian original of the sixteenth century. It founded the romance of terror and supplied the machinery, the castle and the curse that the following generation of writers inherited.
works.plot: Manfred's son Conrad is crushed to death by an enormous helmet on the day of his marriage, and Manfred, needing an heir, designs to divorce his wife and take the young Isabella himself. Isabella flees through the castle's secret passages, and the captive Theodore is discovered and released, Manfred's daughter Matilda being killed by her father's mistake in the dark. The prophecy is fulfilled as the castle falls and the true possession is restored to Theodore, Manfred retiring to a cloister.
works.significance: It is the founding work of the Gothic and the origin of a whole century's popular fiction; its prefatory theory of romance made it also a piece of criticism, and its imitation of the old tales defined the literature of terror.
works.meter: A rapid, dramatic prose of portent and exclamation, modelled on the phraseology of the old translation and the tragedy of the stage; the inserted supernatural actions are reported in a plain chronicle manner.
works.context: Written at Strawberry Hill amid the antiquarian revival and published in 1764, in the season of the debate over the licentiousness of fiction and of the quarrel over the authenticity of the old romances; the second edition's confessions of the trick answered the charge of forgery.
works.characters: Manfred; Hippolita his wife; Matilda his daughter; Conrad and the murdered line; Isabella the escaped bride; Theodore the captive; the hermits and Friar Jerome
works.structure: A short continuous romance in five acts or chapters of the drama-like design, with the supernatural machinery appearing at the decisive moments; the second edition added the author's own preface and defence of romance.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published as a translation and a reprint from an unseen Italian original, a device withdrawn in the second edition, which acknowledged the modern authorship.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Castle of Perseverance
works.description: The earliest complete English morality play (c. 1400–25, 3,649 lines): the life of Mankind (Humanum Genus) from birth to judgement, staged on the famous circular 'place' with its central castle and five scaffolds, as the virtues and vices battle for his soul through the Seven Ages. The most ambitious play of the English medieval stage.
works.plot: Mankind, born in sin, is led by his Bad Angel through World, Flesh, and the Devil to the seven deadly sins; rescued by Confession, he is garrisoned in the Castle of Perseverance with the virtues; the sins' siege fails, but Covetousness wins him in old age, until Death strikes and the debate of the four daughters of God — Mercy, Peace, Righteousness, Truth — yields his salvation.
works.significance: The foundational English morality: its stage diagram, its allegorical cast, and its theology of mercy set the pattern for the genre through Everyman to the Elizabethan stage.
works.meter: Thirteen-line stanzas (rime couée with wheel), with stage directions prescribing the elaborate fixed staging.
works.context: Composed c. 1400–25 in East Anglia (the manuscript's language is Norfolk), in the milieu of the great fifteenth-century moralities; preserved uniquely in the Macro manuscript (Folger Shakespeare Library, MS V.a.354, c. 1440) with Mankind and Wisdom.
works.characters: Mankind (Humanum Genus); the Bad and Good Angels; World, Flesh, and the Devil; the Seven Deadly Sins; the Seven Virtues; Confession; Death; God; the Four Daughters of God
works.structure: A four-scaffold cosmic drama (God; World; Flesh; Devil) around the central castle, with the banns, the siege, the death scene, and the parliament of heaven as its great movements.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

editions.title: The Macro Plays

works.title: The Changeling
works.description: Middleton and Rowley's tragedy of desire and madness: Beatrice-Joanna, betrothed to Alonzo but in love with Alsemero, commissions the ugly servant De Flores to murder her fiancé; his price is her virginity, and the play follows the pair's descent through murder, the bed-trick with the maid Diaphanta, and madness to the final deaths — while the comic sub-plot of the madhouse, where the pretended fools and madmen perform, doubles the theme of 'change'.
works.plot: De Flores kills Alonzo and claims Beatrice-Joanna; the wedding to Alsemero proceeds through the virginity-test and the Diaphanta substitution; the castle catches fire (in the plot), the murders of Diaphanta and the witnesses follow, and the final scene's confessions — Beatrice-Joanna's 'I am that of your blood was taken from you' — end with the lovers' deaths and the madhouse's ironic close.
works.significance: One of the great Jacobean tragedies — the study of complicity and self-loss ('the deed's creature') that T. S. Eliot would single out as the age's masterpiece of moral horror.
works.meter: Middleton's verse in the main plot — swift, ironic, and chilling — against Rowley's prose farce in the madhouse.
works.context: Performed by the Lady Elizabeth's Men in 1622, at court in 1624, and printed in 1653; based on Reynolds's God's Revenge Against Murder (1621).
works.characters: Beatrice-Joanna; De Flores; Alsemero; Alonzo de Piracquo; Tomazo de Piracquo; Vermandero; Diaphanta; Jasperino; the madhouse crew (Alibius, Lollio, Antonio, Franciscus, Isabella)
works.structure: A two-plot structure unique in the canon: the main tragic plot (by Middleton) and the madhouse comedy (by Rowley) run in deliberate counterpoint, never meeting until the thematic rhyme of the final scene.
works.attributionNotes: Middleton (main plot) and William Rowley (madhouse sub-plot) as stated on the title page; the division is uncontested.

editions.title: The Changeling (Revels Plays)

works.title: The Changes
works.description: An early Shirley comedy of romantic change and constancy, in which lovers exchange and re-exchange partners before the final matching; it is Shirley's first play on the theme of inconstancy that would dominate his later work.
works.plot: Two pairs of lovers in London and the country undergo reversals of fortune and affection, and the title's 'changes' resolve into a stable set of marriages.
works.significance: One of Shirley's earliest plays and an example of the Caroline comedy of manners in formation.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Cockpit in 1626; published 1632.
works.characters: Phillipa; Vincentio; Annibell; Clarinda; the Duke of Florence; Antonio
works.structure: Five acts alternating between court and city settings.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shirley; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Chief Promises of God unto Man
altTitles: A Tragedy or Interlude Manifesting the Chief Promises of God unto Man
works.description: John Bale's interlude of the covenants of God from Adam to Christ, composed c. 1538 and printed at Wesel in 1547; a dramatic sermon on the promises fulfilled in the gospel.
works.plot: God the Father, in seven acts, makes his successive promises to man — to Adam of the woman's seed, to Noah of the rainbow covenant, to Abraham of the blessing of nations, to Moses of the law, to David of the everlasting throne, to Isaiah of the virgin's son, and to John the Baptist of the Lamb of God — each act closing with a prayer or antiphon, the whole demonstrating that the Old Testament is fulfilled in Christ.
works.significance: The most accomplished of Bale's biblical interludes and a model of Reformation dramaturgy: its covenant structure turned the mystery-cycle tradition to doctrinal ends and influenced the biblical drama of the Elizabethan church.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages with antiphons
works.context: Written c. 1538 during Bale's service as a Protestant dramatist under Cromwell, and printed at Wesel in 1547 in the collection of Bale's biblical plays; the play embodies the Protestant programme of replacing the old mysteries with doctrinal drama drawn from scripture alone.
works.characters: God the Father (Pater Coelestis); Adam; Noah; Abraham; Moses; David; Isaiah; John the Baptist; Baleus Prolocutor
works.structure: Seven acts, each a dialogue between God the Father (as Pater Coelestis) and a biblical figure, framed by a prologue (Bale as Prolocutor) and an epilogue; the play is a doctrinal pageant of the covenants.

editions.title: The Complete Plays of John Bale, vol. 2

works.title: The Christian Hero
altTitles: The Christian Hero: An Argument, That no Principles can be effectual to encourage Vertue and Goodness, but those of Christianity
works.description: Steele's devotional and moral argument that unassisted virtue is unsustainable and that Christianity supplies the only adequate motive to goodness; a confession of his own past profligacy and the book he feared would be thrown in his teeth.
works.plot: The author proves from experience and from the passions that honour, interest and good nature leave a man unprotected against himself, then argues that the Christian rule alone both forbids and enables, and closes with the picture of the hero of piety.
works.significance: It is the periodical essay's other face, the serious religious self-examination that made Steele's name a byword for professional conscience, and it supplied the model of the reforming tract of the century.
works.meter: Plain, earnest, familiar prose, deliberately free of ornament, with the short imperative sentence and direct address to the reader.
works.context: Written early in Steele's army years and published as his public career made him a target, at the height of the deist and anti-deist controversy and in the year of his quarrel with Addison and of his entry into party politics.
works.characters: the penitent author; the man of the world
works.structure: A continuous argument in numbered sections, moving from autobiography and diagnosis through scriptural proof to the exemplary character.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Spectator, 4 volumes

works.title: The Christian Religion, as Professed by a Daughter of the Church of God
works.form: Practical divinity and conduct treatise in prose, a devotional and moral system rather than an occasional controversy.
works.description: The longest and most systematic of her prose works, published in 1705 and reprinted through the century, a practical divinity written in the manner of a moral essay. It argues that Christianity is a reasonable and orderly scheme of duty, and then lays out the devotional, moral and social conduct proper to a churchwoman, with sustained sections on the government of the passions and on the duties of the single and the married state. The title announces the standpoint: an account of religion written from within the communion, and addressed to practice rather than to controversy.
works.plot: The first division establishes the grounds of belief, the evidence of revelation and the authority of the church, and answers the pretences of free enquiry and of latitudinarian moderation which would relax those grounds for the sake of ease or of party. The second division reduces the Christian life to a method: a settled rule of devotion, periodical self-examination, the ordering of the affections towards the love of God, and the practice of charity and of the duties of each station. Along the way she argues that the Passions, esteem, and the love of the world are the real enemies of a devout life, and that the conscience must be disciplined by the church's rule instead of left to its own temper. The whole is intended as a complete guide to conduct for a reader who means to think and to believe consistently.
works.significance: It is her most ambitious prose work and the one by which she was best known to readers who never reached her scheme of female education. Its blending of conduct book, practical divinity and moral philosophy is the fullest evidence of the religious content of her case for women, and the number of its editions measures the reach of a woman's prose theology in the early eighteenth century.
works.context: It appeared in 1705, after the occasional conformity controversies of the last years of the war had sharpened the language of church party, and between her earlier philosophical writings and the high-church polemic of the following decade. Its assertion that Christianity is a reasonable service answers the latitudinarian and deist vocabularies then current, and its tone is that of a woman writing within the communion's discipline for readers of both sexes. The bookseller who issued it had printed her occasional prose, and it passed through many editions without the name of its author on the title page.
works.structure: Treatise in two main divisions, speculative grounds followed by a rule of life in numbered practical sections; the manner is sententious and hortatory, with long periodic sentences and frequent appeal to the reader's own experience.

works.title: The Citizen of the World
altTitles: The Citizen of the World; or, Letters of a Chinese Philosopher, Respecting His Residence in London
works.form: Periodical essay and spectator paper in epistolary form: short papers of character and custom, mixed with fable, translation and reflection, written for a daily newspaper and reprinted as books.
works.description: Goldsmith's periodical essays cast as the letters of a Chinese philosopher resident in London, first contributed to a daily newspaper and then collected in two volumes. The device of the observing foreigner, familiar from the 'Persian Letters' tradition, is used to make English manners, laws, learning, commerce and show appear strange, and to let a writer of little consequence comment on a great city with the immunity of an outsider.
works.plot: The letters are connected not by plot but by the persona of Lien Chi Altangi, a Chinese merchant-philosopher in London, whose correspondence with friends at home reports and judges everything he meets: the exchange, the playhouse, the auction, the coffee-house and the critics, the luxury of the rich and the misery of the poor, the laws, the duels, the salons and the political factions. His outsider's eye produces the two characteristic effects of the series, an invention of British society as a system of contradictions, and a defence of simple virtue and of the 'mandarins' of his own country against European pretence. As the letters proceed, the philosopher's own family misfortune is woven into the papers, so that the spectators' pleasure is gradually seasoned with sentiment and with a plea for benevolence. Its most quoted material is its account of the 'golden fairies' of British credit, the paper money and the phantom wealth of a commercial nation.
works.significance: It is the most accomplished of the mid-century spectator series and a central text of the literature of politeness, commerce and national self-observation; its letters shaped the essayistic treatment of commercial society for a generation. It also shows the sentiment of the 1760s turning the essay from a machine of wit into a machine of sympathy.
works.context: It appeared in the efflorescence of the English periodical paper after Addison and Steele, when a contributor could supply a newspaper with a series of essays and when the foreign-letter conceit had become a standard means of criticising national manners. Its publication belongs to the years when Goldsmith was moving between the magazines, the book trade and the great houses, dependent on the very world he describes.
works.characters: Lien Chi Altangi, the Chinese philosopher; his correspondent Hoamsy and the family at home; the London citizens, critics, tradesmen and great whom he observes
works.structure: A sequence of independent periodical letters in two collected volumes, unified by the persona of the Chinese correspondent and by the seasonal and topical round of London life, with a few serial threads, chiefly the philosopher's domestic sorrows, running through.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the papers were known to be Goldsmith's and were collected under his name. Some letters appeared in the newspaper press before the collected edition and were revised for it, so the exact order and dating of individual papers is not fixed here.

works.title: The City Madam
works.description: Massinger's comedy of a citizen's wife, Lady Frugal, whose ambition to be a lady leads her husband to fake a departure for the Indies and to test her virtue and her daughters' constancy.
works.plot: Sir John Frugal pretends to embark for Virginia; Lady Frugal and her daughters, believing themselves rich, cast off their modest lives; the test exposes their vanity and they are sent to the colonies as punishment.
works.significance: Massinger's fullest treatment of London citizen society and one of the most striking Caroline comedies of female ambition and colonial punishment.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed at the Blackfriars in 1632 and published posthumously in 1658.
works.characters: Sir John Frugal; Lady Frugal; Anne; Mary; Lord Lacy; Sir Maurice Lacy; Ramble; Luke Frugal
works.structure: Five acts of a Jonsonian testing-comedy with a moralising conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Massinger; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The City Mouse and Country Mouse
altTitles: The Hind and the Panther Transvers'd to the Story of the Country Mouse and the City Mouse
works.description: A burlesque of Dryden's The Hind and the Panther (1687) by Matthew Prior and Charles Montagu, retelling Dryden's fable of the mice in mock-heroic terms to ridicule his conversion and his religious argument — a celebrated example of Whig literary mockery and Prior's early wit.
works.plot: Following Aesop's fable (used by Dryden), the country mouse visits the city mouse and, after witnessing the dangers and hypocrisies of town and court, returns to the safety of the country, applied as satire on Dryden's religious and political position.
works.significance: A notable Whig burlesque of Dryden and an early showcase for Prior's wit; it reflects the literary politics of James II's reign and the quarrel over Dryden's conversion.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in a witty, parodic mock-heroic register.
works.context: Written in 1687 by the young Prior and Montagu (later Earl of Halifax) against Dryden's Catholic poem, and published anonymously; it launched Prior's reputation.
works.characters: the City Mouse; the Country Mouse
works.structure: A burlesque verse fable in heroic couplets parodying Dryden's poem.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative, by Matthew Prior and Charles Montagu; Montagu is not in this database, so only Prior is linked.

works.title: The Cloud of Unknowing
works.description: The classic English treatise of apophatic contemplation, written in the late fourteenth century by an anonymous master (perhaps a Carthusian or secular priest) for a young disciple: the soul seeking God must enter the 'cloud of unknowing' between itself and God, striking down every thought with the dart of longing love and the 'naked intent' of the single word. The most intellectually rigorous work of the English mystical canon.
works.plot: The author teaches his disciple the work of contemplation: the forgetting of all creatures, the rejection of discursive meditation, the piercing of the darkness with love — and warns throughout against the false mysticism of physical fervour and deluded visions, prescribing the discipline of the single word ('God' or 'love') repeated in the heart.
works.significance: The supreme English expression of the negative way and a work of the first rank in the European contemplative tradition; its psychology of attention and intention has given it a continuing modern readership.
works.meter: Precise, sinewy prose, paradoxically articulate about the ineffable; vivid negative imagery (clouds, darts, nakedness).
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400, probably in the north-east Midlands, in the orbit of the Carthusian order; it circulated with the author's other works (The Book of Privy Counselling, the translation of pseudo-Dionysius's Mystical Theology) and was read by the English Benedictine revival and by modern contemplatives (Thomas Merton).
works.characters: the author (spiritual director); the young disciple (addressee)
works.structure: Seventy-five short chapters of graduated instruction, in the apophatic tradition of pseudo-Dionysius, with the 'cloud' as its organizing image.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the author is often identified as a Carthusian on grounds of the work's transmission, but the identification is conjectural.

works.title: The Comedy of Errors
works.description: Shakespeare's shortest play and his only pure farce, built on Plautus's Menaechmi: twin masters and twin servants, both pairs named Antipholus and Dromio, are separated by shipwreck and reunited by coincidence in Ephesus, where the confusions of mistaken identity multiply until the family is restored in the recognition scene before the Abbess.
works.plot: Antipholus of Syracuse and his servant Dromio arrive in Ephesus, where their long-lost twins live; the day becomes a cascade of wrong beatings, wrong dinners, and wrong arrests, until the Duke's judgment and the Abbess's revelation untangle the knots and reunite husband, wife, and sons.
works.significance: The most technically perfect of the early comedies and Shakespeare's demonstration that classical comedy could be outdone in English.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose for the servants' comedy; the play includes the verse 'discourse' scene between Antipholus of Syracuse and Luciana.
works.context: Probably written for Gray's Inn's Christmas revels of 1594; the frame of Egeon's doom under Ephesian law darkens the farce with the threat of execution.
works.characters: Antipholus of Syracuse; Antipholus of Ephesus; Dromio of Syracuse; Dromio of Ephesus; Adriana; Luciana; Egeon; the Abbess (Emilia); the Duke
works.structure: A single-day, single-city action — the closest Shakespeare came to the classical unities — with the errors compounded scene by scene to the recognition finale.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Comical Revenge; or, Love in a Tub
works.description: George Etherege's first comedy, a witty Restoration intrigue play that alternates heroic verse scenes of courtship with prose scenes of low comedy, and gave the stage its first true Restoration rake in Sir Frederick Frollick.
works.plot: Two brothers love two sisters; Colonel Bruce and the Widow Rich clash in the main plot, while Sir Frederick Frollick pursues the Widow with comic irreverence; all is resolved in marriage.
works.significance: The first of the great Restoration comedies of manners; Sir Frederick Frollick established the type of the gallant-rake that Dorimant would perfect.
works.meter: Rhymed couplets in the high plot and prose in the low comedy.
works.context: Performed by the Duke's Company at Lincoln's Inn Fields in March 1664; it made Etherege's reputation immediately.
works.characters: Sir Frederick Frollick; the Widow Rich; Colonel Bruce; Graciana; Beaufort; Palmer; Dufoy; Mrs Gudgeon
works.structure: Five acts with three parallel plots of differing social register and metre.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Etherege; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Commonwealth of Oceana
works.description: James Harrington's utopian treatise on the ideal commonwealth, in which he argues that political power follows the distribution of landed property and proposes an elaborate republican constitution with a bicameral legislature and rotation of office.
works.plot: The Archon of Oceana, after the dissolution of the old government, establishes a commonwealth founded on an agrarian law limiting landed property, with a Senate proposing, a popular assembly resolving, and a magistracy executing; the model is Venice and ancient republics rather than monarchy.
works.significance: The most original political theory of the Interregnum; its theory that power follows property influenced Marx, and its constitutional model directly shaped the constitutions of the American colonies and of the early United States.
works.meter: A mixture of narrative and constitutional prose.
works.context: Written during the Protectorate and dedicated to Cromwell, who is said to have suppressed it until Harrington's friends obtained its release; published in 1656.
works.characters: the Archon; Olphaus Megaletor; the Council of Legislators; Parthenia
works.structure: A narrative frame of the founding of Oceana followed by the text of the proposed constitution and the Model of the Commonwealth.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Harrington; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Commonwealth of Slaves
works.form: Heroic tragedy in five acts, the continuation of an adaptation already recorded, written for the patent house and printed from the acting text.
works.description: The second part of the stage adaptation of the Oroonoko story, brought out for the Drury Lane stage at the turn of the century and printed in 1701. Where the first part had made the African prince's constancy and betrayal the substance of a tearful tragedy, the continuation carries the consequence into rebellion, siege and execution, and keeps the comedy of planter appetite running beneath it. The very title, a commonwealth of slaves, makes the plantation a scene of political danger as well as of pity.
works.plot: Oroonoko, sold into the plantations and still honoured as a prince by those about him, finds that the colony's laws leave him no redress, and combines the captives into an armed community resolved to win its liberty or to die. Imoinda, who has followed him into bondage and bears him a child in the new world, is the occasion both of his tenderness and of his exposure. The English planters conduct the suppression with a cruelty that the play invites its audience to measure against their Christian profession: the widow of fortune who had pursued the slave with her purse, the governor and the trading captain who first cozened him, and the young heiress whose suit is disputed among them, all pursue their several bargains while the revolt is being crushed. The rising is betrayed and put down, Oroonoko is taken, scourged and destroyed, and the subordinate plots close in marriage or in the discomfiture of the greedy. The tragedy is thus carried from the pathos of betrayal to the politics of a slave republic and its suppression.
works.significance: It completes the most influential stage version of the tale and, by converting the first part's pathos into a slave revolt and its suppression, brought the politics of plantation slavery into the tragedy of the patent theatre. Its two-tier handling of African heroism and English avarice became the standard framework for later treatments of the subject, and it remains a fixed reference in the history of the stage Oroonoko.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic five-beat line for the heroic roles, with couplets closing the scenes of the prince's speeches; the planter underplot is in prose, with the song matter of the earlier part reduced.
works.context: The adaptation had held the London stage since the middle of the 1690s and was the most frequently revived treatment on the English theatre of African slavery and of African nobility. The continuation appeared in the years when the royal trade in captives was a matter of charter and of parliamentary dispute, and when the plantations were becoming a visible political question. Its title plays upon the vocabulary of rebellion and of contested government which the previous century had made familiar to every playhouse audience.
works.characters: Oroonoko; Imoinda; the widow of fortune who designs upon the hero; the governor of the colony; the captain who betrayed him; the planter family about whom the underplot turns; the followers of the slave community
works.structure: Tragedy in five acts with a two-tier design, the heroic line in verse and the plantation underplot in prose; the first part's single movement of betrayal is here expanded into plotting, discovery and military suppression.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Complaint, or, Night Thoughts on Life, Death and Immortality
altTitles: The Complaint: or, Night-Thoughts on Life, Death, and Immortality
works.description: Young's long meditative poem on the night, death and the immortal life, spoken by a grieving soul under the patronage of the personified Night: the central work of the century's cultivation of melancholy and of the thought of death.
works.plot: Across nine nights the poet addresses Night, the stars, the tomb and his own losses, passes through the tales of the ruined house, the physician and the fallen ambition, and rises from the meditation on mortality to the argument for immortality, the proof of religion and the triumph over the fear of death.
works.significance: It made the gloomy meditative night-piece the most influential English verse form of the later eighteenth century, supplied the imagery of the graveyard and the ruin to the Gothic, and was read across Europe in translation.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines of great variety, with the abrupt short line, the capitalised abstraction, the exclamation and the suspended period of the night piece.
works.context: Issued in the season of the century's mourning culture, the burial-ground and the fashionable garden, and in the same years as the debate over enthusiasm, ridicule and the reality of religion; the separate numbers were sold as they appeared and were gathered into a single poem as it grew.
works.characters: the poet; the personified Night and her daughters; the auditor of the tales; the dead whom the poem mourns
works.structure: A serial of nine numbered nights, each a continuous meditation with the inset narrative and the address to an auditor, first issued one by one and afterwards collected.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Compleat Angler; or, The Contemplative Man's Recreation
works.description: Izaak Walton's pastoral dialogue on fishing, in which the angler Piscator instructs Venator, combining practical lore on the taking of fish with songs, poems, and reflections on the contemplative life; the fifth edition of 1676 added Charles Cotton's second part.
works.plot: Over five days of dialogue, Piscator teaches Venator and Auceps the arts of angling and defends the quiet life of the angler against the pursuits of the hunter and the falconer.
works.significance: One of the most reprinted books in English (over 400 editions), a founding text of the English pastoral tradition, and the standard expression of the ideal of quiet country retirement.
works.meter: Gentle, conversational prose with interpolated songs and verses.
works.context: First published in 1653, in the Commonwealth, when Walton had withdrawn from public life; revised and expanded in five editions to 1676, when Charles Cotton's part on fly-fishing was added.
works.characters: Piscator (the angler); Venator (the huntsman); Auceps (the falconer); Peter Manwood; Piscator's scholar
works.structure: A pastoral dialogue in five chapters or days, interspersed with songs, verse quotations, and digressions.
works.attributionNotes: Parts I-III by Walton; the 1676 edition adds Part II by Charles Cotton (not in this database), who is named on the title page.
