editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Epistle to Curio
works.description: Akenside's political verse epistle, the fiercest party attack of the mid-century, denouncing the statesman who passed from the opposition to the administration and warning the nation against the corruption of its liberty.
works.plot: The poet addresses Curio as the traitor to the public cause, traces his progress from the patriotic platform to the rewards of the court, and sets the example of the true patriot against the train of ministers, place-holders and corrupt senators.
works.significance: It is the ablest of the century's verse political attacks and the work by which Akenside's public career as a moral and political poet began, and the person intended was understood at once by the party readers of the year.
works.meter: Heroic couplet of the Juvenalian and Swiftian hardness, with the long arraigning period and the closing sententia.
works.context: Written in the year of the fall of the long administration and published at the moment when the conversion of the old country leaders into the new ministry seemed to the patriot writers the ruin of the country cause; the pamphlet presented itself as an old manuscript now first printed.
works.characters: Curio the converted minister; the poet as the patriot monitor; the court and the corrupted senate
works.structure: A single long epistle of invective, moving from the character of the minister to the history of his treason and to the general argument about the fate of British liberty.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously and long uncertain in its authorship, with other names proposed by its enemies; Akenside's claim is established by his circle and by the manuscript evidence, though he is said to have wished the piece suppressed in later life.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Essays
altTitles: Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
works.description: Francis Bacon's essays, published in three successively enlarged editions (ten essays in 1597, thirty-eight in 1612, fifty-eight in 1625): counsels civil and moral on studies, truth, death, revenge, marriage, gardens, masques, and the conduct of public life, in the aphoristic prose that made the form an English genre.
works.plot: No plot: each essay is a compact meditation on its subject — the 1625 title calls them 'counsels, civil and moral' — moving from observation through maxim to practical advice, with the famous 'Of Studies' ('Reading maketh a full man') and 'Of Truth' as its touchstones.
works.significance: The book that naturalized the essay in English — the prose counterpart of Bacon's philosophical revolution, and a schoolbook of English style for three centuries.
works.meter: Prose of aphoristic compression — antithesis, balance, and the telling image — deliberately plain and packed.
works.context: The 1597 edition was among the first English essay collections, after Florio's Montaigne was still to come; the 1625 edition, published the year before Bacon's death, is the canonical text and the foundation of the English essay tradition.
works.structure: A collection of fifty-eight numbered essays in the final edition, each a self-contained meditation in the Senecan and Montaignian modes.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Essayes or Counsels, Civill and Morall (Oxford Francis Bacon)

works.title: The Essays of Montaigne
works.description: John Florio's translation of Montaigne's Essays (1603), made from the 1595 French edition: the first complete English Montaigne, in which the Frenchman's scepticism, self-portraiture, and humane wisdom enter English prose in Florio's expansive, inventive idiom — the book Shakespeare read and quarried for The Tempest.
works.plot: No plot: the Essays proceed by subject — custom, cannibals, coaches, friendship, experience — Montaigne's 'I' the matter of the book, and Florio's version enlarging the French into the rich Elizabethan English of the translator's own invention.
works.significance: One of the great translations in the language — the book that gave English thought its sceptical conscience and Shakespeare his New World speech.
works.meter: Prose of Florio's characteristic copiousness — Montaigne's sentences doubled and ornamented into the idiom that Shakespeare knew.
works.context: Published 1603, dedicated to the Countess of Bedford and others; Shakespeare's Gonzalo in The Tempest paraphrases 'Of Cannibals' from this translation, the most famous borrowing in English drama.
works.characters: Michel de Montaigne (as speaker); his friend La Boétie (in 'Of Friendship'); the cannibals; the ancients quoted throughout
works.structure: Three books of essays in the 1595 arrangement, with Florio's dedicatory epistles, his preface 'To the Reader', and his appendix of the author's life.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by John Florio from the 1595 French text; uncontested.

editions.title: Shakespeare's Montaigne: The Florio Translation of the Essays, A Selection
editions.editor: Stephen Greenblatt and Peter G. Platt (eds.)

works.title: The Examinations of Anne Askew
altTitles: The First Examination of Anne Askew
The Latter Examination of Anne Askew
works.description: Anne Askew's first-person accounts of her two examinations for heresy before the ecclesiastical authorities, printed in 1546 and 1547 with prefaces by John Bale; the most important English text written by a woman in the first half of the sixteenth century.
works.plot: Askew narrates her arrest and first examination before the bishop's chancellor (March 1545) and the second, harsher examination before Bishop Bonner, Bishop Gardiner, Wriothesley, and the privy council (1545–46), recording her scriptural answers on the eucharist, her refusal to name her fellow evangelicals, and her racking in the Tower — 'I answered that I would not deny my master and my God'; the account ends with her condemnation, the burning following on 16 July 1546.
works.significance: The first sustained autobiographical narrative by an English woman in print and the founding text of the English martyr tradition; Askew's scriptural self-defence under torture made her a model of the speaking female subject for later centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in prison in 1545–46, smuggled out, and printed by Bale at Wesel in 1546 (first examination) and 1547 (latter examination) as Protestant propaganda against the Henrician church; John Foxe incorporated the Examinations into the Book of Martyrs, making Askew the most famous of the Henrician women martyrs.
works.characters: Anne Askew (narrator); Bishop Edmund Bonner; Bishop Stephen Gardiner; Thomas Wriothesley; Christopher Dare; John Bale (editor)
works.structure: A first-person testimonial narrative in two parts, with Bale's framing prefaces and his 'elucidations' printed alongside; the latter examination includes the exchange with the council and the account of the rack.
works.attributionNotes: The text is Askew's own account, edited (and heavily framed) by John Bale; the record attributes authorship to Askew, with Bale's role as editor noted.

editions.title: The Examinations of Anne Askew
editions.publisher: Oxford University Press (Women Writers in English 1350–1850)

works.title: The Examiner Papers
works.description: The thrice-weekly ministerial paper which Swift took over and turned into the ablest organ of Harley's peace administration: a sequence of party essays examining the Whig conduct of the war, the church in danger and the state of the nation.
works.plot: The examiner reviews the party in office, the dissenters, the moneyed interest and the allies, and examines the arguments of the opposing papers, closing with the defence of the negotiation for the peace.
works.significance: It marks the moment at which periodical prose became the chief weapon of English party politics, and it is Swift's school of the ironical examination that Gulliver and the Drapier later extend.
works.meter: Swift's bare and forceful prose style, the short closing sentence and the rhetorical question, in deliberate contrast to the periodic manner of the essay papers.
works.context: The paper ran through the winter of the peace negotiation and the trial of the Sacheverell cause, and was conducted by Swift from about the autumn of 1710; Addison's Spectator was in part a reply to its method, and the contest of the two papers defined the political middle.
works.characters: the Examiner as the speaking editor; the ministry in office; the dissenting clergy; the confederate allies
works.structure: Serial numbered papers, each a self-contained argument, with the occasional re-print of an opposing text for examination.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative: the paper before Swift's direction and several numbers around him belong to other hands, and the division between Swift's papers and those of the associated writers remains a matter of bibliographical argument.

editions.title: Jonathan Swift: Critical, Scholastic, and Variorum Edition

works.title: The Example of Virtue
works.description: Hawes's first major poem, an allegory of the soul's life: Youth, guided by Discretion, journeys through the world and learns virtue's lessons from Lady Sapience, marries Cleanness, and passes through Age to the vision of Eternity. Printed by Wynkyn de Worde about 1504.
works.plot: Youth, counselled by Discretion, crosses the sea of the world, defeats the dragon of vice, and is led by Sapience and Fortune's lessons to the marriage with Cleanness; Age overtakes him, and the soul enters Eternity.
works.significance: A minor but characteristic example of the late medieval moral allegory, showing the tradition Spenser was to transform.
works.meter: Rhyme royal in the Lydgatian manner, with aureate vocabulary.
works.context: Written early in the reign of Henry VII, when the court still sustained the allegorical tradition of the fifteenth century.
works.characters: Youth; Discretion; Lady Sapience; Cleanness; Fortune; Age; Eternity
works.structure: A moral allegory in the pilgrimage form, moving from instruction through trial to the vision of eternity.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Exeter Book Riddles
works.description: A collection of some ninety-five riddles in the Exeter Book, ranging from the majestic (the swan, the iceberg, the storm, the bookworm) to the bawdy double entendres (the onion, the key, the churn), all spoken in the first person by their subjects — the largest surviving body of riddles in any early medieval vernacular.
works.plot: Each riddle presents an oblique first-person self-description — 'I am a wonderful creature...' — inviting the reader to name the hidden subject; subjects include weapons, tools, animals, natural forces, writing, and domestic objects, with several deliberately suggestive 'obscene' solutions masking innocent ones.
works.significance: The cornerstone of the English riddle tradition; a unique window onto the everyday and the marvellous in Anglo-Saxon imagination.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the riddles vary from four lines to over a hundred.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 101a-115a and elsewhere); the genre descends from the Latin enigmata of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
works.characters: the speaking objects (swan, iceberg, bookworm, onion, key, etc.)
works.structure: A sequence of independent enigmas, likely arranged by the compiler in thematic groups; the collection ends with a famous series of double-entendre riddles.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the collection may include compositions by several poets over centuries.
themes: The sublime, terror, and the ruin

editions.title: The Old English Riddles of the Exeter Book

sources: Essays in the History of Ideas

works.title: The Expedition of Humphry Clinker
altTitles: The Expedition of Humphry Clinker. In a Series of Letters
works.form: epistolary novel of travel and opinion
works.description: The account of a family tour through England and Scotland, given in letters by five correspondents whose temperaments make the same scenes appear as five different books. It is at once the century's most successful comic novel of opinion, a handbook of the bath, road and fishery, and a study in the politics, medicine and morals of the late Georgians.
works.plot: An old bachelor of fortune, his maiden aunt, his ward and their two servants set out for the waters at Bath and travel by Bristol, Wales, Liverpool and the Scottish Highlands home to London. Each correspondent reports the places and the people - the pump-room, the manufacturers, the Highland hospitality, the electors and the mobs - according to his or her interest, and the servants' own histories turn out to matter. Humphry Clinker is discovered to be an heiress's lost lover, the aunt is married against her principle of scorn, and the invalid is cured by the journey.
works.significance: It is the richest of the eighteenth-century comic novels and the standard literary source for the geography of Georgian taste, reform and travel; its plural correspondence method was much imitated and remains a touchstone of narrative theory.
works.meter: Five sharply distinguished prose idioms - the politer satiric period, the fussy feminine epistle, the young man's essay, the servant's blundering record - the comedy arising from their collision over a single fact.
works.context: Written in the last years of the author's life at Nice and in London, and published in 1771, in the season of the heated politics of the Middlesex election and its riots, of the craze for the waters and for the Scottish tour, and of the debate on emigration and the fishery.
works.characters: Matthew Bramble Esq.; his sister Tabitha; their ward and nephew; Humphry Clinker the footman-gardener; Mrs. Winifred Jenkins; the assistant of the Scottish journey
works.structure: A correspondence in five hands, arranged so that the same events are reported at a distance by different letters; the plot is carried by the delayed recognition of the servants' histories.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and documented in the letters of its composition.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Fable of the Bees
altTitles: The Fable of the Bees: or, Private Vices, Publick Benefits
The Grumbling Hive, or Knaves Turned Honest
works.form: allegorical poem with prose philosophical essays
works.description: Mandeville's paradox poem and prose commentary, developing the thesis that private vices - luxury, pride, avarice, sensuality - are publicly beneficial because they set trade, ingenuity, and civility in motion. The first edition paired the 1705 poem 'The Grumbling Hive' with an enquiring essay; the enlarged edition of 1723-29 added a second fable, part of a play, and an extended discussion of the moral origins of virtue.
works.plot: A hive of prosperous bees, 'full of knaves', thrives on fraud, luxury, and emulation until a divine reformer makes them honest; virtue then starves trade, and the hive falls to a despicable abject state, the moral being that neither saints nor knaves can make a 'hiv' well governed. The prose essays that follow argue, paradox by paradox, that the most corrupt societies may be the most flourishing, that honour and shame are artificial engines of social cooperation, and that self-denial for its own sake is a sophism. Mandeville's later Defence and Enquiry extend the argument against 'virtue without renunciation' and against the church's account of moral self-love, distinguishing the 'fine gloss' of virtue from its real, self-interested sources.
works.significance: It is the century's most provocative contribution to the luxury debate, a decisive influence on Hume, Adam Smith, and the ideas of unintended social order, and a landmark of paradoxical prose satire.
works.meter: The fable is written in tight, dry heroic couplets of iambic pentameter in the manner of Auguean didactic satire; the commentary is plain, colloquial argumentative prose.
works.context: Developed from the 1705 poem printed for a Whig club, published as the Fable in 1714 and greatly enlarged in 1723-29, when it provoked formal presentments by the Grand Jury of Middlesex and a flood of replies; it belongs to the debates over luxury, commerce, and national decline opened by the 1720s economic writings.
works.characters: the bees of the hive; the God of the hive; Mandeville as essayist and respondent
works.structure: A short allegorical poem in heroic couplets followed by increasingly long prose essays, a defence, and enquiries; the second edition added a further fable, a dramatic poem 'The Grumbling Hive' turned into a play, and an examination of the reviewer.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Faerie Queene
works.description: Spenser's unfinished national epic and allegorical romance: twelve projected books of the adventures of knights who embody the private virtues, of which six were completed — Holiness (Redcrosse), Temperance (Guyon), Chastity (Britomart), Friendship (Cambell and Triamond), Justice (Artegall), and Courtesy (Calidore) — together with the fragmentary Mutabilitie Cantos (printed 1609), all moving through the fairyland that shadows Elizabeth's England and court.
works.plot: In each book a knight-errant undertakes a quest under the commission of the Faerie Queene (Gloriana): Redcrosse defeats the dragon and wins Una; Guyon destroys the Bower of Bliss; Britomart seeks Artegall through her founding vision of Britain; Artegall dispenses justice against Grantorto; Calidore wins Pastorella; the whole is shadowed by the giants, enchanters, and false knights of moral and political evil.
works.significance: The supreme poem of the English Renaissance and the fountain of English romantic narrative; Milton, Keats, and Tennyson all took their bearings from it.
works.meter: The Spenserian stanza: nine lines, eight of iambic pentameter and a final alexandrine, rhyming ababbcbcc.
works.context: Composed across the Armada decade; dedicated to Elizabeth I, with Books I–III printed in 1590 and IV–VI in 1596 during Spenser's service in Ireland; its allegories address the Reformation, the conquest of Ireland, and the cult of the Queen.
works.characters: Gloriana (the Faerie Queene); Prince Arthur; Redcrosse; Una; Guyon; Britomart; Artegall; Talus; Calidore; Archimago; Duessa; Acrasia
works.structure: Six completed books of twelve cantos each in interlaced romance structure, unified by the figure of Arthur, Prince of Britain, and by the allegorical design announced in the Letter to Ralegh.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Faerie Queene
editions.editor: A. C. Hamilton (ed.), text by Hiroshi Yamashita and Toshiyuki Suzuki

works.title: The Fair Jilt; or, The Amours of Prince Tarquin and Sister Henrietta
works.description: Behn's short prose fiction based on the real scandal of Sister Henrietta of the Convent of the Holy Sepulchre at Antwerp, who was tried for attempting to murder her sister; Behn, who sat on the jury, presents her as a beautiful and irresistible temptress.
works.plot: The beautiful Henrietta, forced into a convent, is pursued by the friar Tarquin; her intrigues with a nobleman and her attempt to murder her sister lead to her trial, and she is finally reconciled to the church.
works.significance: An important example of the Restoration scandal narrative and of Behn's exploitation of the boundary between reportage and fiction.
works.meter: Restoration prose of the scandal-chronicle type.
works.context: Published in 1688; Behn claimed to have witnessed the events while in the Spanish Netherlands in the 1680s.
works.characters: Sister Henrietta; Prince Tarquin; the Prince of Antwerp; the Prioress
works.structure: A short prose narrative with a documentary frame, presented as a true history.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Behn; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: Kissing the Rod: An Anthology of Seventeenth-Century Women's Verse
editions.editor: Germaine Greer, Susan Hastings, Jeslyn Medoff, and Melinda Sansone (eds.)

editions.title: The Works of Aphra Behn
editions.publisher: William Pickering / Ohio State University Press

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Fair Penitent
works.description: Rowe's tragedy of Calista, a woman of quality betrayed into a private guilt which is discovered and judged: the most acted and most read English tragedy of the first half of the century, and the founding play of the pathetic drama of female frailty.
works.plot: Calista, long yielded to the gay deceiver Altamonte and still engaged elsewhere, is exposed by the discovery of her correspondence; her father Sciolto pronounces and executes the family judgment, and the play closes in the deaths of the offenders and of the injured.
works.significance: It made the betrayed and penitent woman the central pathetic figure of the English stage and supplied the plot and the vocabulary that the sentimental drama and the novel of seduction later prosified.
works.meter: Blank verse of sustained pathetic declamation, with the broken address and the long-completed sentence of the penitential speeches.
works.context: Written for the players of the patent theatre in the years when the reformation of the stage was being argued in print, and long identified with the acting of the century's chief tragic actresses.
works.characters: Calista; Sciolto; Altamonte; Lavinia
works.structure: Five acts of discovery and judgment, with the private correspondence as the mechanism of exposure and the father's sentence as the catastrophe.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Family Expositor
altTitles: The Family Expositor: or, A Paraphrase and Commentary on the New Testament
works.description: Doddridge's great posthumous work, a paraphrase and commentary on the New Testament in weekly family portions, published from his manuscripts from 1756 into the 1760s. It was designed to make each section of scripture a complete act of family worship: text, sense, improvement, and devotion together.
works.plot: Each week's portion gives the biblical text with a running paraphrase that supplies the idioms and links, a commentary of doctrine and criticism, and then the practical improvement for the heart and life. Doddridge draws on the best earlier annotators, joining scholarship of a learned temper to pulpit directness. The improvements turn each passage into meditation on providence, the Saviour's love, and the duties of the common hour. The work runs its course through the Gospels and Acts into the epistles, the later volumes completed from his papers by friends.
works.significance: It set the model of the devotional commentary for family worship and, through its completion and constant reprinting into the nineteenth century, formed generations of Protestant reading of the New Testament.
works.meter: A smooth, meditative prose of paraphrase and application, the rhythms of prayer woven into exposition.
works.context: Long prepared at Northampton for the academy and for the family devotions of his people, and published after his death from 1756, it became the most popular Protestant family New Testament of the later eighteenth century.
works.structure: A continuous paraphrase-commentary in weekly family lessons through the books of the New Testament, each lesson a unit of text, paraphrase, comment, and improvement.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
altTitles: The Further Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
The Second Part of the Life of Robinson Crusoe
works.form: novel; prose voyage narrative with an inherited fictional persona
works.description: The second of the three Robinson Crusoe volumes, issued in August 1719 after a spurious continuation had appeared in London. It returns the narrator to the island, then carries him through the East Indies, the Cape and across the deserts of Central Asia in a series of voyages that replace settlement with motion.
works.plot: Crusoe revisits his island, now peopled by the mutineers he left there and by newly arrived Englishmen and Spaniards, and settles disputes over worship and government before sailing on. He is attacked off Madagascar, trades and travels through the Malay coast, China and Persia, and after a near-fatal crossing of the Great Tartary desert reaches Moscow and travels overland to England, where he finds himself unexpectedly wealthy. The volume closes with a third voyage contemplated rather than narrated.
works.significance: It fixed the model of the sequel and the return-novel, and its colony-building episode has been much discussed as a fable of plantation government, toleration and colonial ownership.
works.meter: Plainer and more hurried prose than the first volume, dominated by dates, distances and commoditues of trade; the meditative periodic sentence gives way to the listed itinerary.
works.context: Composed within months of the first volume's success, it draws on East India Company and privateering narratives and expressly supersedes the pirating Continuation of the World of Robinson Crusoe published in London in mid-1719.
works.characters: Robinson Crusoe; the island governor; Friday's brother; the Portuguese pilot; the Tartar and Muscovite guides
works.structure: First-person retrospect in an episodic voyage sequence, the island episode framing a picaresque chain of traverses and encounters; less concentrated than the first volume and more dependent on reported incident.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was advertised as the true second part to displace the anonymously pirated continuation.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Fatal Marriage; or, The Innocent Adultery
works.description: Thomas Southerne's most successful tragedy, an adaptation of two of Behn's novellas, in which Isabella, believing her husband Alonzo dead, remarries and is destroyed when the first husband returns.
works.plot: Isabella, in poverty, believes Alonzo dead and marries Biron; Alonzo returns; Isabella, unable to bear the guilt, kills Biron's brother and then herself.
works.significance: The most popular she-tragedy of the 1690s and an important adaptation of Behn's prose fiction for the stage.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1694 and published the same year; Elizabeth Barry's Isabella was one of the great performances of the age, and the play held the stage into the nineteenth century.
works.characters: Isabella; Alonzo; Biron; Baldwin; Carlos; Anne
works.structure: Five acts in blank verse with a subordinate comic plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Southerne; he acknowledges the debt to Behn in the dedication.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Fatal Sisters
altTitles: The Fatal Sisters: A Translation from the Norse
works.description: Gray's imitated translation of an old Norse poem of the women of the battle, in which the fatal sisters sing the names of the doomed and the course of the fight while they ply the wound and the hair.
works.plot: The daughters of the whirlwind and the battle chant their terrible weaving of the fates of the warriors, name the king whose hour is come and the land that is to be won, and ride away to the north and to the night after the song.
works.significance: It introduced the imagery and the machinery of the northern mythology into English verse, and it is the most exact of the century's poetic reconstructions of primitive poetry.
works.meter: The short paired lines of the reconstructed northern measure, with the heavy alliteration and the repeated burden.
works.context: Written in the same year as The Bard out of Gray's study of the Danish and Norse poetry in the antiquarian editions, at the moment when the northern and the primitive were being made the models of a new sublimity.
works.characters: the fatal sisters of the battle; the king whose doom is chanted; the warriors of the two hosts
works.structure: A short series of antiphonal stanzas of the imitated Norse measure, with the refrain and the enumeration of the slain.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Gray's, though the piece is an imitation rather than a literal translation and the identification of his Norse original is a matter of the antiquarian scholarship of the following century.

editions.title: The Poems of Thomas Gray, William Collins and Oliver Goldsmith

works.title: The Fates of the Apostles
works.form: religious catalogue poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 122 lines cataloguing the deaths and missionary fields of the twelve apostles, signed by Cynewulf in a runic acrostic that spells his name. The catalogue frame encloses a meditation on the poet's own need for grace, the best-known of the four Cynewulfian signatures.
works.plot: The poet, speaking as a weary traveller, enumerates the apostles in order — where each preached and how each died (Peter crucified, Paul beheaded, Andrew in Achaia, John at Ephesus, and so on) — then turns to himself: begging the prayers of the reader, weaving the runes of his name into a meditation on the gifts of God and the terror of judgment.
works.significance: The earliest signature of an English poet in his own verse; a key document for the Cynewulf canon.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the runic acrostic spells CYNEWULF.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 52v-54r) and in the same collection as Andreas and the homilies.
works.characters: the twelve apostles; the poet (Cynewulf)
works.structure: A thula-like catalogue of the apostles followed by the runic signature passage, which modulates from report to prayer.
works.attributionNotes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes; accepted as authentic.
themes: Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
sources: The Rise of the Novel: Studies in Defoe, Richardson and Fielding

works.title: The Female Husband
works.form: fictional biography and scandalous tale in prose
works.description: A fictionalised life of the woman who passed as a man and married several women, published on the occasion of her trial at the Bristol court in 1746. It is a short scandalous biography in the Newgate manner, mixing report, invention and moral comment on the boundaries of sex and marriage.
works.plot: A young person of masculine appearance and no fortune takes to the road in male dress, learns the practice of a physic, and courtships and marries women in several counties. The marriages are consummated or refused, the wives complain of deformity and distance, and the pursuit of an affectionate partner leads at last to detection, trial and punishment. The narrative reports the exposure with a mixture of sensational detail and professed moral horror.
works.significance: It is a central text for the history of cross-dressing, gender impersonation and the legal fiction of sexual identity in eighteenth-century print culture, and evidence of the novelist's movement from amatory to documentary material.
works.meter: Plain narrative prose with the abrupt, evidential sentences of the trial report and the raised register of the moral reflection.
works.context: Published in 1746 out of the reports of a real prosecution for bigamy and deceit at the Bristol sessions, and in the same decade as the author's own conduct-oriented fiction; the case touched the law of marriage and the definition of sex.
works.characters: the female husband; the successive brides; the constables and prosecutors; the Bristol court
works.structure: A continuous pseudo-biographical life in two short parts, following the trial report and the confessional narrative conventions of criminal biography; detection serves as the structural hinge.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution generally accepted on stylistic and publishing grounds and recorded as single; the text was published without the writer's name, and its subject is a real person whose own account differs.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Female Quixote; or, The Adventures of Arabella
works.form: comic novel; moralities of reading in prose
works.description: The comedy of a young heiress who, having read nothing but romances, governs her conduct by their laws and reads every man as a knight and every civility as a homage. It is the most sustained English treatment of the madwoman of the reading plot and one of the century's central statements about fiction's power over its readers.
works.plot: Arabella, beautiful and rich, insists upon the ceremonious courtship prescribed by the romances and refuses the plain addresses of the man she ought to marry. Her lover and her friend try various devices to cure her, including a counter-romantic treatment which makes her believe herself admired in the old style. The exposure of a designing admirer at last breaks the illusion, and the closing reconciliation is effected by a physician who prescribes history and religion against romance.
works.significance: It gave the century its most influential figure of the female reader corrupted by fiction and supplied the model for later treatments of romantic delusion, from its own imitators to the nineteenth-century novel of reading.
works.meter: A clear ironic prose that quotes and parodies the diction of the heroic romance in the heroine's speeches, the comedy lying in the mismatch of registers.
works.context: Published in 1752, in the season of the quarrel over the danger of novel-reading and of the author's own friendship with the leading writers of the day, including the lexicographer who advertised the book; its target includes the surviving vogue of translated romance.
works.characters: Arabella; her lover and friend; the designing admirer who works on her delusion; the physician and the moralist of the conclusion
works.structure: Third-person narration in two volumes, the plot a single sustained irony maintained by the heroine's misreadings; the episodes are arranged as trials of her interpretive system and resolved by an anti-romance cure.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and long, wrongly, credited to another hand by early bibliographers before being firmly reassigned.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Female Reader
altTitles: The Female Reader: Pieces, Prose and Verse, Selected from the Most Classick Writers and Calculated as a Practical Guide to the Review of a Female Education
The Female Reader. A Practical Guide to the Review of a Female Education
works.form: anthology and critical guide to reading
works.description: An anthology of prose and verse selected for the use of young women and furnished with rules of reading and with the editor's remarks on taste, elocution and the choice of books. It was planned as the practical completion of a female education and issued in several volumes.
works.plot: The collection passes in order through the species of composition - description, argument, narration, the drama, the epic, lyric and the letters of history - each being illustrated by extracted specimens and preceded by directions for reading it well. Remarks on the choice of books, on the cultivation of the ear and on the danger of incorrect reading supply the connective argument. Its design is to make a woman's taste an instrument of judgement rather than of amusement.
works.significance: It is an important document of the pedagogy of taste for women at the end of the century and evidence of the author's methods as a critic and teacher before her political writing.
works.meter: A didactic prose of rule and remark for the connecting matter, the verse extracts being given as specimens of the several measures and the prose as models of style.
works.context: Published in 1789 in the same season as the author's work on the education of women and within the dissenting and Bluestocking projects for female improvement, the anthology genre then being a principal means of literary instruction.
works.structure: A systematic anthology in classes with the editor's dissertations and notes interposed; the order of the species governs the sequence, the extracts supplying the examples.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution established by the publisher's records and by the correspondence of the period, the work having been issued without the name of the editor; part of the compiling labour has been associated with a sister's hand, and the record is held as partial.

editions.title: The Works of Mary Wollstonecraft, 7 volumes
editions.editor: Janet M. Todd and Marilyn Butler (general editors)

works.title: The Finnsburh Fragment
works.manuscriptDate: lost; preserved in an early eighteenth-century transcript
works.description: A fragment of about 48 lines of an older heroic lay describing the night attack on the hall of Finn, king of the Frisians, in which the Danish prince Hnæf and his men defend the doors for five days. The story — later told allusively in Beowulf's 'Finnsburg episode' — is one of the great Germanic tales of feud and loyalty.
works.plot: A watchman sees the gleam of weapons as Finn's men attack the hall by night; Hnæf's Danes hold the doors, and the fight lasts five days without a man falling, until the fragment breaks off. The fuller story, reconstructed from Beowulf and other sources, involves the peace-pledge of Hildeburh, the death of Hnæf and Finn's son, and Finn's eventual slaying by the Danes.
works.significance: The sole surviving example, alongside Beowulf, of the heroic hall-fight; indispensable for reconstructing the legend and the older lay tradition.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of an archaic, compressed kind.
works.context: The story belongs to the fifth-century Germanic migrations; the text survives only in the transcript made by George Hickes for his Thesaurus (1705) of a manuscript leaf (Lambeth Palace MS 487) now lost.
works.characters: Hnæf; Finn; Hildeburh; Hengest; Sigeferth; Garulf; Guðlaf; Ordlaf
works.structure: A single vivid scene of hall-fighting, extended by speeches (the door-defenders Garulf and Guðere, the veteran Sigeferth); the poem's brevity and compression suggest the style of the older lays behind Beowulf.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: The Fleece
works.form: Didactic and topographical poem in the Thomson school, in books, with the technical instruction of a husbandry poem combined with the survey of a trade; issued after subscription proposals and dedications.
works.description: John Dyer's principal poem: a didactic and topographical work on the English wool trade, from the feeding of the sheep and the shearing to the staple, the marketing and the international commerce that carried the fleece to the world's ends. It was published by subscription and carries the name of the clergyman who wrote it. The ambition is at once technical and moral: to make the whole circuit of a national industry the subject of elevated unrhymed verse.
works.plot: The poem moves outward in stages from the pasture to the ocean. Its first care is practical: the breeds, the feeding, the shearing and the management of the flock, with the shepherd and the shepherdess introduced as figures of a vanishing rural order. From the fleece in the fold it passes to the wool in the warehouse and the market, and then to the merchant, the ship and the ports of the Mediterranean and the north, arguing that this single commodity has bound England into the world's trade. A moral anxiety runs under the praise: the growth of wealth threatens to corrupt the labour and the independence that produced it, and the prospect of national fullness is shadowed by the fear of decline. The argument is therefore a sustained piece of political economy in verse, closer to a discourse of the wool trade than to any earlier English poem.
works.significance: It is the most ambitious of the eighteenth-century attempts to put a national industry into elevated verse, and the crucial link between Thomson's meditative topography and Goldsmith's 'The Deserted Village' in the poetry of rural labour, commerce and depopulation. Samuel Johnson's account of its crabbed sublimity made it the standard example of a poet who mistook harshness for strength, and it remains a primary document of the age's thinking about commerce and its discontents.
works.meter: Blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) of notoriously harsh and laborious texture, with long compounds, stretched and hypermetric lines, and an evident attempt to bend English measure to the weight of Latin and Italian syntax.
works.context: It was written in the decades when the wool and cloth trade was the acknowledged foundation of English national power, and when the staple, the export markets and the growing manufactures were matters of public debate. Dyer, a Welsh-born curate with a small living and large schemes for rural industry, published by subscription after earlier ventures failed, and the poem carries those projects' hopes and disappointments.
works.characters: The shepherd and shepherdess of the English hills; the wool merchant; the mariner; the labouring poor of the staple towns
works.structure: A didactic poem in books, each gathering its own department of the subject, with descriptive digression, apostrophe to the labouring poor, and an ascending sweep from local husbandry to global commerce.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was published in the author's own name in the collected editions and its composition is documented in Dyer's correspondence with his friends. Precise years of composition for the individual books are not fixed here and are left null.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Forc'd Marriage; or, A Night's Intrigue
works.description: Aphra Behn's first play, a tragicomedy of forced marriage and intrigue in which Alcander is compelled to marry Erminia while loving another, and the complications are resolved in a set of marriages.
works.plot: The King forces Erminia to marry Alcander, who loves Aminta; disguises and mistaken identities lead to a night of intrigue, and the plot ends with the rightful pairings.
works.significance: The first play by a woman to be performed on the English public stage, marking the beginning of professional female authorship in English drama.
works.meter: Rhymed heroic couplets.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in December 1670 and published in 1671; it ran for six nights, a modest but respectable success for a first play, and by a woman.
works.characters: Alcander; Erminia; Aminta; Cleontius; Lisander; the King; Galliard
works.structure: Five acts of heroic tragicomedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Behn; authorship undisputed.
