editions.editor: Germaine Greer, Susan Hastings, Jeslyn Medoff, and Melinda Sansone (eds.)

editions.title: The Works of Aphra Behn
editions.publisher: William Pickering / Ohio State University Press

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Forest
works.description: Jonson's collection of fifteen poems printed in the 1616 Folio, including the country-house poem 'To Penshurst', the odes 'To Celia' and 'To Heaven', the song 'That Women Are but Men's Shadows', and the epistle 'To Sir Robert Wroth' — the volume that made the estate, the court, and the virtuous life the matter of English lyric.
works.plot: No plot: the poems move from the celebration of Penshurst's hospitality and Sidneyan estate-life, through the songs and odes of love and devotion, to the epistles and epitaphs that map Jonson's moral world of patrons and friends.
works.significance: Home of the English country-house poem and of Jonson's most enduring lyrics — the classical counterweight to the metaphysical fashion.
works.meter: Couplets, odes, and songs of classical restraint, including the famous lyric 'Drink to me only with thine eyes' (a cento from Philostratus).
works.context: Collected for the 1616 Folio; 'To Penshurst' (c. 1612) founded the country-house poem that Lanyer, Carew, and Marvell would continue.
works.characters: the poet; the Sidney family (at Penshurst); Celia; Sir Robert Wroth; the Countess of Bedford
works.structure: A miscellany of fifteen poems organized by theme — place, love, virtue, mortality — with 'To Penshurst' as its opening masterpiece.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, 7 vols.
editions.editor: David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (gen. eds.)

works.title: The Form of Living
works.description: Richard Rolle's English epistle of spiritual guidance, written c. 1348 for Margaret Kirkby, the anchoress of Ainderby, and the most influential of his English works: a rule of the devout life in twelve chapters, from the love of God and the practice of prayer through the discernment of true contemplation to the joy of the heavenly song. It became the classic handbook of English anchoresses after Ancrene Wisse.
works.plot: Addressed to Margaret 'in the form of living', the epistle teaches the love of God above all things, the exercise of prayer and meditation on the Passion, the temptations and consolations of the solitary life, and the discernment of the true 'song' of contemplation from delusion.
works.significance: The bridge between Ancrene Wisse and the fifteenth-century devotional manuals, and the classic of the Rolle tradition in English.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative prose of the Rolle school.
works.context: Written c. 1348 for Margaret Kirkby, recluse of Ainderby, in the last year of Rolle's life; the most widely copied of his English writings, it circulated into the fifteenth century and was printed by Wynkyn de Worde.
works.characters: Rolle (writer); Margaret Kirkby (addressee)
works.structure: Twelve short chapters of practical and mystical instruction, in the epistle form of the Rolle canon.
works.attributionNotes: Rolle's authorship secure.

works.title: The Forme of Cury
works.description: The earliest English cookery collection: some 200 recipes compiled c. 1390 by the master cooks of King Richard II, from potages and roasted meats to the subtleties and spiced dishes of the royal table, including the first English recipe for pasta ('macrows') and dishes with olive oil. It is the foundation document of English culinary literature.
works.plot: The collection proceeds from the 'furmenty' and potages through flesh and fish days to the elaborate final courses, with the spices of the East (saffron, cloves, mace) and the French culinary vocabulary of the court marking the recipes' royal provenance.
works.significance: The first English cookbook and the classic document of medieval English courtly cuisine; its recipes are still cooked by food historians today.
works.meter: Prose: terse, practical recipe English with French technical terms.
works.context: Compiled c. 1390 by the chief master cooks of Richard II, and preserved in the manuscript BL Additional MS 5016 (with the closely related manuscripts of the Curye on Inglysch group); first printed by Samuel Pegge (1780).
works.characters: none (recipe collection)
works.structure: A recipe collection in the medieval cookbook tradition, organized by course and occasion, with the royal headnote claiming its authority.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous (compiled by the king's cooks).

works.title: The Fortunes of Men
works.description: A poem of 98 lines cataloguing the fates that befall men — one dies young, one by the sword, one from a fall, one on the gallows; the hawk dies, the wolf mourns, the singer is praised — closing with the assurance that God apportions all gifts. A companion to The Gifts of Men.
works.plot: The poem surveys the deaths and destinies of men (and, in an admired passage, of a hawk), then turns to the arts — one man learns song, one harp, one the law — and concludes that the Measurer shapes each man's lot, bestowing craft, wealth, and wisdom as he will.
works.significance: A finely crafted example of the catalogue poem and of the period's providential view of human diversity.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 87a-88b), following Widsith.
works.characters: none
works.structure: A double catalogue (fates, then gifts) closed by a doxological gnome on divine providence.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
sources: Encyclopedia of the Enlightenment

works.title: The Four Elements
altTitles: A New Interlude and a Mery, of the Nature of the Four Elements
works.description: John Rastell's pedagogical interlude on the four elements and the new geography, printed by the author c. 1520; the first English play designed to teach natural science.
works.plot: Humanity, instructed by Nature and Studious Desire, is taught the four elements, the roundness of the earth, and the new-found lands of America; he is then tempted by Sensual Appetite into the tavern, where he wastes his learning in drinking, and the fragment (the play survives incomplete) breaks off with Experience promising his restoration.
works.significance: The first English play to teach science and geography, and a pioneering attempt to harness the stage to the new learning; it documents the arrival of the Age of Discovery in English popular culture.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic songs
works.context: Printed c. 1520 by Rastell, More's brother-in-law, who had himself attempted a voyage to the New World in 1517; the play's geography lesson celebrates the discovery of America, and its music survives in the unique fragment (British Library).
works.characters: Nature; Humanity; Studious Desire; Sensual Appetite; Experience; Ignorance; The Taverner
works.structure: A morality framework used for instruction: a series of lectures on cosmology and geography alternating with scenes of temptation and fall, with songs (including one with music) and a dance.

works.title: The Four PP
altTitles: The Play Called the Four PP
works.description: John Heywood's best-known farce, a lying contest among a Palmer, a Pardoner, a Pothecary, and a Pedlar; the earliest surviving edition is that of William Middleton, c. 1544.
works.plot: A Palmer, Pardoner, and Pothecary each boast of his trade and its profits, and the Pedlar proposes a contest: whoever tells the greatest lie wins the wager. The Pothecary's tale of a marvellous cure and the Pardoner's account of a soul released from hell's pains — capped by the Palmer's claim that he has met a woman patient and uncomplaining — end the contest, the Palmer winning the palm and the company concluding in good fellowship.
works.significance: The most famous of the Tudor interludes and the classic English stage farce before Shakespeare; its tale of the woman patient in all things circulated into later jest-books and remains the play by which Heywood is chiefly remembered.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Composed c. 1520–30 in Heywood's period as a court entertainer and virginal player to Henry VIII; the lying contest reworks the fabliau tradition (the tale of the patient wife appears in Boccaccio) and the satire of pardons and relics reflects pre-Reformation criticism of popular piety.
works.characters: The Palmer; The Pardoner; The Pothecary; The Pedlar
works.structure: A single-scene farce built of successive set-piece tales, with the Pedlar as proposer and judge of the wager.

editions.title: The Plays of John Heywood

works.title: The Fox and the Wolf
works.description: The earliest English beast fable, a comic tale of some 300 lines in which the fox, trapped in a bucket down a well, persuades the gullible wolf that he is in paradise, and escapes by the wolf's folly. It inaugurates the English Reynardian tradition that runs to Caxton's Reynard the Fox.
works.plot: The thirsty fox climbs into one well-bucket and is stranded; when the wolf asks what he does there, the fox claims the well is paradise, induces the wolf to descend in the other bucket, and is drawn up as the wolf goes down.
works.significance: The beginning of the English Reynard tradition and the earliest English fabliau-fable; an essential witness to the continental debts of early Middle English narrative.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with lively dialogue.
works.context: Composed c. 1250–75, adapted from the French Roman de Renart; preserved in the late thirteenth-century Digby MS 86 (Bodleian Library).
works.characters: the Fox; the Wolf
works.structure: A single comic episode built on the trickster's persuasive lie and the dupe's comeuppance.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Freeholder
altTitles: The Freeholder: a Collection of Papers
works.description: Addison's late political essay paper, written in support of the Hanoverian settlement during the Jacobite rising of 1715 and addressed to the freeholder electorate; it argues the case for limited property-based liberty against both arbitrary power and popular licence.
works.plot: A freeholder addresses his constituents and a succession of imaginary opponents, tracing the constitution from the feudal conquest, defending the settled succession, and warning that a standing army, Jacobite intrigue and the demagogic temper threaten the same liberty from opposite sides.
works.significance: It became a standard textbook of the moderate Whig constitutional argument, reprinted in America through the 1760s and 1770s as an elementary school of British liberty.
works.meter: Clear argumentative prose of the Spectator manner, with heavy use of balanced pairs, historical example and closing sententiae.
works.context: Published during and immediately after the '15 rising, in the season of Whig pamphlet warfare that also produced Swift's and Steele's party papers and Addison's breach with Steele over The Drummer's circle.
works.characters: the freeholder-writer; the party opponent; the Jacobite conspirator
works.structure: A short serial of letter-like papers addressed to a named friend or to the freeholders, each taking up one branch of the argument, with an inserted historical dissertation.
works.attributionNotes: Addison's authorship is uncontested, though the paper was issued without his name; his official connection with the administration has encouraged readers to treat it as ministerial writing.

editions.title: The Spectator, 4 volumes

works.title: The Gamester
works.form: domestic and sentimental tragedy in five acts
works.description: A domestic tragedy of a gentleman undone by the gaming table, whose weakness is exploited by those about him until he destroys his family and himself. It was one of the most effective and most imitated of the century's moral tragedies and remained a stock piece of the repertory.
works.plot: Beverley, an honest man with a passion for play, is drawn on by a cheating companion and by the artifices of a serving man who wins his own ends by the ruin. His wife's remonstrances and the losses at the table drive him to despair, and he is led by a false report of her infidelity to a fatal act. The discovery of the cheat and of the innocent wife comes too late, and Beverley dies penitent on a bed of straw in the playhouse's most quoted scene of domestic ruin.
works.significance: It is the most successful of the eighteenth-century plays on the ruinous passions of the middle class and a central text of the sentimental theatre, its ending being a byword for the pathos of the domestic catastrophe.
works.meter: A grave and affective blank verse of the middle style, with the homely sentences of the domestic scenes and the long dying periods of the last act.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in February 1753, in the season of the new statutes against gaming and of the vogue for moral domestic tragedy; the writer was a periodical essayist and editor of the same years.
works.characters: Beverley the gamester; his wife; the designing servant; the cheating friend at the table; the family and the creditors of the ruin
works.structure: Five-act regular domestic tragedy, the action contracted about the game and the house, with the villainy of the inferiors supplying the machinery of the fall; the catastrophe is a death-bed discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with a dedication that argues the moral design.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Garden
works.description: Marvell's meditation on the pleasures of a garden and the withdrawal from worldly ambition and sensual love into contemplative solitude, culminating in the famous image of the mind as a sea that 'Annihilates all that's made / To a green thought in a green shade'.
works.plot: The poem rejects the vain pursuits of ambition and the grosser pleasures of love for the superior delight of the garden, then rises to a Platonic vision of the soul's meditation and the paradise of the solitary, innocent mind.
works.significance: A central poem of retirement and contemplation in English, admired for its wit, its green imagery, and its metaphysical meditation on the mind.
works.meter: Iambic tetrameter quatrains with a serene, meditative wit and paradox.
works.context: Composed probably in the 1650s, published in Miscellaneous Poems (1681); it reflects the Neoplatonic and Epicurean ideal of retirement valued by Marvell and his contemporaries.
works.characters: the poet; the soul
works.structure: A nine-stanza lyric meditation moving from satire of worldly pursuits to celebration of the garden to visionary contemplation.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; there is a Latin companion poem 'Hortus' by Marvell.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Poems of Andrew Marvell
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Garden of Cyrus
altTitles: The Garden of Cyrus: Discourse on the Quincunx
works.description: The companion piece to Hydriotaphia, a learned and increasingly mystical discourse on the quincunx — the five-point arrangement — as it appears in the gardens of Cyrus, in nature, and in art, and as an emblem of cosmic order.
works.plot: Browne traces the quincunx from the Hanging Gardens of Cyrus through Roman military formations, botanical patterns, and the arrangement of the stars, arguing that the figure reveals a divine geometrical order in creation.
works.significance: A unique experiment in emblematic natural philosophy and one of the strangest and most beautiful works of English prose; it has been a touchstone for critics interested in the seventeenth-century imagination.
works.meter: Dense, incantatory prose; the concluding 'night-piece' is famous for its drowsy cadences.
works.context: Published in 1658 together with Hydriotaphia and dedicated to Nicholas Bacon.
works.structure: Five chapters of accumulating pattern and digression, ending in a nocturnal vision.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Browne; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Garland of Laurel
works.form: dream vision in rhyme royal and Skeltonics
works.description: Skelton's self-crowning dream vision: the poet, wandering in a forest, is brought before Queen Fame and the assembled court of the Countess of Surrey at Sheriff Hutton, where Pallas and the ladies of the court intercede for him and Fame grants him the laurel — the poem including a catalogue of his own works that is the first English poet's bibliography.
works.plot: The dreamer debates with Occupation and Fame whether he deserves the laurel; the ladies of the court, led by the Countess of Surrey, petition on his behalf; Fame crowns him, and the poet wakes to compose the envoy of praise.
works.significance: The first English poem to canonize its own author, with a bibliography of his works; a unique document of the poet's self-understanding at the Tudor court.
works.meter: Mixed rhyme royal and Skeltonic passages; the courtly and the demotic styles deliberately alternated.
works.context: Written at Sheriff Hutton in Yorkshire, in the household of the Countess of Surrey, in 1523, when Skelton's laureate claims needed the court's support against Wolsey.
works.characters: the poet; Queen Fame; Pallas; the Countess of Surrey; Occupation
works.structure: Dream vision with debate and pageant; the catalogue of the poet's works embedded in the intercession of the court ladies.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Gentle Craft
works.description: Deloney's fiction of the shoemakers' craft: the legendary origins of the 'gentle craft' in the saints and heroes who took up shoemaking — St Hugh, St Crispin and Crispianus, Sir Simon Eyre the shoemaker Lord Mayor, and the apprentice who married a king's daughter — the book that gave Dekker his Shoemaker's Holiday and the trade its mythology.
works.plot: The frame of the shoemakers' feast encloses the tales: Hugh's love for the king's daughter Winifred and his martyrdom; Crispin and Crispianus serving the king in disguise; Simon Eyre's rise to the mayoralty; and the apprentice Tom Drum's wooing of a great lady — each tale proving the craft's gentility and the shoemaker's wit.
works.significance: The classic of the craft romance — the book that made the shoemaker's bench a seat of English legend.
works.meter: Prose of Deloney's popular register, with songs and the frame's festive setting.
works.context: Published about 1597–98; its Eyre story supplied the plot of Dekker's The Shoemaker's Holiday (1599), and its craft-patriotism answered the decade's civic pride.
works.characters: St Hugh; Winifred; St Crispin; Crispianus; Simon Eyre; Tom Drum; the master shoemakers and their guests
works.structure: A frame-tale collection in the manner of the Decameron, with each story a romance or jest of the craft's legends.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Works of Thomas Deloney

works.title: The Gentleman Dancing-Master
works.description: Wycherley's second comedy, a satire on affectation of French and Spanish manners, in which a would-be Spanish grandee is fooled by his daughter's suitor disguised as a dancing master.
works.plot: Monsieur de Parelle, an affecter of foreign fashions, is outwitted by St Jago, who courts his daughter Hippolita by posing as her dancing master; the plot exposes the emptiness of the gentleman's pretensions.
works.significance: An important link between Wycherley's first comedy and his two masterpieces, notable for its satire on cultural affectation.
works.meter: Prose dominant.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in 1672 and published in 1673.
works.characters: Monsieur de Parelle; Hippolita; St Jago; Madame Caution; Don Diego; Mrs Flareit
works.structure: Five acts of intrigue comedy with a strong comic central figure.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Wycherley; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Gifts of Men
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A catalogue poem of 113 lines celebrating the diversity of human talents as gifts of God: one man is strong, another wise, another skilled in song, hunting, navigation, smithing, or counsel. The poem's theme is that every gift comes from the Lord and none should be despised.
works.plot: The poet enumerates the many endowments distributed among mankind — physical strength, beauty, eloquence, song, learning, craftsmanship, skill in the hunt, the sea, the harp, and the council — and concludes that God, the giver of all gifts, has so ordered the world that no one possesses everything and each talent has its place.
works.significance: A major statement of the Old English wisdom tradition's social vision, and a companion piece to The Fortunes of Men; both poems treat the same theme of distributed human destiny.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the catalogue form is carried by parallel clauses of the 'sum... sum...' (one... another...) type characteristic of Old English gnomic verse.
works.context: The poem belongs to the Exeter Book wisdom tradition alongside Maxims I and II and The Fortunes of Men, with which it is often compared; it reflects the Anglo-Saxon conviction that society is knit together by complementary gifts under divine providence.
works.structure: A sustained catalogue organized by successive human activities and skills, framed by an opening assertion of God's generosity and a closing meditation on the ordered distribution of gifts.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Golden Legend
works.description: William Caxton's translation of Jacobus de Voragine's Legenda Aurea, printed at Westminster in 1483: the great medieval collection of saints' lives and feasts of the church year, in nearly 450 leaves and the first English printing of the work. It became the standard English legendary for a century, reprinted repeatedly into the 1520s.
works.plot: Following the church year, the collection narrates the lives and martyrdoms of the saints — from St Andrew through the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins — with the great feasts (Advent, Christmas, Passiontide) expounded and the legends moralized for the reader's instruction.
works.significance: The great bestseller of Caxton's press and the principal English channel of the Legenda Aurea; its saints' lives nourished English devotional reading into the sixteenth century.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's mature plain style at its most ample.
works.context: Translated by Caxton from French and Latin sources and printed at Westminster in 1483, in the orthodox devotional market of pre-Reformation England; nine editions appeared by 1527, before the Reformation ended the cult of the saints it served.
works.characters: the saints of the calendar
works.structure: A calendrical legendary in the Voragine tradition, with Caxton's additions (including lives of English saints) and his prologue explaining the work's purpose.
works.attributionNotes: Caxton's translation is documented in his own prologue.

editions.title: Caxton's Golden Legend
editions.editor: Mayumi Taguchi, John Scahill, and Satoko Katsumata (eds.)

works.title: The Good-Natur'd Man
works.form: Comedy in five acts, in dialogue prose with sententious and tender passages, written for the London stage in the reforming 1760s and prefaced in print by epistle and dramatis personae.
works.description: Oliver Goldsmith's first produced comedy, and the play with which he entered the quarrel about sentimental comedy: an essay in the 'laughing comedy' of which he became the theorist, in which goodness of disposition, not wit or contrivance, is made the subject and the instrument of the plot. Its unhappy first run gave it a place in theatrical history larger than its later performance on the stage would suggest.
works.plot: The comedy is built on a generous young man whose very openness of temper makes him the prey of everyone with a claim upon him, and on the confusions his readiness to oblige produces in his own affairs of the heart. He is in love with a lady under the control of an interested guardian, and the artful about him exploit his good nature in order to advance their own designs, so that the action consists less of a scheme than of a series of impositions. Against these the play sets the worth of uncalculated kindness, and its resolution restores the lovers and exposes the designs. The moral interest is deliberately affective rather than satirical: the audience is asked to laugh with good humour and to approve benevolence, and the antipathy of the malicious and the calculating is what the comedy finally defeats.
works.significance: It is the first of the two plays in which Goldsmith tried to restore mirth and national character to the English stage against the fashion for distress, and its failure and its defence shaped the subsequent history of the sentimental-comedy quarrel. It supplies the practical counterpart to his theoretical case for laughing comedy.
works.context: It belongs to the theatrical controversy of the 1760s between the laughing comedy of manners and feeing and the sentimental comedy of distress, a debate Goldsmith had already entered as a critic and was to state formally in his essay on the theatre, which argued for laughing against sentimental comedy. It was produced in the season when the managers were remaking the repertoire and when the 'sentimental' piece was at its height.
works.characters: The good-natur'd young lover at its centre; the lady he loves and the guardian who controls her; the artful claimants upon his generosity; his friends and dependants
works.structure: A five-act comedy of character and imposition, with a double amatory plot and a succession of deceptions worked upon the protagonist's generosity, resolved by exposure and restitution.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the play is Goldsmith's and its production is documented. The dating of the surviving manuscript and the extent of the revisions made after the first run are matters of editorial detail, not of authorship.

editions.title: The Poems of Thomas Gray, William Collins and Oliver Goldsmith

works.title: The Governess; or, Little Female Academy
works.form: children's fiction; framed school story with embedded tales
works.description: A story of a boarding school for girls, in which a wise governess governs by letting her pupils tell and judge one another's tales. It is the first English book written deliberately for the entertainment and instruction of girls of that age, and a foundation text of the children's novel.
works.plot: Ten or eleven girls arrive at the academy, each with her own fault of temper, vanity or falsehood, and the governess discovers their characters by observation rather than by rule. The girls are set to tell stories of their own invention - tales of lovers, of servants and of the adventures of the world - and to pass judgement on one another's conduct. The book closes with the reformation of the stubborn and the reward of the modest, the governess's method having turned amusement into moral discipline.
works.significance: It invented the English school story for girls and is a landmark in the history of a literature designed for female childhood, influencing the didactic fiction of the following century.
works.meter: Simple conversational prose suited to young readers, with the inset tales adopting the diction of the popular romance they parody.
works.context: Published in 1749, in the season of new attention to the education of girls and of the didactic tales of the day, and written by an author already associated with conduct-oriented fiction and school teaching.
works.characters: the governess of the academy and her pupils, each standing for a fault or a virtue of temper
works.structure: A framed collection: a continuous school narrative enclosing tales told by the pupils, the frame supplying the judgement and the tales the example; the sequence is orderly and episodic.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name and with a preface addressed to the parents of the pupils.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Grave
works.form: Meditative blank-verse poem in the continuation of the 'Night Thoughts' tradition of the 1740s; descriptive and declamatory passages alternate with direct address and apostrophe; passages were afterward used as hymns and as anthology pieces.
works.description: Robert Blair's meditation on death, buried bodies and the resurrection, the poem that gave the graveyard school its name and its characteristic atmosphere. It is written in a heavy, sonorous blank verse and moves through the churchyard, the coffin, the worm and the general dissolution, turning the contemplation of putrefaction into an argument for immortality. It is also a work of the devotional edge of the Augustan age: Blair was a friend and fellow-minister of the evangelical circle around Ralph Cudworth the younger, and the poem's religious weight is not merely decorative.
works.plot: There is no story, only the sustained exercise of a single thought. The speaker first dwells on the physical facts of burial and decay with a candour that the age found almost indecent, and describes the churchyard at night as the place where these facts are most visibly assembled. From the darkness of the grave the poem argues upward: the same dissolution which appals the unbelief of the worldling is for the believer the avenue to a resurrection, and the dead body becomes a 'seed' committed to the ground. The meditations on the last judgment, on the sleep of the dead and on the triumph of the living over the grave are the poem's true conclusion, and they justify its terrible preliminary imagery. Its characteristic mixture of horror and hope is what later readers of the 1740s and 1790s recognised as a new seriousness in English verse.
works.significance: It is the founding text of what later historians have called the Graveyard School, and its title gave the group its name. Its blend of physical realism about death with evangelical hope marks the transition from Augustan meditation to the preromantic taste for terror, and it shaped the devotional and funereal vocabulary of Gray, of Blair's Irish and Scottish successors and of the Gothic romance of the following generation.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of great weight and latinity, with long suspended syntax, repeated keywords and a deliberate harshness of sound which contemporaries admired as sublimity and others censured as inflation.
works.context: It belongs to the religious current running under Augustan neoclassicism: the evangelical revival of the 1730s and 1740s, Blair's friendship with the ministers of the London 'British' Presbyterian meeting, and the vogue for poems upon the last things which produced Parnell's and Young's meditations and Gray's early essays in terror. It was published in the decade of the 'graveyard' imagination and soon associated with an engraving design by William Hogarth.
works.structure: A continuous meditative argument in a single voice, loosely articulated in sections following the progress of thought from the churchyard and the coffin to the resurrection and the last day; no dramatis personae and no narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested: published anonymously or initialed at first and afterward with Blair's name, and edited with a memoir by William Mason in the mid-century editions, which fixed the text and the biography. The years of composition are uncertain and are not asserted.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Grave (Hugh Blair)
works.form: published sermon and graveyard meditation, in the solemn descriptive manner of the mid-century
works.description: The sermon on death and the grave that made Blair's reputation while he was still a young minister in Carrick, and one of the most quoted pieces of Scottish pulpit prose of the mid-century. Preached at Colmonell and published at Edinburgh in 1743, it meditates on the burial place, the bodies of the dead and the terrors and consolations of the last hour, and passes from the spectacle of the grave to the hope of the resurrection. It belongs with the graveyard verse of the same decades as an expression of the new taste for solemn meditation.
works.plot: Blair leads his auditors to the graveyard and holds before them the equality of the dead, the silence of the tomb and the uncertainty of the hour of death, pressing each hearer to imagine himself laid there. He then turns the meditation upon the resurrection and the judgment, so that the terrors of the grave are answered by a reasoned hope. The argument moves by description and appeal rather than by doctrine, and its aim is the reformation of present conduct through the continual thought of death.
works.significance: It is the classical prose statement of the graveyard meditation and helped to fix the rhetoric of solemnity in Scottish preaching for a generation. It also supplies the link between sermon and poem in the preromantic interest in death, and its reputation was long maintained by its place in collections of elocution.
works.meter: Prose; deliberately sonorous and cadenced, with the balanced period, the pause and the climax of the elocutionary school that Blair later theorised.
works.context: Preached and issued in the tradition of graveyard meditation opened by Parnell's night piece and by Edward Young's Night Thoughts, and some years before Robert Blair's poem of the same name; it belongs to the religious atmosphere of the Scottish west before the Moderate ascendancy, and its success marked the arrival of a new taste for the awful and the pathetic in Scottish discourse.
works.structure: A single preached discourse moving from the meditation on the grave and the dead, through the contemplation of mortality and judgment, to the consolation of the resurrection and the practical application.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the sermon's publication at Edinburgh in 1743 is given in the usual bibliographical reckoning, and the later enlarged editions are Blair's own revision.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Great Bible
works.description: The first authorized English Bible, a revision of Matthew's Bible (itself based on Tyndale and Coverdale) carried out by Miles Coverdale and printed in Paris and London in 1539 under Thomas Cromwell's patronage; the Bible ordered to be set up in every parish church.
works.plot: A complete Bible in large folio format, with the title page by Hans Holbein showing Henry VIII handing the Word to Cranmer and Cromwell; the text revises the Matthew Bible's Old Testament against the Hebrew and Latin, and its 1540 second edition carried Cranmer's preface, giving the book its later name.
works.significance: The Bible that made the English Bible a public institution: chained in the churches, read aloud to the people, it established the vernacular scriptures at the centre of English religious life and supplied the psalter of the Prayer Book.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Commissioned by Cromwell and begun in Paris (the French printing was seized by the Inquisition, and the presses moved to London), the Great Bible of 1539 was ordered by the injunctions of 1538 to be placed in every parish church; its psalter entered the Prayer Book tradition, and it remained the standard English Bible until the Bishops' Bible of 1568.
works.structure: The full biblical canon with prologues, summaries, and the famous illustrated title page.
works.attributionNotes: The revision is Coverdale's, on the basis of the Matthew Bible (edited by John Rogers from Tyndale and Coverdale); the record attributes the work to Coverdale as revising editor, following standard usage.

works.title: The Grounds of Criticism in Poetry
works.description: Dennis's systematic companion to the treatise of 1701, which sets out the foundations of a critical art: poetry is an imitative and designing craft whose ends are to instruct and delight, whose means are the passions, and whose highest achievements depend upon enthusiasm, both ordinary and poetical. The argument grounds the rules in nature and in the reason of things, and then argues from the same premises that the religion of a modern nation is a necessary foundation of its poetry. It is the most rigorous of Dennis's attempts to hold neoclassical rule and Augustan sublimity in one system.
works.plot: Dennis first disposes of the sceptical objection that criticism is a vain art, insisting that as surely as the rules of music produce harmony the rules of poetry, learned from nature and from the ancients, produce pleasure; he then distinguishes the passions that a poet must know from the craft that copies them, and derives from this the doctrine that great poetry requires an enthusiastick elevation which no mere rule-making can supply. He next argues that a religion of terrors and of grandeur such as Christianity provides gives the modern poet materials the pagan epics never possessed, while the machinery of a revealed faith is at once more awful and more instructive than the personifications of the heathens. Finally he tests the moderns against the ancients in the several genres, and finds that the critic's office is to reconcile the love of the ancients with the claims of a more knowing age.
works.significance: It is the chief English link between Renaissance poetics of the rules and the eighteenth-century psychology of enthusiasm, the sublime and genius, and much of what Addison, Hughes, the Blairs and the French theorists said on those subjects was worked out first in these pages.
works.meter: Prose, in the emphatical and heavily coordinated style Dennis associated with grandeur, with long periods, balanced clauses and repeated key terms.
works.context: Published in the last years of the reign of Queen Anne's precedent period of the Whig war and the expedition to the continent, when Dennis, an ardent Williamite, was writing against the Tory revival in letters; it was reprinted after his death, in the age of the Scottish enquiry into taste, because it was one of the few native treatises on enthusiasm available to eighteenth-century readers.
works.structure: A treatise advancing in numbered sections and argumentative heads from first principles to the doctrine of enthusiasm, then to religion as the foundation of modern poetry, then to an evaluation of the modern genres, with a closing defence of the critical enterprise itself.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Guardian Papers
works.description: Steele's thrice-weekly paper of 1713, conducted in the guardian mask and chiefly against the deism of Anthony Collins, the free-thinkers, the pretenders and the married men's project; the most openly party-political of the essay papers and the occasion of the Addison-Steele breach.
works.plot: The guardian reports the transactions of his ward, the public, attacks the trick of ridicule against religion, stages the Married Men's claim to be governed by their wives, and defends the Christian foundation of moral obligation.
works.significance: It documents the moment at which the periodical essay became an instrument of party and of religious polemic, and its controversy with the anti-theatrical and deist press shaped the later eighteenth-century debate on ridicule and morality.
works.meter: Colloquial, urgent argumentative prose with the interrupted sentence and the indignant apostrophe, less periodic than Addison's.
works.context: Published in the months of the Asylum Bill and the fall of the Harley ministry, when Steele turned from the moderate essay to high-church and Whig polemic; the paper's attack on the Married Men drew the rebuttals of the female writers of the period.
works.characters: Mr. Guardian; the Married Men; the female correspondents; the free-thinker
works.structure: Serial papers alternating party argument, fictional letter and project, character writing and the dialogue between the guardian and his correspondents.
works.attributionNotes: Chiefly Steele's, with numbers by Addison, Hughes, Prior and Berkeley; the disputed shares are the occasion of one of the century's first collaborations dissolving in print.

editions.title: The Spectator, 4 volumes

works.title: The Harley Lyrics
works.description: A collection of some forty secular and religious lyrics preserved in the Ludlow scribe's anthology, BL Harley MS 2253 (c. 1340), the richest single manuscript of early Middle English lyric: love songs, laments, satires, and devotional poems in French, Latin, and English, including such masterpieces as 'Alysoun', 'Wynter wakeneth al my care', and 'Blow, northerne wynd'.
works.plot: The poems range across the lyric repertoire: the lover's springtime longing and complaint, the satire of corrupt clergy and unjust lords, the meditation on death and the Passion, and the praise of the Virgin.
works.significance: The indispensable witness to the early Middle English lyric tradition at its best, and the principal source of the poems that bridge early and Ricardian poetry.
works.meter: A remarkable variety: tail-rhyme stanzas, alliterative long lines, and French-derived stanza forms, often with refrains.
works.context: Copied c. 1340 by a professional scribe working near Ludlow, Herefordshire, for a gentry household, from materials of the later thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries.
works.characters: the lovers and speakers of the lyrics
works.structure: An anthology, not a sequence: the manuscript's trilingual arrangement (with English poems often paired with their French and Latin analogues) supplies the order.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the poems are the work of many hands, assembled by the scribe.

works.title: The Hermit
works.description: Parnell's tender narrative tale of a hermit drawn from his cell by a pleasing guide, of a betrayed country maid, and of the care exercised over the tempted soul: one of the most reprinted English short poems of the century.
works.plot: An old hermit, peevish at the world and at his own past, is allured from his cell by a fair guide who leads him through the country night to a cottage, where he learns the story of a maid seduced and lost; the tale turns on the discovery of the guide's errand and on the hermit's humbling.
works.significance: It supplied the century with one of its most quoted examples of pathos and of the supernatural tale, and its reprints, translations and schoolbook presence made it a conduit for the sentimental ballad.
works.meter: Plain couplet and short lyric stanza of the old ballad manner, with the night description in a slower measure.
works.context: Published in the years when the ballad, the romance tale and the tender religious narrative were displacing the heroic manner, and when Pope and the Scriblerans held Parnell's verse to be the model of easy native simplicity.
works.characters: the hermit; the guiding spirit; the seduced maid of the inset tale; the rural household
works.structure: A single romance tale in verse, with the inset narrative of the maid and a closing revelation.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Hind and the Panther
altTitles: The Hind and the Panther: A Poem in Three Parts
works.description: Dryden's great beast-fable of religious controversy, written after his conversion to Roman Catholicism: the milk-white Hind (the Roman Church) is pursued and slandered by the Panther (the Church of England) and the other beasts of the English sects.
works.plot: The Hind, immortal and unafathed, seeks her lost children; she debates authority and interpretation with the Panther, recounts her own conversion, and the poem ends with the fable of the Swallows and the Martins.
works.significance: The longest and most serious of Dryden's poems and the fullest statement of his Catholic apologetic; a masterpiece of sustained argumentative verse that influenced Pope's Essay on Man.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of sustained eloquence, with the most complex syntax of Dryden's verse.
works.context: Published in April 1687 under the Declaration of Indulgence, when James II's policy of toleration for Catholics briefly encouraged open Catholic argument; it was parodied within weeks by Montagu and Prior in The Hind and the Panther Transvers'd.
works.characters: the Hind (the Roman Catholic Church); the Panther (the Church of England); the Bear (Independents); the Hare (Quakers); the Wolf (Presbyterians); the Ape (Freethinkers); the Swallow (Titus Oates)
works.structure: Three parts: the characters of the beasts, the theological debate at the Hind's house, and the concluding fable; framed by an extended address to the poem itself.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The History and Present State of Electricity
altTitles: The History and Present State of Electricity, with Experiments and Observations
works.description: Joseph Priestley's definitive survey and experimental history of electricity, written with Franklin's encouragement and the Royal Society's papers in hand. It gathered a century of electrical discovery into a single narrative and added Priestley's own experiments, including the charged cylinder that opened the age of large machines.
works.plot: Priestley narrates the history of electricity from Gilbert and the philosophical trials of the seventeenth century through the improvements of his own age, arranging the phenomena, instruments, and controversies into a chronological and analytical account. His inserted experiments establish the inverse-square law of electrical attraction, the conductivity of charcoal, and the identity of lightning with the electrical discharge, and his account of the electrical cylinder records the machine that made experiments on a great scale possible. The history ends with the state of the theory, the sparks, the shocks, and the promised uses of the science. The book is at once a museum of discovery and a programme for the next, its experiments pointing toward the chemistry of gases.
works.significance: It became the standard history of electricity and the model of the scientific survey, and its success funded and framed Priestley's pneumatic chemistry, the empirical foundation of his natural theology and his radicalism.
works.meter: Plain, businesslike experimental prose with a historian's synoptic periods, apparatus described in working detail.
works.context: Written in the wake of the Leyden jar's craze and Franklin's experiments, at Priestley's early Leeds and London period; published 1767 with the Royal Society's encouragement, it made its author a Fellow and the historian of a science whose next chapter he would himself write.
works.structure: A chronological history interleaved with numbered reports of the author's own experiments and theoretical commentary.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The History of America
works.description: Robertson's history of the Spanish discovery and settlement of America, the standard English account for a century, the first volumes appearing in 1777 and the later books on the other European colonies completed after his death. It turned the conquests and colonial histories into a philosophical narrative of the extension of Europe.
works.plot: The narrative opens with the state of the American nations before 1492, their arts, governments, and religions treated with Robertson's blend of wonder and condescension, then follows Columbus from the enterprise to the governorship, the voyages, and the discovery of the mainland. It chronicles the conquest of Mexico and Peru with Cortes and Pizarro, the establishment of the Spanish colonial system, the treatment of the natives, and the rise of the other European colonies in North America and the West Indies. The closing volumes, completed after his death, carry the history of the British plantations, their constitutions, and the temper of the new societies. The whole reads as a science of colonies: climate, soil, constitution, and commerce explaining the destinies of the European America.
works.significance: It was the received history of America in English well into the nineteenth century, the book through which generations read Columbus and the conquests, and a foundation of the historical geography of the Atlantic world.
works.meter: The capacious balanced periods of late philosophical history, campaign and constitution set in stately alternation with the moralist's clauses of judgment.
works.context: Published from 1777 as the American revolution broke out, drawing on the historians of the Indies and the accumulated voyage literature; it stood at the centre of Robertson's late work as the great historical geographer of the Atlantic.
works.characters: Columbus; Cortes; Pizarro; the American nations; the colonial projectors
works.structure: Volumes published from 1777 with the later books completed after the author's death: the discovery, the Spanish conquests, and the northern colonies forming one history of America under Europe.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The History of England
altTitles: History of England, from the Invasion of Julius Caesar to the Revolution in 1688
works.description: Hume's six-volume history of England, written backwards from the Stuarts to Caesar and the earliest ages, and the most widely read history of the century. It narrates the growth of the constitution, party, and commerce from a philosophical standpoint hostile alike to Whig martyr legends and Tory divine-right tales.
works.plot: The Stuart volumes first show the fatal collision between the prerogative and the commons, the errors of Charles I and of his opponents, and the way enthusiasm and faction made civil war and then commonwealth plausible; the Tudor volumes trace the centralizing monarchy, the reformation, and the rise of the people's claims; the early volumes from the invasion of Caesar through the Plantagenets and the establishment of the commons narrate how law, property, and civility emerged slowly out of conquest, feudal anarchy, and monastic learning. Throughout, Hume explains events by the opposition of authority and liberty, the interests of ranks, and the unnoticed moral effects of commerce and the laws, refusing providential and party readings alike. The volume covering the accession of the house of Stuart to the revolution of 1688 closes his own published series.
works.significance: It was the standard English history for half a century, shaped nineteenth-century historiography and the Whig-Tory synthesis, and is still studied as the monument of history written as the science of human nature applied.
works.meter: The level, capacious, periodic historiographic prose of the philosophical historian, marked by balanced judgment clauses and sardonic character portraits.
works.context: Written while Hume was librarian of the Faculty of Advocates in Edinburgh and supported by copies of records from London, the History drew furious party reviews and episcopal remonstrance, yet made Hume financially independent and a European name.
works.characters: Henry VIII; Elizabeth I; Mary Queen of Scots; James I; Charles I; Cromwell; William III
works.structure: Six volumes issued in reverse chronological order between 1754 and 1762, each a continuous political narrative with inserted constitutional, legal, and economic remarks.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
