works.title: The Testament of the Papyngo
altTitles: The Testament and Complaynt of Our Soverane Lordis Papyngo
works.form: verse satire in the testament tradition
works.description: Lindsay's satire of court and church: the king's parrot, dying after a fall from the palace wall, makes her testament — leaving her heart to the king, her body to the courtiers, and her counsel to the clergy — and delivers a dying bird's-eye satire of the bishops, the court, and the vices of the age.
works.plot: The Papyngo, perched high on the palace wall, falls and dies; before death she disposes of her estate in a testament that satirizes each legatee in turn, closing with an epistle to the bishops on their duties.
works.significance: The wittiest of Lindsay's satires and a classic of the Scots complaint; its parrot looks back to Skelton's Speke Parrot and forward to the beast satires of the later century.
works.meter: Scots couplets and stanzas; the mock-legal diction of the testament handled with satirical point.
works.context: Written in 1530 as the Scottish church's wealth and the court's corruption became the subjects of Reformation debate; the parrot speaks with the licence of the dying.
works.characters: the Papyngo; James V (legatee); the courtiers; the bishops
works.structure: The testament form — the dying bird's will and last counsel — used as a vehicle for estates satire; mock-legal framework, satirical legacies, and a closing sermon.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
works.description: Adam Smith's first great work, the fullest elaboration of the moral-sense tradition through the mechanism of sympathy and the impartial spectator. It explains how fellow-feeling, admiration, and the desire for praiseworthiness generate moral judgment, duty, and virtue, and it remains the century's most comprehensive treatise on the social psychology of ethics.
works.plot: Part I shows that we judge the propriety of another's feelings by imagining ourselves in his situation, sympathy being the imaginary transposition of spectator and agent, and that the senses of propriety and justice arise from this exchange of perspectives. Part II traces the feelings of merit and demerit, the rules of justice and beneficence, and the influence of custom and fashion on moral sentiment. Part III introduces the impartial spectator as the internal judge and the desire for praiseworthiness as the mature moral motive. Parts IV and V analyse the corruption of the moral sentiments by the love of riches and rank, and survey the rival systems of ethics from the ancients to the moderns. Part VI completes the taxonomy of the virtues of prudence, justice, beneficence, and self-command. The whole grounds society not on contract but on the mutual mirror of sympathetic sentiments.
works.significance: It supplied the moral psychology for commercial society's self-understanding, is the necessary companion to the Wealth of Nations, and anchors the modern revival of sympathy-based ethics and the study of the Scottish Enlightenment.
works.meter: An expansive, illustrative lecture prose dense with social observation, its famous generalizations stated in balanced declaratives, addressed alike to polite and philosophical readers.
works.context: Grown from Smith's Glasgow lectures begun in the early 1750s and published in London in 1759 with Hume's encouragement, it appeared in the season of the Edinburgh and Glasgow debates on scepticism and the French materialists and was revised by Smith through five later editions.
works.structure: Six parts of graduated argument, from the analysis of sympathy through the general rules and the impartial spectator to the history of ethical systems and the taxonomy of the virtues.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The Tomb
works.form: Meditative blank-verse poem, a planned sequel or pendant to 'The Grave', surviving among the manuscripts Blair left and printed posthumously; short in relation to its companion and incomplete in the sense that its author left it.
works.description: Robert Blair's projected companion to 'The Grave', left in manuscript at his death and printed among his posthumous poems. It pursues the same subject in the same measure, but narrows the focus to the sepulchre itself and to the monuments and inscriptions by which the living attempt to keep the dead in mind.
works.plot: Like 'The Grave', the poem is an exercise of thought rather than a narrative. It meditates upon the tomb as a structure, an inscription and a hope: the masonry and the heraldry of memorial are surveyed and found insufficient, while the Christian tomb is read as the pledge of a resurrection. The turn from the vanity of monumental fame to the faith of the buried believer is the argument, and the piece supplies a closing reflection to the open-ended contemplation of its predecessor.
works.significance: It completes the conception of 'The Grave' and shows how far the graveyard meditation had become, in Blair's hands, a structured sequence rather than a single performance. It is a minor but authentic document of the preromantic contemplation of death.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter in the same weighty, Latinate manner as 'The Grave'; the diction is funerary and lapidary, with the compressed phrasing of an epitaph.
works.context: It was written in the same period as 'The Grave', when Blair was assembling a sequence of poems on the last things, and it stands within the 1740s fashion for churchyard, tomb and resurrection meditation. Its survival in manuscript and its posthumous printing are part of the history of that fashion, since the editors of Blair's papers were also the editors of his reputation.
works.structure: A continuous meditation addressed to the tomb, in the same sectional, associative movement as 'The Grave', with apostrophe and epitaph-like reflection taking the place of events.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Blair is not contested; the difficulty lies in its publication history. Because it was not printed in the poet's lifetime and because the several posthumous collections and reissues of Blair's poems are differently dated, no first-print year is asserted here and the publication field is left null rather than guessed.

works.title: The Tournament
works.form: Antiquarian romance in verse among the Rowley poems; long, irregular and catalogue-driven, in the archaic orthography Chatterton supplied, with glosses of the obsolete words attached in the manuscripts and collections.
works.description: One of the longest and most ambitious of the poems Thomas Chatterton put into the name of the fifteenth-century Bristol monk Thomas Rowley, and a centrepiece of the forgeries he sent to Horace Walpole in 1764. It presents itself as an antiquarian account of a medieval tournament, complete with lists of champions, devices and heraldic blazon, in a deliberately archaized spelling and diction. Its interest is double: as an early achievement of the primitive-genius vogue, and as a document of a Bristol apprentice's furious self-education in the literature of the past.
works.plot: The poem narrates the summoning, the gathering and the running of a great tournament, and dwells on the heraldry, the armour, the ladies' favours and the encounters of the champions with a minuteness meant to look like a period chronicler's rather than a modern poet's imagination. Chivalric honour, religious invocation and the pomp of the field are combined without any neoclassical sense of proportion, so that the piece reads as a series of illuminated tableaux. Its frame is the more important fiction: Rowley is made to be an eyewitness and recorder of the scene, an authority older than any modern antiquary. The result is the most complete of Chatterton's impersonations, in which the medieval is not described from outside but re-enacted in a language the eighteenth century was willing to believe.
works.significance: It is the largest single exercise in the Rowley impersonation and an important text in the history of literary forgery, of medievalism, and of the cult of the primitive genius; its mixture of heraldic learning and genuine imaginative power is what later readers from the Romantics onwards remembered. It also helped to establish the vogue for an invented national antiquity which the same decade received from Macpherson and from Percy.
works.meter: Rowley's supposed measures: long lines with medial caesura and mixed rhyme formations, imitating fifteenth-century verse rather than any Elizabethan or Augustan practice.
works.context: It belongs to the Rowley correspondence of 1764, when Chatterton, a clerk in Bristol, supplied Walpole with parchment 'originals' and letters in a fabricated antiquarian persona, at the moment when the taste for chivalry and for national origins was being formed by Walpole's own circle at Strawberry Hill. The forgery was detected within a few years, but the poems continued to be read as poetry.
works.characters: The framing chronicler 'Thomas Rowley'; the knights and champions of the listed tournament; the ladies whose favours are proclaimed
works.structure: A chronicle-poem in the supposed voice and hand of Rowley: annalistic opening, catalogue of champions and devices, narrative of the field, and devotional and heraldic digression, without regular stanzaic closure.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship is recorded as single because Chatterton, not any medieval monk, wrote the poem. The ascription in the manuscripts is to 'Thomas Rowley', a fictitious fifteenth-century Bristol priest and chronicler whose parchment 'originals' and glosses Chatterton supplied; the deception imposed upon Walpole and other antiquaries before it was seen through. The year 1764 refers to the Rowley correspondence in which the piece was produced.

works.title: The Tragedy of Tragedies; or, The Life and Death of Tom Thumb the Great
works.form: burlesque tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: A burlesque tragedy on heroic subjects, in which the tiny hero of the old ballad is placed inside an exact parody of heroic verse, with its declamation, its mono-syllabic names and its catastrophes of absurd magnitude. It is the most sustained English exercise in tragicomical burlesque of the century and was revised into a two-act form with a dedication that became a manifesto.
works.plot: Tom Thumb, in miniature and married to the queen, discovers his beloved's intrigue with a courtier and sends his rival on errands that end in death. King Arthur's court supplies the dignity, the giants and the fathers the ceremony, and the accumulating duels and poisonings grow past all probability. The finale buries nearly the whole cast, the survivors being left to moralise on the fragility of heroic design.
works.significance: It is the classic English parody of heroic tragedy and a key document of the quarrel between the legitimate theatre and the little houses; its preface and dedication are primary statements of the comic theory later applied in the novels.
works.meter: Heroic couplets and the inflated blank verse of tragedy used exactly for nonsense, with the famous mono-syllabic names and the tautological similes of the high style.
works.context: First played at the Haymarket in 1731 and revived in altered form at Drury Lane in 1737 with a prose dedication to the reader and a preface critical of contemporary tragedy; the season was one of heroic revival and of managerial dispute.
works.characters: Tom Thumb; King Arthur; Queen Huncamunca; Doodle; Grumio; Glumdalca; Meridanta
works.structure: A regular five-act burlesque tragedy in the heroic manner, reduced later to two acts, with the parody sustained scene by scene against the conventions of tragic structure; the deaths are stacked for cumulative effect.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the revised edition of the late 1730s carries the author's name, prefatory matter and a dedication much debated as criticism.

works.title: The Traitor
works.description: Shirley's most successful tragedy, a political play on the assassination of the Duke of Florence by his favourite Sciarrha, loosely based on the murder of the Florentine Duke Alessandro de' Medici in 1537.
works.plot: The Duke's favourite Sciarrha, ambitious and jealous, conspires with the Duke's rival to assassinate him; the conspiracy succeeds, but Sciarrha's sister Amidea refuses the Duke and the murder destroys both plotters.
works.significance: The finest Caroline political tragedy and a principal influence on later plays of tyrannicide, including the Restoration heroic drama.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Cockpit in 1631 and read at court by Charles I, who is said to have remarked that it was 'a tragedy'.
works.characters: the Duke of Florence; Sciarrha; Amidea; Cosmo; Lorenzo; Depazzi
works.structure: Five acts following the rise, execution, and ruin of the conspiracy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shirley; authorship undisputed.
