works.title: The Traveller; or, A Prospect of Society
works.form: Philosophical-reflection poem in the tradition of Pope's 'Essay on Man', cast as a verse epistle to a friend and organised as a comparative survey of nations; issued as a separate pamphlet in quarto.
works.description: Goldsmith's first published poem and the work that established him as a poet: a reflection in heroic couplets on the forms of society and on the place each gives to human happiness, written in the manner of the Augustan philosophical essay in verse and addressed to his friend the painter Sir Joshua Reynolds. It takes the traveller's survey of the nations of Europe as the frame for an argument about happiness, government and contentment.
works.plot: The poem opens with the traveller's farewell to his family and his retirement from the world's noise, and proceeds as a survey of the chief states of Europe, each examined for the kind of happiness its institutions secure or refuse. The commercial states of Flanders, the hardy independence of the Swiss cantons, Italy under priestcraft, smiling but servitude-prone Gaul, proud and darkly policed Spain, and England with its liberty, its commerce and its unequal distribution of enjoyments, are each allowed their plea and then judged. The argument is that happiness does not follow from any single form of policy or condition of life, since every state has its own peculiar miseries and every rank its own discontents, and that felicity depends rather on the mind and on the balance of the whole. The close withdraws from the prospect of society to the poet's own retired lot, content to have failed in the world if he has kept his integrity.
works.significance: It made Goldsmith's poetical reputation at the moment when the couplet tradition was beginning to be questioned, and it remains the best example of the Augustan philosophical survey in verse written in the 1760s. Its doctrine that forms of society do not determine happiness, and its portraits of national character, were much quoted, and it prepared the moral manner of 'The Deserted Village'.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, in the polished Augustan manner with balanced antithesis, sententious closure and a good deal of the epigrammatic turn Goldsmith took from Pope.
works.context: It was composed largely during a country retirement in the English midlands and published at the height of the debate about commercial society, national character and the comparative history of government, in which the Scottish and English moral philosophers were then engaged. Its survey of Europe drew on the Grand Tour and on the travelling literature of the age, and on the post-war confidence and anxiety about British commerce.
works.characters: The traveller-poet and his own family left behind; the nations of Europe as collectively personified conditions of society
works.structure: A single sustained argument in the epistle-reflection form: opening retirement and apostrophe, a sequence of national portraits each with its own balance sheet of good and evil, general conclusion on the dependence of happiness on the mind, and personal peroration of retirement.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was published anonymously at first but was known and acknowledged as Goldsmith's, and its history is documented in his letters and in the contemporary accounts of its subscription publication.

editions.title: The Poems of Thomas Gray, William Collins and Oliver Goldsmith

works.title: The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo
altTitles: The Treatise of the Two Married Women and the Widow
works.description: William Dunbar's scandalous Midsummer Eve debate (c. 1500–07, 530 lines): the eavesdropping poet overhears three women — two wives and a widow — exchanging frank confidences on marriage, their husbands' inadequacies, and the arts of deceiving them, in the most sustained exhibition of female licence (and male ventriloquism) in medieval English verse. The most brilliant of Dunbar's alliterative poems.
works.plot: Hidden in the hedge on a June night, the narrator hears the first wife anatomize her husband's age, impotence, and jealousy, the second mock hers as a coward and braggart, and the widow — dismissing both as amateurs — advise on choosing, managing, and surviving husbands, until the dawn and the lark's song end the colloquy.
works.significance: The supreme comic-satiric poem of the Scottish tradition: its frankness and metrical brilliance made it a scandal in its own day and a touchstone of medieval misogyny debate in ours.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line in Dunbar's hands — colloquial, obscene, and metrically audacious.
works.context: Composed c. 1500–07 at the court of James IV, in the makars' revival of alliterative verse; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508) and preserved in the Bannatyne manuscript.
works.characters: the narrator (Dunbar); the two married women; the widow
works.structure: A debate-frame of three long monologues, each more outrageous than the last, in the tradition of the débat and the Wife of Bath's prologue.
works.attributionNotes: Dunbar's authorship secure.

editions.title: The Poems of William Dunbar

works.title: The True Intellectual System of the Universe
works.description: Ralph Cudworth's massive learned work against atheism, in which he argues that the ancient philosophers were not atheists and that a rational theism is the true intellectual system of the universe.
works.plot: Book I sets out the various forms of atheism and refutes them; the work argues for the existence of plastic natures, for the immateriality of the soul, and for the eternity of moral truths against Hobbesian materialism.
works.significance: The most learned philosophical work of the seventeenth-century English Platonists; its concept of 'plastic nature' influenced Leibniz and later vitalist philosophy, and its refutation of atheism was a standard reference.
works.meter: Dense, heavily cited scholarly prose of the Cambridge Platonists.
works.context: Published in 1678, the year of the Popish Plot, and licensed by Samuel Parker; Cudworth was Master of Christ's College, Cambridge.
works.structure: A single vast treatise in four books (only the first volume was published), with enormous learned apparatus.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Cudworth; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Tunning of Elinour Rumming
works.description: Skelton's carnivalesque masterpiece: a Skeltonic account of the alewife Elinour Rumming of Leatherhead and the procession of women who come to drink her noxious ale, a low-life gallery from drunken Alice to the beggarly Maud Ruggy — ugliness, appetite, and disorder rendered with gleeful verbal energy.
works.plot: The poem describes Elinour's brewing and her customers in turn — their poverty, their lechery, their brawling — as the alehouse degenerates into a riot of appetite without plot or moral.
works.significance: The most vivid low-life poem in English before the eighteenth century; its catalogue form and demotic energy made it a model for later satire.
works.meter: The Skeltonic at its most anarchic — breathless rhymes, macaronic puns, and tavern speech.
works.context: Set at Leatherhead in Surrey; the poem belongs to the alehouse satire of the early sixteenth century and reflects the moralists' anxieties about disorderly women.
works.characters: Elinour Rumming; her customers (drunken Alice, Maud Ruggy, and others)
works.structure: A catalogue or procession of drinkers, framed by the description of the brewing; no plot, but a mounting carnival intensity.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: John Skelton: The Complete English Poems

works.title: The Turkish Embassy Letters
altTitles: Letters Written During the Turkish Embassy
works.description: The correspondence of the ambassador's wife at Constantinople and Adrianople, describing the seraglios, the baths, the Greek church and the women's society of the Turkish capital, and reporting the inoculation practice she afterwards brought to England. It is the most vivacious of the century's travel writing and the classic account of the East seen by a woman.
works.plot: The letters follow the party from Vienna through the Hungarian and Bulgarian roads to Adrianople and Constantinople, giving an account of the way of travelling, of the houses and of the ceremonies of the embassy. They describe the women's baths and the seraglio, the Greek ladies and their usages, and the cathedral of the Phanar, with the writer's own freedom of access to a society closed to other travellers. The later letters from the embassy report the smallpox operation, and the correspondence closes with the return into Poland and Germany.
works.significance: It created the literary image of the Turkish women's world for English readers and is a foundational text of the travel letter and of the female account of the East, its evidence on inoculation being of the history of medicine as well as of letters.
works.meter: An animated epistolary prose of the quick phrase, the parenthesis and the indignant comparison, its sentences built on the sudden turn of observation rather than on the balanced period.
works.context: Written during the embassy of 1717-18 at the time of the Turkish war and the settlement of the Passarowitz season, in the current of the correspondence of the diplomatic corps, and returned to by the writer's own account of inoculation in the English medical press.
works.characters: the writing lady of the embassy; the friend at home to whom the letters are addressed; the begum or lady of the seraglio and her attendants; the Greek ladies of Constantinople; the ambassador and his household
works.structure: A continuous family correspondence, chiefly to a single friend, ordered by the route and the stay, and rising to the set descriptions of the baths and the seraglio; there is no plot beyond the journey and the observation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the letters remained in manuscript and were given to the press after the writer's death, so that no publication year in her lifetime can be asserted here.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Twa Dogs
works.form: beast fable and debate poem in the Scottish vernacular, in the tradition of Ramsay's and Dryden's dialogues of creatures
works.description: Burns's animal fable of the two dogs - Luath the farmer's working stock-dog and Caesar the gentleman's pampered spaniel - who meet at a tavern door and compare the conditions of their lives. Under the covering of the beasts the poem delivers a searching social analysis of rank, idleness, hire and hunger in the agricultural west of Scotland, and one of the sharpest indictments of the privileges of great families in the century. It is among Burns's earliest considerable poems and the first open declaration of his egalitarian creed.
works.plot: Caesar, kept warm and idle by his laird, and Luath, the working dog of a farmer, meet and dispute their respective happiness. Caesar reports the luxuries and the boredom of the hall, the squire's dogs, horses and flatterers, and the uselessness of his own life, while Luath describes the labour, the weather, the hunger and the honest dependence of the poor. The dialogue arrives at the poem's famous conclusion that the rank of the creature makes no difference in its worth, and that the poor dog and the poor man have at least the merit of usefulness.
works.significance: It established Burns's characteristic politics of the worth of the common creature and supplied the imaginative ground of his later songs on rank and equality. As a dialect fable it is the most successful modern descendant of the Scots 'Makkar' tradition of talk between beasts, and it remains a standard text for the literature of the nations and for social analysis in verse.
works.meter: The six-line Burns stanza (Standard Habbie), four long and two short Scots lines with the a-a-a-b-a-b rhyme, used for sustained dialogue.
works.context: Begun about 1784 and revised for the Kilmarnock volume, in a decade of enclosure, of improving agriculture and of depressed rural wages in Ayrshire; the poem's comparison of the idle and the useful draws on a long native tradition of estates criticism and on the contemporary debate about the condition of the labouring poor.
works.characters: Luath; Caesar; the poor laird; the farmer and his bailiff; the tavern company
works.structure: A framed tavern scene followed by a matched dialogue of the two dogs, each speech elaborating the conditions of its master, closing with the moral of the fable.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Burns dated the poem in his own memoranda as an early attempt, and the standard editions record his successive revisions of the text.

editions.title: The Poems of Robert Burns, 3 volumes

works.title: The Two Gentlemen of Verona
works.description: Shakespeare's early romantic comedy of friendship and betrayal: Valentine and Proteus, the 'two gentlemen' of Verona, both fall in love with Silvia; Proteus betrays his friend and his own beloved Julia, and the play moves through disguise, forest outlawry, and attempted rape to a reconciliation whose abruptness has troubled audiences ever since.
works.plot: Proteus, sent to Milan, falls in love with Valentine's Silvia and betrays him to the Duke; Valentine joins the outlaws, Silvia flees to the forest, and Proteus's assault on her is stopped by Valentine's intervention, leading to the double reconciliation and the play's famously compressed ending.
works.significance: The first of Shakespeare's romantic comedies and the seedbed of themes — friendship versus love, the heroine in disguise, the green world — he would develop for a decade.
works.meter: Blank verse and prose, with songs; among Shakespeare's earliest surviving verse.
works.context: An early play, probably written about 1590–91 from the Spanish romance Diana Enamorada (via its French and English versions); not printed until the 1623 First Folio.
works.characters: Valentine; Proteus; Silvia; Julia; the Duke of Milan; Launce; Speed; Crab the dog
works.structure: Five acts of alternating Milan and forest scenes, built on the paired lovers plot with the comic servants Speed and Launce (and his dog Crab) as counterpoint.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: The Two Noble Kinsmen
works.description: Shakespeare's last play, written with John Fletcher from Chaucer's Knight's Tale: the cousins Palamon and Arcite, kinsmen and friends, both fall in love with Emilia from their prison window; their rivalry is settled by the tournament for her hand — Arcite wins and dies in a riding accident, and Palamon marries her, while the Jailer's Daughter's mad sub-plot runs its course.
works.plot: The cousins swear eternal friendship, then break it over Emilia; Arcite is released, Palamon escapes; the tournament appoints the winner; Arcite's victory is followed by his fatal fall from the horse; the dying Arcite bequeaths Emilia to Palamon; Theseus closes the play on the riddle of fortune, while the Jailer's Daughter is cured by the doctor's masque of her wooer.
works.significance: The closing chord of the Shakespeare canon — a return to Chaucer, and to the question of friendship and love with which his career began.
works.meter: The collaboration's two styles are audibly joined — Shakespeare's ceremonial verse (the prayers at the altars) with Fletcher's supple fluency.
works.context: First performed about 1614, after the Globe fire, probably at Blackfriars; printed in quarto in 1634 as 'by the memorable worthies... Mr John Fletcher and Mr William Shakespeare'; omitted from the First Folio.
works.characters: Palamon; Arcite; Emilia; Theseus; Hippolyta; the Jailer; the Jailer's Daughter; the Wooer; Pirithous; the Doctor
works.structure: A tragicomedy of friendship and fortune in five acts, with the Jailer's Daughter's madness as a tragic sub-plot and the Morris dance and tournament as spectacle.
works.attributionNotes: Joint authorship with John Fletcher is established on title-page and stylistic evidence and is universally accepted; the division of scenes is broadly agreed.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: The Two Ways
altTitles: The Boke of the Two Ways
works.description: Sir John Clanvowe's devotional prose tract on the two ways of life and death — the narrow way of virtue and the broad way of the world — a Lollard-leaning meditation written in the circle of the 'Lollard knights' of Richard II's court, probably in 1391. It is the earliest prose work of the English reforming tradition by a lay courtier.
works.plot: The tract expounds Christ's teaching of the two ways, contrasts the few who walk the narrow path with the many on the broad road to perdition, and anatomizes the sins of the world — pride, avarice, gluttony — with a particular Lollard sharpness against clerical wealth and display.
works.significance: A principal document of the Lollard sensibility among the courtly elite and the earliest lay devotional prose of the Ricardian court.
works.meter: Plain, earnest prose with scriptural quotation.
works.context: Composed c. 1391 by the courtier-knight Clanvowe (d. October 1391), in the company of the Lollard knights at the court of Richard II; preserved in Bodleian MS Eng. th. c. 39 and later copies.
works.characters: the writer (as penitent teacher)
works.structure: A single homiletic meditation organized by the scriptural image of the two ways, with catalogue of sins and exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Clanvowe in the manuscripts.

editions.title: The Works of Sir John Clanvowe

works.title: The Unfortunate Traveller
works.description: Nashe's picaresque novel: the page Jack Wilton travels through the wars and cities of Europe — tricking the camp at Tergou, fleeing the sweating sickness and the plague, witnessing the massacre of the Anabaptists at Münster, courting in Italy, and escaping the rape-and-execution plot of the Jew Zadoch and the courtesan Juliana — in the first English novel of adventure and the grotesque.
works.plot: Jack's tricks in the army, his travels with the Earl of Surrey (and the Italian Diamante in boy's disguise), the horrors of Münster and of plague-struck Rome, the anatomies and executions, and the final escape through the villain's own engines carry the narrative to its abrupt, comic close.
works.significance: The first English picaresque novel — the ancestor of Defoe, Smollett, and the English novel's roguish line.
works.meter: Prose of Nashe's most violent invention — the grotesque, the comic, and the lyrical in rapid succession.
works.context: Published 1594; its continental horrors answered the decade's appetite for travel lies and martyrdom pamphlets, and its Italian scenes the anti-Catholic mood.
works.characters: Jack Wilton; the Earl of Surrey; Diamante; Zadoch; Zachary; Juliana; the Pope; Heraclide; the Anabaptists
works.structure: A first-person travel narrative in the manner of Lazarillo de Tormes, episodic and sensational, with the set pieces of horror (the anatomies, the executions) as its climaxes.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Works of Thomas Nashe, 5 vols.
editions.editor: R. B. McKerrow (ed.), revised by F. P. Wilson

works.title: The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York
altTitles: The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancastre and Yorke
works.description: Edward Hall's chronicle of the Wars of the Roses and the triumph of the house of Tudor, from the deposition of Richard II to the death of Henry VIII; printed posthumously by Richard Grafton in 1548 and continued by Grafton in later editions.
works.plot: Hall narrates the dynastic strife between Lancaster and York as a providential drama culminating in the union of the two houses in Henry VIII, with long set-piece speeches and a moralizing emphasis on the ruin brought by ambition, faction, and rebellion; the reign of Henry VIII occupies the final section ('The Triumphant Reign of King Henry the VIII').
works.significance: The principal source of Shakespeare's English history plays (the second tetralogy follows Hall closely) and the classic statement of the Tudor myth of union and providential kingship; its dramatic speeches made it the most literary of the Tudor chronicles.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Compiled over the 1530s and 1540s by Hall, a lawyer and MP, drawing on More's Richard III, Polydore Vergil, and Fabyan; the 1548 edition was supervised by Grafton, who added continuations in the editions of 1550.
works.characters: Henry IV; Henry V; Henry VI; Edward IV; Richard III; Henry VII; Henry VIII; Cardinal Wolsey
works.structure: Chronicle divided by reigns, from Richard II through Henry VIII, framed by a preface on the theme of union and enriched with speeches invented in the manner of classical historiography.

works.title: The Unnatural Combat
works.description: Massinger's dark tragedy in which the Marseilles admiral Malefort, under pressure from his son, kills him in single combat, and the son's ghost returns to expose the father's crimes.
works.plot: The young Malefort, corrupted by the villain Beauford junior, demands a combat with his father; the father kills him; the ghost reveals the unnatural deed and the father's earlier crime, and Malefort dies in madness.
works.significance: One of Massinger's most powerful tragedies, notable for its psychological intensity and its treatment of paternal guilt; it was long thought to have influenced later Jacobean and Caroline revenge drama.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men at the Globe c. 1624-26 and published in 1639.
works.characters: Malefort senior; Malefort junior; Beauford; Theocrine; Montrevile; Rochefort
works.structure: Five acts of revenge tragedy with a ghost and a catastrophic recognition.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Massinger; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Vanity of Dogmatizing; or, Confidence in Philosophy
works.description: Joseph Glanvill's sceptical defence of the new philosophy, which attacks Aristotelian scholastic dogmatism and argues that only experimental enquiry can extend knowledge; it was revised in 1665 as Scepsis Scientifica.
works.plot: Glanvill argues that human understanding is weak and prone to error, that the schools' dogmatism is vain, and that the experimental method of Bacon and the Royal Society offers the only path to reliable knowledge; the work contains the famous witchcraft narrative of the Drummer of Tedworth.
works.significance: The most readable early statement of the case for experimental philosophy in English and a source for the sceptical tradition that influenced Hume; the 1665 revision Scepsis Scientifica was widely read.
works.meter: Elegant, persuasive prose admired by the Royal Society.
works.context: Published in 1661, a year before the Royal Society's charter; Glanvill became a Fellow in 1664 and one of its most eloquent apologists.
works.structure: A series of chapters of sceptical argument with illustrative narratives.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Glanvill; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Vanity of Human Wishes
altTitles: The Vanity of Human Wishes: The Tenth Satire of Juvenal Imitated
works.form: verse satire and meditative poem in the Juvenalian tradition, with a strong native elegiac and devotional undertone
works.description: Johnson's greatest poem, an imitation of Juvenal's tenth satire on the emptiness of human desire, transposed from Roman invective into a Christian meditation on providence. Its catalogue of disappointed wishes - the scholar, the statesman, the general, the great man, the beauty, the aged - moves from the fall of Sejanus to the quiet exemplary death of the virtuous widow. The poem replaces the satirist's confidence in exposure with the recognition that only prayer and resignation remain.
works.plot: The speaker invites History to reveal the disasters produced by human hope, surveying ambition in learning, in public office, in arms and at court, and showing that each wish, granted or refused, destroys the wisher. The celebrated Sejanus passage enacts the sudden collapse of a favourite's power, and the fall of Wolsey gives the argument a distinctly modern and Christian dimension. The portraits of the beauty and of the aged wretch extend the miseries of the body and of dependence, and the poem ends by surrendering choice to providence in the prayer for wisdom that closes Johnson's verse.
works.significance: It is generally held to be the finest poem Johnson wrote and one of the major moral poems of the century, matching Pope's Essay on Man with a darker and more Scriptural account of desire. Its Sejanus and its closing widow supplied later poets with a model of the meditative satiric couplet, and the poem stands at the centre of the preromantic interest in melancholy, mutability and resignation.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, famously varied by dactylic and trisyllabic substitutions that give the line an unusual weight; the couplet is often enjambed and the antithesis strained to the breaking point.
works.context: Published on 28 January 1749 from Johnson's lodgings in Gough Square in the same season as the opening of his periodical labour; the fate of ministers and favourites was a live topic after the fall of Walpole and the recent rising of '45 made the instability of power and the misery of civil war immediate experience.
works.characters: The speaker; Sejanus; Wolsey; the beauty; the aged wretch; the virtuous widow; History
works.structure: A single invective movement organised as a series of exemplary portraits after the manner of the satire, framed by an invocation and closed by a devotional turn to prayer and wisdom; the examples accumulate rather than develop.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Johnson described the poem in his own correspondence and it was published under his name.

editions.title: The Yale Edition of the Works of Samuel Johnson (21 volumes)
editions.editor: W. Jackson Bate and James L. Clifford (general editors)

works.title: The Vicar of Wakefield
altTitles: The Vicar of Wakefield: A Tale, Supposed to be Written by Himself
works.form: Sentimental and domestic novel in the picaresque line, in short numbered chapters, with the first-person narrative of an amiable patriarch; mixed comedy and pathos, with inserted songs and moral reflection.
works.description: Goldsmith's novel, and one of the most read and most translated prose fictions of the century: the story of the family of Dr Primrose, a country chaplain, reduced from competence to poverty and tried by a succession of calamities, which it narrates in the first person with an unaffected and comic seriousness. It is the exemplary domestic and sentimental novel of the 1760s, and its fame has rested ever since on the question of whether its virtue is sincere or merely naive.
works.plot: The Primroses, happy and prosperous in their parish, lose their fortune when a trust in which their savings were lodged fails, and they retire to a smaller house where the family's learning, vanity and simplicity are displayed in the father's sermons and in the accomplishments of the daughters. Squire Thornhill, the dissolute nephew of a local great man, seduces and abandons the elder daughter Olivia, while the younger Arabella is courted in turn; the father's resentful attempt at revenge by letter ruins him further, and the family is reduced to a jail in which the father's philosophy, the mother's indignation and the children's several fates are all tested. A disguised benefactor, appearing as the humble Mr Burchell, is revealed at the close as the real power who has been testing them throughout, and the novel ends with restitution, recovered fortune and marriage. The movement is thus from prosperity through a series of calamities to a providential restoration, with patience and benevolence as the family's governing virtues.
works.significance: It is one of the two or three novels that fixed the sentimental domestic form for later generations, and its portrait of family virtue under trial was admired and ridiculed in equal measure, the most durable of the ridicule being Samuel Johnson's objection that its whole design sacrificed probability to affecting circumstance. Its influence on the country-pastoral novel, on the fiction of trials and providential restoration, and on the nineteenth-century reading of Goldsmith as a man of feeling, is considerable.
works.context: It appeared in the decade of the sentimental comedy and of Richardson's moral fiction, when the novel was being taken up as an instrument of instruction and when the 'good-natur'd' philosophy of the moral sense school was a subject of public debate. It was published at a stroke by a writer otherwise known as a poet, essayist and hack, and its scene of rural retirement speaks for an age anxious about the decay of the country and of the paternal clergyman.
works.characters: Dr Primrose, the vicar; his wife; Olivia and Arabella; Moses and Dicky; Squire Thornhill; the disguised benefactor Mr Burchell; the gaoler and the minor friends of the family
works.structure: A picaresque-sentimental novel in fifty-two short chapters, told in the first person by the vicar, with a continuous linear sequence of prosperity, fall, trial and restoration, and with the narrator's own simplicity as the source of the comedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the novel was published with Goldsmith's name, and its sale to the trade was famously negotiated for him by Samuel Johnson. Disputed questions concern the order of composition and the extent of revision, not the authorship.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Virtuoso
works.description: Shadwell's comedy satirising the Royal Society and the new experimental philosophy through the figure of Sir Nicholas Gimcrack, an amateur scientist who wastes his fortune on absurd experiments.
works.plot: Sir Nicholas pursues swimming-lessons for frogs and the extraction of air from cucumbers while his nieces and suitors conduct a normal intrigue; the satire is aimed not at science itself but at its pedantic misuse.
works.significance: The most important dramatic satire on the early Royal Society and a key text in the history of the quarrel between the wits and the philosophers; Gimcrack became a byword for the foolish virtuoso.
works.meter: Prose dominant.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in May 1676 and published in the same year; Shadwell claimed to have attended Royal Society meetings for two years to get his material, and the portrait was taken as an attack on the Society's Fellows.
works.characters: Sir Nicholas Gimcrack; Lady Gimcrack; Hazard; Longvil; Clara; Lucia; Mrs Figgup; Snarl; Sneak
works.structure: Five acts with a Jonsonian comic central figure and a conventional love plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shadwell; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Vision of Leofric
altTitles: The Old English Vision of Leofric, Earl of Mercia
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 367, part II (eleventh century)
works.description: An Old English account of four visions granted to Leofric, earl of Mercia (d. 1057), written soon after his death: a vision of the cross and the hand of God during a mass at St Mary's, a miraculous vision through the mist at Wednesbury, a visit to the shrine of St Peter in Rome, and a vision of the soul's judgment at Christ Church, Canterbury. It is the earliest vernacular prose vision narrative in English.
works.plot: The text narrates Leofric's visionary experiences in order: at mass he sees the cross of light and God's hand blessing the congregation; at Wednesbury the mist parts to reveal the church as God sees it, with Leofric guided by a mysterious companion; in Rome he kneels before St Peter; and at Canterbury he witnesses a dying man's soul weighed in judgment and rescued by the saints through Leofric's intercession.
works.significance: The earliest surviving prose vision narrative in English, anticipating the great medieval genre of Piers Plowman and the Pearl-poet, and a precious first-person witness to eleventh-century English devotional practice.
works.context: Written in the Confessor's reign by a writer close to Leofric's household, the text documents the piety of the last great Old English earl and the penitential spirituality of the eleventh-century church on the eve of the Conquest; it is contemporary with the earliest continental prose visions that shaped later medieval vision literature.
works.characters: Earl Leofric, the mysterious guide, St Peter
works.structure: Four discrete vision episodes in chronological order, each grounded in named places and dates and framed by Leofric's devout response; the Wednesbury and Canterbury visions are developed at length, the others briefly.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the author writes from within Leofric's circle and is otherwise unknown.

works.title: The Wallace
altTitles: The Acts and Deeds of Sir William Wallace
works.description: Blind Hary's epic life of William Wallace, composed c. 1477 in some 11,800 lines: the hero's outlawry after the killing of Selkirk's sheriff, his battles against the English — Stirling Bridge, the invasion of England, Falkirk — his betrayal and execution at London (1305), and his posthumous vindication. For four centuries it was, after the Bible, the most read book in Scotland, and it fixed Wallace in the national memory.
works.plot: Wallace, driven to outlawry by English oppression, gathers his men, defeats the English at Stirling Bridge, harries England as far as York, and is named guardian of Scotland; betrayed at Falkirk and by the treachery of Menteith, he is taken to London, tried as a traitor to a king he never acknowledged, and executed — his dismembered body displayed, his fame immortal.
works.significance: The great popular epic of Scotland: its Wallace shaped the national hero for five centuries, and its influence on Burns and the romantic revival of Scottish identity is incalculable.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in Older Scots, declamatory and rapid.
works.context: Composed c. 1477 by Blind Hary, who recited it before James IV for payment, drawing on John Blair's lost Latin life and oral tradition; printed by Chepman and Myllar (c. 1508) and endlessly reprinted — Burns acknowledged it as his first poetic inspiration.
works.characters: William Wallace; Edward I; Menteith; Graham; Bruce (epilogue)
works.structure: Twelve books of epic narrative, from outlawry through triumph to martyrdom, in the minstrel chronicle manner, with the poet's appeals to his audience throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Blind Hary (Henry the Minstrel) by the poem and the treasurer's accounts.

editions.title: Hary's Wallace

works.title: The Wanderer
works.description: An elegy of 115 lines in which a solitary exile, deprived of lord and hall, meditates on the transience of earthly joy and arrives at a hard-won Christian consolation. One of the most admired poems in the Exeter Book and the supreme statement of the Old English ubi sunt theme.
works.plot: The speaker, an 'eardstapa' (earth-stepper) wandering the frozen seas since the death of his lord, remembers the lost joys of the hall and laments the ruin of the world's splendour ('Where is the horse? Where is the young warrior?'); the poem closes with the famous gnomic consolation that a wise man keeps faith and seeks mercy from the Father in heaven, where all stability dwells.
works.significance: The classic Old English elegy; a locus classicus for the ubi sunt topos and for the Christian reframing of the heroic ethos.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre with the formulaic diction of the heroic tradition, turned to meditative ends.
works.context: Preserved only in the Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 76v-78r), a late tenth-century anthology; the poem's heroic nostalgia is often read against the upheavals of the Viking age, though its date of composition is unknown.
works.characters: the Wanderer (speaker); the lost lord
works.structure: A movement from personal lament through the ubi sunt catalogue of vanished glories to a generalizing wisdom passage and a prayerful conclusion; framed by the figure of the wise man who speaks little and reflects much.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Old English Literature, 2nd edition

works.title: The Way of the World
works.description: Congreve's last and greatest comedy, the supreme achievement of the English comedy of manners, in which Mirabell and Millamant negotiate the famous 'proviso' scene and outwit the jealous Lady Wishfort and the treacherous Fainall.
works.plot: Mirabell needs the consent of Lady Wishfort, whose fortune Millamant depends on, and has pretended to court the old lady; Lady Wishfort is enraged when she learns the truth; the villain Fainall tries to seize the estates, and Mirabell defeats him with the deed of trust.
works.significance: Universally regarded as the greatest comedy of manners in English and one of the supreme achievements of Restoration literature; it was decisively revalued in the twentieth century by T. S. Eliot and Bonamy Dobrée.
works.meter: Prose of the most refined and musical precision; the proviso scene is the high-water mark of English comic dialogue.
works.context: Performed at Lincoln's Inn Fields in March 1700 and published the same year; its relative coolness at first performance ended Congreve's dramatic career at the age of thirty.
works.characters: Mirabell; Millamant; Lady Wishfort; Fainall; Mrs Fainall; Mrs Marwood; Sir Wilfull Witwoud; Petulant; Waitwell; Foible; Witwoud
works.structure: Five acts of intricate intrigue culminating in the proviso scene (IV.i) and the discovery scene (V), each with a formal balance and symmetry unmatched in English comedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Congreve; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Wedding
works.description: Shirley's first surviving comedy, a witty intrigue play in which the Duchess of Florence tests her suitors by pretending to favour the wrong man, and the various disguises and misunderstandings are resolved in a set of weddings.
works.plot: The Duchess of Florence entertains several suitors, among them the noble Beaufort and the disguised soldier; through feigned favour, a fake death, and a discovered plot, the true lovers are matched and the court is reconciled.
works.significance: Announces Shirley's characteristic mode — elegant, urbane intrigue comedy — and marks the transition from Jacobean to Caroline drama.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose in the low comic scenes.
works.context: First performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Cockpit c. 1626 and published in 1629.
works.characters: the Duchess of Florence; Beaufort; Rawliff; Gratiana; Jane; Annabel; Sir Ambrose Marlove
works.structure: Five acts in the standard Caroline comedy structure of parallel love intrigues converging on a multiple wedding.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shirley on the 1629 title page; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Wedding of Sir Gawain and Dame Ragnelle
altTitles: The Weddynge of Sir Gawen and Dame Ragnell
works.description: A fifteenth-century Arthurian romance on the loathly lady theme: to save Arthur's life, Gawain marries the hideous Dame Ragnelle, who holds the answer to the riddle 'what women most desire' — sovereignty — and his courtesy at the wedding night transforms her into a beauty. The wittiest of the Gawain romances and the source of the Wife of Bath's Tale's plot.
works.plot: Arthur, challenged by Sir Gromer Somer Joure, must learn what women most desire; Ragnelle supplies the answer (sovereignty) in exchange for Gawain's hand; Gawain's free gift of choice on the wedding night breaks the enchantment, making Ragnelle fair by day and night, and the two live happily until her death.
works.significance: The most entertaining of the late Gawain romances and the fullest English statement of the 'sovereignty' motif central to late medieval debates on marriage.
works.meter: Six-line tail-rhyme stanzas with comic energy.
works.context: Composed c. 1450 in the East Midlands; preserved uniquely in Bodleian Library, Rawlinson MS C.86 (c. 1500); the loathly lady plot derives from Irish and English folk tradition (and parallels Chaucer's Wife of Bath's Tale).
works.characters: Gawain; Dame Ragnelle; Arthur; Sir Gromer Somer Joure
works.structure: A riddle-romance in two movements (the quest for the answer; the marriage and its testing), resolved by the courtesy test.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The West-Saxon Gospels
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, University Library Ii.2.11 (c. 1075) and five other copies including Oxford, Bodleian Library, Bodley 441 and Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 140
works.description: An anonymous translation of the four gospels into late West Saxon, made in the last decade of the tenth century, probably in the south-west of England. It is the first complete translation of the gospels into English and circulated widely, with six surviving manuscripts and copies reaching into the twelfth century.
works.plot: The translation renders Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John continuously, in a plain, literal but idiomatic Old English prose that follows the Vulgate closely while producing natural vernacular sentences.
works.significance: The first complete English translation of the gospels, the ancestor of the Wycliffite and later English bibles, and a cornerstone of the Old English prose corpus studied by every student of the language.
works.context: Produced in the aftermath of the Benedictine Reform, when vernacular preaching and reading were encouraged; Ælfric's biblical translations belong to the same movement, and the gospels' circulation shows the demand for scripture in English among clergy and laity alike.
works.characters: Christ, the apostles, Mary, John the Baptist, Pilate
works.structure: Four continuous gospel narratives in traditional order, with chapter divisions supplied in the manuscripts; the translation is a continuous prose version without glossing apparatus.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. No convincing attribution has been proposed; the language is late West Saxon with south-western features.

editions.title: The Old English Version of the Gospels
editions.publisher: Early English Text Society (Oxford University Press)

works.title: The Whale
works.description: A poem of 89 lines on the legend of the whale (Fastitocalon) that lies like an island: sailors moor to it, light fires, and are dragged down when the beast dives. The poem reads it as an allegory of the devil, who lures sinners with the appearance of safety and plunges them into hell.
works.plot: Mariners mistake the whale's back for an island, anchor and kindle fires; when the creature senses the heat it dives, drowning the crew. The allegory applies the story to the devil, whose deceptive promises — the sweet sins that seem secure ground — drag the unwary soul into the abyss.
works.significance: The earliest English version of the whale-island legend, later famous in the Navigatio Sancti Brendani and Mandeville; a vivid allegory of temptation.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book with The Panther and The Partridge.
works.characters: the Whale (Fastitocalon; the devil); the mariners (sinners)
works.structure: Narrative exemplum followed by allegorical application, in the Physiologus manner.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Life of Samuel Johnson, 6 volumes (Birkbeck Hill edition)

works.title: The White Devil
works.description: Webster's first independent tragedy, of the Italian court: Vittoria Corombona, married to Camillo, loves Duke Brachiano, whose wife Isabella is murdered by the lovers' plot; Vittoria's great trial for her husband's death follows, then the revenge of Isabella's brother Francisco — poisoned portrait, masque of murderers, and the final bloodbath in which Brachiano, Vittoria, and her brother Flamineo all die.
works.plot: Flamineo panders his sister to Brachiano; Isabella and Camillo are murdered; Vittoria's arraignment — 'I am summoned to appear before the wolf' — is the play's trial centrepiece; the counterfeit letter and Francisco's disguised revenges pursue the lovers; and the last act's masque of revengers kills Brachiano, with Vittoria and Flamineo dying in the mutual treachery of the close.
works.significance: One of the two masterpieces (with The Duchess of Malfi) of Jacobean tragedy — the play that defined Webster's theatre of corruption and splendour.
works.meter: Webster's dark, emblematic blank verse — the arraignment speeches and the dirges are its heights — with the prose of the panders as counterpoint.
works.context: Based on the historical Vittoria Accoramboni (d. 1585); performed at the Red Bull in 1612 to a hostile audience, as Webster complains in his preface; printed the same year.
works.characters: Vittoria Corombona; Flamineo; Duke Brachiano; Francisco de Medici; Cardinal Monticelso; Isabella; Camillo; Cornelia; Marcello; Zanche; Lodovico; Gasparo; the Ambassadors
works.structure: A five-act revenge tragedy of the Italian court, built on the trial scene and the double masque, with the choric comments of the ambassadors and the ghost of Isabella.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The White Devil (Revels Plays)

works.title: The Widow Ranter; or, The History of Bacon in Virginia
works.description: Behn's last play, produced posthumously, a tragicomedy set in colonial Virginia during Bacon's Rebellion of 1676, combining a love intrigue with an unprecedentedly sympathetic treatment of Native Americans.
works.plot: The wealthy tobacco-planting Widow Ranter loves the dashing Dareing; Bacon leads a rebellion against the colonial government to defend the settlers from Indian attacks; Bacon falls in love with the Indian queen Semernia, kills her accidentally, and dies, while the comic plot resolves in marriage.
works.significance: The first English play set in colonial America and one of the earliest literary treatments of the Atlantic slave economy and of Anglo-Indian relations; it has become central to postcolonial readings of Restoration drama.
works.meter: Prose and verse mixed.
works.context: Written c. 1688-9, produced at the Theatre Royal in November 1689, and published posthumously in 1690 with a preface by an unknown hand.
works.characters: the Widow Ranter; Dareing; Nathaniel Bacon; Semernia; Caverno; Hazard; Friendly; Chrisante; Flora
works.structure: Five acts with a tragic historical plot and a comic plantation plot set in the same Virginian world.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Behn; published posthumously.

editions.title: Kissing the Rod: An Anthology of Seventeenth-Century Women's Verse
editions.editor: Germaine Greer, Susan Hastings, Jeslyn Medoff, and Melinda Sansone (eds.)

editions.title: The Works of Aphra Behn
editions.publisher: William Pickering / Ohio State University Press

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Wife's Lament
works.description: An elegy of 53 lines, unique in the corpus for its sustained female voice: a woman separated from her lord laments her exile in an earth-cave beneath an oak tree and curses the man responsible for her misery.
works.plot: The speaker tells how her lord departed over the sea, how his kin plotted against them, and how she was banished to a desolate dwelling in the wilderness, where she sits weeping through the long days; she ends by wishing upon her beloved the sorrow of one who sits apart, remembering a happier home.
works.significance: The first sustained female voice in English poetry and a key text for feminist criticism of the period.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; unusually personal and passionate diction.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; the poem has been read as autobiography, as allegory (the Church or the soul lamenting Christ), and as a riddle-like exercise — a famous crux of Old English scholarship.
works.characters: the Wife (speaker); the absent lord
works.structure: A first-person lament moving from past happiness through separation and exile to a bitter wish against the absent beloved; the obscurity of the situation (which lord, which feud) is itself part of the poem's design.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
sources: The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: The Wild Gallant
works.description: Dryden's first play, a prose comedy of intrigue performed before the court at Whitehall and a conspicuous failure that he later revised.
works.plot: Lord Truceville pursues Lady Constance while pretending to be a wild gallant; a series of mistaken identities, a faked ghost, and an inn intrigue lead to a double marriage.
works.significance: Dryden's dramatic debut; its failure taught him to move toward the rhymed heroic play, which he began with The Rival Ladies.
works.meter: Predominantly prose.
works.context: Performed by the Duke's Company at the Theatre in Lincoln's Inn Fields in February 1663 before Charles II and the court, who found it dull.
works.characters: Lord Truceville; Lady Constance; Colonel Fairly; Bibber; Mrs Gripe; Set-Star; Mr Trice
works.structure: Five acts of low comedy and intrigue.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Winter's Tale
works.description: Shakespeare's romance of jealousy and resurrection: Leontes of Sicilia, seized by groundless suspicion, destroys his queen Hermione and orders the exposure of their newborn daughter; the child Perdita grows up a shepherd's daughter in Bohemia; sixteen years later the flight to Sicilia, the revelation of her birth, and the 'statue' scene bring Hermione back to life and the family together again.
works.plot: Leontes' sudden jealousy condemns Hermione; the oracle's verdict comes too late and the prince dies of grief; Perdita is exposed and found; the Bohemian pastoral of the sheep-shearing and the courtship of Florizel occupy the middle acts; the flight to Sicilia unravels Perdita's birth; and Paulina reveals Hermione, preserved in secret, in the play's miraculous final scene.
works.significance: The most moving of the romances — the play of grace, time, and forgiveness that defined the tragicomic art of the late Shakespeare.
works.meter: The late style at its richest — the flower speeches of Perdita, the ballads of Autolycus — with the trial scene's forensic verse as the tragic core.
works.context: Written about 1610–11 from Greene's Pandosto; performed at court in 1611 and at the Globe; the statue scene's art-life paradox crowns Shakespeare's last engagement with Ovid and Pygmalion.
works.characters: Leontes; Hermione; Perdita; Florizel; Polixenes; Paulina; Camillo; Antigonus; Autolycus; the Old Shepherd; the Clown; Time (the Chorus); Mamillius
works.structure: A two-part structure — tragedy in Sicilia, pastoral in Bohemia — bridged by Time the Chorus and resolved in the resurrection ending, with the bear's exit as the most famous stage direction in English.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: The Witch of Edmonton
works.description: Dekker, Ford, and Rowley's tragicomedy of the real Elizabeth Sawyer, hanged as a witch at Edmonton in 1621: the old woman, cursed and beaten by her neighbours, sells herself to the devil in the shape of the black dog Tom; the parallel plot of the bigamist Frank Thorney and his murders runs alongside; and the play ends with Sawyer's execution and Thorney's confession, the village's two sins joined in one scaffold.
works.plot: Old Banks's curses and the villagers' cruelty drive Sawyer to the dog Tom; her witchcraft plagues the village while Frank Thorney, secretly married, stabs his second wife Susan and is pursued by the law; the two plots converge in the final acts, where Sawyer's repentance and execution and Thorney's scaffold confession close the play on the wages of desperation and greed.
works.significance: The most humane of the English witch plays — the first to make the witch's persecution, not her malice, the tragedy.
works.meter: The three authors' mixed verse and prose, with Sawyer's curses and the dog's speeches as the play's remembered scenes.
works.context: Performed at court in December 1621, within months of the real Sawyer's execution in April of that year; printed in 1658; its sympathetic witch answered the decade's pamphlet wars over witchcraft.
works.characters: Elizabeth Sawyer; the Dog (Tom); Frank Thorney; Susan Carter; Winnifred; Old Thorney; Sir Arthur Clarington; Cuddy Banks; Old Carter; Katherine Carter; the Justice
works.structure: A two-plot tragicomedy — the witch and the bigamist — built on the documentary record of the 1621 trial and the pamphlet of Henry Goodcole.
works.attributionNotes: By Dekker, Ford, and Rowley, as stated on the title page; the division of scenes is partly conjectural.

editions.title: The Witch of Edmonton (Revels Plays)

works.title: The Witlings
works.description: A five-act comedy of the blue-stockings and the tea-table wits of the town, written for the stage but never performed in the author's lifetime, its rehearsal being stopped by the interference of her father and of the leading players. It survives in manuscript and in modern print as the sharpest contemporary attack on the society of wit.
works.plot: A young lady of the school of the witlings is set by her friends against the plain suitor her family approves, while the club of the blue-stockings, its critics and its authors, divides the conversation of the town between pretension and malice. The several devices of the wits, the verses and the reviews, expose the vanity of the set. The comedy was withdrawn before performance, and its argument about the price of literary reputation was left to be read.
works.significance: It is a primary document of the century's argument about women's literary sociability and of the practical censorship of the stage, and its suppression has become a central case in the history of women's access to publication.
works.meter: A brilliant conversational prose of quotation, review and affected sensibility, the jargon of the witlings being reproduced for exposure.
works.context: Written in 1779 in the season of the quarrel between the author's father and the theatres, and suppressed at the rehearsal stage with the intervention of the leading manager; the Bluestocking society and the review trade supplied its immediate targets.
works.characters: the young lady of the witlings; her mother and the friends of the circle; the plain suitor disapproved by the set; the critics and the authors of the tea-table club
works.structure: A regular five-act comedy of conversation and pretension, the satire concentrated in the scenes of the blue-stocking circle; the text is that of the withdrawn manuscript.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the comedy remained in manuscript and in the author's papers, and was not printed until modern times, so that no first edition date is asserted here.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Wonder: A Woman Keeps a Secret
altTitles: The Wonder, A Woman Keeps a Secret
works.form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: A comic drama of jealousy and female reticence, set in a Spanish-Portuguese court and its island, and the author's most popular play with the following generation of readers and managers. Its title phrase passed into proverb, and its heroine's refusal to explain her secret supplies the plot's mechanism.
works.plot: A jealous governor suspects his sister's conduct and confines her, while a rival lover's designs on an heiress are pursued in the island scheme. The women keep their counsel through apparent betrayals, the men misread every signal, and the discovery of the secret clears the innocent and unites the lovers. The comedy ends with the governor's jealousy turned into an emblem of the sex's power over male inference.
works.significance: It consolidated the comedy of female discretion as a civic virtue and became the stock example of a woman dramatist's command of regular construction; its proverbial title marks its penetration into everyday language.
works.meter: Heroic couplets mixed with prose for the lower scenes, in the post-Dryden comic manner; the repartee depends on balanced half-lines and the interruption of the couplet.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1714 and revived throughout the century, including in the altered version of the 1740s; its Spanish setting belongs to the vogue for Iberian comic scenes inherited from the Restoration.
works.characters: Inez, the wondering woman; her brother the jealous governor; Caesario; Clara; Blazina; the rival gallants
works.structure: Five-act regular comedy in verse and prose, with a tightly interlocked intrigue of jealousy and a delayed revelation; the secret is structurally held until the fifth-act discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the play was published with the author's name and was claimed for her in the biographical prefaces of the collected edition.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Wonders of the East
works.form: travel and wonders literature in Old English prose
works.description: The Old English catalogue of the marvels of the East, preserved in the Nowell Codex beside Beowulf and illustrated with vivid drawings: dog-headed men, giants, serpents, the phoenix's nest, the hens that burn men, and the gold-guarding ants of Gorgoneus — the fantastic geography of the age compiled for an English audience.
works.plot: The text proceeds place by place through the wonders of Egypt and the East — the two-headed beasts, the monoculi, the cynocephali, the generous king of the Hostes, the locusts and dragons of the desert — describing each marvel's appearance and habits, with the famous closing account of the gold-digging ants as large as dogs.
works.significance: The fullest English witness to the medieval geography of marvels and to the monstrous races that haunted the period's imagination.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated from a Latin original (itself from the Epistola Alexandri tradition) in the late tenth or early eleventh century; preserved in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv), the Beowulf manuscript, and in Cotton MS Tiberius B.v.
works.characters: the monstrous races and beasts of the East
works.structure: A catalogue of marvels organized by region, each entry a short description.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Order and degree: the body politic
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Milton, 2nd edition

works.title: The Wooing of Our Lord
altTitles: On Wel Swuðe God Ureisun of God Almihti
works.description: A group of lyrical prose meditations on the love of Christ, in the AB language: the Wooing of Our Lord, On Ureisun of Ure Louerde, On Lofsong of Ure Louerde, and related prayers. Addressed to a female recluse, they figure Christ as a knightly wooer whose love and Passion the anchoress must return, in prose of extraordinary affective intensity.
works.plot: The speaker addresses Christ as lover and spouse, meditating on his beauty, his suffering on the cross, and the soul's answering love, weaving prayer, praise, and erotic-spiritual longing into a single meditation.
works.significance: The earliest English expression of the bride-mysticism and Passion devotion that culminate in Rolle, Julian, and the lyrics; a landmark of affective prose.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative, incantatory prose with lyric repetitions and refrains.
works.context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands for a woman recluse, in the same milieu as Ancrene Wisse; preserved in BL Cotton MS Nero A.xiv and Titus D.xviii.
works.characters: Christ as wooer; the anchoress speaker
works.structure: A sequence of meditative addresses, each moving from invocation through Passion meditation to petition.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Works of Mr. Martinus Scriblerus
altTitles: Memoirs of the extraordinary Life, Works, and Discoveries of Martinus Scriblerus
works.form: Collaborative satirical miscellany: mock-biography, mock-didactic essay, eclogue and parodic scholarly apparatus
works.description: The collected issue, in two volumes, of the papers of the Scriblerus club, printed seven years after Arbuthnot's death and four after Swift's and Parnell's. Its centrepiece is the Memoirs of the imaginary pedant Martinus Scriblerus, a burlesque life and catalogue of false discoveries, accompanied by the club's earlier pieces against false learning, bad taste and the abuse of scholarship. The volume is the published monument of the greatest joint satirical project of the Augustan age.
works.plot: The Memoirs recount how Martinus, the posthumous son of a great man, is educated by a circle of projectors who teach him every system of error: false philosophy, obsolete scholarship, the art of digging for hidden treasure, and the machinery of pedantic invention. Thereupon he devotes his vast industry to useless discoveries, among them a treatise on the shadow of a bat and a mechanical device for travelling by pinning the wind, and ends in a universal scheme of knowledge that teaches everything and signifies nothing. The accompanying tracts attack the modern critick, the moneyed interest and the corrupt clergy, converting the club's private jests into a public indictment of learning without sense and of wit in the service of dullness.
works.significance: It fixed the type of the pedant and of organised dullness for two centuries and is the foundational document of Augustan collaboration. Its model of satire as a joint construction of fictitious scholarship runs directly from here through Fielding, Sterne and the nineteenth-century mock-book, and it remains the best evidence of the Scriblerans' theory that ridicule is the test of imposture.
works.meter: Chiefly prose in a parodic latinised period style, with interspersed Hudibrastic and Augustan verse pieces
works.context: Drawn up during the club's Oxford and London meetings of roughly 1710-1714 and assembled for the press in the literary quarrels of the 1730s, the volume reflects the Scribleran campaign against the criticks, the projectors and the Whig learning of the age, and Pope's use of club material in the Dunciad.
works.characters: Martinus Scriblerus; his tutors and projectors; the club's personae of invented editors
works.structure: Miscellany: a Mock-biographical Memoirs in continuous narrative, followed by separately titled essays, eclogues, notes and pieces of club origin, with an apparatus of fabricated scholarship.
works.attributionNotes: Club composition: the shares of John Arbuthnot, Alexander Pope, Jonathan Swift and John Gay, with Thomas Parnell and Bishop Atterbury, are much debated and cannot be assigned with confidence; the Memoirs are chiefly Arbuthnot's with Pope's revision, and the 1741 text was prepared with Pope's involvement. Recorded here as a single collaborative volume, with the four principal club members credited in the map.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Works of Ossian
works.form: Collected translated epic and lyric corpus with editorial dissertation and annotation: the founding edition of the Ossianic canon, and the vehicle for its scholarly defence.
works.description: The collected edition in which Macpherson gathered the fragments and the two epics, with a large scholarly apparatus of dissertations, imitations of ancient poems and a history of the era, and which gave Europe 'Ossian' as a single book. This is the form in which the poems were read, translated, attacked and imitated for the rest of the century, and the volume round which the authentication quarrel hardened.
works.plot: As a collected work it presents a complete imagined literature: the epic actions of Fingal and of his grandson, the shorter poems of lament and of love, and the critical dissertations that supply a chronology, a bardic religion and a theory of ancient heroic poetry. Its argument throughout is that the northern nations possessed, before letters, a poetry of passion and of the moral imagination equal to the classical epic, and that this poetry can be recovered by a modern translator. The shorter pieces add the tender and domestic register: the dead mourned by women, the ghosts of the fallen, the last departures of a failing race. The volume closes the circle by making the reader's own sensibility the proof of the poems' truth.
works.significance: It is one of the most influential books of the second half of the century across Europe, the standard reference for the primitive sublime, for the poetry of melancholy and for the idea of a national bardic literature; its influence is traceable in poetry, in the Gothic, in music and in painting. It is also the most celebrated case in the history of literary forgery or reconstruction, and it forced the age to define the evidence required for a text's antiquity.
works.meter: The uniform cadenced unrhymed measure of the Ossianic books, with the shorter poems in a more purely lyric and elegiacal movement; apostrophe, epithet and inverted syntax carry the rhythm.
works.context: Published in 1765, after the controversy had already become public and political, and at the moment when the Highland Society, Irish antiquaries and English critics were all examining the claims. The edition's apparatus is an answer to that scrutiny, and its confidence provoked the more systematic denials of the later eighteenth century.
works.characters: Ossian as the supposed ancient author and speaker; Fingal; his sons and successors; the bards, spirits and mourning women of the shorter poems
works.structure: A collected two-volume edition: preliminary dissertations on the era and on the heroic poetry of the ancients, the epics, the shorter poems and translations, with arguments and notes; the sequence is encyclopaedic rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: The collection is Macpherson's in every recoverable sense, and the ancient authorship it asserts, that of the bard Ossian, is recorded here as disputed: the claimed Gaelic and Irish originals have never been authenticated, and the case for composition rather than translation was made within a few years of publication and renewed since. The edition's own dissertations are Macpherson's defence.

works.title: The Works of Virgil Translated into English Verse
altTitles: The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Aeneis
works.form: epic translation; pastoral translation; didactic translation
works.description: Dryden's complete translation of Virgil — the Eclogues, the Georgics, and the Aeneid — undertaken over more than a decade and published by subscription in three folio volumes in 1697.
works.plot: A translation of all of Virgil: ten pastoral eclogues, four books of didactic georgic poetry, and the twelve-book epic of Aeneas's journey from Troy to the foundation of the Roman race.
works.significance: The dominant English Virgil for over two centuries and a decisive influence on the Augustan verse style; Johnson judged it 'such a translation as no age or nation could hope to see again'.
works.meter: Heroic couplets throughout; Dryden's translation method is 'paraphrase' — sense for sense rather than word for word.
works.context: Begun after Dryden lost his laureateship in 1689 and completed as his chief source of income; the subscription edition raised some £1,300, an unprecedented sum for a translation.
works.characters: Aeneas; Dido; Turnus; Anchises; Tityrus; Meliboeus; Aristaeus
works.structure: Three sections following Virgil's own tripartite oeuvre; Dryden's prefatory essays on pastoral, georgic, and epic theory accompany each.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Theron and Aspasio; or, A Scriptural and Critical Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians
works.form: Prose devotional and doctrinal treatise in epistolary and dialogic form with embedded biblical commentary
works.description: James Hervey's devotional-argumentative masterpiece, issued in three volumes in 1755, casts the doctrines of grace and the righteousness of faith into a frame of letters, dialogues and a running commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians. Its ornate, balanced prose was admired across denominational lines even by readers who disliked its Calvinism. The work immediately became the occasion of John Wesley's furious reply, because Wesley read its teaching on justification as antinomian and disparaging of holiness of life.
works.plot: The letters and dialogues between Aspasio, a Christian nobleman, and his friend Theron trace the grounds of natural religion, the corruption of human nature, and the necessity of an imputed righteousness. Hervey then appends a scriptural and critical commentary on Galatians, arguing that the epistle establishes justification by faith alone and excludes all human boasting. The intermediate dialogues dramatise the contrast between a moralist religion of self-effort and a gospel religion of reliance on Christ, and press home the practical duties of the regenerate life. The whole is designed to be at once devotional reading, doctrinal instruction, and exegetical argument, and to show that profound Calvinism can be spoken in the most polished and affecting English.
works.significance: For a century Theron and Aspasio was quoted as a model of English religious prose, and Samuel Johnson and Robert Hall admired its eloquence. Its publication provoked one of the most energetic pamphlet exchanges of the century, Wesley's Defense of his own letter and the long controversy with the label "Calvinism" attached to it. The book remains the clearest instance of how evangelical doctrine could be accommodated to polite Augustan diction.
works.meter: Prose only, in a highly wrought periodic style of balanced clauses and cadenced rhythm
works.context: Published in the middle of the Calvinistic-Arminian revival controversies, the book belongs to the effusive piety associated with the Countess of Huntingdon's connection and to Hervey's own late meditations at Weston underoclic. It also belongs to the broader eighteenth-century fashion for ornamental religious prose and to the growing use of dialogue and epistle as vehicles for theological argument.
works.characters: Aspasio; Theron
works.structure: Three volumes arranged as a sequence of letters and dialogues framing a verse-by-verse commentary on Galatians, so that meditation, conversation and exegesis alternate throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by James Hervey is established and undisputed.

works.title: Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species, Humbly Submitted to the Justice of Great Britain by the Africans
altTitles: Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil of Slavery
works.form: Polemical essay in natural-law, scriptural and legal argument
works.description: An abolitionist polemic by Ottobah Cugoano, a Fante man kidnapped and sold in 1769, who by the 1780s was a literate servant in the London household of the artist Richard Cosway. The book argues from natural law, scripture and British law that the slave trade and West Indian slavery are crimes against God and humanity, and it demands immediate remedy rather than gradual relief. A short abridgement for wider circulation followed in the same year, and a second edition with an appendix on the slave insurrection in Jamaica appeared in 1788.
works.plot: Cugoano first states the natural right of every human being to liberty, so that enslavement is a violation of the law of God written on the conscience. He then examines the scriptural evidence and shows that neither Hebraic servitude nor the New Testament's household codes sanction the modern traffic, and he presses the legal argument that a Christian cannot lawfully hold a fellow Christian in perpetual slavery. Turning to practice, he denounces the planters' plea of necessity and property, refutes the political arithmetic that counts colonial wealth as national strength, and proposes remedies: the recall of British subjects from the colonies, the education of the enslaved, and the establishment of lawful commerce in Africa in place of the trade in persons. The conclusion warns that Britain's national guilt for the trade will draw national judgment.
works.significance: It is the first published abolitionist argument written by an African in England to confront the slave trade as a national crime and to claim the authority of reason and scripture against the planters' case. Its insistence that liberty is a divine and natural right, and its refusal of gradualist compromise, make it a foundational text of black Atlantic political writing and a necessary companion to Equiano's narrative.
works.meter: Prose only, in an urgent, latinate, sermon-like style marked by biblical cadence
works.context: Written between the Somersett decision of 1772 and the first parliamentary abolitionist campaign of 1788, it joins the printed output of the Committee for Abolishing the Slave Trade and the black London community of Equiano, Sharp and Ramsay, and reflects the evangelical moral-language of natural rights then current.
works.structure: Continuous argumentative treatise in short numbered sections, moving from first principles to scriptural, legal and commercial refutation and then to proposals for remedy.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Cugoano is accepted; the extent of assistance from friends and patrons in a household of artists and literati is discussed but does not displace his authorship, which the text signs as an African speaking for Africans.

works.title: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters
altTitles: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters, in the Early Part of Life
Thoughts on the Education of Daughters. In the Early Part of Life; with Remarks on the Management of Children, from Birth to the Age of Ten Years
works.form: conduct and educational treatise in prose
works.description: A conduct and educational treatise for the management of girls from earliest childhood, drawn from the author's experience as a governess and a schoolmistress. It argues for the cultivation of reason, truthfulness and independence in girls, and for the reform of the needlework and accomplishments curriculum of the day.
works.plot: The work sets out the duties of the mother and the governess in the first years of a girl's life, treating the government of the temper, the formation of habits of veracity and the dangers of false modesty. It criticises the female academies and their round of accomplishments, recommends the study of religion and of reason, and gives directions on health, amusement and the choice of company. Its conclusion is that a woman's virtue depends on her understanding being taught to act for itself.
works.significance: It is the first published work of the century's most influential advocate of women's rational education and supplies the practical ground of the later argument about the rights and the cultivation of women's minds.
works.meter: A clear, earnest and direct prose of instruction, with the occasional apostrophe to mothers and the sententious summation of the section.
works.context: Published in 1787 after the author's keeping of a school for girls and her service as a governess, in the season of the public debate on female academies and on women's rational education, the same debate that occupied the Bluestocking writers of the day.
works.structure: A continuous didactic essay in numbered heads and reflections, with the instance and the practical direction alternating; the argument is orderly rather than systematic.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was issued without the writer's name in the first edition, its authorship being established by her correspondence and by the later issues.
