works.title: Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous
altTitles: Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous, in Three Parts
works.description: Berkeley's immaterialism restated in dialogue form, his most readable and most-quoted philosophical performance. Over three consecutive conversations on a walk, the sceptical materialist Hylas is led to concede that matter is unintelligible and that only spirits and their ideas exist, to the vindication of common sense and religion.
works.plot: In the first dialogue Philonous drives Hylas from the dispute about secondary qualities to the concession that no sensible thing can exist unperceived. In the second, the doctrines of absolute space, time, and motion, and of matter as an inert occasion or unknown cause of ideas, are dismantled, and the real is redefined as what is perceived by minds. The third dialogue answers the charge that immaterialism breeds scepticism, solipsism, and atheism: the stability of things is secured by the divine perception, the senses give real knowledge of a world, and God is nearer to us than matter ever was. Hylas ends convinced, Philonous having shown that the paradox destroys only a philosophical fiction and leaves the garden, the table, and the body exactly as they were.
works.significance: It supplied the century's model of dialogue as philosophical argument and remains the standard entry to immaterialism; its Hylas-Philonous exchange shaped later philosophical dialogues from Hume to the Victorians.
works.meter: Lucid dramatic prose of question and retort, with the courtesy, warmth, and scene-painting of the Platonizing dialogue tradition.
works.context: Published in London in 1713 as a popular companion and corrective to the difficult Treatise of 1710, after the furor over the Principles had made Berkeley a marked man in Dublin and London intellectual society.
works.characters: Hylas; Philonous
works.structure: Three consecutive dialogues framed by a brief narrative introduction of the speakers and their walk, rising from sensation to substance to theology.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Threnodia Augustalis
works.description: Dryden's funeral ode on the death of Charles II in February 1685, a public lament that mourns the king and welcomes the accession of James II.
works.plot: The poem opens with an ominous vision of a bleeding comet, narrates the king's last illness and death, laments the nation's loss, and turns to consolation in the new reign.
works.significance: A significant example of the Restoration public ode and of Dryden's adaptation of Cowley's Pindaric form to serious occasion.
works.meter: Irregular Pindaric stanzas with varying line lengths and rhyme schemes.
works.context: Written within weeks of Charles II's death on 6 February 1685 and printed in the same year.
works.characters: Charles II; James II; the mourning nation
works.structure: A Pindaric sequence of irregular stanzas moving from omen through narrative to consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Timon of Athens
works.description: Shakespeare's (with Thomas Middleton's) unfinished-seeming tragedy of misanthropy: the prodigal Timon of Athens bankrupts himself in bounty, is abandoned by his flatterers, and retires to the woods to curse Athens and mankind — digging for roots and finding gold, which he flings to the whores, thieves, and the general Alcibiades, whose sack of Athens the play leaves hanging.
works.plot: Timon's feasts and gifts draw the parasites; his creditors call; his friends refuse him; at his last banquet he serves them warm water and curses them; in the woods his gold draws a new parade of leeches; Alcibiades marches on Athens; and the play ends with Timon's epitaph and the city's submission, its loose ends never fully tied.
works.significance: The most extreme of the tragedies — a play of pure negation that has found its moment in every age of financial crisis.
works.meter: A verse of savage curses — Timon's tirades against gold and mankind are its glory — with the prose of the flatterers' scenes.
works.context: Probably written about 1605–08, in the phase of Lear and Coriolanus; its satire of the Jacobean credit economy has made it a favourite of economic criticism.
works.characters: Timon; Flavius; Apemantus; Alcibiades; the Poet; the Painter; Lucullus; Lucius; Sempronius; Phrynia; Timandra; the Fool
works.structure: A two-movement structure — Athens and the woods — with the masque of the false banquet as hinge; the play's rough edges suggest an abandoned draft revised for the press.
works.attributionNotes: Thomas Middleton's share (the banquet scene and parts of the middle acts) is generally accepted on stylistic evidence.

works.title: Tirocinium
altTitles: Tirocinium; or, Advice to Parents on the Point of Sending Their Sons to Public Schools
works.form: didactic poem and conduct piece in blank verse, belonging to the century's writing on education and domestic duty
works.description: Cowper's poem of advice to parents on the education of their children, urging home and day-school teaching against the boarding public school. It sets the school-boy's loneliness, the tyranny of his seniors and the hardness of classical drudgery against the supervision of a father and the example of a Christian household, and extends its argument to the education of daughters. The poem is the most vigorous poetical statement of the eighteenth-century attack on the boarding-school.
works.plot: The speaker urges parents to keep their sons at home, arguing that the public boarding school exposes childhood to fear, vice and an idle learning of words rather than of sense. He describes the boy's first day at school, the austerities of the seminary, the return home with its spoiled affections, and the mischief of friendships formed under such confinement. The close passes to the education of girls and to the plea that the domestic and religious instruction of the family is the true seminary of the mind.
works.significance: It is the strongest poetical intervention in the eighteenth-century quarrel over boarding, and its appeal to the domestic and imaginative life of childhood belongs with the growing cult of the child that leads to the Romantic poets. Its influence on later conduct and educational writing was considerable, and it remains a primary document for the social history of schooling.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of the Task's school, more abrupt and hortatory than Cowper's meditative verse, with pointed sententious closures.
works.context: Written in 1784, when the boarding public school was already a target of moral and educational writers and when the debate over classical curriculum, parental authority and the religious training of children was active in Evangelical and dissenting households; Cowper's own schooling and its hardships lie behind the picture.
works.characters: The advising speaker; the parent addressed; the school-boy of the description; the masters and ushers of the seminary
works.structure: A continuous didactic argument in several thematic sections, opening with the direct advice to parents, proceeding through the picture of school life, and closing with the extension to female education and the commendation of home.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is given in Cowper's own account, while the year of first separate impression has been variously reported, so publication_date is left null with the uncertainty stated.

works.title: Titus Andronicus
works.description: Shakespeare's first tragedy, written in collaboration with George Peele: the Roman general Titus returns from the Goths with the captive queen Tamora, whose revenge — the rape and mutilation of Titus's daughter Lavinia, the deaths of his sons — drives the play to its banquet of horrors, where Titus serves Tamora her own sons baked in a pie.
works.plot: Titus sacrifices Tamora's son and refuses the empire; Tamora, empress through Saturninus, avenges herself through her lover Aaron and her sons Chiron and Demetrius; Titus feigns madness, discovers the rapists, and executes his revenge in the cannibal banquet that ends the play.
works.significance: The most performed of the early tragedies and a laboratory of Shakespeare's tragic art — revenge, madness, and the stage as charnel house.
works.meter: Early verse of rhetorical set pieces — Lavinia's mute testimony, Titus's mad wordplay — with Ovid's Metamorphoses as the play's internal book of horrors.
works.context: Performed from 1594 and printed the same year; its extreme violence answered the vogue for Senecan blood inaugurated by Kyd's Spanish Tragedy.
works.characters: Titus Andronicus; Tamora; Aaron the Moor; Lavinia; Saturninus; Bassianus; Marcus Andronicus; Lucius; Chiron; Demetrius; young Lucius
works.structure: A Senecan revenge tragedy of symmetrical atrocity and counter-atrocity, with Aaron the Moor as its gleeful vice-figure.
works.attributionNotes: George Peele's co-authorship of Act 1 (and possibly other scenes) is now widely accepted on stylistic evidence.

works.title: To a Mouse
altTitles: To a Mouse, On Turning Her up in Her Nest with the Plough, November, 1785
works.form: occasional meditative lyric and address, in the tradition of the 'To a' poems of the Scottish vernacular
works.description: The shortest and most quoted of Burns's ploughman poems, addressed to a field mouse whose nest has been laid bare by the poet's plough in November 1785. Pity for the small creature turns into a meditation on provision, fear and the human lot, since the mouse at least lives in the present while mankind is tormented by memory and forecast. It is the classic lyric instance of the eighteenth-century cult of sympathy extended to the lower creation.
works.plot: The speaker apologises to the frightened mouse for the destruction of its winter house, and reflects that its pains in storing for the winter have been laid aside by an accident it could not foresee. He then envies it, because its troubles are but of the moment, whereas man looks backward and forward and is wretched. The poem ends in a prayer that the mouse may be spared the cruel human remembrances, and that its fate may teach the poet himself to bear his own disappointments of hope.
works.significance: Its lines on the best laid schemes of mice and men passing often ago became among the most familiar proverbs in English, and the poem is a standard example of the preromantic lyric that reasons outward from a small accident of feeling. It also fixed the figure of the thinking ploughman as a poet of sensibility and of providential anxiety.
works.meter: The six-line Burns stanza (Standard Habbie): four four-beat Scots lines and two short trimming lines, with the rhyming pattern a-a-a-b-a-b and an insistent colloquial rhythm.
works.context: Written at Mossgiel in the autumn of 1785, when Burns's farming prospects were failing and his poems were being prepared for the press; the mood of disappointed hope and of dependence on the weather of a small farm belongs exactly to that season, and the poem's ethic of pity for animals draws on the contemporary debate about sympathy and the moral sense.
works.characters: The mouse; the ploughman-speaker
works.structure: Six short stanzas moving from the immediate incident to apology, comparison and general conclusion, the argument of the meditation rising steadily out of a single act of ploughing.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is Burns's own, entered in his memorandum of the poem, and the printed title carries that date.

works.title: To His Coy Mistress
works.description: Marvell's most famous lyric, a carpe diem argument to a reluctant mistress: had we world enough and time, coyness were no crime, but time's winged chariot hurries near, so let us rather devour time than languish — a brilliant fusion of logic, wit, and urgency.
works.plot: A three-part syllogistic argument ('Had we but world enough and time ... But at my back I always hear / Time's winged chariot ... Therefore ...'), urging physical love against the pressure of mortality.
works.significance: One of the most anthologised and admired English lyrics, a supreme example of metaphysical wit applied to the carpe diem theme.
works.meter: Iambic tetrameter couplets with metaphysical conceits and a witty, urgent tone.
works.context: Composed probably in the 1650s, unpublished in Marvell's lifetime and printed in Miscellaneous Poems (1681); it draws on the classical carpe diem tradition of Horace and Ovid.
works.characters: the speaker; his coy mistress
works.structure: A dramatic monologue structured as a logical argument in three movements, in iambic tetrameter couplets.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: To the Ladies
works.form: ironic address in verse; poem of the women question
works.description: A short ironic poem addressed to women, remonstrating against the conditions of marriage and against the education that makes a wife a dependent. It is one of the most anthologised lyrics of the debate about women, and its couplets turn the commonplaces of gallantry against the law and custom that they conceal.
works.plot: The poet addresses her sex with a complaint of their treatment, showing that they are educated only to please and are then governed by the men they have pleased. Marriage is represented as a condition in which the wife's person and estate pass into another's keeping, and the language of superiority used against women is turned back upon it. The poem closes on the advice that the ladies improve their minds and their use of them.
works.significance: It is a landmark of early feminist verse and one of the most quoted of the period's poems on marriage and women's condition, much used in the modern recovery of the writing of women before the eighteenth century.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of the plain Augustan manner, the point of the argument closing on the rhyme; the idiom is that of the conversation poem of the debate about the sexes.
works.context: Written in the circles of learned women of the south-west in the last years of the seventeenth century, circulating in manuscript, and appearing in print among her poems in 1703, in the season of the pamphlet and stage war about women's abilities that produced the essays and the verse poems of the question.
works.structure: A single continuous address in closed couplets, moving from complaint to argument to counsel; there is no narrative, the argument being carried by the sequence of the retorts.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to the poet is settled by the manuscript tradition and by the printed collections that carry her name; the poem existed in more than one state, so the year recorded here is that of the printed collection and not of composition.

works.title: To the Memory of Mr. Oldham
works.description: Dryden's elegy for the young satirist John Oldham, who died of smallpox in December 1683; a short masterpiece of restrained praise that compares Oldham's early death to that of Marcellus and Nisus.
works.plot: The poem laments the loss of a kindred wit, concedes the difference in style between the two poets, and consoles with the thought that Oldham's early death spared him the decay of age and dulness.
works.significance: Often judged the finest short elegy in English between Lycidas and In Memoriam, and a canonical instance of Dryden's capacity for personal warmth.
works.meter: Heroic couplets with frequent enjambment and a deliberately unpolished, masculine roughness suited to the subject.
works.context: Written in the winter of 1683-4 and prefixed to the 1684 edition of Oldham's Works.
works.characters: John Oldham; the speaker; Marcellus (alluded to)
works.structure: A single continuous elegiac meditation of twenty-seven lines.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Tottel's Miscellany
altTitles: Songes and Sonettes, written by the ryght honorable Lorde Henry Haward late Earle of Surrey, and other
works.form: anthology of sonnets, lyrics, and epigrams
works.description: The first great printed anthology of English poetry: 271 poems by Surrey, Wyatt, Nicholas Grimald, and other courtly poets, published by Richard Tottel on 5 June 1557 under the title Songes and Sonettes. It fixed the public canon of the Henrician lyric and went through nine editions by 1587.
works.plot: An anthology without narrative frame: sonnets, songs, elegies, and epigrams arranged by author, beginning with Surrey, whose name gave the volume its selling title.
works.significance: The founding anthology of English poetry: it created the reading public for the lyric, fixed the reputations of Wyatt and Surrey, and supplied the Elizabethan poets with their metre and manner.
works.meter: The full range of the early Tudor lyric: sonnets, poulter's measure, short-line songs; the anthology standardized the decasyllabic line for a public audience.
works.context: Printed two years after the Marian restoration began; the miscellany carried the Henrician court's poetry into the Elizabethan age and made the court lyric a national possession.
works.characters: the courtly poets (Surrey, Wyatt, Grimald, and others)
works.structure: Miscellany organized by poet, with the Earl of Surrey's poems first; the arrangement itself constitutes the first printed history of the English lyric.
works.attributionNotes: Compiled by Richard Tottel (publisher); the authorship of the 'uncertain authors' poems remains largely unknown. Recorded as collaborative with no author links, per the validator's anonymity rule.

works.title: Towneley Plays
works.description: The Towneley (Wakefield) cycle of thirty-two plays, from the Creation to the Last Judgement, preserved in the Towneley manuscript (c. 1500) and long associated with Wakefield: famous above all for the six plays in the nine-line 'Wakefield stanza' attributed to the Wakefield Master — including the Second Shepherds' Play, the comic masterpiece of the English cycles, with its sheep-stealing Mak and its nativity of the stolen lamb.
works.plot: The cycle retells salvation history from Lucifer's fall through the patriarchs to Christ's Passion and the Judgement; the Master's plays — Noah and his scolding wife, the two Shepherds' plays, Herod, and the Buffeting — transform the biblical matter with a vernacular comedy of Yorkshire shepherds, shrews, and ranting tyrants unmatched in the other cycles.
works.significance: The Second Shepherds' Play is the most famous English medieval drama: the cycle's blend of farce and nativity embodies the mystery tradition at its theatrical summit.
works.meter: The unique nine-line 'Wakefield stanza' (aabcccbddb with internal rhyme) in the Master's plays; thirteen-line stanza and couplets elsewhere.
works.context: Composed and compiled c. 1400–1500, probably at Wakefield, where the plays were performed on Corpus Christi day; the manuscript (Huntington Library, MS HM 1) belonged to the Towneley family of Lancashire, from which the cycle takes its name.
works.characters: Mak the sheep-stealer; Gill; the shepherds (Coll, Gib, Daw); Noah and his wife; Herod; Christ; Pilate
works.structure: A pageant cycle of thirty-two plays, partially dependent on York but transformed by the Wakefield Master's comic and homiletic genius.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative; the 'Wakefield Master' is a scholarly construct for the author of the six stanza-linked plays.

works.title: Toxophilus
works.description: Ascham's dialogue on the art of archery, presented to Henry VIII as both a practical treatise and a model of English prose style — the first book on a sport written in the English language.
works.plot: Two speakers, Toxophilus ('lover of the bow') and Philologus ('lover of learning'), debate whether study or shooting better befits a gentleman; Toxophilus vindicates archery as recreation, describes the bow, its parts, and the craft of shooting, and argues for the health and military value of the sport, while the dialogue itself demonstrates the eloquence the English tongue can achieve.
works.significance: The first English treatise on a sport and a deliberate demonstration of the capacities of English prose for learned subjects; together with The Schoolmaster it established Ascham's reputation as a stylist and educational theorist.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written 1544–45 when Ascham was reader in Greek at St John's College, Cambridge, and presented to Henry VIII in 1545 in the royal library at Westminster, for which Ascham received a pension; archery's military role had been reaffirmed by statute in 1541.
works.characters: Toxophilus; Philologus
works.structure: Two-book dialogue framed by a preface to 'all gentle men and yeomen of England', with a systematic technical exposition embedded in the conversational form.
